title: Trip Report #1
content_raw:
An epic kayak trip...
Most kayakers want to be on the river. The open lake is loaded with boats. Small rivers offer kayakers the ability to get away from big boats, but there's a catch, the water has to be right. Most of the time, when I talk about kayaking rivers in middle Tennessee, I share a chart from the United States geological survey, that allows you to see the flow on any given river. You have to know the flow before you go, to be safe! Fortunately, there's one trip in middle tyennessee, that should be kayak friendly, every single day of the week, for the next few months, and that's where I went today...
I started at 8:00 a.m. at the Kirby road put in...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/z8vRmoZNjG8ZfBZCA
This is a small, gravel parking lot, that's open to the public, 24 hours a day. This gives you access, to the river, 10 miles below Center Hill dam. That is important, because that means that the generating water doesn't reach this area, until very late in the afternoon, sometimes, the evening. That far away from the dam, it would take the generating water a little more than 3 hours to get there. Tomorrow's generating schedule starts with one generator at 2:00 p.m. that means, the water wouldn't start showing up where we started our trip, until around 5:00 p.m. by then, we would be off the water, and never had to deal with the generating water!
When you get to this parking lot, just across the gravel road, there is a steep, muddy bank, with a well-beating path, for you to get down to the water's edge. Unfortunately, it's super slippery, because it's been raining everyday, and they've been bringing the water level up as well. That makes getting kayaks down to this location, a 4 out of five on the effort scale. It's not the hardest thing I've ever done to get a kayak in or out of a river, but it's pretty close! Fortunately, when you get 5 miles downstream, to the end of the trip, there is a boat ramp for you to pull your car down and load up...
Stone Wall Boat Ramp (Gordonsville Access) https://share.google/Qd5SWiMRE8W9zIhQl
The only other piece of the puzzle, is knowing the generating schedule. I always include the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, because it's important for you to check it every, single, time, you go fishing there! No matter what you're doing on the river, you need to know what the generators are doing first. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#CEHT1
While we're on the subject of the generators, when I was fishing yesterday from my boat, and I was catching trout out there on the Caney fork, there was a kayaker who had just started her trip downstream. Shortly after she got about a half mile downstream, the dam started releasing water, and she was trying to paddle her way back upstream. That wasn't going to happen, obviously, so I asked if she needed help, and she said she did. We rode my boat over to her, she hopped in the boat from her kayak, we picked the kayak up out of the river, and drove her back up to the boat ramp. It was her first time out on the Caney Fork, and she was coming from Nashville. Just some anecdotal evidence about why you need to check the generating schedule...
Anyway, back to today, where we had a stellar day catching trout! As we headed down the river after we launched our kayaks, there is an island immediately after you launch from this location. That's Betty's island, and I like to go to the left side to fish for trout. Using my patented better days setup, with an ultralight rod and reel, with 4 pound monofilament, a number 6 eagle claw bait holder hook with a number four eagle claw split shot about 1 foot above that hook. For my bait, I always use the same thing! One pink Berkeley Magnum floating power bait for trout, and half of a Canadian nightcrawler. That setup got it done again today!
I like to get out of the kayak at the spots that look the best, and cast at these fish from the bank. I like to cast directly across, not upstream, get my rod tip directly into the air, and keep that line tight as that worm bounces along the bottom of the river. Those fish were hot today! We got three nice juicy hogs at the very first stop, and then filled up the stringer at the last stop of the day. In between, we got out and fished at the bank at the confluence of the Smith Fork, which is right past the end of Betty's island. You can't miss it, because there is a giant railroad bridge going over the mouth of the creek. In that area, there are thousands of fish!
Most of the fish in that area are rough fish. Carp, gar, drum, Buffalo as well as plenty of bait fish. But there are always lots of bass in that area! We got out, walked around in waist deep water, and threw bass lures. We threw top water, and even a coike... But those bass wanted a peanut butter jelly Ned rig, as bass often do. They were small, but there were a handful of them. If you stayed there, and fished all day, you could probably catch as many bass as you would like. We were booked for a 6-hour trip, so we stayed on the move most of the time. It's tough to get this trip done in 6 hours! Especially if you want to fish. If you're going to do this trip, I would devote all day, and pack a lunch!

title: Trip Report #2
content_raw:
Big trout on fire!
Yesterday, I got the Buffalo valley boat ramp at 5:00 a.m...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/NJlQyZZEyfomIgVHt
I've been taking my boat down the Caney Fork River from Center Hill Dam, at Buffalo Valley boat ramp, for the past few weeks, targeting trout in the afternoons, when they turn the generators on. I wanted a chance to go after them early morning. That was silly. If you've been following these reports, you know, trout on the Caney Fork River don't like early morning conditions. There's always a heavy fog on the water and those fish don't like the fog. You can still catch fish, anytime of day, but they are more productive, during the hottest part of the day, during the hottest time of the year.
But there's just so many! Each time I go up there, I keep seeing more and more big brown trout. In my mind, I thought that I could be there for that magical hour when the Sun rises, and there would be some type of massive feeding event, but that didn't come to fruition. In reality, I was just up there in the dark, casting big lures.
I had my 7 foot, medium heavy rod and reel with 65 pound braid, and a 5 inch glide bait that looks like a gizzard shad. I was casting it in the area around the waterfall, but I wasn't having any luck. Since the big trout didn't want to cooperate, I turned my attention to underneath the waterfall, where I like to fish either at night, or early in the morning, for largemouth bass. Fortunately for me, there was a nice big two and a half pounder sitting underneath each waterfall. If you're familiar with that area, there are two main waterfalls, one in the corner that flows against  the wall of the dam, and another, prettier, taller waterfall. They are all a product of the same leak, from the other side of the dam, where the lake is making its way through the rock face. They both bring lots of oxygen to the river, and you can almost always catch a bass sitting underneath those waterfalls.
That wasn't the only luck I had. Those two fish were nice, but they weren't what I was looking for. I put on a peanut butter jelly Ned rig, and headed over to the middle, deepest part of the river, directly below the dam. It's about 18 feet deep directly below the dam, and walleye like to pile up on the bottom down there. I simply use a light setup, not necessarily an ultra light, more like my 7 foot bass fishing setup with 8 pound line, and drop my Ned rig to the bottom and jig it around for a while.
To fish for walleye below Center Hill dam, or anywhere really, you don't necessarily have to make long casts. If you can find where they are, you can vertical jig for them. Simply drop The lure down to the bottom, and then quickly lift it up off the bottom, and then slowly lower it back down. Often, they will hit your lure as it falls to the bottom. Most people use spoons for this type of vertical jigging, but I like my ned rig! I didn't catch any walleye yesterday morning, but I did catch a really tiny striped bass, which is funny. It was the smallest striped bass I have ever caught, but a good indication that there should be plenty of other big ones in the area.
At 8:00, I had enough of trying to catch trout in the early morning. I've been pressing the issue for years, but just like I've said before, those fish wait till later in the day to bite! I loaded up my kayak, and headed for Nashville. As you know, both my parents tore their rotator cuffs, so I've been mowing their yard, and taking care of a lot of their household needs. As I was heading there direction, I got the call from my mechanic that my vehicle was ready. I wasn't expecting it to get finished that soon, I had just given it to him the day before, and now it was just after 8:00 a.m., the next day, and I needed to get back to Murfreesboro to pick up my truck.
That changed my plans dramatically! I wasn't anticipating having my truck back, and I wasn't anticipating going back to Murfreesboro. Since I was so far away from my parents house, and it was already getting really hot out, I decided to delay mowing the yard for another day or two, load up my boat, and go right back to Center Hill dam. This time, I went to the boat ramp on the other side of the river, at Long Branch campground...
https://share.google/8RAtLVtOne75QGi7I
There isn't a pin on Google maps for the actual boat ramp, but it's right here next to this campground. It's very steep, and when the water is all the way down, I cannot get my boat off the trailer. As a matter of fact, I can't get my boat off of either one of the boat ramps at the dam, when the water is down. That's because the water is so shallow, even when you back into the river, my boat won't float off the trailer. That's not a big deal, because I know when the water comes up! You can always know the generating schedule for Center Hill Dam by checking here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#CEHT1
The generator was scheduled to turn on at 12:00 p.m., and I was there exactly at 12:00 p.m.! I backed my boat down the ramp, and then put it in the water, unstrapped, holding the rope, waiting for the water to come up. It came up right on time, lifting my boat off the trailer, and I was able to set it over on the bank, park my car, and then come back down and safely launch. For what it's worth, if we're ranking boat ramps on an effort scale of one to five, the one across the way at Buffalo valley boat ramp is a 5 out of five on the difficulty scale for most boats! It's as hard as it gets, because it doesn't have any angle! It's practically flat, which means you almost have to drive your car way out into the river to get your boat off the trailer. The other side, one out of five! I've been sleeping on that other boat ramp. When I got done with my trip, I could easily pull off the current, to the side of the boat ramp, and set my boat there, while I backed my trailer down. Then, because the boat ramp was so steep, I was able to leave the bunk boards a few inches out of water, and drive my boat up onto them, centering my boat perfectly!
A quick public service announcement, while we were out there yesterday afternoon in my boat, my buddy and I saw a kayaker struggling to paddle upstream against the generating water. We offered them some assistance, and she gladly accepted! She hopped in my boat, and we picked her kayak up, and put it in the boat with us, and drove her back up to the dam. It was her first time coming to kayak the caney, and she thought she was going to go downstream a mile or two, and then paddle back up. When she headed down, that's when they turned on the generating water. She had no idea they would be doing that. For what it's worth, you can't go up against the generating water with anything less than horses! You need at least 10 horsepower! I have 15 horsepower on my outboard, and that pushes me and one friend, up that river, at about 13 miles an hour. Much less power, and you're not going to make it up that river at all.
Now for the good stuff, the fishing! It was on fire! I've got my setup pretty well figured out...
I picked up a five and a half foot light cherry wood from berkeley. If you don't know, Berkeley does make fishing poles, and the one they make that I like, is called cherry wood. It's a red fishing pole, and I got the light, not the ultralight. I put a 1000 series reel, which is relatively small. On that real, I have 10 pound braid as my main line, and I've been attaching 6 pound monofilament as my leader. I've been attaching a clear monofilament leader line when I'm going walleye fishing, which is what this setup is for. I like about 8 feet of leader line, just because I know I'm going to cut some of it off and retie different lures. Having a long leader, allows me to fish an entire trip without having to retie a new leader line.
I mentioned that this setup is for catching walleye, because I needed a short, stout setup, to generate the type of twitching action I wanted on the jerkbaits I was using. I have been using the Rapala HJ 8 husky jerk, with great success! I caught a few walleye with it, using the standard twitch twitch pause retrieve that you use when casting a jerk bait, but I've been having most luck catching trout!
The generator was scheduled to run one generator from 12:00 until 2:00 p.m., which meant, we could float down for a couple of hours using my drag chain off the front of the boat, to slow us down, and twitch those jerk baits for trout. Mission accomplished! I think my favorite part about twitching jerkbaits for trout, is that you can watch them come up and eat it. It's a very exciting, visual bite, and very many times, they miss. If you're watching closely, you're going to see lots of attacks that don't land. That's when you see some really big fish!
I knew there were giant trout in there, so I wanted to give them a giant bait. On my jerk bait, I caught a 10 inch rainbow trout. I put that on the biggest hook that I had, and put a balloon on the line, about 3 foot above that trout. I let the fish swim out the back of the boat, and because the drag chain was keeping us relatively slow, the balloon went downstream, and I was able to set the rod down in the boat, loosen the drag, and allow the fish to swim freely underneath the balloon. We floated for about a mile, caught a few fish, and the balloon just stayed out behind the boat, presenting that rainbow trout is bait.
The rod I was using was a 7 foot medium heavy stiff action rod with 65 pound braid. This is a big setup for casting big lures and catching big fish! And that's exactly what it did! The rod doubled over, the drag started screaming, the balloon went under, I picked the rod up, calmly tightened the drag down, and then gently set the hook. It was a 22 inch brown trout! I had hoped for it to be much bigger, to keep a brown trout, they have to be 24 inches long, but I'll take it! It was my first fish of the year using a bait underneath a balloon, and it was a lot of fun! Unfortunately, no one will see it. I was so excited to get my truck back, that I forgot to put my camera in my car. I got no video footage of yesterday's afternoon trip. This report will be the only account...

title: Trip Report #3
content_raw:
The newest boat ramp in Middle Tennessee...
I got a chance to kayak the Barren Fork River in McMinnville Tennessee. The city recently added a new boat ramp that is really nice, at Rocket Park...
https://share.google/7wgbkWIY2zBoPJtpr
This is a kayak trip that allows you to start at this location, and finish, about 5 miles downstream, at the VFW boat ramp...
VFW Boat Ramp https://share.google/MQW19lpSBxzDHNxkQ
I had hoped that I could launch from that boat ramp in my Jon boat, and go either, upstream, or, downstream, to the VFW boat ramp. The only way to find out, would be to take my kayak through that area. As it turns out, no, it would not be a good idea to take my fiberglass jon boat in either direction from that boat ramp. Even though the ramp will definitely accommodate Jon boats, I do not think it's a good idea to travel all the way to McMinnville just to launch on this stretch of river.
You can't go upstream, because there is a shallow area, and as you go downstream, some of those rocks will rip your boat to shreds! There are jagged pieces of limestone that reach up near the surface, and they were scratching deep gouges out of my kayak! It's a real shame, because that stretch of river is absolutely loaded with small mouth bass! The scratching of the kayak wasn't so bad that I wouldn't do it again, but I could feel it in my soul every time it pulled a long piece of plastic off the bottom of my boat.
The water is fairly low for that area. I don't believe there are any USGS monitoring stations on the Barren Fork river, I could be wrong about that. There is a USGS station at the takeout point at the VFW boat ramp, and it was reading around 300 cubic feet per second. If you did that trip above 400 cubic feet per second, you would definitely scrape your kayak less! It's a great trip to do, because you start at a boat ramp, and you end at a boat ramp! That means, on the effort scale of one to five, it's a one out of five! This trip is as easy as it gets! You can find the USGS website for the Collins river, where you will be ending your trip, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03421000/all-graphs/#period=P7D
Basically, the Barren Fork will end when it hits the confluence with the Collins river. That confluence is about halfway through this trip. Because the Barren Fork flows into the Collins, you have the potential to catch muskie, all the way down this trip! Unfortunately for us, we did not catch any muskie. We weren't really trying, we were more targeting bass.
I was using a paddle tail, and a Whopper plopper, and my buddy was throwing a Ned rig and a buzzbait. We were getting a little top water action, but we weren't catching the fish. The bite was finicky, until around lunch time. That's when the fish started committing to the lure, no matter what we were throwing. From noon until 3:00, the fishing was pretty hot! We finished our trip in about 8 hours. If you fish every inch of the water, from beginning to end, without paddling through any areas, and without stopping, that's about how long it will take you.
All of the trips on the Collins River are going to have low water like this! When I shared the USGS chart a moment ago, the water was down to 268 cubic feet per second, and that's a no-go on most sections! You will be dragging your kayak! Conversely, if you look out at the Buffalo river, that River isn't viable, because they have too much water!
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03604400/all-graphs/#period=P7D
It's currently sitting at 2800 cubic feet per second and falling, but that River is best kayaked when it's under 1000 cubic feet per second. So it's not going to be an option this week either... That's not common for Middle Tennessee in the summertime. We don't usually see extremes where one river isn't viable because of drought and another river isn't viable because of flooding. But when that happens, we've got great alternatives!
Reservoirs that are held back by dams provide controlled releases that are predictable! Below these dams, you can expect the water to stick to the schedule that is given by the corps of engineers. The schedule they provide can change at any time without notice, but they usually stick to it, for the safety of the public! Percy Priest Dan has been spilling, since the reservoir has recently gone above summer pool. Summer pool on reservoirs is measured in feet above sea level. Percy Priest Lake is considered at summer pool when it is at 490 feet above sea level. It's currently more than a foot above summer pool, so they are releasing water from the floodgates, which should create fantastic fishing below the dam this week! You can find the water release schedule for Percy Priest lake, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#JPHT1
When I went to grab this link, the water in the lake has dropped fast! It's currently only 3/4 of a foot above 490 ft, so it may not be spilling much longer. Unfortunately, the website never updated to mention that they were spilling from the floodgates at Percy priest. When you look at that link, it's going to say that the cone valve is open, and that may be true, but they also have the floodgates open. I have driven by, and seen them personally, but you can tell by the discharge. The cone valve only discharges 130 cubic feet per second. I know this from experience. The floodgates are currently open, because I have seen them, but the outflow is registering 650 cubic feet per second. That's a very typical number when they are releasing water from the top of the dam at the floodgates.
It's not very deep below Percy Priest damn, but lots of quality fish come up there to feed. You could use lures that don't run very deep, like a rooster tail, or you could try a spoon, and try keeping it near the surface. You could definitely try top water lures like a spook! There should be hybrid bass out there as well as striped bass! When the water stops, that first day, and the next day, there should be some quality fish hanging around, they get trapped in the low water. That should happen sometime at the end of this week.
Hybrid bass are being caught out at Jefferson Springs boat ramp area...
Jefferson Springs Boat Ramp. https://share.google/rHyar8nB0UNUBPQWJ
I tried to go there for myself to catch some a few days ago, but I got a flat tire at the boat ramp. Then, that night, my truck wouldn't shift into gear. I had my truck towed today, and the shop said they should have it ready tomorrow. If I could go out there tomorrow morning, before sunrise, to chase hybrid bass busting on the surface, that's where I would be!
The hotter it gets outside, the more they will have to generate for power at Center Hill dam. Today, they turned on three generators! They only have three, so that was the full electrical capacity today. That was because of the extreme heat. They will have to turn on three generators in the afternoon, again, tomorrow. After the heat breaks, and we get back to regular July heat, Wednesday Thursday and Friday of this week, they will back off on the generating schedule, and that will mean two things...
First and foremost, lots of fish from Old hickory lake, where Center Hill Dam dumps into, use the three generator water like a super highway to come up to the dam. That much cold water discharge, into that hot lake, grabs the attention of lots of different fish. From crappie to walleye, and everything in between, they will be using that river like a highway, right now as I type this out! When they get there, and they reduce the generating schedule, they will be much easier to catch! Look for the end of this week to have one generator running during the daytime, that would be a great time to get them from not only a boat or a kayak but also from the steps!

title: Trip Report #4
content_raw:
A complete snafu!
Right after that cold front came in, and we had a couple of nice days Thursday and Friday, I had tons of vehicle problems! You'll see in the next two videos. Things weren't going my way!
I went to Jefferson Springs boat ramp right before sunrise...
Jefferson Springs Boat Ramp. https://share.google/j7RGtY8IWgZAkW60h
I had heard there were some striped bass and hybrid bass being caught in that area, and I figured I could get on them early morning, before the sun came up. Worst case scenario, the last time I was out that way, I was catching crappie, underneath the bridge. At least, that's what I thought. The actual worst case scenario was not being able to fish at all. By the time I got to the boat ramp, I could hear air quickly escaping from my tire, the result of a huge screw in the sidewall! Fortunately, I wasn't far away from walmart, so I just had to wait for about an hour until the tire department opened. After I got everything squared away, it was far too late for the morning bite, so I regrouped, got some yard work done, and then went for a quick fishing trip to see if I could get a smallmouth bass on the West Fork Stones River...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/LCZff5qVcbMKCs8N6
That's a small gravel parking lot on the side of the road that gives you access to the river, in a really nice bend of the river. If you take the trail from the gravel parking lot, there are a few different access points, I like the middle trail. This was one of those spots that I've cleaned several times, because people constantly dump trash there. A little birdie told me they caught a really big small mouth down there, so I went just down the street to Big Charlie's bait shop to get a dozen shiners...
Big Charlie's Bait Shop https://share.google/AslyVzYBKnwBxWcCc
I was using a bobber and a mosquito hook with a number four eagle claw split shot about 6 inches above my hook. I put that shiner at a depth of about two and a half feet, because this is a pretty deep spot in the river. It's really nice! Within a few minutes, I figured out exactly where a couple different fish were sitting, after they took my bait. After a couple more attempts, I finally hooked up with the first one, a beautiful little smallmouth. Then, I hooked into a gigantic fish! It could have been a really big bass, or a hybrid bass, or even a big catfish, who knows! It gave me one heck of a fight, and then I saw it go under a rock, and get away. I had a dozen shiners, and I only hooked those two fish, but it was a pretty good hour of fishing!
I was using my medium action bass fishing rod that had 12 pound monofilament. Hindsight being 20/20, I definitely should have had a heavier setup. I knew, because I had been told, that there were really big bass in the area, and I simply couldn't handle the fish that I hooked. Not a big deal, I had bigger fish to fry, I needed to get ready for the next day's trout fishing trip with clients.
I was scheduled to meet two gentleman, who wanted to kayak fish down the Caney at 6:30 in the morning. I got everything loaded up into my truck, now that it had a brand new tire, and then loaded the three kayaks onto the trailer, and then went to back my truck to the trailer hitch, but the gear shifter wouldn't make the transmission respond! Once again, not a big deal. My little Mazda has a trailer hitch, so I was able to move everything from the truck, into the car, and attach the trailer to the car instead of the truck. That's probably going to take me out of commission one of these days soon, because I need to take my truck to the shop and get that fixed. As for today's trip with my clients, that was a complete success! We launched from Buffalo valley boat ramp...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/ix9of63vi9VDULUzp
It rained on us quite a bit, and that's a problem! Those trout hate the rain, and they really don't like heavy fog. Unfortunately, when it rains out there, the warm rainwater hits that cold river water and makes a thick blanket of fog on the surface. That was the case today, and the Sun never really came out, and the wind never really picked up, so it was a really tough day! Fortunately for us, we had some pink Berkeley powerbait.
Using ultralight rods and reels, with 4 pound monofilament, and a number 6 eagle claw bait holder hook, with a number 4 eagle claw split shot about 1 foot above the hook, we were able to get almost a couple of limit of trouts! We came up one rainbow trout short. Here's how we made that set up work for us...
There are two main ways I like to fish with Berkeley powerbait on the Caney Fork river. I'm almost always going to add half of a Canadian nightcrawler to the setup. Adding a live worm, changes the game! Those fish will see the power bait from a long distance, but once they find out the worm is attached, they won't leave it alone until they eat it! If I'm not using a worm, I will use a mosquito hook instead, because it's much smaller, and that big bait holder hook isn't necessary. When I do that, I usually only use one pink ball. I prefer pink Berkeley Magnum powerbait.
There are two main ways that I like to present that to fish on a Caney Fork river. Most of the time, I'm going to get out at my favorite spots, and stand in the water, about ankle deep, cast in front of me, and allow that setup to bounce along the bottom. As it drifts, at the speed of the river, that's when you get the bite! If you add a piece of worm, you can let it sit on the bottom, for as long as you like, and they will eventually pick it up! The way I fish it from the kayak, is to throw it behind the boat, and drag it as I slowly float down. It's a little trickier to get the hook set, but it's a great way to get them to bite!
We tried throwing every different lure in the book at these trout! I think one client caught a fish on a Rapala countdown in brown trout pattern, but it was probably only just one. These fish were not happy with the rain and the fog! You pretty much had to force feed them a worm. We were getting lots of bites, but the bite was finicky, at best! It took a very patient, very steady hand, to actually hook these fish. I think the video that comes out, in a couple of days, will make it look like we did better than we did! We fished the entire 6 mile stretch, and only had nine keepers. We actually stayed out there a little longer, we were on the water about 7 and 1/2 hours! It was really slow going, but it won't be, on those hot, sunny days! That's when you can go to the Caney Fork river, and anticipate catching lots of fish.

title: Trip Report #5
content_raw:
Bigger trout out on the Caney...
The best time to get the biggest trout out on the Caney Fork river, as well the generators are running. I explained, with great detail, how using a drag chain could slow you down, while you're in a boat. That's what I did yesterday, while they were running one generator, from 11:00 a.m. until 7:00 p.m. I launched my boat exactly at 11:00 a.m. when the generators turned on from Buffalo valley boat ramp...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/OixCKsz5eTZyeuUDo
Here's a few things that I have figured out wow drifting down the Caney Fork with a drag chain...
Occasionally, you're going to drift a little too far left or right. The best way to correct the boat, and get yourself to the center of the river, is to get on the main motor, and just move yourself quickly. The trolling motor on my boat is mounted to the front, and if I try to use it, I could get tangled up in my drag chain line.
I like one generator. If they are running two or more generators, the water gets a little too deep, and too swift for the drag chain. Days where they run one generator for several hours at a time, are going to be the days that I look for. Unfortunately, you don't know the generating schedule until about 2:00 p.m. on the day before. That makes it tough to make advanced plans. It's best to go to Center Hill on a whim, wind conditions are right. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#CEHT1
Don't have a boat? Go fishing on the steps! Take a 7 foot, medium heavy rod, with 15 pound braid, and throw spoons in the generating water from the steps...
https://goo.gl/maps/YrmmZUucaRiUHcvr5
The water down there is cold! I take a hoodie with me when I'm riding up and down in my boat. The fog can get really thick, and it can get cold fast, even in the middle of the day! You're going to have the opposite experience on the steps. It's going to be as hot as it can be in Tennessee! To cool off, you can go to the bottom of the steps, and get your feet in the water...
The biggest fish right now are being caught on the steps with spoons, or from the boat with jerk baits. I've been using a Rapala hj8, which is a suspending jerk bait, but it's pretty small. My buddy has been using a giant HJ 12, and he has been catching much bigger fish! It's definitely jerkbait season on the Caney Fork river! I don't think you can go too big, we have found trout with 7-inch gizzard shad in their stomachs! Just get out there and throw your favorite jerkbates, and see what sticks to the wall.
This is going to be the most important thing when it comes to running a boat up and down that river... YOU NEED TO KNOW WHERE THE CHANNEL IS!
When the water goes all the way down, there is a clear path for the deepest part of the river. When one generator comes up, you can go up and down the river in a boat, but you really need to stick to the main channel. The places that are dry when the river goes down, may not be deep enough for you to run up at full speed. There are trees in the river that are just under the surface when the generator is on, but are out of the river when the water is off. It helps to know where these are, so that you can easily avoid them on your way back up the river.
The best way to learn how to run the river when the water is down, is to take a kayak trip! If you don't have a kayak, or access to a kayak, you could rent one at one of the many different outfitters on the Caney Fork river. The one that I have used most is canoe the Caney...
Canoe the Caney https://share.google/bK7BuY3O5O8zk8TgW
I haven't seen them running the first 6 miles of the river, which is the stretch you need to do to familiarize yourself so you can run your boat. They have primarily been running from Betty's Island down to stonewall, which is much farther downstream. If they are not doing this trip, you should check with another outfitter

title: Trip Report #6
content_raw:
This week's fishing forecast...
One thing I can say about middle Tennessee, there are always some type of fish, going crazy. No matter what time of year it is. Cold weather, hot weather, every different time of the year has different fish that fire up. Right now, trout are going crazy on the Caney Fork river!
Today, I had clients booked for a 4-Hour bank fishing trip on the Caney Fork river. It was a grandfather and his son and his grandson, and he wanted to not only catch some fish, but to make some memories... Mission accomplished! We met at 8:00 a.m. at Betty's Island boat ramp...
Bettys Island Boat Ramp https://share.google/Ntlr6cESv1utlOukf
The fish were cooperative from start to finish, mostly because we were using live bait. When I have clients, trying to catch trout on the Caney Fork river, I like to use my ultralight rods and reels with a number 6 eagle claw bait holder hook and a number four eagle claw split shot about 1 foot above that hook. First I put on one piece of Berkeley Magnum floating power bait for trout, I like the pink color, then I put on half of a Canadian nightcrawler. The bait holder hook helps to hold the worm on, so the fish can't pull it off the hook.
Getting the fish to bite wasn't a problem today, setting the hook was tough! Just because a trout bites, doesn't mean the lure is in their mouth. Quite often, they have taken an investigative bite, and spit it back out. You have to wait for them to pick it up and start swimming with it a little bit, before you can set the hook. It's incredibly tough to teach someone that, but my 9-year-old client got it right away! He was able to catch his limit of keeper size rainbow trout, and even a little brown trout. That is somewhere you can go this week, and every week through the summer!
The Caney Fork River is always a great option, just make sure you check the generating schedule first. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#CEHT1
When I went to check that schedule, it says that tomorrow will have one generator from 11:00 a.m. to 7:00 p.m. . For the past few days, they have been running two generators, most of the day. That's fine if you're in a boat, but it's not ideal. The ideal situation would be to have one generator on, so you can use your drag chain that I told you about! Looks like tomorrow will be ideal, to run your boat up and down the Caney Fork River, especially if you have a drag chain!
Fish are still fired up in the morning at 7 points boat ramp...
Seven Points Boat Ramp https://share.google/J994kdtxLCTmfyqh3
Around the corner from the boat ramp, at the point, hybrid bass continued to blow up in the mornings. I caught one there a couple of days ago, and that trend looks like it's going to continue. I had been starting at the point, but there has been more action across the way, I'll drop you a pin for that location right now...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/r5L2E1Uan1KxujSE6
This bank has been blowing up with hybrid, as opposed to the other bank. Unfortunately, there's no bank fishing access here, you'll have to get there by boat or kayak. Some good news about this spot, I always see bass boats sitting there. I never knew why, but I suspected they were catching bass. Fast forward to the other day, and there are massive schools of bass all over this bank! Seems like that might be a spot on the lake where they like to live.
Crappie are still relatively accessible on Center Hill lake. By the time I left the other day, the water temperature at the surface was reading 90°! I suspected that those fish would move 50 feet or deeper, but I don't think they can, because of the thermocline. I'm no water scientist, so I don't know exactly how the thermocline works, except that, oxygen levels get depleted below that level. I'm not 100% certain what depth the thermocline is on Center Hill lake, but those fish were no deeper than 25 feet, which makes them easy to find, if you have forward facing sonar.
Speaking of finding fish easily on Center Hill lake, something I forgot to mention in the report I made the other day, was that, that lake is overwhelmingly loaded with bluegill! There are gigantic School of bluegill everywhere you look. From the boat ramp, to the backs of coves, at the surface, all the way down to 30 feet deep! I did manage to catch one, to confirm they were bluegill, but I had no interest in fishing for them!
You can expect the recent heavy rains and tonight's anticipated heavy rain to keep the flow going below Woods reservoir...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/3QV9iCK77Rotg2m96
This spot is the honey hole! Not only are people catching hybrid bass, every single morning, but they're also catching really big striped bass and lots of nice walleye! You'll have to park in the provided parking lot, but then ignore the sign that says the area is closed. I can assure you, I have spoken with the Air Force security on the grounds, and the area is open! It's a short walk, downhill, about a quarter of a mile, to a relatively treacherous bank. This is bank fishing, but it's one of the tougher spots, not necessarily a 5 out of 5 on the effort scale of one to five, more like a four. The boulders down there are big, and you have to climb on them, as opposed to walk on them. Everybody needs to be going to this spot, you've just got to experience it for yourself.
Tonight, we get our second cold front of this summer. The first one came in the first few days, after June 21st, so it's been about a month... After a cold front, when we have a north wind, with bluebird skies, I like to go bass fishing on our middle Tennessee rivers. Something about those conditions, when Lake fish tend to typically shut down, according to old wives tales, river fish go crazy!
Unfortunately, most of our Rivers don't have enough water to kayak. I can point you in the direction of some that should be good to go...
Number one on the list is always the Piney River. There is no public access, you'll have to either rent a kayak or canoe, or shuttle your own, with Pinewood canoe and campground...
Pinewood Canoe & Camp LLC https://share.google/SWVGL9QWTHFYWSPEr
The Buffalo River in Linden Tennessee or near Waverly Tennessee is a great spot, but I don't necessarily know all the outfitters out there. As I utilize their services, I will inform you of where they are, and what you can expect on those trips. For those of you already familiar with the Buffalo river, this is going to be a great week out there!
Too much rain ruins so many of these trips, but we're going to need quite a bit of rain tonight to get the Stones River in Murfreesboro to an acceptable level for kayaking. This is my home stretch of river, and I'd like to invite everybody down to murfreesboro, to kayak the Stones River from Thompson Lane trailhead to Nice Mill Dam... It's a technical stretch of river, not a 5 out of five but definitely a 4 out of five on the effort scale! There is a boat ramp at the beginning at the Thompson Lane trailhead, but you will have to move your kayak a significant distance at the end, either up a set of stairs, or through the woods, to get to the parking lot on either side of the river. You can start this trip at the Thompson Lane trailhead in Murfreesboro...
Thompson Lane Trailhead https://share.google/vPi9yjBorckHkEmKc
From there, it's about 8 and 1/2 mi downstream to nice mill dam, where you're going to take out...
https://share.google/9J1y44ylTVNWBQGsl
There are public parking lots on either side of the dam. I would suggest checking both of them out, and the access to the water, to decide which way you would like to take out.
That River will need significant amount of rain, which hopefully, we will get tonight. To kayak down that river, without rubbing a hole in the bottom of your kayak, or having to get out and drag the entire way, you need at least 140 cubic feet per second of flow. You can find the flow for the West Fork Stones River on the USGS chart, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D
I have kayaked this river all the way up to 440 cubic feet per second, and it's fun at that level! The river is swift, and the rapids are exciting, the fishing is good, no matter what level the river is that. At lower levels, the obstacles become harder to avoid, for some reason. When the water gets a little higher, you can easily float over some of them more difficult rapids.

title: Trip Report #7
content_raw:
Putting in work on Center Hill Lake...
My biggest problem with Center Hill lake, I don't know where to launch! The boat ramps out there are very different than Percy Priest. I never know if I'm going to show up to a boat ramp and it's not going to be open! That literally happened at Cookeville boat dock. I met my buddy there early in the morning, and they don't open the gate until 9:00 a.m... Fast forward to today, and I found a spot where you can pay to go fishing anytime you want to!
I launched my boat at 7:00 a.m. at Sligo boat ramp...
Sligo Resort and Marina https://share.google/0jz1ACIvJn5u4sNea
Disregard the hours for the marina. That has nothing to do with the boat ramp! They don't have a gate at this location, so you will be able to launch 24/7, 365 days a year! There's one caveat, it cost $8. They have a lockbox, with envelopes, so you will need to bring a pen, and exact change. I only had $10, I didn't have any ones, so they got a little bit of extra money from me today, but it was well worth it!
I stayed on the water, in one branch of the lake, for 11 hours... There were plenty of fish out there, but they were not in a good mood today! I drew you a map of the area I covered. This spot had more of the type of fish that I was looking for than the last spot I went to on Center Hill Lake. I was able to find a few different big school of BIG crappie, as well as, what I think, were walleye.
I slowly worked my trolling motor all the way around this area, counterclockwise, looking at the bank from 100 feet away with my forward facing sonar. I used to keep the forward distance set to 70 feet, but I've gotten a lot better with it, and I'm starting to look a little farther away from the boat, successfully. That's crucial out on Center Hill lake, because it's so deep! You won't be able to cruise very close to the bank, and get a good look at the fish that you want to find. To see fish that are 20 to 30 feet deep, you will have to be at least 70 to 100 feet away from the bank, as you scan. I adjusted not only the forward distance, but also the down distance, to try to get the best picture that I could, when I found a school of fish.
As I scanned, I found one crappie structure that had obviously been placed by someone, but it wasn't the TWRA, because it wasn't marked...
https://goo.gl/maps/xtMMbvRnkesXz4tp6
The next two spots were brush piles, but they didn't look like they were placed by anyone, they were just stuck on something underwater, and the fish were hanging out there...
https://goo.gl/maps/pmSrw92ouNTMtMmc9
https://goo.gl/maps/oFk8xfYFnbLSCVL98
These schools of fish were gigantic! Hundreds of fish! They had a terrible disposition! Each time I found a school of crappie, the top of the pile was at 20 feet, and the bottom of the pile was at 25 feet. They weren't suspended, they were in 25 feet of water. That means, the bottom of the pile was touching the bottom of the lake, and the top of the pile, extended up, about 5 feet. Typically, crappie will stack up pretty tall in the water column, just a couple weeks ago, on Percy Priest, I found them under a bridge, stacked from the surface, all the way down to the bottom, on a bridge piling. Today, these fish out on Center hill, we're spread out flat like a pancake. I think, because they were favoring the temperature of the water at that depth. The surface of the water was reading 90° by the time I left today!
The whole time I was there, I was beating up the bank with a Whopper plopper, trying to catch bass, but I only got a couple little blow ups, and I didn't catch any bass at all today! Typically, if bass are biting really well, I will catch them while I'm catching crappie. Today, despite my best efforts, I couldn't catch a bass. They were there, they just had as bad and attitude as the crappie did!
I also saw some other fish, that I don't see in other bodies of water. I'm fairly certain they were walleye, but I couldn't catch them either! There were several of them, hanging out around a school of crappie. It's important to point out, that each time I found a school of crappie, they were surrounded by schools of blue gill. I don't usually see that, but that's the way it was today. There were thousands of bluegill! But they were really small. They were all hanging out at that 20 foot of depth, and I only managed to catch one of them.
Each time I go to Center Hill lake, I look for schools of bait fish, to see if there are fish underneath them, so I could try to target those fish. I saw plenty of action like that today, and I was able to get lots of different fish to look at my lures, but I wasn't able to catch them in that scenario either. The only luck I would have, would be using my ultralight rod and reel with 4 pound monofilament and two 1/32nd of announced jig heads. But even with two jig heads on, my setup wasn't falling fast enough. These fish were 20 feet down, at least, and then, farther down. I needed to get down quicker, so I added a number four, eagle claw split shot, about a foot above my jig heads.
Each time I found a school of crappie, it was the same thing. First, I would try running my lure way above their heads, about 10 feet. Super active fish will make the swim, 10 feet straight up, to grab that lure! These were the opposite of Super active fish. I had to drop down to their level, and then run it right past their eyes. But even that, would only get their attention, and not get them to bite.
The only thing that would consistently get a bite, was the fall. Not only allowing the lure to get to there depth, but allowing it to fall right past them. That's the most finicky crappie bite, and it's the hardest one to feel. By the time you actually feel the bite, it's a little too late to set the hook. I was able to consistently get these fish to bite, but because they were so far down, and that bite is so light, I wasn't able to catch very many fish. But the ones I did catch, we're very sizable, they were all keepers!
I had one more trick up my sleeve, and that worked pretty well. I allowed the jigs to sink all the way to the bottom, and then, started a painfully slow retrieve, through those fish, dragging the bottom... That worked for a couple of fish as well!
On the day, I ended up with five or six slab crappie, and a couple of rock bass, one of which was a trophy fish! If you're not aware, the state of Tennessee classifies any rock bass that you catch, over 10 inches, as a trophy fish. The one I caught today was right at 10 and 1/4 inches. I caught both of them while I was dragging those crappie jigs along the bottom. Not sure if that's a reliable method for the future, but it was one of the only ways I could get fish to bite today.

Sligo Resort and Marina https://share.google/0jz1ACIvJn5u4sNea

Disregard the hours for the marina. That has nothing to do with the boat ramp! They don't have a gate at this location, so you will be able to launch 24/7, 365 days a year! There's one caveat, it cost $8. They have a lockbox, with envelopes, so you will need to bring a pen, and exact change. I only had $10, I didn't have any ones, so they got a little bit of extra money from me today, but it was well worth it!

I stayed on the water, in one branch of the lake, for 11 hours... There were plenty of fish out there, but they were not in a good mood today! I drew you a map of the area I covered. This spot had more of the type of fish that I was looking for than the last spot I went to on Center Hill Lake. I was able to find a few different big school of BIG crappie, as well as, what I think, were walleye.

I slowly worked my trolling motor all the way around this area, counterclockwise, looking at the bank from 100 feet away with my forward facing sonar. I used to keep the forward distance set to 70 feet, but I've gotten a lot better with it, and I'm starting to look a little farther away from the boat, successfully. That's crucial out on Center Hill lake, because it's so deep! You won't be able to cruise very close to the bank, and get a good look at the fish that you want to find. To see fish that are 20 to 30 feet deep, you will have to be at least 70 to 100 feet away from the bank, as you scan. I adjusted not only the forward distance, but also the down distance, to try to get the best picture that I could, when I found a school of fish.

As I scanned, I found one crappie structure that had obviously been placed by someone, but it wasn't the TWRA, because it wasn't marked...

https://goo.gl/maps/xtMMbvRnkesXz4tp6

The next two spots were brush piles, but they didn't look like they were placed by anyone, they were just stuck on something underwater, and the fish were hanging out there...

https://goo.gl/maps/pmSrw92ouNTMtMmc9

https://goo.gl/maps/oFk8xfYFnbLSCVL98

These schools of fish were gigantic! Hundreds of fish! They had a terrible disposition! Each time I found a school of crappie, the top of the pile was at 20 feet, and the bottom of the pile was at 25 feet. They weren't suspended, they were in 25 feet of water. That means, the bottom of the pile was touching the bottom of the lake, and the top of the pile, extended up, about 5 feet. Typically, crappie will stack up pretty tall in the water column, just a couple weeks ago, on Percy Priest, I found them under a bridge, stacked from the surface, all the way down to the bottom, on a bridge piling. Today, these fish out on Center hill, we're spread out flat like a pancake. I think, because they were favoring the temperature of the water at that depth. The surface of the water was reading 90° by the time I left today!

The whole time I was there, I was beating up the bank with a Whopper plopper, trying to catch bass, but I only got a couple little blow ups, and I didn't catch any bass at all today! Typically, if bass are biting really well, I will catch them while I'm catching crappie. Today, despite my best efforts, I couldn't catch a bass. They were there, they just had as bad and attitude as the crappie did!

I also saw some other fish, that I don't see in other bodies of water. I'm fairly certain they were walleye, but I couldn't catch them either! There were several of them, hanging out around a school of crappie. It's important to point out, that each time I found a school of crappie, they were surrounded by schools of blue gill. I don't usually see that, but that's the way it was today. There were thousands of bluegill! But they were really small. They were all hanging out at that 20 foot of depth, and I only managed to catch one of them.

Each time I go to Center Hill lake, I look for schools of bait fish, to see if there are fish underneath them, so I could try to target those fish. I saw plenty of action like that today, and I was able to get lots of different fish to look at my lures, but I wasn't able to catch them in that scenario either. The only luck I would have, would be using my ultralight rod and reel with 4 pound monofilament and two 1/32nd of announced jig heads. But even with two jig heads on, my setup wasn't falling fast enough. These fish were 20 feet down, at least, and then, farther down. I needed to get down quicker, so I added a number four, eagle claw split shot, about a foot above my jig heads.

Each time I found a school of crappie, it was the same thing. First, I would try running my lure way above their heads, about 10 feet. Super active fish will make the swim, 10 feet straight up, to grab that lure! These were the opposite of Super active fish. I had to drop down to their level, and then run it right past their eyes. But even that, would only get their attention, and not get them to bite.

The only thing that would consistently get a bite, was the fall. Not only allowing the lure to get to there depth, but allowing it to fall right past them. That's the most finicky crappie bite, and it's the hardest one to feel. By the time you actually feel the bite, it's a little too late to set the hook. I was able to consistently get these fish to bite, but because they were so far down, and that bite is so light, I wasn't able to catch very many fish. But the ones I did catch, we're very sizable, they were all keepers!

I had one more trick up my sleeve, and that worked pretty well. I allowed the jigs to sink all the way to the bottom, and then, started a painfully slow retrieve, through those fish, dragging the bottom... That worked for a couple of fish as well!

On the day, I ended up with five or six slab crappie, and a couple of rock bass, one of which was a trophy fish! If you're not aware, the state of Tennessee classifies any rock bass that you catch, over 10 inches, as a trophy fish. The one I caught today was right at 10 and 1/4 inches. I caught both of them while I was dragging those crappie jigs along the bottom. Not sure if that's a reliable method for the future, but it was one of the only ways I could get fish to bite today.

title: Trip Report #8
content_raw:
Explosions at the lake...
I got up and at them early this morning! I was 45 minutes away from my house, at 4:45 a.m., at seven points boat ramp...
Seven Points Boat Ramp https://share.google/wvlaCKUii1KHEikov
Hybrid bass have been blowing up consistently, at this location, every morning, for a few months! It defies what most people consider common knowledge on Percy Priest lake. Typically, these fish move so much, that you won't find them in one spot like this, every single morning. Fortunately, they've been there so consistently, that I was able to go catch one this morning!
Unfortunately, they were blowing up everywhere, insanely, and I was only able to catch one. I was hanging out near my buddy, while he was in his boat, and he was only able to catch one. We were in the middle of boiling water, hybrid bass chasing bait everywhere, but we could not get them to pay attention to our lures. I suspect, we probably would have had better luck, with live bait. The problem, is that it's tough to have live bait, unless you get it the night before. Then, it's tough to keep it alive, especially as warm as it is lately. I will probably just keep trying lures.
I actually caught my hybrid bath this morning, on my ultralight crappie setup, with a 2-inch Berkeley realistic. If you don't know, that's a small plastic minnow, typically used to catch crappie. I wasn't having any luck with my typical lures, things that I like to use, include, but are not limited to, 4 inch paddle tail swimbaits, 5 inch flukes, top water lures, and silver spoons. None of those were doing the trick today, so I downsized, and almost immediately caught a fish.
One thing I can say for sure, people who aren't using forward facing sonar, tend to have better luck. If you're watching your lure, and watching the fish, and how they react, you will almost always do the wrong thing. Something about not watching the fish, and just retrieving your lure, haphazardly, creates more bites. I believe, it's because the lure doesn't act like it knows the fish is there. What that means, is when I see a fish look at my lure, I start to do stuff with it. Either bring it up in the water column, to take it away from them, or jig a little, or perhaps let it fall, to see if that's what they want. The reality is, if it just stays moving steady, and keeps an attitude like it doesn't know that predator fish is there, it may get eaten!
These fish are all over this area, and hundreds of yards, and any direction, every morning. This morning, there must have been 20 boats out there catching fish! And then, around 7:00 a.m., everything stops! Not only do the hybrid quit busting on the surface, you can't even see them on the screen anymore. They go somewhere else! But you don't have to...
Right there, at seven points, at the green buoy that marks the channel, crappie are loaded in great numbers! I'm going to drop a pin, exactly where I found them, on an underwater hump, in the middle of the channel...
https://goo.gl/maps/199Xti64izexYJ9p6
If that pin looks familiar, it's because we were catching crappie there back in March! It has been since then that I saw crappie loaded up in great numbers at this location. They have been favoring somewhere else, I couldn't tell you exactly where, but today, I found them 20 foot down, sitting on underwater timber. They were there in great numbers, but I could not make them bite. I am 100% certain they are crappie, because of how they acted. No matter how many times I brought my lure through, or how I tried to present it to them, they wouldn't move. They never budge off the underwater structure they were preferring, and I couldn't get them to chase anything. Typical of crappie behavior, when they're not biting. I suspect, if I had live bait, like a minnow, I probably could have caught them. The good news, there in about 20 foot of water, and they're definitely in this location!

title: Trip Report #9
content_raw:
Three videos from one location...
Starting today, for the next 3 days, you're going to see videos that I made on the same day, on the same fishing trip. I went to the Kirby road access area...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/JnMU7hg2nZ87Ust86
This isn't a marked location on maps, but it is a public access area! I've been parking here my whole life, to go fishing on this end of the river. You are definitely allowed to be here! It's a gravel parking area, with enough room for about 7 or 8 vehicles. It gives you access to the Betty's Island area, where you can fish the left side or the right side of the island, for trout. Lots of people come here to get in the water, either in chest waders, or to do some wet wading, when it's hot outside. When you hop out of your vehicle, you go directly across the street, and down a steep, muddy bank, to the water's edge. Going down the hill and back up is physically strenuous, but it's not as hard as it can be! I would rate this trip at a four out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. There was an older gentleman down there, he had to be 70 years old, and he was in his chest waders. If he can do it, you can do it! I will make sure to leave him in the video, so you can see who I was talking about. He was a very nice guy!
So if you park there, you can do a lot of trout fishing. It's great for people who use fly rods. There's lots of room to move around, and it's loaded with fish. I made two different videos that day, catching trout. My first video, was using a panther Martin that I had found. If you don't know, that's an inline spinner, a lot like a rooster tail. In the next video, I tried using my fly rod, but those fish weren't having it. Mostly because I don't know what fly to use. So I picked up my spinning rod, and started beating up the fish. I ended up making the video, fly rod versus spinning rod, and of course, the spinning rod won out.
The third video I made was a little farther downstream. I had taken my kayak down that hill, which you're allowed to do, and paddled down, past the island, where the confluence of the Smith Fork River comes into the Caney Fork river. That area is known as Sebowisha, and it's loaded with smallmouth bass right now! Actually, it's loaded with all types of fish, but I was targeting smallmouth. I wanted to make a video using top water lures, and the fish were attacking it, but I only ended up catching one. With so many bass in the area, I wasn't willing to only catch one fish, and call it a day, so I put on my peanut butter jelly Ned rig, and started catching really big bass!
To get back to my vehicle, I simply went around the left side of the island, on my way upstream, and paddle as far as I could, and then got out of my kayak, and then dragged it behind me with a rope. There were only a couple of spots where I had to get out, because the water was too swift, or too shallow. But it was really lovely, because it was a hot day, and the water felt nice! I never got in water that was deeper than my knee. So if you time it just right, you can do the same thing. The timing is everything! If you don't time it right, you could be injured, or worse! Here's how to make sure you stay safe, doing this trip...
THE MOST IMPORTANT THING TO KNOW IS THAT THE GENERATING WATER ARRIVES TO THIS AREA IN ABOUT 4 HOURS TIME!
That means, if they're not discharging water from the dam, for several hours at a time, this area will be allowed to get low and slow. That creates the perfect condition for us to fish and kayak. Lately, they've been turning the generators off at night, between 8:00 and 10:00 p.m. They haven't been turning them back on, until 12:00 p.m. or later. That creates a 12 to 14 or perhaps even 16 hour stretch, when the water is down.
The water doesn't move like a train, where the beginning and the end are moving at the same time... When the water stops at the dam, it takes a long time to go down in this area! Also, when the water is down, downstream, it takes a long time for the water to get from the dam, to that area. Because the water travels at about 3 mph, and this spot is about 10 miles away, you can expect it to show up, right inside that 4 hour time frame. The day I went, the generators were scheduled to turn on at 3:00 p.m., and they had been off since the night before. That meant, when I showed up at 8:00 a.m. the water was almost all the way down, and it wouldn't come back up, until around 7:00 p.m. that evening. So I had all day to fish! You can do the same thing, you just have to know the generating schedule, which you can find, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#CEHT1
Here are some worst case scenarios, and what you might be able to do in that situation...
If you are in chest waders, and the water starts to come up, you need to get to the bank where your vehicle is as quick as possible. If you can get across the river, even if you have to float downstream a little, you can scurry up the bank, and the road is just up that hill. You can walk back down to your vehicle, and that could save your life! If you can't get across the river, you could consider staying on the island. The water doesn't go over the island, and you might have to stay there all night, but you will be safe. If you have your phone, you can call for help, and you can be rescued. For those of us who kayak, the answer is quite simple...
If the water starts to come up, unexpectedly, and you can't get back upstream in your kayak, consider floating downstream! If you will go about 5 miles, on the left, you will find gordonsville boat ramp...
Stone Wall Boat Ramp (Gordonsville Access) https://share.google/8Wln9bqvpdPhnRadu
From there, you could call an Uber, or call a friend or family member, but you wouldn't be stuck, and you wouldn't need to be rescued. These are the type of contingency plans that you have to keep in place, if you want to get to the good fish! Fishing on rivers is inherently dangerous... Having a plan for your safety is of the utmost importance.

title: Trip Report #10
content_raw:
I found the bass on Center Hill Lake!
I'm trying really hard to find all the crappie spots, as well as, learn how to catch walleye on Center Hill Lake. I've got a little bit figured out... If you stay off the main lake channel, and in the fingers of the lake, you stand a better chance at finding fish. The main lake is really deep, and unless you have sophisticated electronics, it's going to be tough to find fish out there. The lake has lots of fingers that reach far away from the main channel, get much shallower, and are loaded with fish! I went to one of the biggest fingers on the lake, Indian Creek boat ramp...
https://share.google/ehPqDwcxXsLa5KMPm
First of all, this boat ramp is open 24 hours a day. I have never been to a lake like Center Hill, where, they have so many boat ramps that don't open till 8:00 or 9:00 a.m... I am certain you can launch here anytime of night or day. I wish I could tell you I have a whole bunch of pins for you to go look at, where I found crappie, but that's not the case! This is the north end of the lake, pretty close to the dam. The water in this section is relatively clear, and I couldn't find any crappie, because if they were there, they were way too deep for me to see.
I was also hoping to find walleye. From what I've learned, you can use your forward facing sonar to find schools of bait fish, and then scan that school to see if there are fish below. In many cases, those fish will be walleye, on Center Hill lake. What I found was that exact scenario, except the fish were bass! Everywhere! This was, the most loaded stretch, of any body of water, that I have ever seen! There were literally bass everywhere! I fished from the boat ramp, all the way out to the mouth of the creek, where it turns into the main lake, and all the way back. I was able to find bass on every bank, in every depth of water chasing bait, and at one point, I saw a school of at least 200 fish! They all darted to the crappie jig that I was using, and I hooked up with one, and then it got off, and then another one ate the lure and I caught that fish! It was truly a sight to see!
I also ran into a friend of mine who was on his kayak, and he's an avid bass fisherman. That's all he does! He won't even catch a crappie if he's in the boat with you and you're catching crappie... He was throwing a Whopper plopper on top water near the banks, and he was catching giant fish! 3 pound smallmouth and 4 pound largemouth,  he even caught one right in front of me while we were talking! I ran into him at about 10:00 a.m., and he had been catching them like that all morning, and he was still catching them!
I believe, the reason I couldn't find any crappie, is because they are deep in that clear water. I suspect, if I go to the south end of the lake, where the water is more stained, I will have better luck finding crappie and walleye, as they have very sensitive eyes, and like to hide from the daytime sun.
For those of you keeping score at home, the water temperature at the surface, according to my electronics, was 86°. I was catching fish with crappie jigs and my ultralight setup with 4 pound monofilament, but you could literally catch them with most types of presentation! The area is fantastic for kayakers, because boats don't come that far back, unless they launch at that boat ramp. You have lots of area to explore, and there are trees in the water everywhere! Not the type of trees you're thinking of, that are underneath the water, or laying over in the water, trees that were recently growing in the lake, and still standing in the water! It's a truly beautiful spot, everyone should go check it out!
The boat ramp is fantastic! It's only a single wide, but it's like a one and a half ramp. It's plenty-wide, it's plenty steep, but there is no courtesy dock. You will have to put your boat on the bank, which is gravelly, or the boat ramp, which is concrete. There's not a lot of parking, I could see this place filling up during the weekend. Fortunately, there are some overflow parking spots outside of the parking lot, in a grassy area. It looks like lots of people have been parking there!
content_markdown:
I found the bass on Center Hill Lake!

I'm trying really hard to find all the crappie spots, as well as, learn how to catch walleye on Center Hill Lake. I've got a little bit figured out... If you stay off the main lake channel, and in the fingers of the lake, you stand a better chance at finding fish. The main lake is really deep, and unless you have sophisticated electronics, it's going to be tough to find fish out there. The lake has lots of fingers that reach far away from the main channel, get much shallower, and are loaded with fish! I went to one of the biggest fingers on the lake, Indian Creek boat ramp...

https://share.google/ehPqDwcxXsLa5KMPm

First of all, this boat ramp is open 24 hours a day. I have never been to a lake like Center Hill, where, they have so many boat ramps that don't open till 8:00 or 9:00 a.m... I am certain you can launch here anytime of night or day. I wish I could tell you I have a whole bunch of pins for you to go look at, where I found crappie, but that's not the case! This is the north end of the lake, pretty close to the dam. The water in this section is relatively clear, and I couldn't find any crappie, because if they were there, they were way too deep for me to see.

I was also hoping to find walleye. From what I've learned, you can use your forward facing sonar to find schools of bait fish, and then scan that school to see if there are fish below. In many cases, those fish will be walleye, on Center Hill lake. What I found was that exact scenario, except the fish were bass! Everywhere! This was, the most loaded stretch, of any body of water, that I have ever seen! There were literally bass everywhere! I fished from the boat ramp, all the way out to the mouth of the creek, where it turns into the main lake, and all the way back. I was able to find bass on every bank, in every depth of water chasing bait, and at one point, I saw a school of at least 200 fish! They all darted to the crappie jig that I was using, and I hooked up with one, and then it got off, and then another one ate the lure and I caught that fish! It was truly a sight to see!

I also ran into a friend of mine who was on his kayak, and he's an avid bass fisherman. That's all he does! He won't even catch a crappie if he's in the boat with you and you're catching crappie... He was throwing a Whopper plopper on top water near the banks, and he was catching giant fish! 3 pound smallmouth and 4 pound largemouth, he even caught one right in front of me while we were talking! I ran into him at about 10:00 a.m., and he had been catching them like that all morning, and he was still catching them!

I believe, the reason I couldn't find any crappie, is because they are deep in that clear water. I suspect, if I go to the south end of the lake, where the water is more stained, I will have better luck finding crappie and walleye, as they have very sensitive eyes, and like to hide from the daytime sun.

For those of you keeping score at home, the water temperature at the surface, according to my electronics, was 86°. I was catching fish with crappie jigs and my ultralight setup with 4 pound monofilament, but you could literally catch them with most types of presentation! The area is fantastic for kayakers, because boats don't come that far back, unless they launch at that boat ramp. You have lots of area to explore, and there are trees in the water everywhere! Not the type of trees you're thinking of, that are underneath the water, or laying over in the water, trees that were recently growing in the lake, and still standing in the water! It's a truly beautiful spot, everyone should go check it out!

The boat ramp is fantastic! It's only a single wide, but it's like a one and a half ramp. It's plenty-wide, it's plenty steep, but there is no courtesy dock. You will have to put your boat on the bank, which is gravelly, or the boat ramp, which is concrete. There's not a lot of parking, I could see this place filling up during the weekend. Fortunately, there are some overflow parking spots outside of the parking lot, in a grassy area. It looks like lots of people have been parking there!

title: Trip Report #11
content_raw:
Trout going crazy!
Yesterday, I got in two trips on the Caney Fork River. As I had suggested, the generating schedule will allow for downstream fishing from the bank or, like I like to do in this hot weather, getting in the water to wade. The generating schedule was perfect for me to do a short trip downstream from the dam, and then go up to the dam and fish the generating water. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#CEHT1
With the water all the way down because it had been off all night, I headed to Betty's Island boat ramp at about 11:00 a.m...
https://share.google/F2a9GmnJjPEV8ysJq
The generators were scheduled to turn on at noon, so I knew that I could fish down there until at least 3:00 p.m. before the water would start to rise. Betty's Island boat ramp is 9 miles away from the dam on the river, and the water flows at about 3 mph, so it takes it about 3 hours to get down there. I wouldn't need that much time! You've seen my favorite method, my ultralight rod and reel with 4 pound monofilament, I added a slight wrinkle to my typical setup. Instead of a split shot and a hook with one piece of Berkeley powerbait and a nightcrawler, I found some Berkeley powerbait that was in the shape of a nightcrawler and pink in color, so I tried that out, and it worked really well!
Here is an Amazon associates link for the specific product that I found...
https://amzn.to/4x1LMSn
I used it the same way you would a real worm. I made a short cast, allowed it to sink to the bottom, and then bounced through the current. Rainbow trout and brown trout alike were loving it! I made a quick video about that product, and then headed up to the dam, to fix the generating water in my kayak...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/p4YsayabLq6hi8iWJ
By the time I got up there, it was a little after 2:00 p.m., and they had gone from one generator, to two generators. The river was full, and flowing fast, but if you put in at Buffalo valley boat ramp, the water is relatively calm on that side of the river. It's really nice! You're able to easily paddle on the side of the river where there is no current, all the way up to the dam if you'd like.
I fished for more than 4 hours, and never caught a single fish, but I still had an amazing day of fishing... So how does that work? I'm glad you asked!
I've done a lot of fishing from those steps beside the generators, while the generators are running. I've probably done more from my kayak. In all the times I've been out there in my kayak, I have never seen them get into the boils like they did yesterday. When I say them, I mean extremely large trout! I have been on the steps, several times, when the surface erupts with trout chasing threadfin shad. I have not seen that from the boat or the kayak, until yesterday. Here's how it went down...
I always assumed that the generators were too deep to pull fish through. I was wrong! Especially, after they turn on two or more generators, the current that they pull from the lake, according to all the information I've read online, is enough to pull big schools of threadfin shad through the generators, and spit them out on the riverside. When that happens, the fish come out of the bottom of the generators, and then make their way to the surface, flapping around, stunned, dazed, and sometimes killed. That usually triggers every trout in the area to come up to the surface and attack those shad. That's exactly what happened yesterday, and it was insane!
The sheer volume of big fish at the dam was what blew my mind. I can't sit at Center Hill Dam and fish everyday, but I wish I could! What I witnessed yesterday, was one of those life-changing events, that let me know, lots of my assumptions are wrong! There are way more big fish hanging around in that generating water then I thought there were. Unfortunately, I couldn't catch any of them!
I tried running a rooster tail, jigging a spoon, I even tried a weightless fluke, but they weren't having it. When they would come to the surface to target one of these fish, they would attack it until they successfully got it down. I was able to throw my lure right beside these fish, and they wouldn't pay it any attention. So what I did, was paddle around with my long net, and scoop up some of these bait fish off the surface. They were huge thread fin shad! Most of them at least four to five inches long, some of them longer. I put one on a hook with no sinker, and allowed it to sit on the surface and flop around in the heavy current, and I was able to get a few different trout to smack my bait up into the air, but none of them would eat it.
It's that time of year, the trout are going crazy on the Caney Fork river!
