title: Trip Report #12
content_raw:
Tough Fishing and this week's fishing forecast...
For the past few days, I've tried to go fishing, but it's been really tough! On friday, I went to the Murfreesboro greenway, in the afternoon, to try to catch bass with live bait...
Cason Trailhead https://share.google/jhCR0CL51vPTY3hTg
I could see, from an elevated position on the greenway, that it was loaded with really big bass! Big largemouth and smallmouth, cruising around, looking for an easy meal. I got down in the river, caught some bait with my cast net, and then tried my hand at these fish. A few of them took my bait under, but they were wary! They knew I was there, and it was really tough to get them to bite, and when they did, they wouldn't put the hook in their mouth. When I finally hooked a fish, it was a very big small mouth, and the first time it jumped out of the water, it spit my hook...
Then, once the weekend got here, so did the lightning. I had clients booked to float the Caney Fork River, to fish for trout on Saturday, and we had to cancel that because of early thunderstorms. Sunday wasn't as bad with lightning, but my family had to get together, and I wasn't able to go fishing. Fast forward to this morning, and I was chomping at the bit to get out on Percy Priest lake, to fish for some crappie.
I woke up early, before the sun, and got everything packed into my boat, and headed down to Stewart Creek boat ramp...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/yIeTGZJiIMuAgVRTK
I have dozens and dozens of crappie pins on this end of the lake, and I wanted to check those locations, to see a few things... Were there any fish on this end of the lake, what depth are they located at, and are they in a mood to bite? Unfortunately, what I saw when I got to the boat ramp, sent me right back to the house... The lake had white caps! The wind was already blowing so hard this morning, right at sunrise, that waves were scooting across the surface, and crashing against the boat ramp. My little John Boat doesn't do very well in the wind, anything over 5 mph is a constant battle. I turned around, headed for home, and put the boat in the garage.
It's been tough! This isn't our typical weather pattern for this time of year. I'm not as brave as some people, I will not go fishing when there's a chance of thunderstorms. Despite the fact that I take every precaution, I've already been caught in a couple of heavy thunderstorms this year. I wouldn't recommend it!
So what do you do when conditions are like this? Where can you go when it's thunderstorms everyday? I'm glad you asked...
Some people, only fish in one spot. For instance, using Percy Priest Lake as an example. Maybe they have a boat that's already in a slip in a marina, or they live nearby, and they don't really want to drive past their home lake, to visit other lakes. All of that makes perfect sense! For me, since I like to go fishing every day, it's not really practical. There are a few different ways, that I like to get out on the water, when the weather is inclement.
First of all, it doesn't usually rain everywhere, all at once. I will check the forecast, and run the radar for 24 hours into the future, and see where it thinks storms will pop up. I will do my best, to pick a fishing location, away from that area. It's not an exact science, but you've got to give yourself the best opportunity to get some fishing in!
This morning, I could tell, that I had a few hours on Percy Priest, before any rain was going to fall. I checked the wind speed, and it said 4 to 5 mph for the next few hours. By the time I got close to the lake in my vehicle, I noticed that the flags on the flagpoles were flying stiff! The wind was already too much to be out on the open lake in my boat, or kayak for that matter.
With a brief window before rain, and too much wind to be on the open lake, I would typically opt for a bank fishing trip. I would steer clear of the lake, all together, because there's nothing out there to break up the wind. Today, the wind is predicted to be double digits by lunch time, so I'm going to look for somewhere in a river basin. In the woods, below the tree line. You're still going to have to deal with wind, but it will definitely be busted up...
A really good place, that meets all those requirements, it's below Woods reservoir...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/J6CC488twkdMaAS26
This location is on an Air Force Base, and they recently reopened it to fishing. It had been closed for a while, because people had been leaving their trash. People had been leaving their trash, because it is an unbelievably good fishing spot! If you park in the parking lot where I drop this pin, you will see a sign, that says the area is closed, but that is not true. It is reopened, and there is a trail, straight down to the water's edge. If you're going to fish below this dam, it's a 5 out of 5 on the effort scale of one to five. The rocks below the dam are slippery, and they're very large, and you kind of have to hop or crawl in between. It's one of the more difficult places that I bank fish, but it's worth going to, because it's loaded right now!
Recent rains have brought the level of Woods reservoir up, and they are releasing water from the floodgates, all day every day, right now. The type of fish stacked up below Woods reservoir include, but are not limited to, lots of striped bass! Every morning, at sunrise, striped bass are blowing up on the surface below the dam. People are catching them with top water lures, as well as paddle tails, weightless flukes, just about any type of lure you can think of. During the early morning melee, the striped bass have been joined by very large hybrid bass. Not necessarily large schools of hybrid bass, but hybrid bass that weigh a lot! Most of them, over 8 pounds! You can catch these fish, in the same exact manner in which you would catch striped bass. I've been using a 7 foot medium action rod with 15 pound braid, and that seems to work really well to not only cast all the way across the river, but to drag these fish in.
Walleye have started to come up from Tim's Ford lake, which is the next body of water below this dam. The last few days, people have been standing on the bank, using rapala jerk baits, and having pretty good success catching keeper walleye. For that, I like to use a lighter rod and reel, with a stiff tip, and 8 pound braid with a 6 pound monofilament leader. I've been using a pretty long leader, about 8 feet, just because walleye are so tough to catch! I've been using clear line, to try to give myself an advantage, so that the fish don't see the line, and get spooked away from the lure. I'm almost certain they can see the braid, especially in the daylight! Typically, people will fish for walleye at night, but they've been catching them during the daytime below the dam!
There are also a lot of really big bass. Most people are catching largemouth, but I have seen some smallmouth caught as well. In reality, most people aren't fishing for bass, they're fishing for walleye, or striped bass, or hybrid bass, and then catching these bass as a bycatch. It's been a pretty good bycatch, one day, a buddy of mine, caught eight largemouth!
Last week I told you conditions were right below Tim's Ford dam, to go trout fishing... Fast forward to this week, and it rained so much, that they are releasing a deadly torrent of water from that dam. When I got home this morning, after being defeated by the wind, before I even started fishing, I had turned my sights towards trout fishing, in the hopes that I could go down below Tim's for dam, and catch 100 fish, and make myself feel better. I like fishing below Tims ford, because it's almost a guaranteed thing. There are so many trout in there, mostly brown, that you can't help but catch fish, with every method. That won't be an option this week. They are releasing too much water to utilize the area below the dam, in any capacity. You cannot stand on the bank, you cannot use a kayak and there are no options that close to the dam for using a boat.
Typically, during the summer, that dam will release 235 cubic feet per second, all day everyday. They did that this weekend, to accommodate recreational fisherman and kayakers, but as of this morning, their plan is to ratchet up discharge, to an unsafe level... Thousands of cubic feet per second, through a little stretch of river, that is no more than a creek, making it unusable this week. You can find the water release schedule for Tim's Ford dam, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#TMFT1
For the first time this year, Percy Priest Lake has reached summer pool. That's the level at which, they like to keep the lake, during the summer months. They usually achieve that level, by April 15th. We didn't hit summer pool, until the middle of July. Because of that fact, fishing below Percy Priest Dam was not really much of an option, so far this year. Now that the lake is at summer pool, they will have to do regular water releases, to keep it at that level. When they release water from Percy Priest dam, it's a great place to go during the summer, to try to catch striped bass and hybrids. Not unlike Woods reservoir, when the water is coming out of that dam, fish will come up from the next body of water, which is the Cumberland river. The correct time to go below Percy Priest dam, is when they have one generator on, or, the floodgates open. You can find the water release schedules, for Percy Priest dam, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#JPHT1
Center Hill Lake has been on fire for walleye! That's where I want to be, but I need a break in the thunderstorms. I'm not willing to drive that far from my house, to get stuck in a thunderstorm. Once we have a break, that's where I'll be this week. Out in the lake, trying to use my live scope, or troll some crankbaits, for walleye. Here's how I intend to go about doing that, as I'm very unfamiliar with the lake, and incredibly unfamiliar with walleye fishing.
From what I've observed, on my limited amount of time on the lake, simply scanning around for piles of crappie, can be very effective! Once I find them, I'm able to sit on an anchor, and fish for them. While you're doing that, you will see, not only the crappie that you're fishing for, but schools of bait fish, and other fish in the area, as well. When I'm on Percy Priest lake, most of the time, those other fish are bass. When you're out on Center Hill lake, quite often, those fish are walleye! I have learned, from several good friends, that if you take your crappie lure, and jiggle it in front of a walleye, they will bite it, much the same way that bass do! It is my intention, to go looking for crappie, and then, fish for other fish that I see on my forward facing sonar.
It's also prime time of year below Center Hill dam. I will probably say that in every week's fishing forecast. It's always good to go fishing below Center Hill dam! Here's why it's going to be especially good this week...
Recent rains have meant that they have to run the generators every day, rather predictably, around 12:00 p.m., until around 8:00 or 9:00 p.m. at night. That provides excellent opportunities in the morning, for Bank fishermen and people who want to get out in the river in chest waders. You have plenty of time to fish not only below the dam, while the water is down, but also, downstream, before the water comes up in the afternoon. Because the water comes on every day, that allows people in boats, to get out there, rather reliably. I just made a short video, explaining the benefits of using a drag chain on the Caney Fork river, and now is the time for the drag chain to shine! You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#CEHT1

The rocks below the dam are slippery, and they're very large, and you kind of have to hop or crawl in between. It's one of the more difficult places that I bank fish, but it's worth going to, because it's loaded right now!

Recent rains have brought the level of Woods reservoir up, and they are releasing water from the floodgates, all day every day, right now. The type of fish stacked up below Woods reservoir include, but are not limited to, lots of striped bass! Every morning, at sunrise, striped bass are blowing up on the surface below the dam. People are catching them with top water lures, as well as paddle tails, weightless flukes, just about any type of lure you can think of. During the early morning melee, the striped bass have been joined by very large hybrid bass. Not necessarily large schools of hybrid bass, but hybrid bass that weigh a lot! Most of them, over 8 pounds! You can catch these fish, in the same exact manner in which you would catch striped bass. I've been using a 7 foot medium action rod with 15 pound braid, and that seems to work really well to not only cast all the way across the river, but to drag these fish in.

Walleye have started to come up from Tim's Ford lake, which is the next body of water below this dam. The last few days, people have been standing on the bank, using rapala jerk baits, and having pretty good success catching keeper walleye. For that, I like to use a lighter rod and reel, with a stiff tip, and 8 pound braid with a 6 pound monofilament leader. I've been using a pretty long leader, about 8 feet, just because walleye are so tough to catch! I've been using clear line, to try to give myself an advantage, so that the fish don't see the line, and get spooked away from the lure. I'm almost certain they can see the braid, especially in the daylight! Typically, people will fish for walleye at night, but they've been catching them during the daytime below the dam!

There are also a lot of really big bass. Most people are catching largemouth, but I have seen some smallmouth caught as well. In reality, most people aren't fishing for bass, they're fishing for walleye, or striped bass, or hybrid bass, and then catching these bass as a bycatch. It's been a pretty good bycatch, one day, a buddy of mine, caught eight largemouth!

Last week I told you conditions were right below Tim's Ford dam, to go trout fishing... Fast forward to this week, and it rained so much, that they are releasing a deadly torrent of water from that dam. When I got home this morning, after being defeated by the wind, before I even started fishing, I had turned my sights towards trout fishing, in the hopes that I could go down below Tim's for dam, and catch 100 fish, and make myself feel better. I like fishing below Tims ford, because it's almost a guaranteed thing. There are so many trout in there, mostly brown, that you can't help but catch fish, with every method. That won't be an option this week. They are releasing too much water to utilize the area below the dam, in any capacity. You cannot stand on the bank, you cannot use a kayak and there are no options that close to the dam for using a boat.

Typically, during the summer, that dam will release 235 cubic feet per second, all day everyday. They did that this weekend, to accommodate recreational fisherman and kayakers, but as of this morning, their plan is to ratchet up discharge, to an unsafe level... Thousands of cubic feet per second, through a little stretch of river, that is no more than a creek, making it unusable this week. You can find the water release schedule for Tim's Ford dam, here...

https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#TMFT1

For the first time this year, Percy Priest Lake has reached summer pool. That's the level at which, they like to keep the lake, during the summer months. They usually achieve that level, by April 15th. We didn't hit summer pool, until the middle of July. Because of that fact, fishing below Percy Priest Dam was not really much of an option, so far this year. Now that the lake is at summer pool, they will have to do regular water releases, to keep it at that level. When they release water from Percy Priest dam, it's a great place to go during the summer, to try to catch striped bass and hybrids. Not unlike Woods reservoir, when the water is coming out of that dam, fish will come up from the next body of water, which is the Cumberland river. The correct time to go below Percy Priest dam, is when they have one generator on, or, the floodgates open. You can find the water release schedules, for Percy Priest dam, here...

https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#JPHT1

Center Hill Lake has been on fire for walleye! That's where I want to be, but I need a break in the thunderstorms. I'm not willing to drive that far from my house, to get stuck in a thunderstorm. Once we have a break, that's where I'll be this week. Out in the lake, trying to use my live scope, or troll some crankbaits, for walleye. Here's how I intend to go about doing that, as I'm very unfamiliar with the lake, and incredibly unfamiliar with walleye fishing.

From what I've observed, on my limited amount of time on the lake, simply scanning around for piles of crappie, can be very effective! Once I find them, I'm able to sit on an anchor, and fish for them. While you're doing that, you will see, not only the crappie that you're fishing for, but schools of bait fish, and other fish in the area, as well. When I'm on Percy Priest lake, most of the time, those other fish are bass. When you're out on Center Hill lake, quite often, those fish are walleye! I have learned, from several good friends, that if you take your crappie lure, and jiggle it in front of a walleye, they will bite it, much the same way that bass do! It is my intention, to go looking for crappie, and then, fish for other fish that I see on my forward facing sonar.

It's also prime time of year below Center Hill dam. I will probably say that in every week's fishing forecast. It's always good to go fishing below Center Hill dam! Here's why it's going to be especially good this week...

Recent rains have meant that they have to run the generators every day, rather predictably, around 12:00 p.m., until around 8:00 or 9:00 p.m. at night. That provides excellent opportunities in the morning, for Bank fishermen and people who want to get out in the river in chest waders. You have plenty of time to fish not only below the dam, while the water is down, but also, downstream, before the water comes up in the afternoon. Because the water comes on every day, that allows people in boats, to get out there, rather reliably. I just made a short video, explaining the benefits of using a drag chain on the Caney Fork river, and now is the time for the drag chain to shine! You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...

https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#CEHT1

title: Trip Report #14
content_raw:
Smallmouth bass in the Smoky mountains...
Today I'm fishing in Pigeon Forge. Most people come up here for the trout that they stock in the rivers. That's something that I like to do, but not this time of year. The trout have been heavily pressured, the weather is warmer, and the trout fishing is slow and sluggish. This time of year, people go for Smallmouth bass! If you're going to make your way to the Smoky mountains to do any fishing, you've got to stop by The Old Mill!
The Old Mill Restaurant https://share.google/fVDibzQZK3PShnOg8
This restaurant overlooks the river that flows through the center of town. The restaurant is called The Old Mill because it has an Old Mill and a dam that backs up the river. There is a spinning water wheel that is still in function, but I don't believe it's operating anything inside. It's probably just for looks at this point. If you drive just past the restaurant, on the right, there are public parking lots. These lots are free, until they fill up, usually around 8:00 or 9:00 a.m. You should show up before then to do your bass fishing. If you get down there just after sunrise, you will have plenty of free parking. If you show up late, there is a paid parking lot, on the left hand side of the street, after you pass the restaurant.
Now for the good stuff, the fishing! We didn't have to stay long, before we caught seven mallmouth bass! The first few came rather quickly, you guessed it, peanut butter jelly ned rig!
When I'm using the Ned rig, I like a rod with a stiff tip! Two things happen, you can feel the bite quicker with a stiff tip, and you can set the hook quicker. A quick hook set is important with a Ned rig because it's so small. Fish will pick that lure up, decide they don't like it, and spit it back out before you ever feel a thing. To improve my odds, I like to use a 7 foot medium, ultra fast action tip. That phrase, ultra fast action, means that the rod tip will set the hook quickly. That typically refers to a very stiff rod tip. I've got 15 pound spider wire braid on my reel, but when I'm using a Ned rig, I like to add about 6 foot of monofilament leader line.
When you're attaching monofilament to braid, it's important that the diameter of both fishing line be comparable. If one is significantly thinner or thicker than the other, it's going to be tough to get them to tie together. I like to use what's called an Acapulco knot, with one small deviation. I will do a video about that knot in the near future... 15 pound spider wire is about the same diameter as 8 pound monofilament, so that's what I use.I like to use a length of clear monofilament, because I feel like fish can see the braid. I'm not 100% certain that it helps, but on this day, I was able to catch a nice big bruiser of a smallmouth bass, directly under the dam at the old mill.
After a few small mouth came in, I headed over to Walmart to pick up a cast net and a bucket for some live bait. I suspected that there were a lot more fish in that area, and they might be easier to catch with some live bait, but I didn't bring any of my stuff from home to facilitate that type of fishing trip, so I headed to the closest sporting goods section at the Walmart to pick up what we needed to continue smallmouth fishing, with live bait from the river.
There are lots of bait fish in the river, but they're not super easy to catch, because the river has lots of rocks and boulders that will snag your cast net. We were able to catch a few fish with live bait, but I probably wouldn't do that again, just because getting the bait was so difficult.
If you would like to fish from the bank in this area, it's not necessarily easy! The rocks are slippery and boulderous and it's easily a four out of five on the effort scale of one to five... The banks are steep, and treacherous, but if you're the adventurous type, I say go for it!

title: Trip Report #15
content_raw:
A holiday summary and your weekly forecast...
Friday, July 3rd, I headed down the Piney River with my buddies, and a few hundred of my closest friends ( not actual friends, just people who are also kayaking the Piney River )! I thought I was ready to go fishing with that many people on the water at the same time, like a party atmosphere, but I was wrong! There were a little too many people, even for me, and I'm a socialite! By now, you've already seen the video, I wished everyone a Happy Independence day, and released that video on Saturday, the 4th. You can see how many people are on the water, but that didn't stop the fish from biting! They were going crazy, until they weren't. Once the thunderstorms lit up, and started slapping really hard, the fish stopped biting, and most people got off the river! For what it's worth, this river is loaded with smallmouth bass, and I believe they are there for the long haul. You should be able to catch bass on the Piney river, on the stretch provided by Pinewood canoe and campground, for the rest of the summer. You can facilitate a kayak trip down the Piney by getting in touch with pinewood canoe and campground, or just showing up, they are open 7 days a week...
Pinewood Canoe & Camp LLC https://share.google/Y44K9pH0VIFqrLaq6
You can take your own kayak and they will shuttle you or you can rent one of theirs if you don't have one. It's a fantastic service, it's about a four mile trip, and on the effort scale of one to five, it comes in at a 4. You're going to have to navigate some difficult rapids and there are some hairpin maneuvers that are necessary to avoid flipping. Plan on getting wet!
I tapped out on the weekend! I do that from time to time, where I just let people have at it, and stay at the house and do some cleaning and gardening. I even made a short video about my preferred style of kayak. I waited until the weekend crowds slowed down, and then headed out to try my hand at some hybrid bass fishing this morning. In last week's weekly forecast, I told you that hybrid bass were on fire, first thing in the morning, at Seven Points on Percy Priest Lake...
Seven Points Boat Ramp https://share.google/XzCRUozY47XrOLpOJ
This morning, I met my buddy with his boat, at 4:45 a.m. We motored around the corner, to fish at the point, where the hybrid have been blowing up consistently, every morning, for 8 to 10 weeks now...
https://goo.gl/maps/dWoPzdU33APDT9hk9
That's a pin in Google maps of the location where I usually start out in the morning. There's an underwater hump, and these fish come off the hump, into the deep channel, between the bank and where I sit, to feed. We got there just before 5:00 a.m., and between 5:15 and 6:00 a.m. these fish went crazy! They were blowing up everywhere, but we couldn't get a single one to bite. That's been happening lately, I've been getting reports of people that have been catching fish, but mostly with live bait. The preferred live bait, is small bluegills. Drop one of those under the boat, and just hang on!
I've been using lures like a quarter ounce jig head with a 5 inch plastic fluke or a white paddle tail of the same size or a top water lure like a Whopper plopper. I even tried throwing a glide bait, and my buddy was throwing an Alabama rig, but those fish just weren't having it! We kept seeing them blow up by the boat, and we would cast in their direction, and usually that's all it takes, but it's like they had tunnel vision. They had their sights set on something, and they weren't going to come off of it to feed on something else.
As usual, the people on the bank did a little better than the people in the boats. When we got there, there weren't any other boats there, and only one other boat showed up while we were there. There were half a dozen people on the bank, and they caught at least half a dozen fish! If you want to fish from the bank, you have to park in the parking lot at the boat ramp. Access to the park isn't open until well after these fish stop biting. The way that people get to the bank, is to park in the assigned parking, at the boat ramp. There are spots that say parking for trailers only, and then other ones, where that writing has been blacked out. If you park in those spaces, you can walk down the road, to the point. I will drop you a pin where you need to be, if you would like to fish from the bank, to catch these hybrid bass...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/KpHNArcCJ7ogbJXx5
I'm going to tell you about my setup, because it's perfect from the bank, or the boat. I've been using a 7 foot medium action bass rod with 15 pound braid tied directly to my lure. I used to put on a leader line, but that would break too often. I find that 15 pound braid allows me to cast very far, and is still super strong enough to pull in these fish. People on the bank don't take a net, it's very easy just to pull the fish right up on the bank! If you're going to walk through the dark, to get to this spot, most of the walk is on the pavement. You can walk almost all the way to the spot, and then, there's mowed grass with picnic tables. It's only a short trail through a little bit of wooded area, so it's not actually that difficult! On the effort scale of 1 to 5, I'd call it a three, just because you do have to walk pretty far.
This week is shaping up to be a good week for fishing! Rain fell in different sections of the mid-state, which is going to make some areas better than others, and some areas unfishable. When I'm looking to go fishing, I check the water levels of the lake or river that I'm heading to. Sometimes, just by checking the water levels, I can know exactly where I want to go! For instance, just now when I started typing up this weekly forecast, I first looked at Tims Ford Dam to see what it was doing...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#TMFT1
For the last few weeks, Tim's Ford has been releasing water during the week, but not on the weekends. Below Tims Ford dam is the only other place beside below Center Hill Dam in Middle Tennessee, where trout can live year-round. They always release a little bit of really cold water, but they had been releasing so much, that it was unfit to fish. As of this week, they're back to regular summertime operations, which is 245 cubic feet per second, all day every day! That is the ideal number for every type of recreation on the Elk River below Tims Ford dam. You could take your kayak and fish directly below the dam like I like to do or, you could stand on the bank or, wade. If you would like to get in the water, you can go really far downstream. You can either walk in the water, OR there is a trail from the boat ramp below the dam, that gives you access to the first mile of fishing. You can park to launch your kayak or to fish for trout below Tim's for dam, here...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/jyxGXe3Qp48xYzdKA
If you have friends and want to do a kayak shuttle, you can start at the dam, and finish at the Farris Creek bridge access...
Farris Creek Bridge https://share.google/1U20dTzolFHarOrTi
That's an eight and a half mile stretch of river that's going to take you all day long. There are some challenging spots, so this is a four out of five on the effort scale of one to five. If you're not an experienced kayaker, I wouldn't recommend it. If you are, I would send it! This will be one of your favorite places in Middle Tennessee. The water is cold and clear, and it's full of rainbow trout and brown trout all the way!
I don't see any chance those hybrid bass stop biting first thing in the morning out at Seven Points, for the foreseeable future. On Percy Priest Lake this morning, the water temperature was around 85°, and those fish seemed really happy! We don't have any severe changes to the temperature in the forecast, so I don't see any reason why they won't be there, in the mornings, for the foreseeable future.
Center Hill Dam isn't operating any generators from midnight until 2:00 p.m. today. That means, not only could you go fish below the dam, until 2:00 p.m., when they turn the generators on, but you could also get in the river downstream, all day! Because the river only travels at about 3 mph, that gives you several hours, when you are downstream, after the generators turn on, to stand in the water to try to catch trout. Always check the water release schedule before you go fishing below Center Hill dam. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#CEHT1
Here are some locations downstream where you could go fish, and the approximate time the water will show up to that location...
Happy Hollow Boat Ramp https://share.google/jtxRJaoGyy0bHhgYf
This location is 6 miles from the dam, so you would be able to stay in the water, without being affected by the generating water, until 2 hours after water release. Because the water release is at 2:00 p.m. today, you wouldn't start feeling the effects of the generating water until closer to 4:00 p.m. at that point, you would have to get out of the water for your safety, and move to higher ground.
Bettys Island Boat Ramp https://share.google/2ThWIYBA94CbofiKT
This location is 9 miles from the dam, so you would get an extra hour versus the 6 Mile location. Because the water travels at about 3 mph, and we're using today as an example, the 2:00 p.m. water release, would reach this area, around 5:00 p.m. at that point, you would need to get out of the water for your safety, and move to higher ground.
I mentioned Pinewood canoe and campground, and if you've never been, I suggest it! The rain that fell on that area brought the level of the river up, and you won't have to drag as much as you usually do. It's not a very big river, so sometimes, it gets very shallow when we don't get any rain. As of right now, if you check this graph, you can see, the levels are up...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03602500/all-graphs/#period=P7D
This is a smallmouth bass fishing kayak trip, and there are no public access points on this river. You won't be able to do any Bank fishing, or get in the water to wade. The only effective way to fish this river, is through the private access allowed by Pinewood canoe and campground.
The Collins River in McMinnville Tennessee finally has some water in it! I've done extensive videos chasing Muskie out there, as there are a handful of locations where you can access the river. I can see, from the USGS chart provided, that the rain filled the river up, and it's at a fantastic level! Anything between 500 and 1,000 out there is a good number. Once it starts getting around a thousand, it's too fast for most people. Of course we're talking, cubic feet per second. As of the time of this report, it was running at 793 cubic feet per second, which means, if it doesn't get too much more rain this week, it should be perfect all week! You can check the chart to see the flow of the river, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03421000/all-graphs/#period=P7D
If you would like to do a trip on the Collins, you can facilitate a kayak shuttle with mad musky water sports...
https://share.google/8WxJh9ydYoYsSEmc2
I didn't get a chance to do any crappie fishing on any of the area lakes last week, but I did see that Percy Priest was 85° this morning. That bodes well! If that number starts getting towards 90⁰, those fish will move very deep! As of right now, I would expect them to be in 15 to 25 foot of water. If you're looking for bluegill, I would start looking for the schools of larger bluegill, at 25 feet down.
Since we did get quite a bit of rain, there's a good chance water will be flowing below Woods reservoir. The area below the dam has been hot for striped and hybrid bass for the last couple of months. Access below the dam is a nightmare! The boulders are gigantic, and you have to crawl around to avoid breaking your legs. On an effort scale of one to five, it is a solid 5! If you're daring enough to try to go below Woods dam, I would try top water, or a paddle tail on a light jig head. The setup I mentioned earlier, for fishing at Percy Priest lake, would be ideal. You can access the area below Woods Dam, after a short downhill walk, from this parking lot...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/ex572ANG9W3a2fqc7
Unfortunately, you never know if the water is going to be running or not. There are no generators at Woods, they only use floodgates. There is no information about Woods reservoir, because it's controlled by the Air Force. Woods reservoir is on Arnold Air Force base, and they don't give out public information about what they do with the water there. It's hit or miss if you go, whether or not the water will be on, it's always best to go after a heavy rainstorm, because it's best to go when the water is flowing through the floodgates. Hope this week's report helps, happy fishing, and have a better day!

You can take your own kayak and they will shuttle you or you can rent one of theirs if you don't have one. It's a fantastic service, it's about a four mile trip, and on the effort scale of one to five, it comes in at a 4. You're going to have to navigate some difficult rapids and there are some hairpin maneuvers that are necessary to avoid flipping. Plan on getting wet!

I tapped out on the weekend! I do that from time to time, where I just let people have at it, and stay at the house and do some cleaning and gardening. I even made a short video about my preferred style of kayak. I waited until the weekend crowds slowed down, and then headed out to try my hand at some hybrid bass fishing this morning. In last week's weekly forecast, I told you that hybrid bass were on fire, first thing in the morning, at Seven Points on Percy Priest Lake...

Seven Points Boat Ramp https://share.google/XzCRUozY47XrOLpOJ

This morning, I met my buddy with his boat, at 4:45 a.m. We motored around the corner, to fish at the point, where the hybrid have been blowing up consistently, every morning, for 8 to 10 weeks now...

https://goo.gl/maps/dWoPzdU33APDT9hk9

That's a pin in Google maps of the location where I usually start out in the morning. There's an underwater hump, and these fish come off the hump, into the deep channel, between the bank and where I sit, to feed. We got there just before 5:00 a.m., and between 5:15 and 6:00 a.m. these fish went crazy! They were blowing up everywhere, but we couldn't get a single one to bite. That's been happening lately, I've been getting reports of people that have been catching fish, but mostly with live bait. The preferred live bait, is small bluegills. Drop one of those under the boat, and just hang on!

I've been using lures like a quarter ounce jig head with a 5 inch plastic fluke or a white paddle tail of the same size or a top water lure like a Whopper plopper. I even tried throwing a glide bait, and my buddy was throwing an Alabama rig, but those fish just weren't having it! We kept seeing them blow up by the boat, and we would cast in their direction, and usually that's all it takes, but it's like they had tunnel vision. They had their sights set on something, and they weren't going to come off of it to feed on something else.

As usual, the people on the bank did a little better than the people in the boats. When we got there, there weren't any other boats there, and only one other boat showed up while we were there. There were half a dozen people on the bank, and they caught at least half a dozen fish! If you want to fish from the bank, you have to park in the parking lot at the boat ramp. Access to the park isn't open until well after these fish stop biting. The way that people get to the bank, is to park in the assigned parking, at the boat ramp. There are spots that say parking for trailers only, and then other ones, where that writing has been blacked out. If you park in those spaces, you can walk down the road, to the point. I will drop you a pin where you need to be, if you would like to fish from the bank, to catch these hybrid bass...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/KpHNArcCJ7ogbJXx5

I'm going to tell you about my setup, because it's perfect from the bank, or the boat. I've been using a 7 foot medium action bass rod with 15 pound braid tied directly to my lure. I used to put on a leader line, but that would break too often. I find that 15 pound braid allows me to cast very far, and is still super strong enough to pull in these fish. People on the bank don't take a net, it's very easy just to pull the fish right up on the bank! If you're going to walk through the dark, to get to this spot, most of the walk is on the pavement. You can walk almost all the way to the spot, and then, there's mowed grass with picnic tables. It's only a short trail through a little bit of wooded area, so it's not actually that difficult! On the effort scale of 1 to 5, I'd call it a three, just because you do have to walk pretty far.

This week is shaping up to be a good week for fishing! Rain fell in different sections of the mid-state, which is going to make some areas better than others, and some areas unfishable. When I'm looking to go fishing, I check the water levels of the lake or river that I'm heading to. Sometimes, just by checking the water levels, I can know exactly where I want to go! For instance, just now when I started typing up this weekly forecast, I first looked at Tims Ford Dam to see what it was doing...

https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#TMFT1

For the last few weeks, Tim's Ford has been releasing water during the week, but not on the weekends. Below Tims Ford dam is the only other place beside below Center Hill Dam in Middle Tennessee, where trout can live year-round. They always release a little bit of really cold water, but they had been releasing so much, that it was unfit to fish. As of this week, they're back to regular summertime operations, which is 245 cubic feet per second, all day every day! That is the ideal number for every type of recreation on the Elk River below Tims Ford dam. You could take your kayak and fish directly below the dam like I like to do or, you could stand on the bank or, wade. If you would like to get in the water, you can go really far downstream. You can either walk in the water, OR there is a trail from the boat ramp below the dam, that gives you access to the first mile of fishing. You can park to launch your kayak or to fish for trout below Tim's for dam, here...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/jyxGXe3Qp48xYzdKA

If you have friends and want to do a kayak shuttle, you can start at the dam, and finish at the Farris Creek bridge access...

Farris Creek Bridge https://share.google/1U20dTzolFHarOrTi

That's an eight and a half mile stretch of river that's going to take you all day long. There are some challenging spots, so this is a four out of five on the effort scale of one to five. If you're not an experienced kayaker, I wouldn't recommend it. If you are, I would send it! This will be one of your favorite places in Middle Tennessee. The water is cold and clear, and it's full of rainbow trout and brown trout all the way!

I don't see any chance those hybrid bass stop biting first thing in the morning out at Seven Points, for the foreseeable future. On Percy Priest Lake this morning, the water temperature was around 85°, and those fish seemed really happy! We don't have any severe changes to the temperature in the forecast, so I don't see any reason why they won't be there, in the mornings, for the foreseeable future.

Center Hill Dam isn't operating any generators from midnight until 2:00 p.m. today. That means, not only could you go fish below the dam, until 2:00 p.m., when they turn the generators on, but you could also get in the river downstream, all day! Because the river only travels at about 3 mph, that gives you several hours, when you are downstream, after the generators turn on, to stand in the water to try to catch trout. Always check the water release schedule before you go fishing below Center Hill dam. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...

https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#CEHT1

Here are some locations downstream where you could go fish, and the approximate time the water will show up to that location...

Happy Hollow Boat Ramp https://share.google/jtxRJaoGyy0bHhgYf

This location is 6 miles from the dam, so you would be able to stay in the water, without being affected by the generating water, until 2 hours after water release. Because the water release is at 2:00 p.m. today, you wouldn't start feeling the effects of the generating water until closer to 4:00 p.m. at that point, you would have to get out of the water for your safety, and move to higher ground.

Bettys Island Boat Ramp https://share.google/2ThWIYBA94CbofiKT

This location is 9 miles from the dam, so you would get an extra hour versus the 6 Mile location. Because the water travels at about 3 mph, and we're using today as an example, the 2:00 p.m. water release, would reach this area, around 5:00 p.m. at that point, you would need to get out of the water for your safety, and move to higher ground.

I mentioned Pinewood canoe and campground, and if you've never been, I suggest it! The rain that fell on that area brought the level of the river up, and you won't have to drag as much as you usually do. It's not a very big river, so sometimes, it gets very shallow when we don't get any rain. As of right now, if you check this graph, you can see, the levels are up...

https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03602500/all-graphs/#period=P7D

This is a smallmouth bass fishing kayak trip, and there are no public access points on this river. You won't be able to do any Bank fishing, or get in the water to wade. The only effective way to fish this river, is through the private access allowed by Pinewood canoe and campground.

The Collins River in McMinnville Tennessee finally has some water in it! I've done extensive videos chasing Muskie out there, as there are a handful of locations where you can access the river. I can see, from the USGS chart provided, that the rain filled the river up, and it's at a fantastic level! Anything between 500 and 1,000 out there is a good number. Once it starts getting around a thousand, it's too fast for most people. Of course we're talking, cubic feet per second. As of the time of this report, it was running at 793 cubic feet per second, which means, if it doesn't get too much more rain this week, it should be perfect all week! You can check the chart to see the flow of the river, here...

https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03421000/all-graphs/#period=P7D

If you would like to do a trip on the Collins, you can facilitate a kayak shuttle with mad musky water sports...

https://share.google/8WxJh9ydYoYsSEmc2

I didn't get a chance to do any crappie fishing on any of the area lakes last week, but I did see that Percy Priest was 85° this morning. That bodes well! If that number starts getting towards 90⁰, those fish will move very deep! As of right now, I would expect them to be in 15 to 25 foot of water. If you're looking for bluegill, I would start looking for the schools of larger bluegill, at 25 feet down.

Since we did get quite a bit of rain, there's a good chance water will be flowing below Woods reservoir. The area below the dam has been hot for striped and hybrid bass for the last couple of months. Access below the dam is a nightmare! The boulders are gigantic, and you have to crawl around to avoid breaking your legs. On an effort scale of one to five, it is a solid 5! If you're daring enough to try to go below Woods dam, I would try top water, or a paddle tail on a light jig head. The setup I mentioned earlier, for fishing at Percy Priest lake, would be ideal. You can access the area below Woods Dam, after a short downhill walk, from this parking lot...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/ex572ANG9W3a2fqc7

Unfortunately, you never know if the water is going to be running or not. There are no generators at Woods, they only use floodgates. There is no information about Woods reservoir, because it's controlled by the Air Force. Woods reservoir is on Arnold Air Force base, and they don't give out public information about what they do with the water there. It's hit or miss if you go, whether or not the water will be on, it's always best to go after a heavy rainstorm, because it's best to go when the water is flowing through the floodgates. Hope this week's report helps, happy fishing, and have a better day!

title: Trip Report #16
content_raw:
An exceptionally long day...
Yesterday, I pulled a double shift... I fished overnight for walleye again, on the heels of the previous day's success. Unfortunately, I wasn't able to reproduce the action that I had the night before. I fished out of my kayak below Center Hill Dam at Buffalo valley boat ramp all night long!
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/K8NZo3QWIslYCckEh
The fish weren't biting! I wasn't doing anything wrong, I was using the same lure as the night before, and the same retrieve, standing in the same spot, but I wasn't having any luck! It's like the fish just weren't biting. I got out of there before the sun came up, so I could get home to get just a little bit of rest. The generators were scheduled to turn on at 10:00 a.m., and I wanted to float on the river, in my boat. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels#CEHT1
They were scheduled to generate with one generator from 10:00 a.m. until 3:00 p.m. and then two or more generators after 3:00 p.m. I wanted to hit that magical 5 hour spot, with one generator on. I call that magical, not because the fishing is necessarily good with one generator, but because it's fantastic to do out of a boat! If you have a small boat, like a Jon Boat, that river is a lot of fun, when the generators are on. I have a 15 horsepower on mine, and it's more than enough to run up the river at 13 miles an hour, with my friend in the boat with me. That allows us to float several miles at a time, do a lot of fishing, and then run back up the river to the dam, to do the whole thing over again.
If you would like to run this river in a boat, I suggest you float it several times in a kayak or canoe, before you do so. This is the real pro move of this Pro report! Learning where the trees and islands are, is crucial to understanding how to run back up the river. There is a main channel, and if you stay in that, when you're running back up, you will have to zig and zag to avoid areas that go completely dry when the water goes down. The generator comes up enough for you to run a boat up and down the river, but not enough for you to run wide open from bank to bank. There will be several areas in the middle of the river that are still shallow, and there are giant trees in the way that could eject you from your boat if you hit them at full speed! If you know where those are, when the water is down, it's much easier to go up the river, at full speed.
DO NOT TAKE YOUR SAFETY ON THIS RIVER LIGHTLY! YESTERDAY, AT STONEWALL BOAT RAMP, 15 MILES DOWNSTREAM FROM THE DAM, THEY HAD A HELICOPTER EVAC SITUATION! PLEASE USE CAUTION BELOW DAMS, WATER MAY RISE RAPIDLY WITHOUT WARNING!
Now that I've got the public service announcement out of the way, I want to tell you how the fishing went... It was lackluster. It seems like the sluggish fishing from the night before carried over right into the daytime. I had my buddy with me in the boat, and we fished from 10:00 a.m. until 6:00 p.m., and we only got three fish to the boat all day! They were trout, because that's what we were targeting, but that's a low number of fish to catch on a day where you put in that much effort. They just weren't biting very well!
The ones that did bite, ate my Rapala husky jerk. That's a Rapala HJ 8 and I'm not 100% sure that the color is as important as the lure. The action that lure imparts is fantastic! As you start it, it dives down a little, then when you give it a twitch twitch, it really takes a shot down, but instead of floating up really fast, it's suspends, right in the water column, which triggers trout to bite! Well, it triggers them on most days, I was able to trigger a few yesterday, but that's the way it goes! We tried several different methods, lots of different lures, but nothing was effective.
I'll still always go when they have several hours of one generator. It's the ideal condition for me to use the drag chain on my boat. That's something that I learned about recently, from one of my Pro report subscribers, shout out to Jeff! Here's how it works, and why you might consider it...
A drag chain is about a 3 foot section of really heavy chain that's attached to a rope, that's attached to the front of your boat, with two zip ties. From there, there's another length of rope attached to the interior of the boat, think one of the forward facing cleats. You make the chain and rope just long enough so that when you motor up, it can't reach the propeller at the back of your boat. For most boats, let's use mine as an example, I have 14 and 1/2 foot from the front of the boat to the propeller, so I'm able to drop 13 and a half foot of rope and chain. When I run the motor to go back upstream, the chain and rope lift up and then get pressed underneath the boat, but they can't reach the propeller, to mess anything up. That way you don't have to lift it up and down when you're riding back up the river. Once you get upstream, the chain falls back down to the riverbed, and then drags along the bottom, slowing you down, allowing you to fish more!
But it doesn't just slow you down. It really helps to keep you centered, so you don't have to stay on the trolling motor as much. When you have the drag chain deployed, it acts as a reverse rudder, and keeps you on position, in the center of the river. Without it the current pushes you left and right and you constantly spin around in a circle!
I realize now, after trying to type out an explanation of what a drag chain is, that I should just do a video! I'm going to do an in-depth video of not only how to install your drag chain, but how it works on the river. I don't necessarily want a whole bunch of boats out there competing with us for space on the Caney Fork river, so I'm going to make this video private, just for my Pro report subscribers. I'm going to put it on youtube, but I'm not going to make it a public video. I'll make sure to get that video out next week, so that you guys can enjoy the summertime, from your boat, on the Caney Fork River.

title: Trip Report #17
content_raw:
A lesson in patience...
I'm not a good walleye fisherman. But I know where walleye are! So that changes the game. Now all I have to do, is figure out how to fish for them, effectively. If you've been reading my reports, you know, I'm well on my way. The last time I went, I figured out, that if you get out of the kayak, and stand on the bank below Center Hill dam, you greatly increase your odds. Fast forward to this morning, at 1:30 in the morning, and that's exactly what I did...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/T80nFhyJF7Klo8raw
I paddled my kayak up to the dam from the boat ramp, and got out on the slippery, rocky bank, to try to ground myself, so that I stood a better chance to catch these fish. I've been trying to catch them from my kayak, but it's been a struggle, mostly because I don't know what I'm doing. Things are starting to turn around, though, and it's happening fast! After just a couple of casts with my Rapala husky jerk, I had an 18 and a half inch walleye on the hook, and in the net! For me, the biggest mystery, was how I was supposed to retrieve the lure. In reality, it's a jerk bait, so all you have to do, is cast it as far as you can, and then start your retrieve with a twitch twitch pause and then continue that same retrieve. Start the lure with the reel, and then give it a twitch twitch, and then stop everything and wait for a bite. Wait for a few seconds, and then start the reel, and then give it a twitch twitch. That's how you use a jerkbait, and it works really well!
Unfortunately, the bank is treacherous! Even getting out of your kayak you stand a risk of falling in the water. Those rocks go underwater every day, when they turn the generators on, and they are covered in a thick layer of grass and moss. If you're going to try this, keep in mind, that standing on this bank is a 5 out of 5 on the effort scale! Not to worry, you have easier options, on the other side of the river...
https://goo.gl/maps/QFPv96QJyzN6XWZ26
This is the parking lot on the other side of the river where you can access the bank using the steps that come down from the top of the dam. It's much more forgiving for people who can't stand on those rocks, or, don't have a kayak.
So why would I mention the other side of the river if I'm catching walleye so far away that you can't possibly cast over there? Good question! Here's why... After 3 hours of standing there, fishing my guts out, I had hooked four fish. One of them got away before I got it to the net, one of them was too small to keep, and two of them, were the same size, 18 in fish, that went on the stringer, and into the cooler! But that was it, in 3 hours! I expected a much better showing, especially, since I got there so early. At that point, at 4:30 in the morning, you can start to see a little bit of light developing in the sky. When that happens, the walleye tend to shut down with their bite.
Because my bite window was ending, and I was curious, I got back in my kayak, and turned on my headlamp, so that I could look down in the water, in front of where I was fishing, to see what types of fish were swimming around. To my amazement, I could only see a couple of walleye! Just a few days ago, there were scads! SCADS!!
So where did they all go? Did they go back downstream to the lake? While it was still dark enough out for me to see in the water with my headlamp, I wanted to look for them. I started paddling around aimlessly, in the corner, by the waterfall, expecting to see their eyes light up. That's the spot they've been favoring, for the past couple of weeks. When I couldn't see any, I had to take off in all directions. As it turned out, they were sitting next to the wall where the steps are! All loaded up, all together, pressed up against the wall, facing downstream. By the time I found them, my lights hit their eyes, and they scurried away, but that put a whole new light on how I believed they were behaving out there.
I thought they were just sitting in the corner by the waterfall, waiting to feed, just off the edge of the current. As it turns out, they're gathered in great numbers, sitting in stillwater, next to the relative safety of the wall. If you were to go out there at night with a lighted bobber and some minnows, you could allow those to sit and soak while you cast and retrieve lures. It's a great way to beat the summer heat, and still try to get your fishing in!

So why would I mention the other side of the river if I'm catching walleye so far away that you can't possibly cast over there? Good question! Here's why... After 3 hours of standing there, fishing my guts out, I had hooked four fish. One of them got away before I got it to the net, one of them was too small to keep, and two of them, were the same size, 18 in fish, that went on the stringer, and into the cooler! But that was it, in 3 hours! I expected a much better showing, especially, since I got there so early. At that point, at 4:30 in the morning, you can start to see a little bit of light developing in the sky. When that happens, the walleye tend to shut down with their bite.

Because my bite window was ending, and I was curious, I got back in my kayak, and turned on my headlamp, so that I could look down in the water, in front of where I was fishing, to see what types of fish were swimming around. To my amazement, I could only see a couple of walleye! Just a few days ago, there were scads! SCADS!!

So where did they all go? Did they go back downstream to the lake? While it was still dark enough out for me to see in the water with my headlamp, I wanted to look for them. I started paddling around aimlessly, in the corner, by the waterfall, expecting to see their eyes light up. That's the spot they've been favoring, for the past couple of weeks. When I couldn't see any, I had to take off in all directions. As it turned out, they were sitting next to the wall where the steps are! All loaded up, all together, pressed up against the wall, facing downstream. By the time I found them, my lights hit their eyes, and they scurried away, but that put a whole new light on how I believed they were behaving out there.

I thought they were just sitting in the corner by the waterfall, waiting to feed, just off the edge of the current. As it turns out, they're gathered in great numbers, sitting in stillwater, next to the relative safety of the wall. If you were to go out there at night with a lighted bobber and some minnows, you could allow those to sit and soak while you cast and retrieve lures. It's a great way to beat the summer heat, and still try to get your fishing in!

title: Trip Report #18
content_raw:
An exciting new development...
I've been looking forward to this week, all my life. I look forward to it every year. It's the first week of the summer, where every single day, is going to be brutally hot. We will get breaks from this heat during the summer, it won't be this hot everyday, but during the heat wave, I always look forward to getting in the trout rivers in middle Tennessee, so that I can beat the heat.
Today, I went to Buffalo valley boat ramp, but I didn't bring my boat or my kayak. I left my chest waders at home and I opted not to bring my hip boots. I got straight into the crystal clear, extremely cold, Caney Fork river, to do some fly fishing...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/kE6Pj0NVwvMx8XuyQ
I didn't get down there until 10:00 a.m., and the generators were scheduled to turn on at 1:00 p.m., so I didn't have much time to fish. I drove all that way, a little more than an hour for me, each way, just to stand there for a few hours. I ended up catching three little trout, which was exciting for me, because I'm not much of a fly fisherman, yet. I started off throwing the little fly that I found last week, but today, they weren't having it! Because I don't know the name of flies, I don't know what it was that I used to catch fish, but I got a great video of it. I can tell you this much, it wasn't something you float under a strike indicator. It was a small hook with some different colored shiny ribbon that you strip through the water. I was able to get a couple of fish on that, as well as one fish on an Adam's parachute dry fly. Before you go to the Caney fork, always check the generating schedule, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels/Center-Hill
As I was standing there, enjoying catching fish that I knew I would catch, because every year during these conditions, they like to cooperate, it hit me, I need to be telling you guys this stuff!
THE NEWEST ADDITION TO MY PRO REPORTS WILL BE A WEEKLY FISHING FORECAST, PROVIDED ON MONDAYS!
Most weeks of the year, I already know where I'm going to be fishing that week, based on the weather, the time of year, and the type of fish that like to eat during those conditions. Lots of people make reports about where they've caught fish, I'm going to start giving forecasts about where you should be able to catch fish, during the upcoming week. Here's what I've got figured out for this type of weather, during this time of year...
Crappie fishing on Percy Priest and Center Hill Lake...
On both lakes, the water temperature is right around the mid 80s. These fish are still loving the warm water, and they haven't moved super deep just yet! Fish will be scattered throughout the water column from the surface, if they have a shady area, all the way down to 25 feet.
Bluegill on Percy Priest...
You can always find bluegill near every bank, all the way around the lake. Those small, three to four inch fish, that are super aggressive, you can catch really easily. The schools of bigger bluegill are hanging out deep! I kept finding what I thought were schools of crappie, that turned out to be bluegill. They are sitting about 20 feet deep, in 25 to 30 foot of water.
Hybrid and striped bass on Percy Priest Lake...
People are still catching both from the bank and from boats every morning at 7 points...
Seven Points Boat Ramp https://share.google/sk48z1WzqD7jQKkzC
If you're fishing from the bank, you're going to want to park in the boat ramp parking lot, and then walk down the road, to the point. I'll drop you a pin here, there are usually about a half dozen people out there every morning...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/Qu1fog7weaEBNQJq8
I'd get there around 4:15 a.m. and make the walk over there. By the time you got there, it would start to get light out, and those fish should fire up. People are using top water lures, but they're not having as much success as they were earlier in the season. The majority of people in the bank are using one quarter of an ounce or a 3/8 of an ounce jig head with a soft plastic. Something 5 inch long like a fluke or a paddle tail. They are making long casts, allowing their lure to sink for 10 to 12, maybe even 15 seconds, and then starting a slow retrieve, with a couple of twitches. If you have a boat, you can try the same methods, but you could also put live bait down, under the boat. If you can't use a cast net to catch live bait, you could catch some bluegills with a hook and line and try that, or you could buy some bluegills for bait from Big Charlie's bait shop...
Big Charlie's Bait Shop https://share.google/kdcDBFkFAJx6aoJKF
Trout on the Elk River below Tims Ford Dam...
If I could, I'd be going down to the Elk River this week! Unfortunately, they got a lot of rain, and they are running water, which makes the river too fast to fish! They had the water turned off for the weekend, so people could do recreation like fishing and kayaking, but as of today, they turned the water back on, and it's unsafe to do anything out there! This time of year, we usually don't get very much rainfall all at once, so the water is usually down, 7 days a week, below Tims Ford Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/i4yCMxqQxufyPtYT7
Directly below the dam, there's plenty of parking! It's like a playground, if you're a trout fisherman. You can walk all over, up to the dam, or way downstream. Here's your forecast, you can definitely go this weekend! Just based on previous experience, they're going to turn the water off for Saturday and Sunday. Since this is going to be a holiday weekend, they may turn it off for Friday and Monday as well. You can always know before you go. The magic number on the Elk River, is 245 cubic feet per second. That's the number you want to see them releasing. That's what it was last weekend, and I'm confident they will do that again this weekend. Always know before you go! You can check the water release schedule for Tim's for dam, on the Elk river, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels/Tims-Ford
When they are releasing 245 cubic feet per second, you can not only fish the bank below the dam, but you can get in the water as well! It's not too swift, and it's very cold! I like to put my kayak in, and paddle upstream. There's a little bit of room up there to move around, and there are lots of trout! That would be a great place to go to cool off this weekend.
Two different suggestions for going walleye fishing...
I already went to the Caney Fork today, and I'm going a lot more this week. I always do when it gets this hot. I like to go at night. There have been lots of walleye hanging out below the dam, and I want to get a stringer full! If you've been reading my reports, you know that I am not the best walleye fisherman. I've been trying really hard, and only catching a couple. I'm going to try to change my luck in the future, by using some minnows. You could do the same, below the dam, or, if you have a boat, you can go up on the main lake.
Center Hill lake, has been on fire for walleye lately! I haven't been able to catch any, but I haven't targeted any. I've got a few things figured out, for when I get started. First of all, most people troll for walleye on that lake. Instead of just driving around, and wondering if you can catch them, it's best to hug the bank, and try to keep your boat in about 15 feet of water. They are going to go really deep, once to lake heats up, but as of right now, people are catching them trolling deep diving crankbaits and lures like Berkeley flicker shads, that get down at least 10 to 12 feet. Also, if you know how to use a nightcrawler harness, that seems to be a very effective method for loading the boat with walleye, this time of year.
Another night fishing idea, and something that I've been itching to do, is to head out to Center Hill Lake, and fish overnight for walleye. When I get the chance, I'm going to anchor in 15 foot of water, and put out one of those green lights, to attract bait fish. Then, I'm going to drop minnows under the boat, and sit and wait. According to a good friend of mine, and an avid fisherman, that's all it will take to load the boat on a hot summer night on Center Hill Lake!

title: Trip Report #19
content_raw:
What's going on at Center Hill Dam...
I got to Center Hill damn just before 3:00 a.m...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/xQ67Ct746rNs67ltv
I launched my kayak and I started over in the corner by the waterfall, fishing for walleye. I could see, with the light strapped to my head, that there were scads of them! As many as you will ever see you loaded up at the dam. Plenty of really big walleye. I was using my ultralight rod and reel with 4 pound monofilament, so that I could go as stealthy as possible. I've been having trouble getting these fish to bite, mostly because I don't know what I'm doing.
In reality, I did know what I was doing, I was just doing it from the wrong spot. It's not necessarily tough to catch walleye, when they are biting, you just have to give them the correct presentation. Walleye, notoriously, like lures that are being trolled. That presents The lure at a steady pace. Conversely, they also like lures, like a floating Rapala minnow, if you're working it correctly. That involves a slow retrieve, with a twitch twitch of the lure, and then a pause. According to everything I've read, and studied up on, that pause should be as long as 10 seconds in cold water! My problem was, I was trying to use a Rapala jerk bait minnow, from my kayak. That would have been fine, if my kayak was anchored, but I have not been. That imparts action to the lure that is apparently not what they want! Here's how I decided to try to overcome that.
In the middle of the night, in very dark conditions, I hopped out of my kayak, onto the bank, next to the waterfall. Probably not the smartest move, definitely high up there on the effort scale of one to five, but it was the necessary move. As I stood there, next to that waterfall, casting as far as I could, using a slow retrieve with the twitch twitch paws, it was only my second cast when I hooked up with a walleye! I had casted the lure as far as I could, started a slow retrieve, gave it a twitch twitch, and then a pause, and then I actually felt the fish smack the lure on the pause! I had wondered if I would feel the bite, and I did! I think it helps to have light line, and a sensitive rod and reel.
I'm going to share a link for the exact jerk bait that I've been using. It's a suspending jerkbait, which means, after you get it started, it will hang in the middle of the water column, as opposed to floating directly to the surface. It works really well for walleye, and exceptionally well for trout on this river!
https://amzn.to/4gLFd13
Just about the time I got something figured out, it started to get light out. My plan in the future, fish up there all night long, so I can try to get a limit of walleye. In the meantime, with the sun coming up, it was time to shift my attention to trying to catch trout. Unfortunately, they did not want to be caught!
I tried a few of my typical tricks, I left that jerk bait on for a while, and eventually, tied on a white rooster tail. But they said there was no way... One of my favorite options, is a trout magnet, which is a 1/64th of an ounce jig head, and a 1 inch gulp minnow. That little presentation, albeit hard to cast, is deadly!
It doesn't matter that you can't cast it very far, you can watch the fish eat the lure! Just keep your rod tip up, after you make the cast, and start a painfully slow retrieve, watching your lure, near the surface. Every once in awhile, give it a quick twitch. Right after that twitch, when it starts to settle down, you will see a fish come up and smack it! Now, is the tough part. Getting them to bite, is the easy part. Setting that hook, is tough. You have to be ready! You can't have any hesitation. Mastering this style of fishing took me years, but it's been the most productive style of trout fishing, for me, up to this point, outside of using a nightcrawler on the bottom.
That's not something I was willing to do, because I didn't bring any worms, and I was actually hoping to use my fly rod. I had recently been on a trip with some clients, and found someone else's flies, still attached to their strike indicator. On that day, I attached their flies to my fly rod, and immediately started catching trout! Fast forward to this trip, and the results would be exactly the same!
Not long after that strike indicator started to dangle my fly about 18 inches under the surface, I saw a big trout come up to take it! Unfortunately, I'm not as keen on that hookset as I am with my spinning rod, so I missed that fish. After that, I made a concerted effort to be ready when the fish would bite. And it paid off! These fish were going crazy, for that particular fly. In the video, about this day of fishing, that will come out on Monday morning, I asked for help, identifying the fly that I found. Fortunately for us, I went looking for them yesterday, and I found them!
It's called a pheasant tale, and it looks to be a number 16. If you don't know what that means, basically, flies are numbered by the size of the hook that they are tied to. A number 20 is extremely small and a number one is very large. Most of the trout flies, that work well on the Caney Fork River, are in the 14 or 16 or 18 size range. I picked up a whole bunch of pheasant tail, in those sizes. I grabbed some with gold beads on the head, as well as silver. Because you never know which color is going to work better for you.
What type of fly works best on the Caney Fork River will change, depending on the time of year, and what types of flies are hatching at that time. I know I have some avid fly fisherman reading, so I will always keep my ear to the ground, to try to find out what types of flies are doing really well, at the time.
