title: Trip Report #20
content_raw:
Crappie fishing on Percy Priest...
I had a short amount of time to take my boat out to try to find crappie on Percy Priest. I didn't want to have to look around too far, I was hoping to find some near a boat ramp. It was super bright and sunny, so I went to sit underneath the bridge, near Jefferson Springs boat ramp...
Jefferson Springs Boat Ramp. https://share.google/KHHRHZywqSmrgbryn
There are eight concrete pillars that support the bridge, that are in the water. Each one of those had crappie all over them! Literally, all over them! From the surface, all the way down to 20 feet. I sat there on an anchor, for a couple of hours, and targeted those pillars. Making long casts, and running my crappie jigs beside them, at different depths. Sometimes, I would run them near the surface. Other times, I would allow them to sink, the name of the game was just trying to get the lure in their face.
I could see these fish on the forward facing sonar, and I could see my crappie jigs. What I couldn't see, was the fish having any interest in what I was doing. At first, I tried what I always start with, running my lures about 5 feet above their head. Because there were fish at just about every depth from the surface to 20 feet down, I had to pick out individual fish, and try to target them. I would allow my lure to sink, until it was just about 5 feet above their head, and then start twitching it. That method will make active fish come directly up for the lure! Unfortunately, there wasn't a fish on any of those pillars who was looking for that type of action.
My setup is just right to try to finesse these fish. A 7 and 1/2 foot ultralight rod and reel with 4 pound monofilament and a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head. Instead of my usual Bobby Garland, I was using some soft plastics that my friend Chris made... They look very similar, and they have the same shape and profile, and he makes them in the color that I like, pearl white. You can get some at tastytreatz.com if you would like to shop local.
It's the combination of the long rod, with the light line, and the light lure, that allows me to twitch above their head, for several seconds at a time, which typically, with active fish, will entice a bite. I could see with my forward facing sonar that they didn't have any interest. At that point, I moved to my next crappie retrieve, which is to bring that lure down to about one foot above their head, and give it some twitches, to see if I can get their attention. Once again, they did not go for that action. For the record, it's not like I threw that lure out, and expected the first fish to come up and eat. I gave each method more than it's fair share of time! Trying on several different piles of fish, on several different pillars. None of them wanted the lure above their head at any level.
The next thing I do is start going directly into the piles. I can see the fish, so I just let my lure fall down to their level. Most of the time, I start with a nice slow retrieve, directly through the fish. If that doesn't work, I will incorporate a couple of twitches, while the lure is right there beside them. Once again, this tried and true method, wasn't getting me any bites!
At that point, it had been more than an hour. I feel like most people would give up, but I didn't want to leave the comfort of the shade that was provided by the bridge I was sitting under. The relative comfort of the area, coupled with the fact that I could see crappie on the forward facing sonar, meant that I just had to double down, to figure out how to catch them.
Going slow wasn't working! I had that much figured out. When that's the case, I will add a number four split shot, about 1 foot above my jig head. That serves to do two things, get that lure down to their level faster, and make the lure move through their area faster. I had gone as slow as I could, and I wasn't getting any bites. For me, the next step, is to go fast.
I go through my entire routine. I just do it a little faster. I start with that lure, about 5 foot above their heads, jiggling it, to try to get attention. But this time, it's moving real fast. Then, if I don't have any luck, which I didn't, I start going down closer to them. When I still wasn't having any luck, I started going directly through those fish. With a quick moving lure, and sometimes, adding some twitches. Nothing was working! Until I figured it out...
They wanted the pendulum! It had been a while since I caught crappie using the pendulum. Basically, you throw that jig out there, and allow it to sink through them, and continue falling straight down past them. These fish were looking to feed down! Once I figured that out, almost completely on accident, it was Katie bar the door! Something about the speed at which my lure was sinking, after I added that split shot. That's what triggered them. Here's how I figured it out...
I was bringing my jig, behind a sinker, through the fish that were at the surface. They were gathered around the pillar, and there were lots of them, but none of them wanted to bite. Below them, about 10 to 12 feet straight down, there were other fish, that were extended a little bit out from the pillar. I could tell that, if I allowed my lure to sink directly down, it could potentially reach those fish. As it started to drop, to the pile of fish that were down at the base of the pillar, all of the fish at the surface started to chase my lure! They did the exact same thing that crappie usually do, in reverse! Instead of going directly up for a lure that's above their head, they followed this thing down, fast! The faster it dropped, the faster they swam for it.
Unfortunately, when you're allowing a lure to sink like this, you won't be able to feel a bite. Because I have forward facing sonar, I was able to estimate when they bit the lure, extremely successfully! Here's what that looked like...
As the lure would sink, these fish would follow it down, and then eventually, if they were going to eat it, they would close the gap. When I could no longer see my jig head, because the fish and the jig head had become one on the screen, I gave a quick hook set. That worked out really well! On the day, I ended up landing 27 crappie in the boat. And I did it, in relatively short order, after it took me more than an hour to figure out how to get them to bite.
This is a tough way to catch these fish, because if you can't see them, you're going to miss a lot of bites. I've had days like this before! When I was sitting on a cliff, on Percy Priest lake, on the bank, casting out, and just doing the pendulum, back to the cliff. If you can figure out exactly how deep the fish are, you can cast the lure that far out, and it will swing into position, on a vertical cliff. That's really effective, on days when they won't bite any other way.

title: Trip Report #21
content_raw:
Winds from the north, don't go forth?
You may have heard this traditional weather rhyme, used by fishing anglers, to predict fishing success. It's cute, but it's not really based on any facts. It's an opinion, about what type of fishing will happen, after a cold front comes through, and a north wind takes over. That was exactly what we had yesterday, to start the summer!
In the middle of Tennessee we are blessed to have four very distinct seasons. Each one arriving right on time, and typically lasting the full 90 days. One thing I look forward to, every summer for the last 3 years, are summertime cold fronts. On the first full day of summer this year, we got our first cold front of the season! Monday, a cold front came through with a bunch of rain and thunderstorms. On Tuesday, the forecast was for temperatures that would barely reach 80°, low humidity, blue skies, and a 10 mph wind.
When we get conditions like this in the summertime, I make it a point to go on kayak trips for Smallmouth bass. Something about the day after a cold front, when conditions are typically unfavorable for fishing, makes the smallmouth bass go crazy! There's only one problem, when you get a bunch of rain with a thunderstorm, it has a tendency to fill the rivers up, making them unsafe to kayak. That was definitely the case with this particular storm system.
Several of the kayak locations that I had in mind were unviable! My first option was going to be the Buffalo River. The only way to know if the water was going to be safe to kayak, would be to wait until Tuesday morning and check the flow of the river. The Buffalo River is more than an hour and a half away from my house, so I can't physically check the river, but I can do so with help from the United States geological survey. The USGS has sensors on almost every river, creek, and stream in the country, and if you know the name of the waterway, and a nearby town, you can simply Google search those two pieces of information and find the nearest river sensor.
The sensors provide real-time information about the flow of the river. We measure rivers, and their flow, in cubic feet per second. One cubic foot per second, is about the size of one basketball. So if a river is reading 100 cubic feet per second, when you are standing on the bank, in any given one second, about 100 basketballs worth of water will move past your spot, downstream. Unfortunately, cubic feet per second doesn't translate between waterways. If a waterway is really large, 100 cubic feet per second would be a very small number. Waterways like creeks, can barely hold 100 cubic feet per second, before they pop out of their banks. It's all relative to the size of the waterway. The only thing that stays consistent, is the way we measure the water.
Because of that fact, looking at the information on the USGS website won't help you very much, until you become familiar with that particular waterway. I already know what types of numbers are acceptable for kayaking on the buffalo river, because I have extensive experience going out there. I know that, any number below 1,000 cubic feet per second, is a good amount of flow for that river, and the trip will be safe, and potentially productive. Unfortunately, yesterday, the Buffalo River at one point in time, reached over 7,000 cubic feet per second! That meant, not only would the river be unsafe to kayak, it would be out of its banks, and into flood stage. I was able to find that information on the USGS website, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03604400/all-graphs/#period=P7D
When I went to copy and paste the link for you guys just now, it said that the Buffalo River was over 10,000 cubic feet per second! For some reference, the American side of Niagara Falls has a peak flow of 10,000 cubic feet per second... That means, right now, the force of nature, and tourist attraction, has about the same flow as our little Buffalo River on the west side of middle Tennessee. So the Buffalo River was not an option!
My next option was to try and do a little musky fishing. This would be one of my last trips of the season, if I could get it in, because I typically won't go musky fishing during the months of August and September. Muskie are very large fish, and the fight that they give wears them out. If you catch them during the summer, when the water is really warm, it will hold less oxygen, and it will make it hard for them to recover, after you fight them. For that reason alone, I only fish the other 10 months of the year, which is plenty! Since we're coming up on July now, and we can see hot weather in the forecast, I like to get these trips in. So I checked the USGS website for the Collins River in McMinnville, and even though the flooding wasn't as extensive as it is on the Buffalo river, the water levels were still way too high to take out a kayak! Once again, I know from extensive experience, that anything less than 1,000 cubic feet per second is the only acceptable number on the Collins river. Once again, when I checked, there were a couple of thousand cubic feet per second rolling through, which is way too much. You can find the USGS website for the Collins river, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03421000/all-graphs/#period=P7D
When I went to copy the link just now for the Collins river, it had dropped significantly! The Buffalo River was still rising, which you could see on the chart, but the Collins River had made a precipitous drop. As of the time of this report, it was around 1400 cubic feet per second, and within a couple of days, would be ready for kayakers!
Because I have dozens of trips on lots of different rivers, I'm able to continuously check to see if any of the rivers in our area are viable for kayaking. It's just a matter of time, before you find a spot, where it didn't rain as much as the others. That's exactly what happened yesterday! Just for some reference, not because I went out there, I'm going to tell you about the Smith Fork Creek... It's in the heart of middle tennessee, and it empties into the Caney Fork river. I already mentioned that the Collins was way too much to kayak and that the Buffalo was literally flooding, but then when you check the Smith fork, it looks like it didn't receive much rain at all, if any! Here is a link to the USGS website for Smith Fork Creek...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03424730/all-graphs/#period=P7D
As of the time when I released this report, it's sitting at 20 cubic feet per second! For some reference, this River needs at least 150 cubic feet per second, just for your kayak to float downstream. This is drought level! Extreme drought level! All the rain that fell over tennessee, and this creek, which is 99 miles long, appears to have not received any! Traditional thinking, for those people who have private access to this body of water, is that they can do a float after a nice rainfall. It just depends! I think most people assume, that when it rains in Middle Tennessee, it rains everywhere. The rivers tell a drastically different story!
There was one River in the Goldilocks zone! The Piney River had received just the right amount of rainfall, to make the level rise enough to float, but not too much to make it muddy and brown, or flood. The window of opportunity on that river is very small. Anything over 300 cubic feet per second, it's too much! Fortunately, the majority of the year, it stays well below that number. Yesterday, the flow is fantastic, at 120 cubic feet per second! You can find information about the flow of the Piney River on the USGS website, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03602500/all-graphs/#period=P7D
So I found a river that I could kayak, because I wanted to go after smallmouth bass. I like rivers, specifically, after a cold front, because the fish tend to go crazy. I'm not sure if they do the same thing out on the lake, for the last few years, every summer time cold front, has found me out on the river, enjoying a spectacular bite! Yesterday would be no exception! As soon as we got in the water, the fish were chasing bait! I used my cast net, to catch a mess of bait fish, and put them in my bait bucket alongside my kayak. But I didn't have to! I had a couple of lures tied on, a Whopper plopper, and a chatterbait, and I was able to catch fish on both of those!
The Piney River is very clear, and it's typically tough to get these fish to bite any type of lure. On days like yesterday, the water gets a little stained from the rainfall, and they're also all fired up for some reason. That makes them much easier to catch on lures, which makes it much more fun! I still have lots of fun catching them with bait, but that's the way you get them, on a daily basis. I've perfected my setup for using live bait to get these fish to bite, I'll tell you about it...
I've been using 12 pound monofilament on a medium action bass rod. I've got a bobber about 2 ft up from a eagle claw, gold Aberdeen hook. Depending on the size of my bait, I will use a hook as large as the number one, or as small as a number six. Any of the sizes in between work great! About 4 inches up from my hook, I like to put a size 4 split shot. That's it! That will make these fish go crazy on this river, and most Middle Tennessee creeks and streams.
Yesterday, it did just that! I was catching fish left and right, until I wasn't. The only problem with this setup, and the reason I shouldn't have used the word perfected, it's too light! You would think, 12 pound test, would be more than enough. Unfortunately, sometimes, it's not. Yesterday, there were two different times, when my 12 pound monofilament, wasn't up to the task. Each time, a trophy sized smallmouth came out from underneath a rock, and then, before I could do much to stop them, they went directly underneath that rock with the bait in their mouth, and then rubbed my line against the rock, breaking me off. The two biggest fish of the day, got away with a hook in their mouth, and that's terrible!
The only logical step is to go with heavier line. I think I will double up, and go to 25 pound monofilament. Why not go even heavier? Just to make sure that they can't get broken off? Diminishing returns. At some point, the line is going to be so thick, that they can see it, and you're going to get diminishing returns on your bites. Right now, that 12 pound monofilament is almost invisible to them. That means, they don't see it, and they just key in on the bait, and you get a lot more bites. Start using thicker, or more visible line, and you might experience, diminishing returns.

I think most people assume, that when it rains in Middle Tennessee, it rains everywhere. The rivers tell a drastically different story!

There was one River in the Goldilocks zone! The Piney River had received just the right amount of rainfall, to make the level rise enough to float, but not too much to make it muddy and brown, or flood. The window of opportunity on that river is very small. Anything over 300 cubic feet per second, it's too much! Fortunately, the majority of the year, it stays well below that number. Yesterday, the flow is fantastic, at 120 cubic feet per second! You can find information about the flow of the Piney River on the USGS website, here...

https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03602500/all-graphs/#period=P7D

So I found a river that I could kayak, because I wanted to go after smallmouth bass. I like rivers, specifically, after a cold front, because the fish tend to go crazy. I'm not sure if they do the same thing out on the lake, for the last few years, every summer time cold front, has found me out on the river, enjoying a spectacular bite! Yesterday would be no exception! As soon as we got in the water, the fish were chasing bait! I used my cast net, to catch a mess of bait fish, and put them in my bait bucket alongside my kayak. But I didn't have to! I had a couple of lures tied on, a Whopper plopper, and a chatterbait, and I was able to catch fish on both of those!

The Piney River is very clear, and it's typically tough to get these fish to bite any type of lure. On days like yesterday, the water gets a little stained from the rainfall, and they're also all fired up for some reason. That makes them much easier to catch on lures, which makes it much more fun! I still have lots of fun catching them with bait, but that's the way you get them, on a daily basis. I've perfected my setup for using live bait to get these fish to bite, I'll tell you about it...

I've been using 12 pound monofilament on a medium action bass rod. I've got a bobber about 2 ft up from a eagle claw, gold Aberdeen hook. Depending on the size of my bait, I will use a hook as large as the number one, or as small as a number six. Any of the sizes in between work great! About 4 inches up from my hook, I like to put a size 4 split shot. That's it! That will make these fish go crazy on this river, and most Middle Tennessee creeks and streams.

Yesterday, it did just that! I was catching fish left and right, until I wasn't. The only problem with this setup, and the reason I shouldn't have used the word perfected, it's too light! You would think, 12 pound test, would be more than enough. Unfortunately, sometimes, it's not. Yesterday, there were two different times, when my 12 pound monofilament, wasn't up to the task. Each time, a trophy sized smallmouth came out from underneath a rock, and then, before I could do much to stop them, they went directly underneath that rock with the bait in their mouth, and then rubbed my line against the rock, breaking me off. The two biggest fish of the day, got away with a hook in their mouth, and that's terrible!

The only logical step is to go with heavier line. I think I will double up, and go to 25 pound monofilament. Why not go even heavier? Just to make sure that they can't get broken off? Diminishing returns. At some point, the line is going to be so thick, that they can see it, and you're going to get diminishing returns on your bites. Right now, that 12 pound monofilament is almost invisible to them. That means, they don't see it, and they just key in on the bait, and you get a lot more bites. Start using thicker, or more visible line, and you might experience, diminishing returns.

title: Trip Report #22
content_raw:
From snafu to success!
I tried to go to Cookeville boat dock with my buddy, at 6:50 in the morning...
Cookeville Boat Dock https://share.google/uYjdfcuv07nbJQP2M
It's a boat ramp, so I didn't consider that it would be closed at 6:50 in the morning. Recently, I encouraged you guys to launch your kayaks and boats from this boat ramp, so that you could visit Fanchers Falls, which is only two and a half miles away. The first day I went, I showed up at 12:00 noon. The next time I went, I tried to get started early, and the gate was locked up tight! For some reason, you can't access Cookville Boat Dock, until 9:00 in the morning. That was going to be more than 2 hours for us, so we had to find the closest boat ramp, and that is an adventure!
The closest boat ramp isn't a boat ramp, in the strictest terms. It's a gravel parking lot, and you can launch a boat or a kayak, but I wouldn't recommend it! It's called Austin Bottoms...
https://goo.gl/maps/ogE294zTprP8LxcHA
You can technically go to this location, and back a boat into the water. It's a primitive boat ramp, so it's gravel. If you don't have four wheel drive, or front wheel drive, like my little suv, you may not be able to get your boat out of the water. You need to have good grip, and a light boat. There is no parking lot, the area is gravel, and because of that, and the steep nature of the area, there are giant ruts, not only in the parking lot but also in the gravel road on the way down to the bank. My buddy got his vehicle stuck in one of those ruts, and we had to get a Jeep to pull us out! Bottom line, this is the most difficult place that you can launch a boat or kayak, a 5 out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5! You need a sure-footed vehicle, or this isn't the place for you!
Once we got into Center Hill lake, everything was great! On that day, I was with a friend of mine who only likes to bass fish. He was happy to allow me to do some crappie fishing, whenever we came across a pile of fish, but mostly, we beat the banks around that area, trying to catch bass. And we were 100% unsuccessful!
That happens from time to time. I'll go fishing with someone who wants to target a particular fish. When I go fishing, I like to target the type of fish that are biting. Unfortunately, even though we fished for 10 hours, we never caught a single bass, while we were bass fishing. I caught a few while I was crappie fishing, but nothing of consequence. In reality, the crappie fishing was the story of the day!
Right out of the boat ramp, I found crappie that were sitting on a tree, that was in 25 foot of water. They were suspended at the top of the tree, at 15 feet. I'm going to drop you some pins, where I found crappie on underwater structure. All of these locations, are subject to change at any moment. These were trees that were underwater, that were holding fish, but they like to move around, and there's no guarantee they will be on any particular tree, at any particular time. Anytime I drop a pin in Google maps where I found crappy, it's always a good idea to look there first...
https://goo.gl/maps/rwVTSPmagihai7cDA
https://goo.gl/maps/9sm1sHp7uKw9MFyQ6
https://goo.gl/maps/5WqiaunaUY4R4QUF8
https://goo.gl/maps/vaQwWsrsJLqyTQeq5
https://goo.gl/maps/d5oFErVj6zQiFVVr9
https://goo.gl/maps/VMNsW3EruToCRwms7
https://goo.gl/maps/awNon14nPTDdqXEQ7
This next pin I'm going to drop is actually a TWRA fish attractor. Unlike other underwater sticks, these type of attractors tend to have fish almost every time you show up! This attractor is right around 20 foot of depth right now, which is the perfect number on Center Hill lake, at the moment. Most of the water out there is between 80 and 84°, and these fish are feeling really comfortable down at about 15 to 20 feet...
https://goo.gl/maps/4mcEEFCu3JUSnjm57
This location is clearly marked with a buoy that says "fish"! By far, this was one of the best locations that I found on that side of the lake. The TWRA has placed dozens of attractors by this bouy, and there were thousands of fish! For what it's worth, each one of these locations where I found crappie, not only did I catch fish, all of them were keepers! Like I said, I had a friend with me who wasn't necessarily keen on crappie fishing, so I only caught a few fish at each location, and then we continued trying to catch bass. Each time I caught fish, they were keepers!
I was told by someone, earlier this season, that once I got out to Center Hill lake, and started fishing for crappie, I would like it better than Percy priest, and that person was right! Every time I find fish, they are big ones! That's not the way it is on other lakes, but so far, that has been my experience out on Center Hill lake.

title: Trip Report #23
content_raw:
Bluegill on bed!
If I didn't see it with my own eyes, I wouldn't believe it... I saw bluegill, actively guarding beds! Typical understanding of bluegill behavior is that they spawn when water temperatures reach around 70°. Right now, they are way beyond the optimum window for spawning in shallow water. But, there they were! I was walking the Murfreesboro Greenway, and I was trying to catch bass with topwater lures. I was walking upstream, from the Manson Pike trailhead...
Manson Pike Trailhead https://share.google/neTaLxW1RHMJiRmTb
It's a long walk, but they will be there for at least a few more days! They always stay on their bed until their eggs hatch, and swim away. They were actively fanning the beds, to try to keep sediment from settling. I'm going to drop a pin, where they were...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/SoN698qcmYkVXT1d7
There's a dam on the river, and they were just above that. I had never tried to fish above the dam, but we are still in the throes of a drought, so the water above the dam is very low. In the area that is usually a lake, you can walk around on the old lake bed. Because the ground is typically underwater, it's very muddy! Also, because you have to walk more than half a mile up the greenway to get there, those two factors combine to make this trip a three out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. It's not super physically demanding, you just have to go a long way, and you're going to get dirty.
Once you get up there, above the dam, it's obvious where to go. There is a bench, that allows you to sit and overlook the lake, but there's no water right in front of you! You can easily hop over the small retaining wall, on to the dry lake bed, and down to the water's edge.
There were at least a dozen really big bluegill on bed! When I got there, I didn't have anything for them. All I had were giant topwater lures, as I was trying to catch bass. When I found those fish, I immediately walked back the half mile to my car, and then drove home, to pick up my fly rod. I was hoping, I could present some tiny flies to these fish, and get them to bite. I was wrong! I tried several different flies, and I could get them to show interest, and even nip at them, but I couldn't get them to commit, until I could!
There was one fly, that looks like a little worm, that lays on the bottom, that I was able to trick a fish into eating. I made the perfect cast, the fly landed in his bed, he saw it hit the ground, and he swam over to it and picked it up. These fish are good sized! As big as your hand! And crazy beautiful... They're also right next to the bank. Within a foot of the bank, in 4 inches of water. That makes them really tough to catch!
When you arrive, they will all turn to face you. As you move around the bank, they will follow your every move. Every single one of them, staring at you the entire time. It's really tough to get fish like that to eat, but they will do it. Typically, they sit on those beds for 2 to 3 weeks, so they have to eat! If I were going back, I would take some red wigglers and a tiny hook. Maybe even a tiny little bobber.
Fast forward to today, and I had clients booked for a kayak trip on the first 6 miles of the Caney Fork river, starting at Buffalo valley boat ramp...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/6TiplR4j5O0RDSK8R
Today, they weren't scheduled to turn on any generators until 2:00 p.m. That meant, we were free to float the river as long as we would like, with one caveat, there were heavy thunderstorms expected around lunch time. In an effort to get our trip in, we started at 6:00 a.m., and finished at noon. Finishing at noon meant that we wouldn't have to deal with any generating water at all. I like to avoid the generating water when I am with clients, it's just too dangerous, when people aren't familiar with the waterway. To avoid kayaking while the generators are on, you can find the generating schedule, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels/Center-Hill
Today, the fishing was stellar. You can't always say that, because trout can be finicky. Today, they started off gangbusters! Including myself, there were three of us on the trip, and we all immediately started catching trout, using ultralight rods and reels, and a 1/8 of an ounce roostertail. One of us using yellow, two of us using white. Although today, the color wasn't really important. These fish were making it easy on us, when we got started. As the day went on, it got tougher and tougher!
By the end of the trip, heavy rain was approaching, and we got everything loaded into our shuttle vehicle, just as a downpour fell on the area. Our timing was immaculate, and the fishing was a total success! We opted for the first 6 miles of the river, a trip that you can get done in about 6 hours, if you're trying. The takeout point for that trip, is Happy Hollow boat ramp...
Happy Hollow Boat Ramp https://share.google/nyrhKq9pgrKiveHzs
If you have a high profile vehicle like an SUV or a truck, you can drive out on the boat ramp at the beginning of the trip, to put your kayaks at the river's edge, and you can do the same at the boat ramp at the end of the trip! If you drive slowly, the rocks are relatively well packed, and you can idle your way right next to the water's edge. That makes loading and unloading on this trip, easier than just about any other trip in middle Tennessee! Because loading and unloading your kayaks into the water is so easy, and that's usually the hardest part of any kayak trip, this kayak trip is a one out of five on the effort scale of one to five. It doesn't get any easier than this trip!

title: Trip Report #24
content_raw:
Center Hill lake, loaded with fish!
Today, I took my boat to a waterfall! I launched from Cookeville boat dock just before 12:00 p.m...
Cookeville Boat Dock https://share.google/mqHcdtCEbPDu6LqcJ
This particular boat dock has lots of amenities! There's a restaurant. Lots of slips that have people's personal boats. A place to get gas on the water, as well as rental boats like pontoons and jet skis. They also rent kayaks, which is a fantastic idea! This boat ramp is super close to one of the most photogenic waterfalls in all of middle Tennessee, Fanchers Falls. If you're going to Cookeville boat dock, you're going to have to pay. It cost $10 to use the boat ramp. There were lots of people there who brought kayaks, but they came in one vehicle, so they only had to pay a $10 fee. It's not $10 per person to launch, it's $10 per vehicle. If you bring lots of kayaks, you can save money!
I paid the $10 so that I could launch my boat, and I was super glad that I did! I had never been to Fanchers, and I heard the fishing was great. What I heard was right! Here's how you get there...
Go directly out of the boat ramp and go to the left, around the entire marina. You will have to go slow, that area is in no wake zone. It takes a few minutes to get through the no wake zone! Once you get through, it's a short drive before you reach the mouth of the creek, then you have to wind your way all the way back to the falls. It's about two and a half miles from the boat ramp, to the base of the falls. It's a very short boat ride, or a lovely kayak paddle...
If you're in a kayak, you can paddle really close to the falls, before you have to get out, and walk to the base. If you're in a boat, you're going to have to stop considerably farther away, and get in the water, and wade. The water is relatively clear, and you can see, that the bottom is mostly flat. It's a little slippery, and because of that, this trip is probably a four out of five on the effort scale of one to five. Believe it or not, it's not as hard as it can be! Once you get to the base of the falls, there are some slip and fall hazards, but it's really not as treacherous as the base of other waterfalls! It's nice!
The waterfall is epic. Pretty much, below the waterfall, is a perfect swimming pool! Take a float, and lay there all day! I had a picnic lunch, and it was lovely. Then, I got turned around, and started fishing my way back out.
The water was unbelievably warm! 87° at the surface! I had no idea Center Hill Lake could get that warm at any point in time. I just assumed, that the water would be clear. But this far away from the dam, the water looks more like it does on other lakes in Middle Tennessee. You can't see past the first foot! That's fantastic! I was super happy to see that, because clearwater, makes fish go really deep.
Even though the water was 87° at the surface, I was still able to find a nice school of crappie, that was sitting on the top of a tree, 15 feet underneath the surface. That tree, was standing in 35 feet of water. The top of it was at 15 feet, and so were the crappie. They were balled up, down to about 20 feet. I know they were crappie, because I caught a couple of them! This is a major milestone for me, this represents the first crappie that I have found, and caught, on Center Hill lake, from my boat. I'm going to drop you a pin in Google maps where I found those fish, but I can assure you, they probably won't be there ever again. This Lake is loaded with trees underwater, and I'm sure they find different spots to hang out. Either way, I dropped a pin, just in case...
https://goo.gl/maps/rM7krnM2jGoNvq616
When I started going downstream from the boat ramp, there were fish everywhere on the fish finder! From the very shallows, near the falls, all the way down to where I dropped this pin, there were fish in every depth of water, hanging out on every type of structure. I was able to catch lots of bluegill, and in the places where I found bluegill, there were other fish that I could see on the scope. Today, I took my boat to a waterfall! I launched from Cookeville boat dock just before 12:00 p.m...

Cookeville Boat Dock https://share.google/mqHcdtCEbPDu6LqcJ

This particular boat dock has lots of amenities! There's a restaurant. Lots of slips that have people's personal boats. A place to get gas on the water, as well as rental boats like pontoons and jet skis. They also rent kayaks, which is a fantastic idea! This boat ramp is super close to one of the most photogenic waterfalls in all of middle Tennessee, Fanchers Falls. If you're going to Cookeville boat dock, you're going to have to pay. It cost $10 to use the boat ramp. There were lots of people there who brought kayaks, but they came in one vehicle, so they only had to pay a $10 fee. It's not $10 per person to launch, it's $10 per vehicle. If you bring lots of kayaks, you can save money!

I paid the $10 so that I could launch my boat, and I was super glad that I did! I had never been to Fanchers, and I heard the fishing was great. What I heard was right! Here's how you get there...

Go directly out of the boat ramp and go to the left, around the entire marina. You will have to go slow, that area is in no wake zone. It takes a few minutes to get through the no wake zone! Once you get through, it's a short drive before you reach the mouth of the creek, then you have to wind your way all the way back to the falls. It's about two and a half miles from the boat ramp, to the base of the falls. It's a very short boat ride, or a lovely kayak paddle...

If you're in a boat, you're going to have to stop considerably farther away, and get in the water, and wade. The water is relatively clear, and you can see, that the bottom is mostly flat. It's a little slippery, and because of that, this trip is probably a four out of five on the effort scale of one to five. Believe it or not, it's not as hard as it can be! Once you get to the base of the falls, there are some slip and fall hazards, but it's really not as treacherous as the base of other waterfalls! It's nice!

title: Trip Report #25
content_raw:
Back to back days on the Caney Fork River...
My friend had some relatives come into town, so Friday, the five of us kayak down the Caney Fork River, starting at Buffalo valley boat ramp...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/14hNaKsxWEdkXtHYN
Both days, Friday and Saturday, I had to figure out some strategic kayak shuttling. Every trip down any stretch of river has its own logistical challenges. In this report, I'm going to discuss how to facilitate trips, when you have multiple kayakers, but only a couple of vehicles that can move kayaks.
On Friday, my buddy was coming with his three cousins. There were four of them, and they had three kayaks strapped to the roof of his car. The way we do it, is to sandwich them, one on top of the other, and strapped them tight, so they don't fly away. It was my mission to bring one extra kayak, for the other person that they didn't have a kayak for. I strapped the two kayaks to the roof of my car, and met them at the beginning of the trip, at Buffalo valley boat ramp.
We met around 7:00 in the morning and dropped all of our kayaks on the river's edge. His cousins were able to immediately launch and do some fishing below the dam, while we drove down to the end of the trip, at Happy Hollow boat ramp...
Happy Hollow Boat Ramp https://share.google/cW4s0biLCpcYn4Gm2
We left his vehicle in the parking lot at the boat ramp, and then he got in my vehicle, and we drove back up to the dam. Then, we hopped in our kayaks, and we all floated down 6 miles, from the dam, to Happy Hollow boat ramp. The fishing wasn't great. Most fish were caught with worms on bottom, and between the five of us, we ended up with 40 fish. I caught two rainbow trout that were in the slot limit. If you don't know, on the Caney Fork river, rainbow trout between 14 and 20 inches, are considered in the slot, and must be released immediately.
When we finished our trip, the five of us pulled up on the bank at Happy Hollow boat ramp, and once again, his three cousins were able to fish, and guard our gear, while he and I took his vehicle, up to the dam, where I hopped in my vehicle, and we came back down, to load our kayaks.
Fast forward to Saturday, and I had a client who wanted to go on a kayak trip down to Caney Fork river, but his vehicle didn't have a roof rack, and wasn't able to haul any amount of kayaks. Here's the way I handled that trip, for the two of us...
He wanted to do the trip that starts at Betty's Island Access...
Bettys Island Boat Ramp https://share.google/DBSPo89Vs5GCeJuCe
This is another location where, you can put your kayaks right on the river's edge. I got there at 6:45 a.m., and there were already a few people fishing the bank. Here's how I handled things, but you have to have a lot of faith in humanity...
When I got there, there were a couple gentleman fishing, and I said hello, and quickly unloaded my kayaks. My hope, was that their proximity to my fishing equipment, would keep it relatively safe. I didn't necessarily ask them to watch my gear, although I probably should have. In the past, I have asked people, and they were extremely cooperative. I have also set my kayaks there, when there was no one else out there, and then trusted that they would be there when I got back.
So far, I haven't had any problems. That doesn't mean, that my kayaks won't get up and walk away in the future. What I've been doing, is unloading my kayaks, and then driving down to the end. For this stretch of river, it's a 6 mile trip, that starts at Betty's island boat ramp, and ends at Stonewall boat ramp...
Stone Wall Boat Ramp (Gordonsville Access) https://share.google/92SJxV9sQCyJx4lyf
It's a 10 minute drive from Betty's Island boat ramp to Stonewall boat ramp. I leave my kayaks unattended, for those 20 minutes. So far, like I said, so good. When I get down to the end, I hop in the car with my client, and have them drive us up to the parking lot at the beginning. From there, we can walk down to the kayaks, provided they are still there, and float down to my vehicle, where I can load everything up, and then take them back up to their vehicle, after the trip is over. This is one of those situations, we're having a third person, would come in extremely handy. They could guard the kayaks, at the beginning, and the end, while you do the shuttling.
On that trip, on Saturday, my client wanted to catch some Smallmouth and some trout. Mission accomplished, but just barely! We struggled for a couple of hours to try to catch the first trout of the day, and when we did, it would be the only one! After we finally bagged the trout, we spent some time fishing at the confluence of the Smith Fork Creek and the Caney Fork River...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/EjZzhS82KV93vGg39
Smallmouth bass tend to stay in this location, year-round. They like the warm water that comes out of the Smith Fork Creek, and the cool water, from the Caney Fork, that flows by the mouth of the creek. Fortunately for us, they would cooperate rather quickly. Typically, in that area, all you need is a peanut butter jelly Ned rig, and a little bit of patience. If you will throw that lure near the bank, and jig it around on the bottom, you will definitely catch some small mouth!
Because each one of these locations has a boat ramp, you can load and unload your kayaks relatively easy. I like to fish when the generators are off, but even if the generators were on, and the river were full, you could still pull your kayak up to the end of the boat ramp, and load there. The physical aspect of loading and unloading your kayaks on this river are not as strenuous as other locations, because of that, I would rate these trips at a two out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. As long as you have some friends, and another vehicle, these trips are relatively easy to facilitate!
Always check the generating schedule, not only the day before you go, but the day you go! Generating schedules are subject to change, without notice. Times are given in local times. Please use caution below dams, water may rise rapidly, without warning. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://www.tva.com/environment/lake-levels/Center-Hill

title: Trip Report #26
content_raw:
Back to back days in the wrong spot...
Let's say you go fishing everyday. Let's say you know lots of great fishing spots. Now, let's pretend that sometimes, you pick the wrong spot!
That's what happened to me the last two days! Yesterday, I went back to Woods Dam to fish for striped and hybrid Bass... I HAD JUST MADE A REPORT TELLING YOU WHICH SIDE HAD BETTER FISHING... I went against my own advice, went to the far side, walked more than a mile to get to the spot, just to realize, I knew what I was talking about.
When I got there, the fish were going crazy on the other side. I took 30 minutes out of the best part of the day, to hike back the entire mile, and drive around to the other side of the dam. Had I just gone over there in the first place, I probably could have had an epic day. As it was, I only ended up catching one hybrid Bass. I'm going to drop you a pin, where you can park, to get down below Woods Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/AuQVLGpHBMj4PJAd9
When you get there, there is actually a fence that says the area is temporarily closed. That's not true! We have spoken directly with the powers that be at Arnold Air Force base, and as of right now, the area is open. If it were not open, you would not be able to access this parking lot!
So anyway, walk around that temporarily closed sign, and you will see a nice trail, all the way downhill to the water's edge. Unfortunately, when you get there, those boulders are gigantic! Treacherous! That makes this bank fishing trip a five out of five on the effort scale of one to five. Maximum effort!
By the time I made it to the other side, sunrise had already happened, and I had missed the best bite window. I didn't catch enough fish to make a video, and if I wasn't already feeling bad enough, I heard from a friend of mine that was fishing on the bank at seven points on Percy Priest Lake...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/3soBPsidYNKD6Foz6
There were a handful of people standing on this bank, which can accommodate many more, and between them, they landed 20 hybrid bass! So not only did I pick the wrong side of the dam to fish on, I also picked the wrong location altogether. I could have easily taken my boat to Seven Points boat ramp and been out there for the melee...
Seven Points Boat Ramp https://share.google/yAYU7ICqDEuXM0SZX
Fast forward to this morning, and I wanted to get in on the action! I went to seven points, just as I had done so many mornings before, but this morning, I got there really early. At 3:38 a.m., I was on the water, headed around to the point. It's only a short boat ride, so if you would like to take your kayak, you should probably do that! Just don't do it this morning...
When I got there this morning, I couldn't see any hybrid bass on the forward facing sonar. I scanned the area for a little more than half an hour, and then, they just appeared. A huge school of hybrid bass, swimming in single file, about 25 feet deep. Cruising fast around the underwater cliffs in front of the bank at seven points. Faster than usual! So fast, that it looked like they really weren't interested in feeding.
They must not have been! My boat was one of nearly half a dozen, and they were just as many fishermen on the bank. Between all the boats, and all the bank fishermen, I only saw five fish caught. Everyone was throwing different types of lures, they just wouldn't commit to them.
I could see fish following lures, not only mine, but lures that people were throwing from other boats. These fish would come to investigate, sometimes in a hurry, and then just stop, look at it, and then swim away slowly. That's not something that I had seen these fish do, for some reason, this morning, they had a very bad disposition. That happens! It would be impossible for those bank fishermen to know that those fish were out there today. Yesterday, they caught 20, today, I only saw three go into the bank. They might have assumed that the fish weren't there in great numbers, like they were the day before, but that's not true! They were loaded in there, they just weren't biting.
At 6:30 in the morning, just like clockwork, those fish disappeared from that area. I have yet to figure out where they go, I think they just cruise all day... From there, I headed over to a spot where I dropped some brush piles in concrete buckets...
https://goo.gl/maps/VKWtTYK745DHReQKA
Typically, this location holds crappie. Last week, I went there with a client, and we got a trophy crappie off this spot. This morning, it was loaded, and I caught a fish, but they were all bluegill. I think it's important to note, any of the places that I have marked that hold crappie, could potentially be covered up with nice bluegill. That was the case today! The bluegill I caught was a monster! I'm certain, there were many more in there, I just don't have any interest in catching bluegill.
If you did, a bobber and some minnows would be the way to go! I'm sure they would eat worms, and probably even crickets, but minnows are cleaner, it allows you to dip your hands into the water, to keep cool, and I'm certain, if you got small minnows, they would go for those quickly!

At 6:30 in the morning, just like clockwork, those fish disappeared from that area. I have yet to figure out where they go, I think they just cruise all day... From there, I headed over to a spot where I dropped some brush piles in concrete buckets...

https://goo.gl/maps/VKWtTYK745DHReQKA

Typically, this location holds crappie. Last week, I went there with a client, and we got a trophy crappie off this spot. This morning, it was loaded, and I caught a fish, but they were all bluegill. I think it's important to note, any of the places that I have marked that hold crappie, could potentially be covered up with nice bluegill. That was the case today! The bluegill I caught was a monster! I'm certain, there were many more in there, I just don't have any interest in catching bluegill.

title: Trip Report #27
content_raw:
Hybrid and striped bass, back to back days...
Yesterday, I launched my boat from Seven Points boat ramp at 4:00 a.m...
Seven Points Boat Ramp https://share.google/0Z1A2lGrbyf4Eflr1
In the past, I would wait until it started to get light out, before I even showed up. I know better now! When you know of a spot where these fish are feeding heavily, consistently, you can catch them anytime of night or day! I got there as quick as I could, and that just happened to be 4:00 a.m. When I came around the point to the main area where these fish blow up on a daily basis, I could see them on my fish finder everywhere! The biggest schools that I had seen out there yet. I'll drop you a PIN to the cliff face where they have been hanging out every morning...
https://goo.gl/maps/trRNf75PEqdNjsmTA
I just pull up to this spot, check my forward facing sonar, and typically, they are there! When I see them, I just cast at them. I've been using my 7-foot 2-inch cast King Royale Pro with 15 pound braid. I've been tying directly to a 1/4 of an ounce jig head and putting on a 5-inch white, fluke.
I know what they look like on the forward facing sonar, so that makes it a lot easier. When I see them, I cast directly above them, allow it to sink almost down to their depth, and then start to give it some twitches. Maybe even a little jiggle jiggle jiggle. I tried allowing it to sync all the way to them, and that will get their attention, but when they follow it up, they usually won't bite it. I have found, that the most effective method, is to try to twitch it above them a few feet. If you do it just right, you will see them come up and crush the bait!
That's really hard to do! Even if you're really good at reading a fish finder, you may struggle to find your lure. There are so many fish, and so many bait fish, that it's tough to tell what is what. The best thing to do, is to figure out exactly how long it takes your lure to sink. That way, you can cast above fish, and count it down, to the right depth. I know exactly how long it takes my quarter ounce jig head with a 5 inch fluke to sink to 10 feet. Quite often, when I see these fish, I will cast in their direction, and then count it down to what I think is the correct depth. Then I will start my retrieve. That has been working really well! Most of the time, there's too much stuff on the screen to know what is what. It's best to just fish for them, when you find them.
Don't have a boat? If you have a tremendous sense of adventure, you may be able to get to these fish! Each morning, there are at least half a dozen fishermen standing out on the bank. This is a long bank! There is plenty of room to stand! No one is shoulder to shoulder. Everyone is having a great time, and they typically catch more fish than the people in the boats. Here's what you're going to have to do...
Park in the seven points parking lot, just like those of us who have boats and trailers. Just don't park in the spots that say, for trucks with trailers only... They would probably tow you. Reason being, they have spaces for vehicles who don't have trailers. They are still really long spaces, but they have painted over the wording, that says trucks with trailers only. You are allowed to park in these spaces! From there, you just have to walk on the road, through the park, before it opens, to get to the spot. You are allowed to do that as well! Now that I finally have the whole entire thing nailed down, I can tell you, that this is probably a three out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. You have to walk a pretty long way! I'll draw you a map...
You can walk along the road most of the way! There is a gate, prohibiting people from driving, but you are allowed to walk into the park. You can walk almost all the way on the pavement, until you get to the trail that is in the parking lot near the point. It's a well-beaten path, and if you're going early in the morning, you may have some people who will travel with you! I know these people, and I can assure you, they are awesome! Great fisherman, and good people, and they will be really nice to you if you go all the way out there. I would still throw my quarter ounce jig head and my fluke, but top water works great when you're standing on the bank! Most of them are using spooks, but you could also use a Whopper plopper.
Typically, by about 6:30 in the morning, everything is over. The fish move away from that area, for some reason, and the bite dies completely. Everybody leaves, at pretty much the same time...
Fast forward to 4:00 a.m. this morning, and I was pulling up at Woods reservoir. You can fish below the dam, but it's really hard! This morning, I made the mistake of going to the far side. Basically, there are two sides to access fishing, below the dam. On one side, they have a parking lot, and it's only a quarter of a mile straight downhill, to the bank, where you can fish. Unfortunately, on both sides, they have giant boulders! The biggest that I've ever tried to stand next to the water and fish. Because the boulders are so large, they are tough to walk on. No matter which side of the reservoir you park on, to access the area below the dam, it is a 5 out of five on the effort scale of one to five!
I said I made the mistake of parking on the far side, because there is no parking lot! There are only a couple of spaces, where you could possibly park in the mud, and if you don't get completely off the road, you might be towed! The Air Force owns the property around Woods reservoir, and they patrol it very heavily! There are gates where you have to park, that will keep you from getting in. You're also more than a mile away. Because of those two facts, I'm going to go to the other side next time. If you go to that side, keep in mind, do not block the gate! They use it regularly, and if they have to tow you out of there, I'm not 100% sure you would even get your vehicle back. I'm not sure who you would call, and I'm not sure where they would take it.
The other side is fantastic! It has a parking lot and everything! I'm going to drop you a pin right here, because it's the easiest way to access fishing, below the dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/fVkwiEVKx6FfzLDU8
This spot is great! You are allowed to park here, and there's plenty of parking for everybody! It's only a quarter of a mile, straight down the hill to the water's edge. Keep in mind, once you get down there, it's tough to stand! There are some places, a little farther downstream, where the bank is more forgiving. Unfortunately, most of the action happens, closer to the dam, where the spillway is letting water flow.
Once you get there, it's mostly hybrid and striped bass. Today, I caught a large mouth, on accident. There are several different types of fish in there! I saw a catfish pulled in today, as well as several yellow bass and bluegill. There are lots of different types of fish, but because you have to walk at least a quarter mile, and the bank isn't necessarily great to stand on, not very many people go there. Today, there were probably 8 to 10 people.
I did fantastic! I ended up catching three striped bass, one hybrid bass, and a 4 pound largemouth. Everything on that fluke on a 1/4 of an ounce jig head. It helps if you have a really long net. The boulders are big, and it can be tough to get to the water's edge. If you have a long net, you can reach out farther, to scoop up your fish.
So it's a great spot, and you catch a lot of fish. So why haven't I been there before now? Great question! Here's the skinny...
You never know if you're going to catch anything. There is no water release schedule for Woods reservoir, because it's controlled by the air force. They actually keep that information hush hush. You kind of just have to know, instinctively, that they're going to be releasing water. Here's what I figured out...
After prolonged rains, like we've had the last few weeks, or a heavy rain that falls in the area, they're going to have to release water. They don't have generators, so they just open floodgates. When they do that, it can be fantastic. It can also be really tough. If they open all three floodgates, the water is too fast, and you won't be able to fish. Today, they had the middle of three floodgates open. That was a tremendous condition for fishing, but I was told by the locals, that it's better when they have one of the side Gates open. That brings the flow closer to the bank, which brings the fish closer to the fisherman.
For what it's worth, today, with the middle floodgate open, they were actually blowing up on the other side, until about 6:30 a.m. We were having to cast as far as we could, which you will see in the video that will come out either today, or tomorrow, just to get a bite. At that point in time, we packed everything up, and went to the Hardee's at the exit where you get off to go to this location, to have some breakfast.
Just in case you'd like to go, and you're apprehensive, I will draw you a map. Once you get to the parking lot, it's super obvious where you are supposed to go, it's straight downhill, through a trail that has been there for a very long time...
Actually, when I went to draw the map, Google maps already has the trail drawn in for us! I'll just drop the screenshot right here...

title: Trip Report #28
content_raw:
Hybrid bass are still biting in the morning...
Yesterday morning, I got up early and drove to the other side of Percy Priest Lake, to Seven Points boat ramp...
Seven Points Boat Ramp https://share.google/wxjZG8Zhi2vgFQz87
I've got it all figured out! You can catch these hybrid Bass from the bank, quite easily! You just have to put in the effort to get there. Here's how people are doing. If you will arrive to Seven Points boat ramp around 4:00 a.m., you can park in the parking spaces that are for everyone. They have some spaces that say trucks with trailers only. They have other spaces, where they have painted over that writing. You are allowed to park in these spaces!
From there, just walk back out the boat ramp on the road. When you get to the top of the hill where you enter the boat ramp, you can go left, into the park. The park gates are closed, but you can still access it by foot. Walk all the way through the park, and then down to the water's edge, where everybody is standing on the bank, and catching these fish. I'll drop a pin right here, where you can stand at the point...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/K7EwtjKsjc5bUv4J9
It's a long walk! But the majority of it is on the road, so that makes it a little easier. I haven't done this hike yet, but I'm certain that it's right around a three out of five on the effort scale of one to five. You're still going to have to be fairly capable to do this.
If I were going to stand there on the bank to try to catch these hybrid bass first thing in the morning, I would use my 7 foot rod and reel with 15 pound braid. That would be strong enough to pull in any of these fish, but also allow you to cast your lure far enough, to get into the action. Fortunately, they're blowing up right near the bank, so it won't be difficult to catch these fish. That's why at least a handful of people are making this walk every single morning of the week. I've been out there a few times now, and there's always someone standing on the bank, and they're always catching nice fish.
Most of the people on the bank are using topwater lures like a spook or a Whopper plopper. Some of them are using jig heads with a fluke. That's what I would use! A 1/4 of an ounce jig head with a 5 inch white fluke. That's what I was using yesterday, when I was in my boat, and I was doing really well! I had the benefit of forward facing sonar, so I was able to cast at fish that I could see on the screen, and jiggle my lure in front of them, to make them bite. When you're standing on the bank, you'll want to cast as far as you can, and then start your retrieve. If you're using a jig head, keep your rod tip up, and start a nice slow retrieve. Every once in awhile, give the lure a little jiggle jiggle jiggle. I learned that from my buddy yesterday.
I got to the boat ramp at 4:00 a.m. I had seen people on the bank, and I knew they were getting there early to walk there. But I didn't know how! Fortunately for me, one of the first people to pull up, was someone that I know, named Lester. He informed me about how they walk to that spot, and I offered him a ride in the boat in exchange. He and I sat far enough away from the bank so that the people fishing the bank couldn't hit us with their cast. Then we started fishing. I was looking at the forward facing sonar and catching fish, and he was using the technique I just described, casting a jig head with a fluke, not allowing it to sink, getting his rod tip directly up, starting a slow retrieve, and then every once in awhile, giving it a jiggle.
He was catching fish simply by using that retrieve. He's a fantastic fisherman, so I watched him like a hawk! It's that retrieve that is so enticing to hybrid bass. He didn't need to look at the live scope, and he out fished me in my boat.
In the past, I would keep my lure at the ready, with my finger on my line and my bail open, so that I could make a quick cast if I saw these fish blowing up near the boat. That would work, to get me some fish, but I wasn't really having epic days. Then when I went fishing with Lester, I had a realization... Instead of waiting for these fish to start hitting at the surface, and casting near them, and hoping to get a bite, you should just fish! If you're in the area where these fish are, it doesn't hurt to have forward facing sonar, and cast in their direction, but if you're in their general vicinity, you should just fish! They will find your lure, and they will hit it!
That's how people on the bank are having so much success. They aren't worried about casting to a fish that's actively feeding on the surface, and they're not watching forward facing sonar. That's exactly what Lester was doing from my boat, and he caught the biggest hybrid that I've seen all year, a 10-pounder!
If you have a boat or a kayak or a dinghy or a raft, you need to get out there! From the boat ramp, around the corner to the point, is less than a half of a mile by water! Make sure to have navigational lights on your boat, and even though you don't have to have navigational lights on your kayak or canoe in the state of Tennessee, I would suggest that you do when you are out on Percy Priest lake!

Make sure to have navigational lights on your boat, and even though you don't have to have navigational lights on your kayak or canoe in the state of Tennessee, I would suggest that you do when you are out on Percy Priest lake!

title: Trip Report #29
content_raw:
A long day at Center Hill Dam...
Yesterday, I had two different client trips booked below Center Hill dam. The first, a 4-Hour trip from 7:00 a.m. until 11:00 a.m. fishing on the bank. We met at the steps just below the dam...
https://goo.gl/maps/NAFsbkzhMeBj6aqw7
This is a great spot to fish because you don't have to get in the water. Not everybody wants to be in the river. My clients wanted beginner instructions about fishing for trout at the Caney Fork river, and this was the place that I chose to begin our day.
First of all, this was a family. Grandfather and son and grandkids. So I wanted a location with a bathroom. This spot has a really nice restroom facility, that gets cleaned daily. I also wanted a location where I could show them how to work a lure, and they could see the lure, performing correctly, in the water. Because the steps are above the water, and the water is relatively clear, I was able to make short casts with lures like spoons and rooster tails, to show them how they should retrieve them through the water. On my example casts, we saw fish come up and chase the lures! That type of immediate result is fantastic for beginners, because it gives them hope that they will be able to catch fish.
So you can stand on the steps to fish, and you don't have to get in the water, and you can park right by where you're fishing, and there is a bathroom in the parking lot. Really ideal for us to do some instruction. While I was showing them how to use different types of trout lures, we also threw a minnow on a bobber into the river, as well as some power bait on bottom, and a nightcrawler. While we were going over instructions, we caught a couple of small trout. It's important to note, for the most part, people fish this location when the generators are on. I opted to go there yesterday, when the generators were off. It made it much easier for us to teach, and learn. Just because people go there when the generators are on, does not mean you cannot catch fish when they are off! I've had some tremendous days fishing from the steps, when they weren't running any generators at all. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
From there, we went across the river, to put everything we had learned, into practice. We headed over to Buffalo valley boat ramp, to walk down the nature trail, to one of my favorite bank fishing locations on the Caney...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/IY0SLpQQdohmEFfbw
If you park in this parking lot, directly in front of the handicap parking spaces, there is a nature trail that will take you about a quarter mile downstream, where you can walk into the river, and fish in front of the first Creek that flows into the Caney Fork...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/yeFfWFp5rUNZVMwt8
From the parking lot, there's a gravel road, all the way to the river's edge, where there are steps down to the river. You will have to walk in the water, but we did not wear chest waders. We opted to just get wet! On the effort scale of 1 to 5, just because you have to walk around in the river bed, this is probably a two. It's definitely not hard, but you need to be able to wade.
This is a magical location! One of the first places I like to stop with clients whenever we are on a kayak trip. Typically, there are people standing there, so I don't get to stop. When we got there yesterday, no one was there! There was one gentleman standing a few hundred yards away, but by and large, we had the whole place to ourself! Most of us used a worm on bottom with an ultra light setup, and caught fish quickly and often. One person did not want to wait for the fish to bite, and wanted to throw lures, and that worked out great! I tried handing him a couple of different lures, but the one that would do the trick, was a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail. For what it's worth, that's my favorite trout lure!
At 11:00, our time was up, and I had another client booked to do the 6 hour instructional fishing trip in kayaks below Center Hill Dam...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/FX50c7Sx1JzfSSkcz
He wanted basic information about what different types of fish you could catch below the dam, and how you could target them. I explained, that my favorite thing to do, is to sit in the very center, directly below the dam, and the deepest spot, which is about 18 feet. It is in that location, when the generators are off, that I like to catch every type of fish that swims below Center Hill dam. Most of the time, it's as simple as dropping a minnow, or a worm, underneath the kayak. I like to sit on an anchor, and just wait for the fish to come to me.
Yesterday was no exception! Within a little while of trying, a crappie decided to take down the minnow that he had under his boat. Shortly thereafter, a 3 foot long sturgeon gobbled up the nightcrawler that we had on an ultralight setup with 4 pound monofilament. It would take 30 minutes before we could get that fish in, and something happened during those 30 minutes. I can't tell you exactly what it was, but we went from catching fish all morning with my first clients, and then a couple of quick fish with my second client, to nothing!
The fish got tight-lipped, and we couldn't even catch a bass with a Ned rig under the waterfall. We tried lots of different techniques, from vertical jigging with spoons for walleye, to using rapid countdown minnows and a slow retrieve, in an effort to catch trout. It wasn't for lack of effort on our part, but we could not get the fish to bite! Just after 4:00, we called it a day. By then, the generators had been on for a little over an hour, which I hoped would turn the bite on, but it did not.

title: Trip Report #30
content_raw:
A mountain of information...
I've been booked the last couple of days with clients, so I've been neglecting my duties to write Pro reports. Fortunately, I haven't forgot any of the information!
People are still catching hybrid bass every morning at 7 points boat ramp...
Seven Points Boat Ramp https://share.google/VLnK1DjTpMgcdcMmx
There are people standing on the bank every morning. I was there two mornings ago, on Tuesday morning, and I launched my boat at 4:45 a.m. I hit the motor and went directly around to the cliffs at the end of the park...
https://goo.gl/maps/2kGqP4ZFqNFPVGCe6
When I got there, the bank was loaded with people. It was already starting to get light out, and they were hybrid fishing. Throwing as far as they could out to the middle, with top water lures and paddle tails. I'm not sure how they're getting there! I know they are walking from the boat ramp, but I'm not sure if they are walking through the woods, or if they are walking on the road. At the boat ramp, there are places for people without trailers to park. I'm certain there are parking there, because there where cars in the parking lot when I got there. The trail through the woods is tough! Five out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. It's half a mile, and you have to hike up a huge hill, and then back down. I wouldn't do it in the daytime right now, and they are getting there while it's still dark out. That makes me think, but they are walking on the road.
If you park in the parking lot, you can just walk the road all the way to this location. After 6:00 a.m. they open the gates, and you could drive there, but you would be too late, because the fishing is already over. I'm going to drop a pin where they are standing, and you can go check it out for yourself...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/Sma2okeCfFPWkbSV9
If you look at the maps, you can see that there's a parking lot not far from here. Unfortunately, the recreation area is only available for day use. They lock the gate every night, and they don't let us back in until well after the Sun comes up. When I was there on Tuesday, all the fish were done biting, and everybody had left the bank, by around 6:30. That's exactly when my client showed up, so I scooted over to the boat ramp to pick him up, and we started cruising around the area, mostly just hanging out, looking for bass near the bank with a top water lure. We didn't do any good at all, so I went to a couple different spots that I know of that usually hold crappie.
The first spot is in a cove across the lake from seven points, there's a brush pile that holds fish, and I even dropped three concrete buckets with brush in this area. Both the brush pile, and my concrete buckets, we're holding fish. We didn't stay there long, because the wind was kicking our butt! We tried to put down an anchor, and we managed to catch one fish. It was a trophy white crappie! 14 inches long. But the wind was screaming from the northeast, a very untypical direction, and it made it impossible to sit on this spot. So we had to move, but I'm going to drop you a pin for these brush piles...
https://goo.gl/maps/CmyDAiDVy1V6qqzv5
From there, we went way up into the cove, at Viveret Creek. There is a fish attractor near the bank there, that we fish all winter long, and I wanted to see if there were any crappie on it. I haven't heard about anybody fishing at this location from the bank, in a long time, so I didn't expect to catch any crappie. But I was wrong. Guys, this fish attractor still has fish on it, and you can walk there and fish it from the bank!
https://goo.gl/maps/euZq1WJAyY9vmdMi9
Just park at Viverette Creek boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/kkcDNtpskrj9oEGBA
There's a trail through the woods that goes directly to this spot! This is not a terribly long trail, and I would walk it this time of year! It's probably a three out of five on the effort scale of one to five. Just because you have to hike through the woods, but it's not very far, only about a quarter mile. Once you get there, there is a buoy that marks the spot! There's plenty of room to stand on the bank, and when we showed up in my boat, I caught a crappie on the first cast! Unfortunately, the wind was whipping at that location as well, that was going to be the theme of the day. We fished for 6 hours, and I only caught those couple crappie, and he got one bass on a crankbait. That was it!
Fast forward to Wednesday, and I had a family booked to kayak the first 6 miles of the Caney Fork River, from Center Hill Dam...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/zBG3yL9HpcAcpndSZ
To Happy Hollow boat ramp...
Happy Hollow Boat Ramp https://share.google/FRyENqLjGmPiBUFOB
The first 6 miles of this River are the easiest for people who are beginning kayakers. There are no rapids, and there are no boulders, and there are very few trees in the way. When the generators are off, the water is smooth, and the surface is level. We did our trip while there was zero chance of generation, which made it optimum! You can find the generation schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
We were scheduled to start our trip at 8:00 a.m. so I got there at 4:00 a.m. I wanted to do some fishing below the dam, before it got light out, to try to catch either striped bass, or walleye. Once again, I didn't have any luck. I did the same thing that I've been doing the last couple of weeks when I go up there, when I don't have any luck. After long, frustrating hours of fishing, I tie on a peanut butter jelly Ned rig, and throw it in the waterfall, and catch bass. At least I got that going for me, which is nice. One of these days, I will learn how to catch walleye, and I will catch those fish! Until then, I'm going to keep trying.
By 8:00, I met up with my clients, and we started heading downstream. Yesterday was a fantastic fishing day! I've been on this trip, at least half a dozen times this year, so far. Up to this point, we have not had good days. Yesterday was fantastic! We stopped at several different locations, where the river gets narrow, and the current gets swift, to fish with worms on the bottom while using ultra light rods and reels. We stopped at five different locations, and at each location, we caught fish! At the very last stop, one of my young clients caught a nice big brown trout!
