title: Trip Report #31
content_raw:
The orifice gate is online...
Every year, for the summer and fall, Center Hill Dam operates the orifice gate. That is a small gate, at the base of the dam, that allows 250 CFS to flow at all times, starting on June 1st, and closing on December 1st. Today is June 1st, and I was there for the opening. I was there on December 1st, when they closed it as well. The orifice gate adds water to the river during the time of year when we get the least amount of rain. That is very beneficial for the fish. However, I am not a fan.
First of all, if you're wondering about how this release of water affects the river, effectively, it doesn't. If you regularly wade the river, there will be a small amount more flow, but it won't affect your ability to go where you like to go and do what you like to do. If you use your boat, or a kayak, things will stay the same, relatively speaking. When the generator comes on, the effect will be the same. When the generators go off, the water will go back down, and this amount of water coming from the orifice gate won't necessarily change the river much, to the naked eye.
The one thing it does, that I do not like, is make the river cloudy. I was there this morning, before they opened the orifice gate at 8:00 a.m., and I could see fish everywhere! I actually got a striped bass on video. I put it in today's video, three different times. You'll have to look closely, because I don't point it out, but it's clear as day! It looks really big, but that's one of the little ones! There are some really big striped bass in there, but they are very skittish, and I haven't been able to get them to bite.
I got to Buffalo valley boat ramp around 2:00 a.m...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/NvwSAxWZIwNhEaAtq
I paddled up to the dam, in the dark, hoping to catch one of those striped bass, or a walleye. I fished for quite some time, without a bite, and I knew that the generators were going to turn on at 4:00 a.m... You can find the generating schedule, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
Just before 4:00 a.m., I hadn't had any luck, so I decided to throw a Ned rig under the waterfall. It was loaded with largemouth bass! Mostly just one and a half pounders, but they were fun to catch, on my peanut butter jelly Ned rig, and it gave me something to do, while I was waiting for them to turn on the orifice gate. For me, it's kind of like, an event. I just like to be there when they do things!
After I caught a few largemouth, they turned on one generator. I tried to fish the generating water with some big lures, for whatever, striped bass, or giant trout, anything, but the only attention I would get, would be from gar. For what it's worth, if you ever wanted to catch a long nose gar, you could do so easily, below Center Hill dam. They will eat any lure, and you can catch them all day and all night. If you wanted to catch a thousand fish in one day, you could do it there.
After the sun came up, I could see fish everywhere! Schools of giant largemouth bass, striped bass cruising, walleyes, laying on the bottom. There were schools of redear sunfish as well as bluegill... And even some large schools of tiny yellow bass, hanging out in the grass. And then it happened, they flashed blue lights at me from above the dam, and broadcasted their voice over a loudspeaker to tell me that I needed to move away from the dam, because they were about to open the orifice gate for the season.
I paddled back down to the boat ramp, where the corps of engineers were waiting on me, to make sure that I stayed safe. He explained, that even though it would only be releasing a small amount of water, and that it should be relatively safe, if anything went wrong, they wanted an abundance of caution. Fortunately, everything went exactly as planned, and the orifice gate is now open for the rest of the season, until December 1st.
As soon as they opened it, the clarity went away. The ones pristine, crystal clear water of the Caney Fork river, replaced with red rust. Water that looks more brown than clear. Silt deposits, that had settled on the bottom of the lake, in front of the orifice gate, since the last time it was opened, in December of last year. Will it clear up? Maybe. If it does, when will it be? Nobody knows. All I know for sure, is that the increased debris in the water is actually nutrients for the grass. Each year, the grass grows thicker on the Caney Fork river, now that it has extra nutrients flowing from the orifice gate.
If you have ever tried to fish on the Caney Fork river, you know that most of the time when you cast, if you don't catch a fish, you're going to catch some grass or some river snot. And it's only getting worse! Fortunately, it's great for the fishing. It's not great for fishermen, because we have to deal with the grass, but the fish love it! According to all metrics, from the TWRA, the river is super healthy, and the fish population is fantastic! It's not the best it's ever been, but it's better than it has been in a long time!
content_markdown:
The orifice gate is online...

Every year, for the summer and fall, Center Hill Dam operates the orifice gate. That is a small gate, at the base of the dam, that allows 250 CFS to flow at all times, starting on June 1st, and closing on December 1st. Today is June 1st, and I was there for the opening. I was there on December 1st, when they closed it as well. The orifice gate adds water to the river during the time of year when we get the least amount of rain. That is very beneficial for the fish. However, I am not a fan.

First of all, if you're wondering about how this release of water affects the river, effectively, it doesn't. If you regularly wade the river, there will be a small amount more flow, but it won't affect your ability to go where you like to go and do what you like to do. If you use your boat, or a kayak, things will stay the same, relatively speaking. When the generator comes on, the effect will be the same. When the generators go off, the water will go back down, and this amount of water coming from the orifice gate won't necessarily change the river much, to the naked eye.

The one thing it does, that I do not like, is make the river cloudy. I was there this morning, before they opened the orifice gate at 8:00 a.m., and I could see fish everywhere! I actually got a striped bass on video. I put it in today's video, three different times. You'll have to look closely, because I don't point it out, but it's clear as day! It looks really big, but that's one of the little ones! There are some really big striped bass in there, but they are very skittish, and I haven't been able to get them to bite.

I got to Buffalo valley boat ramp around 2:00 a.m...

Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/NvwSAxWZIwNhEaAtq

I paddled up to the dam, in the dark, hoping to catch one of those striped bass, or a walleye. I fished for quite some time, without a bite, and I knew that the generators were going to turn on at 4:00 a.m... You can find the generating schedule, here...

https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill

Just before 4:00 a.m., I hadn't had any luck, so I decided to throw a Ned rig under the waterfall. It was loaded with largemouth bass! Mostly just one and a half pounders, but they were fun to catch, on my peanut butter jelly Ned rig, and it gave me something to do, while I was waiting for them to turn on the orifice gate. For me, it's kind of like, an event. I just like to be there when they do things!

After I caught a few largemouth, they turned on one generator. I tried to fish the generating water with some big lures, for whatever, striped bass, or giant trout, anything, but the only attention I would get, would be from gar. For what it's worth, if you ever wanted to catch a long nose gar, you could do so easily, below Center Hill dam. They will eat any lure, and you can catch them all day and all night. If you wanted to catch a thousand fish in one day, you could do it there.

After the sun came up, I could see fish everywhere! Schools of giant largemouth bass, striped bass cruising, walleyes, laying on the bottom. There were schools of redear sunfish as well as bluegill... And even some large schools of tiny yellow bass, hanging out in the grass. And then it happened, they flashed blue lights at me from above the dam, and broadcasted their voice over a loudspeaker to tell me that I needed to move away from the dam, because they were about to open the orifice gate for the season.

I paddled back down to the boat ramp, where the corps of engineers were waiting on me, to make sure that I stayed safe. He explained, that even though it would only be releasing a small amount of water, and that it should be relatively safe, if anything went wrong, they wanted an abundance of caution. Fortunately, everything went exactly as planned, and the orifice gate is now open for the rest of the season, until December 1st.

As soon as they opened it, the clarity went away. The ones pristine, crystal clear water of the Caney Fork river, replaced with red rust. Water that looks more brown than clear. Silt deposits, that had settled on the bottom of the lake, in front of the orifice gate, since the last time it was opened, in December of last year. Will it clear up? Maybe. If it does, when will it be? Nobody knows. All I know for sure, is that the increased debris in the water is actually nutrients for the grass. Each year, the grass grows thicker on the Caney Fork river, now that it has extra nutrients flowing from the orifice gate.

If you have ever tried to fish on the Caney Fork river, you know that most of the time when you cast, if you don't catch a fish, you're going to catch some grass or some river snot. And it's only getting worse! Fortunately, it's great for the fishing. It's not great for fishermen, because we have to deal with the grass, but the fish love it! According to all metrics, from the TWRA, the river is super healthy, and the fish population is fantastic! It's not the best it's ever been, but it's better than it has been in a long time!

title: Trip Report #32
content_raw:
Too much fishing, not enough writing!
The fishing has been fantastic! I've been going every waking moment, and I haven't been writing as much as I'd like. The last report I did was Thursday afternoon when I had just paddled down the Caney Fork river, and back upstream against the current. That day was epic, but that wasn't the end of the day. From there, I drove up to Betty's Island Access where I set up to do a little night fishing...
https://share.google/PViQmBHJXtJFHha9o
Typically, on the weekends during the summer, they run the generator for 1 hour at a time, every 8 hours. That creates a situation, at Betty's Island Access, where you can fish all day and night! Because that location is 9 miles away from the dam on the water, the generating water has time to spread out before it gets there, and it doesn't arrive with as much force, and it tends to just bring the level up slightly. Only a few inches, before it starts to drop back down. This makes conditions fantastic for fishing at any time of day or night! The area is unbelievably large and you can put on chest waders and go upstream or downstream. It's like a playground for trout fishermen.
I don't like to get in the water. You can stand right next to the water's edge, and cast all the way across to the other side. It's not very wide, and it always has current, which makes it a fantastic choke point, that always holds trout. I actually didn't have any luck, but there was another guy fishing there, and he was using worms on bottom. He was wearing them out! I didn't bring any bait with me. I was using a few different lures, and they didn't work, and that's okay. I fished until about 11:00 p.m., and that's when the generating water started to come up. That location is 9 miles downstream from Center Hill dam, and it takes the generating water about 3 hours to get there, because the water moves at about 3 mph. The generating schedule stated that they were intending to release water at 8:00 p.m., and that's exactly what they did. I always check the generating schedule, even if I'm not going fishing in Center Hill dam. Just so I know what they are doing. Here is a link to where you can find information about the generating schedule at Center Hill Dam...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
The next morning was Friday morning and we had a short window before light rain moved in that lasted pretty much all day. I took my boat out to check on some crappie spots near Stewart Creek boat ramp...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/EHLJOCxSawz0O12VE
It's been a while since I checked any of the pins that I had on Percy Priest lake, so I started near the boat ramp... Unfortunately, I forgot my camera, so I didn't get a video, but I also didn't leave the boat ramp area. They were crappie stacked all over the cliffs at Stewart Creek boat ramp! They were mostly hanging out on or underneath, or around the trees that are in the water on those cliffs. I pulled my boat up onto one of the trees, right by the bank, and just sat there and dropped my pearl colored Bobby Garland directly under the boat and wiggled it around in about 4 to 5 feet of depth, and I was catching crappie left and right!
Overall, the water directly off the cliff is about 25 feet deep, and fish were stacked from the bottom, all the way up to about 4 feet from the surface. I sat there and caught crappie, until it started to rain. Unfortunately, none of those fish were very large. Most of them would have been just barely keeper size, or shorter than that, but there were hundreds! I wasn't able to scan the entire cliff, because there were some people who were fishing on the cliff. It looked like they were crappie fishing, but I couldn't be sure. You could definitely catch them from the bank, especially if you went at night with a bobber and a minnow. I would probably just use a Bobby Garland with an ultralight setup and 4 pound monofilament.
Today, I had a client booked to do the 6 mile kayak trip on the Caney Fork river. It was going to be his first ever kayak trip going downstream on a river, and he wanted something that would be good for a beginner. I like the Caney Fork River for that type of situation, because it's wide, and the water is flat, there aren't many obstacles in the middle of the river to navigate, and the river moves very slowly when the generators are off. There are no waterfalls or low head dams that you have to go over and no spots where you need to portage. When the generators are off, it's a fantastic place for beginners!
We opted to start at Betty's Island Access, which I already linked above, and paddle downstream to Stonewall boat ramp...
Stone Wall Boat Ramp (Gordonsville Access) https://share.google/E1QxmKGAgwHNS6gT4
This is mostly a trout fishing trip, but if you stop at the confluence of the Smith Fork river, where it enters the Caney Fork river, you can catch any number of species of fish! At that point in our trip, we were getting rained on heavily, so even though we stopped at the confluence, we only managed to land three smallmouth bass and one Gar. The rest of the trip, was dry, and the trout fishing was stellar! Simply using an ultralight rod and reel, and a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail, my client had a day for the ages! We were catching fish left and right, everywhere they were supposed to be, and they were biting, on command.
Casting that lure downstream, getting the rod tip up quickly, and starting a slow retrieve, is the method that makes these fish go crazy. Especially if you're in a kayak, floating downstream, because as you float to your lure, and reel at the same time, the roostertail will practically sit still, presenting itself in one location, for a long time, which is irresistible to trout.
We did that 6 mile trip in exactly 6 hours, caught tons of fish, got rained on heavily, and had an epic day. A lot of Pro report subscribers ask me how long it takes to do a particular kayak trip. It just depends! How long do you want it to take. For a trip of six miles, using a little bit of current to help you paddle, you could get done in a couple of hours! But if you fish slowly, and get out of the kayak to fish, it could take all day!

title: Trip Report #33
content_raw:
How to kayak fish Sebowisha by yourself...
In the past, you've heard me mention Sebowisha. That's the confluence of the Smith Fork Creek and the Caney Fork River...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/UNzB1JHVDsje4xbn6
Anytime you have a river confluence, that's somewhere you want to fish. This is a very special confluence, because it's the end of a very long creek, that holds a lot of nice Smallmouth bass, and it flows into the Caney Fork river which is crystal clear and really cold. Bass don't like to be too cold, so they will come up that river, and then stick their nose in that creek, and hang out in that warmer water that flows out of the creek. It was right where that warmer, cloudy water meets the cold, clear water of the Caney Fork, that I had a day for the ages today!
When you get there, just fish for bass. Anyway you know how. I was using a topwater lure as well as a Ned rig and even a weightless fluke. Pretty much, the area is loaded, and they're keying in on anything you throw in there. The trick is getting there. Because the river has daily generation that causes the water level to rise up and down several different times per day, you have to get the timing just right. Here's how you can go about trying to do, what I did today.
First of all, you need to know the generating schedule. Here's where you can find the generating schedule for Center Hill Dam...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
I put in at Kirby road access...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/zi3GuwcaKJd4gm7y6
This is a small gravel parking lot underneath the interstate where you can park, and take your kayak down to the water's edge. This is a public place to launch a kayak or if you would like to put on some chest waders, and do some trout fishing. The trail down to the water's edge is steep and muddy and slippery, but someone has added a rope to aid in your descent, but it's more helpful, on the way back up the hill. Because you have to go up and down this mud bank, and you're going to have to paddle against the current to get back up to this location, this trip is a 5 out of five on the effort scale of one to five. This is only for the most hearty of souls, and even then, it's going to test your abilities.
So now you know where you're going, and what to fish for, but you need to know when to go. I can use today as an example, because tomorrow's generating schedule is exactly the same. Here's the way I facilitate this trip...
The access point at Kirby road is about 10 miles away from the dam. I know from experience, that it takes a little more than 3 hours for the generating water to reach that point. They were scheduled to generate from 4:00 a.m. until 5:00 a.m. That water started showing up near Kirby road access just after 7:00 a.m. it takes a couple of hours, that far away from the dam, for the water to get all the way up, and start going back down. Even though it was only one hour of release from the dam, the water will continue to rise for 2 hours, this far away from the dam. I got there at 9:00 a.m., when the river was as full it was going to be, before it started dropping back down. I rode the river down to the confluence, where I fished for a few hours, before I paddled back upstream to my vehicle.
On your way down, the river splits left and right. On the right side, it's deeper, and a little more swift. On the left side, it's shallower, and the water is a little more lazy. I rode down on the right side, and caught trout, and on the way back up, I paddled up the left side. It is not easy to paddle up stream on this river, even when the generators are off! I was a little nervous about getting there before the generating water showed up, so I played it safe, and left early. I got back up to my vehicle, just after 2:00 p.m. then I sat there and waited. I wanted to know exactly when that water starts showing up underneath that bridge on Kirby road. Just after 3:30, the water started to rise. So now we know, because they generated today at 12:00 noon, that it takes three and a half hours for that water to get to Kirby road. In the future, I could fish for a little while longer, before I made my way upstream, but today, it was better safe than sorry...
I mentioned that you can wear chest waders and do some fishing in this area. Lots of people do that! Way more than actually kayak here. It's a great spot for that, but as far as trips in your chest waders go, this is another one, that is a 5 out of 5 on the effort scale. Not only do you have to get up and down that muddy bank, but you're going to have to cross the river. If the water were to rise, without warning, you would definitely be stuck. I was speaking with someone today who had that happen to them twice! One time, they started to set up a camp and build a fire, before some kayakers came along and allowed him to hop in their canoe and they paddled him to the other side of the river where his vehicle was. The generating schedule doesn't change often, but you always have to be prepared for it to change, without notice.

title: Trip Report #34
content_raw:
I finally did it!
Last night, I got to Center Hill Dam and launched my kayak at 2:00 a.m....
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/6adAIPfv9WP4AdhHh
I've been trying to catch walleye for the better part of a week now. I know they're in there, because I can see them at night, and in the daytime. I've been going continuously, determined to get one, at least one. Today is finally happened, but not the way I thought it would.
I got to the dam at 2:00 a.m. so that I could fish for about an hour before they turned the generator on, at 3:00 a.m. I had every intention of targeting walleye, but there are also massive striped bass swimming around below the dam, so I couldn't help throwing some giant lures to see if I could catch one of those as well. I could not.
To target striped bass below Center Hill dam, I like to throw a large glide bait. Most glide baits are very expensive, so a good alternative, would be a large paddle tail swimbait. Live bait is always a good idea, if you can catch some. I like to use a whole rainbow trout. I have a 7 foot, heavy action rod and reel, with 65 pound braid. I don't like to use a leader line, I like to tie directly to the braid.
Once again, I know these striped bass are in there, because I saw them Monday, while I was up there. I spent the majority of my time while it was dark out fishing for them. I saw a school of three, that was cruising around in the shallow area near the waterfall, and each one of them was no less than 4 feet long. That's not hyperbole! I saw these fish from a standing position in my kayak. Fast forward to last night, and I fished for that first hour while the generators were off, the next hour while the generator was on, and all the way until sunrise, and never so much has got a bite.
Once it got light out, I really focused on trying to catch those walleye. In my opinion, it should be easier to catch in the daytime, because they don't like to spread out in the shallow water as much. Their eyes are sensitive, and they like to move into the deepest part, directly below the dam.
I like to troll a Berkeley flickershad. They dive deep, and wobble side to side really well. It's a favorite lure for walleye fisherman all over the country, especially people who like to troll. That's how I finally got one on the line this morning! I was using my ultralight rod and reel with 4 pound monofilament. You can get Berkeley flicker shad that dive to any number of depth, but I was using the 7-foot diver today. The same lure that I have been using the last week. I simply cast behind the kayak, and then paddle around in a circle, allowing that lure to troll behind me... Today, with one major exception, I put out a ridiculous amount of line!

People have been using top water Spooks as well as Whopper ploppers and having great success, catching as many as 25 or 30 stripers and hybrid bass in one trip!
There is a small parking lot, and you will have to walk a relatively long way down to the water's edge. It's straight downhill, and you will have to walk back uphill! Because you have to stand on rocks on the bank, and walk a relatively far distance from your car this bank fishing trip rates at a three on the effort scale of 1 to 5. It's going to be relatively difficult, for a bank fishing trip. If you're up to it, you should definitely go as quickly as possible, here's where you need to park...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/uo9aQTPzHA6eLcRz7
From there, you can't miss it, but I'm going to draw you a map of exactly where you need to walk...
It's easiest to walk through the woods, there is a well-beating path. I mentioned that this location was closed for a few months, maybe even longer, that was because people were leaving their trash. If you don't mind, pack some of that out with you when you go. This is a fantastic location! Lots of really good fish to catch, from the bank, easily! Doubtful you will ever see any boats at all, it's treacherous trying to get this far up the river. It's truly the perfect place for people who want to catch striped bass and hybrid bass from the bank.

title: Trip Report #35
content_raw:
Hoping you had a safe and memorable memorial Day weekend...
I have spent the whole weekend going back and forth between Center Hill dam. Launching my kayak at every hour of the day and night from the boat ramp, directly below the dam, Buffalo valley boat ramp...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/BxalYeh70BPU9d9RH
At this point, I've completely lost track of each trip. I started going in the middle of the night. Then early in the morning. Then the middle of the day. Each time, I've been trying to catch walleye. Each time, I have been unsuccessful. Today, I was there pretty much all day. I got there just after breakfast time, and left just before dinner time. I tried to speak with everybody I could about catching walleye. No one was reporting any catches! I didn't have any luck either.
Lots of other fish are being caught. Plenty of trout. An incredible amount of bass! When the water gets low, after the generator has been off for a couple of hours, it's really clear and shallow, and you can see fish everywhere! There's lots of every different type of fish to catch from crappie to sturgeon, and everything in between. People are catching fish, but no one is catching walleye! A little birdie told me, that for a brief period, on sunday, from 11:00 a.m. until noon, while the generator was on for 1 hour, people in kayaks were catching walleye. I cannot confirm that, but it makes sense. I know, as a matter of fact, that they are loaded in there.
I've been reporting to you guys that I can see them at night with my flashlight. As you scan around in the water, you can see their eyes light up. It's a lot like the way cats eyes are reflective. They are unmistakable, and they are everywhere! Fast forward to the daytime, and today, I could see them swimming around!
There were lots of people below Center Hill Dam today. Some Pro report subscribers, and some friends that I haven't seen in a long time. Every type of method was being used, from nightcrawlers on the bottom, to minnows under a bobber, and every type of lure that you could ever possibly use for walleye. Jerk baits mostly, but lots of people were also vertical jigging. There were at least a handful of people who were actively targeting walleye, and we all failed to get one. Not even one!
Everyone was catching fish though. There are no shortage of different species to target. Today, while I was trying to catch walleye, I caught a crappie, a few bass, some trout and even a nice big bluegill. I saw other people catch drum as well as skipjack herring. One of my buddies was using a legal sized rainbow trout, underneath 14 inches, as bait. He was using an extra heavy rod and reel with very heavy line and a huge hook that he stabbed through the throat of the trout and dragged it around behind his kayak trying to get some of the bigger fish to bite. It didn't work out for him today, but it's never a bad idea to use big baits on the Caney Fork River. You never know what you might catch!
The most popular way to fish for walleye below Center Hill Dam at night, is to use a floating or suspending jerkbait from rapala. A standard retrieve, with a couple of twitches and then a short pause, is typically all it takes to load the boat. During the daytime, the sensitive eyes, positioned on top of the head of these fish, typically forces them to move deeper in the clear water below Center Hill Dam. When I first started going to Center Hill Dam in 1992, I would see people in boats, sitting below the dam, vertically jigging. They would use gold and silver spoons, drop them down to the bottom, which is about 18 feet deep in the deepest spot. Then they would reel any slack out of the line, and twitch The lure up off the bottom a couple of feet and allow it to flutter slowly back down. Then they would wait for 10 to 15 seconds before they would twitch it back up and then allow it to flutter back down. This is called vertical jigging, and this is the most popular way to fish for walleye below Center Hill Dam during the daytime.
There's another really good way, but it's kind of tough, especially when there are other people in kayaks or boats. I like to troll a Berkeley flicker shad, which is a deep diving jerk bait. I simply cast it behind my kayak, and paddle around in a large circle below the dam. That has been the most effective method for me, in years past. So far this year, I've tried everything that I know how to try, including using live nightcrawlers on, or near the bottom, as well as minnows, and I have come up empty-handed, more than half a dozen times now!
At some point in time, these fish are going to get caught. They keep coming upstream, from Old hickory lake, and they're going to do so, all summer. As the summer goes on, our odds for catching these fish will get better and better! Typically, by July and August, we're catching lots of them, sometimes, even a limit! If you're not familiar, or unaware, in the state of Tennessee, which includes below Center Hill dam, you are allowed to keep five walleye per day, provided they are at least 16 inches in length. Always make sure you have a way to measure your fish, the TWRA has been patrolling heavily, as they tend to do at this location. I have seen them out there each day, for the last 3 days, working hard to ensure not only that people are safe, but also catching fish.

title: Trip Report #36
content_raw:
Finally getting some rain...
Yesterday, I took my kayak up the Stones River from Manson Pike trailhead...
Manson Pike Trailhead https://share.google/ecfGMCRDLWRTUgZ8h
I go to lots of different locations in Middle Tennessee, to paddle my kayak upstream in search of fish. This spot is on the Murfreesboro greenway, and it requires that you have wheels to roll your kayak. If you cannot roll your kayak to this location, you will not be able to fish this spot. If you park in the parking lot at Manson Pike trailhead, and load your kayak onto your kayak cart, you can roll up the greenway, and launch above Ransom Mill dam. I'll drop a pin right here, on the water's edge, where you can safely launch your kayak. Believe it or not, other than rolling your kayak, this is a very easy trip! The fact that you have to have a kayak cart makes it a two out of five on the effort scale of one to five. The water is flat, and loaded with fish, and easy to paddle...
https://goo.gl/maps/E5QvaTJrAm6tCV6C8
I go bass fishing on this stretch of water, and yesterday, I did really well! The fish weren't particularly happy, it was raining off and on, but I was able to catch bass on a top water Whopper plopper, two different color crankbaits, both that dove to about 4 feet of depth, and even a chatterbait! If you don't know, a ChatterBait is a bladed jig. Something that people used to fish on the bottom, but once the blade was added, you could run it more like a swimming lure. Basically, it's a swim jig with a shiny blade. I was using my purple spinnerbait that I have been catching bass with since last fall, and it didn't even get a look! That's the first time that I've gone bass fishing this year, when that lure let me down. They wanted anything but a spinnerbait. For what it's worth, spinnerbait season is year round, there's a good chance they just didn't want that particular action yesterday.
Not a big deal, I was still able to catch plenty of fish! This stretch of river is loaded, and if bass fishing isn't necessarily your thing, bring your ultralight gear. There are plenty of bluegill and even crappie in the trees along the banks. Yesterday, I was able to see gar that were spawning. They were chasing every type of lure I had, and I even hooked up to a couple! If you wanted to go catch gar, on purpose, this would be a good place. This stretch of river is loaded, and they hangout near the surface.
You can paddle more than a mile, before you reach the golf course. That's Old Fort golf course, and there is a bridge, for the golfers to drive over the river. I go up there to clean up golf balls, feel free to take as many as you would like! From what I can tell, it's perfectly okay for us to do this, I've never been discouraged in any way. I'm 100% certain we can be on this body of water because it's public. I'm 100% certain we can access this location from the greenway, because it's public. I'm not 100% certain we can gather these golf balls, but I do it anyway.
This is a long stretch of river that starts out deep, but after you paddle a couple of miles up to the golf course, becomes very shallow. It has every type of structure, from limestone cliffs to deep underwater trees. It's quickly becoming one of my favorite places to go bass fishing, especially when I know I don't have much time. I can easily get in, and get out, and get some fish. It's also a two-for-one location!
In the parking lot at Manson Pike trailhead, there is a boat ramp. You cannot access upstream, in this area, but you can access downstream areas. Right now, with all the rain we are receiving, the water will be a little swift, so it's going to be tough to paddle back up to the boat ramp. During the heat of the summer, when the river slows back down, you can launch from the boat ramp in this parking lot, and go downstream a little more than a mile. Then, you can easily paddle back upstream. There's nothing in your way to prohibit you from moving around. And the first shallow water is a little more than a mile away, so you don't have to go over any rapids, and you can easily make your way back to your vehicle.
This boat ramp is also where you would start one of the most adventurous trips in Middle Tennessee. In the heart of Murfreesboro, on the West Fork stones river, there are a couple of rapids that have steep drops, and make for an exciting adventure! My friends and I do not take this stretch of river, because the first time we did, I flipped my kayak, and lost a bunch of my fishing gear. It's not unsafe, it's just a steep drop, and it's a 5 out of five on the effort scale of one to five. You have to be a good kayaker, and even then, you may still flip your kayak.
If you're considering doing this trip, it's a little less than 5 miles long, and you will put in at Manson Pike trailhead, and you will take out at Thompson Lane trailhead...
Thompson Lane Trailhead https://share.google/FfECpfPmNNU7es7fn
Under no circumstances should this be your first ever downstream trip. You should become proficient in using a kayak before you ever attempt to do this stretch of water. For what it's worth, the majority of the trip, isn't very challenging, just a couple of spots, right in the center of town. If you can handle these rapids, you will be able to handle every waterway that I kayak middle Tennessee. Nothing is more technical, or difficult, then these couple of rapids.

Under no circumstances should this be your first ever downstream trip. You should become proficient in using a kayak before you ever attempt to do this stretch of water. For what it's worth, the majority of the trip, isn't very challenging, just a couple of spots, right in the center of town. If you can handle these rapids, you will be able to handle every waterway that I kayak middle Tennessee. Nothing is more technical, or difficult, then these couple of rapids.

title: Trip Report #37
content_raw:
The fish you're not supposed to target...
Yesterday, I went back to Center Hill dam, to try to target those walleye. I went the day before, at night time. Fished all night long, saw walleye everywhere, but couldn't catch any. Then I decided to change my tactic. I was going to go the following night, but instead, opted for a daytime trip. Here's my reasoning. At night, those fish were spread out, from the steps, to the waterfall, and everywhere in between. During the daytime, you can still see in the water! As you paddle around during the day, you noticed that they are not in those locations. It's a little too shallow, it would be easy for people or predators to see them, and I don't think their eyes are fond of the bright light from the sunshine. During the daytime, they all move to the safety of the deep hole, directly in front of the dam.
My plan was to put an anchor in that spot, directly in the middle, in front of the dam, and sit there and fish for walleye. There were three ways that I caught them pretty consistently last year. First and foremost, I was using a Ned rig on bottom. Just a peanut butter jelly Ned rig, with an ultra light setup with 6 pound monofilament. Typically, I use a 1/10 of an ounce jig head, but just about anything will do. I like to let it sit on the bottom, and then occasionally, twitch it around. Vertical jigging, is one of the tried and true methods for getting walleye, and last year, I was doing it very successfully, most of the time, catching one on my first cast!
I was also trolling quite effectively. Using a Berkeley flicker shad, I would simply paddle around in a big circle, and drag those lures behind me. Usually two of them. One day I caught 15! Fast forward to this year, I still haven't caught one using either one of those methods.
The other way I was getting them, not as often, but fairly consistently, was to drop a worm, directly under my boat or kayak, and let it sit near the bottom, or on the bottom. That worked out great! Until it didn't. Last year, the only types of fish that I would catch doing that were my target species, walleye, and the occasional bluegill. This year, the first time I dropped a worm down to the bottom, I hooked into a 4 foot long sturgeon.
Of course I was using my ultralight rod and reel. I only had 4 pound monofilament. The fight was 37 minutes, and ultimately, I had that sturgeon in my lap, in the kayak. It was the fight of a lifetime, it was a true test of my gear, and the knot that I had tied onto my hook. It was a tremendous amount of fun, and it's illegal to do it intentionally. Unfortunately, the state of Tennessee has determined that targeting sturgeon, is illegal. Fortunately for me, I was targeting walleye. I only mention this, so that you know the rules and regulations. If you find yourself hooked up with a sturgeon, it was always accidental! There is no reason to tell anyone that you had any intention other than trying to catch a catfish or a walleye or some other type of fish. In reality, you're not going to be able to set live bait anywhere near the bottom of that river, without the chance of catching a sturgeon.
So what now? Well, these walleye are in that river, for the long haul. They literally won't turn around and go downstream until September. We typically fish for them all summer long, and even when you catch a bunch, and keep them, new fish keep coming up from downstream. The Caney Fork river flows into Old hickory lake, and if you are not aware, that is where the world record walleye comes from. Every year, the TWRA stocks thousands, if not hundreds of thousands of walleye, in the Cumberland river/ Old hickory Lake. For those of you who don't know, the Cumberland River has several different dams and lakes through middle Tennessee. Old hickory dam, in Nashville, backs up the Cumberland River all the way to Cordell Hull Dam. The Caney Fork dumps into the Cumberland / Old Hickory, just below Cordell Hull Dam. That's why it constantly replenishes itself with fish. They are able to come upstream, and if there are not already too many fish there, they will stay, because it's nice for them.
My next course of action will be dictated by the rain. We have lots of rain in the forecast, thank goodness! I will utilize breaks in the rain to go fishing. Whenever I find a long break, that's when I will get out to target these fish. I plan to use some spoons to do some vertical jigging, as well as some soft plastics along the bottom. I may even get a quarter pound of minnows to try and tempt them with live bait. I just need to get the ball rolling, and get a few walleye on the stringer, to build my confidence. That's the way it works! You've got to figure something out!

title: Trip Report #38
content_raw:
A hard Day's night...
Last night, I got to Center Hill Dam at about 10:30 p.m...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/D5M4QanQ202PjNRq7
I launched my kayak in the dark, and planned on fishing for walleye, while the generators are off. If you go in a kayak, below Center Hill dam, while the generators are off, it's as easy as it gets! A one out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. To find the generating schedule from Center Hill dam, you can look here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
The best part about fishing for walleye below Center Hill Dam is the clearwater. Because the water is clear, and shallow, the headlamp that you use to see what you are doing will show you where the walleye are! Their eyes light up like cats in the dark. When you see them, they are typically schooled together, unless they are really big, those are roaming around by themselves. Last night, walleye were everywhere! From the steps, where you could easily fish for them from the bank, all the way over to the corner by the waterfall, and everywhere in between. Here is a link to where you can park to fish for walleye at night, from the steps, if you would like to...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/1L5cVBh9i9d1ZNpd6
I fished all night, until it got light out this morning. I was there for 7 hours, and I could not make a walleye bite. In the past, I have always used a Berkeley flicker shad...
https://amzn.to/43gy7tt
I'm a little early in the season right now, but the fish are already there. I tried doing what I did last year, last night. Last year, around the middle of july, I was able to put one of these Berkeley flicker shad on my 6 lb monofilament with an ultralight, cast it behind the kayak, and then troll around in a circle below the dam. On one day alone, I caught 15 walleye doing this.
Another incredibly successful method for me, last summer, was simply throwing a peanut butter jelly Ned rig on the bottom...
https://amzn.to/4eQfMKZ
You can put those on any type of jig head, but I prefer these specific jig heads...
https://amzn.to/4v0KExh
Once again, last year, all I had to do was throw that thing on the bottom, in the deepest part below the dam, about 18 feet of water, and leave it down there and jiggle it around, until I caught one. I can't tell you how many times I went out there and caught a walleye on my first cast doing that.
I tried both of those methods, extensively last night, but didn't have any luck. I also tried a method that I typically only employ at night... Running a traditional rapala slowly, with twitches and pauses, like you're supposed to for walleye...
https://amzn.to/4tHA1Ow
Nothing that I did could attract the bite of a walleye. I don't even think I got a single bite! I know I can catch these fish, I've limited out several times before, but last night, I just didn't have it! Fortunately for me, the night wasn't a total let down.
While I was dragging that peanut butter jelly Ned rig along the bottom, I was getting bites, and catching fish, but it was mostly largemouth bass. Each time I would hook up, I would get excited, and think that I might have a walleye. Each time, it would be a bass. One of them was a pretty large smallmouth, and a few of them, jumped into the air, and spit the hook. I wasn't necessarily trying to catch bass, so I wasn't giving a very big hook set. Typically, you don't need much of a hook set to stick a walleye. They won't jump out of the air, and try to spit your lure, like a bass will.
While using my headlamp to look for walleye, I noticed lots of different schools of largemouth bass. Really big fish! It's that time of year, where I like to go bass fishing at night, below Center Hill dam. I usually don't get started this early in the season, but the bass came up, earlier this year. It's a good thing! If you would like to go out there and try to get some walleye, even if you're striking out, you should be able to catch some bass, if you just keep a soft plastic, slow and low, on the bottom. You don't have to use a Ned rig, you could use a soft plastic worm on a Texas rig or a Carolina rig if you would like. That should do the trick!

title: Trip Report #39
content_raw:
A magical confluence on the Caney Fork River called Sebowisha...
There's a 99 mile long creek that is completely uninterrupted by dams, and flows unencumbered, into the Caney Fork River below Betty's Island Access. This is the Smith Fork creek, and even though it holds untold numbers of really large smallmouth bass, it's almost impossible to fish, because the entire length is all private property. The only way that I'm ever able to legally fish the Smith Fork, without trespassing, is to paddle up the mouth of the creek. That trip is something that I look forward to every summer, as it can only be facilitated when the water is down. Going up the creek, when the water is down, would not be possible for any sizable type of boat, even most jet boats won't make it up.
The area at the confluence of the Smith fork and the Caney Fork is a magical place known as Sebowisha. There's a lot of controversy about how the area got the name, none of that really matters. That's the name of the area at the confluence. Not unlike most river confluence in the state of tennessee, it is a fantastic place to target fish! Seems like they are always hanging out there. Mostly, I like to target smallmouth bass.
When most people think about kayaking the Caney Fork river, they think about trout fishing. We caught a lot of trout yesterday when we did this trip, but the main attraction is fishing for bass in the first half mile, up that creek. The water in the Caney Fork River is cold, and the water coming out of the creek is a little warmer. The fish that find the creek, make their way into that shallow, warm water, to feed, mostly on top water! When I go on this trip, and I paddle up the Smith Fork creek, I usually fish with a Whopper plopper, because that's the type of action they are looking for, this time of year, in this location.
They didn't let us down yesterday! I had three buddies with me, and the four of us paddled up this creek, and then back down, and all of us caught nice bass! But if you don't get the timing just right, it's not going to work out that way. Timing is everything! You're almost always going to have to do this trip on the weekend, because they usually run the generators during the week, for electricity. On the weekend, they usually reduce generating schedules so that people can do more recreational activities, like this one! Here's how you can work out the timing...
Saturday and Sunday of this weekend, they ran their typical weekend generating pattern, that they do in the summertime, provided there's not much electrical demand, or flooding. On a typical summer Saturday and Sunday, they will run one generator for 1 hour, every 8 hours. Those short bursts of water, will not fill the river, and that keeps the levels low, so that people can kayak, and wade fish. The farther away from the damn you are, the less impactful the generating water will be. It will rise slowly, it won't rush as fast, or get as high, and it will fall slowly. Where we started our trip, was significantly downstream, mitigating how much generating water would affect us, 9 miles away from the dam on the river, at Betty's Island Access...
https://share.google/g46naPWhy88lmJC3c
This boat ramp is a little more than a mile upstream from the confluence at the Smith Fork Creek. That makes it the ideal location to load your kayak, so you can float down, and do some fishing. Unfortunately, when the water is down, you either need a truck to drive out on the riverbed, or you will have to carry your kayak a long way! The boat ramp doesn't go to the water's edge, when the water is down. I was able to drive out there with my suv, and we put our kayaks on the side of the river, which made it an easy launch. If you do not have a high profile truck or suv, you will not be able to drive out there, or you may get stuck. That makes this trip difficult, if you don't have the right vehicle. With the right vehicle, loading and unloading is as easy as it gets, a one out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. It will be more difficult if you have to carry your kayak to the water's edge from the boat ramp.
Now you know what generating schedule to look for, and you know where to start your trip. You know you're going to the confluence to try to catch smallmouth bass, and that top water will do the trick, but you should be prepared to use other lures. Yesterday, the biggest fish of the day, was caught on a drop shot plastic worm. If you don't know, that's a soft plastic worm, with the sinker, below the worm. Basically, you tie a hook on the line and leave a long leader, and then you attach a drop shot sinker to the end of the line, leaving the plastic worm suspended, about a foot off the river bed, when you drop it to the bottom. Any type of bass lure will work, we just usually use top water.
From beginning to end, this trip is loaded with trout! It is, a trout river after all. We were able to catch trout all day, mostly using rooster tails. I like a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail, or, if the fish are being particularly aggressive, I will use a 1/6 of an ounce white rooster tail. Either way, I don't go to the Caney Fork River without white rooster tails. Yesterday, the fish were biting really well, so I opted for the bigger, 1/6 of an ounce, white rooster tail. The reason I do that, is because with the heavier weight, I can run it faster. The lightweight lure, when you start to run it faster, it comes up to the surface. A heavier lure, will stay down lower, in the water column, and allow you to run it faster. Aggressive fish, like to strike at things as it moves by, quickly!
There are only a couple of rapids on this trip that are "kinda" tough to navigate. Lots of beginners do this trip, every weekend, but most of the time, they aren't in fishing kayaks with hundreds, or even thousands of dollars worth of gear. That's something that I have never mentioned before, that I suggest all kayak fishermen, including myself, should consider doing. When kayaking a new stretch of river, it's probably a good idea to take a minimum amount of gear! It just now dawned on me, as I was about to suggest that you do the same. If it's your first time taking this trip, consider taking two fishing poles, instead of three or four. Consider taking a small tackle pack that floats, and some essential gear, to do a scouting trip. That way, if you encounter water that you can't handle, or you flip your kayak, you won't have as much to lose.
I don't think that's going to be an issue on this trip! This is flat water, except for a couple little spots, that are relatively easy to navigate. However, it is a long trip! Because you want to do this trip when they are not generating much water, you are going to have to paddle, most of the 6 miles. This stretch of the river is wide, and when they are not pushing water, it moves slow, or sometimes not at all. You will feel every bit of those six miles, so be prepared! We like to pack a lunch, we always stay out there all day.
The end of the trip is a boat ramp that actually goes into the water, even when the water is all the way down! It's a fantastic boat ramp, and it's relatively safe! It's in the town of Gordonsville, and the police regularly patrol the area. It's even got a really cool name, Stonewall boat ramp...
Stone Wall Boat Ramp (Gordonsville Access) https://share.google/rICHqRet1gXsKdgPn
Now, I'm going to try to explain how the timing with the generators works. For simplicity's sake, most stuff happens in threes on the Caney Fork river. For example, the first boat ramp, happy hollow, is 6 miles from the dam. The second boat ramp, where we started our trip yesterday, Betty's Island access, is 9 miles from the dam. Stonewall boat ramp, where we ended our trip, is 15 miles from the dam. When they release water from the generators, that water travels a little more than 3 mph. To keep everything with even numbers, most of us just use 3 mph as a general rule of thumb.
That means, after 2 hours, the water out of Center Hill dam, we'll have reached the six Mile boat ramp, or, Happy Hollow boat ramp. And 1 hour later, 3 hours after release from the dam, the water will reach Betty's Island Access. In reality, it's a few minutes before that, but it's really easy to understand, if you use those metrics. That would mean, 15 miles away from the dam, where we ended our trip, the generating water won't show up for 5 hours after release.
Knowing how fast the water arrives to any given location is one of the greatest factors for my success on this river. It takes years of study, to finally understand exactly how everything works. Once you understand, it's powerful knowledge, because things don't change. The water always moves at a predictable pace, and arrives right on time! For example, yesterday, they were scheduled to generate one generator, for 1 hour, from 11:00 a.m. until noon. We were 1 mile downstream from Betty's Island access, at the confluence. That means we were 10 miles away from the dam. That means it was going to take a little more than 3 hours to get to us. Sure enough, right around 2:30 in the afternoon, that short burst of generating water began to arrive.
Having just finished lunch, and packed up all our kayaks for the day, we rode that wave of water, for the next 5 miles, down to the boat ramp at stonewall. That push of water, if you paddle alongside, don't get out ahead, and don't fall too far behind, we'll take you all the way down there, but you have to move at that three mile per hour pace. If you go any slower, it will move ahead of you, leaving you in still water. If you go any faster, you will outpace it, and find yourself in still water. After a long morning of fishing, and hanging out with your friends, it's nice to not have to paddle very hard to cover those last few miles.
While we floated downstream, we continued to throw those rooster tails, and catch trout. One thing I know about the trout on the Caney Fork river, for sure, is that they don't like that afternoon, low light condition. Around 4:00 p.m., as the sun started to fall behind the trees, and not shine directly on the surface any longer, we couldn't get any more bites. After catching fish non-stop, while floating down the river, as soon as the sun quit shining on the surface, the bite quit as well.

Saturday and Sunday of this weekend, they ran their typical weekend generating pattern, that they do in the summertime, provided there's not much electrical demand, or flooding. On a typical summer Saturday and Sunday, they will run one generator for 1 hour, every 8 hours. Those short bursts of water, will not fill the river, and that keeps the levels low, so that people can kayak, and wade fish. The farther away from the damn you are, the less impactful the generating water will be. It will rise slowly, it won't rush as fast, or get as high, and it will fall slowly. Where we started our trip, was significantly downstream, mitigating how much generating water would affect us, 9 miles away from the dam on the river, at Betty's Island Access...

https://share.google/g46naPWhy88lmJC3c

This boat ramp is a little more than a mile upstream from the confluence at the Smith Fork Creek. That makes it the ideal location to load your kayak, so you can float down, and do some fishing. Unfortunately, when the water is down, you either need a truck to drive out on the riverbed, or you will have to carry your kayak a long way! The boat ramp doesn't go to the water's edge, when the water is down. I was able to drive out there with my suv, and we put our kayaks on the side of the river, which made it an easy launch. If you do not have a high profile truck or suv, you will not be able to drive out there, or you may get stuck. That makes this trip difficult, if you don't have the right vehicle. With the right vehicle, loading and unloading is as easy as it gets, a one out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. It will be more difficult if you have to carry your kayak to the water's edge from the boat ramp.

Now you know what generating schedule to look for, and you know where to start your trip. You know you're going to the confluence to try to catch smallmouth bass, and that top water will do the trick, but you should be prepared to use other lures. Yesterday, the biggest fish of the day, was caught on a drop shot plastic worm. If you don't know, that's a soft plastic worm, with the sinker, below the worm. Basically, you tie a hook on the line and leave a long leader, and then you attach a drop shot sinker to the end of the line, leaving the plastic worm suspended, about a foot off the river bed, when you drop it to the bottom. Any type of bass lure will work, we just usually use top water.

From beginning to end, this trip is loaded with trout! It is, a trout river after all. We were able to catch trout all day, mostly using rooster tails. I like a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail, or, if the fish are being particularly aggressive, I will use a 1/6 of an ounce white rooster tail. Either way, I don't go to the Caney Fork River without white rooster tails. Yesterday, the fish were biting really well, so I opted for the bigger, 1/6 of an ounce, white rooster tail. The reason I do that, is because with the heavier weight, I can run it faster. The lightweight lure, when you start to run it faster, it comes up to the surface. A heavier lure, will stay down lower, in the water column, and allow you to run it faster. Aggressive fish, like to strike at things as it moves by, quickly!

There are only a couple of rapids on this trip that are "kinda" tough to navigate. Lots of beginners do this trip, every weekend, but most of the time, they aren't in fishing kayaks with hundreds, or even thousands of dollars worth of gear. That's something that I have never mentioned before, that I suggest all kayak fishermen, including myself, should consider doing. When kayaking a new stretch of river, it's probably a good idea to take a minimum amount of gear! It just now dawned on me, as I was about to suggest that you do the same. If it's your first time taking this trip, consider taking two fishing poles, instead of three or four. Consider taking a small tackle pack that floats, and some essential gear, to do a scouting trip. That way, if you encounter water that you can't handle, or you flip your kayak, you won't have as much to lose.

I don't think that's going to be an issue on this trip! This is flat water, except for a couple little spots, that are relatively easy to navigate. However, it is a long trip! Because you want to do this trip when they are not generating much water, you are going to have to paddle, most of the 6 miles. This stretch of the river is wide, and when they are not pushing water, it moves slow, or sometimes not at all. You will feel every bit of those six miles, so be prepared! We like to pack a lunch, we always stay out there all day.

The end of the trip is a boat ramp that actually goes into the water, even when the water is all the way down! It's a fantastic boat ramp, and it's relatively safe! It's in the town of Gordonsville, and the police regularly patrol the area. It's even got a really cool name, Stonewall boat ramp...

Stone Wall Boat Ramp (Gordonsville Access) https://share.google/rICHqRet1gXsKdgPn

Now, I'm going to try to explain how the timing with the generators works. For simplicity's sake, most stuff happens in threes on the Caney Fork river. For example, the first boat ramp, happy hollow, is 6 miles from the dam. The second boat ramp, where we started our trip yesterday, Betty's Island access, is 9 miles from the dam. Stonewall boat ramp, where we ended our trip, is 15 miles from the dam. When they release water from the generators, that water travels a little more than 3 mph. To keep everything with even numbers, most of us just use 3 mph as a general rule of thumb.

That means, after 2 hours, the water out of Center Hill dam, we'll have reached the six Mile boat ramp, or, Happy Hollow boat ramp. And 1 hour later, 3 hours after release from the dam, the water will reach Betty's Island Access. In reality, it's a few minutes before that, but it's really easy to understand, if you use those metrics. That would mean, 15 miles away from the dam, where we ended our trip, the generating water won't show up for 5 hours after release.

Knowing how fast the water arrives to any given location is one of the greatest factors for my success on this river. It takes years of study, to finally understand exactly how everything works. Once you understand, it's powerful knowledge, because things don't change. The water always moves at a predictable pace, and arrives right on time! For example, yesterday, they were scheduled to generate one generator, for 1 hour, from 11:00 a.m. until noon. We were 1 mile downstream from Betty's Island access, at the confluence. That means we were 10 miles away from the dam. That means it was going to take a little more than 3 hours to get to us. Sure enough, right around 2:30 in the afternoon, that short burst of generating water began to arrive.

Having just finished lunch, and packed up all our kayaks for the day, we rode that wave of water, for the next 5 miles, down to the boat ramp at stonewall. That push of water, if you paddle alongside, don't get out ahead, and don't fall too far behind, we'll take you all the way down there, but you have to move at that three mile per hour pace. If you go any slower, it will move ahead of you, leaving you in still water. If you go any faster, you will outpace it, and find yourself in still water. After a long morning of fishing, and hanging out with your friends, it's nice to not have to paddle very hard to cover those last few miles.

While we floated downstream, we continued to throw those rooster tails, and catch trout. One thing I know about the trout on the Caney Fork river, for sure, is that they don't like that afternoon, low light condition. Around 4:00 p.m., as the sun started to fall behind the trees, and not shine directly on the surface any longer, we couldn't get any more bites. After catching fish non-stop, while floating down the river, as soon as the sun quit shining on the surface, the bite quit as well.

title: Trip Report #41
content_raw:
I told you at the end of April to save the date, we're doing a meet and greet this Saturday, May 16th! The time has come, and the final arrangements have been made. I've settled on a location where we can picnic in the shade, there's plenty of parking, people can fish from the bank, there is a boat ramp for people who would like to meet and greet, and then go out on their boat, and there is even a men's and women's restroom!
We're going to meet at Fate Sanders recreation area...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/F86RrZGWhehcwNWk9
I'm going to get there early so that I can pick a premium location and get set up. I will get there just before 8:00 a.m. and be ready to go at 8:00. I'm planning on meeting, and greeting, anyone who would like to show up early, and then take off, to enjoy their day. From 8:00 a.m. until 11:00 a.m. we can hang out. I will answer any type of fishing questions that you have, so come prepared! There is no information that I covet, I will share anything and everything I know with you guys!
Not sure how the generating schedules work, I will be glad to explain it. Want me to investigate a particular body of water or a certain lake, you got it, just say the word! Tomorrow is your day, to have full access! I try to include all the pertinent information in my Pro reports, but there's still so much information that I haven't gotten out, if there's any amount of information that you are seeking, I will do my best to help  figure it out.
At 11:00, I'm going to start preparing some lunch for myself and my parents. I have invited them to come down to have lunch in the park, and if you're so inclined, there are several other picnic tables with grills that are available. There are probably half a dozen or more picnic tables with grills, so there should be plenty of space for anyone who would like to stay and have lunch. I won't be providing lunch for anyone, except for myself and my parents. We will be staying to have lunch, and I hope you do as well!
If you have a boat, and would like to come to the meet and greet, you could consider bringing it! The boat ramp does not have a courtesy dock, but if you're comfortable putting your boat on the bank, or the boat ramp, it's a good place to get in and out of the lake. I went to check at 11:00 a.m. last Saturday, and there were only a handful of boat trailers in the parking lot. That was one of the biggest reasons I chose this location, there weren't many people there last Saturday. For the most part, we should have the park to ourselves.
If you have any questions at all, you can respond to this message, and I will make sure to get back to you! Hope to see you guys on Saturday!

title: Trip Report #42
content_raw:
Finally got to go fishing, twice...
I've had a lot of responsibility so far this May, and I haven't been able to do as much fishing as I would like. Yesterday, for the first time in a while, I got a chance to double dip, on two different fishing trips in one day. There was a unique set of circumstances that presented itself as Center Hill dam, so my buddy and I floated the first 6 miles of the Caney Fork River, in kayaks, from Center Hill Dam at Buffalo valley boat ramp to Happy Hollow boat ramp...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/o0UfD1h5FBSd0dC5f
Happy Hollow Boat Ramp https://share.google/hcANC5RamrD1L7sFj
As of right now, 6:00 a.m. on Wednesday May 13th, the generators are on, and we would not be able to facilitate the trip that we did yesterday. That's typical for this time of year. They usually don't have the generators off, in the morning, during the warm months. The only exception, is on the weekends, when they turn the generators off, to allow for recreational activities. Yesterday, they were running their summertime weekend pattern during a weekday, so we took full advantage!
There was only one generator on for 1 hour from 6:00 a.m. until 7:00 a.m. and then it was turned off until 1:00 p.m. that gave us a 6-hour window with the generators off, where we could float down the river, and catch trout. Unfortunately, yesterday wasn't a fantastic day of trout fishing. My tried and true method of using a worm on bottom wasn't getting any attention at all! We ended up catching probably a dozen fish, and most of them came on the rooster tail. I was throwing my favorite, 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail with a silver blade, but my buddy was having better luck, with his 1/8 of an ounce black rooster tail with a silver blade.
Before he got there, I had a little time to fish below the dam by myself. Even though the water was off, and the level was down, I headed over to the corner by the waterfalls to see if I could catch a crappie. This time of year, there are so many crappie in there, you never know. Typically, I like for the generators to be on to fish in the corner for crappie, but when there are great numbers, you might be able to get them, just about anywhere below the dam. That was the case yesterday! I was able to catch crappie in the corner, with the water all the way down. Using a Bobby garland, and a slow retrieve, that's all it takes!
The generators turned on at 1:00 p.m., and we had paddled almost all of the six miles to Happy Hollow. Just before we got to the boat ramp, the water caught up to us, and started overtaking the island below Happy Hollow boat ramp. If you don't know, or haven't been, when the water is off, the boat ramp will allow you to drive out onto dry ground. That's where you can load and unload your kayaks. As we were loading up, at 3:00 p.m., the water was coming up, covering the area. We got out of there just in time, exactly as I planned, because the water moves predictably, each time it is released. You can expect it to overtake the Happy Hollow area, 2 hours after the dam starts releasing water. If you get out of there, before then, you are good to go! If you wait any longer, it may be difficult to get out, and you may have to load your kayak, on the boat ramp. That's not necessarily a bad thing, that's what they're for!
This trip is as easy as it gets. I would rank it as a one out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. You can drop your boat on the water's edge at the beginning, drop your boat on the water's edge at the end, and float on flat water. If you choose to go out when the generators are on, this trip is as hard as it gets! The generators are merciless! They never stop, the water is incredibly swift, and really cold. I wouldn't suggest this trip for anyone who doesn't know how to read the generating schedule. You can find the link to the Center Hill Dam generating schedule, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
As soon as I got home, I grabbed my boat, and headed over to Stewart Creek boat ramp...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/qqGQQyhkhNgs5pLOL
I know the crappie have been starting to gather together on fish attractors at every depth, so I wanted to go out and get some, before sunset. Mission accomplished! The first spot I headed to was directly across the lake near the Poole Knob area. It's directly across from Fate Sanders marina, that I have some pins dropped in a cove where there are some fish attractors.
https://goo.gl/maps/uJvqqGJBGkpYf6f66
https://goo.gl/maps/1B12JnSqFChRSGu38
https://goo.gl/maps/Y9rafEw3oW2mUjYLA
These spots were loaded! I hit so many yesterday I can't recall the depth of every location, but I remember they were all different! From 40 feet of water, hanging out at 25 feet of depth to 8 ft of water from the bottom to the surface, these fish were scattered all over different types of structure, and all over different depths. I caught some really nice crappie at this location, and then headed to another one around the river's bend Island area...
https://goo.gl/maps/zs77M6sLCPBHiyBM7
https://goo.gl/maps/TkqyYiAdEpEjKng7A
I caught crappie at both locations, and they were keepers at both locations! So now that I had a few crappie on the stringer, I tried to do a little bass fishing on this backside of Rivers Bend island. I usually catch bass pretty well on top water here, but I only had one blow up and one hook up. So I headed over to some really deep structure on the cliffs near Poole Knob boat ramp...
https://goo.gl/maps/CC5YNPBH2YH4zqSD9
This spot was loaded as well, but by this point it was getting so dark, that I wanted to head back, so I could get off the lake. I only fished for a little while, and then made my way home. We have other pins in this area that I passed, I just wanted to check these particular ones. I had a feeling they would be loaded, and I was right! For what it's worth, the fish were relatively large, most of the fish that I caught were keepers, I only threw a couple little ones back. That's what these fish will do all summer, they will school together, in great numbers, and they will be easy for us to find, and catch!

You can expect it to overtake the Happy Hollow area, 2 hours after the dam starts releasing water. If you get out of there, before then, you are good to go! If you wait any longer, it may be difficult to get out, and you may have to load your kayak, on the boat ramp. That's not necessarily a bad thing, that's what they're for!

This trip is as easy as it gets. I would rank it as a one out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. You can drop your boat on the water's edge at the beginning, drop your boat on the water's edge at the end, and float on flat water. If you choose to go out when the generators are on, this trip is as hard as it gets! The generators are merciless! They never stop, the water is incredibly swift, and really cold. I wouldn't suggest this trip for anyone who doesn't know how to read the generating schedule. You can find the link to the Center Hill Dam generating schedule, here...

https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill

As soon as I got home, I grabbed my boat, and headed over to Stewart Creek boat ramp...

Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/qqGQQyhkhNgs5pLOL

I know the crappie have been starting to gather together on fish attractors at every depth, so I wanted to go out and get some, before sunset. Mission accomplished! The first spot I headed to was directly across the lake near the Poole Knob area. It's directly across from Fate Sanders marina, that I have some pins dropped in a cove where there are some fish attractors.

https://goo.gl/maps/uJvqqGJBGkpYf6f66

https://goo.gl/maps/1B12JnSqFChRSGu38

https://goo.gl/maps/Y9rafEw3oW2mUjYLA

These spots were loaded! I hit so many yesterday I can't recall the depth of every location, but I remember they were all different! From 40 feet of water, hanging out at 25 feet of depth to 8 ft of water from the bottom to the surface, these fish were scattered all over different types of structure, and all over different depths. I caught some really nice crappie at this location, and then headed to another one around the river's bend Island area...

https://goo.gl/maps/zs77M6sLCPBHiyBM7

https://goo.gl/maps/TkqyYiAdEpEjKng7A

I caught crappie at both locations, and they were keepers at both locations! So now that I had a few crappie on the stringer, I tried to do a little bass fishing on this backside of Rivers Bend island. I usually catch bass pretty well on top water here, but I only had one blow up and one hook up. So I headed over to some really deep structure on the cliffs near Poole Knob boat ramp...

https://goo.gl/maps/CC5YNPBH2YH4zqSD9

This spot was loaded as well, but by this point it was getting so dark, that I wanted to head back, so I could get off the lake. I only fished for a little while, and then made my way home. We have other pins in this area that I passed, I just wanted to check these particular ones. I had a feeling they would be loaded, and I was right! For what it's worth, the fish were relatively large, most of the fish that I caught were keepers, I only threw a couple little ones back. That's what these fish will do all summer, they will school together, in great numbers, and they will be easy for us to find, and catch!
