title: Trip Report #43
content_raw:
Calling all kayakers!
Most rivers don't have great access for kayak fishing. Public launch points, like boat ramps and parking lots are hard to come by. Most rivers, only have a couple public access points, if any at all. Today, I started my work on the Buffalo river, which has lots of access!
The Buffalo River is like the Piney river, except it's gigantic! If you've ever been to the Piney river, you know that it's small, and clear, and beautiful. The Buffalo River is all of those things, except small! It has lots of twists and turns, and lots of backwater areas that are loaded with fish!
There are lots of public access locations on this river. Too many to list in one pro report. Today, I'm going to focus on the five mile stretch of river that I did in Linden, Tennessee.
First of all, I planned my adventure to be a solo trip, so I was going to utilize the services of "honeyhole camping"...
https://www.facebook.com/share/g/1CZGQfiCvu/
That is a link to the Facebook group for honey hole camping. Basically, it's a nice lady named Danielle, that owns a small piece of property on the side of the river, that has a boat ramp. She allows you to park there, and she will shuttle you, upstream, so that you can float back down to your vehicle. What I did, was go to the put in location, drop off my kayak, and then drive to her spot, and park my vehicle. Then, she drove me back up to the boat ramp, where my kayak was eagerly waiting. I planned to use her, because that service is great for someone if they are by themselves. I didn't know, last second, my buddy was going to tag along. For the two of us to be shuttled up to our kayaks, it was only $20.
Her location, where you take out, is a primitive boat ramp. That means it's made of mostly gravel. It's a little steep, but it's a great takeout spot! The location where you put in, is an actual boat ramp! It is concrete, it is public, and the parking lot is big enough for lots of vehicles. You could put in a boat, but it would have to be a jet boat. There is zero chance that you would get up or down this river with a traditional propeller. The location where you put in, is wide, and relatively deep, which means it's not very swift, and it's easy to launch. Here is a PIN to the public boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/VR6yYnXgGydb425c9
As far as kayak trips go, this one is fantastic! Lots of beautiful scenery, and a perfect length, 5 miles. Any less is not enough for a full day's trip, and much more than that, is too long of a day. This is the ideal length for weekend warriors! On the effort scale of 1 to 5, the put in and the takeout are both about as easy as it can get. Where you put in, you can back your vehicle all the way to the water's edge. Where you take out, it's a little steep, and if you don't have four wheel drive, you might not want to back down. On an effort scale of one to five, I would give this trip a two, based simply on that fact. You will have to carry your kayak a little, or have four-wheel drive. Other than that, there are no rapids that have drops or surprise boulders in the way. There was a tree in the way, but only because we went the wrong way! We clearly should have gone right, and we went left. We will know better next time, but it was pretty obvious, so most people wouldn't make that mistake. Fortunately for us, we were able to limbo under the tree. That's because the water wasn't too swift.
I talk about this a lot, it's probably the most important aspect of kayak fishing. Cubic feet per second. The way we measure rivers, is cubic feet per second. One cubic foot, is about the size of one basketball. Today, before I started this trip, this stretch of the Buffalo River was measured right around 840 cubic feet per second. That means, in one second, about 840 basketballs worth of water pass by the monitoring location. Knowing that number is crucial! I have been out to this River before, and I know that it is safe, even when it is at 1,000 cubic feet per second. That number would be devastating on most small rivers. It would be a class four or a class five rapid. Out there, on that wide, sometimes deep, river, it was the perfect amount of flow to make sure that we didn't have to paddle too much, but still allowed us to slow down and fish, as much as we would like. You can find the flow of the Buffalo River on the USGS chart, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03604400/all-graphs/#period=P7D
As of 7:30 on Monday May 11th, while I'm writing this report, the river has dropped significantly since the last time I checked, yesterday evening. Currently, the cubic feet per second are around 770. That's great! Realistically, the lower it goes, the better it will be. The obstacles that are in the water, like downed trees, won't come at you as fast, and you will be able to fish, what equates to, a lazy river. With no rain in the forecast for the next 10 days, it should only get better!
I asked Danielle if she would like me to give out her phone number. She did not. She will give you her phone number, but she wants you to interact with her through that Facebook page. She is fantastic, the service you provides is invaluable, and this stretch of river is stunning!
There are a few more outfitters on this river that will either rent you a kayak or shuttle yours. I will be going out there several times in the next few weeks, to try to inform you of all the different locations that I can find. I already have a couple in mind.
I wish I could tell you there was some kind of magic secret or perfect lure, but the reality is, I'm still throwing that same purple spinnerbait. It worked for me all day, again today. If you don't recall, or haven't heard, they sell $1 spinner baits on the shelf at walmart, and I've been buying the purple one with two silver blades. I've been throwing it since the fall, and I just can't put it down. I tried top water, a Ned rig, a weightless fluke among other lures, but they just weren't effective. The best thing I've had going, lately, has been that little spinnerbait.
The blades work pretty well to make it weedless, so I throw into heavy cover, and bring that thing through the grass, and over logs and tree limbs. It doesn't work in crystal clear water, because you need to trick these fish. As long as there is a little bit of tint, and you run this thing through those types of areas, they will come out and smash it! Most of the time, you can see them, which makes it that much more exciting. That was the case today, the fish were coming out, from under the tree limbs, to take the bait!
I was having success with the spinnerbait, but my buddy was not. He was continuing to throw that Ned rig, and fish the bottom. Because the Buffalo River is much larger than other rivers that I kayak, much longer than other rivers that I kayak, and dumps into a substantial body of water, it gets filled with lots of different types of fish. We were targeting bass, but with his Ned rig, he caught not one, but two crappie! They were nowhere near each other, miles apart on the river, and it just goes to show, this river is filled with lots of different species of fish.
Speaking of different species, I caught my first ever, chain pickerel today. It was in one of the backwater areas that this river is loaded with. It was my plan, to get out of the current, into some of the coves and lagoons that are off to the side of this river. Because this river doesn't have many dams that I know of, it's still runs rather naturally. That causes it to become very wide, and reach out around the river, and fill areas in with water. As you're paddling, you can pass by an area that looks like a little creek mouth, but if you go to investigate further, you might see, that it opens up, into a small lake. Those are the types of areas, that I look forward to fishing, on this river. A few years ago, before I started my Pro reports, I caught a 5 pound largemouth in one of those locations. Today, when I went back into a backwater slew, I was throwing my spinnerbait, over some tree limbs, when I hooked my first ever chain pickerel!
At first, I thought it was a muskie, because they look almost identical. Fortunately, my buddy knew how to distinguish them, and he let me know, that it was a chain pickerel. Apparently, they're located all over, but I've never even seen one, let alone caught one. Until today! That's part of the draw of this river, we were catching plenty of bass, but we also hooked into some crappie and a brand new species checked off the list!

title: Trip Report #44
content_raw:
Happy Mother's Day!
Today, I was fortunate enough to have breakfast and lunch at my parents house before I mowed the yard for them. If you hadn't already heard, or weren't aware, both my parents had rotator cuff surgery. I've been helping them out, and I haven't been fishing as much. Today, I got up bright and early, to try to find some exciting fish for you guys to catch, mission accomplished! Here's the kicker, whether you are fishing from the bank, or you have a kayak, or you have a boat, all of you can target these fish!
This morning, I launched my boat, before sunrise, at Seven Points boat ramp...
Seven Points Boat Ramp https://share.google/pAZTGuTrnSQ7AsyOL
When I got there, at around 5:30, there were no other boats in the parking lot. No trailers, no trucks, nobody but bank fishermen. I realize it's mother's day, but there should have been some people at the boat ramp, the fish were there in great numbers, and they were going crazy!
Before we get into all that, let's talk about the boat ramp. It is safe to use this boat ramp, but it's not very steep. That means, some people will have to get wet to get their boat on and off the trailer. When you do get the boat into the water, there is a courtesy dock, but only the very end of it is in the water, and unless your boat floats really shallow, you may not be able to use it. We are still in the throes of a drought, and the lake is about 5 feet below where it should be, this time of year.
A little birdie told me that the hybrid bass, which schooling great numbers on Percy Priest lake, we're blowing up top water, in the mornings, at Seven Points. That little birdie was right! Here's how it works for everybody who's in a boat or a kayak...
When you launch, don't go left, that would be into the cove, towards shallow water, in the Viverett Creek area. You want to go out to the right, in the direction of the main lake. You don't have to go very far, it's probably not even half a mile! Right when you come around the corner, the main point, at Seven Points, that's where everybody is standing on the bank. There was only one boat when I got there this morning, but when word gets out, lots of people will be in this area! Don't get discouraged if you are trying to bank fish or fish from a boat. Most people know that these fish school heavily, in certain areas, and we all have to share that location. For the most part, everyone I have met has been very helpful, and friendly! You can expect the same. I wouldn't be afraid to pull into this area if there were 20 boats out there! There is plenty of room, and the fish were going crazy everywhere!
There is a green buoy at the point that marks the channel for that area. That's where you want to be before sunrise. I'm going to drop a pin, but you don't necessarily need to be on that pin, you just need to be in the general area, before sunrise, or 2 hours before sunset. Here is the pin...
https://goo.gl/maps/CSLgUKisnNRDn1RK8
Bank fishing this spot is a little tricky, because the closest access, is gated, until after sunrise. I believe they open the gate at 6:30 in the morning, but don't quote me on that. That's too late though! These fish were only biting from 5:30 a.m. until 6:30 a.m. after that, I switched to crappie fishing. I know one way to get there, but it's awful! It's a long way through the woods. I'm not sure how those people were there, when I got there this morning, but they were there before the gate to the recreational area had been opened. I will find out how they got there, and I will let you guys know.
Here is a pin for where everybody stands to catch hybrids and striped bass from the bank. For what it's worth, they were about 8 to 10 people out there today, and they probably caught about that many, nice sized, fish...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/aKq4ZgpF9ZLuwLAH7
If you look at the maps, you will see that the recreation area allows you to drive almost all the way to this point. But not until they open the gate. By the time the majority of the people made it out there on the bank this morning, the fish weren't biting anymore. Everyone left the bank, by 7:30 a.m. If you really wanted to, you could park at the seven points boat ramp, because there are spaces for people who don't have trailers. It's a long walk through the woods, or, if you just wanted to hoof it, and walk past the gate, into the recreation area, you can definitely do that. It's a long way, but the fishing is on fire!
I could see that the people on the bank were throwing the same lures that I was throwing. I like to use a 3/8 of an ounce jig head and a three to four inch white paddle tail swimbait. If you don't know, that's just a soft plastic, with a rounded tail, that looks like a small swimming fish when you put it on a jig, and give a steady retrieve. For these types of fish, people will give the lure lots of different action. I'm still not 100% adept at targeting striped and hybrid bass, so I try lots of different retrieves. It looked like, most of the people on the bank, were casting as far as they could, allowing the lure to sink for several seconds, before they started their retrieve. Where they are casting, is about 45 ft deep. That's where these fish are hanging out, not far from where they are standing. The people on the bank are technically on the cliff. It's an underwater cliff, so they are standing at the water's edge. Some of them stand in the water. About 15 to 20 feet in front of them, it drops off, and that's where they get the majority of their catches, directly out in front of them.
Today, the water temperature on this end of the lake was 72°! That's actually warmer than it has been on the south end of the lake, we're fishing has been a little tougher. I was hopeful I could get one on top water, because they were busting on the surface. I tried a Whopper plopper, and I could see that some people on the bank were trying that as well, but no one had any top water success. Typically, hybrid bass, we'll go crazy for a Whopper plopper. It took me awhile to figure it out, but these weren't hybrid bass, they were striped bass!
Striped bass are notoriously more finicky. They like what they like, and when they figure out what they like, they go crazy on it! Unfortunately, even though fish were busting all around, for the better part of an hour, I was only able to catch two. Fortunately, two is the legal limit! If I were keeping striped bass, which I usually do not, they would have to be over 15 inches, and you would be allowed to keep two, per day. Since both of mine were plenty long, I technically, limited out, which is always nice!
When these fish quit biting, they didn't just hang around, they left the area! Using my forward facing sonar, I could see, that all of the large fish that were previously chasing bait, had moved on, just after 7:00 a.m. I started looking around, right by the green buoy. I had seen people, anchored in that area, catching crappie. I have caught plenty of copy in that area, before I had forward facing sonar. I didn't necessarily know why, but today, I put some pieces together.
Right by that green buoy, on that pin that I dropped in the water, there is an underwater forest! On this lake, there are several places, where they did not bulldoze all of the trees to the ground. They left some standing timber, in some select areas, and this is one of those areas!
That buoy is strategically placed, because the ground comes up there. It's no longer 45 feet deep, at the most shallow spot, by that buoy, it's only about 12 feet deep. All around that underwater hump, there are standing trees. A couple of them have fallen over, and they are loaded with crappie! There were plenty of crappie, at every depth, where there was underwater structure. If the water was only 12 ft deep, but had a tree laying over, it was loaded with crappie. The same was true at every depth, all the way down to 45 feet! There was a tree, standing from 45 feet down, to 15 feet underneath the surface. From the top of it, at 15 feet, down to 25 feet, it was loaded with crappie!
This time, I could be certain they were crappie, because I caught them! I didn't have much time, because I was going to have breakfast with my parents, but I didn't need much time! Finally! Finally! Finally, these fish are coalescing together, in great numbers, on underwater structure. Now that the spawn has come to an end, they have paper thin bellies, and they are hungry again! Best part, the water temperature is still nice and cool, so they are comfortable at every different depth, which means, you should be able to find them, on most of the pins that we have, on Percy Priest lake. If those pins are under 7 feet of water, there should definitely be fish!
This time last year, that was the secret recipe. 7 feet of depth. Of course, last year, we had one of the wettest years to get started. So the lake, was full at this point. We were able to catch fish, on the stake beds that the TWRA has provided, as long as they were under 7 feet of water. Right now, there aren't any stake beds on Percy Priest Lake that meet that criteria. In my opinion, if and when the lake comes up, it will be too late for the stake beds to be a viable option for crappie.
If you haven't previously been informed, or weren't aware, the wooden stakes that the TWRA has driven into the ground, to attract crappie, are marked with 2 inch PVC pipes, that stick way out of the water, so you can see them from across the lake. Typically, you could hop from one of those to the other, on most parts of the lake, looking for crappie. Unfortunately, like I said, that simply won't be an option this year.

Here's the kicker, whether you are fishing from the bank, or you have a kayak, or you have a boat, all of you can target these fish!

This morning, I launched my boat, before sunrise, at Seven Points boat ramp...

Seven Points Boat Ramp https://share.google/pAZTGuTrnSQ7AsyOL

When I got there, at around 5:30, there were no other boats in the parking lot. No trailers, no trucks, nobody but bank fishermen. I realize it's mother's day, but there should have been some people at the boat ramp, the fish were there in great numbers, and they were going crazy!

Before we get into all that, let's talk about the boat ramp. It is safe to use this boat ramp, but it's not very steep. That means, some people will have to get wet to get their boat on and off the trailer. When you do get the boat into the water, there is a courtesy dock, but only the very end of it is in the water, and unless your boat floats really shallow, you may not be able to use it. We are still in the throes of a drought, and the lake is about 5 feet below where it should be, this time of year.

A little birdie told me that the hybrid bass, which schooling great numbers on Percy Priest lake, we're blowing up top water, in the mornings, at Seven Points. That little birdie was right! Here's how it works for everybody who's in a boat or a kayak...

When you launch, don't go left, that would be into the cove, towards shallow water, in the Viverett Creek area. You want to go out to the right, in the direction of the main lake. You don't have to go very far, it's probably not even half a mile! Right when you come around the corner, the main point, at Seven Points, that's where everybody is standing on the bank. There was only one boat when I got there this morning, but when word gets out, lots of people will be in this area! Don't get discouraged if you are trying to bank fish or fish from a boat. Most people know that these fish school heavily, in certain areas, and we all have to share that location. For the most part, everyone I have met has been very helpful, and friendly! You can expect the same. I wouldn't be afraid to pull into this area if there were 20 boats out there! There is plenty of room, and the fish were going crazy everywhere!

There is a green buoy at the point that marks the channel for that area. That's where you want to be before sunrise. I'm going to drop a pin, but you don't necessarily need to be on that pin, you just need to be in the general area, before sunrise, or 2 hours before sunset. Here is the pin...

https://goo.gl/maps/CSLgUKisnNRDn1RK8

Bank fishing this spot is a little tricky, because the closest access, is gated, until after sunrise. I believe they open the gate at 6:30 in the morning, but don't quote me on that. That's too late though! These fish were only biting from 5:30 a.m. until 6:30 a.m. after that, I switched to crappie fishing. I know one way to get there, but it's awful! It's a long way through the woods. I'm not sure how those people were there, when I got there this morning, but they were there before the gate to the recreational area had been opened. I will find out how they got there, and I will let you guys know.

Here is a pin for where everybody stands to catch hybrids and striped bass from the bank. For what it's worth, they were about 8 to 10 people out there today, and they probably caught about that many, nice sized, fish...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/aKq4ZgpF9ZLuwLAH7

If you look at the maps, you will see that the recreation area allows you to drive almost all the way to this point. But not until they open the gate. By the time the majority of the people made it out there on the bank this morning, the fish weren't biting anymore. Everyone left the bank, by 7:30 a.m. If you really wanted to, you could park at the seven points boat ramp, because there are spaces for people who don't have trailers. It's a long walk through the woods, or, if you just wanted to hoof it, and walk past the gate, into the recreation area, you can definitely do that. It's a long way, but the fishing is on fire!

I could see that the people on the bank were throwing the same lures that I was throwing. I like to use a 3/8 of an ounce jig head and a three to four inch white paddle tail swimbait. If you don't know, that's just a soft plastic, with a rounded tail, that looks like a small swimming fish when you put it on a jig, and give a steady retrieve. For these types of fish, people will give the lure lots of different action. I'm still not 100% adept at targeting striped and hybrid bass, so I try lots of different retrieves. It looked like, most of the people on the bank, were casting as far as they could, allowing the lure to sink for several seconds, before they started their retrieve. Where they are casting, is about 45 ft deep. That's where these fish are hanging out, not far from where they are standing. The people on the bank are technically on the cliff. It's an underwater cliff, so they are standing at the water's edge. Some of them stand in the water. About 15 to 20 feet in front of them, it drops off, and that's where they get the majority of their catches, directly out in front of them.

Today, the water temperature on this end of the lake was 72°! That's actually warmer than it has been on the south end of the lake, we're fishing has been a little tougher. I was hopeful I could get one on top water, because they were busting on the surface. I tried a Whopper plopper, and I could see that some people on the bank were trying that as well, but no one had any top water success. Typically, hybrid bass, we'll go crazy for a Whopper plopper. It took me awhile to figure it out, but these weren't hybrid bass, they were striped bass!

Striped bass are notoriously more finicky. They like what they like, and when they figure out what they like, they go crazy on it! Unfortunately, even though fish were busting all around, for the better part of an hour, I was only able to catch two. Fortunately, two is the legal limit! If I were keeping striped bass, which I usually do not, they would have to be over 15 inches, and you would be allowed to keep two, per day. Since both of mine were plenty long, I technically, limited out, which is always nice!

When these fish quit biting, they didn't just hang around, they left the area! Using my forward facing sonar, I could see, that all of the large fish that were previously chasing bait, had moved on, just after 7:00 a.m. I started looking around, right by the green buoy. I had seen people, anchored in that area, catching crappie. I have caught plenty of copy in that area, before I had forward facing sonar. I didn't necessarily know why, but today, I put some pieces together.

Right by that green buoy, on that pin that I dropped in the water, there is an underwater forest! On this lake, there are several places, where they did not bulldoze all of the trees to the ground. They left some standing timber, in some select areas, and this is one of those areas!

That buoy is strategically placed, because the ground comes up there. It's no longer 45 feet deep, at the most shallow spot, by that buoy, it's only about 12 feet deep. All around that underwater hump, there are standing trees. A couple of them have fallen over, and they are loaded with crappie! There were plenty of crappie, at every depth, where there was underwater structure. If the water was only 12 ft deep, but had a tree laying over, it was loaded with crappie. The same was true at every depth, all the way down to 45 feet! There was a tree, standing from 45 feet down, to 15 feet underneath the surface. From the top of it, at 15 feet, down to 25 feet, it was loaded with crappie!

This time, I could be certain they were crappie, because I caught them! I didn't have much time, because I was going to have breakfast with my parents, but I didn't need much time! Finally! Finally! Finally, these fish are coalescing together, in great numbers, on underwater structure. Now that the spawn has come to an end, they have paper thin bellies, and they are hungry again! Best part, the water temperature is still nice and cool, so they are comfortable at every different depth, which means, you should be able to find them, on most of the pins that we have, on Percy Priest lake. If those pins are under 7 feet of water, there should definitely be fish!

This time last year, that was the secret recipe. 7 feet of depth. Of course, last year, we had one of the wettest years to get started. So the lake, was full at this point. We were able to catch fish, on the stake beds that the TWRA has provided, as long as they were under 7 feet of water. Right now, there aren't any stake beds on Percy Priest Lake that meet that criteria. In my opinion, if and when the lake comes up, it will be too late for the stake beds to be a viable option for crappie.

If you haven't previously been informed, or weren't aware, the wooden stakes that the TWRA has driven into the ground, to attract crappie, are marked with 2 inch PVC pipes, that stick way out of the water, so you can see them from across the lake. Typically, you could hop from one of those to the other, on most parts of the lake, looking for crappie. Unfortunately, like I said, that simply won't be an option this year.

title: Trip Report #45
content_raw:
The other trout river...
In middle Tennessee, we have two dams that allow cold water release, and support trout, year-round. The best, and most famous, is the Caney Fork River below Center Hill Dam. The other is smaller, and lesser known, the Elk River below Tims Ford Dam. Today, I took my kayak so that I could fish directly below the dam. It's a spot where most people don't think to go, either because they don't know they're allowed, or just don't think about it. There is a parking lot directly below the dam where you can drive your vehicle to the water's edge to drop off your kayak...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/Z5gCcQ8nyB9Jdef76
Be wary of this pin on Google maps. I tried to follow it earlier, and it put me on the other side of the river. If you get to this location, you will figure it out! There are signs that point to Tim's Ford dam, and they even have a picture of a canoe and a fish, because you're allowed to canoe and fish!
This is the Elk river. It's cold year round, and it's usually very clear. They stock brown trout and rainbow trout, and sometimes Brook trout. There are no size regulations for the brook or the rainbow trout, but you're only allowed to keep one brown trout over 20 inches, per day. You are allowed to keep a total of seven fish. In any combination. But you're only allowed to have one brown trout, and it has to be a big one! Now that you know where these fish are, and the regulations, let's talk about this area specifically.
The best thing about the Elk River below Tims Ford Dam is that they don't run generators on a daily basis like they do on the Caney. Most of the time, there is a steady release of cold water, that doesn't fluctuate, for days, or weeks, or even months, on end. That makes it ideal if you would like to fish from the bank, or put on your chest waders and get into the water. You won't have to worry about rapidly rising water, because that type of thing just doesn't happen very often out here. As of right now, the dam is only releasing 120 cubic feet per second of water. Typically, they released twice that much. The river still has just as many fish, but there's half as much of it! It's absolutely loaded up there! I should say, down there, because it's pretty close to the Alabama border.
You always need to know before you go! It's crucial to check the website before you head down, just to make sure they're not releasing more than a couple hundred cubic feet per second. The magic number is typically 235. That's usually what they release, all day everyday. Right now, because we're in a drought, they're only releasing 120 cubic feet per second. Always know before you go! Here is where you can check the schedule for Tim's Ford Dam...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/tims-ford
If you like to get in the water, and catch fish while you are wearing waders, this is a great place! Not just because the water stays steady, and you don't have to worry about generators, but the bottom of the river really lends itself to wading. There aren't lots of giant boulders, it's nice smooth river rocks. They are slippery, because they are smooth, the people I saw today, had those sticks that you carry with you while you wade. Like the poles that skiers have, but only one. You can get in the water right at the parking lot, and go downstream, or a little upstream. Or, you can take a trail through the woods, and go way downstream! Either way, there's lots to explore. There are fish everywhere! Don't think you have to walk too far, unless you just want to get away from it all.
I put my kayak in right by the parking lot. If you're careful, you can drive down to the water's edge, unload your gear, and then drive your vehicle back to the parking lot. Make sure not to park on the river, there is a sign that indicates that you are not allowed to park, past the parking lot. You are allowed, to unload. After I got unloaded, I paddled the opposite way that most people go, I went, upstream. It's not very far, but it put you right at the base of the damn, where the cold water is coming out of the spillway.
I like going up there every once in awhile, because there's never anyone there. I get the whole place to myself, I have a nice lunch, and I catch trout with multiple different methods. Today, I had my ultralight rod and reel with 4 pound monofilament. There wasn't one particular lure that they were keying in on, I was catching them a few ways.
First and foremost, they wanted that 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail. Those things come with three hooks, I cut two of them off, so it would be a little more accommodating for the fish. I had plans on releasing them, so I didn't want to hurt them too badly. If you're wondering about the hook up ratio, at this location, it won't matter. The fish bite, on almost every cast.
I also threw a1/64th of an ounce trout magnet with a 1 inch gulp minnow. That's a tough lure to fish, but when you get the hang of it, it's really effective, especially out there on the Elk. It's great for shallow water situations, and you don't have much deep water, below that dam. The way I work it, is like a crappie lure! I cast it as far as I can, keep my rod tip up, and give it a quick twitch. They like to hit, just after the twitch. Setting the hook, can be a little bit tricky. Basically, you just have to try it for yourself. Make sure to use 4 pound monofilament, or lighter!
I also used my favorite method, a sinker and a hook on bottom with a worm. When I got tired of trying to set the hook, I just started feeding them food. With a worm on bottom, and a small hook, they will do all the work! I like to use nightcrawlers, because they are big and fat! Those tiny little red worms, just don't stay on the hook. I like to pinch a Canadian nightcrawler in half, and put that on the hook, and let it sit on the bottom, until I feel a bite. Then, it's just a quick flip of the wrist to set the hook!
Another fantastic feature about this river, are the takeout and put in locations. Obviously, you can start a trip, at the dam, the location that I'm sharing with you right now, but you need to know where to take out. The first take out spot, downstream from here, is about 8 and 1/2 miiles, on the water. It's called Ferris Creek bridge access...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/RZfTP9R5qhwY2N5z9
Once again, this location can be kind of tricky. Google maps is doing its best, but this is way out in the country! It looks like there is access on the other side of the river, but you will need to cross the bridge, and make a right. Then, you will see a TWRA boat ramp. This is a nice location! It's gravel, it won't accommodate any boats, but you can back right down to load your trailers up, after a long day! It's great for kayaking if you intend to spend a full day on the river. It's an 8 and 1/2 Mile trip, and it's going to take you a minimum of 8 hours. Especially now that the water is flowing half as much as usual. Be prepared to paddle! It's a long trip.
Unfortunately, unless you have a jet boat, you're not going to be able to get on this river. Even if you do have a jet boat, you probably won't get it off the trailer. It's a tiny river! It's hardly worth trying to get a Jon boat, or a jet boat, on this body of water. I've never seen one out there, and it would be really out of place. It's heaven for kayakers, and it's as good a place as any if you would like to wade for trout.

title: Trip Report #46
content_raw:
Massive amounts of shell crackers...
Yesterday, I took my kayak upstream, on Fall Creek from Fall Creek boat ramp...
Fall Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/1dZjNjB9qpZEZMrT7
I have been seeing people park on the side of interstate 840 for years. They are parking right next to the bridge that goes over Fall creek, and fishing underneath the bridge. It's the next bridge over from Hurricane creek, so I just suspected they were catching bass and crappie, just like we have been, on Hurricane creek. But, I wanted to find out for myself.
First of all, the last time I went to Fall Creek boat ramp, the water in Percy Priest Lake was all the way down at winter pool. As of right now, it's up about two and a half feet from winter pool, but it's still way down from Summer pool. At winter pool, you could barely launch a kayak! The water is so shallow, and there are so many boulders everywhere, that it's like a minefield. As of right now, you could launch a boat, but you wouldn't go very far! You definitely wouldn't be able to put your motor down. As you head upstream, from this boat ramp, there are stumps, and boulders in the water, everywhere!
There were bass galore in this stretch! Just like the other creek, a couple of miles away, largemouth are up here, in great numbers. It's a fantastic spot right now, for kayaking, because most boats won't go this shallow. And there is a lot of area to kayak! It seems like it was more than a mile to the interstate 840 bridge. It was a pretty long paddle. I just wanted to see what the conditions were like underneath, because from above, as you're traveling past at 70 mph, it looks like it's very shallow, doesn't have enough water to hold fish, and has a lot of scum and algae. What I saw when I got down there, was quite different than that.
First of all, just before you get to the bridge, the water turned crystal clear! It is not like that on Hurricane creek. It stays cloudy all the way to the back. So now, it's really wide, it's really clear, and there is a bunch of algae, but you can see fish everywhere! And then I saw it, the trash that they had left from fishing underneath that bridge. Most of it, was red worm buckets. They have been using red wigglers, under bobbers, to catch bluegills and shellcrackers. There were large schools of red ear sunfish, or shellcrackers, everywhere! I'm going to drop a pin, on the side of the interstate, where they are walking down. I don't think it's safe to park on the interstate. Admittedly, this has been happening, since 840 was built. Hunters and fishermen have always been parking on the side of this particular interstate, and to my knowledge, they have never faced any repercussions. I can't suggest doing it, it doesn't sound safe, but here is where people are fishing...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/Amz4vXbjsHBHXvJq5
This wouldn't be a very easy spot to fish from the bank because of all the algae that's on the surface. Unless you are using a bobber and worms, and the fish are coming to you. If you're trying to cast lures, for the bass that are in there, you're going to have a tough time. There are large patches of algae floating on the surface everywhere, and the clear water has allowed algae to grow on the rocks on the bottom. Clearwater allow sunlight to pass through, and grow grass and algae more effectively. It also creates tons of areas for these fish to hide! There were large schools of red ear sunfish, hiding underneath these patches of algae!
I thought it was going to be all bass fishing, so I didn't have anything to present to these red ear. It's just as well, I didn't have much time to fish. I was on an exploratory mission. I wanted to know what they were targeting there. Mission accomplished!
From there, I headed over to my parents house. I haven't been able to do as much fishing as I would like the last couple of weeks, because, both of my parents have now had rotator cuff surgery. My mother had her torn rotator cuff repaired along with her biceps tendon, which had ripped apart. She is currently doing physical therapy, and recovering slowly, but on Friday, my father had to have his left arm repaired. He had also torn his rotator cuff. I've been helping them out, because between the two of them, they only have two arms. He starts physical therapy this Friday, and they are going to schedule both of them on the same day, to make it more accommodating for us.
I will still do as much fishing as I can, whenever I'm not helping them out. Mostly vacuuming and dishes and laundry and stuff like mowing the yard. Once they get their strength back, I'll be finding lots of great fishing spots, all day everyday, that I can share.
I would like to personally thank all of you, for subscribing to my Pro reports. Everything I am able to do, is because of the support that I receive from you, thank you!

First of all, just before you get to the bridge, the water turned crystal clear! It is not like that on Hurricane creek. It stays cloudy all the way to the back. So now, it's really wide, it's really clear, and there is a bunch of algae, but you can see fish everywhere! And then I saw it, the trash that they had left from fishing underneath that bridge. Most of it, was red worm buckets. They have been using red wigglers, under bobbers, to catch bluegills and shellcrackers. There were large schools of red ear sunfish, or shellcrackers, everywhere! I'm going to drop a pin, on the side of the interstate, where they are walking down. I don't think it's safe to park on the interstate. Admittedly, this has been happening, since 840 was built. Hunters and fishermen have always been parking on the side of this particular interstate, and to my knowledge, they have never faced any repercussions. I can't suggest doing it, it doesn't sound safe, but here is where people are fishing...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/Amz4vXbjsHBHXvJq5

This wouldn't be a very easy spot to fish from the bank because of all the algae that's on the surface. Unless you are using a bobber and worms, and the fish are coming to you. If you're trying to cast lures, for the bass that are in there, you're going to have a tough time. There are large patches of algae floating on the surface everywhere, and the clear water has allowed algae to grow on the rocks on the bottom. Clearwater allow sunlight to pass through, and grow grass and algae more effectively. It also creates tons of areas for these fish to hide! There were large schools of red ear sunfish, hiding underneath these patches of algae!

I thought it was going to be all bass fishing, so I didn't have anything to present to these red ear. It's just as well, I didn't have much time to fish. I was on an exploratory mission. I wanted to know what they were targeting there. Mission accomplished!

From there, I headed over to my parents house. I haven't been able to do as much fishing as I would like the last couple of weeks, because, both of my parents have now had rotator cuff surgery. My mother had her torn rotator cuff repaired along with her biceps tendon, which had ripped apart. She is currently doing physical therapy, and recovering slowly, but on Friday, my father had to have his left arm repaired. He had also torn his rotator cuff. I've been helping them out, because between the two of them, they only have two arms. He starts physical therapy this Friday, and they are going to schedule both of them on the same day, to make it more accommodating for us.

I will still do as much fishing as I can, whenever I'm not helping them out. Mostly vacuuming and dishes and laundry and stuff like mowing the yard. Once they get their strength back, I'll be finding lots of great fishing spots, all day everyday, that I can share.

I would like to personally thank all of you, for subscribing to my Pro reports. Everything I am able to do, is because of the support that I receive from you, thank you!

title: Trip Report #47
content_raw:
An adventure for the young and foolhardy...
Yesterday, I took on a tremendous challenge in my kayak. 10 miles of river that I have never seen, that I suspected, would be quite technical. I was right! I use the effort scale of one to five to portray how difficult or easy these fishing trips are. This trip was off the scale! This was as hard as it gets, a 5 out of five! I kayaked the East Fork Stones River from Goochie Ford, to Guy James road.
Let's start with the end first, because it's less complicated. Where it is, and, and park your vehicle, is state property. Like I have said before, I have an app on my phone called "OnX Hunt", which shows me property lines and the owners for every location in the state of Tennessee. There are some gravel parking spots right by the entrance to the Middle Tennessee agricultural school. Those spots have been utilized for fishermen for as long as the state has owned that property. You are allowed to park here! I will drop a pin of this location...
https://goo.gl/maps/dv9aFvJriAtAoWJt9
The beginning is much more complicated. It's a relatively popular place, with a handful of parking spots, that locals go to hang out near the water. Unfortunately, the land next to the river at this location is private property. Where people hang out is private property. Where people park their cars, is private property. Locals have been relying on this spot to hang out, for generations. The owners of this property, have been allowing it to happen. If, someone were to take advantage of this spot, by leaving trash, or making it less pretty than it already is, we may lose access. I know all of my Pro report subscribers are very responsible conservationists, so if you see something out of place, please make it your job to clean it up. This location does have a Google maps listing, because it's so well known, but it is not a public location! This land is owned by the Reed family living trust. They own 1.8 acres of land, there are no homes on this land, and no one that owns this particular stretch of river lives nearby. Long story short, it's private, but they allow it to be public, and I would like to keep it that way, so let's make sure we keep it clean!
Goochie Ford https://share.google/3pcxDtLohLfKj75lp
Putting in and taking out are very straightforward! At each location, there is a short trail down to the water's edge. Both of them are very steep, and there's certainly a trip and fall hazard. That's just part of the five out of five on the effort scale. This trip, is incredibly difficult!
First of all, it's a little more than 10 Miles long. Most kayak trips aren't more than five. That's a lot of water to cover in one day! I think the second most important thing are the obstacles. Right out of the gate, you have to deal with white water rapids that are created by underwater boulders. Less than 2 miles into the trip, there are a series of boulders that stick up out of the water, and there is only enough room to squeeze between them for one kayak. Because the water is flowing, and the boulders aren't in a straight line, you have to weave your way through, and it would be really easy to mess up and flip your kayak.
Then you come to a limestone shelf, where, my buddy just decided to portage. He got out of his kayak, into the water, and allowed his kayak to float over the edge. I made my way over the cliff, and down the other side, and it was a lot of fun! For what it's worth, if you are an extremely good kayaker, you can probably do this trip. For everyone else, I wouldn't suggest it!
From there, there are many more miles of shallow situations that you have to carefully pick your way through, or get stuck. Trees down, all over the river, creating an obstacle course, that you can almost always pick your way through. But only if you're good! On this trip, if your kayaking skills aren't extremely technically sound, you will find yourself getting out of the kayak, a lot!
Now for the good stuff, the fishing! This is a smallmouth bass fishing river. We never even saw a spotted bass or a largemouth! Because there are so many obstacles and so many trees in the water, there are countless places for fish to hide. Also, it's worth mentioning, that the water, still hasn't reached 70°. That means, these bass are still pre-spawn, with an angry disposition, looking to fill their bellies!
Because the water temperature is still in the 60s, these fish haven't committed to hitting top water, yet. Yesterday, my buddy kept trying to catch one on top water, but it wasn't going to happen. These fish are still locked in on that small spinnerbait that I've been using. It's just a purple spinnerbait with two silver blades that I picked up at Walmart for $1. That has been fantastic this season for pre-spawn fish in rivers. I've been using my 7 foot, extra fast medium action rod. It's a one-piece bass rod that was given to me by a client. I've got 15 pound braid on there and that's what I've been tying directly to my lure. In the past, I would add some leader line onto my braid, but I went away from that, when I realized it wasn't necessary. Tying straight to the braid, is the way to go!
If this river wasn't already technically tough enough, it's about to get a little tougher. I got really lucky yesterday. The water level, was optimum. In this situation, when you don't know what a river looks like, what i do, is look to the USGS chart for that river, to see what the flow is. That way, I know what to look for in the future. You can find the USGS chart for the East Fork Stones river, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03427500/all-graphs/#period=P7D
When we started our trip, the water was right around 100 cfs, and falling fast. If you don't know, cfs, or cubic feet per second, is how we measure the flow of rivers. One cubic foot per second, is about the size of one basketball. So that river was flowing at about 100 basketballs per second. The reason I say that number was optimum, is because, there were places where we would scrape bottom, and nearly have to get out and drag our kayak. We made it through every single time, but any less water, and we would have got stuck, a lot. Any more water, and obstacles like the row of boulders that were in the middle of the water, would suddenly become way too fast to handle. Because the water was at its slow, low level, yesterday, we were able to pick our way through those boulders, making hard left and right turns. Those quick turns, wouldn't be possible, if the river was flowing faster through those rocks.
It was the same way when we had to pick our way through downed trees. There were some areas, where you had to weave, back and forth, to get downstream. Those areas, would be really tough sledding, if the water moving any faster. We decided, then and there, 100 cubic feet per second is the number for this river.
So now you know where to go, and now you know that it's going to be one of the most difficult trips that you've ever taken. Two things to remember, it's completely loaded with fish, and we have to keep it super clean! If you see any signs of trash at the put in or take out, please take it upon yourself, to remove it.

title: Trip Report #48
content_raw:
A lake completely full of fish...
Yesterday, I started my work on Cordell Hull Lake. This is a river lake. It's on the Cumberland river. Lakes on the Cumberland River are much different than other reservoirs. They have high traffic from commercial ventures like barges, that move up and down the river on a daily basis. They have a system of locks that allow large and small vessels alike, to pass up and down the river. On a daily basis, the lakes on this river system will have some current, to extremely swift current. Conveniently enough, the best place to fish on Cordell Hull lake, is a giant cove known as Defeated creek. I launched at the day use area at Defeated creek...
Defeated Creek Day Use Area https://share.google/A4XR2fgNG6lpIA4Lf
This place has it all! First of all, the boat ramp is steep. Not out of the water, in the water, the most important place. For those of you who aren't aware, launching a boat at a shallow boat ramp is difficult, because the boat won't float off the trailer until you back way out. Not at this location! Most people won't even have to get their feet wet. Once you launch, there is a courtesy dock, and it's floating! Because this body of water has barge traffic, it doesn't experience the severe fluctuations in elevation like other reservoirs. I expect this courtesy dock to be usable, year-round.
This is a day use area. Typically, that means you have to pay for access. Yesterday, April 30th, was the last day of unpaid access. I took full advantage of the fact that it didn't cost me anything to enter the park. As of today, it will cost $5 per vehicle to enter the park. There is a booth as you enter, and they will accept your money there. You get a whole lot for your $5!
The park is fantastic! It's well-kept, and it has a lot of amenities. There are extensive hiking trails. There is a huge beach! Nice white sand, and an area for swimmers that has been blocked off from boats. There are tennis courts on the property as well as a nice playground and a couple different bathrooms. One in the day use area, and one over by the playgrounds in tennis courts. Now for the good stuff, the fishing!
There were people fishing from the bank, but the side of the lake where they have the day use area is very shallow. At best, you might be able to catch bluegill or bass. Directly across from the boat ramp, on the other side, the water is nearly 30 feet deep and there are cliffs. Those cliffs were holding fish, but you wouldn't be able to get to them without a boat.
I handled yesterday the same way I do anytime I'm launching from a new boat ramp to explore the area. My forward facing sonar is positioned on the left side of my boat, so I ride with the bank on my left side and go clockwise around the area, scanning for fish, and fish structures. What I found, was nothing short of amazing!
As soon as I put the transducer in the water, there were fish everywhere! Not unlike the coves on Percy Priest lake, there were massive schools of bait fish, schools of bass hanging out near the bank, and schools of crappie, on underwater structure. Everything has its place, so here's where the fish were positioned...
This cove is aligned due north to south. The west side, is where I launched my boat. As I left the boat ramp, I headed north, up the west bank. That bank is very shallow! It's only two or three feet deep, hundreds of yards from the bank, in most cases. If you work your way through there slowly, it's bass fishing heaven! I fished yesterday afternoon. While I was there, scanning the other side of the lake, at 5:00 p.m., a bass tournament launched out of the marina that is in the same cove. Most of those boats headed directly back into the cove, on this side to fish. By then, I was already on the other side of the cove, but I watched it all unfold. They raced each other to their favorite spots, at 70 mph!
Bass were up shallow, near the bank, under the overhanging brush. Because this lake was completely full yesterday, bass were able to make their way into one foot of water. The only reason I mention that it was full yesterday, is because it will drop out on you, even while you're fishing. When I arrived, they had just started running the generators, and they dropped the water nearly half a foot while I was there! But that's about as far as it goes, before it fills back up overnight, and they drop it again the next day. You can always know exactly how much water they will be pulling out of the lake, while you are fishing, if you check the generating schedule for Cordell Hull dam. The more generators they are running, the faster the water will drop. No matter how much it drops, it won't be unsafe, and it won't drop so fast that you get stranded. It's a relatively safe place to fish! Especially if you're in a boat or a kayak. You can find the generating schedule for Cordell Hull dam, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/cordell-hull
As you go farther back into the cove, there are two bridges that you can go under. It's 10 feet deep, and clear passage under the first bridge. I could see the second bridge in the distance, but I couldn't make it that far up, because I couldn't find the channel, and the water got to shallow. It was about 2 feet deep everywhere I looked, and I didn't feel comfortable, going any farther. I will drop a pin for exactly how far I made it...
https://goo.gl/maps/PPtveaFPM1nDJn3e7
At that point, I started my way back down on the east bank, which you can see, has limestone cliffs. That side of the cove is much deeper, and there has been extensive work done, by private individuals, putting fish attractors near those cliffs. I'm certain that it was done by individuals and not the TWRA, because the TWRA has marked all of their fish attractors. They don't have any on this end of the cove. From the boat ramp, upstream, there are no fish attractors that are marked. If you go downstream, near the main river, which I did not do yesterday, there are dozens of them! There is even a map, at the boat ramp, on the bulletin board, that shows you where the fish attractors are, downstream.
None of the pins that I am about to share with you are marked, but they are as good as gold!
Most of these are trees that have fallen off the cliff and gotten lodged under water at a depth of, between 15, and 5 feet. The water temperatures on the lake we're still over 70°, and crappie had spawned out, for the most part, and they were stacking up on these underwater structures. For what it's worth, yesterday was an incredibly tough day of fishing! I did manage to catch bass, confirming what I was seeing. And I did manage to catch crappie, confirming what I saw on the forward facing sonar, but it was tough! I used every tactic in my arsenal, but a great day of fishing, wasn't in the cards.
Fortunately for me, the fish were everywhere! I could see huge schools of bait fish, just like I do on Percy Priest lake. The underwater structures that had either fallen, or were placed there, we're loaded with fish! Everywhere I found structure that was at least 5 feet deep or more, there were schools of crappie, and sometimes, bluegill. Big schools! I'm going to drop these pins, some of them are close together, because there has been extensive work done, trying to attract fish to this area. All of them are along the east bank, where the water is deepest, and the fish tend to congregate...
https://goo.gl/maps/6H3NdbMCxJMCCSqV6
https://goo.gl/maps/se4MZkN3tMBa6sxu7
https://goo.gl/maps/xXzz6EBQ39z3oJUQ6
https://goo.gl/maps/8hWzTa5thPcTJVGe9
https://goo.gl/maps/mkVJupDw2bVTnSg16
https://goo.gl/maps/hpJzZPyx6jDcBhhJA
https://goo.gl/maps/yZWXyx89XtxkAHrf7
https://goo.gl/maps/NrxURXqgbcdyv7J57
https://goo.gl/maps/3FVWAcPsRf3viaAz9
https://goo.gl/maps/qu8xMGf6cfgRL2Rk7
https://goo.gl/maps/1ckaK4cW8aNTQiRK6
This is just one half of this cove on Cordell Hull lake. I keep calling it a cove, because that's what it is, but it's more like an entire lake, unto itself. This area is massive! It took me half a day to meticulously pick through this area and find those pins. The next time I go to this area, I will go the other direction. If you're going, keep in mind that it does cost $5 per vehicle. That includes launching your boat or kayak. There couldn't be an easier boat launch! As far as effort goes, this trip is a one out of five on the effort scale of one to five! If you have a boat or a kayak, getting to these fish, is as easy as it gets!

The only reason I mention that it was full yesterday, is because it will drop out on you, even while you're fishing. When I arrived, they had just started running the generators, and they dropped the water nearly half a foot while I was there! But that's about as far as it goes, before it fills back up overnight, and they drop it again the next day. You can always know exactly how much water they will be pulling out of the lake, while you are fishing, if you check the generating schedule for Cordell Hull dam. The more generators they are running, the faster the water will drop. No matter how much it drops, it won't be unsafe, and it won't drop so fast that you get stranded. It's a relatively safe place to fish! Especially if you're in a boat or a kayak. You can find the generating schedule for Cordell Hull dam, here...

https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/cordell-hull

As you go farther back into the cove, there are two bridges that you can go under. It's 10 feet deep, and clear passage under the first bridge. I could see the second bridge in the distance, but I couldn't make it that far up, because I couldn't find the channel, and the water got to shallow. It was about 2 feet deep everywhere I looked, and I didn't feel comfortable, going any farther. I will drop a pin for exactly how far I made it...

https://goo.gl/maps/PPtveaFPM1nDJn3e7

At that point, I started my way back down on the east bank, which you can see, has limestone cliffs. That side of the cove is much deeper, and there has been extensive work done, by private individuals, putting fish attractors near those cliffs. I'm certain that it was done by individuals and not the TWRA, because the TWRA has marked all of their fish attractors. They don't have any on this end of the cove. From the boat ramp, upstream, there are no fish attractors that are marked. If you go downstream, near the main river, which I did not do yesterday, there are dozens of them! There is even a map, at the boat ramp, on the bulletin board, that shows you where the fish attractors are, downstream.

None of the pins that I am about to share with you are marked, but they are as good as gold!

Most of these are trees that have fallen off the cliff and gotten lodged under water at a depth of, between 15, and 5 feet. The water temperatures on the lake we're still over 70°, and crappie had spawned out, for the most part, and they were stacking up on these underwater structures. For what it's worth, yesterday was an incredibly tough day of fishing! I did manage to catch bass, confirming what I was seeing. And I did manage to catch crappie, confirming what I saw on the forward facing sonar, but it was tough! I used every tactic in my arsenal, but a great day of fishing, wasn't in the cards.

Fortunately for me, the fish were everywhere! I could see huge schools of bait fish, just like I do on Percy Priest lake. The underwater structures that had either fallen, or were placed there, we're loaded with fish! Everywhere I found structure that was at least 5 feet deep or more, there were schools of crappie, and sometimes, bluegill. Big schools! I'm going to drop these pins, some of them are close together, because there has been extensive work done, trying to attract fish to this area. All of them are along the east bank, where the water is deepest, and the fish tend to congregate...

https://goo.gl/maps/6H3NdbMCxJMCCSqV6

https://goo.gl/maps/se4MZkN3tMBa6sxu7

https://goo.gl/maps/xXzz6EBQ39z3oJUQ6

https://goo.gl/maps/8hWzTa5thPcTJVGe9

https://goo.gl/maps/mkVJupDw2bVTnSg16

https://goo.gl/maps/hpJzZPyx6jDcBhhJA

https://goo.gl/maps/yZWXyx89XtxkAHrf7

https://goo.gl/maps/NrxURXqgbcdyv7J57

https://goo.gl/maps/3FVWAcPsRf3viaAz9

https://goo.gl/maps/qu8xMGf6cfgRL2Rk7

https://goo.gl/maps/1ckaK4cW8aNTQiRK6

This is just one half of this cove on Cordell Hull lake. I keep calling it a cove, because that's what it is, but it's more like an entire lake, unto itself. This area is massive! It took me half a day to meticulously pick through this area and find those pins. The next time I go to this area, I will go the other direction. If you're going, keep in mind that it does cost $5 per vehicle. That includes launching your boat or kayak. There couldn't be an easier boat launch! As far as effort goes, this trip is a one out of five on the effort scale of one to five! If you have a boat or a kayak, getting to these fish, is as easy as it gets!

title: Trip Report #49
content_raw:
Topwater bass fishing time in Tennessee...
In middle Tennessee, people have been catching bass on top water lures, for at least a month, sometimes longer. I never really try very much, unless it's going to be a sure thing. As of yesterday, for the rest of the summer, the topwater bite is going to be a sure thing! Yesterday, I took my kayak up Hurricane creek. You can park on the side of Maddox road and easily launch your kayak into the lake. Here is where you can park to launch your kayak and fish this part of the lake...
https://goo.gl/maps/XLVdStLaLiR1r1vr9
It's a short walk from your car on the side of the road, to the water's edge, and that's the most difficult part of this trip. Because you have to carry your kayak, or use wheels if you have them, this trip is probably a three out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. There is no boat ramp, so it's not going to necessarily be easy.
All of this area is accessible from the bank, right now. Because we didn't receive much spring rain, the lake level is still low, at winter pool. You can park in this area, and walk around almost the entire lake! If you don't have a kayak, you could still go bank fish this area, for bass, and do pretty well! I paddled up the creek. If you don't have a kayak, you can still bank fish up there, as well! A couple of months ago, I told you guys about a spot on Hurricane creek, that is open to the public. Once again, because the water is so low, you can bank fish most of the creek, if not all of it!
To bank fish the creek, you can park here...
https://goo.gl/maps/NJcppbaQKSk3q4yW7
This spot is really nice! There are a few places to park at the end of a gravel road. You will be able to see a gate, that will not allow you to go any farther. Park in the little parking spaces, provided, before you reach that gate. Then, walk toward the gate, on the gravel road that is provided. This is a foot traffic only area. That's why the gate is blocking the path of your vehicle. You are allowed to be here! Keep taking the gravel trail, down to the water's edge. It's a lovely spot, and there is even a bench to sit on! You can fish all the way up and down this bank, and I guarantee, you will wear out largemouth bass!
Because the bank is relatively steep, and you have to navigate your way around cliffs and boulders and rocks, this fishing excursion ranks at a four out of five on the effort scale of one to five. It's going to be tough to get next to the water's edge, but it will be easy to do for most people who are fleet of foot.
When I went yesterday, I got there at 2:00 p.m. I had my six and a half foot medium heavy bass rod with 15 lb braid tied directly to a Walmart brand Whopper plopper. They don't put the size on those, but if I had to compare it to a brand name Whopper plopper, I would say it was a size 110. Basically, it's about three and a half inches long. That's my go-to size for bass fishing topwater. Fortunately, this lure also catches hybrid bass and striped bass. When you're out on Percy Priest lake, you never know what's going to blow up on top water!
I had a good feeling that these fish were going to go off yesterday, and I was right! Not necessarily because of that day, or that time of day, but more, because of the location. Those fish are in that creek, after they spawned, feeding heavily. They are hungry, their bellies are skinny, and they are looking to get full.
I didn't waste any time. As soon as I got in my kayak, I was in the back of that cove, and I was facing due south. The wind was blowing heavily out of the south, so I knew I wanted to get not only into the creek, to get out of the wind, but a very least, to the opposite bank that I was on, the north facing bank. The wind was screaming in my face, so I paddled directly across, and there was immediate relief provided from the trees. As soon as I got across the lake, which isn't very far, and out of the wind, I made my very first cast toward the bank, with a slow retrieve. On my first cast, a nice big large mouth hammered home, and I got him in the net!
It would be like that, for the next 2 hours. Despite my best effort with other lures like a ChatterBait and a spinnerbait, I was unable to generate any type of interest outside of topwater. It was like the siren song for a largemouth bass. I would end up catching about a dozen bass, and none of them were spotted bass, and none of them were smallmouth bass. All largemouth, with a bad disposition!
At 4:00, the bite was over. I was in the same location where fish had been going off for 120 minutes. Then they stopped. I kept fishing until 5:30! I never got another bite. They may have turned back on at sunset, but I wasn't going to stick around to find out. I learned everything I needed to know. The bass on Percy Priest lake, are ready to hit top water!

title: Trip Report #50
content_raw:
An epic adventure on the plateau...
Yesterday, I went to a spot that I've had marked for years. Downtown Sparta Tennessee has a boat ramp on the Calf Killer River...
https://goo.gl/maps/2j1cHUkQvNXb6Vdb6
This is a small boat ramp with no amenities. There is a parking lot for maybe 10 to 15 cars. It's perfect for kayaks or canoes and you could even get a small Jon boat in there. I took my kayak, but my boat would have easily fit. I didn't take my boat, because I wanted to go upstream, past the area where boats can venture. The boat ramp itself is concrete, and steep enough to launch most boats. You can only go downstream from this boat ramp about an eighth of a mile before there is a low head dam that backs up the area. You can go upstream, in a boat, about two and a half miles. After that, there are trees that block the river. You can easily paddle over them in a kayak, but you would not be able to go over them in most boats.
I went up exactly 5 miles. At that point, it turns into a very narrow, scenic river. There are steep bluffs, and limestone cliffs, and huge boulders in the water. I stopped there, to turn around and head back downstream. You could definitely go up much farther! It just gets more beautiful, and there are plenty of fish everywhere along the way.. here is where I stopped, to have lunch, and turn around...
https://goo.gl/maps/1icMwyd6ise9NzTy5
This trip is pretty well known for its stunning, natural beauty. There are massive waterfalls and caves that people like to use as backdrops for a beautiful day on the water. There aren't any houses on this stretch of river, just a few cabins. If you go all the way up as far as I went, and come back down, it will be in all day affair. Because the water where you begin at the boat ramp is 12 feet deep, you won't feel the effects of any current until you get a few miles upstream. That makes the paddle relatively easy, and because the boat ramp is nice, and easy to launch, I would put this trip at a two out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5.
This is a bass fishing trip. You will want to take your favorite bass fishing lures, the ones you have the most confidence in. It's that time of year where you can catch fish top water everyday. I have been throwing the same purple spinner bait that I bought at Walmart for $1, all spring. That's what I threw yesterday, and I was beating them up! I believe, most types of lures would have worked well. Any type of crankbait or moving lure of any kind.
This entire stretch of river is a lot like the Elk River on Woods reservoir that I explored last week. The banks are mostly dirt, and there are trees laid over in the water, everywhere! There are so many good places for fish to hide, and they were coming out of the woodworks, left and right! These fish aren't heavily pressured, because you have to paddle a few miles upstream to get to them. Most people won't put in that type of effort, so these fish don't see a lot of lures. You won't see a bunch of trash on the bank, and there is not a lot of fishing line hanging from the trees. Bottom line, it's a fantastic place to get away from it all!
This is the Calf Killer River, and it's one of several rivers in the area that flow into Great Falls Lake...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/oJGX5exsmr7B7vCg6
Great Falls Lake is backed up by Great Falls Dam. That Lake is known for holding muskie. Most of the tributaries, including the Calf Killer, have Muskie in them. Unfortunately, because of the low head dam that creates the deep water area where the boat ramp is, muskie have not been able to go upstream, since that dam has been built. As a result, there are no longer any muskie in this upstream stretch of the Calf Killer river. Because of that fact, the largemouth bass has become top dog! There are plenty of small mouth in this stretch of river, but yesterday, it seemed like the large mouth outnumbered them four to one!
Because the banks are steep, and mostly made of dirt and mud, there are not very many good places to stop and rest, or get out of the kayak along the way. That was the biggest reason why we stopped where we did. 5 miles upstream from the boat ramp, at the pin that I dropped, there are some nice flat limestone rocks that are at the surface of the water. They are shaded, and it makes for a great spot to stop and have lunch, before you head back downstream.

title: Trip Report #51
content_raw:
Back to back days at Center Hill Dam...
Thursday, I had a client booked below Center Hill dam. He wanted to take his kayak out, and learn everything I know about catching every different species of fish below Center Hill dam. The most important thing to know is the generating schedule. The most common question that I get asked about fishing at Center Hill dam, is what condition is my favorite. Do I prefer the generators off? Would I rather there be one generator on or two generators on or three generators on? I don't have a preference. The fishing can be bad, or fantastic, in any condition. Some days, the fish bite better than others. What I have learned, is how to fish, no matter what the dam is doing.
Know before you go! If the most important thing is the generating schedule, then you need to have this link on your phone. Put it on your homepage, and check it everyday. Even if you're not going to the river or lake, make sure you know what the river or lake is doing. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, along with the lake level at Center Hill lake, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
On Thursday, one generator turned on at 4:00 a.m. A second generator was scheduled to turn on at 5:00 a.m. Then, at 8:00 a.m., they were going to drop back down to one generator, and then at 9:00 a.m., completely turn the water off. My client wanted to go at 9:00 a.m., which is understandable, because the generators would be off. That would be a great time to be on the water, in your kayak, if you're unsure about fishing in that area. I've been doing it for a long time, so I'm comfortable fishing with the generators on. I went before sunrise, to fish for Crappie in the corner by the waterfall while there were two generators on.
When the water is off, there is not enough depth in the corner to hold fish. Lots of different fish go in there, but not schools of crappie. The water is only about 3 feet deep, and you can see the bottom. When one generator comes on, the water level rises about 4 feet. That's good, and it brings other fish into the corner, but crappie still won't come in there and great numbers. When a second generator turns on, it raises the water level another three or four feet. That is the perfect amount of depth for these fish! At that point, they start stacking up in that corner, looking for bait.
I sat there for a couple of hours before he got there, and hammered away on some nice crappie, and put a few on the stringer, just to make sure he had some to take home. By the time he got there at 9:00 a.m., the water was starting to drop, and the fish moved out of that corner. We spent our time trying to target them in the center of the river.
The majority of the area below Center Hill Dam is so shallow, that when the water is off, you can see the bottom from your kayak or boat. Only in the very center of the dam, directly below the dam, is there any depth. When the water is off, there is one spot, that looks like a very steep bowl underwater. That's where all the fish pile up when the water gets low. That's where I like to drop my anchor, and fish around and find out what I can catch.
His main concern was learning how to catch the different types of fish that live down there. We went over lots of different techniques, and lots of different lures. Most people go below Center Hill Dam to target trout. There are lots of different ways to catch those! Anything shiny like a spoon or a rooster tail should do the trick. If you can't get them to bite an artificial lure, they will always eat a worm on bottom.
I honestly don't know what the number two targeted fish at Center Hill Dam is. If I had to guess, it's probably walleye. Most people fish for walleye on the bottom. They drop something like a spoon or a heavy jig directly underneath their boat, and vertically jig. They will lift their lure up off the bottom and allow it to fall back down to the bottom. That technique draws walleye and sauger, but any type of fish that sees your lure on the bottom jumping up and down might just bite it, including really big trout!
My favorite thing to target is crappie. The ones that make it up to the dam from Old hickory Lake are usually pretty big. You don't catch a whole lot of small crappie below Center Hill dam. We went over how to catch them, extensively. Like I said, if there are two generators running, I will sit in the corner by the waterfall. When the water is off, like it was yesterday, I like to sit in the middle, and fish in a circle, until I find where they are sitting.
Fast forward to Friday, and my client and I went out in my boat. There is a boat ramp below Center Hill dam, where I launch my kayak, and my boat. Unfortunately, if the water is off, and the level is down, I cannot get my boat off the trailer. There is not enough depth at the boat ramp, to float my boat. So we waited for the generators to turn on at 12:00 noon. Here is a link for where I launch my boat blow Center Hill Dam at Buffalo valley boat ramp...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/NsW8XGnDD8TQn6poy
Yesterday's client wanted to learn all the same information, but mostly target trout, instead of crappie. We went over the same techniques, and the same lures.
When the generator is turned on at noon, it was one generator. We waited for a while for the river to fill up, and then we floated downstream in my boat, twitching a rapala husky jerk bait for trout, along the way. At 1:00 p.m., they turned on a second generator, which allowed the water to come up enough for those crappie to pile up into the corner. After successfully fishing for, and catching some small trout, we made our way over to the corner to sit on an anchor, and go after a stringer full of crappie, for him to eat at the campground.
I wanted to make sure we had success, so I brought a bucket of minnows. Live minnows work almost every time!
