content_markdown:
Back to back days at Center Hill Dam...

Thursday, I had a client booked below Center Hill dam. He wanted to take his kayak out, and learn everything I know about catching every different species of fish below Center Hill dam. The most important thing to know is the generating schedule. The most common question that I get asked about fishing at Center Hill dam, is what condition is my favorite. Do I prefer the generators off? Would I rather there be one generator on or two generators on or three generators on? I don't have a preference. The fishing can be bad, or fantastic, in any condition. Some days, the fish bite better than others. What I have learned, is how to fish, no matter what the dam is doing.

Know before you go! If the most important thing is the generating schedule, then you need to have this link on your phone. Put it on your homepage, and check it everyday. Even if you're not going to the river or lake, make sure you know what the river or lake is doing. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, along with the lake level at Center Hill lake, here...

https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill

On Thursday, one generator turned on at 4:00 a.m. A second generator was scheduled to turn on at 5:00 a.m. Then, at 8:00 a.m., they were going to drop back down to one generator, and then at 9:00 a.m., completely turn the water off. My client wanted to go at 9:00 a.m., which is understandable, because the generators would be off. That would be a great time to be on the water, in your kayak, if you're unsure about fishing in that area. I've been doing it for a long time, so I'm comfortable fishing with the generators on. I went before sunrise, to fish for Crappie in the corner by the waterfall while there were two generators on.

When the water is off, there is not enough depth in the corner to hold fish. Lots of different fish go in there, but not schools of crappie. The water is only about 3 feet deep, and you can see the bottom. When one generator comes on, the water level rises about 4 feet. That's good, and it brings other fish into the corner, but crappie still won't come in there and great numbers. When a second generator turns on, it raises the water level another three or four feet. That is the perfect amount of depth for these fish! At that point, they start stacking up in that corner, looking for bait.

I sat there for a couple of hours before he got there, and hammered away on some nice crappie, and put a few on the stringer, just to make sure he had some to take home. By the time he got there at 9:00 a.m., the water was starting to drop, and the fish moved out of that corner. We spent our time trying to target them in the center of the river.

The majority of the area below Center Hill Dam is so shallow, that when the water is off, you can see the bottom from your kayak or boat. Only in the very center of the dam, directly below the dam, is there any depth. When the water is off, there is one spot, that looks like a very steep bowl underwater. That's where all the fish pile up when the water gets low. That's where I like to drop my anchor, and fish around and find out what I can catch.

His main concern was learning how to catch the different types of fish that live down there. We went over lots of different techniques, and lots of different lures. Most people go below Center Hill Dam to target trout. There are lots of different ways to catch those! Anything shiny like a spoon or a rooster tail should do the trick. If you can't get them to bite an artificial lure, they will always eat a worm on bottom.

I honestly don't know what the number two targeted fish at Center Hill Dam is. If I had to guess, it's probably walleye. Most people fish for walleye on the bottom. They drop something like a spoon or a heavy jig directly underneath their boat, and vertically jig. They will lift their lure up off the bottom and allow it to fall back down to the bottom. That technique draws walleye and sauger, but any type of fish that sees your lure on the bottom jumping up and down might just bite it, including really big trout!

My favorite thing to target is crappie. The ones that make it up to the dam from Old hickory Lake are usually pretty big. You don't catch a whole lot of small crappie below Center Hill dam. We went over how to catch them, extensively. Like I said, if there are two generators running, I will sit in the corner by the waterfall. When the water is off, like it was yesterday, I like to sit in the middle, and fish in a circle, until I find where they are sitting.

Fast forward to Friday, and my client and I went out in my boat. There is a boat ramp below Center Hill dam, where I launch my kayak, and my boat. Unfortunately, if the water is off, and the level is down, I cannot get my boat off the trailer. There is not enough depth at the boat ramp, to float my boat. title: Trip Report #52
content_raw:
Lots of crappie news...
Yesterday, I took my boat out from Stewart Creek boat ramp...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/fhssYA4Un6nQayE1k
A little birdie told me, that crappie were stacking up on underwater brush piles between 8 and 15 feet. That little birdie was right!
First of all, the area around the boat ramp is completely loaded with crappie right now. While I was loading my boat, someone standing on the bank caught two keepers. Before I was able to get my boat out of the lake, and back onto my trailer, when I was leaving, I was scanning the area in the very center of the cove. It's too far away to reach from the bank, but there are fish attractors out there, and they were overwhelmingly loaded with crappie!
I left that area, across the lake, to check on some locations that I knew were in the appropriate depth. I wanted to look in water that was 15 ft deep, and had brush piles. Either naturally occurring, like old stumps or old trees, or something someone had placed in the lake. There are a few good locations directly across from the Fate Sanders Marina area, near the bank at the Poole Knob recreation area. You wouldn't be able to get to these locations from the bank, unfortunately. They are a little too far out for that. They were just perfect for crappie though!
What I saw, was nothing short of a miracle. After what seemed like forever, probably four or five weeks now, since crappie started spawning on Percy Priest Lake, these fish have finally started grouping back together. During the spawn, the male spread out in shallow water, and make beds. If you can find an area where there are beds, you can catch a lot of fish, but that was impossible for me to do this year! The females roam around. They're not necessarily looking for a bed, they are waiting to pop. When they are ready, they hop on the nearest bed, and then leave the area. The males are the ones who tend to the bed. I couldn't catch males or females! I tried. I was unable to catch fish during the spawn. Don't get me wrong, I caught some fish, but I didn't catch my limit of crappie, like you expect to, every time you go out. It was really hard this year!
Fast forward to yesterday, and I went to this location to check on these three pins...
https://goo.gl/maps/LAGT2anVFVwnTyZu8
https://goo.gl/maps/8pCeSN45MVEDcBVSA
https://goo.gl/maps/AL2XjDTX6iJCpr7Y8
All three of these locations were holding fish. I was having a really tough time keeping my boat in position. As you know, I have spot rock. That is a 40 pound chunk of limestone, attached to a rope, that I used to keep my boat in position. It's probably the most important tool on the boat. Without it, I would never be able to sit on these fish, make an accurate cast, drop the lure down to their depth, and then get them to bite. That's really the secret to my success. There is no magic touch. There are no magical lures. Using a small soft plastic, and a light jig head, with light line, and getting that lure in front of their face, or just above their head, is the only way to do it. Yesterday, I would have needed a 100 pound chunk of limestone. I just kept getting blown off my spot.
I knew a location, close to a cliff, where the wind was being blocked. I made my way over there, and I found what I had been looking for. I took a picture on my phone, so I can show you exactly what it means, when someone says, they found fish in eight, to 15 feet of water. Instead of attaching a video to this report, I'm going to attach this picture. Patreon won't allow me to attach both. Apparently, it's either pictures, or a link to a YouTube video. I'm going to drop the picture, and then explain what you're looking at.
On the left side of the screen, where it says lowrance, you see numbers in groups of five. Five, and then 10, and then 15, and then 20 all the way down to 25. That is the depth. The image on the right, correlates to that depth, on the left, and distance, on the top. That number 10, on the top is 10 feet away from the transducer. The transducer, is the part of the fish finder that is sending out the signal. That is 0, in the top left corner.
So these fish, were hovering around a structure, and the top of them was about 8 feet deep, and the bottom of them, was a little more than 15 feet deep. This is what it looks like when someone says they found fish between 8 and 15 feet. This is what I have been waiting for, for about a month! When I got positioned on these fish, out of the wind, I pulled out my trusty,  seven and a half foot ultra light rod and reel. I've got 4 lb monofilament, and I was using a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head. For me, I'll always use a pearl colored body garland. I just feel like white does a great job, but any color will do. If you can get into position, and get one of those small soft plastics across their face, or above their head, they will bite!
And bite they did! One right after the other! Finally, things are starting to get back to normal. For the rest of this calendar year, these fish will be holding on structure, and they will only get deeper as the months get warmer. Fortunately for us, on Percy Priest lake, they never really get much deeper than about 25 feet. That makes them easy to find, and easy to catch. The majority of the pins that I have dropped on Percy Priest lake, will be perfect until next spawning season. Here is a pin that correlates with where I took that picture. I haven't been able to see what type of structure is under there. It could be a stump, or it could be a man-made fish attractor. It was too covered up with fish, for me to tell...
https://goo.gl/maps/DK3cDguDsW1kDkW87
This is a new location that I have never found until yesterday. I was scanning the cliffs, because we have a spot that we went to all winter that I found where we could fish from the bank. If you're new here, or don't remember, I'm going to go ahead and drop a pin on that location, even though I didn't find any fish there...
https://goo.gl/maps/4bY9mFt1tFtLC4NB7
Here's the thing about this location, it's great during the winter pool. Now that they are slowly starting to raise the level of the lake, and with next week's expected rain, you will no longer be able to stand at this spot. It is a cliff, and you have to stand on the edge, and that will be underwater. It's a great spot, to have on your list of locations, because it was a Non-Stop producer, all the way up until the spawn. Crappie love to hang on cliffs, on Percy Priest lake, year-round. But during the pre-spawn, they load up! Mostly, because there are a lot of bait fish. I didn't see any fish in that location yesterday and that's what led me to start scanning around the area. In the past, I had seen lots of crappie fishermen that were having great success, loaded up in this area. As it turns out, there are a lot of underwater stumps. That's probably what this is, but the main feature, is that drop off.
You can see in the picture I have provided, that the bank isn't necessarily, slowly sloping. It seemingly drops off, but those aren't cliffs, that's mud! For some reason, crappie love the mud. If they had the choice between a tree that was hanging on a limestone cliff, and a tree that was in the mud, they would always prefer the mud. I'm not sure why, but they gravitate toward it. This area, is a long stretch, with an underwater drop off, and lots of stumps! It's no wonder, I had seen so many crappie fishermen in that area, when I was fishing from the cliffs.
Fast forward one more time, and now we're caught up. Today, I went out on my friend's boat, from the Nashville shores Marina...
Nashville Shores Marina https://share.google/gtyhLoETrj8fgdI47
This is the smallest Marina on a lake! It's tiny. Only a few docks. The whole area is completely loaded with crappie and bluegill! It's not public, and there is nowhere to legally hang out and fish. You have to have a boat slip. But if you have a boat, you can go in there! There are thousands of bluegills. They hang out, everywhere. All around the boats, all around the bank. The crappie, hang out underneath the boats, just like they do in most marinas. But that's just during the daytime. At night, they wander around, and there are lots of people out there currently, fishing at night for them. Like I said, you can't fish from the bank, but you can take your boat!
We went across the lake, to the cliffs near where the corps of engineers has their own boat ramp on the lake. We found crappie, in 35 feet of water, that were suspended, on the cliff face, 25 feet down. They were loaded! We were able to sit directly on top of them, cast straight down, and vertical jig for them. If you haven't done that, essentially, you just let slack out of your line, until you get down to their depth. Once you get down there, you just hold the jig in place, and give it a little wiggle jiggle wiggle. Typically, they take the bait, every time! It's probably the easiest way to catch a crappie. I'm going to drop a pin for you, but they weren't hanging on any structure. They were just on the cliff. You may be able to find them there in the future, or you may have to look up and down the cliffs. Either way, they're going to be nearby!
https://goo.gl/maps/Mp3hfzQvA3EZu8EG9
For what it's worth, The cove at Nashville shores Marina was also completely loaded with bass. They didn't necessarily look like they would win the tournament, but there were hundreds of bass between the one and a half and three pound range! They were hanging close to the bank, within 18 inches most of the time. I'm pretty sure they were on bed, because the water on that end of the lake has just now reached 70°. Each time you would walk by, when you were loading stuff into the boat from the car, they would quickly scoot away, and then come right back! I'm pretty sure each one of those fish had a bad, that they were guarding. Most of the bass on the south end of the lake have already spawned, as the water temperatures have recently been as high as 75°. On the North end of the lake, the water is much cooler, and while those crappie just finished up, the bass are just getting started!
If you know somewhere on the North end of the lake, that you can Bank fish, you could probably get bass there, right now! The best spot, would probably be the recreation area near the dam. I haven't fished there since I was a kid, but you may be able to get a top water bite, especially early in the morning, or late in the evening, close to the bank. I'm going to drop a pin for that park, because it's a great place to go fishing, not just for bass that might be spawning right now, but because there is a fish attractor there! It's a really big one! It's marked with a buoy, and it's right in front of where you park. There were no fish on it today, but it will be loaded up soon!
https://maps.app.goo.gl/WKTuCNU2DkbEB65F6

It's a really big one! It's marked with a buoy, and it's right in front of where you park. There were no fish on it today, but it will be loaded up soon!

title: Trip Report #53
content_raw:
A couple of productive spots...
Yesterday, I kayaked upstream from Ransom Mill Dam, on the Murfreesboro greenway, at the Manson Pike trailhead...
Manson Pike Trailhead https://share.google/yyH7XgIQcxyYMdaEn
To do this trip, you will need wheels for your kayak. Here is a link to the type of wheels that I use to roll my kayak long distances...
https://amzn.to/4cpwKhC
There is a kayak launch in the parking lot at the Manson Pike trailhead. You can take that downstream, and paddle right back to the same spot. You can go, almost a mile, before it gets too shallow, and you have to turn around. That area is loaded with fish! Lots of different types of sunfish as well as catfish, and lots of big bass. I like to go above the dam. I get my kayak loaded up in the parking lot, and then set it on my wheels, strap it down, and then roll up the greenway, and launch at a little gravel spot that is provided on the river's edge. I'm going to drop a pin for that location, right here...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/bNHGSJ5sTnpU2wFY8
Rolling up the greenway to this spot, loading into the river, and paddling around this area, is it difficult, but it's not easy. This trip falls at a three on the effort scale of 1 to 5. It's impossible if you don't have wheels for your kayak. Once you get there, you have lots of area to explore! Directly across from the kayak launch, there is a creek that you can paddle up, that is typically loaded up with largemouth bass. Yesterday was the first time that I have taken my cast net to catch some live bait, at this location. In the past, I've always used lures, and had great success! I thought I had it pretty well figured out, I would usually catch bass in the same locations. Those locations do hold bass, but so does everywhere else!
I went below the dam with my cast net to get some live bait from the waterfall. There are some shiners and some small bottom feeders that are perfect for big bass. I like to use my medium action rod and reel with 12 pound monofilament and a bobber and a number one eagle claw Aberdeen hook. Yesterday, I experimented with a small, number four split shot, about 6 inches above the bait, like I usually do, but also, with no split shot. I really enjoy the action of no split shot, because the bait fish swims to the surface when it gets chased, and then it gets eaten on the surface, which is exciting! That stretch of river is completely loaded! I started with lures, and was having a pretty good day, then I started throwing bait fish. Everywhere you cast, there are bass!
I knew I'd be fishing for bass, so I got there around 11:00 a.m. the bite was hot until about 3:00 p.m. I stayed out there until about 5:30, and I only caught one bass after 3:00 p.m. I have mentioned before, river bass don't typically act like lake bass. They prefer midday, when they feed the heaviest. Bass on the lake are notorious for biting heavily, first thing in the morning, right at sunset, and all night long. That is not the way river bass behave, so I usually don't show up very early.
On this stretch of river, you can paddle more than a mile before you get to the bridge at Old Fort golf course. Under that bridge, you would have to get out and drag your kayak upstream, if you wanted to go any farther. You can, but you won't go very far, until you have to get out and drag your kayak again. Unfortunately, above this area, is not very navigable, when the water is low. Low water, on the West Fork Stones river, is anything below 100 cfs. The flow of rivers are measured in cubic feet per second, and one cubic foot, is about the size of one basketball. You can find the flow of West Fork Stones River on the USGS chart, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D
If you're going out there, take your top water lures! The pollen, and significant amount of debris that had built up on the surface, got washed away with the rainfall a couple of days ago.
Today, I took my boat out on Percy Priest Lake in search of crappie. I had heard that they were holding on underwater brush at a depth of 8 to 15 feet. I went to an area of the lake that I know has lots of brush piles below the surface, and that type of depth, consistently. You can find water that doesn't reach more than 30 feet of death for a couple of miles, at West Fork boat ramp...
West Fork Boat Ramp https://share.google/rj7Xy6mZiDAbDiTI4
I started scanning immediately, as soon as I pulled out of the boat ramp. There have been crappie stacked up, near the boat ramp, over the winter, and during the pre-spawn season. They weren't there during the spawn, because they were in very shallow water. They have started to come back to the area now, but, no matter how hard I tried, I couldn't sit still, because of the wind. Everywhere I looked, no matter the depth, if there was a tree underwater, or a stump, it had a few fish on it. I wasn't able to catch them, to ensure they were crappie, but they were everywhere!
The wind was screaming through that area, so I headed to the confluence of the East and West Fork stones river, to see if the fish were in that area, or if it were a little more blocked from the wind. Both of those things turned out to be true...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/HH6U5JGHXnQgxzV77
I didn't launch my boat until about 2:30 p.m. and I spent a little more than an hour looking around the boat ramp area, trying to sit on my anchor, and catch those fish, to no avail. By the time I made it to the confluence, it was just after 4:00, and I could see bait, as soon as I pulled up. There were huge schools of bait fish everywhere. It wasn't long, before fish started blowing up that bait. At first, I was throwing a chatterbait, and then a top water lure. They didn't want that, so I switched to a 3 and 3/8 of an inch white paddle tail. I was using a 3/8 of an ounce jig head, on 10 pound monofilament on my 6 foot 8 inch, medium action, extra fast rod.
Fish were blowing up, in every direction, right at the surface. It didn't take long, before I started nailing them! For the most part, they were giant white bass. Most of the fish were 14 to 16 inches in range, which is really large for white bass. Every once in awhile, a school of largemouth bass would blow up on bait, and we would catch some of those. I had my buddy with me, and we beat up on those fish for exactly 2 hours, until just after 6:00 p.m., when the water got still, and everything went quiet. The water was literally boiling for 2 hours!
If you're going to West Fork boat ramp, it's important to note, that there are no amenities. There are no bathrooms, and there is no courtesy dock, for you to load your boat. You will have to put your boat on the boat ramp. Fortunately, it's a very steep boat ramp, so it's easier to launch, and load your boat, without getting wet. Simply because there is no courtesy dock for your boat, this probably ranks at a one and a half on the effort scale of one to five.

title: Trip Report #54
content_raw:
Where you can get away from it all...
Yesterday, I began my work on Woods reservoir. I have never been on that body of water in any kind of boat or vessel, and I have never fished it from the bank. It was literally my first time. Woods reservoir has one primary tributary, the Elk river. I found a quiet boat ramp, that is not suitable for full size boats. It is a primitive boat ramp, made of gravel. It's very shallow, and it's very narrow, and unless you have a small Jon boat, 14 foot or less, you definitely would not be able to get your boat in at this boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/NhEVse4H8N2GR41W7
It's the perfect spot for kayaks and canoes, because most boats would never come this far up the lake. The parking lot that is provided is relatively shady from all the overhanging trees, and there is a sign that states that you are on a wildlife management area. There are no amenities at this boat ramp like a restroom or picnic tables, and they also have specific regulations that state, no alcohol may be on the premises. You're not even allowed to possess it in this area. It's for hunting and fishing only!
I launched my kayak around 11:00 a.m. I had the intention of paddling as far upstream as I could until the Elk River turned into a creek. The water at the boat ramp was clear, and cold, and there is lots of hydrilla grass growing! It's a neat, natural area, that doesn't look like any of the other places that I fish. As you go upstream, instead of having rock cliffs that bend the river to their will, the banks are made of mud! They get very steep, sometimes vertical, and deposit untold of mounts of trees into the water! This location is a bass fishing paradise!
I paddled 3 miles upstream, until I couldn't go any farther. I will drop a pin, where the river ends, and turns into a creek that is so shallow, and so swift, that it's not fun to continue going up...
https://goo.gl/maps/wdwYaHVXRjAgnM7J6
The three miles between the boat ramp and the pin that I just dropped are some of the best bass fishing that I have ever seen in my life. The sheer volume of trees in the water, mean that there are limitless hiding spots! There is grass, every inch of this river! Not necessarily in the middle, but on both banks. It's a fantastic place to use a topwater frog, right now, because the surface is covered with pollen. It piles up heavy into corners, creating great hiding places for big bass. I didn't spend much time fishing, cuz it takes a long time to paddle 3 miles upstream. On the handful of casts that I did make, I was receiving great interest in my spinnerbait from really large bass! Unfortunately, that would be there motive operandi on the day... I could get fish to follow, but I couldn't get very many to bite.
That was fine with me! I just wanted to know they were there. When I started driving that direction, I had no idea what it was going to look like! This is the headwaters of Woods reservoir. I didn't know if it would be a gravelly bottom or limestone cliffs, or if I would be able to paddle upstream at all! When I got there, I was stunned! The area is pristine, I didn't see any trash in the river. It's barely used, I was the only person at the boat ramp, until a few people came out to paddle around at sunset.
The water is cold! I was surprised. It's not deep. You can see the bottom, most of the way. There were only a couple of places where it looked like it got more than 7 feet deep. I did manage to catch a couple bass. For the most part, I was throwing my spinnerbait that I've been doing really well with the last couple of months. Bass were very interested, and would follow all the way to the kayak, but most of them would not commit to the lure. I didn't spend much time, trying to figure out exactly what they wanted. I went all the way upstream, had lunch, and then made my way back to my vehicle. By the time I got there, it was nearly 6:00.
This will be one of my go-to locations next spring. Woods reservoir is loaded with fish like white bass and hybrid bass and even striped bass. Those fish, along with crappie, will go up this stretch of river in great numbers! They have already turned around for now. I was able to catch one white bass up the creek, but the majority of them have finished their run for the year. Not unlike the tributaries on Percy Priest lake, crappie will go all the way up to that creek, where the water is only a foot deep! They weren't there yesterday, the only panfish that I saw were bluegill and red ear. That's how it works for these fish. The crappie go way upstream when they are pre-spawn, and then they go to a comfortable area to spawn. Then, bluegill and other panfish swim up the tributaries during their pre-spawn.

title: Trip Report #55
content_raw:
When and where to go musky fishing...
A friend of mine owns a business in McMinnville Tennessee called Mad Musky Watersports. Her name is Stacy, and she is the biggest driving factor in my ability to continuously catch muskie. She offers a shuttle service for kayakers. Yesterday, I utilized her services to take my kayak down the Collins River from Turner's bend back to my vehicle at Myers cove boat ramp. I will be giving you her phone number, and you can give her a text to set up a time to meet.  She has a truck that can haul a couple of kayaks, maybe even three if they are small.
Here's how it works. After you confirm your date and time, if you have your own kayak, you can show up at Myers cove boat ramp, which will be the end of your trip...
https://share.google/a6F1B9Ye3Tg1X2TZY
You will load your kayaks into her truck, and then she will drive you up the river about 5 miles upstream, where you will launch your kayak down a relatively steep hill that is perfectly designed to slide kayaks to the water's edge. Once at the water's edge, you will get loaded into the river, and float back down to your vehicle, at your leisure. You can take all day, or you can paddle right down to the takeout point, which is where you met her, at Myers cove boat ramp. This is a great stretch of river, because no matter how low the water gets, you can always paddle from beginning to end. Even during times of drought, this stretch of river will hold enough water to not only float your kayak, but also have plenty of fish to catch.
Once again, her name is Stacy, and she has requested that you text, as opposed to call. Simply send a text message, tell her who you are, and that better day since you to do a kayak trip. The cost for her to shuttle your kayak is $30. Right now, this is the only service she is offering. During the summer time, she has a shop with kayaks, that she will rent. If you don't have your own kayak, that will be an option, after the school year ends. All of her helpers are school-age students, and she doesn't begin renting kayaks until they can do the heavy lifting for her. If your kayak is too heavy for you to pick up by yourself, you probably shouldn't do this trip. You need to be able to load your kayak into her truck. That's the one caveat. Here is her phone number...
931-743-7566 Mad Musky Watersports
Now for the good stuff, the musky fishing! Yesterday, my buddy and I didn't catch any muskie. That happens a lot! I can't remember exactly, but it seems like, the first five or six times that I kayaked this river, I never saw a muskie, let alone never caught one. After several trips, I broke the ice, and caught my first muskie. It seems like that happens a lot. When I take people out here for their first time, they very rarely ever catch a muskie. These fish are very elusive, after all, they're called the fish of 10,000 casts for a reason.
Yesterday, we had a muskie follow a 4-inch white paddle tail on a 1/4 of an ounce jig head all the way back to the boat. When that happens, you need to do what's called a figure eight. You literally stick your rod down in the water with your lure on about 2 feet of line and then try to swing it back and forth beside the kayak to get the Muskie to follow, and eventually bite. My buddy was giving his best effort! It's really hard to do a proper figure eight in a seated position from a kayak. Despite his best effort, and the fact that the musky followed all the way around his kayak, eventually, it turned off, swimming back into the deep, without so much as a nip at the lure.
After that, we would see a few more fish, that didn't have much interest in what we were doing. We saw two musky fighting, presumably over spawning grounds. The musky spawn should be pretty much over. They spawn when the water temperature reaches 55°, and that happened early this year. Typically, they spawn between mid-march and mid-april. I would say everything is wrapping up now. The only reason that's important, is because when they're spawning, they're usually pretty tough to catch. They're always pretty tough to catch, but they get even tougher during the spawn. Right now, post spawn, is the best time to go get them!
During the hottest months of the summer, August and September, I will not target these fish. The water temperatures get too warm, and they are so big, and they fight so hard, that recovery is often impossible. Many times, during the summer, once these fish get caught, it will be the last fight of their life. Colder water holds more oxygen, and more oxygen in the water allows these fish to recover faster, after they get into a fight with a fisherman. It's best to go fishing for these fish between now and the end of July.
Unfortunately, it's really tough to catch other types of fish in this stretch of water. Because these giant muskie rule the area, I have never had much luck catching bass. There should be great numbers of smallmouth bass in this river, but these musky keep them out of the area. THIS IS NOT WILD SPECULATION! I HAVE RECEIPTS!
Two different times when I have gone fishing at this location, TWRA has been at the Myers cove boat ramp with three shocking boats. Their intention, to cover as much water as possible and shock musky to do a population survey. What they told me, each time, is fact. From the Myers cove area, upstream, there aren't many smallmouth bass to be found. Even when they run their shock boats, they only occasionally find a few. The reason, that stretch of river is loaded with muskie.
A few years ago, the TWRA was doing a smallmouth bass movement study. They had tagged about 30 fish in the Collins River with yellow tags sticking out of the back, near the dorsal fin, that had instructions to call a telephone number and indicated a $100 reward. I caught two of those fish. The procedure was, to call the number on the tag, and report exactly how it where you caught the fish. Each time, that I caught one of these fish, it had been tagged in the same location. I was considerably downstream from Myers cove, as far as 10 miles. That's how far away the smallmouth bass are from these musky. To facilitate their smallmouth bass movement study, they needed to place tags on bass up and down the river. When they tried to shock for bass from the Myers cove area upstream, they weren't able to find any! They had to go downstream, catch some bass, put the tags in them, and then put them back upstream. What they found out was, those fish quickly moved away from that area, back downstream, where there are less musky, and they felt more comfortable. Bottom line, you're going musky fishing.
Now that you know where you're going, you need to know when to go. If you don't want to know the science behind when I go to a particular river, you don't have to for this one. You can simply text Stacy, and she will tell you if River conditions are right. The way you monitor River conditions is by using the USGS website. The United States geological survey provides us with sensors on most rivers, creeks, and streams, that give us real time data about how the water is flowing. Like I mentioned before, no matter how low the flow gets on this stretch of river, you will always be able to float! There is an operational maximum. I don't like to float this River when it goes over 500 CFS... At that point, you don't have much time to fish, you're just floating all the way back to your car. Yesterday, the river was flowing at 270 CFS when we started our trip. Cfs, or cubic feet per second, is how we measure the flow of rivers. One cubic foot, is the size of one basketball. Yesterday, the flow of that river, was 270 basketballs per second, passing by anyone given point. That's nice and low! I loved it, and you can find that information, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03421000/all-graphs/#period=P7D

I wish I could tell you. As much as I have fished for them, I am certain, they do what they want. They feed when they want, on what they want, from where they want. There isn't necessarily a magic corner on this stretch of river, or a deep pool, where they gather. You can find these fish pressed up against a rock face in 10 feet of water, or sitting in grass in six to eight inches sunning themselves. They truly are a mystery, but I have one thing figured out. Don't fish for them! Fishing for them will drive you nuts. Unless you're a really good muskie fisherman, I would suggest fishing for bass.
But you already told us there aren't any bass in this stretch of river. That's correct! There are not. But you still want to use your favorite Bass lures. Whatever type of lure you have the most confidence in, that's what you want to throw at these fish. You will know how to work it, and that will make the lure effective. Effective lures will draw the attention of muskie, no matter what type of lure they are. The most important thing, is to have extremely oversized gear. You need a really heavy pole, really heavy line, a really big net, some really long pliers, and a pair of small bolt cutters.
If the fish gets its mouth pinned with treble hooks, you will want to cut the hooks with your bolt cutter. If the hooks are in the fish, but you can remove them, you will want really long pliers, so that you don't have to reach near the thrashing fish. If you've hooked a fish, you want to get it into a net where it can safely swim around. Find the biggest rubber net that you can! I can stand up in my net! It needs to be big enough for a 3 foot long fish to swim around on his own, without being cramped. I use my 7 ft medium heavy rod. It's very stiff, and it would drag in a truck, if you have the right line. I like to use 65 pound Berkeley triline braid. On that heavy line, you want to attach a 100 pound steel leader. I like a 6-inch leader. The reason this is the only appropriate setup, is because it allows you to get the fish in quickly. Having heavy equipment minimizes the fight. You will still have an epic fight! But if you have the right equipment, it will be a lot shorter. You want these fish to be released happy, and healthy. The best way to do that, is to have the right equipment.
This is a long trip! The last mile of river has no flow. The water is deep, and you will have to paddle the whole way. Because you will have to load your kayak into her truck, and then down the hill, into the river, this trip is probably a three out of five on the effort scale of one to five. It's definitely going to be moderate, to difficult.
I like to throw lots of different lures. Top water lures, paddle tails, spinnerbaits, and even some of my favorite musky lures. You'll have the most success, if you will just fish. Try not to worry too much about targeting them, just go fishing in the spots that look like they should hold fish. Enjoy your time, and keep an eye out! One of the most fun things about this trip, is that the water is typically very clear. That means, you should see muskie! Yesterday, we saw seven different muskie. One followed my friends lure, all the way around the kayak, and one followed my lure, and took a quick swipe at it, before it swam away. On my best day, we caught a handful of muskie, and saw a total of 22! Keep your eyes peeled, and your head on a swivel!

I will be giving you her phone number, and you can give her a text to set up a time to meet. She has a truck that can haul a couple of kayaks, maybe even three if they are small.

Here's how it works. After you confirm your date and time, if you have your own kayak, you can show up at Myers cove boat ramp, which will be the end of your trip...

https://share.google/a6F1B9Ye3Tg1X2TZY

You will load your kayaks into her truck, and then she will drive you up the river about 5 miles upstream, where you will launch your kayak down a relatively steep hill that is perfectly designed to slide kayaks to the water's edge. Once at the water's edge, you will get loaded into the river, and float back down to your vehicle, at your leisure. You can take all day, or you can paddle right down to the takeout point, which is where you met her, at Myers cove boat ramp. This is a great stretch of river, because no matter how low the water gets, you can always paddle from beginning to end. Even during times of drought, this stretch of river will hold enough water to not only float your kayak, but also have plenty of fish to catch.

Once again, her name is Stacy, and she has requested that you text, as opposed to call. Simply send a text message, tell her who you are, and that better day since you to do a kayak trip. The cost for her to shuttle your kayak is $30. Right now, this is the only service she is offering. During the summer time, she has a shop with kayaks, that she will rent. My buddy was giving his best effort! It's really hard to do a proper figure eight in a seated position from a kayak. Despite his best effort, and the fact that the musky followed all the way around his kayak, eventually, it turned off, swimming back into the deep, without so much as a nip at the lure.

After that, we would see a few more fish, that didn't have much interest in what we were doing. We saw two musky fighting, presumably over spawning grounds. The musky spawn should be pretty much over. They spawn when the water temperature reaches 55°, and that happened early this year. Typically, they spawn between mid-march and mid-april. I would say everything is wrapping up now. The only reason that's important, is because when they're spawning, they're usually pretty tough to catch. The water temperatures get too warm, and they are so big, and they fight so hard, that recovery is often impossible. It's best to go fishing for these fish between now and the end of July.

title: Trip Report #56
content_raw:
Public ponds you can kayak or bank fish...
Today I went to the Percy Priest wildlife Management area at Poole Knob. This area is only open Monday through Thursday, September 1st until April 30th. That means, soon, it will be open 7 days a week. There are a few ponds in the area, and you are allowed to fish there as well as kayak...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/VgKYZocLz8zKAPta8
I have already confirmed with the TWRA that you are allowed to kayak these ponds. There are six ponds, but a couple of them are dried up because of the drought. There are two main ponds, and I fished the biggest one today. I loaded my kayak into the pond, after I had a picnic lunch under a shade tree, right around 12:30 p.m...
https://goo.gl/maps/T1grRKWMckQtp9uK6
I have fished in this pond before, from the bank. Today, I wanted to take my kayak, and my fish finder to see how deep this body of water is. The center is about 6 feet deep, and the middle is about 5 feet deep for a few hundred yards in any direction. The lake itself is probably about 3 acres. When I went there before, I used my crappie setup to fish from the bank, and caught a handful of nice crappie as well as a catfish. When I scanned today, I saw that it was loaded with fish! Not only were there plenty of crappie and catfish, there were also giant carp, and lots of largemouth bass that were on bed near the bank.
I didn't spend much time fishing for crappie. I have caught them before, and I know they're in there. I started with my crappie setup, quickly caught a small crappie, and then focused on bass fishing. This little lake is full of bass! Almost all of them are largemouth. They didn't want anything to do with food! They were in the middle of spawning. The water temperature at the surface was 76°, and these fish only had one thing on their mind. I tried catching one, while it was on its bed, with a crappie jig under a bobber. I was twitching it, above the bass, when it ate the bobber! That was when I made the change to a Whopper plopper, and started fishing top water.
I worked my way all the way around the pond, found lots of different fish, but none of them wanted to hit topwater. Until one of them did. I could see a bass on bed, so I casted my lure directly on top of it, like I had so many others, and it exploded on it! A nice big large mouth, and what I thought, would be one of the biggest bass in the pond. I was wrong! Around the corner, and the next cove, I made a cast near some of the only rocks that are in the pond. I started my Whopper plopper, with a slow retrieve, and then, made it come to an abrupt stop. As it lay there, motionless on the surface, a really big bass exploded on it! It would turn out, there are plenty of three plus pound bass in this lake.
Don't worry if you don't have a kayak, you can walk almost all the way around this bank! The grass is starting to get tall now, but the water is low, and the bottom of the pond is exposed. It's pretty dry, and hard-packed, so it's good to walk on! I went, a couple of weeks ago, to do a test run, and caught a couple crappie from the bank, right where I dropped this pin. That is the main point on the lake, and fish cycle, from the deep part of the lake, up to the points, to feed. Every type of fish! I could see all my fish finder, that there were thousands of fish in the center of the lake.
There are no amenities in this area. There are no bathrooms, there are no buildings. There are no benches. There are a couple of ponds that are full of fish, and gravel roads that lead you around the property. The grass is starting to get a little tall, but they keep it mowed all summer. It's a great place to explore. There's lots of natural area, and wildlife, doing its thing, mostly uninterrupted.

title: Trip Report #57
content_raw:
Boatloads of fish at Center Hill Dam...
Today I launched my kayak from Buffalo valley boat ramp at around 12:30 p.m...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/1JuYbGQ0PCakNexuh
This time of year, dozens of different species of fish swim up the Caney Fork River, and get stuck, at Center Hill dam. I like to target crappie, specifically, this time of year. You could probably catch a crappie anytime of day or night, any day of the year, below Center Hill dam. I have definitely caught one every month of the year. This time of year, there are lots of them up there! They are looking to spawn, and they start heading upstream. Today, I kept 11 crappie, most of them were females, that were full of eggs! That's the way it is every year, lots of crappie, looking to spawn, stacked up below Center Hill dam.
These fish are coming from Old hickory lake. That is the Cumberland river. The Caney Fork River below Center Hill dam, flows for a little more than 20 miles, before it reaches the Cumberland River below Cordell Hull Dam. Lots of different species of fish from the river, also known as Old hickory lake, swim up the Caney Fork river, at different times of the year. Right now, crappie have made their annual migration, looking for upstreams spawning grounds. Other fish have made their way to the base of the dam as well, for different reasons.
To catch a stringer full of crappie today, I simply paddled my kayak into the left corner of the dam, next to the waterfall. Not all the way next to the dam, just next to the rock cliffs, where the tree is overhanging. I sat there catching fish for a little while, before I popped out onto the cliffs, to stretch my legs, and get a better angle on these fish. The method I was using was painfully slow, and it was tough to catch these fish with my kayak floating around, and bobbing on the waves. It was much easier to get a feel for exactly what I needed to do, while I was standing on the bank.
Here's how it all went down... I had my seven and a half foot ultralight rod and reel. I've been using 4 pound, Stren, monofilament. Today, I started with a 1/32nd ounce jig head and an electric chicken color Bobby Garland. That would catch me a few eager fish, but the rest of the fish that I would catch, would take a little more patience. While sitting in the corner, next to the current that comes off the waterfall, I would cast into the current, and allow my lure to drift off to the side where it would start to slowly sink. As soon as it got off to the side of the current, I would start a slow retrieve. The first few fish made it easy. They hit as soon as I threw in there, and I put them on the stringer. The next seven keepers were really tough to get.
After the initial hot bite, slowed down. I had to slow down my presentation. I was already reeling my lure painfully slow, with my rod tip up, waiting for the faintest bite, so I could set the hook, but that wasn't slow enough. To slow down even more, I reduced the size of my jig head, in half. I went with a 1/64th of an ounce jig head. This moves through the water so slowly, and sinks so slowly, that it immediately had an effect! On my very first cast with the lighter lure, I smacked another big crappie. Then I started catching a bunch of small ones, so I got out on the cliffs, to not only stretch my legs, but to really try to get dialed in. That's exactly what I did! Here's how it went...
Standing on the flat limestone, underneath the tree, I would make a short cast, and hold my jig head against the current. That was it. Every once in awhile, a crappie would come up, and it would be a good one! One of them, was over 14 inches, a Tennessee trophy crappie! That was how I pushed the number of crappie that I had on the stringer up to 11. I tried to get my limit of crappie, which is 15, but it wasn't in the cards! There were a few other fish in there that we're getting in the way of me catching all of the crappie that I wanted to. Before I got out and started fishing on the bank, I was catching some of those other fish that had made their way, below Center Hill dam.
After I caught my first few fish by casting out with the current, I started making some casts up into the corner, and reeling my lure back down the current. That's a tricky endeavor, but those fish were hot! I started getting bites right away, and then I started catching fish, but they were largemouth bass! The limit in the state of Tennessee is five bass. On this particular body of water, there is no size regulation for black bass, which includes largemouth, smallmouth, and spotted bass. While I was fishing for my kayak, I limited out on largemouth bass! Using my crappie lure, and a crappie retrieve, I caught five little largemouth. That's important, and I'll tell you why...
Every year, usually around May, I like to go bass fishing in this corner, by the waterfalls, before the sun rises. That darkest hour, from 4:45 a.m. until 5: 45 a.m., is when those largemouth come alive! I like to paddle my kayak, into the corner, and cast a peanut butter jelly Ned rig on bottom. Most of the time, my goal is to limit out, with five big bass, in 1 hour. It's a lot of fun, and it's a sure thing this time of year! Catching my limit on a crappie jig, during the daytime, means that, not only are there a lot of them up there, but they should be all over the place! Not just in the corner, but all along the rock wall that goes back to the boat ramp, and even up against the walls of the dam. Most of the biggest bass I've ever seen in my life, have been pressed against the wall, in that crystal clear water.
So now you know that, every year, at this time of year, for the next couple of months, until the heat of summer, you can go below Center Hill dam, and catch lots of crappie, or lots of bass if you would like to. What you already knew, was that, the place is loaded with trout. Today, while I was trying to catch crappie, a 21 and a half inch brown trout ate my Bobby Garland. On my ultralight, that was a fight that I didn't think I was going to win. Ultimately, the fish made it to the net. Unfortunately, brown trout are required to measure 24 inches in length, before you are allowed to keep them. That meant, my fish was short of being legal. I got a few quick pictures, a short video, and then sent him on his way. That's not necessarily a surprise catch. Earlier this year, while I was crappie fishing in the same spot, I hooked a rainbow trout that I was allowed to keep. Big rainbow trout must measure more than 20 inches before you are allowed to keep one. If you catch a rainbow trout over 20 inches, and you would like to keep it, you are only allowed to keep one, per day.
I went after 12:00 p.m., because that was when the generators were turning on. I like to fish for these crappie, when there are two generators on. Today, the generators were scheduled to turn one on at 12:00 p.m., and two or more at 1:00 p.m. Fortunately for me, they went to two generators at 1:00 p.m. This is the only time of year that I will sit in the corner, to target these fish. Most of the year, I like to sit in the center, in the deepest part, on an anchor, while the generators are off. This time of year, there are so many crappie in there, that when the generators turn on, they pile up in the corner. They don't do that the rest of the year. That's what makes right now, so special! You can plan your trip, by looking at the generating schedule, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
To go fishing for bass, in the dark, I like the generators to the off! It's much easier to target bass without all the current. They like to get out and roam around, when the water settles down. Crappie and trout, do just the opposite! They get a move on, and so should you! Next time I'm out at Center Hill dam, I hope to see you there!

These fish are coming from Old hickory lake. That is the Cumberland river. title: Trip Report #58
content_raw:
A cautionary tale...
Several times this year, I have kayak the East Fork Stones River, at the headwaters of Percy Priest lake. This trip is ideal, during winter pool. Winter pool on Percy Priest lake, it's when they draw down the lake, 7 feet, to accommodate for winter and spring rainfall. Typically, they will raise the lake to summer pool, around mid-April. Bodies of water are measured in elevation above sea level. For example, Percy Priest lake, is that summer pool, when the surface of the water at the dam is at 490 feet above sea level. Winter pool, is when the surface of the water at the dam is at 483 feet above sea level. Currently, the lake is just below 486 feet above sea level. That puts it 4 feet below summer pool, and that makes this trip extra fun, at least, it should.
This kayak trip is about 5 miles long. During summer pool, only the first mile is shallow with flowing water. During winter pool, only the last mile is deep, and still. That makes it fun because the moving water, pushes you along most of the way. Because we are in a drought, the water coming down the East Fork Stones River wasn't sufficient to float our kayaks! It turns out, this stretch of river has an operational minimum. Rivers are measured in cubic feet per second. One cubic foot is about the size of one basketball. Today, the East Fork Stones River was measuring 55 cubic feet per second. You can find this river's stream data on the USGS website, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03427500/all-graphs/#period=P7D
No matter where you live, there should be a creek or a stream running nearby your town. You can ask Google to give you the USGS location on your local river, creek, or stream. Most will have a station like this one that I have shared with you. That way, you can check your local waterway, and your chart, and know what water levels are good to fish for which types of fish. When the water is really low, it's easy to target fish like bass. When the water gets really swift, and high, especially during floods, catfish usually make their way near the bank, and easy to catch. I use the USGS website system every single day to determine what type of trips I need to do. Not only where I can find fish, but where I can kayak. As it turns out, you need at least 100 CFS on this river, are you are going to get stuck!
Not only is the river so shallow that you will bottom out in a kayak, and have to get out and push, this spring, at some point in time, a giant sycamore tree fell, blocking the entire river! You will have to get out, and portage, to go around this tree. So that's new, and it's a bummer. That tree doesn't look like it's going anywhere! This trip was already a 5 out of five on the effort scale because the put-in location is not a boat ramp, you have to carry your kayak a couple hundred yards over really rough terrain from the parking lot. Now, it's even more difficult.
It's important to note, that this stretch of river, only really fishes well, in the late winter to end of spring. When the lake comes up, this water will get stagnant. It will be relatively shallow, it will be still, and it won't hold much bait. The majority of the fish that are in there now, will head back out to the main lake. This time of year, it's like being in an aquarium! There are fish everywhere! Unfortunately, today was an unbelievably tough day of catching fish. We saw several other fishermen when we were ending our trip, and everyone had the same report, fish weren't biting. That was truly tragic, because today, I saw more gigantic bass in that stretch of river, then I have ever seen!
I've gotten used to seeing lots of largemouth bass on this particular stretch of river. Today, there were lots of really big smallmouth bass, cruising around in the shallow, clear water. For the first two and a half miles of this trip, the river never really gets more than three feet, and you can see all the fish! Not only were there lots of bass, that we couldn't catch, but there were tons of every different type of sunfish as well as gar and every different type of carp and red horse. There were schools of each different type of bait fish that Percy Priest holds. It truly was like visiting an aquarium!
There won't be a video from this trip, because we didn't catch any fish. If you are young, and have a strong back, you should probably give it a go. It's going to be one of the more strenuous things you will do all week, but it's epic! And if those fish are biting, it's going to be the day of a lifetime. Here's how you facilitate this trip...
You'll want to launch your kayak from Walter Hill dam. There is no boat ramp. You'll have to park in the parking lot, conveniently, right next to the only port a Jon. There is a trail down to the water's edge, but it's got boulders, and steep inclines, and deep gravel. Take your lightest kayak! I have wheels that I can strap to the underneath of mine, and that makes it a lot easier to roll the kayaks down to the water's edge. Easier, definitely not easy. Here is a link to Walter Hill Dam...
Walter Hill Dam https://share.google/CoGAeAlL9y9ayWYV2
If you paddled directly to the end, it would still take you a few hours. If you take your time, it's going to take you at least 7 hours. If you stop, have lunch, fish from the bank, make a day of it, it could easily turn into a 10-hour trip. When the water is down, it takes significantly longer!
There are white water rapids at the very beginning of this trip. My clients today, we're still new to kayaking. They handled tough rapids really well. I think most kayakers could float right over most of the shallow water spots, with very little trouble. There are a couple of strainers, which are trees in the water, in swift moving areas. It's best to get out and walk around, if you don't feel comfortable paddling through.
Other than it being a drag fest, and excruciatingly hard to get your boat in the water, and incredibly difficult to portage around the sycamore tree, it's totally worth it! The stretch of river is loaded with giant bass! The only reason I would subject myself to this stretch of river again, it's because these fish won't be there in the near future. Getting after them now, would be the only time to get after them. So if you're going to go, you need to know where to take out. The end of this trip, is very convenient! It's a boat ramp, on Percy Priest lake, called Mona boat ramp...
Mona boat ramp https://share.google/GIF1m688dpCKtYfNK
Today, we tried throwing only a handful of lures. I've been having tremendous success throwing a spinnerbait. I've also been fishing with lots of people who have been catching non-stop fish with a paddle tail swimbait. If those won't work, right now, probably not much other than live bait, would. There are live bait on this trip that you could catch with a cast net, but we didn't make any stops today, and it still took us 7 hours. We simply didn't have time to use live bait. If I were going out, on this trip, I would take my cast net, and catch some live bait. It would turn it into an all-day affair, but that way, I would at least catch some fish. Those fish were spoiled! They were chasing  bait into the shallows, and blowing up on it, but they didn't want anything to do with lures.

title: Trip Report #59
content_raw:
The final cold front?
The way things are looking right now, the cold front that came through on Easter will be the last cold front of winter. That one was a doozy! Crappie went from being on fire, to being a little tough to catch. The wind didn't make it any better! When the weather gets like that, I will go Bass fishing. By now, you've already seen my reports. I don't like to force the issue with fish that aren't going to bite. When the crappie are tough to get, I will catch other fish. After Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday we're really cold, yesterday, once it started to warm up, I started chasing those crappie again.
I took my boat out from Stewart Creek boat ramp to inspect the different pins that I had dropped in that area...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/IGSSL0CaF7qsj2deI
There were a handful of fish at each different location, but they were tiny! It was also tough to get them to bite. Fast forward to today, and I went out the other direction from Stewart creek, downstream, to find some more crappie structures. Right around the corner from the boat ramp, between there and the bridge at Weekly lane, there were at least half a dozen man-made structures! Most of them had a few fish, and I was even able to catch a couple. I'm going to drop pins for all the new locations that I found...
https://goo.gl/maps/oR1VweucVFyQtqVr9
https://goo.gl/maps/AQDqanjrMLGdzmon6
https://goo.gl/maps/WkQkwa6iiuxMRNnK8
https://goo.gl/maps/z2xcsJSDrnZE9cvk7
https://goo.gl/maps/agsRJQ1UvrLSNmXH6
https://goo.gl/maps/G1ezHNR1pyuBz3XK8
Most of these structures are 8 to 10 feet under the surface of the water. They weren't holding very many fish, but they were holding some fish. The majority of the crappie on this lake are spawning. That means they're not in schools, they are sitting on beds. The males will make a bed, and sit there until a female comes along to lay her eggs. That means, the males are stationary, and the females are cruising around. Unless you find an area, where they are actively spawning, they're going to be really tough to catch!
There was a little birdie at the Stewart Creek boat ramp, who told me that, they were catching crappie in one foot of water, really close to the bank. He said, he was using a bobber, and he had his jig 8 inches under the bobber! He said, they would go to a fish attractor, and then fish behind the fish attractor, closer to the bank. I'm definitely going to give that a shot!
It's time to go to Long Hunter State Park to catch hybrid Bass from the bank...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/bYUmXLLjh8ot7hyo7
People are standing on the bank at this park all day every day right now, catching hybrid bass and striped bass. Most people are using a bobber with about 3 foot of depth and a small bluegill as bait. You could use any number of top water lures as well as a rooster tail or a paddle tail to catch these fish. Get there early, the parking lot is getting full every day! I'm not able to go, because I have clients the next two days, but the fishing has been an outstanding out there! Take a medium heavy rod with at least 15 pound braid, these fish are strong! At this location, you will be standing on cliffs. This is a long bank, and there is room for a lot of fishermen, but it's not necessarily easy. The fact that you have to stand on the cliffs, makes this at least a two on the effort scale of one to five. It's not flat, level ground, and there is no where to sit down or relax. Just hard ground, mostly limestone.

After Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday we're really cold, yesterday, once it started to warm up, I started chasing those crappie again.

I took my boat out from Stewart Creek boat ramp to inspect the different pins that I had dropped in that area...

Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/IGSSL0CaF7qsj2deI

There were a handful of fish at each different location, but they were tiny! It was also tough to get them to bite. Fast forward to today, and I went out the other direction from Stewart creek, downstream, to find some more crappie structures. Right around the corner from the boat ramp, between there and the bridge at Weekly lane, there were at least half a dozen man-made structures! Most of them had a few fish, and I was even able to catch a couple. I'm going to drop pins for all the new locations that I found...

https://goo.gl/maps/oR1VweucVFyQtqVr9

https://goo.gl/maps/AQDqanjrMLGdzmon6

https://goo.gl/maps/WkQkwa6iiuxMRNnK8

https://goo.gl/maps/z2xcsJSDrnZE9cvk7

https://goo.gl/maps/agsRJQ1UvrLSNmXH6

https://goo.gl/maps/G1ezHNR1pyuBz3XK8

Most of these structures are 8 to 10 feet under the surface of the water. They weren't holding very many fish, but they were holding some fish. The majority of the crappie on this lake are spawning. That means they're not in schools, they are sitting on beds. The males will make a bed, and sit there until a female comes along to lay her eggs. That means, the males are stationary, and the females are cruising around. Unless you find an area, where they are actively spawning, they're going to be really tough to catch!

There was a little birdie at the Stewart Creek boat ramp, who told me that, they were catching crappie in one foot of water, really close to the bank. He said, he was using a bobber, and he had his jig 8 inches under the bobber! He said, they would go to a fish attractor, and then fish behind the fish attractor, closer to the bank. I'm definitely going to give that a shot!

It's time to go to Long Hunter State Park to catch hybrid Bass from the bank...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/bYUmXLLjh8ot7hyo7

People are standing on the bank at this park all day every day right now, catching hybrid bass and striped bass. Most people are using a bobber with about 3 foot of depth and a small bluegill as bait. You could use any number of top water lures as well as a rooster tail or a paddle tail to catch these fish. Get there early, the parking lot is getting full every day! I'm not able to go, because I have clients the next two days, but the fishing has been an outstanding out there! Take a medium heavy rod with at least 15 pound braid, these fish are strong! At this location, you will be standing on cliffs. This is a long bank, and there is room for a lot of fishermen, but it's not necessarily easy. The fact that you have to stand on the cliffs, makes this at least a two on the effort scale of one to five. It's not flat, level ground, and there is no where to sit down or relax. Just hard ground, mostly limestone.

title: Trip Report #60
content_raw:
You wouldn't believe it unless it was on video...
Today, I had the most epic day! I went to Big Charlie's bait shop around noon to pick up a quarter pound of minnows and a quarter pound of shiners...
Big Charlie's Bait Shop https://share.google/OklLxURduLzyXnpvY
As I've been reporting, fish are headed up the tributaries, on all the main lakes and reservoirs. Everywhere that water is flowing into a lake, fish are in the shallowest areas they can get to! Recently, I found fish incredibly shallow in Stewart Creek at Volunteer Park...
Volunteer Park https://share.google/ofj0aVCYGIlVDwnuk
I found double digit bass schooled up below the low head Dam at Manson Pike trailhead...
Manson Pike Trailhead https://share.google/8kO5DbInugL1eejFB
I even went to the base of a waterfall to catch bass that were trying to swim up the Little duck River at Old Stone Fort Archaeological Park...
Old Stone Fort State Archaeological Park https://share.google/VEceRy24y3ZREYC7K
At the head of every river, creek, stream and tributary, there will be loads of fish! We know this! It happens every year at this time. One of the places that you can do this, every year, and catch lots of big fish, was right under my nose, and I never thought to go bass fishing there. Today, I went to the head of Percy Priest lake, on the West Fork Stones river, at Nice Mill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/98HnH3cnWwGFgmUM8
I had my 5 and 1/2 foot, ultralight rod and reel, with 4 pound monofilament, and a small bobber with a small split shot and a mosquito hook. I was planning on catching small bass and bluegill at the dam. Mission accomplished! Not only were there plenty of small bluegill and bass to catch, that were willing to eat a minnow, I also caught three rainbow trout! I spent about an hour standing on the dam using those minnows to catch little fish. Then, because I had caught three trout, I decided to go downstream to catch more trout.
There is a trail in the parking lot at this location, that goes straight down to the river's edge, a hundred times over! There are literally, a hundred different places to stand on the bank and fish, along this trail. It's a very long trail, and it's mostly pretty flat. On the effort scale of 1 to 5, this ranks right around a two.
I was looking for places where the current got swift, and then dropped off into a deep pool. There aren't many places out there like that, so when you find one, it's pretty obvious. I was casting my minnows into those spots, trying to catch a trout, with no luck. Eventually, using my same ultra light setup, I put a shiner on the hook instead of a minnow. If you don't know, a shiner is like a minnow, it's just a lot bigger. These are fantastic for bass!
It wouldn't take long at all before I hooked into a 2 pound smallmouth bass. On the next cast with a shiner, a giant fish broke my 4 pound test! At that point, I realized there were a lot of big bass in there, so I loosened the drag on my real, and made another cast, and then caught a trophy smallmouth, over 20 inches long! Then another bass, then another trophy smallmouth! Then a couple of more bass, then I was out of bait. So I headed back up to Big Charlie's, got another quarter pound of shiners, went right back to the same spot, and then caught another trophy smallmouth bass! Then, I wasn't getting any bites.
Typically, when you find a spot like this, the biggest bass will eat last. That was the case, again today, and after I caught my third trophy fish, there were no more bass in there to catch. So I took my bobber off, and made a cast with a sinker, and allowed my bait to sit on the bottom. Within 45 seconds, I had a fish pulling on the line. I was very patient, took my time to get a good hook set, and was in a fight with the biggest fish of the day! It was a 4 pound 12 ounce fish, but it wasn't a smallmouth bass, or a bass at all, it was a channel catfish! In the center of that heavy current, laying on the bottom, there was a monster catfish. It took forever to get it in, but it reminded me how much I love catfishing! Especially if they're going to bite within 60 seconds of the bait hitting the bottom.
Today was the third time this spring season that I have gone bass fishing after a cold front. When we have a bluebird sky, and a North wind, like we did today, traditional thinking is, it's going to be tough to fish. On days like today, directly after a massive cold front, I like to go bass fishing. For some reason, they get fired up! I've been doing so well the last couple of years, that I look forward to these cold fronts in the spring and the summer. Cold fronts do not have the same effect on bass in the fall and the winter. Something about this time of year, they love it!

title: Trip Report #61
content_raw:
Lots of new fish attractors...
Yesterday, the wind finally laid down a little, and I was able to do some work on Percy Priest lake. This time, I launched my boat out of Smith Springs boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/rVCou6Kgxh5Nn3zy9
I did the same thing I usually do when I'm exploring a new place, looking for crappie structure... I started scanning the area counterclockwise, and marking fish attractors. I found lots of good places that will hold crappie, most of the year. Right now, on Percy Priest lake, crappie are spawning near the bank. You won't find very many on underwater structure or fish attractors, unless they are very close to the bank, in very shallow water. Most of the locations I found were near the bank, but not close enough to fish from the bank, except for one.
There is a buoy marking a very large fish attractor that has been built by the TWRA. It's located near the bank of the Smith Springs recreation area, but the recreation area is closed. I'm not sure, if or when, it ever opens. During the pre-spawn, which was about a month ago now, this location would have been on fire! Unfortunately, I didn't know about it. I'm going to drop two pins... There were fish attractors everywhere in between both of these pins, and all around them! This was a truly gigantic fish attractor...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/LpG65mCLrHaxDHDS6
https://goo.gl/maps/YAAUutLXaTQ6Zejg8
To get over there, you would have to park in the parking lot with the boat ramp, and then hike through the woods to the water's edge. I didn't see great numbers of fish in this area, but there were some large crappie roaming around. When the spawn is over, they will likely gather on the fish attractors, before the heat of the summer really sets in, and they start to move deep along the cliffs on Percy Priest Lake. This is a massive new spot on my radar! I suspect I will catch lots of fish here, and it's great for crowds of people, 150 people could stand on this bank and everybody could catch fish! I confirmed with a TWRA agent, Ethan Davis, that he inspects people with buckets loaded with crappie, at this location.
The next handful of pins that I am going to drop are all relatively close to one another, but you will have to get there by boat or kayak. It's not terribly far from the boat ramp, and there are lots of pins around this particular peninsula. I didn't see any fish gathered on these fish attractors, but when the time is right, they will be loaded! The best time of year for fish attractors that are located underneath the surface of the water when the lake is at winter pool, is most of the year! Typically, during the spawn, and during the hottest part of the summer, is the only time there won't be fish on these attractors. We can expect these to be loaded for the month of May and June and probably even July...
https://goo.gl/maps/c3tDsF6FskwHWgq96
https://goo.gl/maps/SqrCXBZy7qwHmo8F6
https://goo.gl/maps/pHqwJZJU7o35ZWoQ9
https://goo.gl/maps/rknRgf5EGpUbjDLy9
https://goo.gl/maps/qgkDp3ncgdYy9iCb9
https://goo.gl/maps/VEnDth7T1G6pPMyL6
https://goo.gl/maps/nxtYbeQxGCYsBWaRA
https://goo.gl/maps/kwEBzpoc4sJ32VdT7
Unfortunately, all of these locations are on the bank near a neighborhood. Unless you live in that neighborhood, you're not going to get access from the bank. It's just as well, most of these pens are too far away from the bank to fish, effectively. Most of these structures, were quite unique! I saw large, man-made structures, the likes of which I had never seen before. They were very uniquely shaped, and sized! No doubt in my mind, with the effort that people went to to create these, that they will be loaded with fish, when the time is right. Because I know where these are now, I will continue to inspect them, and let you know when they are loaded up. That way, you can mark the time of year on your calendar, and be sure to go back there, for years to come!
Yesterday was more of an exploratory mission, I would like to slowly scan all of Percy Priest Lake with my forward facing sonar, so that I can find all of the marked fish attractors, as well as all of the unmarked ones. It's my plan, to have no less than 100 pins on Percy Priest lake. That should be easy to accomplish, given the amount of structure that people have planted themselves, in the lake. As I was looking around, I found myself in the cove for the YMCA...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/w8oeX4ufXfnJCGA49
This area was loaded with bass! It's a quick paddle around from the boat ramp, if you'd like to take your kayak, and if you have one of those fast Bass boats, you may be able to win a tournament in this cove! I was fishing with my buddy Chris, and we caught several largemouth and smallmouth bass in this cove, in relatively short order. I was throwing the same purple spinnerbait with two silver blades that I've been throwing all spring. He was throwing a 4-in white paddle tail with a jig head that had a silver underspin blade. We just made a quick pass through the area, looking for fish attractors, and caught half a dozen bass. Had we stayed in that area, we could have loaded the boat! The only fish I saw on the forward facing sonar, we're bass, and there were hundreds of them!
I plan to give every boat ramp in the Middle Tennessee area this type of treatment. There will always be setbacks, like the two weeks my boat was down because I needed to repair my trailer. Before that, I was making pretty good progress, and even got started on Center Hill lake, before it got really windy, which makes it tough to do any work out on the lake. As of right now, the next 10 days have wind in the forecast between 15 and 25 miles per hour every day! That's one of the toughest conditions to fish, especially if you don't know where you're going or what you're looking for. I intend to try my hardest to find as many locations as possible!
