title: Trip Report #62
content_raw:
Those red ear sunfish were right where I left them...
Two days ago I took my kayak down the West Fork Stones River on the Murfreesboro Greenway from the Manson Pike trailhead...
Manson Pike Trailhead https://share.google/HPmpjprdA0lKPY3kA
There's a nice boat ramp here, and it's easy to paddle downstream, and come back up, when River levels are low. A low level for this stretch of river, would be less than 100 cubic feet per second. One cubic foot is about the size of one basketball, so a river flowing at 100 cubic feet per second, would be flowing at about 100 basketballs per second, passing by any given point. You can find the river levels on the USGS chart for the West Fork stones river, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D
I went down as far as you can go without having to go over rapids that you can't paddle back up. It's a pretty long way! Most of a mile. And there's really good fishing for bass everywhere in between. What I wasn't expecting to see, was a school of fish that looks like crappie, but turned out to be red ear sunfish. If you don't know, red ear sunfish are typically called shellcracker around this part of the world. They are beautiful, and they are highly sought after, because they get big, think of them as bigger bluegill. I wanted to see if I could get them from the bank, it definitely looked like they were close enough when I was in my kayak.
I parked at the General Bragg trailhead and started walking upstream toward these fish...
General Bragg Trailhead https://share.google/e4v1U8yXROfuGSsb4
It's about a half mile upstream to the spot where I marked those fish, but I was pleasantly surprised by how much bank fishing access there was along the way. There were several different trails over to the water's edge where you could pop in and potentially catch a nice fish. There was also one area, where there was a lot of neat rapids and shallow water, and I'm 100% certain that it's holding trout! They release trout upstream every year and they make their way down to this spot, and hang out, until the end of May. I was on my way upstream, to some still water, where I saw these fish...
https://goo.gl/maps/TpPxA9iMvjsRQfov6
There's a nice spot to stand right here, just off the greenway. Because you have to walk the Greenway at least half a mile, and go a little off-road, fishing in this area would rank as a two on the effort scale of 1 to 5. It's pretty easy! Once I got to this location, I started fishing the way I had planned, using crickets underneath a bobber. That didn't go as well for me as I thought it would. Instead of catching these giant red ear sunfish, I was catching lots of bluegill and long ear sunfish. There were lots of them! Every once in awhile, I would get a red ear sunfish, but not as often as I had hoped. I did pretty well, made a great video, and then started walking back to my vehicle, and fishing the different spots that I could get in along the way.
Instead of using crickets, I was throwing a rooster tail, 1/8 of an ounce white, on my way back. That allowed me to pop in to several locations, make a few quick casts, and then move along. What I figured out, was awesome! These red ear fish were looking for something like a minnow! The best red ear that I caught all day was on my way walking back to the car, throwing that rooster tail. Manson Pike Trailhead https://share.google/HPmpjprdA0lKPY3kA

One cubic foot is about the size of one basketball, so a river flowing at 100 cubic feet per second, would be flowing at about 100 basketballs per second, passing by any given point. You can find the river levels on the USGS chart for the West Fork stones river, here...

https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D

title: Trip Report #63
content_raw:
Crappie and bass on beds...
I got my boat back! Yesterday, I took a test run out of my local boat ramp from Stewart Creek boat ramp...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/RgkVEvGf7qa651JkC
I wanted to make sure my boat and trailer were in top working order, so I took a quick run around 9:00 a.m. I headed directly back into the creek, to the very large fish attractor that is marked with a buoy...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/va2PnQ3YGUaTq2zR7
At this location, there is a white buoy, that says, fish! All around this buoy, there are corrugated pipe fish attractors. My buddy caught a slab crappie on the first cast! But we were unable to fish, because the wind was crazy. This was just a test ride anyway, so we headed back, to the boat ramp, with the intention of checking my other pins, along the way. I have more than half a dozen pins, in the main channel, between Stewart Creek boat ramp, and the back of Stewart creek. As fish head into the shallows, to spawn, they stage in these areas, in great numbers, to feed heavily. What we found, was nothing short of amazing!
Unfortunately, the wind was way too stiff for us to fish. On each one of these pins that I'm about to drop for you, there were hundreds of crappie! I've already given you these pins before, I didn't drop any new ones. I will do this from time to time, when I find fishing this good. We tried to drop my spot rock anchor, and catch these fish, but before we could get a cast on them, the wind would blow us off of position, and way too far away. Despite that fact, we were still able to catch a handful of crappie, just to determine that we were actually looking at crappie, and not some other type of fish like bluegill. Here's where we found lots of crappie...
https://goo.gl/maps/hoNUNwPE3HA2a3Yx9
https://goo.gl/maps/jNrMNAMZ5mKMLQ3U6
https://goo.gl/maps/eud9gPDRiDHDVyFS8
https://goo.gl/maps/6eAf7TZ3RfZrLn1t5
Also, there was no one fishing from the bank on the cliffs at Stewart creek. Because there were no fishermen making casts, I went over to check out the trees that are suspended on the cliffs. One tree, that I've been telling you guys about for years, had thousands of crappie on it! If you park in the parking lot, it's a short walk through the trail, to a spot on the cliffs where, if you turn around and look at the cliff face, you will see some graffiti that says "o + d" in Black paint. Right in front of that spot, there are two trees on top of each other, in the water. That spot was loaded with crappie! I mean, loaded! They will be there, ready for you to catch from the bank, until May! Also, that handicapped fishing pier that is in the parking lot here, had lots of people catching crappie. Make sure to keep that thing manned, at all times!
After lunch, I went to do something that I haven't done before. I went to Manson Pike trailhead, on the Murfreesboro Greenway to use the kayak launch. I have launched from this boat ramp before, but only to go downstream. My intention was, to go as far downstream as I could, and then come back up to the boat ramp. I've been asked, constantly, to update people with kayak fishing spots where they could catch some nice fish, but not be exposed to the lake. Because the winds were so heavy yesterday, I decided to get away from the lake in the afternoon, and try fishing somewhere down in the river basin, where I might have a little more luck. After all, wind is one of the toughest conditions to fish in.
I was pleasantly surprised! The boat ramp at Manson Pike trailhead is fantastic! You can back your car or truck right down to the water's edge, and drop your kayak for a quick easy launch. Paddling downstream, almost a mile, was relatively effortless. Coming back upstream, wasn't very hard, because I was able to check the river level on the United States geological surveys website, before I went. I knew, that anything below 100 CFS on that website would be easy for me to paddle back upstream. You can find stream data about the West Fork Stones River on the USGS website, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D
You can launch your kayak from Manson Pike trailhead, here...
Manson Pike Trailhead https://share.google/GHpyimwLJG0dBRd0F
You can make it nearly a mile downstream before the river gets so shallow that you would bottom out, and have to drag your kayak down some shallow rapids. Instead of doing that, I simply paddled back upstream. There's a lot of room to fish, and what I saw, was nothing short of amazing.
First of all, last week, I was standing at this boat ramp, using live bait, when I caught 10 gigantic bass. All of those bats were pre-spawn, as you could tell from their gigantic bellies. They were feeding heavily, in preparation for the spawn, that usually happens around the 1st of may, when the water temperature reaches nearly 70°. This year, everything has moved up a month. Those bass, that were at the Manson Pike trailhead last week, had spread out, downstream, and made beds! There were large Smallmouth bass, and huge largemouth bass, that were guarding beds, in the middle of the river, in 1 to 2 foot of water. Every few hundred yards, I would find another gigantic bass, on a bed. They didn't want anything to do with the lures that I had, they were simply chasing stuff away from their beds.
If I had a Ned rig, or some kind of plastic worm or plastic lizard, I probably could have caught those fish. I really wanted to, but all I had were top water lures and spinnerbaits. At that point, it was more of an observation mission. The things I observed were insane! There were dozens of schooling bass that were roaming around, seemingly trying to move bigger bass out of their beds. Those bigger bass would chase them off, then return right back to their bed. There were also schools of, what I thought were, crappie. They were a little skittish, but they were crappie shaped. It took me a while to do some careful sleuthing, to realize, that these were schools of red ears! Giant shellcrackers, in great numbers, patrolling the same areas where the bass were on bed.
Then I started looking around. The greenway walks right past this area! If you were so inclined, it would be about a half mile walk down the greenway, but you could get to this spot, without a kayak! There were lots of bank access points that had been beaten down, you could either fish from the bank, or get in the river. You could definitely wade in this area, it's going to be tough, just like anywhere on the stones river, but it could be done. If you wanted to get into the river to wade, that would make this trip a four out of five on the effort scale. If you wanted to launch your kayak, while the CFS are registering under 100, paddling back upstream, would be a two and a half out of five on the effort scale of one to five. The majority of the shellcracker that I found were all concentrated at this bend in the river...
https://goo.gl/maps/9J6WxcMFybf76MqH8
There's a little island where there was a bass on bed, and just behind that island, near the bank where the greenway is, the water was about 3 to 4 feet deep, and there were hundreds of red ear sunfish! If I were going to walk into this location, to try to find these fish, I would carry an ultra light rod and reel with a bobber and some crickets. I'm not sure what it's going to take to get those gigantic shellcrackers on the line, but that would be a good place to start.
For me, the most important takeaway, is that these fish are already on bed. We're going to have a huge rain event tonight, hopefully (we desperately need the rain), and that's going to mess everything up. Fortunately for us, it's not going to rain for several days afterwards. That should put these fish right back in the same position, by about Wednesday of next week. Next weekend, until the end of May, should be fantastic for pulling bass off of beds, all over middle Tennessee!

title: Trip Report #64
content_raw:
WARNING ⚠️  Someone recently passed away at this park by falling and hitting their head and then drowning. Please use extreme caution, or don't go at all...
This morning I went to Old Stone Fort Archaeological Park...
Old Stone Fort State Archaeological Park https://share.google/TddMbB0FPLzvemmHz
This is a Tennessee state park, right off of interstate 24 in Manchester. They open the gates at 8:00 a.m. and they close at sunset. There is a playground with bathrooms and a pavilion for grilling, but it's nowhere near where the fishing is. If you drive all the way to the back of the park, there are lots of parking spaces, and a small museum. They have really nice restrooms in the museum. From there, it's an arduous task to get down to the fish!
There is a trail, but it's very steep! It's kind of long, and to get down to the water, you will literally have to climb cliffs. On my way back up, I did a 10-ft vertical wall! I threw my fishing pole am tackle up on top, and scaled the cliff face. This trip is literally off the charts hard! I would say that it's a 5 out of 5 on the effort scale of one to five, but it's harder than anything else that I've done, so I wouldn't suggest anyone try it!
If you're going to, here's what you need to do. Be prepared to get in the water. Most of the rocks are very slippery, be prepared to fall down. Once you get to the riverbed, it's relatively flat, which makes for good wading. Unfortunately, there aren't many fish where the water is good to wade. The best spot, is all the way at the end of the trail, at the base of the main waterfall. I'm going to drop you a pin at the base of the waterfall, and when you get there, you're going to wonder how the heck I got down there...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/nDk4bptc5wHRoiaB8
If you click on this link on Google maps, there is actually a 360° photo that someone has taken from where I was standing. They got down there, I got down there, so potentially, you could get down there. I wouldn't suggest anyone with kids try this. One wrong step, and you will fall down this waterfall. So here's how you get down there...
As you're walking downstream, the left edge of the waterfall is only about an inch deep. The rocks are really slippery, but if you sit down, and get wet, you can slowly lower yourself down the waterfall. After you lower yourself about one full body length down, there are some dry rocks to your left. That's how you get down to the base without falling. Getting back up, was insane! I tried to go back up the way I came, but the force of the water was too much, and the rocks were too slippery. That's when I decided to go vertical. I've never done any intentional rock climbing, and it's not something I'm looking forward to doing very much in the future. If you can't lift your body weight, with your two arms, you definitely shouldn't do this trip.
Once you get to the bottom of the waterfall, everything's great! The rocks are flat and dry, and there is a huge area that's loaded with bass. There may be catfish in there as well, but there are definitely loads of bass and lots of bluegill. It's not a place that I would go because I'm looking to catch a bunch of fish or a bunch of really good fish, it's a place that I like to go because it's so beautiful, and hard to get to. It's like the land before time!
My plan was, to throw my cast net, and get some live bait. Unfortunately, I only got a few bait fish before my cast net got hung, and ripped to shreds. I didn't bring much tackle with me, I was planning on using live bait. I did have the foresight to bring two purple spinnerbaits with silver blades. That's the spinnerbait that I've been using lately, with great success. Today would be no different! Standing at the base of that waterfall, my first catch was a small spotted bass. Throwing that spinnerbait in the heavy current that comes off the waterfall, my second catch was a nice chunky largemouth bass. At that point, I tied on my hook and bobber, and through my bait fish out. On the very first one, I got a smallmouth bass, completing the black bass trifecta! From there, I headed over to lunch at the highly rated Jiffy Burger...
https://share.google/V33DSfJgl4weN0ZRR
They have stalls that you can park in that are kind of like sonic, and you can press a button to make your order. They sell burgers and fries and lots of other things like tenderloin sandwiches. The service was prompt and friendly, and the food was pretty good! After lunch, I headed back to murfreesboro, to regear for an afternoon of chasing crappie on the bank. As it turned out, I wouldn't have to go very far. I went to the handicap fishing pier at Stewart Creek boat ramp, and none of you were there catching crappie...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/EEwZA9t0LvLqkZtzX
It's loaded in there! There was an older gentleman sitting on the fishing pier, using minnows, catching them pretty good, when I got there. I started fishing on the opposite corner from him, and I caught three fat female crappie, real quick! I was using a Bobby Garland. First, on a tight line. If you don't know what that is, basically, it's just 4 pound monofilament on a fishing pole, and a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head with a Bobby Garland. That's it. Tight line means, nothing between the rod tip and the lure. You simply cast out, and give it a slow retrieve. No need to let the lure sink, it's really shallow in this area! The alternative to a tight line, is to add a bobber. I did that as well! That caught me two really big crappie. I gave each of those crappie to the older gentleman, and quit fishing. I wanted to make sure I didn't catch too many, so that you guys can go get them. Not that it matters, like I have stated many times before, those fish will be in this location, until the end of April. As well as the handicapped fishing pier on the other end of the lake at Vivret Creek boat ramp...
Vivrett Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/I8jI1wzsY86Q0ggXB

It's not a place that I would go because I'm looking to catch a bunch of fish or a bunch of really good fish, it's a place that I like to go because it's so beautiful, and hard to get to. It's like the land before time!

My plan was, to throw my cast net, and get some live bait. Unfortunately, I only got a few bait fish before my cast net got hung, and ripped to shreds. I didn't bring much tackle with me, I was planning on using live bait. I did have the foresight to bring two purple spinnerbaits with silver blades. That's the spinnerbait that I've been using lately, with great success. Today would be no different! Standing at the base of that waterfall, my first catch was a small spotted bass. Throwing that spinnerbait in the heavy current that comes off the waterfall, my second catch was a nice chunky largemouth bass. At that point, I tied on my hook and bobber, and through my bait fish out. On the very first one, I got a smallmouth bass, completing the black bass trifecta! From there, I headed over to lunch at the highly rated Jiffy Burger...

https://share.google/V33DSfJgl4weN0ZRR

They have stalls that you can park in that are kind of like sonic, and you can press a button to make your order. They sell burgers and fries and lots of other things like tenderloin sandwiches. The service was prompt and friendly, and the food was pretty good! After lunch, I headed back to murfreesboro, to regear for an afternoon of chasing crappie on the bank. As it turned out, I wouldn't have to go very far. I went to the handicap fishing pier at Stewart Creek boat ramp, and none of you were there catching crappie...

Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/EEwZA9t0LvLqkZtzX

It's loaded in there! There was an older gentleman sitting on the fishing pier, using minnows, catching them pretty good, when I got there. I started fishing on the opposite corner from him, and I caught three fat female crappie, real quick! I was using a Bobby Garland. First, on a tight line. If you don't know what that is, basically, it's just 4 pound monofilament on a fishing pole, and a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head with a Bobby Garland. That's it. Tight line means, nothing between the rod tip and the lure. You simply cast out, and give it a slow retrieve. No need to let the lure sink, it's really shallow in this area! The alternative to a tight line, is to add a bobber. I did that as well! That caught me two really big crappie. I gave each of those crappie to the older gentleman, and quit fishing. I wanted to make sure I didn't catch too many, so that you guys can go get them. Not that it matters, like I have stated many times before, those fish will be in this location, until the end of April. As well as the handicapped fishing pier on the other end of the lake at Vivret Creek boat ramp...

Vivrett Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/I8jI1wzsY86Q0ggXB

title: Trip Report #65
content_raw:
Trout fishing Gatlinburg...
Every year on April 1st, the delayed harvest in Gatlinburg Tennessee ends. Delayed harvest means, that you are not allowed to harvest fish, until the delayed harvest ends. The city of Gatlinburg prohibits people from harvesting trout from December 1st until March 31st. The city has its own trout hatchery, and they stock Giant fish, year-round, on thursdays. They don't allow people to keep fish in the winter time, so that they can grow big! On April 1st, every year, for the last 5 years, the city of Gatlinburg has hosted a trout catching / litter cleanup competition.
I went to participate in this year's event, but I really didn't know how everything worked. Now that I have a better understanding, I plan to win the thing next year! Here's how the tournament works, and how and where you can catch some fish in Gatlinburg, if you're so inclined...
This fishing tournament is hosted out of Herbert Holt Park...
https://share.google/3U3uKBlK3FnnR1w2b
You can pre-register online with the city of Gatlinburg, on their website, or you can register in person, on the day of, starting at 6:00 a.m., that's what I did. It's important to note, sunrise on April 1st in Gatlinburg is 7:20 a.m. You are not allowed to fish at night in Gatlinburg. You will have to wait until 30 minutes before sunrise to start fishing, which is 6:52 a.m. The competition is for your two best trout. You are allowed to keep five trout each day, but only your two best would be entered into the competition. There are five prizes in the children's division, which is under 16 years old. There are five prizes in the adults division, which has no age limit, and second place went to an extremely advanced senior citizen, which is nice!
There is a prize for the most unusual piece of trash collected, that price will be given to a child every year. Once I realized how much this event is for the children, I was really excited to let you guys know about it! I had assumed, that I could go win this thing. After all, I collect garbage professionally! I've made it a habit on my channel of going to fishing spots and picking up litter. I thought that I was a shoe in! I drove up to Gatlinburg on the 31st, stayed that night, checked out at 5:00 a.m. so that I could go to the park to register, and then got started cleaning up the city! I was able to pull six big black trash bags out of about a 1-mile stretch of river. I thought, for sure, that would win me the biggest prize. As it turns out, that prize is also given to a child, which is nice! His parents had clearly gathered more trash than I had, and that was the whole objective!
The prizes aren't inconsequential, but it's not life-changing money. Several different businesses in the Gatlinburg community, got together to donate what they could. There were free rounds of mini golf as well as trips on the sky ride up to the top of Ober Mountain Gatlinburg. Lots of fishing equipment like tackle boxes and fishing poles and lots of trout lures. There were no cash prizes, but there is also no cash entry. Your entry fee, is one small grocery bag filled with trash. As long as you collect that much litter, from the river, you are able to enter the tournament, and win prizes!
For the kids, as well as senior citizens, this one is a no brainer! Where you sign up, at Herbert Holt park, is a children's and senior citizens only fishing area. This area has a long stretch of river, with a very walkable bank, most of it sidewalk! It is intended to be very friendly for small children as well as extremely advanced senior citizens. This is the place to be, if you are a family! No need in taking your children up and down the streets of gatlinburg, trying to find different holes to fish. This is your premiere destination! The park has playgrounds and I believe I even saw a bathroom house.
The rules about where to fish are quite simple, just fish in downtown Gatlinburg. There's lots of access along the river, that allows you to walk straight off the sidewalk, down some steps, into the riverbed. The only problem with that, the river is filled with large round boulders. It's really hard to wade in this river, but people were doing it everywhere! I didn't have any intention of getting in the river. My plan was to win the garbage cleaning competition. I exclusively cleaned trash for the first 3 hours of the tournament. You are allowed to start cleaning trash immediately, so that's what I did. From 6:00 a.m. until 9:00 a.m., when I ran into a local, that told me that the same young person wins the trash cleaning competition every year. I was a little bummed out, but I still didn't understand, this event is all about the kids!
At that point, I had about 3 hours left. The tournament ends at noon, so I grabbed my fishing pole, put down my bucket, and started fishing. And my effort was laughable! I didn't do anything wrong, I know how to catch trout, I like to throw a worm on bottom. Unfortunately, I played myself! I should have got to fishing, as soon as I could. There were, dozens of people, with trout that would have been the biggest trout of my life! I saw people walking around downtown Gatlinburg with 3 foot long rainbow trout on their stringers. It was a massacre! And I didn't get to be a part of it.
Now I know, the key is to start fishing as early as possible, and get your five fish limit, quickly, and then clean up some trash. Hopefully, we can all go out there next year, and take over the event, and clean up the city! If you're planning on going to Gatlinburg at any point in time, you can do what I did, and try to stick to the bank. You will definitely be able to catch trout! If you would like to get in the river, keep in mind, that it's really tough to wade! Just beating up the bank, is a three and a half out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. Walking in that river, is a five out of five! It's literally as hard as it gets.
At first, I was sticking to access points that were provided by the city, on the sidewalk. Then I noticed, it's more of a free-for-all! People use whatever restaurant or hotel access they can find, and just jump over the side to get access where they want. If it's a good looking spot, people just do what seems like trespassing, to get to it. I noticed some locals out, in their cabins, watching people fish, not saying anything about people coming in and out of their yard. I wouldn't suggest that, but it seems like it's not necessarily taboo. Pretty much, if you have a fishing pole, people are going to let you access the river, which is nice!
There's one hard and fast rule that you're going to have to follow, no treble hooks! During the delayed harvest, you're not allowed to use any type of bait, which means no power bait, and no worms. Now that the delayed harvest is over, you are allowed to use things like worms and power bait, but you are never allowed to use treble hooks in this river! One of my favorite trout lures is a roostertail, which has a treble hook. I still wanted to use a rooster tail, so I just cut two of the hooks off! Problem solved. If you like to use jerk baits that have treble hooks, you can simply remove those treble hooks, and add a single hook point.

title: Trip Report #66
content_raw:
Unbelievably epic fishing spots...
To start my day, I launched my kayak from the side of Maddox road...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/qCyq9SX8L2oGEn7x8
There are a handful of parking spots on either side of the road right here. If you would like to launch your kayak here, don't be discouraged if there are a lot of people! There is plenty of room upstream for everybody! If you can find a parking space, you can carry your kayak over to the water's edge. You're walking on the lake bed, so it's not easy, but it's not super difficult. This put-in location rates at a two on the effort scale of 1 to 5. I paddled out of this cove where you launch, to the left, which is upstream on Hurricane creek. It's exactly one mile all the way up to where the creek gets so shallow that you can't go anymore.
I went up there in my kayak, because I was catching a lot of crappie in this location the other day, but I also hooked into a couple of really big bass. Hooking into those bass made me want to go up there and do some bass fishing. On my way up, I made a few casts with my crappie jigs towards the bank. I caught a crappie, which indicated to me that they are still in the area. Then I caught a really big catfish! You never know what you're going to catch up the creek, seems like everything is up there!
Using my 7-foot medium rod, which has an ultra fast tip, and 15 pound braid, I was throwing the same purple spinnerbait, with two silver blades that I've been throwing most of the spring for bass. On my second cast, I caught a nice largemouth bass. From there, it was gangbusters! I simply paddled up the creek as far as I could, casting everywhere I could, and then back down out of the creek, to my vehicle. On the way up, and on the way down, I caught bass, lots of largemouth bass!
When you go as far as you can up the creek, it's crystal clear, and you can see fish everywhere! More bluegill than you can count. Giant largemouth! Lots of little bass, everywhere! And then, I floated right over top of a whole bunch of slab crappie. The water was so clear, I could tell if the crappie were black nose, or if they were white crappie, or if they were males! I didn't try fishing for those crappie, because they were in one foot of water, and it was really clear. In that situation, you may be able to catch them, but it's much easier to catch those bass!
I hit the water at 10:20 a.m. I had prior obligations this morning, so that was as quick as I could get to the lake. I got back to my car at around 2:20 and then went to get some late lunch. After lunch, I grabbed my cast net and my bait bucket and headed over to the Murfreesboro Greenway...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/ckECxaNGnsGn9yB28
This is Manson Pike trailhead, and it sits at the base of Ransom Mill dam. A little birdie told me that there were a lot of large bass hanging out in this area. I went up to the dam, where the bait fish hang out in the shallow area. I made one cast with my cast net, and had more than enough bait. It's loaded in there! I fished around the area below the dam, but I couldn't find any bass. Then I went to fish underneath the bridge, which is a little downstream, but I couldn't find any fish underneath there. So I kept working downstream. As you come out from underneath the bridge, there is a small, low head dam. Just below that low head dam, there was the mother load of big bass.
Using my six and a half foot, medium action rod, with 12 pound monofilament, and a fat orange styrofoam bobber, 2 feet above a number one eagle claw Aberdeen hook, I was able to have the best day of bass fishing I've had in a really long time! I had one medium sized split shot, about 6 iny above my bait fish, just to keep him down in the current. There is a swift current that comes off that low head dam, and I was casting directly into it and allowing my bait to float through that area when the first fish ate. It was a small largemouth bass, and it gave me hopes that I had found the fish I was looking for.
Those hopes were well founded! The next fish I would catch, was a 20-inch, 3 pound 6 ounce, trophy Smallmouth bass. That was my first trophy Smallmouth this year, and I honestly thought that would be the last fish I would catch. Typically, when you find a spot where there is more than one bass on a river, the biggest bass, will eat last. I suspected, that was the biggest bass in the area. I was wrong. I would continue fishing, and after a few minutes, I would hook into a really big large mouth. Then, a handful more smallmouth bass as well as a really big spotted! At this point, it was getting ridiculous! I was having one of the best days of my life, standing in one spot on the Murfreesboro Greenway. The next fish would be the last fish. It was a second, trophy smallmouth. This one weighed in at 3 pounds 12 ounces!
I'm 100% certain that you could catch these fish for the next few days at this location. You will need to catch some of the live bait with a cast net. I saw multiple people fish this area with lures, and have no luck. I waited till all of them cleared out, before I was able to get to this spot. I caught 10 large bass, from 3:15 to 4:15...
I've been catching bass in this location, with live bait under a bobber, since the late 90s. This time of year, they're always going to swim upstream, as far as they can. This is pretty much as far as they can go! They can't go over the dam, so they get stuck right here at the base of it. If you can't make it out this week, or even this spring, that's okay! This is a great location, every year! I have never had a day, at this location, like I had today, but there is always the potential for that to happen! Also, if you know of a low head dam that you have access to in your area, it should be loaded up with bass right now, and for the foreseeable future!

title: Trip Report #67
content_raw:
A new feature to help you catch fish!
I will always continue to evolve my Pro reports to make them better for you. The events that unfolded yesterday, after I posted the video beating down crappie in that shallow creek, gave me a fantastic idea. Essentially, what happened, was that some people, know this public spot. Every spot that I find to go fishing, is public access. That way, I can share the location with you, and we can all enjoy it. In the past, I would try to send out my Pro report, and then immediately release the video. When I did that with my last report, lots of people who knew that area, showed up to catch those crappie. Going forward, I will send you a pro report on the day that find fish or a new location, and then wait for a day or two, to post any of my photos or videos to social media. That will give you guys a chance to get a heads up on any fish that I find.
Today, I've got a great report for all of my kayak fishermen, and people who like to take their boat out for white bass. Yesterday, I kayaked from Walter Hill Dam, down the East Fork stones river, 5 miles, to Mona boat ramp. This is a kayak trip that you can do year-round, but it's the most fun, when Percy Priest Lake is at winter pool. During summer pool, the first mile of this trip is shallow, with rapids. The last four miles, you will have to paddle the whole way. At winter pool, the first 4 miles of this trip are all shallow, with rapids! It makes for a very scenic, swift moving trip, that requires very little paddling. Right now, the lake is up a couple of feet from winter pool. title: Trip Report #68
content_raw:
Super shallow crappie...
This morning I started my day at Stewart Creek boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/uVYY4tP1P8jqSUiG9
There's a handicapped fishing pier in the parking lot that has fish attractors spread around it. As of right now, there's just enough water to almost completely cover them. That doesn't matter to the fish, they are there anyway! When I got there, there were a couple of gentlemen already on the fishing pier, and they said they were catching fish. I know they were, because each one of them caught a keeper while I was there. I caught a short fish, right at sunrise, just to make sure they were there, so you guys would have a spot to go to. You should try fishing for them at that location, from now until the end of April.
From there I headed over to Volunteer Park...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/iFGHuTaMwrymcQbi9
If you park in this parking lot, there is an opening to the creek. Right now, the creek is really shallow, only about 1 to 2 feet deep, and it's crystal clear. I went down it yesterday and my kayak, and because it's so clear, you could see fish everywhere! I mean, everywhere! I went back this morning, and all of those bass and bluegill and red ear were still there! I made a few casts with my rooster tail, caught a nice largemouth bass, just to make sure they were there, so you guys could go and catch them, and then headed to get some breakfast.
I had my sights set on a much bigger prize. The way I like to catch fish, is to look back at what I was doing this time last year, not just in my phone on my photos, but on my Facebook and on my YouTube as well. That not only gives me inspiration about what I should be doing on this day, but could point me in the direction of something that I might have forgot about. That was the case today! After breakfast, I ended up at a spot that I should have been fishing for the last several weeks! It's way up hurricane creek, it's public property, and to get there, you can park right here...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/s8qYW675GSDeQLrz9
This is a dead end road that has a gravel driveway that goes all the way to the river's edge. There is a gate that blocks your path, so you will have to park your vehicle where I have dropped this pin. You are allowed to be here! This is public property, and as long as you walk down to the river, and stay on the bank, you will always be welcome by TWRA. Coincidentally, I have been inspected by them at this spot, so make sure you have your license! This spot is definitely on their map.
The whole entire area is loaded with crappie. That's not an exaggeration, that's not hyperbole. They were everywhere! At first, I thought I was fishing for bluegill, because I could see them on the surface. I was using my ultralight rod and reel, and throwing a 1/64th of an ounce trout magnet with a 1 inch gulp minnow under a trout magnet easy float. That's a great setup to catch little bluegills, but my first fish was a giant slab crappie! I ended up catching four more, before I sent out a quick Pro report to let you guys know where I was, and that you should come down. One of you did, and we absolutely beat the crap out of those crappie! On the day, I ended up with 20 keepers. I put them all back in the river, because they were obviously on beds. These fish are spawning heavily, and I already have enough crappie in the freezer.
Then the north winds came. Unfortunately, it's going to drop down into the mid to lower 30s tonight. I have no idea if those fish are going to stay in that shallow water. It seems like they would have to, because they are spawning! It's not like they can leave their spawning grounds, unless they have to? I really don't know. It's definitely worth going tomorrow, even though it's going to be freezing cold! The good news, just because crappie aren't in one particular location when you go, doesn't mean they won't be there in the future. This spot gets loaded with crappie every year, at this time of year. They won't be there in the coldest parts of the winter, or the hottest parts of the summer, or the driest parts of the fall. They only go there while they are spawning. Simply add this location to the growing list of places that we have already found on Percy Priest lake, and eventually, you will know somewhere to go no matter what time of year it is, no matter what direction the wind is blowing, or no matter what depth these fish are.
I think it's important to note that, not all crappie will spawn at the same time. Not just in different bodies of water, but in the same body of water! Not all of the crappie in this Lake are ready to spawn. They will continue moving up this creek, from now until every single one of them is spawned out. That means, even if they leave this Creek for the next couple of days while it's cold, they will come back in here, when it gets warm again, and we can catch them, at very least, until the end of April.

title: Trip Report #69
content_raw:
Friday at 9:30 in the morning, come fishing right here right now!
I'm at a spot on the side of Fall Creek that you can access legally if you park right here...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/xtU9d9AbgqoCGtis6
I just pulled up to fish this spot, like I do every spring for crappie, and on my first four casts, I caught giant slab crappie! There is a lot of bank to fish here, and plenty of room for everybody! I'm using my ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a trout magnet set up. I'm using a 164th of an ounce jig head with a 1 in golf minnow underneath a trout magnet bobber. If you have minnows, or Bobby garland, that should work! You can get out here right now, and catch these fish all day, before the rain starts this afternoon.
Once you park where my I pin is dropped, walk straight down the gravel driveway to the water's edge. They are lined up everywhere in the middle of the river! There is some scum on the surface, so using a bobber will be best.

title: Trip Report #70
content_raw:
I've never seen so many fish at Volunteer Park...
Because my boat trailer is still in the shop, today, I took my kayak down Stewart Creek, from Volunteer Park boat ramp...
https://goo.gl/maps/WHqn9eBFw1bNw3fA9
This boat ramp is for kayaks and canoes only! You cannot get a full size boat trailer in the water here. Especially not right now! With the lake at winter pool, the end of the boat ramp is dry. It's a great spot for kayaks or paddle boards or, if you wanted to wade. I would probably wear hip waders at least if not chest waders. As you paddle away from the boat ramp, the water is very shallow. You will not be able to paddle back up to the boat ramp. Today, in the shallow areas, I got out, and dragged my kayak upstream. The water wasn't too cold, so I went ahead and got wet. You may or may not want to do that. Because it's a really easy launch, that makes it a nice place. Because it's tough to come back upstream right now, that makes it a three and a half on the difficulty scale of 1 to 5. It's going to be pretty rigorous getting back up.
A few hundred yards downstream from the boat ramp, there were as many bass as I have ever seen in such a shallow spot! Hundreds of large mouth and spotted bass, and I even saw one gigantic trophy smallmouth! These fish were in one foot of crystal clear water. I tried to fish for them, with conventional bass lures, for the better part of half an hour. They weren't going to have it! They were too spoiled. They had everything they needed, in the form of bait fish, and bluegills. There were tons of red ear as well as a few crappie hanging out. It looks more like an aquarium than the lake! They had to be coming up from the main lake, so I decided to paddle downstream a little, where the water wasn't so shallow, and I might be able to trick some of these fish into biting a lure.
Unfortunately, the whole entire area is covered in funk! The surface has grass and moss and pollen, you name it, it's floating on the surface. I was watching the moss on the bottom, release itself from the lake bed and float up to the surface. It was really hard to fish! I tried every different type of lure, but the most effective lure, at not getting as much funk on it, was my trusty silver spinnerbait. Right now, I'm using a purple colored spinnerbait with two silver blades. That has been the magic ticket lately, in these shallow tributaries, that flow into the lake.
As soon as I got away from the surface debris that was trapped in the creek, and made my way out to the main lake, I started catching good numbers of decent size largemouth bass. With a long cast, to shallow banks, and a relatively quick retrieve, these fish were smashing the lure, and making it really easy on me. I was using my 7 foot medium, ultra fast action rod, with 15 pound braid. Lately, I haven't been using any type of leader line, just tying my braid directly to my spinnerbait. Also, I have my drag locked down really tight! I'm probably not going to run into any bass that can break 15 pound braid, and I want to make sure to stab that hook into them as soon as they bite.
I have been on every major tributary of Percy Priest Lake in the last 2 weeks. All of them are on fire with largemouth bass, just like this creek. If you know of a creek or river that flows into a major lake in your area, these fish are going to be really shallow! Ridiculously shallow. The first place this happens every year will be Percy Priest lake. It is one of the shallowest, and one of the warmest lakes in Middle tennessee. Because the water, in the main lake, is usually very cloudy, it not only holds heat very well, but it gains heat from sunlight, very quickly. Clearwater allows sunlight to pass directly through, and doesn't retain heat very well. Most of the fish in Middle Tennessee are not as far in their progression as the fish on Percy Priest lake!
Crappie are already showing their spawning colors, which means they are in full spawn. Bass have headed up the tributaries, in full pre-spawn mode. Bluegill are doing the same thing. Crappie spawn first, then bluegill, then bass. Right now, you should be able to go as far upstream as you possibly can, and find lots of fish.
There's a good chance you could catch some of these fish, tomorrow, from the bank. There is a parking lot at volunteer park, that gives you access to exactly where these fish were stacked up. There are signs, that tell you not to go into the woods, because that is government property. You are allowed to be on the bank, that is Percy Priest lake, and it is corps of engineers property. You will be able to clearly see where they have marked, that you are not supposed to go. If you park in the parking lot, you can walk directly to the water's edge, and try to catch these fish. It's going to be really, really, really hard. There are lots of fish in there, but there is all that funk to deal with, and it's really shallow! Remember, one foot deep. I'm going to drop you a pin for the parking lot, rest assured, you are allowed to fish here, you're just not allowed to go into the woods, OR onto the government property that is clearly marked...

As you paddle away from the boat ramp, the water is very shallow. You will not be able to paddle back up to the boat ramp. Today, in the shallow areas, I got out, and dragged my kayak upstream. The water wasn't too cold, so I went ahead and got wet. You may or may not want to do that. Because it's a really easy launch, that makes it a nice place. Because it's tough to come back upstream right now, that makes it a three and a half on the difficulty scale of 1 to 5. It's going to be pretty rigorous getting back up.

A few hundred yards downstream from the boat ramp, there were as many bass as I have ever seen in such a shallow spot! Hundreds of large mouth and spotted bass, and I even saw one gigantic trophy smallmouth! These fish were in one foot of crystal clear water. I tried to fish for them, with conventional bass lures, for the better part of half an hour. They weren't going to have it! They were too spoiled. They had everything they needed, in the form of bait fish, and bluegills. There were tons of red ear as well as a few crappie hanging out. It looks more like an aquarium than the lake! They had to be coming up from the main lake, so I decided to paddle downstream a little, where the water wasn't so shallow, and I might be able to trick some of these fish into biting a lure.

Unfortunately, the whole entire area is covered in funk! The surface has grass and moss and pollen, you name it, it's floating on the surface. I was watching the moss on the bottom, release itself from the lake bed and float up to the surface. It was really hard to fish! I tried every different type of lure, but the most effective lure, at not getting as much funk on it, was my trusty silver spinnerbait. Right now, I'm using a purple colored spinnerbait with two silver blades. That has been the magic ticket lately, in these shallow tributaries, that flow into the lake.

As soon as I got away from the surface debris that was trapped in the creek, and made my way out to the main lake, I started catching good numbers of decent size largemouth bass. With a long cast, to shallow banks, and a relatively quick retrieve, these fish were smashing the lure, and making it really easy on me. I was using my 7 foot medium, ultra fast action rod, with 15 pound braid. Lately, I haven't been using any type of leader line, just tying my braid directly to my spinnerbait. Also, I have my drag locked down really tight! I'm probably not going to run into any bass that can break 15 pound braid, and I want to make sure to stab that hook into them as soon as they bite.

I have been on every major tributary of Percy Priest Lake in the last 2 weeks. All of them are on fire with largemouth bass, just like this creek. If you know of a creek or river that flows into a major lake in your area, these fish are going to be really shallow! Ridiculously shallow. The first place this happens every year will be Percy Priest lake. It is one of the shallowest, and one of the warmest lakes in Middle tennessee. Because the water, in the main lake, is usually very cloudy, it not only holds heat very well, but it gains heat from sunlight, very quickly. Clearwater allows sunlight to pass directly through, and doesn't retain heat very well. Most of the fish in Middle Tennessee are not as far in their progression as the fish on Percy Priest lake!

Crappie are already showing their spawning colors, which means they are in full spawn. Bass have headed up the tributaries, in full pre-spawn mode. Bluegill are doing the same thing. Crappie spawn first, then bluegill, then bass. Right now, you should be able to go as far upstream as you possibly can, and find lots of fish.

There's a good chance you could catch some of these fish, tomorrow, from the bank. There is a parking lot at volunteer park, that gives you access to exactly where these fish were stacked up. There are signs, that tell you not to go into the woods, because that is government property. You are allowed to be on the bank, that is Percy Priest lake, and it is corps of engineers property. You will be able to clearly see where they have marked, that you are not supposed to go. If you park in the parking lot, you can walk directly to the water's edge, and try to catch these fish. It's going to be really, really, really hard. There are lots of fish in there, but there is all that funk to deal with, and it's really shallow! Remember, one foot deep. I'm going to drop you a pin for the parking lot, rest assured, you are allowed to fish here, you're just not allowed to go into the woods, OR onto the government property that is clearly marked...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/jB4YcVa318SqCGHHA

title: Trip Report #71
content_raw:
Crappie were within arms reach of the bank...
Today, I got a late start, at high noon, fishing from the bank for crappie, at Vivrett Creek boat ramp...
Vivrett Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/Mo0EQIP1F4suPlia5
If you walk about a quarter mile down the bank away from the boat ramp, there is a fish attractor that is marked with a buoy...
https://goo.gl/maps/bgE38wFF6QmqgAze6
That's where most people fish, and where most of the crappie are caught. Today, I marched directly to that spot, and didn't catch any fish. So I started working my way back to the boat ramp, fishing the bank, with my ultra light setup, and two Bobby Garland  underneath a bobber at about 2 foot of depth. Full disclosure, I didn't catch a whole lot of fish! I only caught four crappie, but they were all keepers. Two of them were really dark, indicating that they are males, ready to spawn. Each one of those fish was within a few feet of the bank.
I had tried making long casts and using a slow retrieve. But I wasn't getting any attention. I had noticed that fish were splashing the surface, really close to the bank. I had chosen this location because it faces south. Today, we had a screaming North wind. I wanted the wind at my back, so I could not only make nice long casts, but also, I was hoping the surface of the water would be calm. It was a little too windy to be completely calm, but it was calm enough for me to see that these fish were splashing at the surface. That's when I switched to a bobber, running it's shallow, and casting parallel to the bank, as opposed to directly out into the lake. That would be the move that would prove successful.
There are a handful of trees and man-made structures that are in the water, along this stretch of bank. It was next to those pieces of structure, near the bank, where I would catch my fish. Using a short cast, and twitching that bobber, within 10 feet of the bank, would be the only way I would have any success today. But that's a good thing! These are the very first fish that I have caught this year, that were fully patterned up, for the spawn.
What does that mean? Patterned up? Basically, it's a lot like other animal species. The males get really pretty, when it's time to spawn. Indicating to the females, that they are healthy, and ready to take care of a bed. It's the male crappies that make the beds, for the females to come lay their eggs. The male's garner female attention by wearing an attractive tuxedo. That's what we call it when they get really dark for the season, a tuxedo. They're all dressed up, but they have nowhere to go! These fish were displaying bloody tails. What that means, is that they have used their tail to clear out an area, which will be a bed for the females to lay their eggs. When that happens, they will stay in that area!
Anywhere that you find one crappie spawning, you're going to find lots of others! I suspect, that this bank will be loaded with fish, for the next month! Also, it's worth pointing out, that on the other side of the parking lot, there's a handicap fishing pier. I tried to catch some fish over there, because the area is loaded with fish attractors, but it was still a little too shallow. We need some really good rain to bring the lake level up, or we might miss the prime spawning season on the shallow water fish attractors. That's something to keep in mind, because there are so many crappie spawning in this area, if the water comes up at all, they will definitely go over to that handicapped fishing pier.

title: Trip Report #72
content_raw:
Kayak fishing the Caney Fork River...
Yesterday, I had clients booked to kayak the first 6 miles from Center Hill Dam to Happy Hollow boat ramp. This is the stretch of river that I take clients on, usually during the summer, to fish for trout. Yesterday, we had weather that was summer like, so I had my first trip of the year on this stretch of river. I like to do this stretch of river when the water is off, and there is no threat of the generators ruining our day. This was the earliest in the year that I have taken anyone on this trip.
To start the day, I got to Buffalo valley boat ramp at 6:30 a.m...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/ZmmQsm4eMvEn2LEGH
The generators had run until 5:00 a.m. when they turned off. An hour and a half later, when I showed up, the water had receded, and I was able to drive out off the boat ramp, onto the rocks, and put our three kayaks on the water's edge. I like to unload everything at the beginning of the trip, and then drive to the end, where I meet my clients. I had them meet me at 6:45 a.m. at Happy Hollow boat ramp...
Happy Hollow Boat Ramp https://share.google/Q4Xh2eQv5YYjRzCRg
I had my truck and my trailer to haul the three kayaks. When I met them at Happy Hollow boat ramp, I parked my vehicle there, and hopped into their vehicle. Then they drove us back up to Buffalo valley boat ramp, where we parked, and then walked down to our kayaks, to start our 6 Mile trip. I like to do this stretch of river because when I dropped my kayaks off at the dam, there were lots of other people there, fishing and setting up for the day. I feel like it's relatively safe to leave your kayaks and fishing gear unattended, for a few minutes, especially if you ask someone to watch out for it. I've been doing this for a few years now, and I haven't had any problems. Quite the opposite, I've had a lot of success!
I like the generators to have been off for 2 hours before I start my trip. That way, the river at the dam, as well as all the way ahead of us, will be as low as it can get. I like to fish the water when it's really low for two reasons. First and foremost, it's a nice slow flat float for my clients. No rapids, no swift water, just easy paddling. Another added benefit is the fact that the fish have less options. When they have less room to roam, it's easier to find them! You can look for them in the deeper pockets, and the swifter moving runs. When you find a narrow area that gets deep, it will have some good current, and a lot of fish! The generators weren't scheduled to turn on until noon. Because we started at 7:00 a.m., and our trip is 6 hours, that would have us finishing at Happy Hollow boat ramp, at 1:00 p.m. We ended up fishing a little bit longer than we were supposed to, so we got down to the boat ramp at 1:30 p.m. At that point in time, the generating water, which had started an hour and a half sooner, was just starting to show up at Happy Hollow boat ramp. I was able to drive my vehicle out onto the rocks beside the water's edge, quickly load up, and then get out of there before the water took over the area. Basically, you can drive straight off the boat ramp through a little bit of water, and then get out on to dry ground, as long as the generating water hasn't arrived. You can find the generating schedule, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
Now you know where to start, and where to finish. How to coordinate the logistics, and when to go. Now you just need to know how to catch these fish. Fortunately for us, it's really easy! I like an ultra light rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a number 6 eagle claw bait holder hook with one fat split shot. I used to use two, but one has been working really well for me. The first thing I put on the hook is one pink Berkeley powerbait Magnum floating eggs for trout. This is the one that people have trouble finding. I'm going to drop a link from my favorite Berkeley powerbait, right here...
https://amzn.to/41jib8W
Next I like to cut a nightcrawler in half and then add it to the hook. I'm not 100% certain you need the nightcrawler. Sometimes all I use is the power bait, and I do really well! If I don't feel like going to buy worms, or I don't already have any, or I don't want to get dirt underneath my fingernails, I will just use power bait, with great success. Those worms add the magic touch, especially when fish are being finicky. When I'm taking clients, I always have worms with me, just to make sure we catch fish. And catch fish we did! It wasn't Blockbuster. But it wasn't lackluster either. I wasn't expecting the fishing to be very good, just because it's early in the season. There's just as many trout in there, but I have the best luck on the hottest days, on the Caney Fork river. It's always been that way for me. You can catch trout year round, but on a 100° day in the summertime, every trout in the river is feeding! I don't know why, but I try to take advantage of it, every year.
Some of the best success can be had by getting out of your kayak, in a good looking spot, and standing in the water, with that worm and power bait on the bottom. Especially if you're going to take a break for lunch, make sure you throw that out and leave it on the bottom, with the rod propped up. I have seen some true Giants caught, using a little bit of patience. The longer that worm sits on the bottom, the more likely it is to be seen by a really big fish.
Don't want to fish on the bottom, because you get hung up, and you catch grass? Don't! Use moving lures like a rooster tail or a jerk bait. I have found that fishing for trout with your favorite bass lures is a fantastic idea! Try throwing a spinnerbait or a crankbait. I have caught lots of big trout throwing a 4-inch white paddle tail, something I usually use for Smallmouth bass. When it comes to trout, the sky is the limit! I think it's worth noting that, on our 6 mile trip yesterday, we did not see the fish coming to the surface to take flies. That's probably because of the time of year, but I'm not much of a fly fisherman, so I really couldn't tell you.

title: Trip Report #73
content_raw:
Totally private spot, open to the public...
Today, I kayaked the Piney River via Pinewood canoe and campground...
https://share.google/gDr7eqKRs85BSgmsK
Pinewood canoe and campground owns two different Riverside locations. One location, at the end of the trip, where the office is, and the campground is, and one location a few miles upstream, where you start your trip. If you don't have a canoe, they have canoes and kayaks for rent. If you have your own canoe or kayak, you can take yours, and they will shuttle you upstream from the office and you can float back down to your vehicle. Or, you could shuttle yourself if you would like, if you have two vehicles. They have lots of different services, and they will do whatever it takes to get you on the water. They are open for the season, 7 days a week, from 9:00 a.m. until 7:00 p.m. I got there today at 8:45 a.m. so I could be the first one out.
They have a motto at pinewood canoe and campground, it's "a flipping good time". Unfortunately, most kayakers, even experienced ones, will flip on this trip. The river doesn't have steep drops, but it does have lots of trees in the way. Those trees flip people all the time. I saw someone flip today. Be prepared to get wet. Because where you put in, and take out are not boat ramps, you will have to take your kayak or canoe to the water's edge. Getting it down to the water, and getting it out of the water, it's pretty much the hardest part of the trip. Kayaking is never easy, so this trip falls squarely at a three on the effort scale of 1 to 5.
It's not as important to monitor River levels on this stretch of river as it is other stretches. The USGS has a gauge on this stretch of river, so it's easy to look up, but if the river were flowing at a level that were unsafe, the people at pinewood canoe and campground wouldn't be putting people on the river. Basically, they know best, and they try to make sure everyone is safe. If they are allowing people to go, I would go! If you would like to check the flow of the river, you can look here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03602500/all-graphs/#period=P7D
This is a smallmouth bass river. You can still catch largemouth, but most of the fish are smallmouth. You can almost always find them in the heavy current, especially if there are trees in that current. Some of the biggest fish will be found in stillwater. Deep pockets of water on this River that have trees or rocks hide really big small mouth bass. The best way to get bass on this river, is to use the live bait that the river provides. I like to carry a 4 foot cast net, and catch my own bait.
I like a really simple setup. I've got a six and a half foot medium bass rod that's medium action. I don't like a fast action tip, when I'm using live bait. Fast action tips are very stiff, slow action tips are very flimsy. Medium is right in the middle. I like the rod tip to have a lot of bend, because you don't necessarily need to set the hook hard, when you're using live bait. Typically, the fish will put the food in their mouth, and simply leaning back will set that hook into the corner. That was the case today, I was wearing them out!
Not at first, and that's typical. I started fishing just after 9:00 a.m. and these fish were still really cold. River fish don't act like Lake fish. Especially fish in cold rivers. They like to bite, midday. When the water gets warmest, and The bait fish is easiest to see, because the Sun is high. This trip is a little less than 5 Miles long, and I was more than halfway through, at 1:00 p.m., when these fish started to fire up.
I like to use 12 pound monofilament with a number one eagle claw Aberdeen hook and a small split shot, about 6 inches above the hook, to keep the fish down. About 2 foot above my bait fish, I like to attach a bobber. This is the setup that I have been using for more than half a decade. I believe I finally have it optimized. I get a fantastic ratio of bites to hook ups, and when these fish get hooked, they rarely get away. Those gold Aberdeen hooks are specifically designed for minnows, and if you get the number one, that's a really big hook, for really big minnows. That's what I like to use. When I'm doing these kayak trips with live bait, I like baits that are at least 5 inches.
If you don't have a cast net, or don't know how to use one, or just don't want to try, you could always pick up some shiners from the bait shop. Make sure you have plenty of fresh water, and an aerator to keep them breathing. That gets expensive, for the cost of 1 pound of bait fish, you could buy a cast net, and catch all the bait you need, for the whole summer. It's a worthwhile endeavor, if you're physically capable.

content_markdown:
Totally private spot, open to the public...

Today, I kayaked the Piney River via Pinewood canoe and campground...

https://share.google/gDr7eqKRs85BSgmsK

Pinewood canoe and campground owns two different Riverside locations. One location, at the end of the trip, where the office is, and the campground is, and one location a few miles upstream, where you start your trip. If you don't have a canoe, they have canoes and kayaks for rent. If you have your own canoe or kayak, you can take yours, and they will shuttle you upstream from the office and you can float back down to your vehicle. Or, you could shuttle yourself if you would like, if you have two vehicles. They have lots of different services, and they will do whatever it takes to get you on the water. They are open for the season, 7 days a week, from 9:00 a.m. until 7:00 p.m. I got there today at 8:45 a.m. so I could be the first one out.

They have a motto at pinewood canoe and campground, it's "a flipping good time". Unfortunately, most kayakers, even experienced ones, will flip on this trip. The river doesn't have steep drops, but it does have lots of trees in the way. Those trees flip people all the time. I saw someone flip today. Be prepared to get wet. Because where you put in, and take out are not boat ramps, you will have to take your kayak or canoe to the water's edge. Getting it down to the water, and getting it out of the water, it's pretty much the hardest part of the trip. Kayaking is never easy, so this trip falls squarely at a three on the effort scale of 1 to 5.

It's not as important to monitor River levels on this stretch of river as it is other stretches. The USGS has a gauge on this stretch of river, so it's easy to look up, but if the river were flowing at a level that were unsafe, the people at pinewood canoe and campground wouldn't be putting people on the river. Basically, they know best, and they try to make sure everyone is safe. If they are allowing people to go, I would go! If you would like to check the flow of the river, you can look here...

https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03602500/all-graphs/#period=P7D

This is a smallmouth bass river. You can still catch largemouth, but most of the fish are smallmouth. You can almost always find them in the heavy current, especially if there are trees in that current. Some of the biggest fish will be found in stillwater. Deep pockets of water on this River that have trees or rocks hide really big small mouth bass. The best way to get bass on this river, is to use the live bait that the river provides. I like to carry a 4 foot cast net, and catch my own bait.

I like a really simple setup. I've got a six and a half foot medium bass rod that's medium action. I don't like a fast action tip, when I'm using live bait. Fast action tips are very stiff, slow action tips are very flimsy. Medium is right in the middle. I like the rod tip to have a lot of bend, because you don't necessarily need to set the hook hard, when you're using live bait. Typically, the fish will put the food in their mouth, and simply leaning back will set that hook into the corner. That was the case today, I was wearing them out!

Not at first, and that's typical. I started fishing just after 9:00 a.m. and these fish were still really cold. River fish don't act like Lake fish. Especially fish in cold rivers. They like to bite, midday. When the water gets warmest, and The bait fish is easiest to see, because the Sun is high. This trip is a little less than 5 Miles long, and I was more than halfway through, at 1:00 p.m., when these fish started to fire up.

I like to use 12 pound monofilament with a number one eagle claw Aberdeen hook and a small split shot, about 6 inches above the hook, to keep the fish down. About 2 foot above my bait fish, I like to attach a bobber. This is the setup that I have been using for more than half a decade. I believe I finally have it optimized. I get a fantastic ratio of bites to hook ups, and when these fish get hooked, they rarely get away. Those gold Aberdeen hooks are specifically designed for minnows, and if you get the number one, that's a really big hook, for really big minnows. That's what I like to use. When I'm doing these kayak trips with live bait, I like baits that are at least 5 inches.

If you don't have a cast net, or don't know how to use one, or just don't want to try, you could always pick up some shiners from the bait shop. Make sure you have plenty of fresh water, and an aerator to keep them breathing. That gets expensive, for the cost of 1 pound of bait fish, you could buy a cast net, and catch all the bait you need, for the whole summer. It's a worthwhile endeavor, if you're physically capable.

Don't want to bother with bait? Rather try your hand at casting lures? Go for it! There isn't a single type of bass lure that won't work in this river. I have had fantastic days using a 4-foot diving crankbait or a paddle tail swimbait. I have beat fish up from the beginning of the trip, to the end of the trip, simply using a Ned rig the whole time. The biggest reason I go for live bait, pretty much every time, is because it never lets me down. I don't have to do much fishing, I don't have to do much casting, I just get to do a lot of catching. If that sounds like something you would like to do, you've got to get your hiney, to the Piney.

title: Trip Report #74
content_raw:
A fantastic place for kayak fishing on Percy Priest Lake...
This morning, I started my day bank fishing at my crappie fishing spot that never lets me down...
https://goo.gl/maps/Z9z6gdVW9LTnhWAN9
Unfortunately, this morning, for the first time, I couldn't catch a fish. I got to the bank before first light. It was 10 minutes before 6:00. I watched an incredible sunrise, and fished for an hour and a half. I never got a single bite. More importantly, I didn't really see evidence that there were any crappie there. There were lots of fish in the area, mostly carp jumping out of the water. Just after 7:00 a.m., I headed to get some breakfast. But I had to walk out, half of a mile, to get back to my car. The trail through the woods is really well beaten right now, but I don't know if I will be walking it anymore this year. I don't like walking through the woods when it gets warm out, just because there's too many bugs and snakes. If you want to try your hand at bank fishing this spot, you will need to park right here, on the side of Weekly Lane...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/QXwNsps1D8dVrpik6
The crappie fishing has been tough since the cold front. They still haven't returned to the same pattern that they were before everything got cold. They should be, after this weekend. Until then, I needed something else to do. So I decided to go after bass. If you're in the right spot, you can pretty much always catch bass. Today, I paddled my kayak a couple of miles upstream, against the current, from Mona boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/y5h1Ko9QHUxGu8Aa9
This place is fabulous for kayaks, because no matter how big a boat is, they can't go fast in here. This stretch of river, upstream from the boat ramp, has lots of narrow, shallow spots that require everybody to slow down. If you go far enough up, boats can't go anymore! That's what I did today. I went really far up, before I turned around, and floated back down to my car. The fishing was pretty good, but I missed several fish that I should have caught. Most of the boats that were up this stretch of river, were fishing for white bass. There were some in there, but it wasn't loaded like it was last week, before the cold front. It should be loaded up again, real soon. I was targeting black bass. Largemouth bass, Smallmouth bass, spotted bass, if you can find them.
I had typical bass fishing gear with me. 7 foot medium, fast action rods with 15 pound braid. The first fish I caught was on a 1/10 of an ounce Ned rig, peanut butter jelly color. The rest of the day, I would use a purple colored spinnerbait with two silver blades. Largemouth bass for coming up out of the trees that are in the water to attack that thing near the surface. From the boat ramp, no matter how far you paddle up, there are trees in the water, on the left side and the right side, and sometimes in the middle! That's another obstacle that makes it just about impossible for boats to travel at more than an idle. Sometimes, it's really deep under those trees, but that doesn't matter! I like to cast, over the trees, and real my spinnerbait over top of the limbs. It's tough to do, you're going to get hung up. But if you're doing it right, it can be really effective!
I have no idea what other types of lures might work for these fish right now. I didn't really try anything else. It's safe to assume, that a crankbait would probably pull out plenty of fish. I was able to catch a handful of largemouth and a couple of small spotted, by sticking with my spinnerbait. I like it! I can see it in the water, on its way back to the kayak. When the fish come up to attack it, you can see the whole thing play out. It's really neat!
It's worth noting that, there were several different boats up there that were crappie fishing. They had bobbers, and minnows, and they were fishing around the same trees that I was catching bass out of. No doubt, if you used a really big glide bait, you could probably pull really big bass out of there. I'm sure they're feeding on some of the smaller crappie and definitely some of the bluegill. There are bluegill everywhere in this stretch of river! They were hanging out right at the surface. Some of them were pretty good size!
The water was pretty cold up there. I didn't have a fish finder with me, so I couldn't get a temperature, but the fish I touched, were cold! The water was also really clear. As clear as I've ever seen it! With no rain in the forecast, for the foreseeable future, that water is only going to get clearer, and warmer, which should act like a sirens song for fish out in the main lake. This stretch of river should be loaded from now, until the end of April, maybe even longer!
