title: Trip Report #75
content_raw:
Another seldom used boat ramp on Percy Priest Lake...
There's no such thing as an unused boat ramp on Percy Priest lake. Most of them get used heavily, everyday. Some boat ramps are a little tougher to get to than others, so not as many people go there. Today, I went to hurricane Creek boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/6JztzR9acrYaqPu79
This boat ramp is tucked way up into a neighborhood, in Lavergne. Even on the busiest of weekend days, there won't be as many people at this boat ramp. There is a courtesy dock, but even though the lake is up 2 feet from winter pool, it is still not viable. That courtesy dock will only be able to be used when the lake is completely full. There are no other amenities at this boat ramp. There are no bathrooms, there is no porta jon, and there is no playground or recreation area. It's just a boat ramp, and the bank fishing access is terrible, mostly because it's so shallow in that area. There is no real depth, away from the banks. It's truly a spot for people with boats and kayaks.
Directly across from the boat ramp is four corners marina. There are nearly 20 different arms in this Marina that hold lots of different size boats, from houseboats, to Bass boats, and everything in between. I spent the better part of 2 hours scanning underneath all of those boats. What I found was astonishing! The average depth in the area is about 10 feet, with the water going to as low as 5 feet, and as deep as 15 feet, underneath the boats. There were massive schools of crappie, and bluegill, everywhere underneath these boats. Unfortunately, I couldn't reach back far enough to get to them. That's becoming a repeating trend. Every time I find fish in a marina, they are tucked up too far away for me to get to them. I know they were crappie today, because there was a gentleman standing on the boat dock, and I told him where the fish were, and he went over there and caught one!
There were also a handful of largemouth bass cruising the marina, I suppose they are always there. I was able to catch one of those, on a crappie jig no less. But the crappie were inaccessible. So I headed out of the marina, toward the area of the main lake. I started scanning the banks and the coves in between hurricane Creek boat ramp and the bridge at Hobson Pike. I scanned for several more hours, and skipped lunch time, trying to find crappie. No matter where I looked, I couldn't find any crappie! The only ones that I could locate were in the marina. I'm going to draw a map of everywhere that I scanned today just so you won't waste any time there in the next coming days...
It took me forever, but I scanned this entire area! All around the banks, and most of the interior. The place where I dropped two x's, in between the bank and the island, is a no-go zone! There is a chain of rocks in this area that reaches all the way up to the water surface. I started making my way through there at speed, and just barely noticed them at the last second. If you're going into this area, you want your big motor up, and you're trolling motor down. These are serious boulders, and a couple of thin islands! Not that it matters, you shouldn't be going over there right now anyway. I couldn't find any fish, that weren't bass. Seems like bass are all over this lake.
I did find a handful of really nice fish attractors that were not marked. They were clearly put there by individuals who do not represent the TWRA. I make it a point to Mark these fish attractors whenever I find them, because I know, especially on Percy Priest lake, at some point in time, they will hold lots of crappie. I'm going to drop pins for the handful of fish attractors that I found in this area...
https://goo.gl/maps/j4r8bqsQoy3xkgSh6
https://goo.gl/maps/rQCACNYcm3PFp9CF6
https://goo.gl/maps/Lr3d3mSLExV9sXH99
https://goo.gl/maps/6rdBD2kwHXgie5iK7
https://goo.gl/maps/5yseQDzZgbETLoXR7
So if I didn't find any fish, why am I dropping these pins? I'll tell you why. As I mentioned, at some point in time, they will be loaded with fish. More importantly, I want to have every different location marked, on this lake, that I can. That way, no matter where I am on the lake, I always have lots of places to look. Going out on an expedition like this, even if I don't find fish, it's always worth it, when I find fish attractors like these. The ones I have marked, are really nice structures! They will definitely hold fish, probably pretty soon.
So why don't they hold fish now? Other fish attractors on the south end of the lake, near Jefferson Springs and Stewart Creek are completely loaded with crappie. Why aren't there crappie on the fish attractors in the middle of the lake? Temperature. It's because of the water temperature. Even after the last two cold fronts, the water temperature on the south end of the lake never strayed very far from 60°. It had already reached 65° this year. The water temperature where I was today, at hurricane creek, was 53°! Those fish don't want anything to do with that shallow water, right now. They were staying away from the banks, probably on cliffs, with deep water. Unfortunately, in the hurricane Creek area, there are no cliffs! You would have to go to the islands, or across the lake, to see those kind of features. I needed to get something to eat, so I called it a first half of the day.
I hated home to get some late lunch, and then by 2:30, I was headed back out to the lake. I was going to go to the Stewart Creek boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/2rkdFfvrufUckrfE9
A few miles down the road, the wheel on my trailer exploded. The bearings, and the cat containing them, shot out into the street, and caused me to hobble to the side of the road, and eventually, pull into a business. Fortunately for me, it was a business that repairs tractor trailers. I went in and asked them if they could fix my boat trailer, and they agreed! They said it would take several days, because they needed to order the parts, so they had me back it into their garage. I'm going to include a picture of my trailer tire, with the blown wheel bearing, so you will know what that looks like, if it happens to you. Make sure not to drive very far! Had I not been in their parking lot, I probably would have had it towed to a mechanic, to be repaired.
I just had the bearings and the Caps replaced on this trailer 2 years ago. As often as I use my boat, that time frame is meaningless. Some people will have their boat for a decade and never experienced this type of catastrophic failure, while they are on the road. The more you use it, the more this type of thing will happen. Fortunately for me, the only client trips that I have booked, are to go kayaking. So this happened at a great time! My trailer should be ready, and roadworthy, for summer of 26!

title: Trip Report #76
content_raw:
Where did all the crappie in Stewart Creek go?
This morning, I launched my boat at 6:30 a.m. at Stewart Creek boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/bpNLhh69cjurgv3C9
I wanted to check out all of the spots between the boat ramp and the back of the creek, where I had been catching lots of crappie. I had heard several reports that these fish were not there any longer. That tends to happen when we get major cold fronts, but apparently, they weren't there at the end of last week, when it was still warm. I went to look for myself, and lo and behold, most of the pins that I had dropped where crappie had congregated, we're now barren spots. Sticks underwater that weren't holding any fish. So where did they go? They had to go somewhere.
I went as far back up into Stewart Creek as I had gone previously...
https://goo.gl/maps/rzs2zRD6xRvjc3j57
There were some crappie in this location, on the trees that were hanging off of the shallow cliff, into the water, but it wasn't loaded like it was a couple of weeks ago. So I started looking around the area with my forward facing sonar, and I noticed that there were lots of decent sized fish, swimming around, in the channel. That far back in the creek, the channel is only about 7 feet deep. I started making casts at these fish that were roaming around, with my crappie setup. A 7 and 1/2 foot ultralight rod and reel with 4 pound monofilament and a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head, with a pearl colored body garland. It didn't take long to hook up, these fish were very active, and, they were crappie!
They were everywhere! Typically, by about 8:00 in the morning, these fish gather together, in great numbers, to protect their eyes from the sun. Today, it was nice and sunny, but these fish didn't care! They were on the hunt! Unfortunately, even though they were in a particularly good mood, they weren't gathered together. That makes them tough to get. You never know exactly where you need to cast, because they could be anywhere. We also had very heavy wind moving in this morning, and that made it even tougher to sit still and try to target individual fish. Long story short, the crappie are still very shallow, and it looks like they will stay that way for the next few days, at very least. We have a seriously strong cold front coming in at the beginning of next week, and I'm not certain they will stay in those shallow areas. If they don't stay in less than 8 ft of water, where I found them today, they will probably move to those 10 to 15 foot areas. They won't move very far.
I fished for about three and a half hours this morning, and I probably only caught 10 to 12 crappie. They were just really tough to nail down. After getting blown off the lake, I took my boat to the house, got something to eat, and then headed back out to the bank, where I could stand with my back to the wind, facing north, and try my hand at some crappie, without all of that wind. I went over to the cliffs on the opposite side of Stewart Creek boat ramp, where you have to walk a half mile through the woods to get to the spot...
https://goo.gl/maps/nZc4GRm2HVZkFRJW7
To get to this location, you have to walk a half mile through the woods, and alongside the lakes edge. There is no parking lot, but if you take a left out of Stewart Creek boat ramp, you will come around a curve to the right, and there will be a parking space on your right. It's mostly mud with a little bit of gravel, but most vehicles can get in there fairly safely. There's enough room for two or three vehicles. If you park in this location, and hike to the pin that I dropped, it's about a half a mile, and it's a four out of five on the effort scale of one to five. It's not necessarily as hard as it gets, but the trail is not flat, and you will have to walk on loose rocks, and cliffs that have water constantly flowing on them. There's no parking lot, but I will drop you a pin, relatively near the area where you should be parking...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/Tvtqf8gx7raUfEt36
There's only one trail from the parking spot, and it's a well beaten path. Take it all the way to the lake. When you get to the lake, there will be a white lawn chair hanging about 8 feet up in a tree. That's your trail marker! When you are coming back, you will know to turn down the trail that way, to get back to your vehicle. From that spot, you can walk along the rocks, beside the lake. Some of those rocks are loose! You may be tempted to fish in between the pin that I have dropped, and the end of the trail. It all looks really good! Unfortunately, there is not any underwater structure for crappie to hang on, anywhere along that cliff face, with the exception of that spot, a half a mile away from your vehicle. Once you get there, you will know you are in the right place. Someone has started a fire, and they have left a nice burn spot on the face of the cliff.
Directly out in front of that spot, as far as you can cast, to the left and the right, there are trees under water. Those trees hold crappie, every single time I go there, ever since I found that spot. It's been months! This is a real powerhouse of a location. When I got there today, it took me less than 10 minutes to get my first fish, and within an hour and a half, I had a handful of keepers, and a few small ones. I wasn't doing anything different than I had done earlier, when I was on the boat. My ultralight setup, with a tight line. Casting, and retrieving, with a slow retrieve. The biggest difference, the wind was at my back, and it was much easier to work the lure at the appropriate speed... SLOWLY!
Last week, the warmest water temperature that I saw was 63 and a half degrees. Today, after two cold nights, the water temperature was down to 59° in the back, warmest part of the creek. Typically, crappie spawn when the water temperature reaches 65°. We are definitely a few weeks away from that. That means, at least a few more weeks of pre-spawn! Hopefully, the fishing will get dramatically better.

title: Trip Report #77
content_raw:
What a difference a day makes...
Yesterday, I had the best day ever catching hybrid bass and striped bass at Poole knob boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/geh6Ak38kAskqfYd9
I couldn't wait to get back there this morning at the same time! At 6:30 a.m., I launched my boat from the boat ramp, with a heavy North wind, but I didn't let that stop me. I was convinced those bass would be in the same spot they were yesterday. I was wrong! The first thing I noticed, when I started scanning the area, all of the bait fish that were there yesterday, we're gone. Most people would say it's because of the water temperature, but yesterday morning at 6:30 a.m., the water temperature was 63 and a half degrees, and this morning it was 61 and a half degrees. Yes we had a cold front, yes and north wind came in, but the surface temperature only drops 2°. I wouldn't imagine the water underneath the surface dropped very much, at all.
So where did the bait go? I have a theory. It's long since been confirmed that heavy winds blow bait around. But not the kind of bait that you are thinking about. Not big bait that gets chased by bass or that schools in great numbers, tiny little bait, that you can't see. The stuff that the bait fish eat. That stuff is heavily influenced by the current that is produced by the wind. For the last several days, the winds have been out of the south, keeping us very warm, and blowing into the south facing cliffs that I was fishing on the last couple of days. Overnight, the wind shifted out of the north, and started blowing away from those cliffs. The bait that was hanging on those cliffs, was hanging out there because it was eating. I suspect that it's food got blown the other direction.
I put that theory to the test, and I headed to the north facing side of the channel, which was a shallow mud bank, instead of a deep cliff face. In less than 10 foot of water, pressed up against the bank, I found all the bait fish. Unfortunately, that water was too shallow for those hybrid baths. They like to have a lot of depth underneath them. They had no desire to follow those bait fish into the shallows. The only fish that were over there targeting those shallow water baits were largemouth and spotted bass. They weren't there in very great numbers, that's not a spot where they usually hang out.
That cliff had been holding crappie as well. As long as the bait fish were there, those crappie were hanging out on underwater trees. Now that the bait fish had moved away, all of those trees were empty! There were only a handful of crappie, where there used to be hundreds. When there's only a handful of crappie, that makes them really tough to catch, so I didn't even try. By 8:30, it became obvious that these fish weren't in the area, so I loaded up my boat, and called it a day.

title: Trip Report #78
content_raw:
Hybrid bass and striped bass at Poole knob boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/jRSzpmBTQbQCdhDL9
As you leave the boat ramp, to the left, there is a cliff that runs at least a quarter of a mile. That cliff has water out in front of it that is about 35 feet deep. That water is loaded with bait, and it's also loaded with big schools of hybrid bass and striped bass. Unfortunately, it's a sheer cliff, without much access from the bank. These fish were pressed right up against the cliff, but you can only get to them from a boat of some sort, a kayak would work really well! I sat in one spot in the center of water that was boiling with fish everywhere! Here is where I was sitting...
https://goo.gl/maps/GKs2CksgM3ax1Vvo7
These fish were everywhere, you don't necessarily have to be right in this location, that's just where I was. They were in every direction, for hundreds of yards. They were busting on the surface, everywhere, from 7:00 a.m., until 8:30 a.m. at that point, everything stopped. I literally couldn't get them to bite anymore. I could still see them on my screen, they just weren't biting. When they were biting, while they were busting on the surface, they were biting on every cast. What I would do, was cast where I saw them on the surface, chasing bait, and then catch one, almost every time. Here's how I was getting them...
I was using my 7 ft, medium size, ultra fast action bass pole. I had 15 lb braid tied directly to a 1/4 of an ounce jig head, non-painted. Instead of using a leader of any kind, I just tied my braid directly to my jig, and added a three inch white paddle tail swimbait. That was it. I never broke off, never retied, and never used another lure. That was all it would take to beat up on these fish, cast after cast, 5 pound fish. They were busting on the surface in every direction, so when I was ready to cast, I would throw at, or past where one had just blown up on the surface, and then, immediately start a slow retrieve. Not super slow, you want to make sure that paddle tail is wiggling back and forth really well. Also, I wasn't really letting my lure sink very much. These fish like to come up to the surface to eat.
Typically, I like to use a top water lure instead of a paddle tail. That's what I started with. Using the same setup, but instead of a paddle tail on a jig, I was using a Whopper plopper on top water. Those fish usually respond really well to that presentation, but not even a single fish took a look at that today. Another presentation that I will use to catch these fish, is a white rooster tail. You could use really big ones! Giant ones, one ounce! Or, 3/8 of an ounce, or a quarter of an ounce, or even 1/8 of an ounce. Pretty much any white rooster tail will catch these fish. I didn't try that today, because the paddle tail was having so much success, and it was the second lure that I had picked up.
I'm not sure what these fish do after they're feeding frenzy stops. I haven't spent a lot of time trying to target these fish from my boat, so I'm not real familiar with their tendencies. I know that they can still be caught, midday. I just don't know how, but I suspect throwing a paddle tail will get them. If not, I know that some people use heavy spoons to jig for them in open water. That might be an option if you find yourself in an area where there are a lot of fish, but you can't get them to bite.
I'm going to include a link to the video so you can see exactly how fast my retrieve was, so you can try to mimic that for these fish. There's a certain speed that they really like, I'm not sure exactly what it is, but it's right between one and two miles per hour. I've got the cadence figured out pretty well, it's something that is easy to mimic, and I believe, most people can do.

title: Trip Report #79
content_raw:
Kayaking the Obey river below Dale Hollow Dam...
This is a long kayak trip! Six and a half miles. The first three miles are shallow with slow moving water and, occasionally, rapids. The last 3 miles are dead water! All of that is conditional, except for the distance. The river has to be right for you to kayak, safely. In my opinion, it is safest to kayak this stretch of river, when they are not generating. When I went, the generators had been off since 8:00 p.m. the day before, and weren't scheduled to turn on until 2:00 p.m., the day of my trip. That meant, the water was down as low as it would go, and would be down, until we were finishing up. Knowing the generating schedule is the most important thing about going on this kayak trip. You can find the generating schedule for Dale Hollow dam, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/dale-hollow
Like most kayak trips, you need two vehicles to facilitate this trip. You need to leave one vehicle at the end and take another vehicle up to the beginning, with your kayaks. The end of the trip is six and a half miles downstream, which is almost all of this stretch of river, before it empties into the Cumberland River. Both the put in, at Dale Hollow dam, and the takeout, have boat ramps! That makes this one of the easiest kayak trips to facilitate, that I know of. As far as kayak trips go, this is a one out of five, on the effort scale of one to five. You will want to meet your party at the end of the trip, at Donaldson Park...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/rbQSE7L79okAWKTS7
Unfortunately, when the water is down, you cannot put a boat in at either one of these boat ramps. The water is just too shallow, and most boats will not be able to float off the trailer. That goes for both boat ramps! I'm not sure I will ever run my boat on this stretch of river, it's just too shallow, even when the generators are on, you run the risk of running aground.
To start your kayak trip, you will want to go to the boat ramp below Dale Hollow Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/SPDu13wzo18qTrwT6
There was a little bit of bank fishing access at Donaldson park, but there is tons of bank fishing access at the dam! Even when the generators are on, you can fish from the bank. I know, I did it yesterday, and we caught some fish! The generators at Dale Hollow are not as powerful as Center hill. For example, the water coming out of one generator at Center Hill Dam is over 4000 CFS. The water coming out of Dale Hollow Dam is just over 1600 cfs, or cubic feet per second. That's the way we measure the flow of rivers, cubic feet per second. One cubic foot is the size of one basketball. When I was there, fishing the generating water from the bank, 1600 basketballs of water rolling past in a second, was not too much water to fish, even with ultralight tackle!
So now you know where to start, you know where to end, you know how long the trip is going to be, six and a half miles, and that it's going to take all day. You know you want to go when the generators are off, but you don't know how long the generating water takes to get downstream. Based on my one trip, it took an hour and a half to get to this bridge, nearly the end of the trip...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/jccYFiKj2kwDyoRU8
While we were on the water, the dam started releasing the generators at 2:00 p.m., it took until 3:30 for the water to get to this point, and because the river gets wide, and deep, it came up very slowly, and pushed us to the boat ramp, like a lazy river. You cannot expect it to be a lazy river on the upper stretches! That first 3 miles of river is very shallow, and it will be subject to heavy currents when the generating water comes through. It will rise swiftly, without warning! You should wear your life jacket at all times.
There is also one other boat ramp on this stretch of river. It's called Moody access...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/ddczVydAsjxLUPjB6
It looked like you may be able to get a boat in at this location! I'm not 100% certain, we didn't utilize this boat ramp. It's kind of in no man's land, until you realize, that it has tons of great Bank fishing! There are more than a handful of parking spots, and some really good places to fish from the bank. I know you're allowed to, because they built bank fishing structures! There were also a couple of people there, who looks like they were having pretty good luck. If you're looking to bank fish, because you don't have a kayak, you should try this location, and directly below the dam.
Now for the good stuff, the trout fishing. I've been up to Dale Hollow dam, twice. Once to fish directly below the dam in my kayak, while the generators were off, and this time to kayak downstream while the generators were off. Both times, fish were going crazy everywhere! I had a really great day, catching lots of little fish, but it seems like most fish were eating flies. These fish are crazy for flies on this river! Those are little insects that these things eat all day everyday! That did most of the work for me, catching lots of little trout, all of them rainbows. The only other lure that I used with any success was a husky jerk from rapala. It's a suspending jerk bait, that, when worked like you do for bass, provides pretty good results! My only complaint, when you pause the lure to get that bite, they will smack the lure, but there's no tension on the line, so a lot of times they won't get hooked. That's mostly on the user, I'm sure, with more practice, I could get better at catching fish with that lure.
When we found a good looking spot with swift moving water, we would stop and get out on the bank to fish. That was the only time I was able to use a worm on the bottom with any success. The river bottom is not like the Caney fork. It's chunky limestone rock. You can't really bounce stuff along the bottom, because it's not smooth. Any attempts to fish on the bottom were met with instantly getting hung up, and broke off. https://maps.app.goo.gl/rbQSE7L79okAWKTS7

https://maps.app.goo.gl/SPDu13wzo18qTrwT6

That's the way we measure the flow of rivers, cubic feet per second. One cubic foot is the size of one basketball. Based on my one trip, it took an hour and a half to get to this bridge, nearly the end of the trip...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/jccYFiKj2kwDyoRU8

https://maps.app.goo.gl/ddczVydAsjxLUPjB6

It's kind of in no man's land, until you realize, that it has tons of great Bank fishing! There are more than a handful of parking spots, and some really good places to fish from the bank. I know you're allowed to, because they built bank fishing structures! There were also a couple of people there, who looks like they were having pretty good luck. title: Trip Report #80
content_raw:
Epic fishing from Walter Hill Dam to Mona boat ramp...
This is a kayak trip. You can put a boat in at Mona boat ramp, barely. There is barely enough water to launch a boat, large boats will not be able to launch right now, during winter pool. If you had a small Jon boat, you could go a little ways upstream. There are plenty of fish there right now, but the main attraction is to start in a kayak, at Walter Hill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/FkoSgoWzXxyQFCem8
If you have wheels for your kayak, now is when you need them. If you don't, you will have to carry your kayak all the way to the water's edge. That makes this trip a five out of five on the effort scale. You are not launching at a boat ramp, you are launching below the dam, on the side of the river. The takeout point is 5 miles downstream, and it is a boat ramp! The first place to take out on this trip is Mona boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/m8r9j53MGQoTY688A
You can do this trip year-round, but it's best when the lake is at winter pool. This is the headwaters of Percy Priest lake, and when the water is down, it makes this entire trip swift moving, clear water, that holds lots of really nice bass. Lake elevation is measured in feet above sea level. Percy Priest Lake is full, or at summer pool, when it is at 490 feet above sea level. Winter pool, which is where it is right now, is 483 feet above sea level. You can find the Lake elevation for Percy Priest lake, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/j-percy-priest
You don't want to do this trip after a heavy rain. We did have some rain yesterday, but not enough to flood the river. I won't do this type of downstream kayak trip if the water is brown or muddy looking. I like the water to look pretty! It did today, and I knew it would, because I could look at the USGS chart for the East Fork Stones River and see that it wasn't flowing too heavily from yesterday's rain. A heavy flow for this stretch of river would be anything over 500 cfs. CFS is cubic feet per second, or, the way we measure the volume of a river. One cubic foot is the size of one basketball. So 500 cubic feet per second would be 500 basketballs worth of water passing by any given point in one second. That much water is too much water for this stretch, but we had a lot less than that today. You can find the USGS chart for the East Fork Stones river, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03427500/all-graphs/#period=P7D
I think it's important to note that white bass had made their way all the way up to Walter Hill dam. I'm not sure that you could catch them at the dam, but as soon as we started our trip, we started catching white bass. We weren't using lures that would target white bass, but they were biting bass lures, all the way to the end of the trip. There were even some big ones! We were targeting largemouth and smallmouth, and it went really well!
I had two of my favorite 7-foot medium heavy, fast action bass poles. Each one of those has 10 pound braid. At first, I was trying a Ned rig, because that's what I had been getting bass on lately. That, and a white rooster tail. But neither one of those things were working very well. I started playing tackle box shuffle, which is where I just tie on a bunch of different lures, give each lure a few casts, and then tie on a different one. I started gaining some traction with a silver bladed spinnerbait and a 4 foot diving crankbait.
The bite was slow, until about 11:00 in the morning. We had been on the water for a couple of hours, and we had only caught a handful of fish. But that's typical for these trips. These river bass don't act like lake bass, at all! Lake bass get up very early, before the sunrise, and start hitting top water. These river bass, usually hit best at midday! That certainly was the case today. Running that spinnerbait around submerged timber, largemouths were coming out in great numbers. Throwing the crankbait around the rocks and cliffs would pull spotted bass out. We didn't catch very many smallmouth, but the ones that we caught, were in heavy current. It was truly a prototypical bass fishing day! This is how I expect river bass to behave.
One of the best things, we didn't see a single boat the whole entire trip. This stretch of river is technically Percy Priest lake, so it is subject to the rules and regulations on Percy priest. But it's just too sketchy for most boats. There are lots of underwater trees and stumps that come right up to the surface, and even though it's deep enough, it's just not worth the risk for most boaters. That makes it fantastic for kayakers! For what it's worth, if you can't go downstream, because you don't have two vehicles, or someone to help you facilitate a shuttle, you could always paddle upstream. There were two different couples of people who were paddling kayaks upstream from Mona boat ramp. It's a relatively easy paddle, and it gets you access to lots of good fish! The majority of the best fish that we caught were in the second half of the trip. Not necessarily because there aren't good fish in the first half, that was mostly due to the fact that the fish start firing up, right around lunch time.

comments.text: Terry Harville·5moI paddled upstream myself and probably caught 50-60 white bass on rooster tail. Some 15-20 spotted and smallmouth on crank bait. I didn’t get a largemouth yesterday. Did get a bonus crappie at boat ramp though. It was just one of those magical days yesterday.2

title: Trip Report #81
content_raw:
Largemouth are at the bank, on Percy Priest Lake...
Just before sunrise, bass are going crazy in the cove at Stewarts Creek boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/frDGHxVRpysixNnE7
The whole entire cove! About half an hour before sunrise, to about an hour after sunrise, they are feeding heavily on bait fish that are in three to five inches of water. There are hundreds of small fish and a handful of really big ones.
There are schools of bait fish lining the bank, at the cove, massive schools. During sunrise, and maybe during sunset, these bass fire up into the shallows on bait fish, picking them off, one by one. You're going to be able to get a certain number of these fish using a top water lure. I had a really big bass blow up on my Whopper plopper. He made a couple of jumps, and I got a good look at him, and then he got away. I couldn't get any other fish to bite on top water. I tried for a while, eventually, I settled on a 1/6 of an ounce white rooster tail, and that did the trick! I was pulling in little bass, left and right, and I even got a nice 15 inch largemouth!
It should be like this all over the lake. Anywhere you find a shallow cove, there should be bass, feeding heavily, first thing in the morning. These fish are going to eat all day, they're just not going to sit in the shallows after the sun comes up. About an hour after the day gets going, these fish move away from the bank, to feel a little more comfortable, out of the sun. They still make regular trips into the shallows to blow up on bait, just not as often.
These fish were blowing up right next to the boat ramp! The whole time, trucks were loading and unloading boats into the lake. They only had one thing on their mind, feeding heavily, before they spawn.

title: Trip Report #82
content_raw:
Hybrid and white bass everywhere...
Today, I had a client booked for the 4-Hour instructional forward facing sonar trip, but there was one caveat, we were going to launch somewhere neither one of us had ever been, so I can show him how I go about finding fish. We launched just before 6:00 a.m. out of Poole Knob boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/7txq6ReY9xMWsz6h8
I gave him the full experience. I treated it as if I would any other expedition mission. I typically work the area out of the boat ramp clockwise, in a circle, to see if I can find any fish. My forward facing sonar is positioned on the left side of the front of my boat, so that allows me to scan the bank as I come out of the boat ramp, and go left. When you leave this boat ramp and go left, which is downstream, it's a really long cliff face. The whole entire thing is loaded with fish. More bait than there are stars in the sky. We found lots of underwater trees that were holding crappie, which I will drop pins for, but while we were fishing for those crappie, white bass and gigantic hybrid bass would come in and eat our crappie lures.
There were massive schools of fish, that you might think we're bait, because they were so many, but they were all white bass. There were huge schools of tiny white bass, and small schools of large white bass. We were able to catch a really big white bass, that was only a couple inches away from a trophy. He also got his limit of hybrid bass, which is two. If you don't know, hybrid bass have to be 15 inches to keep. We were targeting crappie on underwater standing timber. These white bass and hybrid were unavoidable! They were everywhere.
At one point, we made our way away from the cliffs, across the channel to the area beside pools knob island. The shallow, muddy flat, had hundreds of thousands of white bass! They were as far as you can see. We caught a handful of those, just for fun, then made our way back to the cliffs, where the crappie were loaded. First I'm going to drop you a pin of where those white bass are sitting on the flats during the day...
https://goo.gl/maps/44q8SaHbzTqMH1o8A
These next three pins are where we found submerged timber or standing timber. These fish were loaded on these structures today, but we also found lots of structure in the area that didn't have any fish. That leads me to believe, just like any spot, crappie pick and choose where they stack up at any given point in time, and may not necessarily be on these pins, at all times. Especially, because they have to spawn soon. These fish won't be able to spawn in this channel. Today, we were fishing water that was a little more than 20 feet deep, but the fish were suspended on structure between 5 and 10 foot of depth. These fish will have to completely move away from this area to spawn. Crappie spawn in shallow water, on beds. So they definitely won't be here forever, but they are there now!
https://goo.gl/maps/T5YPrZtTgn6ebUK26
https://goo.gl/maps/4ZN45rSTw3gukGfB6
https://goo.gl/maps/1vAXb6RxUkfzKKye8
For a couple of hundred yards, on either side of the boat ramp, people were fishing from the bank. It looked like they were fishing for hybrids. I guarantee, if you were patient enough, you could get them. I would use a 1/4 of an ounce white rooster tail and 15 pound braid to cast as far as I could and retrieve that roostertail near the surface. That would be a good way to get not only the hybrids, but the white bass that are swimming through this area.
Surprisingly, the water temperature in this area at the surface, was just over 60°. Unfortunately, this boat ramp does not have a courtesy dock. The ramp is viable, even at winter pool, which is nice. The ramp is steep enough to launch just about any type of boat, but you will have to put it on the ramp, or on the rocks, to get in and out. Not high on the effort scale, but for a boat ramp, it's a two out of five on a scale of one to five. Not as easy as it could be, but definitely not difficult.

title: Trip Report #83
content_raw:
A good spot to wade for trout and Smallmouth on the Murfreesboro Greenway...
I like to park at the Northwest broad Street trailhead, in the 84 lumber parking lot...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/BzLkt4WbrheYzKMv9
From there, I wear some comfortable shoes, that are lightweight, and I walk down to the biggest rapids on the river. I carry my waders with me because it's at least a quarter mile, maybe more. I stop at a bench and put my waders on, and then put my shoes in my tackle bag. Here is where the bench is located...
https://goo.gl/maps/QrkbvWo59xEL4FVj8
When you are sitting here, you can hear the rapids! They are just downstream from this point, only a few hundred feet. There are a couple different access trails, where you can walk through the woods or the brush to get to the water's edge. This is a very popular spot, lots of people go there to swim and sunbathe. If you can catch it when no one else is there, it's a good place to fish! If you want to go to the spot, it's maximum effort. A five out of a scale of 1 to 5 on the effort scale. Walking in the West Fork Stones River is no small task. Even if you have the place to yourself, you're going to have to tread lightly. The bottom of the river is slippery! It's also not gravelly. It would be better if it was sandy or gravelly, but it's mostly flat limestone, which is slippery, and lots of boulders, which present a trip hazard.
I like to fish the river when it's really low, after an extended time with no rain. For me anything around 150 cubic feet per second is the number. As long as it's around 150, or lower than 150, I like to get in the river. It's good to catch fish when the river is moving faster, but I don't like to fight the current. If you don't know, the volume of rivers is measured in cubic feet per second. Basically, one cubic foot of water is around the size of one basketball. So if the river is 150 cubic feet per second, if you're standing there looking at it, in one second, 150 basketballs worth of water will have passed by. That's a lot of force! Fortunately for us, there is a station that monitors the river. Information is provided on the United States geological surveys website, and you can find information about the West Fork Stones river, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D
Check that bottom graph, where it says cubic feet per second... That's what you need to be looking at so that you know the water level before you go. The magic number for me, is less than 150. Depending on your ability, you may like to fish when there's more water, or significantly less. Here's what you're going to be fishing for...
Mostly Smallmouth bass. That's what I was targeting yesterday, but I wasn't able to catch any. The river is loaded with other fish, so that's what I was able to catch. Upstream from this location, they have put in nearly a thousand trout. Most of those fish have made their way downstream to pockets like this. You are not relegated to this one location! You can wade, up or downstream. It's tough sledding, but there's lots of good fishing. Anytime you find somewhere that the current is forming rapids, you will find trout! From now until the end of May.
Most of the other little fish aren't consequential. There are lots of bluegill and longear sunfish, and I was even catching bait fish, all on my 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail. I like to use my ultra light rod and reel, and 4 lb monofilament. It's the same setup that I like for Crappie or trout or panfish. It's my go-to in small water situations. 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail will catch everything in the river! Including a little rock bass that came up out of the current. Pretty much everything that swims in the Stones River will eat a white rooster tail.
Upstream from this location, it gets a little deep. You go back under the Northwest broad Street bridge, and it gets too deep to wade. Up around that bridge, you can fish from the bank, around the pillars that are in the water, and catch Smallmouth all year long! There aren't really many trails down there, because it's such a short walk. You will see where you can get to the water's edge. You can definitely get underneath the bridge, but it's a 4 out of five on the difficulty scale! It's not as hard as it gets, but it's really close. There's a lot of boulders, and some of them are loose. But the water out in front of that location is perfect habitat for big small mouth, and I've caught a lot of them there.
Downstream from that location, the water starts to get predictably shallow. At one point, there's a long stretch where, it never gets more than chest deep. That's a good place to wade as well. The whole entire area is good, if you're careful, and patient, and tread lightly.

title: Trip Report #84
content_raw:
Fighting the wind but finding crappie...
This morning, I made it out to Stewart Creek boat ramp at around 8:30...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/uxmsuMb83dK25SVm9
I went up the creek a little farther, as has been the case each time I have gone after crappie from this boat ramp. They have pushed all the way up, as far as they can go. As far as boats can go. Anywhere you find trees underwater, in less than 6 feet of water, they will be loaded with crappie. Today, most of those fish were keeper size. They had really fat bellies and they were feeding heavily, pre-spawn. When I got there this morning, the water temperature was 61°, when I left this afternoon, the water temperature was 65° at the surface in the creek. Some fish, if they are ready, will start spawning soon! Most of the fish will wait until April. The fish that are ready to spawn have already moved very shallow. Today, I caught 30 keepers, but only kept 16 of the biggest. The majority of the big fish that I caught came from as far up as I have gone yet...
https://goo.gl/maps/AGMd98uPZ4W1Ydr4A
That pin is as far as I have made it up the creek. I have no doubt that there are hot spots upstream from here. The water starts to get really shallow, and I get nervous about getting stuck. I have seen bigger boats than mine go up around the corner, but I haven't ventured that far yet. You have to go slow when you're coming into this area in general, most of the water is 2 to 6 feet deep. There is a channel that's wide enough for one boat, but it's very hard to find, and it's typically about seven to nine feet of depth. That channel pretty much ends at this spot. Fortunately, in the cove, there are some limestone cliffs that have a bunch of trees hanging in the water. Those trees are loaded with big fish! But so were all of the other pins that I passed by. I'm going to drop a whole bunch of pins from the Stewart Creek area that are only accessible by boat. Everything was loaded with fish today!
https://goo.gl/maps/HdQTZTh6CKPuHtZdA
https://goo.gl/maps/GJ3Kh9fgBAhQFGXW6
https://goo.gl/maps/o3xV8nrP6n27J7zG6
https://goo.gl/maps/F3Rupc8QBaqiSNp77
Those last couple are in the middle of the lake on the way to Stewart creek. There were large schools on those underwater trees, but the fish were small. The larger fish, that are ready to spawn, have already made their way to the shallowest areas. I'm certain it's that way all over the lake. I need to get out to East Fork and West Fork of the Stones River to check those areas, I'm sure the crappie have moved up there as well.
When I launched there were people fishing the bank at Stewart Creek all over the place! When I came back, a friend of mine was there and he reported that people had caught lots of crappie from the bank. Anywhere around those cliffs is a good place to fish, but the best place is across the cove at the newest fish attractor at the point...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/nzynYdGXwxhgmrQZ9
There were several people standing at this spot and it looked like they were all catching crappie. Most of the boat ramps on Percy Priest have some type of fish attractor in the area, another really good spot to try right now is the Vivrett Creek area...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/1spZ34hpg6QV7r9j9
The entire area is good fishing but there is a large fish attractor if you walk down the bank. It's a pretty good ways away, but there will always be lots of people there catching fish...
https://goo.gl/maps/57oztf4oqMFGXm8A7
Any of the bank fishing locations that I have mentioned in the past on Percy Priest Lake would be a really good idea right now. Make sure to take your 1/32nd of an ounce jig head and an ultra light rod and reel and pack your patience! The wind has been so intense, then it makes feeling the bite almost impossible. Since the fish have been so shallow, and relatively near the bank, I've been using a fixed bobber, and adjusting my depth between 2 and 4 feet to try to get these fish. It's the best way to see the bite, since it's tough to feel it.

title: Trip Report #85
content_raw:
Lots to catch up on...
Yesterday, I only had a short while to fish in the mid-morning. I was hoping to catch some trout, at Nice Mill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/qDYKjPjHGoBFVvmHA
TWRA has stocked trout at this location three times this winter, and it will have trout for us to catch until the end of May. It's always a good place for me to go to get a quick video, if I don't have a lot of time. Typically, when I'm fishing for recently stocked trout, I will start with a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail. I like an ultra light rod and reel with 4 pound monofilament. When the fish are willing to cooperate, it makes for a quick, easy video. Yesterday, they were not interested in a rooster tail, at all. Fortunately for me, I have the one thing that most freshly stocked trout can't resist, some Berkeley powerbait.
Using my same ultra light, with 4 pound monofilament and one heavy split shot, about 1 foot above a red mosquito hook, I was using one Berkeley powerbait to get the job done. Here is a link to the type of power eggs that I like, I prefer pink, but I think any color will do...
https://amzn.to/4l2y3pi
In the past, I've always used a number 6 eagle claw bait holder hook, and I've added a small piece of live nightcrawler worm. I'm probably not going to do that very much anymore. They seem to eat the power bait just as well. That way, I don't have to buy worms, and I don't have to get my hands dirty! The new type of hook that I've been using is a salmon egg hook. I will share a link for them right here...
https://amzn.to/409lkaQ
This is a link for size 8 hooks but you could use smaller hooks as well. Size 10 or size 12 would be good, especially if you're planning on keeping the fish. These hooks are so small, they go down really easy! The way I like to fish for trout with powerbait, is to cast into heavy current, and allow that sinker to bounce along the bottom. As it bounces on the bottom, if a fish sees the egg, or power bait, they will take it down without you having to set the hook. It's a very effective way to catch these fish, especially if they're being finicky. I had a few takers on the power bait, and I had to call it a day.
Fast forward to today, and the wind has begun! This time of year, when we go from it being winter time, to Spring time, Southwest winds start blowing, and they don't stop for a couple of months! I'll be doing everything I can to try to avoid the wind, but it's just not possible. Today, I was hoping I could avoid the worst of it by fishing on the steps at Center Hill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/HstRWAdEHd96S4r49
I only fish from the steps when the generators are running. Today, the generators were scheduled to be on all day. At least one generator. That was when I fished. There was one generator scheduled to be on from 9:00 a.m. until 5:00 p.m. I got there just after 9:00, but I couldn't make it all the way till 5:00 p.m. by 2:45, I had been fishing for several hours, and caught zero fish, and got zero bites! I employed every tactic that I know how to use, so I will spare you all the details. Basically, nothing was working. There were a handful of boats who were fishing down below us, and at least 10 to 12 people came and went from the steps while I was there. No one caught any fish, and no one got any bites.
That type of thing happens below Center Hill dam. It can be a frustrating place to fish. Just like anywhere! I left Center Hill dam, with the hopes that I could salvage the afternoon, and get on a sunset bite at Percy Priest lake. I took my crappie gear over to the bank at West Fork boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/WnPVuChNfGvJY5YW9
A little more than a month ago, I found some underwater structure, just to the right of the boat ramp. It was accessible from the bank, so I had hoped that I could get on a quick bite, to try to get a video. That spot has been heavily fished! It's marked with a concrete fence post. The fence post has rusted away, so it's just a round concrete cylinder, sitting on the water's edge, about a hundred yards to the right of the boat ramp, if you're looking at the river. There's a short trail through the woods that takes you directly to that spot. Someone has put a bunch of rocks on the water's edge, so you don't have to stand in the mud.
Unfortunately, I couldn't generate a bite. I didn't have much time, only a couple of hours, but I tried every trick in the book for crappie. I tried a tight line, and I tried a fixed bobber as well as a slip bobber. It just wasn't in the cards for me today. So does that mean today was a bad day of fishing? No! Today was a really good day for fishing! I just picked the wrong spots. That happens from time to time. Lots of other people were reporting tremendous catches today, all over the Middle Tennessee area! My plan, to try and avoid the wind, was probably a bad idea. I'm going to have to get out on the lake, and fight the wind, because these fish are going crazy! The arrival of an early spring has the water temperature rising, and the fish in full pre-spawn. I intend to take advantage of it the rest of the week, by getting out on the lake, and fighting the wind. Unfortunately, it will be windy until June. So there's that...

title: Trip Report #86
content_raw:
A hidden gem of a lake on the Murfreesboro Greenway...
Yesterday I used my kayak Wheels to take my kayak off the beaten path, to a spot where most people won't go fish. To get there, you need to park in the Manson Pike trailhead on the Murfreesboro Greenway...
Manson Pike Trailhead https://share.google/riOjByrcfLgIyFifB
There is a boat ramp in the parking lot at this trailhead, but you don't want to use that. That will take you downstream, and that trip is for extreme kayakers only. It has steep drop offs that will flip even the most experienced kayakers, myself included. Where I went was above Ransom Mill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/iBs9hNdi7LPf1oAb8
That small dam creates a lake that has a lot of fish that don't get much pressure. To get to those fish, you need to kayak, and more importantly, you need a kayak cart, so that you can roll your kayak from the parking lot, to the water's edge. Here is a link for the kayak cart that I use...
https://www.amazon.com/dp/B00KX5A7NW/ref=cm_sw_r_as_gl_apa_gl_i_122Q3216K1VDJM10PDJW?linkCode=ml1&tag=richardcpetty-20&linkId=040053a87e1c5f971d51055054016ee7
You're going to need a map. It's not hard to figure out, you need to go above the dam. Exactly where is the most important part. I'm going to drop a pin, but then I'm going to draw you a map...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/au2BSQjzSNu9XUq29
When you're in the parking lot, you need to load your kayak onto your wheels, and then put everything in your kayak that you're going to need for the day. Then you can simply roll down the greenway, until you get to the bridge, where you take a right and go off road. At that point, the spot where you launch will be directly in front of you...
From here, you can paddle a couple of miles upstream to Old Fort golf course. At that point, there's a bridge that allows golfers to go over the river, and underneath that bridge there are heavy rapids that you can't go up unless you get out and go around. That's where I usually turn around and go back downstream, but not before I pick up as many free golf balls as I would like.
The entire stretch of river is loaded with bass! The first mile and a half fishes like a lake, because the water is deep, and pretty. It's not clear, but it's not stained like Percy Priest lake. It's more turquoise in appearance. It's really nice habitat for big largemouth bass, and there are lots of them! I started going to this spot about 6 months ago, and each time I've been I've done really well. I've been throwing a small spinnerbait with two silver blades with no trailer. That seems to do the trick, each time I've been out I've caught decent fish. I've also been throwing a 1/6 of an ounce white rooster tail. As long as it has a flashy silver blade, those fish will go for it. The last half mile before you get to the golf course is shallow water, most of it about 2 to 3 feet deep. I don't catch as many fish up there in the shallows, but when I do, they are Smallmouth bass. They like that current!
Because you can roll your kayak all the way to the water's edge, and the launch point is fairly flat and easy to access, I would rate this trip at no more than a three on the effort scale of one to five. The hardest part will be loading and unloading your kayak and then paddling up the river. Paddling upstream can be difficult, especially if there's heavy current. Fortunately, we are able to check the United States geological survey for this location so that we can see the river speed before we ever go out. For this particular stretch of river, I only ever go when the cubic feet per second or CFS is around 150 or lower. Too much current, and it will be too hard to paddle, and too fast to fish. I like it when it's slow and low. You can find the USGS chart for this stretch of river, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D
If you look at the second graph on that chart, it will be the cubic feet per second. That's how we measure the flow of rivers. One cubic foot is about the size of one basketball. As of 5:00 a.m. on Monday morning when I'm releasing this report, the cubic feet per second is 167. That would mean, if you were standing on the side of the river, in one second, 167 basketballs worth of water would pass by your location. That's how we know how much flow there is, before we go. In the summertime, this thing will get really low! That makes it super easy to catch these fish. They have nowhere to go, and a lot less water to hide in!

title: Trip Report #87
content_raw:
Stunningly beautiful 5 Mile kayak trip that's only viable for less than six more weeks...
Yesterday, my buddy and I kayaked from Nice Mill Dam to West Fork boat ramp. You can kayak this stretch of river anytime. It's never closed, it's always open to the public, but it's not always the same as it was yesterday. This time of year, this trip is really special, for a couple of reasons. First and foremost, the lake is at winter pool. What that means for this 5-mile stretch of river, is that it turns into a white water heaven as opposed to a stillwater lake! The first 3 miles of the trip are relatively shallow and have lots of white water rapids. It's a lot of fun for people who are advanced at kayaking. Fortunately, the rapids aren't too much for fishing kayaks. Which makes this trip optimum for a day out on the water. This is a kayaking trip, so you will be carrying your kayaks and getting in and out of your kayaks along the river. This is a 5 out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5. This is not for the meek of heart.
Now that we know where we're going, and who this trip is for, let's focus on how to facilitate. The first thing you're going to want to do is meet your friends at the end. Logistics about how to shuttle kayaks is often the toughest thing to figure out. No matter how many are in your group, if you all meet at the end of the trip, you can load up kayaks to take to the beginning and figure out which vehicles you're going to leave at the end. Basically, you're going to need vehicles that can move all of the kayaks at the end or the beginning, or you're going to have to drop everything off at the beginning and leave someone there to guard the stuff while you take vehicles back to the end. Outside of physically moving your kayaks, the logistics, typically, is the hardest part to figure out. The end of the trip is West Fork boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/x6Rd5djCcnU455GC6
This is an actual boat ramp on Percy Priest lake. That makes the end of the trip really easy! To load up, all you have to do is back your car or truck down to the water's edge and off you go! The beginning is a little trickier. To put in, there is no boat ramp. The start of the trip is 5 miles upstream from West Fork boat ramp, at Nice Mill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/fYwAtyGBRSZV29Um7
There are two parking lots at Nice Mill, there is a parking lot on the high side of the river, above the cliffs, and this parking lot which I have dropped here, on the low side. This is the side you want to launch your kayak from. There is a gravel path down to the water, but you won't be able to launch there. You'll have to go to the right, downstream a little ways, where there's some calm water on the edge. It's about 250 feet from your car. It's a pretty long ways to carry your kayak, but that's the hardest part of the trip. This is a 5-mile stretch of river, and I often get asked how long it takes. Plan on all day. Start early in the morning, and finish in the afternoon. Take your time, have some lunch! Or don't. If you just want to kayak, you can get this trip done in about an hour. 5 miles in 1 hour? Absolutely. With the amount of current, you could easily paddle your kayak 5 mph. Bottom line, don't be afraid you won't reach the end, it's only 5 miles.
I like to do this trip when the water is below 400 cubic feet per second. Cubic feet per second is how we measure the flow of water in rivers. Basically, one cubic foot is the size of one basketball. So 400 cubic feet per second would mean that if you were standing at the edge of the river, in one second, 400 basketballs of water would pass you. Less than 400 is the sweet spot for this stretch of river. Anything over that and the rapids become a little more than I would like to handle in a fishing kayak. Also, if the water is flowing at that rate, it will probably be brown with lots of debris, which is not a good time to go. I like the water to be clear, or turquoise at worst. You can find the river level, as measured in cubic feet per second, at the USGS website, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D
Now for the good stuff! The fishing on this stretch of river is on fire. First of all, they put 4,000 trout in at Nice mill. Using an ultralight rod and reel, and a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail, we were able to catch trout for the first 3 miles! The first 3 miles have lots of rapids and swift moving water. Perfect for trout! The best part, no boats can go up that far, and no one ever kayaks this stretch of river. There's no way to get to those fish in the middle, you would have to hike in several miles through very rough terrain. There are fish that haven't seen anybody since they came off the truck! And they are loaded! But when this lake starts to come back up at the beginning of April, this trip will change completely. Only the first mile will have rapids, and the last 4 miles will all be deep water lake. Right now, Percy Priest Lake is measured at 483 feet above sea level. That is all the way down at winter pool. 483 is how low they drain the lake to every winter. Summer pool is 7 feet higher. 490 feet. That will cover up most of this area, and there won't be any more moving water. You can find the lake elevation, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/j-percy-priest
After we had our fun catching trout and small sunfish on rooster tails, the river started to get a little deeper, and we lost our flow. We were now in the two mile stretch that is the lake, but the water was still clear, and we could see that there were giant bass swimming around underneath the trees that were laying in the water. I saw two big bass before I tied on my favorite bass lure, a peanut butter jelly ned rig. Basically, it's a small jig with a half of a piece of plastic worm. It's not much to look at, but the fish love it! On my very first cast, I had a big bass come out and take a look at my lure, and then on my second cast, I caught a bruiser of a largemouth bass! And then another! They are loaded up there! The water was about 4 to 5 feet deep, but it was still a little too narrow and a little too shallow for most boats, so no one is up there fishing!
The last mile is loaded with people fishing from the bank as well as folks that were looking for white bass. We didn't see any white bass caught, but that's what the people on the bank were fishing for. There is a way to access the bank, but it's only on the lake side of this trip. The last mile is accessible from a place on the side of the road, but it's about a half mile hike in. I will drop you a pin, in case you would like to go out there and check it out, there were a lot of people out there fishing, which leads me to believe, they know something that we don't. It's the white bass run. They're waiting for those white bass to come up that stretch of river, where they are easily accessible from the bank. That should happen this week, with our warming temperatures! You can fish on the bank by walking in from here...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/5Hz6sLrYuFYD5Vcn7
One important feature to note on this trip, there is a massive spring that flows into the river, that will be underwater at summer pool. This place is a known Haven for not only Giant largemouth, but striped bass in the summertime! They love the cool water that is coming out of the spring, and they sit there in great numbers. I dropped a pin on the location of the spring, and I'm going to drop that, right here...
https://goo.gl/maps/szPBzGT4dYfZM7NR8
At summer pool, you can easily take your boat up to this spring! Unfortunately, it's very well known. You may not have the place to yourself. But it's always worth a look, the scenery is spectacular!

title: Trip Report #88
content_raw:
What a difference a day makes...
2 days ago, I had an epic day at Jefferson Springs boat ramp. There were small schools of large crappie everywhere. There were large schools of small crappie everywhere. Fast forward to yesterday, most of those fish went somewhere else! Yesterday after noon, I took my boat back to Jefferson Springs boat ramp to try to catch the fish that were hanging out right by the boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/zxjUSwCUs6HXabso8
I had dropped a bunch of pins in the immediate area and explained that there were large schools of white bass, everywhere! When I went back to look at those pins, they were just empty trees. The large schools of white bass were now small schools, and there weren't very many of them. Those fish moved! I suspect they went upstream. Here's why I think that...
2 days ago, the maximum water temperature in the afternoon was 51 and a half degrees. Yesterday, after it got warmer in the afternoon, the water temperature at the surface got up to 54°. I think, those fish pushed a little farther upstream. They do that this time of year, following the bait fish. The warmer the water gets, the more it will hold bait, for the bait fish, in shallow areas. When the bait fish goes shallow, to eat, so do the other fish that are following them. The area around the boat ramp is around 20 to 30 ft deep in the channel. There's a good chance they pushed up to where the channel is only 15 to 20 ft deep. Why do I think they pushed up stream, because of the temperature, and because we checked downstream.
I had my buddy with me in my boat, and we went downstream towards trigger Island...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/4J45qfr51z6cB73u6
The channel kept getting deeper, and we scanned the banks where the fish should be, and we kept seeing less and less. We were catching a handful of fish up by the boat ramp, but not even enough to make a video. There won't be a video of my excursion yesterday, because there were that few fish! We were able to catch a handful of crappie and probably 10 to 20 small white bass, but that's it. It was a really tough afternoon of fishing, even though the conditions were stellar.
Unfortunately, stellar weather conditions and great fishing don't always go hand in hand. We've all had the experience where it's an unbelievably beautiful day, a chamber of commerce day they call it, and the fish just won't bite. That was yesterday. We had a bluebird sky, with not a cloud in sight, and 64 degrees with light wind. It literally felt like heaven outside! For some reason, when it gets like that, the fish can be tough to get. The reality is, if you find a good school of fish, you're going to catch them! We did not. Other people I know, did! Yesterday wasn't a bad day of fishing because of those conditions, those fish just moved somewhere they were more comfortable, and I couldn't find them.
I don't think that will be the case moving forward. I think the area by Jefferson Springs boat ramp will stay loaded with fish, and they will be eager to bite. The pre-spawn is in full swing for all species of fish on Percy Priest lake. All of the true bass, which are white bass, yellow bass, hybrid bass, and striped bass, will be making runs up the creeks and tributaries chasing bait fish. All of the crappie will be moving to shallow areas near where they live in the lake. They will have to spawn in 10 ft of water or less, so they will be moving to those areas and feeding heavily.
We've got at least 10 days of warm weather in the forecast! The fishing is going to be stellar in all of the different locations that I have listed for you in the past on Percy Priest lake. The time is now to utilize all these different locations, sometimes going to more than one location in one day, just to find the hungry fish.

The channel kept getting deeper, and we scanned the banks where the fish should be, and we kept seeing less and less. We were catching a handful of fish up by the boat ramp, but not even enough to make a video. There won't be a video of my excursion yesterday, because there were that few fish! We were able to catch a handful of crappie and probably 10 to 20 small white bass, but that's it. It was a really tough afternoon of fishing, even though the conditions were stellar.

Unfortunately, stellar weather conditions and great fishing don't always go hand in hand. We've all had the experience where it's an unbelievably beautiful day, a chamber of commerce day they call it, and the fish just won't bite. That was yesterday. We had a bluebird sky, with not a cloud in sight, and 64 degrees with light wind. It literally felt like heaven outside! For some reason, when it gets like that, the fish can be tough to get. The reality is, if you find a good school of fish, you're going to catch them! We did not. Other people I know, did! Yesterday wasn't a bad day of fishing because of those conditions, those fish just moved somewhere they were more comfortable, and I couldn't find them.

I don't think that will be the case moving forward. I think the area by Jefferson Springs boat ramp will stay loaded with fish, and they will be eager to bite. The pre-spawn is in full swing for all species of fish on Percy Priest lake. All of the true bass, which are white bass, yellow bass, hybrid bass, and striped bass, will be making runs up the creeks and tributaries chasing bait fish. All of the crappie will be moving to shallow areas near where they live in the lake. They will have to spawn in 10 ft of water or less, so they will be moving to those areas and feeding heavily.

We've got at least 10 days of warm weather in the forecast! The fishing is going to be stellar in all of the different locations that I have listed for you in the past on Percy Priest lake. The time is now to utilize all these different locations, sometimes going to more than one location in one day, just to find the hungry fish.

title: Trip Report #89
content_raw:
Fall Creek boat ramp and Jefferson Springs boat ramp on Percy Priest Lake...
This morning I took my boat to Fall Creek boat ramp at 9:00 a.m...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/TwNJWLUrcckkqVzT7
This area is unnavigable. I cannot stress that enough. You cannot launch a boat from this boat ramp during winter pool. The water is too low to get the boat off the trailer. Even if you could, you can see that there is not enough water to float out to the channel. There's not enough water in that area to hold fish! I'm sure they are over in the deeper areas, but for hundreds of yards away from that boat ramp, in all directions, the water is less than a foot deep. So I headed over to the next closest boat ramp, Jefferson Springs boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/H1HJzNuQ4wpCZv2e8
This boat ramp is viable when the water is all the way down, but you have to be careful! You cannot go left or right out of the boat ramp. There are giant boulders under the water that come all the way up to the surface, but you can't see them. When you put in at this boat ramp, you have to go straight out of the boat ramp for about a hundred yards, before the water gets deeper. A little more than a hundred yards away from the bank, the bottom drops dramatically. It goes from 2 to 6 foot deep, straight down to more than 20 feet deep. That drop off runs from the boat ramp, downstream, for hundreds of yards, and it's loaded underwater with trees, and those trees are loaded with fish!
My plan was to go to the Fall Creek area and scout for some new crappie spots. I wasn't able to make it out of sight of the boat ramp! There are overwhelming amounts of crappie and white bass everywhere in the immediate vicinity of the boat ramp. I'm going to drop some pins on some underwater locations where there were trees or stumps that were particularly loaded, but the whole entire area was on fire!
https://goo.gl/maps/WT7AGBGmXDQWnfmAA
https://goo.gl/maps/hAtQuzDWyoyXjhVv6
https://goo.gl/maps/V9eEhTkoYYMQqRso6
https://goo.gl/maps/rNewjVuGPpSLmWr57
https://goo.gl/maps/vZgrRHdnMYfdNr4e6
The deepest part in the middle, was where all the bait was hanging out. On the underwater drop off was where all the desirable fish were. There were big schools of little crappie that were about 10 foot deep. The really big crappie were holding on stumps that were between 2 and 6 foot of depth. They weren't hanging out in big schools, only a handful of fish on each stump, or stick, but they were everywhere! At first, I thought those big fish around the stumps were bass. When you see a bass, on forward facing sonar, and you have a crappie lure, you can cast in their direction and jiggle that crappie jig near the surface, above their heads. That will make those fish rise up relatively quickly, and attack that lure.
That's what I was doing when a really big bass came up really fast, and smacked my crappie jig. Then when I got a look at the fish, I realized it was a nearly trophy sized crappie. That was something that was new to me, I had never seen crappie come up to the surface to attack a jig like that. Typically, I will dangle my crappie jig in front of them on a bobber, or use a tight line to run it through their area, with a couple of twitches. Never, had I danced it at the surface and had them come up and hit like that. That was a new one for me, and it's something to consider for the future! Not only for those of us who have forward facing sonar, but for everybody who goes crappie fishing! If you're in an area, and you know there are crappie, there are a handful of retrieves that work best. We can add this to the list of things to try on days when they are being particularly finicky.
Today, these fish weren't being finicky! All I had to do was figure out that they wanted me to jiggle it, way above their heads, then I started smashing the fish! It didn't matter what color Bobby Garland I was using, they were attacking them all the same way. As long as it was jiggling, at least 4 feet above their head, they would come up quickly to attack it.
Before the storm that came through last night, and the cold front we had a few days ago, the water temperature on this end of the lake was around 60°. As of this morning, the water temperature was 51⁰. With warm weather in the forecast, I expect these fish to be in this area, for the next couple of months! They should be easy picking, in the shallow areas, especially if you have a minnow and a bobber! If that's something you would like to do, I suggest you set that minnow to a depth of 3 or 4 feet. If you're going to use a crappie jig, I would suggest a tight line, unless it's really windy, then you need to try to use a bobber and twitch that jig above their heads. Either way, you need to get out to Jefferson Springs boat ramp!
