title: Trip Report #90
content_raw:
Seven different species today below Center Hill Dam from my boat...
Today, I put my boat in at Buffalo valley boat ramp below Center Hill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/6sycfEpHiyLyYPrX8
This is actually a very difficult boat ramp to use, because it's not very steep. I only utilize this boat ramp when the generators are on. When the generators are off, I cannot get my boat off the trailer, or, on the trailer. Today, the generators were scheduled to be on the entire day. One generator was scheduled from midnight until 6:00 p.m. For me, that's the ideal condition to take my boat below Center Hill dam. To find the generating schedule, look here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
There are more fish below Center Hill Dam than there are stars in the sky! Sitting in the direct center, below the dam, casting a crappie jig, I was able to catch crappie, largemouth, spotted bass, gar and skipjack herring. There are lots more fish to be had, but the crappie bite was slow, so I focused my attention on catching trout out of the generating water.
Today was special not just because the generator was running all day, but it was extra special because they had on the number one generator. If you're on the river, looking at the dam, the generators are numbered backwards. Number one is on the far right, number two is in the middle, number three is on the far left. There are three generators that operate at Center Hill dam, and today, only the number one generator was on.
That generator is in the corner, next to the steps. When the water comes out, it makes its way a long the concrete wall by the steps, and leaves a huge area for boats to sit, right next to where the water comes out. I wouldn't suggest going in there unless you have a sturdy vessel. I wouldn't go in there in a kayak or canoe. It's a little too choppy for that. But it's definitely not too wavy for a decent sized boat. I have a 14 and 1/2 foot Jon boat, and I felt comfortable sitting right next to where the generating water was coming out.
I had my 7 foot bass rod with 15 pound braid already tied up to a half ounce cotton Cordell silver spoon. After only a couple of casts into the heavy boils that come out from the generating water, I hooked into my first nice trout of the day. It was a rainbow trout, and it hit that spoon just after it hit the surface. What you need to do, especially if you're in a boat, is to cast into the heavy boils, and then get your rod tip up so that the spoon doesn't get down to the bottom too quickly. Allow the spoon to flutter with the current while you slowly retrieve any slack. Give the lure a couple of twitches to impart some up and down fluttering action. That's something that trout love. Do your best to keep the lure from hitting the bottom. If that happens, it will get hung up.
On the very next cast, I caught a bruiser of a brown trout! I casted to the same spot, into the heavy boils, but I had to let that lure work its way down the current for a few seconds before I got the bite. One of the nice things about fishing in the heavy current, typically, no matter what type of lure you are using, you won't have to set the hook. There is so much going on down there, that when they hit a lure, they are already on the move, with it in their mouth. They tend to set the hook, themselves.
When I'm getting a good bite on a lure that works the water column, I tend to believe that there are many more fish laying on the bottom who would like to see something that they don't have to chase. To target fish on the bottom, I like to use a Carolina rig. I had a different 7 foot bass rod with 12 pound monofilament as the main line. I slipped on a 1 ounce egg sinker, a glass bead to protect my knot, and then tied my line to a barrel swivel. On the other end of the barrel swivel, I attached about 18 inches of 12 pound monofilament and a number 6 eagle claw bait holder hook. I like to use soft plastics on a Carolina rig and have it bounce in front of these fish, kind of like a conveyor belt of food. On my hook, I put a 2 inch white sassy shad. That's a small soft plastic that looks like a shad.
I cast directly into the boils, and then start to reel out the slack, to help the Carolina rig get down to the bottom. If you don't reel in the slack, the extra line will cause the lure to balloon up off the bottom. When you start to retrieve the slack, you will feel the line get tight and the sinker will find its way to the bottom. The only way to achieve that, is to cast upstream, at a 45° angle, and then start reeling out the slack. I think it might have been my second cast, when a giant female brown trout ate that soft plastic, and set herself into the hook, a good 10 to 15 seconds before I realized she was there.
You can put any type of lure on that hook. You could even put a worm and some power bait! The sky is the limit. Just remember, you're definitely going to get hung up when you're fishing the bottom. Be prepared to break it off. Now that you know when to fish, and how to get them, the toughest thing to do will be getting the boat on and off the trailer.
Even with the generators on, it's still not easy to get the boat on and off the trailer. You have to get used to that shallow boat ramp, and how you have to angle your trailer to make things happen. It's a solid two and a half out of five on the effort scale of 1 to 5, just figuring it out. You also need to have some hip waders or potentially some chest waders, in case you can't get your boat on and off without getting in the water. I have to wear muck boots. Even with the generators on, I still have to get in the water just a little bit. Today, they only had one generator on, but when they run two or three, the water comes up the boat ramp and it actually gets a little bit easier to load and unload the boat.

title: Trip Report #91
content_raw:
Two crappie spots and a trout hole, from the bank...
Yesterday, it was 18° out to start the day. We haven't had a deal with cold weather like that for a couple of weeks, and we won't have to for a couple of more weeks. When it's like that, I find administrative stuff to do. I didn't go fishing until after lunch. I only had a short window, and I wanted to make the best of it. I decided to try to get some crappie from the bank, so I headed over to Percy Priest Lake to a spot that I found with my forward facing sonar. The parking spot is on the side of Weekly lane, and you have to be careful pulling in and out, because it's not paved or gravel, it's just mud...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/tDfw2f9wskVKCYtU6
This spot is about half a mile away from where you park. You have to walk through the woods, and then, down the bank to the cliff where the crappie hang out...
https://goo.gl/maps/5uppf5HAxHtcNxaR9
The trail isn't straight. It weaves through the woods, it's a really old trail. Once you get to the water's edge, there's a white chair hanging in a tree. That is your trail marker! When you're coming back, that's where you need to go to get back to your car. When you're on your way out, that's where I usually hit the rocks on the bank and start walking to the spot. Those rocks are loose! And it's a long walk! This is a four on a scale the effort scale of 1 to 5. It's kind of tough to know you're in the right spot, but fortunately, someone has built the fire there, and there are a couple fire pits right in front of this pin. The water in front of you is 18 feet deep as far as you can cast a light crappie jig, and as much as 7 or 8 feet deep right out in front of the cliff.
There were fish there! In large numbers. There was already one gentleman there, and he had been there for about an hour, and he had six slab crappies! I got to work, casting my ultralight rod and reel with 4 pound monofilament and a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head, with a Bobby Garland. Lately, I've been using whatever color 2-inch Bobby Garland that I have available. I've pretty much decided, that the color doesn't matter. It probably does, on some level, but it didn't yesterday. I was able to generate a bite, after allowing my lure to sink to a depth of 25 seconds, before I started my retrieve. When that lure got about 10 feet away from the cliff, was where I got my first bite, and then, where I caught my first fish, and 11 and a half inch slab crappie. I gave it to that gentleman, and moved on to my next spot.
I went across the street, to see if there was less wind blowing over at Stewart Creek boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/T7yfgD3DygWy1MNy9
It was just as windy on this side of the lake, as it was the other, and that was the main reason why I left my first spot. But there was no one at Stewart Creek boat ramp! I was shocked. I made my way through a much shorter trail, over to the cliffs, to fish by myself, in a location that I already know is loaded!
I drew a map of where I went to. All the other x's are known crappie hot spots. Getting to the edge of the water at each of these spots requires scaling cliffs! This is definitely a four on the effort scale of one to five. You're going to have to be able to lift your own body weight, several times over.
You'll know you're in the right spot, there is a tree sticking out of the water! It's about 15 ft from the bank, and it's a giant tree. I'm convinced this thing stays loaded with crappie year-round. Every time I look at it with my forward facing sonar, there are hundreds of fish! They're just really tough to get. They are underneath that tree trunk, and it's protected at all angles from a cast. All you can hope to do, is run your lure beside the tree and get one of those fish to come out. That's exactly what I was able to do! I was casting over top of the tree, which would literally bring the lure back through the tree, and get me hung up, unless you play it exactly right.
I was using the same setup, to cast across the tree, allow my lure to sink for 10 seconds, and then start a slow retrieve with a couple of twitches. Before my lure got a chance to get to the tree trunk, I would rip it out of there, over the top of it, and cast again. This is very tough! But after a couple of casts, I got my first bite, and then, my first fish. Feeling accomplished, because I'm catching fish in difficult wind conditions, I decided to treat myself to some catching, instead of fishing. I packed my things up and headed over to Nice Mill Dam to do some trout fishing...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/rWhuPGgGwud4zYP28
From this parking lot, there is a trail that walks through the woods for more than a mile! The first half mile of that trail is flat, and takes you to the water's edge, and it's flat! That makes it an easy place to fish. Because you have to walk a little ways from the car, that puts this location at a two on the effort scale of 1 to 5. It's pretty good for lots of people, including families. All of this area is public access, pretty much as far as you can walk. Technically, this is Percy Priest lake, and both banks, all the way around the lake, are public access.
I went there to get out of the wind, mission accomplished, and to catch some fish. I was tired of grinding, which I had to do it both of the first spots. At each location, it took me nearly an hour to generate my fish. It's not that they weren't there, or that they weren't cooperating, you just have to figure something out. That was tough to do yesterday. With trout, everything is figured out. Just go to the trout river, and cast a rooster tail, or some power bait. That's exactly what I did, and I was able to catch a few nice trout. I walked down the trail, instead of standing on the damn, because you're way out in the woods. Really deep in the woods. And that gets the wind off of you, no matter what direction it is coming from.
There are lots of trails in this area, lots of people use it just to hike. Some people ride their horses other people walk their dogs. The trail is heavily used, so it gets muddy after rain. Unfortunately, tomorrow's rain is going to make this area unfishable for several days. Forecasters are predicting as much as 2 inches of rainfall, which will blow this area out completely, most of it will be underwater! That's because it's so flat. The water doesn't have anywhere to go. After the rainfall recedes, we've got some really nice weather, and those trout will run back up to the dam, when these heavy rainfalls come. This year, TWRA stocked around 4,000 trout in this location. I can assure you, at least 3,000 of them are still there!
I've been reporting how shallow the crappie have been the last week or two. They've been in the creek mouths, ready to make a run. I suspect, tomorrow's heavy rain will cause crappie, and white bass, to swim up to these low head dams. By Friday afternoon, I will probably be trying to catch crappie below dams in middle Tennessee. If I can't get them on these smaller creeks, rivers, and streams, I'll end up going to Center Hill dam. They will run up to the big ones too!
content_markdown:
Two crappie spots and a trout hole, from the bank...

Yesterday, it was 18° out to start the day. We haven't had a deal with cold weather like that for a couple of weeks, and we won't have to for a couple of more weeks. When it's like that, I find administrative stuff to do. I didn't go fishing until after lunch. I only had a short window, and I wanted to make the best of it. I decided to try to get some crappie from the bank, so I headed over to Percy Priest Lake to a spot that I found with my forward facing sonar. The parking spot is on the side of Weekly lane, and you have to be careful pulling in and out, because it's not paved or gravel, it's just mud...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/tDfw2f9wskVKCYtU6

This spot is about half a mile away from where you park. You have to walk through the woods, and then, down the bank to the cliff where the crappie hang out...

https://goo.gl/maps/5uppf5HAxHtcNxaR9

The trail isn't straight. It weaves through the woods, it's a really old trail. Once you get to the water's edge, there's a white chair hanging in a tree. That is your trail marker! When you're coming back, that's where you need to go to get back to your car. When you're on your way out, that's where I usually hit the rocks on the bank and start walking to the spot. Those rocks are loose! And it's a long walk! This is a four on a scale the effort scale of 1 to 5. It's kind of tough to know you're in the right spot, but fortunately, someone has built the fire there, and there are a couple fire pits right in front of this pin. The water in front of you is 18 feet deep as far as you can cast a light crappie jig, and as much as 7 or 8 feet deep right out in front of the cliff.

There were fish there! In large numbers. There was already one gentleman there, and he had been there for about an hour, and he had six slab crappies! I got to work, casting my ultralight rod and reel with 4 pound monofilament and a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head, with a Bobby Garland. Lately, I've been using whatever color 2-inch Bobby Garland that I have available. I've pretty much decided, that the color doesn't matter. It probably does, on some level, but it didn't yesterday. I was able to generate a bite, after allowing my lure to sink to a depth of 25 seconds, before I started my retrieve. When that lure got about 10 feet away from the cliff, was where I got my first bite, and then, where I caught my first fish, and 11 and a half inch slab crappie. I gave it to that gentleman, and moved on to my next spot.

I went across the street, to see if there was less wind blowing over at Stewart Creek boat ramp...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/T7yfgD3DygWy1MNy9

It was just as windy on this side of the lake, as it was the other, and that was the main reason why I left my first spot. But there was no one at Stewart Creek boat ramp! I was shocked. I made my way through a much shorter trail, over to the cliffs, to fish by myself, in a location that I already know is loaded!

I drew a map of where I went to. All the other x's are known crappie hot spots. Getting to the edge of the water at each of these spots requires scaling cliffs! This is definitely a four on the effort scale of one to five. You're going to have to be able to lift your own body weight, several times over.

You'll know you're in the right spot, there is a tree sticking out of the water! It's about 15 ft from the bank, and it's a giant tree. I'm convinced this thing stays loaded with crappie year-round. Every time I look at it with my forward facing sonar, there are hundreds of fish! They're just really tough to get. They are underneath that tree trunk, and it's protected at all angles from a cast. All you can hope to do, is run your lure beside the tree and get one of those fish to come out. That's exactly what I was able to do! I was casting over top of the tree, which would literally bring the lure back through the tree, and get me hung up, unless you play it exactly right.

I was using the same setup, to cast across the tree, allow my lure to sink for 10 seconds, and then start a slow retrieve with a couple of twitches. Before my lure got a chance to get to the tree trunk, I would rip it out of there, over the top of it, and cast again. This is very tough! But after a couple of casts, I got my first bite, and then, my first fish. Feeling accomplished, because I'm catching fish in difficult wind conditions, I decided to treat myself to some catching, instead of fishing. I packed my things up and headed over to Nice Mill Dam to do some trout fishing...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/rWhuPGgGwud4zYP28

From this parking lot, there is a trail that walks through the woods for more than a mile! The first half mile of that trail is flat, and takes you to the water's edge, and it's flat! That makes it an easy place to fish. Because you have to walk a little ways from the car, that puts this location at a two on the effort scale of 1 to 5. It's pretty good for lots of people, including families. All of this area is public access, pretty much as far as you can walk. Technically, this is Percy Priest lake, and both banks, all the way around the lake, are public access.

I went there to get out of the wind, mission accomplished, and to catch some fish. I was tired of grinding, which I had to do it both of the first spots. At each location, it took me nearly an hour to generate my fish. It's not that they weren't there, or that they weren't cooperating, you just have to figure something out. That was tough to do yesterday. With trout, everything is figured out. Just go to the trout river, and cast a rooster tail, or some power bait. That's exactly what I did, and I was able to catch a few nice trout. I walked down the trail, instead of standing on the damn, because you're way out in the woods. Really deep in the woods. And that gets the wind off of you, no matter what direction it is coming from.

There are lots of trails in this area, lots of people use it just to hike. Some people ride their horses other people walk their dogs. The trail is heavily used, so it gets muddy after rain. Unfortunately, tomorrow's rain is going to make this area unfishable for several days. Forecasters are predicting as much as 2 inches of rainfall, which will blow this area out completely, most of it will be underwater! That's because it's so flat. The water doesn't have anywhere to go. After the rainfall recedes, we've got some really nice weather, and those trout will run back up to the dam, when these heavy rainfalls come. This year, TWRA stocked around 4,000 trout in this location. I can assure you, at least 3,000 of them are still there!

title: Trip Report #92
content_raw:
Fishing for trout on the steps at Center Hill Dam...
Every winter, I spend extensive amounts of time fishing from the steps below Center Hill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/T1kLXKwB2jUffvnp7
This is a very rigorous activity! Climbing these steps repeatedly, and standing on this metal and concrete to fish is high on the effort scale. On the scale of 1 to 5, it's a solid 3 1/2. These aren't your normal steps, they're not very forgiving, and they're rough on your back! To land these fish properly, after you have hooked them, you will need to walk down the steps to the water's edge to get them in a net. That's really the toughest part. That, and coming back up the steps.
The most important thing that you need to know, when fishing at the steps below Center Hill dam, is the generating schedule. I only fish at the steps when the generators are on. You can fish from the steps anytime you would like. They don't close. 24/7, 365, have at it! I prefer to fish when the generators are on, because all the big fish come into the heavy current to feed. You can find the generating schedule, here....
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
There are a multitude of lures and methods that will work to catch fish from the steps. I have landed on the three most effective methods. The most common, and most effective method, is to use a spoon. Using a 7-foot, medium heavy bass rod, with 15 lb braid, you will have the perfect setup! Use any type of spoon between a half ounce and 1 ounce in weight. Have lots of different options! You can use gold spoons, or silver spoons, or even white spoons! The sky is the limit, just cast them into the heavy current and allow them to flutter through the water. Try to avoid getting hung up on the bottom, but that's going to happen. It's not very deep in this area, when the generators are off, the water is at most, 4 feet deep. When the generators come on, it rises a few feet, but not enough to be considered deep.
My favorite method is to use my 9-foot Shakespeare ugly stick. That's a medium action rod with a lot of bend. I have 20 pound braid and I like to attach a three-way swivel. On one end I like to use 8 pound monofilament to a 1 ounce weight. Any kind of weight will do. I like to make the line for my weight about one foot. On the other end of the three-way rig, I like to attach a 3-foot leader of the same 8 pound monofilament. On that, you can attach anything! A tiny spoon, a 1/64th of an ounce trout magnet, or just a small hook with some power bait for trout or even a worm. I like to use a 2 inch soft plastic called a sassy shad. I like the color white. Simply cast that setup into the heavy current and allow the weight to bounce on the bottom. It will bounce rapidly along the bottom until the current either takes it into a trout's mouth, or lifts the weight up off the bottom. When that happens, simply reel it in, and cast again.
My third favorite method is to use a Carolina rig. I use the same 9-foot setup but instead of a three-way rig, first I put on a 1 ounce barrel weight, then a glass bead, then I tie my braid to a barrel swivel. Then I use a 2 foot leader of 8 pound monofilament to attach whatever type of lure I would like. Typically, I will use a small hook, and that 2 inch soft plastic sassy shad.
Today, they were crushing both lures! My buddy had a fantastic day catching big brown trout with the spoon, and I had a fantastic day catching big brown trout with a sassy shad. The biggest trout was a 22-inch brown that went 7 pounds, but we had several get away before we could get them in the net. Having somebody with you, to run down the steps, to grab the net, before you get the fish down, is crucial. You're going to have to walk the fish down to the bottom of the steps, but you need somebody else in position first so that they can scoop the trout up before it either breaks your line or gets into the railing on the steps. Basically, the railing extends into the water, making it really tough to land a fish if you don't have help.
Make sure you're using a rubber net, with a long handle. Make sure you have some pliers at the bottom of the steps, so you can efficiently remove the hook, and return the fish to the river. Most fish won't be keepers! For rainbow trout, all fish between 14 and 20 inches must be released. You are allowed to keep one fish over 20 inches per day, and you are allowed to keep fish under 14 inches. For brown trout, all fish under 24 inches must be immediately returned. These rules are very important for the future of the fishery! Please also make sure that you wet your hands before you handle any fish.

title: Trip Report #93
content_raw:
My secret to catching fish everyday...
Yesterday I started the day trying to do some crappie fishing. First I went to Stewart Creek boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/EijAVCJ3vNn6WSKL6
My plan was to go Bank fishing. That was a bad plan, if I was intending to fish at Stewart creek. Just because I made that place my first target, I wouldn't necessarily end up fishing there, unless conditions were right. They were not. The wind was screaming out of the northwest, the area was completely windswept, and there were huge waves crashing into the bank. There were no boats and no cars at the boat ramp at 8:30 in the morning. Just because you plan on going fishing somewhere, you don't necessarily need to go there! But that's the heart of today's report, have a backup plan, have lots of backup plans, if you want to catch fish.
When you take a left out of Stewart Creek boat ramp, heading north on weekly lane, there are a couple places to pull over on the side of the road they give you access to the other side of the lake. I thought, potentially, this area might be blocked from the wind. It may have been, but they were a couple cars already parked in that location...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/snkH7F8YQyUNZStz8
As you pass by that location, you pass over the lake on the bridge on weekly Lane. Just after you cross the bridge, going north, there are a few parking spots on the left. No one was there, so I parked and went down to try to fish the cliffs at a spot that I found with my forward facing sonar...
https://goo.gl/maps/8fnatyDxBT3nvHSF8
If you cross the street from where you park, there is a trail that will take you all the way along the lake's edge down to the spot where I have dropped this pin. I've been there twice, on foot, but I still haven't caught any fish. You can wear them out from the boat, but it's been a little tricky to figure out how to get them to bite from the bank. The effort scale is pretty much off the chart for this one. It's a 5 out of five to do this walk. It will get much better, when they open the recreation area. You're technically in Fate Sanders recreation area when you're fishing at this spot, and it will open for the season real soon. As of right now, I'm still not catching any fish there, so I moved on to another location. I went around that end of the lake to Lamar Hill road where there is a spot on the side of the road where you can park to get to the lakes edge...
https://goo.gl/maps/N4LS7fK8VU763Apf9
The hike through the woods to this spot is not nearly as bad. Once you get to the spot, you kind of need to climb down a cliff. If you're not comfortable lifting your body weight, this probably isn't the spot for you. It's definitely a three and a half out of five on the efforts scale. This spot was perfect! I was facing southeast, the wind was at my back, but I was down a cliff and in the woods. The wind was not acting on the surface, so there were no waves! Best of all, I could see crappie flipping, everywhere. Unfortunately, nothing I could do, over the course of an hour, would generate a bite. Also, I got broke off and had to retire no less than eight times this place was loaded with cover, and loaded with fish, they just weren't biting, and I didn't have the touch. So I went to one more spot to try to get my crappy video for the day. Here is where you need to stand if you want to try to catch the crappie at the cliffs at Lamar Hill...
https://goo.gl/maps/DN1TTbSJ7KiBpHX57
You will know you are in the right place because there is a nice rock to stand on near the water's edge, after you climb down the cliff, and a couple of trees that are in the water, that are sticking out. Way out! Right around the corner from there, is where you park to go to the spring on Percy Priest Lake...
https://goo.gl/maps/imo2uZ2W2fCkjXcB9
This isn't necessarily a high effort location, but you do have to walk a half a mile to get in, and a half a mile to get out. That alone puts it at a three on a scale of one to five for effort once you get there, I like to stand in the back of the spring, and cast out as far as I can, with a slow retrieve, to catch crappie. That wasn't an option yesterday. There were a lot of people there, and they were all fishing it wrong. They had bobbers, casted out to the middle, with minnows, at a depth of about 3 to 4 ft. That will catch you some fish, but not very many. That's okay! I fished for a little while, and I didn't catch anything, so ended up having to leave my final crappie spot, without a video. Here is a pin for the spring on Percy Priest Lake...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/ppzyrPo46YeEAUUd7
I get a lot of phone calls and text messages and emails,  asking about where a person should go to fish on any particular day. I went to all these different spots and still didn't catch a fish! That's something that you really need to keep in mind. If I'm going fishing at a handful of locations and striking out, what chance do most people have? That's the biggest secret to my success. Not giving up until I catch some fish. Not fishing at one location, if it just isn't going to happen. I was down, but I wasn't out! I still had the afternoon to go fishing. So I went back to my house, regrouped for trout fishing, and headed over to where they had stocked trout in the river at nice Mill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/FogWm5HCxwiXau7e8
I had my five and a half foot ultra light rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail. That would be all I needed to have an epic afternoon. I was prepared to walk down the trail at nice Mill dam. I usually start by fishing on the dam, and then work my way down the trail to get a maximum amount of fish. If you don't know, there is a trail in the parking lot that extends down The river's edge for at least a mile! That is a relatively low effort trail, it's flat, and it walks right up to the water's edge! That is a two on a scale of 1 to 5 for effort. It's a great place for families as well.
I stayed right on the dam, walked to the end, and instead of casting downstream, below the dam, where they stock the trout, I turned around and fished the narrow trough of Swift running water that was coming from above the dam. It only took me a few casts, before I hooked into my first trout! Throwing that rooster tail upstream, and running it quickly through the water column would generate a bite. Throwing it upstream and running it fast through the water column with generate a strike that would land me a fish, several times over! I only had to fish for about an hour before I caught a little more than a handful of nice trout.
It took all day, I had to drive to all kinds of different locations, hike through the woods several different times, but I finally got a video. That's the type of dedication that's going to take to catch fish as often as I do.

title: Trip Report #94
content_raw:
Drifting the Caney Fork River in a boat to catch trout...
This is kind of tricky. Basically, anytime you want to wade or kayak or take your boat out on the Caney Fork river, you're going to have to know the generating schedule. I check the generating schedule, everyday. Even if I'm not going, just to know what the river is doing. There's a couple things to consider when looking at the generating schedule. First and foremost, the next day's release schedule. That's at the top of the chart, and it tells you whether or not they are generating zero, or one generator, or two or more generators. They have three, but they will only tell you if they are generating two or more. That's the way it is on all of the websites, for each dam, that I know of. Information about the next days release is typically available at 2:00 p.m. on the day before. That prohibits you from making plans on the Caney Fork river, until the afternoon, of the day before your trip. That can make things, tricky, to say the least.
The center panel on the generating schedule is the water release that has already happened. You can easily look up the last 48 hours of water release to see what water conditions might be like downstream. The third panel, is going to be difficult to explain. Basically, it's the predicted outflow for the dam, for the next 3 days, including the day of. It reads a number that is cubic feet per second. Basically, one cubic foot per second is the size of one basketball. The number that it reads for the daily discharge is going to be an hourly average. If that number is lower, around 1,000, or even down in the 100s, they're not going to generate very much that day. When that number gets higher, 4000, 6,000, 10,000 or more, they're going to be doing heavy generation. The more you watch that chart, the more you will understand how much they're going to generate, on a given day, with a couple of days notice.
Here is where you find the generating schedule for Center Hill Dam...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
We had to know the generating schedule, because we wanted to take out my buddies boat. He has a Jon boat with a 40 horsepower outboard propeller, and that boat will not go up and down the Caney Fork River unless the generators are on. The river is far too shallow, and you will bottom out. Ideal conditions are for the generators to be on, because you need a little bit of water to get the boat off the trailer. The boat ramps below Center Hill Dam are notoriously shallow, and only the smallest vessels can be removed from their trailer. You will need the generators on to get your boat off and on the trailer!
We had a 5-Hour window, from 7:00 a.m. until 12:00 p.m. in which to fish. We launched the boat at 7:15, after the generators had been on for 15 minutes. That will add enough water to allow you to get your boat off the trailer. We put our boat back on the trailer at 11:45. Trying to trailer your boat while the water is rapidly dropping is really tough! There will be current, which is fighting against you, and the water is dropping so fast, that by the time you put your trailer where you want it in the water, and get out to get in your boat to put it on the trailer, it will have dropped too far. It's definitely best if you have a two-man operation, and get it done before the water starts dropping.
We put in at the Long Branch boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/BFAt2kU85FXjvYsB6
It's in the Long Branch recreation area, on the opposite side of the dam from where I usually launch. The other side is extremely shallow, and also very flat. It's tough to get a boat off the trailer when the boat ramp doesn't have any angle. The Long Branch boat ramp is extremely steep! That makes it optimum for launching larger boats. His boat wasn't necessarily large. But it is much bigger than mine, and all jon boats are going to need the generators to be on so you can run up and down the river, unless they have a jet drive. Those things can go pretty much anywhere they want to.
Once you get there, you're going to want to throw lures. Throwing something that hits the bottom is not a good idea while you're drifting the Caney Fork river. You're going to get hung up, and it's going to be a nightmare. We threw jerk baits the whole time. A rapala husky suspending jerk bait. I think just about any jerk bait would do, provided it's the right size. These things were about 2 and 1/4 in long, and that's what these fish were keying in on yesterday. We would just work them like you were doing for bass. Make a long cast, and then start a quick retrieve and incorporate a twitch twitch. That's how you work a jerk bait, and that works great for trout! We ended up catching three large brown trout, and having several that got away. We also caught lots of small fish as well.
He stuck with the jerk bait all day and he put on a clinic! He caught lots and lots of trout. I kept changing up my lure, constantly, for some reason, and didn't have as much luck as he did. The only fish that I caught, we're on that suspending jerk bait. That's what they were looking for yesterday. Any number of lures could work, that's why I always try to fish with as many options as I can. You never know when a really big fish is looking for something different. So I tried casting gold spoons and silver spoons, from as heavy as one ounce to as light as half an ounce. I also threw an 11 inch silver spoon, just to see if I could get a giant trout or a striped bass to come up, I could not. I even went super small, with my ultralight rod and reel, and 4 pound test, and a 1/64th of an ounce trout magnet with a 1 inch gulp minnow. Any type of trout lure that you can think of, including bass lures, is on the table, you just have to figure something out.
If you're trying to launch your boat from one of these boat ramps when the water is off, it's going to be a five out of five on the effort scale of one to five. I've tried, I literally can't get my little boat off the trailer, unless the generator is on. If you're trying to launch your boat, and the generators have turned on, and you're by yourself, it's a solid 3 out of five. It's not easy. If you have a buddy, someone who can back the truck down, while you're in the boat, it's still a 2 out of five. It's not the easiest place to launch a boat, under any conditions! Mostly, because once you have some water, you have some current. Now you have to worry about placement of the boat and running into the bank, or even drifting downstream, before you're ready.
Wear your life jacket! Too many people drown on this river, every single year. One is too many!

title: Trip Report #95
content_raw:
The Stewart Creek area is on fire...
This morning, I was able to launch my boat at 6:00 a.m., a half hour before sunrise, and make my way up into Stewart Creek. I launched from the Stewart Creek boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/RzuQVsAUniqADXGo6
Today, I went even farther up into the creek to find crappie. And they were in there in great numbers! They only wanted one particular type of method, but they were biting really well if you did exactly what they wanted you to. On the way into the creek, I saw some of the biggest topwater explosions you'll ever see on the lake. It was either huge striped bass, or massive hybrid bass. I was able to hook one on a rooster tail, but it immediately got away. There were some giant fish, exploding on top water, in Stewart Creek, this morning. They were blowing up in the same spot that I was sitting and catching hybrids and white bass the other day...
https://goo.gl/maps/Pe4iJHsTFTztj8kv6
Be cautious and go slowly when boating in this area. It can get extremely shallow, really quick. It's tough to stay in the channel, it's really small. That being said, if you can make your way to the point that I just dropped on the maps, perhaps you'll be able to go a little farther. Right around the corner from there, there are a few trees laid over in the water, and they are absolutely loaded with crappie...
https://goo.gl/maps/VQbkj5PMTp3mx37g9
This is not one of those spots where crappie will sit year-round. During the coldest parts of the winter, they won't be up in this creek. Today, the water temperature nearly reached 60°. That's going to allow these crappie to go farther and farther up this creek, and all the other creeks in middle Tennessee. These fish were in those tree limbs, as tight as they could be. I tried casting in with a tight line, but I was unable to get these fish to come out of their cover. I was going to have to go in after them.
Using my ultralight rod and reel, with 4 lb monofilament, I attached two 1/32nd ounce jig heads, about 1 foot apart from each other, and put a Bobby Garland, 2 inch, electric chicken soft plastic on each jig head. Typically, I would use Pearl color, but I'm running out of those, and I'm starting to find out, it really doesn't matter. The most important thing, is the presentation. And we got that dialed in this morning! Here's exactly what they wanted...
4 foot of depth between the bottom jig head and my fixed bobber. If you don't know, a fixed bobber, is one that doesn't move up and down the line. It clips on, in one position, like an old school red and white bobber. I like to use pencil bobbers, the long skinny ones. Those provide very little resistance when the fish bites, and also gives a very clear indication of when a fish is biting. That set up, two jig heads, 4 feet underneath my bobber, with electric chicken Bobby Garland, was the magic ticket!
It's worth noting that, the Stewart Creek boat ramp area was also loaded with fish. They were on the cliffs, near the bank, as well as on the fish attractors at the point. They were not, near the fish attractors by the handicapped fishing pier. It won't be long, before they will move that far up, that water is still a little too shallow. Right now, they are favoring water that is 6 to 8 ft deep. The fish attractors by the handicap boat ramp are about 3 feet tall, and the top of them is out of the water. That means they're in less than 3 foot of water, and that's a little too shallow for these fish. Don't get me wrong, they are hanging out 3 feet under the surface, but only in locations where they have a little more depth, underneath.
That's exactly the setup that we have at the new location that I found this morning. These fish were tight inside the cover, and they needed me to dangle these Bobby Garland in front of their face, or they wouldn't bite. In the course of doing so, I put nine slabs in the bucket, off of this one pile. That's pretty tough to do, most piles won't yield that many keepers. It was all about the presentation! Unfortunately, that presentation got me hung up, and broke off, repeatedly! This is not hyperbole, I got hung up, and broke off, and had to retie, at least 12 times. At first, I was counting, but I lost count around eight or nine. It was brutal! But it was the only way I could get to those fish, the nine giant keepers that I put in the bucket.

title: Trip Report #96
content_raw:
How to use a bobber for crappie and why it's important...
Today, I took my boat out from Stewart's Creek boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/nEkDZG1DQLtNaaQ67
It was crazy windy out there! I had no intention of fishing on the open lake. I had caught fish recently, way up the creek, and that's where I intended to fish. I ran right back up to the little cove by the army base, where I had fished a couple of days ago with a client. We were catching white bass and hybrid bass, but I was able to find some schools of crappie...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/iuDt6d2kxHUydYSUA
There is a tiny rock cliff right here that's probably about a hundred yards long and it is loaded with crappie! Unfortunately, it's only about 6 ft deep. So you're in very close quarters with these fish. When that happens, they get a little skittish. When you're really close, they have a tendency to be tough to catch. That was the case today. I harp on the need to get dialed in when you are crappie fishing. I drive it home in almost every single video. You have to intently focus on exactly what you are doing when you generate a bite, so that you can mimic that, to get another bite. That's not the way it was today. These fish wouldn't respond to anyone particular method, over the other. That's when you need to have a lot of tricks up your sleeve!
What I usually do, is called tight lining. I use my seven and a half foot ultra light rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head. I like a 2 inch pearl colored Bobby Garland soft plastic as my lure. I cast that, and then allow it to sink for a few seconds, and then start my retrieve. Sometimes, I use a straight retrieve, sometimes, I Incorporated pause, sometimes, I incorporate a twitch, sometimes you have to give them the jiggle. No matter what you're doing, as long as you don't have a bobber on the line, it's considered tight lining. That method was good for a few fish, but others, wanted something different.
As soon as you add a bobber to the line, it's not tightlining anymore. I have some really light bobbers that I use with my 1/32nd of an ounce jig head. Because I already know the depth, and I could see where the fish were sitting, I put that bobber at a depth of about 4 feet. Cast that past the fish, and then start a slow retrieve, and give it a couple of twitches, right above their head. When that bobber makes a movement that you didn't initiate, set the hook. If it goes under, set the hook. If it lifts up, like they lifted the lure up, and pulled the weight off the bobber, set the hook. Bottom line, if that bobber makes a movement that you don't initiate, set the hook. That method was good for a few more fish, but there were still more fish to get, and another method that I could employ.
Instead of using one jig head and one Bobby Garland, you can use two! I like to tie two different jig heads on, about a foot apart. Then use the same bobber, with a total depth of about 4 feet for these fish, and use the same retrieve. For some reason, crappie on Percy Priest Lake don't really like the two jig method, when you are tight lining. However, they particularly like two jigs underneath a bobber! That method was good for a handful of fish! And some big ones! Seems like the big ones like to hit the bottom lure. Either way, we were starting to put a lot of fish in the boat, and we still had another method we could employ!
This is where things get complicated. This is where you need specialized gear. I have one set up, to run this particular bobber. The whole rod, reel, line, everything is specialized. I don't use this rod and reel for any other lures, or for any other setups. Basically, it's the best method for getting crappie, on a bobber, if you don't have forward facing sonar. It's called a slip bobber, and it's crucial for all crappie fishermen. Here's how it works...
The size of the rod and the size of the reel are not necessarily crucial to this setup. I like to use a 6 ft, medium sized setup, with an ultralight reel. But it's really not that important. The most important thing, is going to be the bobber, but we will get to that in a second. First of all, you're going to want to use braid as your main line. I'm using 10 lb spider wire. That allows you to cast this setup extremely far. Also, it will allow you to retain your very expensive bobber, when you ultimately get hung up, and broke off.
The first thing you put on the line is the bobber stop. A bobber stop is a sliding knot, that prohibits your bobber from going any deeper than you want it to. You can set the depth of your lure, simply by sliding this knot up and down your braid. The reason you have to have braid, is because of this not. These knots, are made of small pieces of rope, and they do not cling to monofilament very well. They will grab, and hold position, on braid, exceptional. The next thing that goes on the line, is a wobble bobber from thill. I use 3/8 of an ounce. I will provide a link, because this is a tough item to find, and they are not on store shelves, like everything else that I'm going to describe...
https://amzn.to/4tKjIBV
Don't get sticker shock from the bobber. They're expensive, but the aim is to never lose them. Here's how. After you slide that bobber on to the braid, then you want to slide on a glass bead. Typically, these are small, orange or red plastic beads. They are referred to as glass beads, it serves as a buffer between your bobber and the knot. It will protect your knot from being damaged by the bobber. Now, you have your bobber stop, your wobble bobber, and a glass bead. Now you need to tie on a barrel swivel.
The barrel swivel will be the thing that always comes back when you get broke off. Reason being, you're going to tie 4 lb monofilament to the other end. When it gets hung up, and it will get hung up, you will pull gently, on your 10 lb braid, until you snap that 4 lb monofilament. That will leave the jig head, and any sinkers that you have, but you will be able to retrieve your bobber, the most important part.
I use about an 18 inch piece of monofilament. It doesn't have to be very long. About 9 inches, or halfway from the barrel swivel, I put a heavy split shot. And then on the bottom, I put my 1/32nd of an ounce jig head, typically with a Bobby Garland. Now, you just need to get to fishing. Here's how you use it...
Start as shallow as you think you can catch these fish. For me, in this situation, I started at about 2 foot of of depth. Since I had 18 in of monofilament, I only had to put my bobber stop about 6 inches up my braid. That gave me a total depth of 2 feet for my lure. I quickly caught a nice big slab. Then, I was able to lower my lure, by sliding that bobber stop up another foot. Now I was fishing at 3 feet of depth, and I was able to get another fish. Then I was able to drop it down to 5 foot, and then 6 foot, and get the fish that were sitting on the bottom. You can slide that bobber stop so far that it goes into your reel. When that happens, you'll be fishing really deep, but sometimes it will get hung up on the way out. That's really the only drawback of this setup. To combat that, you could use a really long pole. That way, you would have a lot more line out so that you could keep that bobber stop from going into the reel. This is the way to get that lure really deep, for those pesky fish, that are hard to target. Just get it in front of them, like dangling a carrot, and give it a couple of twitches. If you are in a location where there are crappie, this will catch them.

https://maps.app.goo.gl/iuDt6d2kxHUydYSUA

There is a tiny rock cliff right here that's probably about a hundred yards long and it is loaded with crappie! Unfortunately, it's only about 6 ft deep. So you're in very close quarters with these fish. When that happens, they get a little skittish. When you're really close, they have a tendency to be tough to catch. That was the case today. I harp on the need to get dialed in when you are crappie fishing. I drive it home in almost every single video. You have to intently focus on exactly what you are doing when you generate a bite, so that you can mimic that, to get another bite. That's not the way it was today. These fish wouldn't respond to anyone particular method, over the other. That's when you need to have a lot of tricks up your sleeve!

What I usually do, is called tight lining. I use my seven and a half foot ultra light rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head. I like a 2 inch pearl colored Bobby Garland soft plastic as my lure. I cast that, and then allow it to sink for a few seconds, and then start my retrieve. Sometimes, I use a straight retrieve, sometimes, I Incorporated pause, sometimes, I incorporate a twitch, sometimes you have to give them the jiggle. No matter what you're doing, as long as you don't have a bobber on the line, it's considered tight lining. That method was good for a few fish, but others, wanted something different.

As soon as you add a bobber to the line, it's not tightlining anymore. I have some really light bobbers that I use with my 1/32nd of an ounce jig head. Because I already know the depth, and I could see where the fish were sitting, I put that bobber at a depth of about 4 feet. Cast that past the fish, and then start a slow retrieve, and give it a couple of twitches, right above their head. When that bobber makes a movement that you didn't initiate, set the hook. If it goes under, set the hook. If it lifts up, like they lifted the lure up, and pulled the weight off the bobber, set the hook. Bottom line, if that bobber makes a movement that you don't initiate, set the hook. That method was good for a few more fish, but there were still more fish to get, and another method that I could employ.

Instead of using one jig head and one Bobby Garland, you can use two! I like to tie two different jig heads on, about a foot apart. Then use the same bobber, with a total depth of about 4 feet for these fish, and use the same retrieve. For some reason, crappie on Percy Priest Lake don't really like the two jig method, when you are tight lining. However, they particularly like two jigs underneath a bobber! That method was good for a handful of fish! And some big ones! Seems like the big ones like to hit the bottom lure. Either way, we were starting to put a lot of fish in the boat, and we still had another method we could employ!

This is where things get complicated. This is where you need specialized gear. I have one set up, to run this particular bobber. The whole rod, reel, line, everything is specialized. I don't use this rod and reel for any other lures, or for any other setups. Basically, it's the best method for getting crappie, on a bobber, if you don't have forward facing sonar. It's called a slip bobber, and it's crucial for all crappie fishermen. Here's how it works...

The size of the rod and the size of the reel are not necessarily crucial to this setup. I like to use a 6 ft, medium sized setup, with an ultralight reel. But it's really not that important. The most important thing, is going to be the bobber, but we will get to that in a second. First of all, you're going to want to use braid as your main line. I'm using 10 lb spider wire. That allows you to cast this setup extremely far. Also, it will allow you to retain your very expensive bobber, when you ultimately get hung up, and broke off.

The first thing you put on the line is the bobber stop. A bobber stop is a sliding knot, that prohibits your bobber from going any deeper than you want it to. You can set the depth of your lure, simply by sliding this knot up and down your braid. The reason you have to have braid, is because of this not. These knots, are made of small pieces of rope, and they do not cling to monofilament very well. They will grab, and hold position, on braid, exceptional. The next thing that goes on the line, is a wobble bobber from thill. I use 3/8 of an ounce. I will provide a link, because this is a tough item to find, and they are not on store shelves, like everything else that I'm going to describe...

https://amzn.to/4tKjIBV

Don't get sticker shock from the bobber. They're expensive, but the aim is to never lose them. Here's how. After you slide that bobber on to the braid, then you want to slide on a glass bead. Typically, these are small, orange or red plastic beads. They are referred to as glass beads, it serves as a buffer between your bobber and the knot. It will protect your knot from being damaged by the bobber. Now, you have your bobber stop, your wobble bobber, and a glass bead. Now you need to tie on a barrel swivel.

The barrel swivel will be the thing that always comes back when you get broke off. Reason being, you're going to tie 4 lb monofilament to the other end. When it gets hung up, and it will get hung up, you will pull gently, on your 10 lb braid, until you snap that 4 lb monofilament. That will leave the jig head, and any sinkers that you have, but you will be able to retrieve your bobber, the most important part.

I use about an 18 inch piece of monofilament. It doesn't have to be very long. About 9 inches, or halfway from the barrel swivel, I put a heavy split shot. And then on the bottom, I put my 1/32nd of an ounce jig head, typically with a Bobby Garland. Now, you just need to get to fishing. Here's how you use it...

Start as shallow as you think you can catch these fish. For me, in this situation, I started at about 2 foot of of depth. Since I had 18 in of monofilament, I only had to put my bobber stop about 6 inches up my braid. That gave me a total depth of 2 feet for my lure. I quickly caught a nice big slab. Then, I was able to lower my lure, by sliding that bobber stop up another foot. Now I was fishing at 3 feet of depth, and I was able to get another fish. Then I was able to drop it down to 5 foot, and then 6 foot, and get the fish that were sitting on the bottom. You can slide that bobber stop so far that it goes into your reel. When that happens, you'll be fishing really deep, but sometimes it will get hung up on the way out. That's really the only drawback of this setup. To combat that, you could use a really long pole. That way, you would have a lot more line out so that you could keep that bobber stop from going into the reel. This is the way to get that lure really deep, for those pesky fish, that are hard to target. Just get it in front of them, like dangling a carrot, and give it a couple of twitches. If you are in a location where there are crappie, this will catch them.

title: Trip Report #97
content_raw:
The steps at Center Hill Dam...
Today I had a client booked for the 4-Hour instructional fishing trip on the steps below Center Hill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/ktzyMdZa5GSedpwy9
There's a parking lot with a bathroom, but the bathroom is closed for the winter. Make sure you go before you get there, this place has cameras everywhere! Also, make sure you check the generating schedule. You can fish from the steps, anytime you would like, 24/7, 365. It's best to fish when the generators are on. That's where my instruction comes in. It's not necessarily easy to do. It helps to have specialized equipment, and lots of know-how. The first thing you need to know, where to find the generating schedule. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
Today, the generators were scheduled to turn on at 10:00. I asked my client to meet me at 11:00 a.m., so we could start fishing after the water had risen completely. I like when the water has been on for a while. We had four hours, so we fished from 11:00 until 3:00 p.m.  That's more than enough time to go over the handful of techniques that work best at Center Hill dam. The way I like to do my instruction, is to start with one technique, and do it until the client is comfortable, or feels like they have mastered that technique.
We started with a Carolina rig on a 7 ft medium heavy pole with 20 lb braid as the main line and a 1 oz barrel weight to a barrel swivel with a glass bead in between. For the leader, I used 8 lb Berkeley trilene monofilament. For the hook, I had a number 6 eagle claw bait holder, and a small soft plastic that looked like a shad, it was white. Technically, the name of that soft plastic, is a sassy shad. Lots of different companies make this lure, it's not necessarily special, it's just the right size and shape. To utilize this setup, you want to cast at a 45° angle, upstream, and then reel out the slack so that the weight can get the lure down to the bottom. Once the lure gets to the bottom, you will feel the weight bouncing on the bottom like someone quickly dribbling a basketball, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump, bump. If you're doing it just right, it will bump hundreds of times in a few seconds, giving you the optimum chance to hook up with a trout.
Within a few casts, he hooked up with a giant female rainbow trout. We fought that fish all the way to the net, and it got one look at us, and turned, and broke the line. That 8 lb monofilament, snapped like a twig. Not a big deal, he got familiar with how to use that setup, and we moved on to my next technique, which is a three-way rig, which presents lures the same way as the Carolina rig.
Using a stunningly similar setup, instead of attaching a leader line to my main line, I attached a three-way swivel. To that, I attached a 1-ft leader of 8 lb monofilament with a 1 oz pyramid weight. On the other end of the three-way swivel, I attached a two and a half foot leader of 8 lb monofilament with a 1/64th of an ounce trout magnet for the hook and a 1 inch gulp minnow for the lure. Within a couple of casts, bumping that lure along the bottom, my client hooked up with a giant brown trout! We got that one down to the bottom of the steps, and to the net, when it got swept away downstream, and into the railing of the steps.
That was the next lesson we worked on. When someone catches a fish on the steps, they need to slowly work it down, and try to get it near the surface, so that someone with a net, standing at the water's edge, can try to quickly scoop their fish, before it either gets off the hook, or gets tangled up into the railing on the steps. Basically, the railing that prevents us from falling into the river, goes down into the water, because the water has risen so high due to the generating waters. Once a fish gets into that railing, it's almost impossible to get it out. You want to avoid that at all costs.
From there, we worked on the 3rd, and most popular technique, casting spoons. He had the ideal setup. A 7 ft, medium heavy action rod, with 15 lb braid and an 8 lb monofilament leader. You can use any number of spoons that you can think of! Silver and gold work best, but today, we saw lots of catches from someone who was using a white spoon with a red tip. Basically, the action of the spoon is what makes these trout trigger.
Casting upstream, at a 45° angle, allow your spoon to sink for a couple of seconds, before you start a yoyo retrieve. What that is, is a slow, meticulous retrieve, that allows the spoon to flutter down after you yo-yo it back up into the water column. Cast out, as far as you can, had a 45° angle, and then immediately get on the reel. Allow that lure to sink, before you lift the rod tip and reel out the slack and then lower the rod tip down. Then lift the rod tip up, then lower the rod tip down and then reel out the slack. You could also, hold the rod tip up, and give the spoon subtle twitches, preventing it from getting too far down in the water column. Another way, and the most popular way, is to try to bounce that spoon along the bottom. Flirt with getting it hung up! Let that thing hit the bottom and then rip it up off, trying to keep it from getting hung up. Sometimes those giant jumps in the water trigger big bites.
This method would prove successful for my client as well! Casting a gold, half ounce cotton Cordell spoon, bouncing it along the bottom, he hooked into a nice big walleye that he took home for dinner.
These are the most effective ways to fish below Center Hill Dam when the generators are running. It's best to go with a friend, so you can have somebody to help you net the fish. Make sure you have your Tennessee fishing license as well as your trout stamp. The rules and regulations for keeping trout are posted at this location, on the chain link fence. Know them! Be very familiar with them. It's important for the future of this fishery, that everyone follow the rules to a t...
Climbing up and down these steps is extremely strenuous! On the effort scale of one to five, this is about a three and a half. The steps aren't normal sized, they're really long, metal steps. They're hard on your feet, they're hard on your back, and the huffing and puffing can be hard on your heart! You need to be physically fit, and make sure you have a friend to hold the net.

title: Trip Report #98
content_raw:
The White Bass run has begun!
Last week, I found white bass on their way up stewarts creek. I was in a few feet of water, in my boat, at this location...
https://goo.gl/maps/t9xWqectfUsX1dB57
Today, I had a client booked to go crappie fishing from Stewart Creek boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/xUnRSKaYkixSivqi7
We found some crappie, but the wind made it impossible to sit on an anchor. When you are crappie fishing, they are sitting on structure, or in a pile, and you need to target them. If you can't sit still, you're not going to be able to do that. That was the case today. So I made the decision to run up Stewart Creek to see if I could find some in a wind protected area. We ended up in this location...
https://goo.gl/maps/adWonTnQnBoCoivk9
The wind was screaming out of the south, so we sat near this north facing bank, in about 3 ft of water, on an anchor, and threw a 1/8 of an ounce roostertail on an ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and had a heck of a good day! Not only were the white bass and yellow bass running through this area in great numbers, we also caught four hybrid bass! Two really little ones, and two nice big sized keepers! In total, we caught six different species of fish sitting in this one spot, white bass, yellow bass, hybrid bass, and a little striped bass. We also caught one largemouth and a couple of crappie. Basically, these fish are going really shallow!
I don't know exactly how far up the creek these fish have gone, but I know somewhere you can target them...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/nJu5QfA4pyrDEzBc6
This is the parking lot at volunteer park, where we have softball fields in Smyrna. If you park in this corner of the parking lot, there is a very short trail to the water's edge! You can walk all the way along the water's edge, very far. You'll need to go at least a few hundred yards downstream. There is a small trail, but it's kind of treacherous. Most people walk along the rocks, but they are very treacherous. Overall, this is a four on the effort scale of 1 to 5. This is not an easy place to walk around. There's a lot of mud, so you're going to want to wear your muck boots. You need to get a little ways downstream, so that the creek has some depth. Go past the rapidly running water, to where it starts to get wide and deep and slow.
Throw rooster tails for hybrid bass and white bass and throw crappie jigs or minnows to see if you can catch some crappie. This is going to be a hotspot for the next few days before they get the water out of the lake, and before the cold weather gets here this weekend. I suspect that the incoming cold temperatures next week will make these fish rush back out into the lake. The time to get them is now through Saturday.

title: Trip Report #99
content_raw:
Mapping the Holmes Creek area of Center Hill Lake...
Yesterday I used my trolling motor to scan the entire area known as Holmes Creek on Center Hill Lake...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/v5fFatGq2xzMsjQr7
First of all, there are two boat ramps at this particular boat ramp. One of them, has a drop off at the end, when the water is all the way down, like it was yesterday, and you cannot get a boat in and out! I tried to back my trailer down, and when I dropped off the ledge, my trailer came off it's tires and ended up on the frame. That's the boat ramp closest to the courtesy dock, which is really inconvenient. Fortunately, they are conjoined, so the other boat ramp is only about 100 feet away. Unfortunately, that boat ramp is really shallow! It's long enough to go into the water, but it's flat LOL it doesn't have any angle. I had to back my truck 40 ft out into the water to get my boat on and off the trailer. Fortunately, I had my muck boots, but you will need some chest waders or hip waders to get your boat in and out there, until we get some spring rains.
Now for some good news... The area is primed for holding crappie. There is one, marked, TWRA fish attractor. It's near the mouth of the creek, near the main Lake channel. It's marked with a buoy, and they have dropped lots of good structure in a spot in a cove, and it will be loaded with crappie, soon. So why isn't it loaded now? All the fish attractors on Percy Priest Lake are completely loaded. That's a good question! Here's the reason. Percy Priest is much shallower, and the water is much more stained. Stained water not only gathers energy from the Sun quicker, but it holds it longer. Clear water can't grab the sunlight, or retain it. Percy Priest Lake is notoriously cloudy while, Center Hill Lake is notoriously clear.
Surface temperatures on Percy Priest Lake have been running around 55° on the south end. I haven't found a surface temperature above 48° on Center Hill Lake. I've only been out there twice, and I've been on the deep end, so I suspect the shallower ends may already have some crappie that are shallow. In this gigantic stretch of lake, that I covered yesterday, I did not find any crappie. But I found lots of crappie structure! Not only did I find the TWRA marked buoy, which is obvious for everyone, but I found eight other underwater locations where people had dropped crappie structure like, crappie motels, which are short and have lots of spikes. In one spot, there were four of those in an area! I also found some crappie condos, which are very tall structures that have lots of limbs that's reach out. These are two different kinds of man-made structures, that are commonly placed in areas where people suspect crappie will gather in great numbers.
Two of the locations that I found were brush piles that had been anchored to the bottom. It looked like someone had used either buckets or cinder blocks to drop a whole bunch of Christmas trees. Whatever it was, it was a brush pile intended to hold crappie. All together, I found nine locations. I'm going to draw you a map of the area that I covered, including the marina that is in that arm of the lake. Once again, the marina is in very deep water, just like at the Edgar Evans Marina that I scanned last week. Unfortunately, the only fish that I found, were in the very center of the structure, way too far away to make a cast at. Fortunately for us, they will come out of there when they need to move to their spawning areas, and that will put them squarely on these fish attractors!
This was a huge project! It took me about six and a half hours. I thought I would see a lot more structure, and fish! I have to say, the only fish I really see, are bass. They're pretty much everywhere in this lake. They don't have anywhere to hide, cuz they like to stay in the shallow water, near the bank. By the end of the day, the water temperature at the surface had reached 50°! I started in the very back, where the boat ramp is, and made my way clockwise, from left to right, around this area. I went into every cove, and scanned every bank. When I left out in the morning, I didn't see any schools of bait fish, which had me really worried! By the time I made my way back, in the late afternoon at the sun was setting, there were schools of threadfin shad had everywhere! Huge schools!
That's fantastic news! Those crappie are going to be quick to follow them into this area. Here is a list of pins on Google maps where you can find crappie structure. The best way to utilize this information, for those who don't know, is to click on the pin, and then save it as somewhere you want to go. content_markdown:
Mapping the Holmes Creek area of Center Hill Lake...

Yesterday I used my trolling motor to scan the entire area known as Holmes Creek on Center Hill Lake...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/v5fFatGq2xzMsjQr7

First of all, there are two boat ramps at this particular boat ramp. One of them, has a drop off at the end, when the water is all the way down, like it was yesterday, and you cannot get a boat in and out! I tried to back my trailer down, and when I dropped off the ledge, my trailer came off it's tires and ended up on the frame. That's the boat ramp closest to the courtesy dock, which is really inconvenient. Fortunately, they are conjoined, so the other boat ramp is only about 100 feet away. Unfortunately, that boat ramp is really shallow! It's long enough to go into the water, but it's flat LOL it doesn't have any angle. I had to back my truck 40 ft out into the water to get my boat on and off the trailer. Fortunately, I had my muck boots, but you will need some chest waders or hip waders to get your boat in and out there, until we get some spring rains.

Now for some good news... The area is primed for holding crappie. There is one, marked, TWRA fish attractor. It's near the mouth of the creek, near the main Lake channel. It's marked with a buoy, and they have dropped lots of good structure in a spot in a cove, and it will be loaded with crappie, soon. So why isn't it loaded now? All the fish attractors on Percy Priest Lake are completely loaded. That's a good question! Here's the reason. Percy Priest is much shallower, and the water is much more stained. Stained water not only gathers energy from the Sun quicker, but it holds it longer. Clear water can't grab the sunlight, or retain it. Percy Priest Lake is notoriously cloudy while, Center Hill Lake is notoriously clear.

Surface temperatures on Percy Priest Lake have been running around 55° on the south end. I haven't found a surface temperature above 48° on Center Hill Lake. I've only been out there twice, and I've been on the deep end, so I suspect the shallower ends may already have some crappie that are shallow. In this gigantic stretch of lake, that I covered yesterday, I did not find any crappie. But I found lots of crappie structure! Not only did I find the TWRA marked buoy, which is obvious for everyone, but I found eight other underwater locations where people had dropped crappie structure like, crappie motels, which are short and have lots of spikes. In one spot, there were four of those in an area! I also found some crappie condos, which are very tall structures that have lots of limbs that's reach out. These are two different kinds of man-made structures, that are commonly placed in areas where people suspect crappie will gather in great numbers.

Two of the locations that I found were brush piles that had been anchored to the bottom. It looked like someone had used either buckets or cinder blocks to drop a whole bunch of Christmas trees. Whatever it was, it was a brush pile intended to hold crappie. All together, I found nine locations. I'm going to draw you a map of the area that I covered, including the marina that is in that arm of the lake. Once again, the marina is in very deep water, just like at the Edgar Evans Marina that I scanned last week. Unfortunately, the only fish that I found, were in the very center of the structure, way too far away to make a cast at. Fortunately for us, they will come out of there when they need to move to their spawning areas, and that will put them squarely on these fish attractors!

This was a huge project! It took me about six and a half hours. I thought I would see a lot more structure, and fish! I have to say, the only fish I really see, are bass. They're pretty much everywhere in this lake. They don't have anywhere to hide, cuz they like to stay in the shallow water, near the bank. By the end of the day, the water temperature at the surface had reached 50°! I started in the very back, where the boat ramp is, and made my way clockwise, from left to right, around this area. I went into every cove, and scanned every bank. When I left out in the morning, I didn't see any schools of bait fish, which had me really worried! By the time I made my way back, in the late afternoon at the sun was setting, there were schools of threadfin shad had everywhere! Huge schools!

title: Trip Report #100
content_raw:
Don't forget to chase the crappie below dams on small creeks streams and rivers today! Here's a report I did about a few places you can go. Crappie will run up this flood water in great numbers!
Where crappie go after a heavy, late winter rain...
Yesterday, middle Tennessee was experiencing some light river flooding due to heavy rains. When conditions are right, those flood waters call to crappie like a sirens song. When they get moving fast, and they get really brown, for some reason, crappie move up! They will do that, after each heavy rainfall, from now until April. They are literally following bait fish so that they can fatten up for the spring spawn. When crappie spawn, males sit on the bed for a few days. They want to get big and bulky before that happens, so they race up these flooded rivers, and then they are easy to catch, at the base of low head dams.
I'm typing this out on Sunday morning, I just released a video on YouTube where I explained in great detail how to Target these fish. What I'm going to do for you here, is drop pins on these locations and explain how to get to these fish. Where are they below the dams, and where do you need to stand. The first location I always go to, is one of the best, Nice Mill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/Wckbcvkyt7fJSA1T7
There are two parking lots at this dam, one on either side of the river. It's best to park in this parking lot, on the high side. Walk through the woods, on the trail provided at the end of the parking lot, just a short way, only a couple hundred feet! Then you can stand on the cliffs that overhang the river. The current will be flowing fast underneath your feet, but you can cast across the current, to the slack water, where crappie stack up in great numbers! Make sure to go there, and all of these locations, the day after a really heavy rain. Those crappie will turn around and leave as soon as the flood waters recede.
The next spot I usually go to is on the East Fork Stones river. Just like Nice Mill dam, it's the last low head Dam on that stretch of river before it turns into Percy Priest lake. That allows great numbers of crappie to swim up to this location, at Walter Hill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/PWiPxVLtYjDnWrqN6
To get to the side of the river I was standing on, where the crappie really stack up, you may want to park where people used to park. Unfortunately, they have fenced that side of the river off. You are still allowed to go down there, you are just not allowed to park there anymore, since they built the new bridge. Not a big deal! You can park across the river in the parking lot that I have pinned for you here, and then walk across the bridge and then down the hill to the water's edge. This is a fantastic location! When I got there yesterday, I realized, that it may be a better spot than over at nice mill. I drew you a map of how to walk over there...
The next location in the video is not somewhere that I have caught crappie just yet, but I suspect you can catch them there. I went to Manson Pike trailhead to fish below Ransom Mill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/8yJwrmFRC1yfhFYL6
At this location, all I can do is speculate that we will be able to catch crappie. I haven't heard any reports, or caught any myself. But that's the way this works. These fish are going to move up to areas like this for the next couple of months. Wherever there are crappie that have access to rivers with dams, they are going to swim towards those dams, and get stuck. There's a good chance there's a small low head Dam on a creek or river in a town where you live, and you don't suspect that they live in there, but you will be able to find out for sure! Try religiously below low head dams until the beginning of April, after heavy rains. I've been living right down the street from Nice Mill for more than 20 years, and I just found out last year that they do this. I could have been targeting these fish, down the street from my house, for decades! I just didn't know they were there.
