title: Trip Report #101
content_raw:
Three different spots to catch crappie from the bank on Percy Priest Lake and why it's important to have lots of spots...
Recently, I've been hitting two spots in the Stewart Creek area really heavily. First of all, the point at Stewart Creek boat ramp has been loaded for the last couple of weeks, and it will be for the next couple of months. If I pull up in the parking lot, and I can see that there is no one standing on the point, I go over there and catch fish...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/FxlmoI0SFmLxCr9dd
Walk over to the point, and stand on those rocks, as close to the water's edge as you can get, and cast out as far as you can, and you will catch crappie. I've been using Bobby Garland, under a bobber, at a depth of about 5 ft. This is a pretty easy walk, albeit long. I would rate this at a two and a half on the effort scale of 1 to 5. Go underneath the second pier, there are two wooden fishing piers, both of them are out of the water right now. Go to the second one, the farthest one, and fish directly out in front of that.
Across the street from Stewart Creek boat ramp, there are a couple different places you can park on the side of the road. If you park in the first spot you can walk to a bank fishing spot that I found, but it's about a half a mile walk, and it's a four on the effort scale of 1 to 5. It's definitely for physically fit individuals only. I will drop you a pin where you need to park, just be careful pulling in, it's a muddy spot, and it's not very level, you need to go slow, especially if you don't have a high profile vehicle...
https://goo.gl/maps/edbFMygf53iDA4js5
There's room for a handful of cars in this location, but it's really muddy! You're going to want to take the trail through the woods, to the water's edge. Then you can walk alongside the lake, to the fishing hole. I'm going to drop you a pin of exactly where you need to be standing, and an impromptu map. It won't be exactly to the scale of each individual twist and turn through the woods, but it'll give you a pretty good idea of where you need to be going. First, a pin on Google maps of where you need to stand...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/9rsBiWd94j25PERw8
When you get to the end of the trail in the woods, just before you reach the water's edge, there is a plastic lawn chair hanging in a tree. That is your trail marker! Make sure to remember to turn on to the trail when you see that plastic chair, when you are returning to your vehicle. When you get to the pin, you will know you are in the right location, because there are a couple of fire pits there. Someone has been burning, in the exact right location! There is a burn stain on the cliff face, and you need to cast directly out from that. The water is about 15 ft, and there are several trees underneath the surface that hold fish, most of the year!
When I go crappie fishing, I will go to the spot where I was catching them the last time, first. I may not catch them, so I will move locations. It's important to remember that, I have listed at least 10 to 15 different crappie fishing locations, on my Pro reports, in the past. All of those locations are viable spots! They don't lose their luster because I don't go, or haven't made a video there in a while. Too many people are focusing on the spring, and not enough on all the other locations. A good example, the side of the road at Lamar Hill...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/5XK8aZt92iLeTQv38
This is another one of those locations where, if you don't have a high profile vehicle, you need to be careful. It's very muddy, and the road is kind of steep, and just drops off to this parking space. Proceed with caution, but at very least check it out. There's never anyone there when I go by! There's a fantastic honey hole, and I will draw you a map and drop you a pin of exactly where to stand...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/ZGoyzCLnejTGe8g49
You will know you are in the right spot because the main trail will have a branch directly to the Cliff face that you need to fish. There is a tree that was cut down, and placed in the water, with the trunk end standing up. It's a relatively long tree, for how skinny it is. I'd say the trunk, is about 8 in across. It's very noticeable! It's not necessarily where the fish are hanging, it's just a good marker. When the water is low enough, there's a rock near the surface that you can stand on. Right now, Percy Priest Lake will be on the rise, so some of these locations will be a little harder to stand at, but this is a cliff, so it will always be above the water!
Once again, this map isn't exactly accurate, but it gives you a pretty good idea of how you need to work your way to the spot. Once you get there, the water is about 10 ft deep, and there are submerged trees. A tight line with a bobby Garland is never a bad idea, but it's that time of year, just put on two Bobby Garland, and stick a fixed bobber at a depth of about 4 to 5 ft. That's been working everywhere! There is a cliff involved, and you may or may not want to climb up or down it. This is squarely at a three and a half on the effort scale of one to five. Not necessarily for the hardiest of individuals, but definitely not easy to do. When you get to this spot, you will see, to your left, there are three points from nearby coves. I have it on good authority, from the twra, that he has inspected people at those points that had buckets filled with crappie! Pretty much, you need to fish in the areas where Fish can be found. Especially this time of year!

title: Trip Report #102
content_raw:
Go to the bank at Percy Priest Lake at any of the crappie spots I have mentioned before!
Basically, the whole entire lake is on fire! All of the crappie are at their typical, February fishing spots... The action has been on fire from the bank! I'm going to drop some pins, get to these locations as quick as you can!
Vivrett Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/Lk5GKIcjkDaUquuX4
I'm just going to draw you a map of where fish can be caught, but the whole entire area is a hotspot! Fishing at the fish attractor in the parking lot is a one out of five on the effort scale! It should have some fish, and it's designed for handicapped persons. Fishing at the end of the trail is a four out of five on the effort scale.
Crappie are moving heavily up and down this bank! People are catching their limit of 30 fish! Hit the hot spots at the "x"... Walk the trail all the way to that last x, there will be people out there fishing, fish with them! They are wearing them out right now. You will have to do a little bit of scaling the cliffs. This hike is a 3.5 out of five on the effort scale.
Bryant Grove recreation area...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/H4nZKgDK62piDNLr7
Make sure not to park at the boat ramp! They are giving people tickets. Wait till at least 7:00 a.m., when they open the gate, and then go fish on the bluffs. The hot spot is in front of the white cross where I drew an x...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/ph9OCmBXwccQB1yyr
It's on fire out here! This is where I launched my boat today, and these banks are loaded with fish! Fishing on the cliffs are a four out of five on the effort scale. Not the most strenuous thing that I do, but for physically fit people only. If you want to walk all the way around, to the fish attractor at the point, it's a long walk, but it's relatively flat. That rates at a 3 out of five on the effort scale.
Found another new bank spot... People have been fishing there for a long time, but I didn't know exactly where it was, or had to get there, until today. You have to park on the side of the road, by the Fate Sanders bridge on Weekly Lane...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/bwj23uPkLzZeHRQHA
The recreation area at fate Sanders is closed for the winter, but you can still cross the street, and walk the trail to the park. This is a maximum effort trail! A five on a scale of 1 to 5, for the physically fit only.
I'm going to drop a pin, where I found these crappie. Basically, there's an underwater cliff that has a tree that these fish love to hang on!
They are about 5 ft down, in 10 ft of water. You will know you are in the right spot because there will be a picnic table behind you, and there is an old cedar tree stump, literally right there on the bank, where you need to be. If you stand right in front of that stump, cast a little bit to your left. The fish are about 15 ft from the bank, from 5 to 10 feet down.
https://goo.gl/maps/X1z85QKfWVB2HME8A
Don't feel like putting in any effort? Just want to take out your boat? I got you... Today, I went upstream from Stewart Creek boat ramp, for the first time, to do a little mapping. I found half a dozen locations where crappie school in great numbers. I was able to catch really big fish today! After you launch from Stewart Creek boat ramp, as you are facing the main lake, start heading left, which is upstream. I will drop you pins, on the brush piles where I found crappie...
https://goo.gl/maps/tyoRjpT3UvVxLdBE8
https://goo.gl/maps/n2RLbqi6pGCJhznv9
https://goo.gl/maps/r8RxFQhgYJv7xrXb9
https://goo.gl/maps/4htCto1E4ns3rUGGA
https://goo.gl/maps/dpS7a55LHMjoJy2B8

title: Trip Report #103
content_raw:
Beginning my work at Center Hill Lake...
Yesterday I launched from the boat ramp just above Center Hill Dam at Ike Park. At least, I think that's what it's called, when I look on Google maps, it doesn't really list it, the boat ramp has always been there, but it's been recently refurbished, and it's brand new, and really nice!
https://maps.app.goo.gl/TMbi8c2d2geHNyiJ6
I wanted to see if there were any crappie on the banks in the area around the dam and at Edgar Evans Marina...
https://share.google/HEdLaodflJuRt1yhw
I started scanning from the boat ramp going clockwise around the area out in front of the dam. I'm going to draw a quick map to show you everywhere that I covered.
It took me 6 hours to scan this entire area, using my trolling motor on low speed. I must have scanned at least a mile of bank, before I decided to enlist some help. I had gone from the rip rap that holds the dam up, across the dam, and along the bluff wall. The water was 200 ft deep! I assumed that I would see crappie, hanging in schools, along the bank. I was wrong! So I asked Google Gemini where the fish would be. It pointed out, rather astutely, that the water on that end of the lake is crystal clear! You can see about 20 feet down. That causes the sunshine to practically blind these fish. Google Gemini suggested that they would be hanging out on submerged tree tops in 55 to 60 ft of water. And it was right!
To find crappie, I had to scan in the open water, provided it was around 100 to 80 foot of depth. Any deeper than that, and there wouldn't be any submerged trees that were standing up. Basically, the lake is only 77 years old, and some of the trees that were underwater when they first filled the lake, are still standing. What I had to find, was a depth of around 80 ft, and then some bait fish that were suspended. If you could find that exact recipe, below those fish, if there was standing timber, there would be crappie, in 55 ft of water! I had no idea they could get that deep! They could get that deep, but I couldn't possibly fish for them with a 1/64th of an ounce or a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head. Before my lure could get down to them, I would already be moving because of the wind. And I had no option to anchor, and I don't have spot lock.
The main attraction in this area, is the massive marina at Edgar Evans State Park. There are hundreds of boats, and lots of structure for Crappie to hang on to. Unfortunately, these boats are sometimes sitting in as much as 100 feet of water. As if that wasn't bad enough, I only found two school of crappie in the entire marina, and both of them were tucked so far underneath, that you couldn't possibly reach them with a cast. The only way to get to them, would be in the center of the marina, on the walkway.
There are plenty of crappie on this end of the lake, they're just really hard to catch right now. In March of 1996, I had an unbelievable day catching crappie from the bank at Edgar Evans State Park. Those fish were on the opposite side of the parking lot from the marina. I went over there to scan the area, and it turns out, it's a relatively shallow cove! The water is about 16 to 18 ft deep and it was absolutely loaded with Bass! I mean loaded to the gills! I expect this area to be the main spawning area for the crappie on this end of the lake. When the time comes, they will have to move into shallow water to spawn, and I suspect I will be able to catch them there.
As for right now, I would completely write off this area for the next month, as far as crappie fishing is concerned. If you want a great place to catch bass, it seems like every single bank was holding good numbers of them, the shallower the better! Those fish were sitting right up next to the bank, in one foot of water!

title: Trip Report #104
content_raw:
Walter Hill Lake in Murfreesboro...
The highly controversial East Fork Stones River above Walter Hill Dam is also known as Walter Hill lake...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/zfj3rYcPHD2huCkn9
There is a boat ramp in this parking lot, and it is technically designed to launch boats. That being said, it's not very easy, which brings us to the effort rating for this trip. If you are trying to launch any size boat from this boat ramp, it's going to be a maximum effort situation. Not only is there no courtesy dock, there's really not anywhere good to put your boat on the bank while you park your car. Best case scenario, you have someone who can be in the boat and someone who can launch them, and then park the truck. Two-man operation, easy peasy. One man operation, maximum effort. If you want to launch a kayak from this location, that is a one on a scale of 1 to 5! This is a fantastic place to launch a kayak, couldn't be any easier!
I wanted to use my forward facing sonar to see if I could find crappie. I should have asked Google Gemini before I left the house. If you don't know, Google Gemini is an AI assistant that you can ask, pretty much anything. I like to ask it fishing questions. I asked if there were any crappie in Walter Hill Lake. It told me, that there were crappie, but they behave more like river fish. It went on to explain, that, these fish won't be schooled up in deep areas, or suspended on cliffs, these fish will be in the brush that hangs off the edge of the river. It was right! I slowly trolled from the boat ramp, using my forward facing sonar, and didn't find any schools of crappie! I went as far as my boat could go, to where the lake turned into a river, about 1 foot deep. I'll drop a pin in Google maps for exactly how far you can go in a boat...
https://goo.gl/maps/Hr2tpDTF4C5Es7gN9
There's plenty of cover for crappie to hide near the bank. Unfortunately, I didn't have any bobbers with me. I'm used to casting and retrieving for these fish. When they are in heavy cover, it's easiest to get them with a bobber. Since I didn't have one, I tried to make the best of a bad situation. Anytime I would see Fish on the sonar, I would make a cast and try to catch them. Each time, they ended up being bass. There are lots of bass in this stretch of water! I wasn't bass fishing, but the video I ended up making was all bass! I have no doubt, that if that was your intention, you could go in there and catch as many as you would like. There's never anybody fishing there, or so I thought...
I got there early this morning. Probably just after 8:00 a.m. I went as far as I could upstream, with only the power of my trolling motor. It took me all day! I didn't turn around to head back to the boat ramp until around 3:30 in the afternoon. At some point in time, after I left the boat ramp, before I got back, someone dumped a limit of crappies, that had their fillets removed. In my experience, that person caught those fish right there! I had already written off this body of water, as somewhere I didn't want to fish, and then I saw those fish carcasses! They were huge! No doubt in my mind, that river is loaded with crappie.
My next move will be to go in there with a Bobby Garland and a bobber with about 2 ft of depth. Just find some trees that are in the water and cast near them and see if you can get a bite. I'll have to cover lots of water to find fish, but that's the way it is in these types of situations. When you don't have a massive reservoir, and places for fish to suspend, they end up hanging out in the trees, where they feel most comfortable. I feel comfortable in saying that, I will eventually find these fish, and this will be a fantastic place for me to go in the future!

title: Trip Report #105
content_raw:
A new addition to all of my Pro reports, will be an effort rating. I will be grading each outing, based on the amount of effort that you must put forth, on a scale of 1 to 5. One, being an easy outing, on flat, level land, that most fishermen, young and old, would be easily able to handle. Five, being an all out effort! Lots of heavy lifting and potentially long hikes through wooded areas.
This trip registers as a 5 on the effort rating! Maximum effort for several hours at a time. From the time you start your trip, till the time you get to the house, you will be working, hard. Most kayak trips require some amount of talent and or know how, this trip requires a little bit of white water kayaking technique!
You're going to need to be proficient with your kayak. If you're not comfortable, this isn't the trip for you. There are a few hairpin turns, and some really swift rapids that require you to make split second movements to avoid obstacles like boulders. This is an 8 mile stretch of river, so if you spend any amount of time fishing, or swimming and enjoying the day, it's going to take all day! Literally, at least 8 hours. Be prepared to flip. I have flipped on this stretch of river two different times. Even the best kayakers will get caught off guard in swift water, by a boulder, that you couldn't avoid. Here's what you should do when that happens.
Both times, I was lucky, my leg didn't get pinned in between rocks, so I was able to stand up, and grab my kayak, and drag it to the bank. Grab everything you can, and get it to the bank, and then stand your kayak up, and drain all the water out of it. This is extremely strenuous! If you don't think you can drag your kayak, upside down, and full of water, against the current, and out of the river, you should avoid this trip. That being said, it's not that hard to do! If you're relatively physically fit, can do a fair amount of hiking or biking or lifting, you should put this high on your list. It's one of the most fun trips in Middle Tennessee! Now let's talk about where to get started...
The beginning of this trip is at Thompson Lane trailhead...
https://share.google/WWJYD1EYdcxWfg5Po
In the main parking lot, there is a road that looks like it goes into the woods. At the beginning of that road, there is a green sign that says, "canoe access" . I spoke with a Murfreesboro police officer who told me I should drive my truck down that access road, and I would find a spot that I could pull into, and then back up to the boat ramp. This spot on the greenway has a sign that says no bicycles! This spot is specifically for our vehicles to drop off our kayaks or canoes. You are allowed to be here, it is encouraged!
Now that you know where to get started, you need to know when to get started. I'm not talking about what time of day. Ideally, anytime you are going to do this stretch of river, you need to be started before 9:00 a.m. in reality, it just depends on how much time you would like to spend on the river. If you paddle, the whole time, for 8 miles, you could probably get it done in about 3 hours. But if you go at a relatively slow speed, to do some fishing, it's going to take 6 to 8 hours. Make sure you have enough time, but make sure you go when the time is right. That was something that took me years to figure out! The very first time I kayaked this stretch of river, I had no idea how lucky I was!
The smallest amount of rain can cause this river to rise to levels that are unsafe to kayak. When I first started kayaking, I didn't know how to look up how fast a river was flowing. I now know, that we have websites that are ran by the United States geological survey that provide us with up to the minute, unregulated, stream data. This data includes everything from water temperatures to observed rainfall and the most important statistic, the cubic feet per second. That is the metric by which water, and it's flow through a given point, is measured. On the West Fork stones river, there is a USGS information station, that is located on this particular stretch. THIS IS THE HOLY GRAIL! THIS IS THE WEBSITE THAT SEPARATES ME FROM OTHER FISHERMEN! THIS IS THE SECRET WEAPON, HOW I KNOW EXACTLY HOW THE RIVER IS FLOWING, BEFORE I EVER SHOW UP!
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D
When you click on that, the first graph you will see, is the river, and it's elevation. That directly correlates with the cubic feet per second, but it's not the important metric. The reason being, that number is different on every river. 2 ft on one river, might be too much to kayak, whereas, 2 ft of elevation on another river, and there might not be any water to kayak at all. It's really hard to explain, but basically, the only number that matters, is cubic feet per second. That number is static! A cubic foot is about one basketball. When I am posting this report, on Tuesday night at 7:00 p.m., the cubic feet per second on that chart was at 188 CFS. That would be 188 basketballs, per second, passing by the observation station.
Pretty much any water way you can think of, will have an USGS observation station somewhere. The way I find them, is with google. Here's a great way for you to try it where you live. Ask for the USGS station at the river that you live near, in the town that you live in. Here is an example, using my location. I would ask Google for the USGS station on the West Fork Stones River in Murfreesboro Tennessee. If you plug in that specific query, you will get the graph that I gave you above! Now you can do that for your hometown, and then you can see what the cubic feet per second are, at any given time! Now we need to talk about the appropriate levels to kayak on the West Fork Stones river, and that number, will be cubic feet per second.
Every river will have an operational minimum. That will be the lowest amount of cubic feet per second that you can have, in the river basin, and still float in a kayak. Pretty much, every single river, unless it is dam controlled, will experience drought and low water conditions that will make them unable to be kayaked. This stretch of the West Fork Stones River gets that way, a lot! As a matter of fact, without the short burst of rain that we are getting tonight, I would expect the West Fork Stones River from Murfreesboro, to Smyrna, to be too shallow to navigate, until this weekend's heavy rainfall.
The river is currently flowing at 188 cubic feet per second, and I have found that, the magic number, the lowest you can go, and still float in a kayak, is 125 cubic feet per second. Any lower than that, and you will have to get out, and drag your kayak. Not just a little, a lot! As a matter of fact, at 125 cubic feet per second, unless you're really good, you're probably going to get stuck a few times.
Technically, rivers don't have operational maximums. In reality, there has to be a limit at which I cut myself off, from every river. I have these numbers memorized, for a dozen different rivers in Middle Tennessee. The only way to figure it out, was to look at the chart, and look at the river. Continuously. For decades. Now I know, what every river looks like, according to its USGS chart, from the comfort of my home. I know, that this stretch of stones river, shouldn't be attempted over 440 cubic feet per second. Why not? What happens at 450 cubic feet per second? Not a whole lot, it's not dramatically different, it's just a little bit faster. And as any river speeds up, it gains difficulty, and it loses fishability. I have fished this particular stretch of river enough to know, if you're starting out over 400, it's going to be swift, and you're not going to get as much fishing in. In my opinion, 440 cubic feet per second, is the operational maximum.
So here's how you gauge that... If you want to start your day, and you check the chart, and it's not already below 440 CFS, and dropping, you probably should consider something else. If that number is below 440, and falling, it's going to be a nice smooth ride. If that number is anywhere near 150 or 140, and falling, it's probably going to get near that operational minimum, 125cfs, before you get off the river. The money zone is right in 260 to 300 cfs.
So you know where to start, and you know when to go, but now you need to know where to finish, and it ain't pretty! There is no boat ramp, no courtesy dock, just a mud bank and a straight cliff! Congratulations, you've made it to the end, Nice Mill dam. Time to earn the rest of that five-star effort rating!
https://maps.app.goo.gl/nfP6gaQKoMyK9MMf8
I take out on the high side. I simply step out into the mud, drag my kayak up a 5-ft, sheer, limestone cliff, on to the steps, and then up to the parking lot. This is maximum effort! This is lifting, your entire kayak, and all your gear, by the handle on the front of the kayak. I've been doing it for years, it's my favorite place to put in, and then take out. You don't necessarily have to do this whole entire 8 mile trip. You can simply go down those steps, drop your kayak into the water, carefully, and then paddle upstream, for about a mile. What you can't do, is get out easily. Maximum effort!
I did this trip yesterday! The fish weren't biting LOL it was terrible. But this stretch of river is absolutely loaded. It's mostly Smallmouth bass, but yesterday, we caught one smallmouth, one largemouth, and one spotted bass. It has all three, but the area is mostly dominated with small mouth. They should hit, just about any Bass lure. Crank baits, Ned rig, jerk bait, spinnerbait, rooster tail, paddle tail, here in a couple of months, anything on top water... Just use your confidence lure, and give it about, 3 weeks. If you can find a window, where you are able to go, and the cubic feet per second is right, pounce on it! This is that stretch of river, that, when the water is right, I drop what I'm doing, and kayak it. The rapids are the most fun in Middle Tennessee! Hands down, out of every different trip, this one is the most exciting!
content_markdown:
A new addition to all of my Pro reports, will be an effort rating. I will be grading each outing, based on the amount of effort that you must put forth, on a scale of 1 to 5. One, being an easy outing, on flat, level land, that most fishermen, young and old, would be easily able to handle. Five, being an all out effort! Lots of heavy lifting and potentially long hikes through wooded areas.

This trip registers as a 5 on the effort rating! Maximum effort for several hours at a time. From the time you start your trip, till the time you get to the house, you will be working, hard. Most kayak trips require some amount of talent and or know how, this trip requires a little bit of white water kayaking technique!

You're going to need to be proficient with your kayak. If you're not comfortable, this isn't the trip for you. There are a few hairpin turns, and some really swift rapids that require you to make split second movements to avoid obstacles like boulders. This is an 8 mile stretch of river, so if you spend any amount of time fishing, or swimming and enjoying the day, it's going to take all day! Literally, at least 8 hours. Be prepared to flip. I have flipped on this stretch of river two different times. Even the best kayakers will get caught off guard in swift water, by a boulder, that you couldn't avoid. Here's what you should do when that happens.

Both times, I was lucky, my leg didn't get pinned in between rocks, so I was able to stand up, and grab my kayak, and drag it to the bank. Grab everything you can, and get it to the bank, and then stand your kayak up, and drain all the water out of it. This is extremely strenuous! If you don't think you can drag your kayak, upside down, and full of water, against the current, and out of the river, you should avoid this trip. That being said, it's not that hard to do! If you're relatively physically fit, can do a fair amount of hiking or biking or lifting, you should put this high on your list. It's one of the most fun trips in Middle Tennessee! Now let's talk about where to get started...

The beginning of this trip is at Thompson Lane trailhead...

https://share.google/WWJYD1EYdcxWfg5Po

In the main parking lot, there is a road that looks like it goes into the woods. At the beginning of that road, there is a green sign that says, "canoe access" . I spoke with a Murfreesboro police officer who told me I should drive my truck down that access road, and I would find a spot that I could pull into, and then back up to the boat ramp. This spot on the greenway has a sign that says no bicycles! This spot is specifically for our vehicles to drop off our kayaks or canoes. You are allowed to be here, it is encouraged!

Now that you know where to get started, you need to know when to get started. I'm not talking about what time of day. Ideally, anytime you are going to do this stretch of river, you need to be started before 9:00 a.m. in reality, it just depends on how much time you would like to spend on the river. If you paddle, the whole time, for 8 miles, you could probably get it done in about 3 hours. But if you go at a relatively slow speed, to do some fishing, it's going to take 6 to 8 hours. Make sure you have enough time, but make sure you go when the time is right. That was something that took me years to figure out! The very first time I kayaked this stretch of river, I had no idea how lucky I was!

The smallest amount of rain can cause this river to rise to levels that are unsafe to kayak. When I first started kayaking, I didn't know how to look up how fast a river was flowing. I now know, that we have websites that are ran by the United States geological survey that provide us with up to the minute, unregulated, stream data. This data includes everything from water temperatures to observed rainfall and the most important statistic, the cubic feet per second. That is the metric by which water, and it's flow through a given point, is measured. On the West Fork stones river, there is a USGS information station, that is located on this particular stretch. THIS IS THE HOLY GRAIL! THIS IS THE WEBSITE THAT SEPARATES ME FROM OTHER FISHERMEN! THIS IS THE SECRET WEAPON, HOW I KNOW EXACTLY HOW THE RIVER IS FLOWING, BEFORE I EVER SHOW UP!

https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D

When you click on that, the first graph you will see, is the river, and it's elevation. That directly correlates with the cubic feet per second, but it's not the important metric. The reason being, that number is different on every river. 2 ft on one river, might be too much to kayak, whereas, 2 ft of elevation on another river, and there might not be any water to kayak at all. It's really hard to explain, but basically, the only number that matters, is cubic feet per second. That number is static! A cubic foot is about one basketball. When I am posting this report, on Tuesday night at 7:00 p.m., the cubic feet per second on that chart was at 188 CFS. That would be 188 basketballs, per second, passing by the observation station.

Pretty much any water way you can think of, will have an USGS observation station somewhere. The way I find them, is with google. Here's a great way for you to try it where you live. Ask for the USGS station at the river that you live near, in the town that you live in. Here is an example, using my location. I would ask Google for the USGS station on the West Fork Stones River in Murfreesboro Tennessee. If you plug in that specific query, you will get the graph that I gave you above! Now you can do that for your hometown, and then you can see what the cubic feet per second are, at any given time! Now we need to talk about the appropriate levels to kayak on the West Fork Stones river, and that number, will be cubic feet per second.

Every river will have an operational minimum. That will be the lowest amount of cubic feet per second that you can have, in the river basin, and still float in a kayak. Pretty much, every single river, unless it is dam controlled, will experience drought and low water conditions that will make them unable to be kayaked. This stretch of the West Fork Stones River gets that way, a lot! As a matter of fact, without the short burst of rain that we are getting tonight, I would expect the West Fork Stones River from Murfreesboro, to Smyrna, to be too shallow to navigate, until this weekend's heavy rainfall.

The river is currently flowing at 188 cubic feet per second, and I have found that, the magic number, the lowest you can go, and still float in a kayak, is 125 cubic feet per second. Any lower than that, and you will have to get out, and drag your kayak. Not just a little, a lot! As a matter of fact, at 125 cubic feet per second, unless you're really good, you're probably going to get stuck a few times.

Technically, rivers don't have operational maximums. In reality, there has to be a limit at which I cut myself off, from every river. I have these numbers memorized, for a dozen different rivers in Middle Tennessee. The only way to figure it out, was to look at the chart, and look at the river. Continuously. For decades. Now I know, what every river looks like, according to its USGS chart, from the comfort of my home. I know, that this stretch of stones river, shouldn't be attempted over 440 cubic feet per second. Why not? What happens at 450 cubic feet per second? Not a whole lot, it's not dramatically different, it's just a little bit faster. And as any river speeds up, it gains difficulty, and it loses fishability. I have fished this particular stretch of river enough to know, if you're starting out over 400, it's going to be swift, and you're not going to get as much fishing in. In my opinion, 440 cubic feet per second, is the operational maximum.

So here's how you gauge that... If you want to start your day, and you check the chart, and it's not already below 440 CFS, and dropping, you probably should consider something else. If that number is below 440, and falling, it's going to be a nice smooth ride. If that number is anywhere near 150 or 140, and falling, it's probably going to get near that operational minimum, 125cfs, before you get off the river. The money zone is right in 260 to 300 cfs.

So you know where to start, and you know when to go, but now you need to know where to finish, and it ain't pretty! There is no boat ramp, no courtesy dock, just a mud bank and a straight cliff! Congratulations, you've made it to the end, Nice Mill dam. Time to earn the rest of that five-star effort rating!

https://maps.app.goo.gl/nfP6gaQKoMyK9MMf8

I take out on the high side. I simply step out into the mud, drag my kayak up a 5-ft, sheer, limestone cliff, on to the steps, and then up to the parking lot. This is maximum effort! This is lifting, your entire kayak, and all your gear, by the handle on the front of the kayak. I've been doing it for years, it's my favorite place to put in, and then take out. You don't necessarily have to do this whole entire 8 mile trip. You can simply go down those steps, drop your kayak into the water, carefully, and then paddle upstream, for about a mile. What you can't do, is get out easily. Maximum effort!

I did this trip yesterday! The fish weren't biting LOL it was terrible. But this stretch of river is absolutely loaded. It's mostly Smallmouth bass, but yesterday, we caught one smallmouth, one largemouth, and one spotted bass. It has all three, but the area is mostly dominated with small mouth. They should hit, just about any Bass lure. Crank baits, Ned rig, jerk bait, spinnerbait, rooster tail, paddle tail, here in a couple of months, anything on top water... Just use your confidence lure, and give it about, 3 weeks. If you can find a window, where you are able to go, and the cubic feet per second is right, pounce on it! This is that stretch of river, that, when the water is right, I drop what I'm doing, and kayak it. The rapids are the most fun in Middle Tennessee! Hands down, out of every different trip, this one is the most exciting!

title: Trip Report #106
content_raw:
Found the crappie on priest...
2 weeks and 2 days ago, we were still pre- epic ice storm. At that point, it had been a warm winter. Since December 21st, we had experienced a few different days with near record highs and a water temperature at the surface on Percy Priest Lake near 60°! Before are two week polar plunge, I had found massive amounts of crappie in the area around Stewart's Creek boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/NBJdgwaAuNZ9TRkE6
This is the lower end of the lake, and it was really shallow, and the water was really warm. Crappie were everywhere! Large schools of small fish. Small schools of large fish. And lots of individual fish roaming around on their own. The deepest spot around that boat ramp is about 20 ft. The majority of it is much more shallow than that. These crappie were hanging out near submerged timber and sometimes, suspended on nothing, from 5 foot of depth to 13 foot of depth. They didn't really care for being in the deep water, but they were always near where the water dropped off to its deepest point. Shallow areas would hold fish, but only if they were near an underwater drop off.
Fast forward to today. It's been 16 days since I have fished Percy Priest Lake in my boat. We had several different days of temperatures near 0° and two weeks where parts of the lake were completely frozen and inaccessible. I made the decision to go right back to the same spot, Stewart's Creek boat ramp, and compare the fishing conditions to the last time I was there.
First of all, the water temperature was 48 and 1/2°. To me, that seemed really high. I thought it would be, at best, in the upper 30s. It hasn't been 48°, at all, at any point in time during the day, for 2 weeks. I have no idea how the lake is so warm, but it is. I got my boat in the water this morning, just after 9:00 a.m. What I saw, shocked me... There were even more crappie in the area than the last time I was there! I started making casts with my ultralight rod and reel and my 1/32nd ounce jig head, and the first four crappie I caught were giant slabs!
The whole area is completely, overwhelmingly, overloaded. The cliffs are loaded with crappie, the channel is loaded with crappie. Anywhere you can find underwater structure, crappie are stuck to it like Christmas ornaments. So I went looking for some new crappie spots.
I started going down lake, away from Stewart's Creek boat ramp, towards the dam. The next boat ramp you pass is Fate Sanders marina. Directly across the lake from fate Sanders marina, is the outskirts of the Poole Knobs recreation area...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/6P2nBFZeXUnRKvej8
All of this area is accessible from the bank, but I haven't walked any of it. But I have some incentive to do so. Today, I found four fish attractors that have been placed close enough to one another that you can sit in the middle, and fish in four different directions. This first location isn't close enough to fish from the bank, but when I find locations in this area, I will walk in, to figure out the trail, and share that information with you guys. Here is a map in Google pins from the location with four different underwater fish attractors...
https://goo.gl/maps/kFzeyRgHKN3CqFSn7
That spot was only about 10 ft of water, and these fish attractors were about 7 ft tall. They were the crappie condo style fish attractors. It looked like they were in buckets and they had corrugated pipe that was designed like a high-rise building with different levels. All four of them were overwhelmingly loaded with crappie! These spots will hold crappie most days of the year, because they are deep enough underwater at winter pool, as well as summer pool. There was another really neat fish attractor, relatively close to here...
https://goo.gl/maps/ixbYTyx7NP2VTTAp9
This one is really neat! It looks man-made, but it's almost impossible. Someone built something very particular, and sunk it in this location. To me, it looks like 15 to 20, 5 inch sized tree limbs, placed together in a rectangular grid, and then dropped perfectly on the bottom in 15 feet of water. They reach up about seven and a half feet, which is halfway to the surface, and they are so tightly packed together, that they were loaded with fish!
Everything on this end of the lake is full of fish! Everywhere I looked, there were fish. Lots of yellow bass, lots of white bass. There were schools of largemouth and spotted bass roaming around as well as more bait than you could ever hope to see. I'm not sure what's happening on the north end of the lake, but the south end of the lake has it going on!

title: Trip Report #107
content_raw:
Massive crappie alert...
Yesterday, I took my kayak to fish below Center Hill Dam...
https://share.google/XDB5ZWBixKdNvATZI
The generators were scheduled to be off from 10:00 a.m. until 3:00 p.m. I arrived at around 8:30 and began fishing at 8:45 a.m. I wanted to fish the generating water, before it turned off. I had about an hour, to try to target trout, with some spoons. During the winter, I have great success from the steps above the generating water, targeting trout. Yesterday, I wanted to go after them from the waters surface. The major difference, you can use much lighter tackle when you're in a boat or a kayak. When you're standing up on the bank, you need relatively heavy gear. You can use ultra light equipment to get to these fish when you're on their level. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
I started off throwing some heavy spoons that got down to the bottom quickly, but I was getting hung up. So I changed to a white rooster tail, and pretty quickly, caught a nice brown trout out of that heavy current. No sooner did I figure out to cast a white rooster tail to catch fish, than the generators turned off. No big deal, all of the same fish are still there, they are just not as easily tricked. When the water turns off, it gets calm, and still, and these fish don't feed as heavily. So I turned my attention to the center of the river, just below the dam, in the deepest part, to try to target some crappie.
Crappie were absolutely stacked under the dam! On my first cast, I used a heavy split shot to get my Bobby Garland down to the bottom quickly. I started a slow retrieve, and immediately caught a crappie. That's when I dropped my anchor, and started fishing intently for crappie. I removed the split shot, and started fishing my crappie jig really slow. At first, I was using one, 1/32nd of an ounce jig head. It wouldn't be long before I would tie two of those onto my line, creating a double rig. Once I started throwing the double rig, I really got into some good numbers of crappie.
Using a slow retrieve, without any twitches, or pauses, these crappie were willing to hit, for about 2 hours. From about 10:30 until about 12:30, the bite was hot! On the day, I caught 11 keeper crappie. I fished for crappie from 10:30 a.m. until 3:00 p.m. The first 10 keepers were caught from 10:30 to 12:30, it took me the next two and a half hours to catch one more keeper. The area was definitely still loaded with crappie, but the bite had turned off.
This will be part of their winter time pattern for the next couple of weeks, until the end of February. These fish will feed heavily midday, in most locations, when temperatures get the warmest. Just a half a degree, or a whole degree in temperature change in the water can cause bait to do fantastic things, that these crappie love. When the bait is happy and active, so are the crappie. That time of day will be the warmest time of day, for the next few weeks.
Conversely, they will also have a prime time bite window at night. Once the sun sets, and low light conditions have turned into dark, these fish will wait until the water temperature regulates. That's usually a few hours, around 9:00 p.m. until 2:00 a.m. should be a prime time bite window for these fish until the end of February. Not just the crappie below Center Hill dam, but the crappie everywhere in middle Tennessee should  acquiesce to this schedule.

title: Trip Report #108
content_raw:
Down at the crappie hole...
Yesterday, I went fishing at what was the "warmest" part of the day, midday. I got to the spring on Percy Priest Lake and started fishing at 1:00 p.m...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/3oDqc44AWbirYmti7
Quite a bit of the north end of the lake is frozen and unaccessible. This is on the south, shallow into the lake, which should be frozen, because there's not as much depth, but this spot never freezes over, because the spring water that flows out is always at a constant 52°. That makes it the ideal place to stand and fish for a couple of hours, during this brutal cold snap.
You have to hike into the spring. There's only one place to legally park, on the side of Maddox road...
https://goo.gl/maps/rWLeop6knCwwFPPG8
There are a handful of places to park off the side of the road. To get to the spring, go under, over, or around the gate that has been placed to keep vehicles from driving back to the spring. This is all public property, you are allowed to be there. There is a straight trail, all the way to the spring.
I had my 6 ft ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament. Before I left the house, I attached a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a 2-inch pearl colored Bobby garland, but I added a little super glue, to make sure that soft plastic would stay put. When I got there, I made a long cast, as far as I could, and counted my lure down to a depth of 13 seconds, followed by a painfully slow retrieve. On my second cast, I counted the lure down to a depth of 7 seconds, followed by a painfully slow retrieve. On my third cast, I counted the lure down to a depth of 17 seconds, followed by a painfully slow retrieve, and success! A nice big keeper crappie, on the third cast.
It would be half an hour before I would get another bite, and a full hour before I would catch another fish! Where there's one crappie, there are usually many, but that doesn't mean that they will bite. When it gets this cold out, they're little metabolism slows down, and the bite slows down as well. With a lot of patience, and many painfully slow retrieves, I was able to get a couple crappie. That's when I decided I needed to change things up. If you can't get more than a couple of crappie in an hour's time, you're not doing something right.
My first move was to go a lot slower, that's typically the way they need you to proceed when the bite is tough. Instead of a 1/32nd sounds jig head, I opted for a 1/64th of an ounce. Being half the size causes the lure not only to sink a lot slower, but also hover in the water, presenting itself to crappie a lot slower than a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head. I tried that for the better part of half an hour, but I wasn't able to generate a bite. My next move would be the one that would pay off. Instead of trying to go a lot slower, I put a 1/8 of an ounce sinker, about 14 inches above my jig head, and started moving it near the bottom, relatively fast.
Making a long cast, and allowing the jig to sink all the way to the bottom, I would start a retrieve that wasn't nearly as slow as I usually do. It would only take a couple of casts at that increased speed to get a third crappie, and then a fourth crappie. Typically, going faster isn't the way to get these fish. If you have a jig head swimming through their area, no matter how slow, they will typically eat. They really didn't want to yesterday. That feels like more of a reaction bite. If the lure is dangling in front of their face like a carrot, and they won't eat it, you may need to get them to respond to the lure in a different way. Running that lure a little faster makes it move through their area quicker, which could trigger the fish to bite instinctually.
This cold weather can't make the bite tough for too long. Here's how it works, all fish love consistency. If it's consistently cold out, for long enough, these fish will have to eat, in great numbers. When it goes from being brutally cold, to a little bit warmer, these fish will feed heavily. The next couple of days are supposed to be above freezing for the afternoon high, and I suspect between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. the next couple of afternoons, these fish will be fired up!

This is on the south, shallow into the lake, which should be frozen, because there's not as much depth, but this spot never freezes over, because the spring water that flows out is always at a constant 52°. That makes it the ideal place to stand and fish for a couple of hours, during this brutal cold snap.

You have to hike into the spring. There's only one place to legally park, on the side of Maddox road...

https://goo.gl/maps/rWLeop6knCwwFPPG8

There are a handful of places to park off the side of the road. To get to the spring, go under, over, or around the gate that has been placed to keep vehicles from driving back to the spring. This is all public property, you are allowed to be there. There is a straight trail, all the way to the spring.

I had my 6 ft ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament. Before I left the house, I attached a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a 2-inch pearl colored Bobby garland, but I added a little super glue, to make sure that soft plastic would stay put. When I got there, I made a long cast, as far as I could, and counted my lure down to a depth of 13 seconds, followed by a painfully slow retrieve. On my second cast, I counted the lure down to a depth of 7 seconds, followed by a painfully slow retrieve. On my third cast, I counted the lure down to a depth of 17 seconds, followed by a painfully slow retrieve, and success! A nice big keeper crappie, on the third cast.

It would be half an hour before I would get another bite, and a full hour before I would catch another fish! Where there's one crappie, there are usually many, but that doesn't mean that they will bite. When it gets this cold out, they're little metabolism slows down, and the bite slows down as well. With a lot of patience, and many painfully slow retrieves, I was able to get a couple crappie. That's when I decided I needed to change things up. If you can't get more than a couple of crappie in an hour's time, you're not doing something right.

My first move was to go a lot slower, that's typically the way they need you to proceed when the bite is tough. Instead of a 1/32nd sounds jig head, I opted for a 1/64th of an ounce. Being half the size causes the lure not only to sink a lot slower, but also hover in the water, presenting itself to crappie a lot slower than a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head. I tried that for the better part of half an hour, but I wasn't able to generate a bite. My next move would be the one that would pay off. Instead of trying to go a lot slower, I put a 1/8 of an ounce sinker, about 14 inches above my jig head, and started moving it near the bottom, relatively fast.

Making a long cast, and allowing the jig to sink all the way to the bottom, I would start a retrieve that wasn't nearly as slow as I usually do. It would only take a couple of casts at that increased speed to get a third crappie, and then a fourth crappie. Typically, going faster isn't the way to get these fish. If you have a jig head swimming through their area, no matter how slow, they will typically eat. They really didn't want to yesterday. That feels like more of a reaction bite. If the lure is dangling in front of their face like a carrot, and they won't eat it, you may need to get them to respond to the lure in a different way. Running that lure a little faster makes it move through their area quicker, which could trigger the fish to bite instinctually.

This cold weather can't make the bite tough for too long. Here's how it works, all fish love consistency. If it's consistently cold out, for long enough, these fish will have to eat, in great numbers. When it goes from being brutally cold, to a little bit warmer, these fish will feed heavily. The next couple of days are supposed to be above freezing for the afternoon high, and I suspect between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. the next couple of afternoons, these fish will be fired up!

title: Trip Report #109
content_raw:
Yesterday, I fished at the Okaloosa Island fishing pier...
Okaloosa Island Pier https://share.google/044cKeNdwcZBzr64I
I had everything set up from the day before, when I was sheepshead fishing. My intention, drop fiddler crabs down by the pilings at the pier. Fortunately for me, I had my underwater camera. I dropped that down, on the bridge pilings, at the end of the pier, and there were no sheepshead to be found. I can provide a link to my underwater camera. It comes in clutch in situations like this...
https://amzn.to/4k2amgk
I can't find the exact version that I bought last year, but this camera is almost identical, for a cheaper price. Basically, you need the infrared so you can see fish in underwater conditions that aren't clear. It's not necessarily just for fishing at night, the infrared works great when you drop it down in a low light situation like Percy Priest Lake, where there is no clear water. This camera shows you everything under the water! So I knew we were wasting our time trying to catch sheepshead.
We could see lots of bait fish, and underneath those bait fish there were some sizable fish. We turned our focus to using a sabiki rig to try to catch bait. If you don't know what that is, basically, it's a long line with a bunch of little flies. You put a heavy weight on the end, and jig it vertically up and down at the pier, to catch a lot of bait fish. This was working well, but our bait fish weren't catching us anything, that's because we were getting the wrong kind of bait. There was another person fishing on the end of the pier and he was using bull minnows from the local tackle shop. We had been there for about an hour and a half with no luck when he caught a flounder on one of those minnows. When he caught his second flounder, I decided to make the run to the bait shop to pick us up a dozen minnows.
This was a great bait shop in this area, but I don't have the name of it, they recently moved, and they're getting established in their new location. I'm going to drop the address right here, because they have everything you need, and they were more than willing to take the time to explain anything we asked about...
102 Eglin Pkwy SE, Fort Walton Beach, FL 32548
I got one dozen live bull minnows. I made my way back to the pier, and I put that bull minnow on my sheepshead setup. I was using my 7 ft medium, extra fast bass rod. I had a 2500 series real and 15 lb braid to a 12 lb monofilament leader that was about 3 ft long. I attached my leader to my braid using an Acapulco knot. Then I slid on a 1 oz barrel weight. I didn't put on any beads, because that's the way my guide did it when we went fishing the day before. Then, on the end of my 3-foot leader, I put a barrel swivel. Then on the end of the barrel swivel, I put 8 lb monofilament at a length of about 14 inches to my small J hook. It's actually a number two hook, which is pretty small for fishing in the ocean.
Traditional method to catch flounder at this pier, is to drop these minnows as close as you can get it to the pilings that hold up the pier, and hold a tight line and wait for the bite. We tried that for a while. Unfortunately, that method really wasn't producing very much. I will admit, I kind of got a little frustrated, because nobody was catching any fish. I took my rods, and instead of dropping it straight down, I made a long cast with it. At least a hundred feet away from the pier, and allowed it to sink to the bottom.
Then I started a slow, meticulous retrieve. The exact same style of retrieve you would use with a Carolina rigged plastic worm or a Texas rigged plastic worm. Allow the lure to sink to the bottom, get the weight of the presentation on your rod tip, by reeling out all the slack, and then slowly draw back on the rod tip, dragging The lure across the bottom. Then, when you get to about 90° with your rod tip, you slowly lower it down and reel out the slack that gets created. Then you start the process over again, until you get the lure all the way back to you. On my very first cast doing that, I caught the biggest flounder anybody caught all day!
Flounder have to be 14 in to keep, and my very first flounder ever was a great big 18-in fish. That would be the only flounder we would get on the day, but we saw several caught, and we have high hopes about catching them here, in the winter time, in the future. There's a couple things you're going to have to have, obviously you need the right setup, so that you can catch these fish. You need some bull minnows from the bait shop, but you also need to keep your minnows! I made the mistake of leaving my minnow bucket open, with the lid off. I went to the restroom that's provided at the end of the pier, and when I came out, a great blue heron had stole all but one of my bull minnows. I caught a fish on the very first minnow that I used, and then I only had one left. That's going to severely hinder your ability to catch these fish.
So you're going to need to keep your bait secure, whether you're using frozen shrimp or squid, any type of food, if it's uncovered, the birds will take it. That's their job, they stand there all day trying to take bait from people. When you bring a fish in, they will try to take that from you as well. One pelican got really close to me, and I tried to clap back a little, and it backed me down! They're very aggressive, and they won't take no for an answer. So you have to keep your stuff covered up.
One of the most important pieces of equipment is your hoop net, or drop net. These are available at every sporting goods store and bait shop in the Florida area. Basically, it's a 3 ft metal circle, a lot like a hula hoop, with a net in it. It's got a long rope, and you can drop it off the pier, and scoop up your fish. That's the only way to get these fish up the pier, especially if they have any size.
Your daily limit of flounder is 5, and I wouldn't be surprised if someone limits out today. This is the best time of year to get these fish at the beach, in the panhandle of Florida, and going out on the pier is the best way to get out to them, if you don't have a boat.

title: Trip Report #110
content_raw:
Ignite the bite...
Yesterday, I took a 4 hour fishing charter out of Fort Walton Beach Florida. Our guide was Captain adam, from Ignite The bite fishing charters...
Ignite The Bite Fishing Charters - Destin https://share.google/KxK3qjFi2rdU6ectF
We left out from Fort Walton Beach in Santa Rosa sound at 10:00 a.m. we made our way about a mile into the gulf, out in front of Fort Walton beach, where we were looking for cigar minnows to use as bait. We trolled around a couple of spots, used a sabiki rig to catch small bait fish, but we were unable to find cigar minnows to use for flounder fishing. The plan was, to go flounder fishing for a couple of hours, and then go sheepshead fishing for a couple of hours. It took us a little more than an hour to realize we weren't going to get any bait, so we immediately moved on to sheepshead fishing.
Here are some things I found out about sheepshead fishing from a boat. You can use a flat shovel to scrape oysters off of bridge pilings. That was how we got all of the bait we needed to nearly limit out on sheepshead. Here's what you want to do...
You need a big net, with small holes, so you can catch the oysters before they fall into the ocean. You get really close to the bridge pillars with your boat, and start scratching the oysters off the wall with your flat nose shovel. Keep your net just underneath the the oysters, against the wall, so they will fall into the net. Then, you simply dump the oysters into a bucket. Yesterday we collected two 5 gallon buckets, and that was more than enough for us to nearly limit out. If we had more time, we would have been able to limit it out, because this method is so effective.
Shucking the oysters and then trying to put them on the hook as best you can, is the most effective way. Inside all of those oysters, there are other little baits! There were dozens of small crabs, and those worked just as well as the raw oysters did!
We fished on bridge pilings at the main bridge between Destin and Fort Walton. Apparently, these sheepshead can sit on just about any of those pilings, even the really shallow ones! You'll just have to fish around different pilings until you find the fish. Fortunately, it's not very deep in this area! I didn't see any depth of more than 30 ft, so it was real easy to drop right down beside the bridge piling and fish. It was so easy, that while we were out there, a person in a kayak paddled up and started fishing next to a bridge piling.
These bridges are heavily influenced by the tide. While we were there, the tide was going in the whole time. Apparently, The tide is always either, going in, or coming out. To anchor to a bridge piling, our captain got out of the boat, on to the concrete bridge piling, and wrapped his anchor around it. That kept us in position really well. The kayaker didn't have an anchor, he paddled over behind a bridge piling and tried to sit in position, out of the current. No matter what, if you're trying to fish these Bridge pilings, there's always going to be some current, going in, or coming out.
I was able to use my fishing pole to catch these fish. I used my 7-ft, extra fast bass rod. That has a 2500 series reel and 15 lb braid. To my braid, our guide attached heavy fluorocarbon. On that fluorocarbon, he put a 1 oz barrel weight. At the end of the line, he put a barrel swivel, and then a smaller diameter, what looks like fluorocarbon. That section was about 14 in long, and on the very end, he put a number two J hook. I got a good shot of the hooks in the video, they were pretty small, for such big fish. That was the ideal setup. We would drop our bait to the bottom, either a crab or an oyster, and then we would reel the slack out of the line so we could feel the weight holding against the rod tip. Then you just let it sit on the bottom, until you feel a small bite. It's actually a lot like a crappie thump!
It didn't take us long to start catching fish, but I hadn't really mastered the technique. Once our guide threw his line down, I was able to watch exactly what he was doing, and emulate him, for better success. The reality is, there's a lot of current, and stuff going on down there. So you almost constantly have to make sure that you are in contact with your sinker. What he was doing, was holding that line tight to the sinker and then lowering his rod tip down to make sure it was sitting on the bottom and then, if it wasn't, he would let a little slack out, and then reel in the slack, to get readjusted. It was a constant process of making sure the line was tight, but there was a little more to it than that.
I think I figured out what was going on underneath the surface. The current was pulling our line just a little bit inland, if you readjust that sinker a couple of times, it should push that bait downstream, effectively pulling against the sinker, that way you could feel the faintest bite! When I say these fish bite like a crappie, I mean it. You will see in the video, I had that aha moment. When you get that line just right, you can feel them thump it, and you can set that hook just like you do with crappie. The only major difference, is that crappie have a paper mouth, and these things have rows of human teeth. They look like molars! So you have to slam that hook into him. When you see these hooks, you will see how small they are, some of these fish were six pounds, but you need these tiny little hooks to catch them. They really get between their teeth, and stick them in the meat.
This time of year, those sheepshead are sitting on the deepest pilings, in the middle of the bridge. Every time of year, they're sitting on bridge pilings, somewhere in this area. If you can't get to a boat, to get out on the water, consider some of the bridges that have fishing from the bridge. Florida offers lots of fishing from bridges, and yesterday, after we knew how to catch sheep head, we realized that some of the people who were standing on the bridges, we're doing just that. As we rode by, after our successful trip, we could see them with Carolina rigs and drop nets. So for most of us, who don't have a boat in Florida, here's what you need to do to try to get these fish from the bank.
You're going to need some live bait. You can buy hermit crabs, but the crabs that come from the oysters off the bridge pilings are a little bit different. Apparently, they will eat live shrimp, but they really prefer oysters! You're going to be fishing really high up from the surface, so you're going to need a drop net. This can also be called a hoop net. These are for sale at most sporting goods stores and fishing supply and tackle stores in Florida. Basically, it's a round net on a rope that you can drop down into the water so that you can scoop your fish up and lift it without having to use the line to pull the fish up.
Apparently, sheepshead will do the same thing on the pilings at the local Piers that reach out into the gulf. I haven't tried that, but if you are fishing on a pier, with paid access, you typically don't need a fishing license. If you are with a guide, in the state of florida, you typically don't need a fishing license. So far, I haven't had to purchase a license yet, because I've been to those two types of locations, exclusively. I have my underwater camera with me, so I will probably go back to the Okaloosa Island Pier and see if there are any sheepshead down there that we can catch...
https://share.google/e0QVs0tIBpP6m9dEf
It cost $2 to go out on the pier and be an observer. It costs $8 to go out on the pier and fish, and this covers your fishing license! Now that I know how to target sheepshead, that will likely be my next stop.

title: Trip Report #111
content_raw:
Florida fishing!
Yesterday, I did some fishing around the Destin, Florida area. The wind was crazy so to start the day I did some scouting. I had found a state park that said they offered kayak and paddle board rentals, so I went there when they opened at 9:00 a.m. It cost $5 to enter the state park, and the website didn't mention that kayak and paddle board rentals were seasonal. I'm going to drop a pin for the state park, so you know where to go to do some freshwater fishing when you're at the beach.
https://maps.app.goo.gl/KziCwdQEVVP8R8b1A
For $5 you get access to the beach and there's a really nice bathroom for men and women. The kayaks and paddle boarding are on a small, freshwater lake. There are signs that say there are gators in the lake, so I'm sure there are fish! Gators have to eat something. From there we went over to Fort Walton to check out a boat ramp that I had used for my kayak once before...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/7k1UU4GoxuUBQhWJA
That's the boat ramp at Ross Marler Park. This park has lots of covered pavilions with grills to cook at each location. There were a couple of really nice bathrooms and a very small beach area that would be good for little children. It's on the back side of the island, so there are no golf waves or deep water. It's sunny, and somewhat wind protected, and there's a really big playground with nice amenities for children. There are two boat ramps that give you access to Santa Rosa sound, and they have long courtesy docs that allow you to launch really big vessels. I launched my 11 ft kayak from here a few years ago, and paddled around in the relatively calm waters of the sound.
This is a public park, and there is no charge to enter. As far as I know, like most parks, it is open during daylight hours. I came to this park once, about 6 years ago, there was nobody there then, and there was nobody there now. It's kind of out of the way, and it seems like most people, especially tourists, don't know about it. It's a wonderful park! From there, just across the street on the beach, is the Okaloosa Island Pier...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/eWXuFz5xfWVDCZDu7
This is a really long pier, that extends out into the gulf. It cost $2 to go for a walk on up here, it cost $8 to go fishing on the pier, that's per person. They have lots of amenities, like a bathroom, and a restaurant/grill. They also have bait, and a select amount of tackle available. They also sell soft drinks and alcohol for people to take out onto the pier. You are allowed to bring your own cooler, and stay all day! I suggest you have some type of cart that you can roll with all of your equipment. It's a long walk to the end of the pier, and most of the time, if you're going to pay to go out there, you want to fish it all.
This time of year, it's tough to catch fish from the piers in the panhandle of Florida. They're just not loaded up with fish like they are in the warm weather months. We heard reports that some Bonita had been caught near the end of the pier, so that's where we started. To fish for bonita, I like to use my 7-foot medium heavy bass rod with 15 lb braid and a rattle trap. I will throw that rattle trap, with the wind, as far as I can, and then allow it to sink for about 5 or 6 seconds. Then I will start to yo-yo that thing back, slowly lifting up on the lure to actuate it, and then allowing it to sink back down for a second or two, before I lift back up on it again. I tried that for the better part of an hour and a half, but we weren't getting any fish.
While walking down the pier, near the very beginning, I had seen a school of fish, so I headed back to try to target those. I had my underwater camera with me, so I dropped that off the pier, to get a good look at those fish. I don't know ocean fish very well, so I looked up a picture of them, and it turns out they were whiting. Whiting are like the bluegill of the ocean. There is no size limit, and there is no creel limit, so you can keep as many as you would like. They also eat like bluegill. We were able to use a Carolina rig with a small circle hook and a small piece of shrimp to catch fish, one right after the other.
These fish were sitting in about 6 ft of water, and the school of fish was hanging out at that depth, exclusively. Occasionally, they moved from one side of the pier, to the other. By in large, they just sat there, and let us catch them. So we obliged! We probably caught a little less than two dozen small, whiting, before the sun started to set. Even though I'm in Florida, it's still really cold, so I called it a day!

title: Trip Report #112
content_raw:
Crappie everywhere!
This morning, I launched my boat at Stewart Creek boat ramp at 7:30...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/dsE1eDPeGiH8XdaaB
Today, I wouldn't use my main boat motor until I loaded my boat up on the trailer. The area out in front of Stewart Creek boat ramp is overwhelmingly loaded with crappie. Lots of schools of little crappie, and lots of big crappie roaming around by themselves. There are fish clinging to the cliffs, and there are fish suspended in the channel. Every piece of underwater structure that is at least 10 ft deep has fish loaded all over them. Most of the time those fish are crappie. Sometimes they are bass, sometimes they are yellow bass, sometimes they are white bass. Everywhere is relatively shallow! There isn't 20 foot of depth anywhere in this area.
Yesterday's rainfall didn't affect the water clarity, it's still relatively clear. Percy Priest never really gets that clear, it's more of a green tint, algae stained. It's perfect! The water temperature is 45° at the surface and these fish are fired up!
We didn't have much wind this morning, so I was able to use my longer crappie rod. I have a 7 1/2 foot ultralight pole that I like to use when there's no wind. That rod has 4 lb monofilament and I like to use a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a 2-inch pearl colored Bobby Garland. Typically, you have to be really patient for that lure to sink to the right depth, today, these fish were screaming straight up! I could start the lure a few feet above their heads and they would fight to be in position to get it first. Those fish were sitting on structure, in about 15 ft of water, in big schools. Most of them were little, not keeper size, but they were very aggressive.
To find bigger fish, most of the time, I didn't have to move my boat, I just needed to turn my forward facing sonar in a different direction. Today, large crappie were spread out all over the area, hanging by themselves, about 5 ft deep, in 10 feet of water. I started targeting bigger crappie, instead of schools of fish.
Unfortunately, the cliffs, where you can fish from the bank, we're only holding small crappie. They were tight to cover, and they were tough to get to. The majority of the good fish were all out in the middle of the lake. Just across from the cliffs there is a mud flat underwater. Anywhere there was a tree stuck in the mud, it was loaded with fish! I went over there, way too far to catch fish from the bank, and had a stellar day catching keeper-sized crappie.
They were in every direction, but you couldn't sneak up on them. The water was only about 10 feet deep at the most, and most of them were hanging at around 5 feet. If you hit the trolling motor at all, even on low speed, they would hear it, and move away. If you put the anchor down, every single fish would leave the area! And they wouldn't come back. Basically, I just had to drift around with what little light breeze there was, and keep turning my forward facing sonar in all directions until I could find a fish to make a cast on. When I found them, they were more than willing to bite! All I had to do was get my lure in their area, and give it a little twitch, to let them know it was there, and they would attack it.
Unfortunately, now that we know where all these fish are, there's a good chance we won't be able to get to them for several days. Tomorrow, it will be really windy, not a great day to be out on the boat. The next day, we get an epic snow and ice storm, and then temperatures that get near zero. I have no idea where those fish are going to move, but when I find them, I will let you know!

title: Trip Report #113
content_raw:
Where is everybody?
Yesterday at noon, I took my boat out from Stewart Creek boat ramp...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/joC10sWvHFH9AHbPx
It was 12° to start the day yesterday, so I waited until the temperature got above freezing, because I was afraid of sliding down a wet and icy boat ramp, into the lake. Those fears were largely unfounded, not because water doesn't freeze when it's that cold, but because there was no water on the boat ramp. Why not? Because no one was fishing. The boat ramp was empty. There wasn't a single car in the parking lot when I arrived. There are two sets of cliffs at the boat ramp at Stewart creek. Both of those cliffs are usually loaded with people catching crappie, but there was no one there!
I typically have to leave the area to do any fishing, because there are so many bank fishermen. That wasn't the case yesterday, so I got to work immediately, looking around those cliffs for crappie. When I got there, because I didn't see anyone there, I just assumed there weren't any fish, and I was wrong. I'm going to draw you a map and circle the areas where the fish are loaded heavily.
This map is not an exaggeration. I started fishing, using my forward facing sonar, and I noticed that, the entire area is overwhelmingly loaded with crappie. Every single underwater tree, stick, or bolder, anything that they could hang on, was loaded with fish! The bait was so thick, sometimes my fish finder didn't know if it was the bottom, or if it was fish. I saw schools of fish, that I thought were 10,000 bait fish, that actually turned out to be white bass, nice sized ones! The whole area was just blown out with fish. I caught bluegill, I caught bass, everything is up there! Everything except people. No one was there yesterday when I was catching those fish, so I went back there this morning, and I had the whole place to myself!
I didn't need my boat, those fish are right next to the bank. I started on the cliffs nearest to the parking lot, at the far end, fishing on the tree that pokes out of the water...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/5gUkNGXzJXR7kiat8
Using my ultralight rod and reel and a 1/32nd ounce jig head I was able to get hung up a bunch! There are a lot of fish in this area, because there are a lot of trees underneath the water. Those trees love to grab a hold of your jig and not let go. Be prepared to get hung up and broke off, and pack your patience. I caught a few fish, using a tight line, but that wasn't the way to go. So I switched to my slip bobber setup. Basically, I have a Bobby Garland on a jig, underneath a bobber. There is a knot on the line that acts as a bobber stop, and that is how I'm able to set the depth of my lure. I set that thing to about 6 ft, and started wearing those fish out!
After I caught a couple fish off of the first tree that sticks out of the water, I started working my way down the bank, just to get a change of scenery. You could stand anywhere out there right now, and fish, and catch them. I was just looking to move around and have some fun! There are so many fish out there right now, you can stand just about anywhere. So I moved down to the next tree that sticks out of the water, and I started putting the screws to those fish!
https://maps.app.goo.gl/THUpAq3WdrgTviG29
I was doing so well, that I decided I was going to make the long hike all the way around the cove, to the other side of the cliff. That would prove to be a big mistake. The wind was blowing so hard on that other side, that I wasn't even able to fish. Not a big deal, I know those fish are over there, but the wind was blowing from the wrong direction. That's a good thing! Today, I figured out, that if there is a south wind, you can fish on the bank nearest to the parking lot, with the wind at your back. On days where there is a north wind, I will just walk around to that other cliff, on the far side of the cove, and then I will be able to fish with the wind at my back!
