title: Trip Report #114
content_raw:
I successfully ran it back...
Going fishing in the same place, back to back days, rarely ends with good results. Unless you're going crappie fishing! This morning, I went right back to the same place that I fished yesterday morning, but today I got there a lot earlier. Before sunrise, I was already a half mile down the bank and going after these fish...
https://goo.gl/maps/NqB4DaammEEG3gmy9
That's the spot where I was fishing on the bank. If you go back to yesterday's Pro report, not only did I do a in-depth dive about how to get there, I also drew you a map.
Something I recently learned about these fish, they like to spread out at night. Wherever they are positioned during the day, once it gets dark out, they start to spread out to feed. I have been out several times in the dark, just before it starts to get light. I have gone to places where crappie gather in great numbers, and set up on an anchor, and watched as timber that is underwater would go from having zero fish on it, to getting completely loaded up by the time the sun comes up over the horizon. Basically, crappies have really sensitive eyes. They like to shield their eyes from bright light. One of the ways they do that is by gathering and piles, and gathering around structure. They also like to sit in the shade.
When I arrived, before the sun came up, I couldn't get a single bite. I fished for an hour! Sunrise is right at 7:00 a.m., the sun doesn't make its way up completely over the horizon until around 7:45. That's when I started catching fish! The area in front of this cliff is loaded with underwater brush piles. These fish school up heavily in this location during the day. From 7:45, until I left at 12:00, it was non-stop action!
This morning there was very little wind. That's one of the best conditions for crappie fishing, in my opinion. That allows me to use my extra long crappie fishing pole, which I prefer. This morning, I was using my 7 and 1/2 ft ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament. I had the exact same jig head that I was using yesterday, a 1/32nd ounce with a 2 in pearl colored Bobby Garland. I was casting to the same spot, directly out, 70 ft, pretty much as far as I can cast that little lure. The only difference, today, I couldn't get them to bite anywhere near the surface. I started by counting the lure down to a depth of 5 seconds. Then seven, then I skipped all the way to 13, and then 15 seconds, that's the depth that I left these fish biting yesterday. I wouldn't find any fish at that depth. It would take counting the lure all the way down to 20 seconds before I started my retrieve. That was the magic number today!
When I say magic, I do mean magic. For about an hour and 30 minutes, I would either catch a fish, or get a bite, on every single cast. Don't get me wrong, crappie fishing is really slow! You have to count your lure down for 20 seconds after you cast, then, once you start your retrieve, you have to retrieve the lure really slow. Unfortunately, today, a slow retrieve wasn't enough. I had to incorporate a twitch. But, I made sure to pay particular attention to the cadence. You don't want to twitch too much, but you don't want to twitch too little. Here was the rhythm I came up with. After I would cast, once the lure had got to the depth that I wanted, I would start my retrieve. After three turns of the handle, I would give a twitch. Then, another three turns of the handle, then, a twitch. That will have you twitching the lure about 7 to 10 times on any given retrieve. That's the magic number.
That spot was on fire today! A few Pro reports subscribers showed up out there, and that was awesome! Everybody that I saw caught fish, and that's not always the case when you're bank fishing with a bunch of other people. It has a lot to do with this spot, these fish aren't highly pressured just yet, get out there and get you some while this weather is really cold, they love it!

https://goo.gl/maps/NqB4DaammEEG3gmy9

That's the spot where I was fishing on the bank. If you go back to yesterday's Pro report, not only did I do a in-depth dive about how to get there, I also drew you a map.

Something I recently learned about these fish, they like to spread out at night. Wherever they are positioned during the day, once it gets dark out, they start to spread out to feed. I have been out several times in the dark, just before it starts to get light. I have gone to places where crappie gather in great numbers, and set up on an anchor, and watched as timber that is underwater would go from having zero fish on it, to getting completely loaded up by the time the sun comes up over the horizon. Basically, crappies have really sensitive eyes. They like to shield their eyes from bright light. One of the ways they do that is by gathering and piles, and gathering around structure. They also like to sit in the shade.

When I arrived, before the sun came up, I couldn't get a single bite. I fished for an hour! Sunrise is right at 7:00 a.m., the sun doesn't make its way up completely over the horizon until around 7:45. That's when I started catching fish! The area in front of this cliff is loaded with underwater brush piles. These fish school up heavily in this location during the day. From 7:45, until I left at 12:00, it was non-stop action!

This morning there was very little wind. That's one of the best conditions for crappie fishing, in my opinion. That allows me to use my extra long crappie fishing pole, which I prefer. This morning, I was using my 7 and 1/2 ft ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament. I had the exact same jig head that I was using yesterday, a 1/32nd ounce with a 2 in pearl colored Bobby Garland. I was casting to the same spot, directly out, 70 ft, pretty much as far as I can cast that little lure. The only difference, today, I couldn't get them to bite anywhere near the surface. I started by counting the lure down to a depth of 5 seconds. Then seven, then I skipped all the way to 13, and then 15 seconds, that's the depth that I left these fish biting yesterday. I wouldn't find any fish at that depth. It would take counting the lure all the way down to 20 seconds before I started my retrieve. That was the magic number today!

When I say magic, I do mean magic. For about an hour and 30 minutes, I would either catch a fish, or get a bite, on every single cast. Don't get me wrong, crappie fishing is really slow! You have to count your lure down for 20 seconds after you cast, then, once you start your retrieve, you have to retrieve the lure really slow. Unfortunately, today, a slow retrieve wasn't enough. I had to incorporate a twitch. But, I made sure to pay particular attention to the cadence. You don't want to twitch too much, but you don't want to twitch too little. Here was the rhythm I came up with. After I would cast, once the lure had got to the depth that I wanted, I would start my retrieve. After three turns of the handle, I would give a twitch. Then, another three turns of the handle, then, a twitch. That will have you twitching the lure about 7 to 10 times on any given retrieve. That's the magic number.

That spot was on fire today! A few Pro reports subscribers showed up out there, and that was awesome! Everybody that I saw caught fish, and that's not always the case when you're bank fishing with a bunch of other people. It has a lot to do with this spot, these fish aren't highly pressured just yet, get out there and get you some while this weather is really cold, they love it!

title: Trip Report #115
content_raw:
The hot new crappie spot...
Yesterday, I found a really good bank fishing spot for crappie. I was out in my boat, using my forward facing sonar, to look for crappie on limestone cliffs. I came across a spot that was not only loaded, but had lots of nice keeper size crappie. I could see from my boat, that someone had been fishing from the bank. Today, I figured out how they get there, and it's not that hard! It's pretty far, you have to walk half a mile. The first half of the trip is on a trail through the woods and the second half of the trip can be a little treacherous. You'll have to do about a quarter of a mile on the exposed lake bed. Fortunately, it's all rocks and cliffs, but some of it is loose, and there's definitely a trip and fall hazard. I'm going to drop you a pin, where you need to stand...
https://goo.gl/maps/RwrXGd6DVvpZXHrHA
Next you need to know where to park. On the side of Weekly Lane, there are two pull offs, if you are traveling north, before you get to Fate Sanders Bridge. The first pull off is where you need to park. I will drop you a pin, right here...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/UTDkQ7sPEbvSvx4L8
Now you need to know how to get to the proper spot. Once you've parked here, there is a trail that goes straight to the water's edge. Straight is a relative term, it kind of curves a little bit left and right. You have to go down a hill. Then you have to go up a hill. Then you're still not there. It's about a quarter of a mile through the woods. Once you get to the edge of the lake, that's when you just walk along the exposed lake bed. That's the quickest way to get to where you're going. I wouldn't worry too much about fishing in between, I didn't see any fish anywhere but this one particular spot. At one point, you kind of have to shimmy along the edge of the cliff. If you're not fleet of foot, you could fall in the lake! Once you get there, you will know you are in the right spot, because there was a fire pit in the crack in the limestone, and I took one of the logs and stood it up as a marker. I put it in the video that comes out tomorrow, so you would know exactly what you are looking for.
Now all you have to do is fish! These fish were pretty deep. They were deep when I found them yesterday, and they were deep when I caught them today. Here's how I got to them. Using my ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a 2-inch pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad, I would cast my lure out as far as I could, about 70 ft, and allow it to sink for 13 seconds. That was the magic number for the first 2 hours. 13 seconds. After I caught several fish at that depth, I wasn't getting any more bites. At that point, I started to count down to 15 seconds and then, 17 seconds, and then, eventually, 20 seconds. I was able to catch fish at every depth. If I waited longer than 20 seconds, The lure would hit the bottom or get hung up in the trees that these fish were hanging in.
Full disclosure, someone else knows that these crappie are there. I found some 2-inch Bobby Garland that someone had left behind. Someone knows about it, but not many people! It's way too far for most people to want to walk, and there's not a parking lot. Only a few little spots in the mud. This is one of those hidden gems, that won't get blown up, because most people won't put in the effort. Now that you know where to park and you know where you're headed, and you know how to catch them, I'm going to draw you a map, just to make sure you know exactly how to get there. The zig zags aren't accurate, I just tried to give some representation of the fact that it's not a straight path through the woods, to the water's edge. Once you reach the water's edge, just walk down the bank.

title: Trip Report #116
content_raw:
Some crappie spots out of Stewart Creek boat ramp...
Yesterday, I took my boat out midday from Stewart Creek boat ramp...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/ZHnLSAsQGIofsogRN
The courtesy dock is laying on the ground, so if you're going to launch your boat at this location, you're going to have to put it on the boat ramp. This boat ramp isn't very steep, but you can back way up if you need to. Make sure to bring your muck boots. I almost got my feet wet getting back into my car. It is currently viable as a boat ramp, but it's just not very steep. It's also subject to a west wind, which is the type of wind we usually have. Yesterday, with the wind that was blowing off the lake, it was tough to get the boat back on the trailer. All things to consider when using this boat ramp.
There were crappie everywhere! This area of the lake has lots of limestone cliffs that hold crappie when the weather gets really cold. Here's why. When the water starts to drop in temperature, crappie wants to know they can go somewhere that doesn't fluctuate too much. When they are on these cliffs, they can easily move up or down in the water column to make themselves more comfortable. Typically that means, most of the crappie will have moved out of the shallow parts of the lake, in favor of these deeper cliffs. With the weather that we have forecasted, it should be like this for at least another two or three weeks. At that point in time, crappie will be fully pre-spawn. When that happens, they will seek out food over comfortability, and that will have them moving all over the lake.
Right now, they're sticking tight to the cliffs! As you drive your boat out of the cove where Stewart Creek boat ramp is, the cliffs on the left are where most people fish for crappie. Those clips had people fishing there, so I just assumed crappie were there. I went to the other side and started dropping pins for you guys, here's how I figure out where to drop a pin...
As I'm using my forward facing sonar to scan toward the bank where the cliffs are, I look for schools of fish that are hanging tight together on structure, or against the cliff face. When I see what looks like crappie, I drop my anchor, and try to catch one. If I can catch one crappie, I can confirm what I am seeing, and I will drop a pin to let you guys know where I found them. As soon as I started looking, I started finding crappie. The biggest school that I saw all day was right there at the bank at Stewart Creek boat ramp. Unfortunately, even though I caught nine fish off of that pile, only two of them were keepers. Here was the best spot that I found to stand on the bank, and try to catch these fish...
https://goo.gl/maps/14yaFCmJHZo4ngy27
It's a long walk from the parking lot. You'll have to go over the bridge, to the end of the sidewalk, and then walk through the trail in the woods. Fortunately, once you get there, there's a pretty good place to stand. It's relatively flat, albeit a little muddy. There were hundreds of crappie in this spot, and I saw them there several months ago before we got into this winter pattern. This is a hotspot! You could use any number of methods, including a minnow under a bobber, but I would use a tight line. An ultra light rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament. To make sure I got the lure far enough, so that I can cast across those fish, and bring it back through them, I would use a 1/32nd ounce jig head. Any type of 2 in soft plastic will do, but I prefer a pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad.
I wanted to find some bigger fish. This pile of fish was large, but the fish in the pile were not. I went around the corner, upstream on the lake, to look for more piles of crappie. I had dropped you guys a pin before, underneath the bridge on weekly lane. There's a place under the bridge where young people cliff jump and rope swing out into the lake. Don't do that! It looks like people fish underneath that bridge from the bank, but I don't know how they get the fish up! It is a really tall, sheer cliff, and I would be afraid to fish up there. Yesterday, there were two boats sitting under the bridge, fishing for crappie against that cliff. I can't confirm to you that crappie were there, but I have caught them there before, and there were two people sitting there, so the math adds up.
As I passed under the bridge, I could see the bend in the river between Fate Sanders recreation area and Lamar Hill boat ramp. That bend in the river has a tall cliff, and every single time I've ever been out on that lake, there have been guys over there crappie fishing. You know they are crappie fishing, because they are spider rigging. If you're not familiar with spider rigging, basically, they have half a dozen rod holders on the front of their boat and they put a whole bunch of lines out off the front and troll around with Bobby Garland's. That was one of the most effective ways to get crappie, before the advent of forward facing sonar.
There were three boats out there, but they were in the wrong spot. People typically fish the mud flat on the inside of the bend in the river. As you can imagine, the outside of the bend in the river, or, channel swing, is limestone rock, that turns, what used to be, the river. Now it's a spot on the lake that people refer to as a channel swing. As we already discussed, those fish are on those cliffs! I don't doubt that some fish have made their way over to the mud flats and are hanging on underwater timber. But the majority of the fish are on those cliffs, where they feel more comfortable. So I started slowly trolling along the cliffs using my forward facing sonar. I came to one spot that had a lot of crappie, but I have told you guys about this spot before. You can park on the side of weekly Lane to get there...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/AGqBVX44dy2QvMD27
There's a trail through the woods, until the trail ends. Most people don't go to this spot, because they don't know about it. You will know you are in the right place, because there will be two trees that are in the water to your left. Cast out in front of you, with a slow retrieve, there are plenty of crappie, most of them hanging close to the cliff that you are standing on. Fortunately, most of this cliff is under water, so it's really easy to get the fish in. I've actually gone to this spot on foot before, and had great success! It's a good place to go when the wind is coming out of the west, because this location faces due east. That will try to keep some of the wind off you as you fish.
As I continued scanning from this location, upstream, it was a long way before I found the next pile of crappie! I was starting to wonder if this cliff was going to hold them. Here was the problem, for more than a quarter of a mile, the cliff didn't have any underwater structure, other than rock face. What you need in that situation, is some underwater timber to be stuck against the cliffs. That's where they load up. From the pin that I just dropped until the pin that I'm about to drop, there was nothing! But this next spot, was the motherload. There weren't very many fish there, but all of them were big!
https://goo.gl/maps/d5KrZEh9Z8Q7gQhw6
There were two distinct underwater structures in this location. There was a crack in the limestone that had gathered up a bunch of underwater timber. As you're facing the wall, the timber that was stuck in the crack was loaded with big crappie. I was casting all the way to the cliff! Sometimes my lure would hit the cliff! Straight down was where those fish were. I caught a bunch of nice keepers! Just to the right of that pile, there's another underwater brush pile that is loaded with fish! When the fish I was targeting would quit biting, I would cast to my right and catch some of those smaller ones. This is truly a magical spot on Percy Priest lake!
The craziest thing, someone has been bank fishing there. That place is in the middle of nowhere! It's an unbelievable spot, so it's worth the hike, but hike from where? I'm not sure, but there was a fire pit in that crack. I'm going to figure out how they got there, and draw you guys a map!

title: Trip Report #117
content_raw:
One of my favorite trout stocking locations...
Yesterday, I extended an invitation to you guys to join me in Lewisburg at Big Rock Greenway...
https://goo.gl/maps/keUxUgSxHvXeUiReA
You can park right there, and you are where you need to be! Just make sure not to fish off the bridge. There is a bridge that gives you access to both sides of the creek, fishing on the bridge is strictly prohibited. They dumped 300 trout, and most of them are still in there. That would be a good place to go today, if you are so inclined, or you could come meet me at Nice Mill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/sQdgjH1Ub1Hi4kTo7
I'll be in the parking lot waiting for the trout to show up at 9:00 a.m. I'm going to wear my waders, because the water is a little higher than it has been the last few years when they stock at this location. They usually show up just before 10:00 a.m.
I'm going to take my four and a half foot ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament. That's a small fishing pole that makes little fish fight real big! I'm going to start off with a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail. That's probably going to be the only lure I will need. These fish come right out of the truck ready to eat, and they usually bring at least 1,000 of them. At the last event, last month, they brought 1500.
Today is Friday January 16th, and this Pro report is going out at 7:15 in the morning. I will probably be down there until 11:00 a.m. or maybe even 12:00 p.m., depending on how late the truck arrives. I'd be happy to say hello, and meet and fish with any of you that would like to come out.

title: Trip Report #118
content_raw:
Lots of different fish below Center Hill dam!
This morning, I went to fish at the steps below Center Hill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/K6LqUw8ePm9VAUKy9
You can park right where I dropped that pin, and fish by the dam. I went this morning from 7:00 a.m. to 11:00 a.m. because that's when the generators were on. In my opinion, the best time to fish from the steps, is during the winter, while the generators are on. To find the generating schedule, you can look here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
There were lots of people on the steps today and usually, people just catch trout. Today, lots of different species were caught, and it's been like that, for the last few days. The hot lure has been a spoon. Ranging in size from 1/2 of an ounce to one whole ounce. Lots of different colors have been effective, but the most effective have been silver or gold. I can tell you how I fish a spoon at the steps, but there really is no wrong way. I like to use my 7 ft medium action bass rod with 10 lb braid, and make long casts. As soon as the spoon hits the surface, I like to twitch it up into the water column and then allow it to flutter back down while I'm quickly reeling out the slack that is being created as the lure works its way downstream.
This week catches that weren't trout include, but we're not limited to, walleye, sauger, and even slab crappie! Several different bass, spotted, and big largemouth bass! Most of these fish are considered a by-catch, as everyone is fishing for trout. As far as I'm concerned, once the generators turn off, the fishing is done. At that point in time, I headed back home to get some lunch, and then went out for round two in the rain at the spring on Percy Priest Lake...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/EwhLRdpenr5FhXt27
To get to the spring, you have to park on the side of Maddox road. There's plenty of parking off the side of the road, but it's a little bumpy, and a lot muddy right now! There's a trail, but you'll have to go over, under, or around the gate. That gate is to stop vehicles, not people! I can assure you, this is all very public property! Park on the side of the road, here...
https://goo.gl/maps/BEa154cRnUczyGTm6
I had one thing on my mind, a crappie dinner. Using my 6 ft ultralight rod and reel, instead of my seven and a half foot, so that I could keep my line down a little bit out of the wind, I went to work. I started with my favorite, a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a 2-inch pearl colored Bobby garland. They did not like that. So I cut the weight in half! I went to a 1/64th of an ounce jig head with the same Bobby Garland. That would be the number that would put me a handful of crappie on the bank, and a few in the bucket, but that's a really tough way to get these fish!
First of all, you can't cast that lure very far. It takes forever to sink, and as soon as you start to reel it, it comes back really fast, so you have to reel, super slow. When I say super slow, I mean barely visible movement of your hand. I'm going to release this video at 6:00 p.m. today. I left a couple examples in the video, where I wasn't speaking, after I had casted, showing exactly how patient I had to be with the reel. It's torture, but sometimes it's the only way you can get these crappie.
For those of you who want to brave the cold tomorrow January 15th, there is a trout stocking event at Big Rock Greenway in Lewisburg Tennessee...
https://goo.gl/maps/G8aieSHHDWBNnsev9
I plan on getting there at around 8:30 in the morning. That's usually a little early, they typically don't show up until closer till 10:00. But I have fomo. Fear of missing out. I want to make sure I'm there when the trout truck shows up. It's a lot of fun! Hope to see you there.

title: Trip Report #119
content_raw:
The steps at Center Hill Dam and a new crappie pile on Percy Priest...
Today I got to double dip. I made it to Center Hill Dam to fish for trout at 5:00 a.m. sharp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/s8qM33jRnV95Ui1o9
There's a parking lot for us right here by the bathroom, but for the first time in my life, the bathroom is closed for the winter. That's a bummer. The closest bathroom that is open is across the river, on top of the dam, at the observation area. That's important to know, because if I'm going to this location, I'd like to be there for quite a while. It's a long drive out there, and if you're going to make the effort, it's nice to stay and do a significant amount of fishing. That's exactly what I did today. I was there for 5 hours from 5:00 a.m. till 10:00 a.m.
The fishing was surprising today. I wasn't surprised that we caught fish. We caught lots of different species of fish, from the steps. That's pretty uncommon, usually, trout will be all that you catch. Today, there were lots of different species in that heavy current. A total of six. Brown trout, rainbow trout, drum, rock bass, sauger and spotted bass we're all caught on spoons in that heavy current. Here's how we got them...
I was using my 7 ft medium action bass rod. It's one of my favorite fishing poles for bass, because the reel has 10 pound braid. That braid allows you to cast a really long way. It also allows you to put a lot more line on the spool. You're going to need a lot of line when you're standing on the steps at Center Hill dam. You need to cast really far, and it's pretty far down to the waters surface.
When I'm using a spoon at Center Hill dam, I usually stand in the middle of the steps. Not at the top, and not at the bottom. When you're right in the middle, I feel like it's the best place to be. You can easily cast a little bit upstream, and then allow your spoon to sink for a couple of seconds before you twitch that thing up in the water column. Then, you allow it to sink for a couple of seconds, and then twitch it up into the water column. This is a yo-yo technique, and you want to yo-yo that spoon right out in front of those fish. Once the lure has passed in front of you, it will start to lift up in the current and make its way to the surface. At that point, reel in quickly, and make another cast.
That's what we did today for 5 hours! The video is going to look like we had a fantastic day of fishing, because it's only going to be 20 minutes. In reality, it took the two of us, 5 hours each, so if you want to look at it that way, there were 10 man hours, put in, trying to get a couple of handful of fish. Just to give you some barometer of what type of success you should expect, that's a pretty good day of fishing on the steps at Center Hill dam. It could be a lot worse, but it could be a lot better.
One thing to note, you're going to want to flirt with the bottom with that spoon. Occasionally, it's going to get hung up on the bottom, and you're going to break off. The bottom is very rocky, and it's also loaded with other people's lures, and lines. Pack your patience!
The generators turned off at Center Hill Dam at 10:00 a.m. When that happens, the river drops dramatically and the surface goes calm and still. It's a great time to fish, but I had my fill of chasing trout, so I headed back to Murfreesboro. You can find the generating schedule, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
After lunch, I went out in my boat at West Fork boat ramp...
https://share.google/YfwjrhHpyMCqzKtuq
I got on the water just before 1:00 and I headed directly to the confluence to see if those fish were still in front of that fish attractor. I caught a couple of crappie, and that was all I needed to see. There are still crappie in this location...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/PoDyXiePRUrxxmiR7
That spot is actually at the confluence. Right where the two rivers come together. There is a fish attractor that the TWRA has installed. It is a wooden stake bed. It is currently out of water, but directly in front of it, about 10 ft, there is a tree underwater that stays loaded with crappie. Each time I've been to this location, I've not only seen crappie on that underwater tree with my forward facing sonar, but I have caught them. From there, I headed upstream on the East Fork Stones river.
The water temperature at the surface was 53°. That's still really warm! As I was headed upstream, the depth in the center was right around 20 ft. I didn't see any crappie on my way upstream, and I thought that was bizarre! The old riverbed, underwater about 20 ft, is loaded with underwater trees! It's like a forest down there! But those trees didn't hold any fish. Eventually, I made my way up to the water intake plant...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/b1SAX2bqBqGhT2PF6
This is a place where lots of people fish from the bank! I could tell, because there's a lot of trash. It looks like, if you're careful, you can cast right into where the water intake is. The whole area is completely covered up with debris. The way it's constructed, the structure gathers trees and logs right there where people are fishing. They are definitely crappie fishing! Those logs were loaded with crappie, but I couldn't get in there to catch them. That was one of those situations where, you probably needed a bobber and a minnow.
In the same bend in the river, there was one of my favorite places to look for crappie. A cliff that came to a sudden end, and turned into a slowly sloping mud bank. That is known as a transition, and crappie love spots like that! Sure enough, this spot was loaded, and, you can get to this spot from the bank. I don't know the exact trail through the woods, but you can park at East Fork boat ramp and get to the bank in front of this spot...
https://goo.gl/maps/bmEJjEFAcNxC2kHi9
When I got to this spot, it was right around 2:30, and the fish were particularly active. They get that way until about 3:30, when the light starts to get low. I found these fish, and then proceeded to beat them up. Relatively quickly, I caught nine crappie. If you've been reading my reports recently, you know that I have been catching one or two fish off of any given pile, and then having to relocate. I attribute their willingness to bite to the time of day. Unfortunately, only two of those crappie were keeper size, but that pile was huge! If you're going to try to get there from the bank, I can tell you where to stand, but like I said, I haven't walked a trail through there just yet.
You'll know you're standing in the right spot when you see a concrete picnic table directly behind you. I believe it said it was number one. There was a black number on the side of the picnic table. It look like the area was relatively cleared out. There is a tall rock over top of the water and if you are standing, looking straight out the lake, at a 90° angle, you need to cast 45° to your right. That will have you casting a little bit upstream. You need to be casting about 40 ft away. That will allow you to retrieve your lure over top of, and through this pile. Eventually, I'll get out there and draw you guys a map. I think this could be a really good spot!

title: Trip Report #120
content_raw:
Crappie hot spots...
I didn't fish today, instead, I opted to tour some of the better bank fishing spots that I know for crappie. I took my bucket, my garbage picker, and some black trash bags, and cleaned up a few different places. My intention, see where people were, and what they were catching. I didn't want to sit in one spot for very long and fish. I wanted to spot hop and see which places were doing better. I started at Vivrett Creek boat ramp...
https://share.google/sNscuGq2nNvjzptuT
You can fish right at the boat ramp. You can also walk the bank way out into the lake. The whole entire area has good fishing. But there is a hotspot, if you walk along the bank, a little more than a quarter mile. There is a place where the TWRA has positioned fish attractors under the water. They are even underwater this time of year! That makes them fantastic for crappie fishing from now until the end of April. I'm going to drop you a pin in Google maps of the location, but you will know you are there, because there is a buoy that marks the fish attractor. It is a standard red and white buoy with a picture of a fish. Stand there, and fish in that area, for crappie...
https://goo.gl/maps/8tomGPfxFv8FnLs49
When I got there today, there were a handful of people who had some nice crappie on their stringers and in their buckets. This place really gets fired up around February, but it's nice to see those fish there in early January. It's a good place to go right now, and in the future, but the next place that I went was on fire! I headed over to the southernmost part of Long Hunter State Park at Bryant Grove boat ramp...
https://share.google/9Drr6fFlBZjmUYUCq
At this location, if you go to the right of the boat ramp, you can walk along the bank, but these rocks are really big boulders. So you kind of have to be careful. There is good fishing all the way along this bank! But the best fishing, is for crappie, and you want to walk, once again, a little more than a quarter mile. You will know that you are in the right spot when you see a white cross on the cliffs. Don't go to the cross, fish just on this side of it. There was a bunch of trash where people were catching crappie, but I cleaned all that up. You will know you are in the right spot, there will be other people there! The crappie that I saw in those buckets today were fantastic! Also, they had several white bass as well as a nice big hybrid!
From there, I headed over to Spring Creek spring...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/5jcf96pFkBjnvbqY8
There's no parking lot for this location, you'll have to park on the side of Maddox road...
https://goo.gl/maps/jKJn3DDWtsFdXKpKA
There's a trail, you guessed it, a little more than a quarter of a mile, to the crappie hole. When I got down there, the water was a little brown, but there were a few guys and they had nice crappies on their stringer! They had one thing in common with each of the people at the other locations, no one was using minnows! Everyone was using 2-in soft plastics, most of them Bobby Garland's. Seems like everybody had a different color, but everybody had fish! Most people were casting as far as they could, and using a slow retrieve. Some people were using a bobber with a fixed depth of about 3 ft.
Bottom line, you've got to get out to these locations, early and often! Looks like the colder weather is here to stay, and that means these spots will heat up.

title: Trip Report #121
content_raw:
Where crappie go after a heavy, late winter rain...
Yesterday, middle Tennessee was experiencing some light river flooding due to heavy rains. When conditions are right, those flood waters call to crappie like a sirens song. When they get moving fast, and they get really brown, for some reason, crappie move up! They will do that, after each heavy rainfall, from now until April. They are literally following bait fish so that they can fatten up for the spring spawn. When crappie spawn, males sit on the bed for a few days. They want to get big and bulky before that happens, so they race up these flooded rivers, and then they are easy to catch, at the base of low head dams.
I'm typing this out on Sunday morning, I just released a video on YouTube where I explained in great detail how to Target these fish. What I'm going to do for you here, is drop pins on these locations and explain how to get to these fish. Where are they below the dams, and where do you need to stand. The first location I always go to, is one of the best, Nice Mill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/Wckbcvkyt7fJSA1T7
There are two parking lots at this dam, one on either side of the river. It's best to park in this parking lot, on the high side. Walk through the woods, on the trail provided at the end of the parking lot, just a short way, only a couple hundred feet! Then you can stand on the cliffs that overhang the river. The current will be flowing fast underneath your feet, but you can cast across the current, to the slack water, where crappie stack up in great numbers! title: Trip Report #122
content_raw:
The most exciting hour of fishing...
Today, TWRA dropped 1,000 rainbow trout below Percy Priest Dam...
Dodson Chapel Access Area https://share.google/jJn8n3R9Rb9r9UuHR
I got there just before 9:00 a.m. That's what I typically do for these trout stocking events, just to make sure I don't miss the dump. I want to be there when they put the fish in the river so that I can get it on video. So I sat there, for about 2 hours, until 10:45, when not only the trout truck showed up, but so did a whole bunch of other fishermen. Before then, I was pretty much by myself. So I asked someone, how did they get there right when the truck did? They said, at this location, they usually show up right before 11:00. Good to know!
I had my 4 and 1/2 ft ultralight with 4 lb monofilament. I only needed one lure today. One, 1/8 of an ounce, white rooster tail. For some reason, at this location, that is the lure! I was up there one month ago, when they stocked at this spot, and it was the same way on that day. The fish come right out of the tube, ready to eat a rooster tail. They may eat some type of fly, I've never taken my fly rod. They always eat a rooster tail.
I always stand right where the tube goes into the river. It seems like the fish hang out in that area for at least the first hour after they come out of the tube. After that, they start to spread out, and become more difficult to catch. During that first hour, it's absolutely magical! There were about 12 to 15 people there today, and fish were coming in left and right! These fish ranged in size from 8 inches to as big as 12 inches in length.
After about an hour of catching those fish, the bite died down. So I went home to Murfreesboro to get some lunch, and then I loaded up my boat for round 2 this afternoon. We got a whole bunch of rain last night, and I wanted to get out to the lake on the southern, shallow end, where I had been catching crappie for the last couple weeks, to take advantage of what I thought would be good fishing, just before those flood waters reach the lake. I put in at West Fork boat ramp at around 2:00 p.m...
I looked around right there at the boat ramp, with my forward facing sonar, but I didn't see any crappie! There were fish hanging out on the structure that usually hold crappie, but I caught a couple of those fish, and they were white bass. So I headed downstream to the confluence of the East Fork and West Fork Stones River to see if the fish that were right at the confluence on Wednesday, we're still there today...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/jM5qKyPXpgGw9SqF7
This location couldn't be any easier for you guys to find. It's right at the confluence, and there is a fish attractor right there! It is a TWRA installed, wooden stake bed. Right now, it is out of the water, but directly in front of it, the water is 15 ft deep and there are two trees that are loaded with crappie! I pulled in there, caught one, and then called over another gentleman who was in a boat nearby. He called a couple of his friends, and they came over in their boat. The three of us sat there on that fish attractor and everybody caught slab crappie! We had a good window from about 2:30 to 3:30. And then the bite completely died.
Getting these fish was really difficult! I'm going to do my best to try to explain it, just so people understand, I probably wouldn't have caught them without forward facing sonar...
Basically, I know where these fish are. I can see them on my forward facing sonar, but I've got a few different conditions to deal with. At the time, I was sitting just inside the mouth of East Fork Stones River. The flow from last night's rain was coming from the West Fork Stones River and it was heading out towards the lake, but it was also backfilling the East Fork Stones.
The current was causing my 1/32nd of an ounce jig head to move off the pile of fish. I could see that on the screen. So my first adjustment was to add a split shot, about 8 inches above my jig. That would help me get down quicker, so I could move my lure through the fish. But that causes it to move much more quickly. They did not like that. What does that mean, "they did not like that"? I could see that my lure was going through the pile of fish, but I wasn't getting a bite. That's not typical for crappie. It was just going too fast.
My next move would be the one that paid off. I removed that split shot, and I started casting a little up current of the fish. I would allow the lure to sink for about 10 seconds. That would get it down to their level. It took me a few different casts, to figure out the positioning, exactly. But once I knew where to cast, so that my jig would sink down into these fish, I was not only able to catch a couple slab keepers, but I was able to tell the other guys in their boat, where they could cast, and they caught nice slabs as well!
Right around 4:00 p.m. this afternoon, the heavy rain that fell this morning in Murfreesboro had made its way to where I was at the confluence. I could see a field of debris coming down the river! There were logs, lots of leaves, and a good bit of trash. The current got wicked, and pushed back against the West Fork, sending it the other direction! That got me looking at the internet to see how much rain fell on each river basin. As it turns out, the West Fork Stones River basin got a lot less rain than the East Fork Stones did. Here's how I found that information. First, I looked at the discharge on the USGS website for the West Fork Stones River. You can find that information, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D
As I'm writing this report at 6:30 on Friday night, the CFS is 365. Cubic feet per second, or cfs, is how we measure the flow of rivers. Basically, one cubic foot, is the size of one basketball. So there were 365 cubic feet of water pushing out of West Fork that were flowing up into East Fork, until the rainfall that fell in the East Fork Stones River basin, made its way to the confluence. That River basin is much larger, and much farther away from the confluence. You can find information about the flow on the East Fork Stones river, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03427500/all-graphs/#period=P7D
As I'm typing out this report, the flow on East Fork Stones River is 2660! That's enough to mess up all the fishing that I have been doing in this area for the last couple of weeks! As I was leaving this evening, I could see not only lots of debris, but lots of brown water. This end of the lake had just gotten cleared out from the last rain event, and it's likely going to be a couple of weeks before it's cleared up again. I'm not 100% sure where the crappie will be after this flooding happens on this end of the lake, but I will look for them, and let you guys know.

title: Trip Report #123
content_raw:
Happy trapped bass...
Yesterday, I took my kayak upstream from Manson Pike trailhead...
https://share.google/UwQRPdouwJj6Ui1ea
There is a kayak launch at this trailhead, but it won't put you on these fish. To get to these fish, you need to go above Ransom Mill Dam...
Ransom's Mill Dam https://share.google/jzMJ891vNbcSQqzpF
To do that, you need your kayak to be on wheels. I have a kayak cart that allows me to roll my kayak anywhere I would like. To get above Ransom Mill Dam, you'll have to follow the map I've drawn for you and left in the pictures.
Starting on the greenway, in the parking lot, and going upstream, there will be a bridge that goes over the river. Go right, off the greenway, just before the bridge. Now you can walk through this grassy area to a nice spot to launch your kayak! It's directly across from the mouth of a creek, and there's really good fishing right there. There's really good fishing everywhere in this stretch of river! Because you have to put in a little bit of effort to get there, most people don't go there to fish.
The day I had yesterday was not indicative of a typical day on that stretch of river. I'm certain that there are an overwhelming amount of bass in there, because I have seen them. But I have not had a good day catching fish there, like I did yesterday. My main focus when I go to this stretch of river, paddle a couple of miles upstream until I get to Old Fort golf course. When I get there, I can help myself to all the golf balls I would like.
On my way up I was using a spinnerbait, one of my favorite lures on that stretch of river. Those largemouth bass really react well to that lure. But they weren't reacting well to it yesterday. I had fished for at least 30 to 45 minutes before I finally got something to bite on that spinnerbait. That's when I realized, it may be a little too big. This time of year, a bass' metabolism has slowed down with the cooler weather, and they usually don't eat big meals, because those are hard to digest. So I downsized to a quarter of an ounce white rooster tail. I put that on my medium action bass Pole that had 8 lb monofilament. That was the perfect setup!
It wasn't long before I hooked into my first nice spotted bass of the day. Then another. Then another! Then a chunky smallmouth. At that point, I found myself up at the golf course, where I had some lunch, collected some golf balls, and then turned around to do some intent fishing. I had the right lure on, and I had a couple of miles of river downstream, ahead of me, with the wind at my back.
Yesterday afternoon could not have went better for bass fishing on the Stones river. If you watch today's video, you're going to see exactly how everything played out, but I'm going to explain it right here. Basically, I was using my rooster tail to make long casts, to try to catch fish before they knew I was in their area. When I would cast into a particularly good looking spot, if I didn't get a bite, I would set that rod and reel down and pick up my other bass pole that had a peanut butter jelly Ned rig. Basically, this is just a soft plastic that you fish on the bottom like a plastic worm. When I saw a spot that I thought a fish should be, but I didn't get a bike, I would follow up with my soft plastic.
I would cast into the spot, and allow the lure to sink to the bottom. Then I would lift my rod tip up and give the lure a little jiggle on the bottom. Typically, that's all it will take! If you're lure is in their vicinity, they will come out and scoop it up within a few seconds. That's the way it was yesterday! Big largemouth bass we're eating on the bottom. My confidence lure in situations like that is a peanut butter jelly Ned rig. Any type of creature bait or plastic worm on the bottom would work for these fish! Just fish it slow. When you cast it into their area, allow it to sit on the bottom and just twitch around for a few seconds. Maybe even half a minute. Before you reel it in and throw it to another spot.
So there's a catch to fishing at this spot... the water has to be right. Yesterday, the river was low and slow. That made it really easy for me to paddle all the way upstream. The rain that is falling right now, is going to make the river swell, and it will be flowing fast, and it will be brown. It will take several days for the water level to low enough for it to be a viable place to fish. It would take more than a week and a half of no rain to get back to the level that I experienced yesterday. The water level yesterday was 62 cubic feet per second. That's just about as low as that river ever gets! To find the river level, and the cubic feet per second, look here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D
My phone is filled with pins that look like this one. Water monitoring stations that paint a picture of what the water looks like before I ever had that way. That's how I decide where I'm going to go fishing. Except for days like today. Today, the TWRA is stocking trout below Percy Priest Dam in Nashville...
Dodson Chapel Access Area https://share.google/PSMxQsxMkqBE4132b
I happen to know from experience, the TWRA needs the dam to release water to be able to put these trout in the river. So I was able to look at the generating schedule at Percy Priest Dam and determine that they will be stocking those trout today between 9:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. because that's when the generating schedule will allow them to do it. To find the generating schedule, you can look here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/j-percy-priest
I like to go to these events because the fish are easy to catch and I get lots of views when I film there. It's a win-win for me! So I will be there today, rain or shine. Looks like it may be a little rainy. I will probably get there a few minutes before 9:00, just to make sure I can be there when the trout truck arrives. I don't want to miss any of the action! All of you are welcome to join me, this is a large location, and there's plenty of room for everybody. Bring your ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/8 of an ounce roostertail. I like a white rooster tail, but any rooster tail with a silver blade will work today. Hope I see you out there!

My confidence lure in situations like that is a peanut butter jelly Ned rig. Any type of creature bait or plastic worm on the bottom would work for these fish! Just fish it slow. When you cast it into their area, allow it to sit on the bottom and just twitch around for a few seconds. Maybe even half a minute. Before you reel it in and throw it to another spot.

So there's a catch to fishing at this spot... the water has to be right. Yesterday, the river was low and slow. That made it really easy for me to paddle all the way upstream. The rain that is falling right now, is going to make the river swell, and it will be flowing fast, and it will be brown. It will take several days for the water level to low enough for it to be a viable place to fish. It would take more than a week and a half of no rain to get back to the level that I experienced yesterday. The water level yesterday was 62 cubic feet per second. That's just about as low as that river ever gets! To find the river level, and the cubic feet per second, look here...

https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D

My phone is filled with pins that look like this one. Water monitoring stations that paint a picture of what the water looks like before I ever had that way. That's how I decide where I'm going to go fishing. Except for days like today. Today, the TWRA is stocking trout below Percy Priest Dam in Nashville...

Dodson Chapel Access Area https://share.google/PSMxQsxMkqBE4132b

I happen to know from experience, the TWRA needs the dam to release water to be able to put these trout in the river. So I was able to look at the generating schedule at Percy Priest Dam and determine that they will be stocking those trout today between 9:00 a.m. and 1:00 p.m. because that's when the generating schedule will allow them to do it. To find the generating schedule, you can look here...

<https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/j-percy-priest>

I like to go to these events because the fish are easy to catch and I get lots of views when I film there. It's a win-win for me! So I will be there today, rain or shine. Looks like it may be a little rainy. I will probably get there a few minutes before 9:00, just to make sure I can be there when the trout truck arrives. I don't want to miss any of the action! All of you are welcome to join me, this is a large location, and there's plenty of room for everybody. Bring your ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/8 of an ounce roostertail. I like a white rooster tail, but any rooster tail with a silver blade will work today. Hope I see you out there!

title: Trip Report #124
content_raw:
11 hours on the water!
Today, I spent an unprecedented amount of time looking for crappie, upstream from the boat ramp at Jefferson Springs boat ramp...
https://share.google/KkR5x0MuWzkaO0ZR8
Crappie are still on the southern end of the lake, which is the shallow end of the lake. The water temperature, 53° this morning, 55 and a half degrees this afternoon. Really warm for this time of year! That's the reason they are so shallow. I'm convinced of it. They were doing their typical thing, schooling together. Typically, pretty large schools, at least 50 to 100 fish. They were hanging on submerged timber in 10 ft or less of water. They had to have at least 10 ft of depth to be comfortable, we didn't find them anywhere that was shallower than 10-ft. But when they did stack up on something underwater that was 10 ft deep, the pile would be stacked up as high as 5 ft from the surface.
Typically, when you find them like this, you can cast into those fish, with whatever method you like. A minnow on a bobber. A soft plastic on a lightweight jig, which is my favorite. Or even a jig under a bobber. There are lots of methods to get crappie once you find them. Most of the time, after you catch a few, they start to get wary. They become increasingly harder to catch, until they become so tight-lipped that, typically, most people will move on to another pile of fish. Today, when we found these fish, if we could pull one out, that would be it. It's not that the fish would quit biting, it's that they would completely move away from whatever structure they were sitting on!
They wouldn't move away slow. They would all get in a single file line, and start swimming away, rather rapidly. Fortunately for us, they would usually move to the next stump, or underwater structure, and then settle down. So today, what we had to do, was continuously move, chasing these fish. Consequently, I ended up with way more pins to drop for you guys! I'm just going to drop a whole bunch of pins on Google maps. Essentially, a road map of where the crappie are between Jefferson Springs boat ramp and the confluence of the East Fork and West Fork Stones river. That was as far as we made it today, before we turned around, and called it a day.
I think it's important to note, when I first started coming out to this boat ramp, at the beginning of fall, when we still had summer heat, crappie were stacked on the cliff. Since then, I haven't seen them on any of the cliffs at all. I have continued to scan the cliffs, each time I have been out, but right now, looking at the rock walls that extend underwater is a waste of time. These fish are not sitting on rock structures! Every single time we found crappie today, they were on the mud flats.
So what's a mudflat? I'll try to explain it. This is a narrow section of the lake. Basically, it looks more like a river. There's not a whole lot of flow, so it functions like a lake. When you're sitting in the middle, you can easily see the bank on both sides. Almost always, one side will be a sheer cliff, that extends underwater, and the other side will be a slowly sloping mud bank. Mud as far as you can see, that used to be underwater, when the lake was up at summer pool. Those slowly sloping mud banks, eventually drop off into the old river channel. It's on those drop offs, sitting on submerged timber, where we found all of the crappie, not only today, but recently.
The only crappie that we found outside of that particular scenario, were the very first crappie that you come to when you leave the boat ramp, headed upstream. To go upstream, you have to go under the bridge at Jefferson Pike,that goes over the lake. Underneath that bridge, there are eight bridge pilings. Four on your left, and four on your right. All eight of them can hold fish, but the four on your right, are overwhelmingly loaded with crappie! They have been every time I've been out there for the last month.
From there, there are a few little pockets of fish in the next half mile. But nothing significant, and nothing that is there all the time. As I drop pins, working my way upstream, I'm going to point out the places where crappie are, every time I come through...
https://goo.gl/maps/d4znS9dxYUZFdTon8
That spot is where the cliff ends and a mud flat begins. That's a transition area. For some reason, crappie love these transitions! These fish were stacked up here this morning, when we went through, but we didn't fish for them. When we came back this afternoon, someone else in a boat was sitting there. Pretty safe to say, that's a good spot. I've even caught them from the bank. If you park on Jefferson pike, it's about a half mile hike through the woods to get to this spot. There's not really a good path, because most people don't know about this spot, so you'll have to just follow the pin on your phone. Be careful picking your way through the woods!
https://maps.app.goo.gl/e2zkUAmt87BKSmqE8
There are two fish attractors in this area that were installed by TWRA. These are wooden stakes that have been driven into the ground. They are marked with a tall PVC pipe that stands in the center of the stakes. In front of these, the water drops off to the old channel. On that drop off, there is some submerged timber that is stuck there. This is a fantastic place! I've seen lots of people fishing there. We came through there this afternoon, and we were able to confirm that it was loaded with crappie!
https://goo.gl/maps/jpDQoNxTLofb66PVA
This is stump row! At this spot, you can see timber that is partially submerged, and partially sticking out of the water. Out in front of each piece of timber or stick or stump that you see, crappie are loaded! In this area, I couldn't drop enough pins.
https://maps.app.goo.gl/CNqQJzX37ifjWruM8
Right as you get to the confluence, on the left, this spot was our most productive spot! It wasn't where we saw the most fish, but it was where we found the most active fish. Here, you could cast all the way to the bank! It was if the mud was making and underwater cliff. The mud drops straight off, and crappie were hanging out there, waiting to ambush prey. That was our most productive spot, but right around the corner, we found the biggest pile of fish we would see all day.
https://maps.app.goo.gl/pxPx9tDoNukV1Giq8
That entire Bank was loaded! For a hundred yards, up and down from the confluence, there are underwater trees, and all of them had crappie on them! They weren't just loaded with crappie, there were several other fishermen in boats there, but they were all targeting white bass. There were huge schools of tiny white bass swimming through this area and attacking anything that you were throwing. The bank on the other side was a slowly sloping mud bank, and it was loaded with crappie as well! I had heard tails about how good the crappie fishing was at that confluence, today was my first opportunity to find out. And find out we did! In total, on a tough day, we ended up with 14 crappie on the stringer. We probably caught around 40 total, with only those 14 being over 10 in, or keeper size, and probably 10 white bass, which we threw back.
Fishing will be fantastic on this stretch of lake until the heavy rainfall comes through on Friday. I can't say for sure what will happen in that area after that point in time, but the getting will be good until then!

title: Trip Report #125
content_raw:
A miniature Center Hill Dam...
Today, I made the pilgrimage out to Dale Hollow dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/NgEpnAC76GekX82S6
This is the boat ramp just below the dam that has the closest access. I took my kayak, because I didn't want to stand in the river in my waders. It's a darn good thing! This is not a good river to wade in. I would have assumed that it would be a lot like Center Hill dam, and you could walk the banks for miles. That is not the case! The banks are extremely steep and muddy, and the river, even though it's incredibly shallow, it's a little too deep to wade. It's really a tough place if you want to try to bank fish. I wouldn't suggest going out there without a kayak or a canoe or a boat.
If you're going out there, you're going to want to fish when the generators are off. I got there today at around 9:45. The generators turned off at 9:00 a.m. I timed my arrival so that when I got there, the water would be down, and I wouldn't have to fight any current. You can't always trust the generating schedule to be accurate, the water release schedule may change without notice. Typically, they stick to the schedule pretty religiously. You can find the generating schedule for Dale Hollow dam, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/dale-hollow
A quick lay of the land... I didn't find any water that was 6 ft deep. Most of it was three to five feet deep. The river is narrow from the boat ramp downstream. From the boat ramp upstream, the river is wide, but it gets increasingly shallower as you get near the dam. Once you get to the base of the dam, the ground is exposed! I would have assumed that there would at least be 10 to 15 feet of depth out in front of the dam. In some places, there's not even 10 to 15 inches of depth! The water is clear and today, it was 48°. You can see the bottom, and you can see the fish!
You won't see the type of fish that you see below Center Hill dam. The river is just too shallow and too narrow. There aren't going to be any sturgeon. You won't find crappie schooled up below the dam. I'm sure there's schools of bait fish that swim through, but I didn't see any today. It's mostly just a bunch of trout! I wouldn't be surprised if there were a few largemouth bass hanging around, they would be tucked into whatever nooks and crannies they could find. But I don't think you'd be able to fish for them. If you're going up there, it's best to target trout.
That's what I did. To start the day, I was using my 4 and 1/2 ft, ultra light rod and reel. That has 4 lb monofilament. I've been using Stren monofilament. It's really inexpensive and really strong! I like the clear color. That's pretty much it, other than my lure. Today, I had a 1/8 of an ounce yellow roostertail with a silver blade tied on. I never had to retie! The fish were biting really well from the time I showed up, until the time it started raining.
They stock the river every Friday. There is a creek on the property called hatchery creek. Dale Hollow national fish hatchery is one of the largest producers of trout in the state of Tennessee, if not the largest. When I say this river is loaded with fish, I mean it's overwhelmingly loaded with fish! When I first got there, there were fish taking flies off the surface everywhere! As far as I know, they stock the river with rainbow trout, cutthroat trout, and brown trout. They may stock it with Brook trout, but I don't think so.
I was able to catch a handful of brown trout just below the dam. Making long casts with my rooster tail, getting my rod tip straight up in the air, and using a retrieve that was just fast enough to keep the blade flipping, those fish were going crazy on my lure! They were hitting it so hard, that they were getting foul hooked. Each time I hook the trout, they would immediately jump out of the water and skip across the surface to try to spit that hook out, something that they did several times today.
There's not much area to explore up there! After paddling around below the dam, checking out everything, and catching a few fish, I was ready to go paddle up hatchery creek. There was only one problem, you can't paddle up hatchery creek. It's way too small. It's way too shallow, and it's way too muddy! When I saw that I wouldn't be able to kayak into the creek, I thought that, perhaps, I would walk up the banks. Upon closer inspection, the banks are super steep, and thick with slippery mud!
The only option was to climb up the bank of the river. At least when I got up there, I was in the parking lot. This parking lot is for patrons of the campground, which is closed right now. So if you wanted to drive to the creek, you wouldn't be able to. This is really the only way to access it, unless you walk through the campground. But I wouldn't recommend it! Once I got to the creek, I realized that the majority of it was either to swift, too shallow, or way too far downhill to access. There were a few different places where people had beaten a path to the water's edge to try to catch fish. But none of those places were ideal. I did find one little pocket, that was almost impossible to fish, and I pulled one out! It was the only rainbow trout of the day, but it was quite the accomplishment!
Some things you need to know before you go to Dale Hollow dam. The bathroom at the boat ramp is open! There is no light switch, it's motion activated. It was a little creepy going in at first, but the lights popped on, and the hot water works well! The boat ramp is really slippery. Mud gets piled up on it, so when I stepped out of my car, I almost fell. Be careful near the water's edge. You have to wear your life jacket from the boat ramp, all the way up to the dam. It's a long way! You can't actually see the dam from the boat ramp. I'd say it's a little less than a half mile paddle. It's about the same distance downstream to the creek.
MOST BOATS WON'T MAKE IT UP OR DOWN THIS RIVER WHEN THE WATER IS OFF!
It's just too shallow. I was paddling in my kayak when the ground came up to grab me! It comes up that quick. You can be moving right along, and then stopped. Unless you have a jet boat, I wouldn't recommend going out there when the water is off. You will get stuck. You may not even be able to get your boat off the trailer. If you can get it off, there's a good chance you won't get it back on. The water is really shallow at the end of the boat ramp. I can't say what the water would be like for a boat when the generators are turned on.
The Fish hatchery is open for tours during normal business hours. I didn't go take the tour, but I wish I would have!

title: Trip Report #126
content_raw:
Are there still stocked trout, weeks after the stocking event?
Yesterday I went to the West Fork Stones River at Nice Mill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/VjsPFqd5y3bsCq7Q9
A few weeks ago, the TWRA stocked 1,500 rainbow trout in this location. I happen to know from experience, that no matter how heavily pressured this location is, we just can't catch all those fish before they restock it again. But I wanted to go to catch a trout, just to make sure they were still in there. The water is really low, less than 100 cubic feet per second, and that makes it really easy to get at these fish! The flow of rivers is measured in cubic feet per second, which is about the size of one basketball. You can always check the internet to see the flow of the West Fork Stones river, here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03428200/all-graphs/#period=P7D
This is a fantastic location for people who want to use their waders. If you want to be in the water to catch these fish, the entire stretch of river in this area is no more than waist deep! That makes it ideal for fly fisherman and spin fishermen alike. I like to stay on the bank, I don't like to get in the water, because I can cast all the way across the river. If I wanted to use my fly rod, that's when I would get out in the water. When I'm using my spinning rod, I just stay on the bank. There's an unbelievable amount of bank to cover if you go downstream from the parking lot. There is a trail through the woods that literally goes for more than a mile!
Unfortunately, right now, there's a massive pile of debris on top of the dam. It makes it really hard to get out there and fish, because it's a giant pile of mangled up trees with trash and debris. It doesn't look like that pile of trees and limbs is going anywhere until the spring floods come to remove it. You can climb over those trees to try to fish on the dam, which is what I did, but I wouldn't recommend it. I followed the trail downstream to hit some of the more beautiful spots, a little more isolated away from people.
I had my four and a half foot ultra light rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail. That's my weapon of choice when I'm fishing this stretch of river. Cast it out as far as you can, get that rod tip directly up into the air, and start a slow retrieve that gets that silver blade flipping just under the surface. Most of the time, trout don't want a rooster tail moving very fast. They will let you know! If you're not getting any bites retrieving it slow, try speeding it up! If that doesn't work, it's time to change lures all together.
That's what I did yesterday. When I can't get them with a lure, I will switch to a better day setup. The way I've been catching these fish for over 30 years, is to put on a couple little split shots, and then about a foot below that, one number six eagle claw bait holder hook. On that hook, I put one Berkeley powerbait for trout. Lately, I've been using the color pink. After I put that one Powerball on, I slide it up the line, and then I add half a Canadian nightcrawler. Then I slide the pink ball back down, making a tasty looking little snack.
If you're going to fish this way, you're going to get hung up on the bottom, and it's going to break off. That's just part of it. But it's going to keep you in the strike zone longer, and you're going to catch more fish! Even if you just use a worm, you would be better off than using the lure that's not getting any attention. Fortunately for me, yesterday, those fish were more than willing to bite my better days set up. I got a few bites, rather quickly, and then landed a nice 10-in rainbow trout. That would be the only fish I would catch on the day, they were being particularly finicky. But I had the information I needed, those trout are still in there, near the dam, and easily accessible!

title: Trip Report #127
content_raw:
The most beautiful trip in Middle Tennessee?
Yesterday, I got an opportunity to kayak a stretch of river that is rarely exposed. The East Fork Stones River from Walter Hill Dam to Mona boat ramp is by far one of the most beautiful kayak trips that I do. It is a 5 and 1/2 mi, all day long, whitewater kayak trip. There are shallow water runs that can flip even the most advanced kayaker. The water is crystal clear and runs a little bit warm for this time of year. There are at least half a dozen Springs that feed the river as you float down. To get started, you want to launch your kayaks from below Walter Hill Dam...
https://share.google/zKQfegzBzSoEe4fUb
It's not easy to do. The parking lot is a long way from the water's edge. We carry our kayaks all the way to the water's edge, and then we launch from here. To get to Mona boat ramp, it's a full five and a half miles. Even though there is significant flow, this trip takes a minimum of 5 hours! If you're trying to do any fishing at all, you're only going to be able to cover ground at a pace of about 1 mph. Ideally, you would like to do this trip a lot slower! Take your time, stop along the way and have a picnic. There are tons of gravel banks that are exposed that make the perfect beach area to sit and enjoy a warm winter day.
So why did I say winter day? Who wants to sit outside and enjoy a winter day? To be honest with you, that's the only time of year you can do this trip. You can do it during the summer, but there will not be any flow, and there will not be any white water. The water won't be clear, it will be stagnant, and still. This is the headwater of  Percy Priest lake. This is where the lake begins. And when the lake is at summer pool, it will back up to this area. Now that the lake is dropped to Winter pool, it has lowered a full 7 ft of elevation! That leaves this upper stretch of river, exposed! It will be that way, until the middle of April. That is when they typically bring the lake back up.
Between now and then, on the nice days, you can get out and kayak this stretch of river, and catch loads of bass! It's full of largemouth and Smallmouth and spotted bass. Unfortunately, yesterday, my buddy and I were only able to catch a few little bass. But that is not typical for this stretch of river! Yesterday was a particularly tough bass fishing day. It was the full moon, and when that happens, they typically feed really well at night, especially if the night is clear, like we had the night before. We did however, noticed that there were fish in the river. Lots of fish! Lots of shad and other types of bait fish as well as big bass that we can see that didn't want anything to do with us or our lures.
Don't let that discourage you! I did this trip last year for my first downstream whitewater kayak trip of the year, and we beat the brakes off the fish! That trip was at the end of February. I got out there a little early this year, so that I could bring the report to all my hardcore kayak Bass fisherman! This trip is second to none! Strap on your life jacket and go after it! The natural beauty of the area is reason enough to go!
The end of your trip will be at Mona boat ramp...
Mona boat ramp https://share.google/1C5u3RfH3vRMOSyB8
Fortunately, this is an actual about ramp! At the end of your day, at the end of a long trip, you'll be glad that you can back the car or truck right down to the water's edge to load up. Lucky you, nobody uses this boat ramp in the winter time! But don't let that discourage you either, it's not because it's dangerous or there aren't any fish, it's because the water at the boat ramp is so low! You will see when you get there. Most boats would not float off of a trailer, because the riverbed is so close to the end of the boat ramp. That makes it ideal for kayakers. We had the whole place to ourselves!
To try to catch bass, I was using my medium action 7 ft rod and reel. I like 10 lb braid with an 8 lb monofilament leader. I was throwing a 5-inch white paddle tail and a 5-inch fluke for most of the day, but neither one of those got any looks. My buddy was throwing a spinnerbait and a crankbait, but those didn't work either. The only thing we could catch a few little fish on would be a Ned rig. Throw it on the bottom, and twitch it around until a bass picks it up. It's one of the least exciting ways to go bass fishing, but sometimes, it's the only way you can generate a bite.
Typically, in a location like this, I would use my cast net to get some bait and then catch bass with the bait that lives in the river. I don't like to do that in the winter time, because you get too wet. It's a little too cold for all of that, so I try to stick to the lures. Typically, that works out really well!
