title: Trip Report #128
content_raw:
The shallow water crappie spot...
Today, I took a client out for the 4-Hour, instructional crappie fishing trip. He was already familiar with catching crappie under a bobber, with a minnow. He wanted to learn my methods for using a Bobby Garland. We launched out of Jefferson Springs boat ramp at 6:00 a.m...
Jefferson Springs Boat Ramp. https://share.google/OvCIcEDXAJGFmDZb3
This is on the south end of Percy Priest lake, but that's where the lake begins. The lake flows from southeast to northwest. The southern end of the lake is the shallow end, and the northern end of the lake is the deeper end. Traditional thinking dictates that crappie move to the deepest part of the lake during the winter months. We are now into January, and I am still catching these fish in less than 10 ft of water!
Today, we went 2 miles upstream from the boat ramp, which is pretty much due south. Heading that direction, the lake only gets shallower. There is nowhere on this part of the lake that is anywhere near 30 ft of depth. Everything is shallower than that, and fish are sitting really shallow, up on mud flats. So what does that mean?
The lake isn't very wide in this area, and you can see the bank, both banks, on either side. Most of the time, one side will be a channel swing, those are typically limestone cliffs. The other bank, a lot of times, will be a slowly sloping mud bank. That's where the fish are sitting! In places where the mud drops off rather quickly, and they have some trees as underwater structure, crappie are hanging in great numbers! I'm going to drop a pin in that area for the people who have boats, just so you know exactly where we were fishing...
https://goo.gl/maps/1iPiKsACDZVWSzps8
There are a few different trees that are sticking up out of the water in this area. Just fish around those! They are completely loaded with crappie. We didn't have any trouble getting fish to bite today, from the very first cast, to the very last cast! That's not hyperbole. On the very first cast, my client hooked up to, and almost landed a really big crappie. It got away right at the boat. On the last cast of the day, he pulled a crappie into the net. For the entire 4 hours while we fished, those fish were not only biting, but they were providing their trademark thump!
When a crappie bites, it is a split second in time, that often results in what feels like a thump. If you use your finger to thump something, that split second in time where you hear that sound, that's how short a crappie strike is. They hit it in that split second of time, thump, and then you have to set the hook. Right then! Right at that split second when they bite. If you don't, you will have missed the fish. Apart from using the same rod and reel, and the same fishing line, and the same lure, that's the biggest difference between being successful at catching these fish, and missing a lot of bites.
I tell you guys about my preferred crappie setup all the time. Sparing no detail. I like to use a 7 1/2 ft ultralight rod. My rod is medium action. I have a 1000 series reel. That's ultralight! I like to use 4 lb monofilament. But not just any monofilament, I use Stren. It's tough, abrasion resistant, and extremely cheap! For my jig heads, I also keep it cheap. On the shelf at the bait shop near where I live, they have 10 packs of 1/32nd ounce jig heads for $1.49. That's 15 cents per hook! When it comes to crappie fishing, I always use the same soft plastic. A 2-inch, pearl colored, Bobby Garland baby shad.
Most of that can be changed out. You could have a longer or shorter rod, you could even use 6 lb monofilament or braid, or maybe even 8 lb monofilament. You could definitely use lighter jig heads, or heavier jig heads. The most important thing, if you're using a small soft plastic where there are crappie, is using a slow retrieve, and you will probably get them to bite. The next most important thing, is setting that hook.
Here's the best way that I have figured out to set myself up for success, when it comes to setting that hook into a crappie's mouth. Once I start my retrieve, I keep my rod at a 45° angle. I make sure to keep the line tight, so that I can feel the slightest bite. As soon as I feel anything, I just assumed that it is a crappie. Quite often, you hit the bottom, or structure, and then you get hung up. That's not a big deal. I still go ahead and set the hook anyway. If I feel anything, I set that hook. If I get hung up, I break it off, I retie, and I try again. When you've got your rod tip up, and your line tight, and you are slowly retrieving your lure, you will feel that thump. When you do, snap your hand that is holding your rod back to your chest. Don't swing it up over your head, just quickly snap it those few inches left between where you're holding your rod at a 45° angle, and your chest.
Too big of a hook set is going to pull this lure away from these fish. Too small, you're not going to hook them, or you're going to be too late. It has to be fast!
Sticking those fish, 40 ft away, with a thin piece of steel is tough! Getting them to bite shouldn't be. If you're in a place that you suspect has crappie, and you're not getting any bites, go to a different spot! One of the key things when it comes to crappie fishing is to be flexible when it comes to changing spots. We found fish that were willing to bite, non-stop. So we never really left their area. I always say, don't leave fish that are biting, to find other fish.

title: Trip Report #129
content_raw:
The pillar my dreams...
Today, I took my boat out at 6:00 a.m. from Jefferson Springs boat ramp...
Jefferson Springs Boat Ramp. https://share.google/ReU5UxLKvHbtHjvC0
From the boat ramp, you can see the bridge on Jefferson Pike that goes over the lake. There are eight concrete pillars that are in the water, holding up the bridge. Each one of those pillars had crappie on them, some more than others.
We got there early. Long before the sun came up. Yesterday, I went crappie fishing at the same time of day, and they went crazy! Every single cast I was catching a crappie. Fast forward to today, and those fish had lockjaw! I could see them on the forward facing sonar hanging on the bridge pilings, but they did not want to bite during that early morning twilight hour. It would be just after sunrise before the fish started biting really well.
I had my buddy with me, and we fished until about 1:30 in the afternoon. We probably caught around 60 crappie, and one white bass. Despite the great numbers, we were only able to catch 11 keepers. That happens a lot on Percy Priest lake. There are so many crappie in that lake, they may be a tad bit overpopulated. After all, wildlife biologist have determined that the proper limit of crappie on Percy Priest Lake should be 30 fish that are at least 10 inches in  length, as opposed to the state limit of 15 fish that are at least 10 in length. Despite the seemingly massive numbers of crappie on the lake, I have never caught anywhere near my limit. Today's results we're fairly typical.
So how did we get these fish? First of all, we put down an anchor. About 30 ft away from those pillars, so we could cast just past them, and then retrieve our lures alongside the underwater concrete columns. That's where these crappie like to hang, right now. When I first started coming out to fish at this boat ramp, a little less than 2 months ago, there were not any crappie on those pillars! I had always heard people say that you could catch crappie around the concrete pilings that hold up bridges, but I wasn't seeing them there, until about 3 weeks ago.
Lately, they've been hanging out there all day. So I've been sitting, 30 ft away, casting with my ultra light rod and reel, with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/32nd ounce jig head. I have been using a variety of colors recently, for no particular reason, and I did the same thing today. Typically, I will throw a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland. Today, I also Incorporated a black and chartreuse 2 in Bobby Garland. Bobby g makes a hundred different colors, you can't go wrong with any of them! As long as you are casting to the other side of the fish, and reeling it either above them, or through them, you should be able to catch them.
You should be able to catch them, but not all day everyday. Today was actually a really good example of needing to be patient. These fish would go through spells where they would bite like gangbusters for about 15 minutes, and then we wouldn't get a bite for 30 to 45 minutes. Then, when you get back to fishing, your lure will sometimes trigger a bite.

I was using a 1/32nd ounce, but it was going really slow, so I added a split shot to make it sink a little faster, which also caused it to move a little faster in the water, as I retrieve it. title: Trip Report #130
content_raw:
Where are the crappie are and where they are not...
I started my day at 6:00 a.m. at the spring on Percy Priest Lake...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/19DrhsEgZqX57Pjo7
You can park on the side of Maddox road and take the trail all the way to the spring. The path is blocked for vehicles, so you will have to go over, under, or around the gate...
https://goo.gl/maps/KLWKStiRjPv9mYwUA
This is where the crappie were. I caught more than 20, and almost all of them were keepers. But by 8:00 a.m., they had almost completely quit biting. I didn't keep any fish today, so presumably, they are all still in there. The fishing was best not just before the sun came up, but while it was still pretty dark out. Here's how I got them... Using my 7 and 1/2 ft ultralight rod and reel, with 4 lb monofilament, and a 1/64th of an ounce jig head with a 2-inch, pearl colored Bobby Garland.
It was dark, so I couldn't see what I was doing, but I didn't need to. I would cast as far as I could, and allow my jig head to sink for 13 seconds. Then I would start a slow retrieve that was quickly rewarded with a thump! That's right! Today, I didn't really have to worry about a finicky bite, those fish were putting on a show! The unmistakable thump that crappie provide had returned, in great numbers! Cast after cast, I would not only get a bite, but I almost always catch a crappie. Until about 7:00 a.m.
When the bite started to slow down, the fish started to get smaller. All of the fish I was catching in the dark and before sunrise we're big slabs, after sunrise, most of the fish were little dinks. In the video that I made for tomorrow, I only included all of the big fish, after the video ends, I went on to catch lots more fish, they were just really small. None of them keepers.
Then I went to get some early lunch and then head out to try to take advantage of the afternoon bite. I went over to stand on the bank at West Fork boat ramp...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/m8BpyVJWUV28Cj1G7
If you take a short trail just to the right of the boat ramp, through the woods, you will come out on a muddy bank. There is a concrete chunk that is a perfect circle with what looks like an old fence post in it. The old fence post has rusted away, leaving just the chunk of concrete, right in the perfect spot to fish. Directly out in front of you, about 30 ft, it's about 10 ft deep, and there is a tree limb stuck underwater that holds crappie. The last time I went there, I beat them up!
Today, I didn't catch a single fish. I did get a couple of bites, and hooked a fish that I thought was a crappie, but I couldn't be sure, because it got away. One thing I did catch, was that tree, a whole bunch! I must have got hung up and broke off at least three or four times. I tried for the better part of an hour, but I just couldn't catch a fish. The last time I went there, it would be impossible not to catch a fish. They were stacked in there! Not so much today.

title: Trip Report #131
content_raw:
Two epic spots, two different results...
This morning I got to Center Hill Dam, to fish on the steps above the generating water, at 6:30 a.m...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/oRifPZywpPgqKm3c6
During the winter time, I will fish from the steps below Center Hill Dam for trout. I will only go fishing there when the generators are on. Today, the generators were scheduled to run all morning long, with the schedule saying two or more. There are a total of three generators at Center Hill Dam. This morning, all three were running. You can find the generating schedule, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
I was just there yesterday afternoon and the fishing was pretty good! Lots of people were catching fish, and we could see trout hitting the surface all afternoon long. This morning was the complete opposite! I threw everything but the kitchen sink at these fish. A three-way rig with soft plastics. A Carolina rig with gulp minnows. Every different kind of spoon I had in the box. We stayed there in the brutal cold until about 8:30, but there were four of us there, and none of us had caught a fish! So I went home to get something to eat, and then head back out for the afternoon shift.
After an early lunch, I went to the spring on Percy Priest Lake...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/XZnzEJG1ar2ieUxo8
The most important part about going to the spring is knowing where to park. The only legal place to park is on the side of Maddox road...
https://goo.gl/maps/9xacPnMcVweQLQUy9
There's plenty of room to park on the side of the road right here, and you can go over, under, or around the gate that prohibits vehicles from driving back to the spring. This is all wildlife management area, so you are allowed to be here, but you probably want to wear a bright orange hat and maybe an orange vest. It is hunting season, and there are hunters in this area.
I made the hike back to the spring with my fly rod, and a bass rod with a hook and a bobber. I was hoping to catch a few little bluegill, and use them as bait to go after some of the really big bass that are in the spring. Unfortunately, despite my best efforts, I couldn't get a bluegill hooked up. So I had to change my plans. Fortunately for me, I brought my ultralight crappie setups. I had my seven and a half foot ultra light rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament. That's my preferred fishing pole for chasing crappie on Percy Priest lake.
Lately, I've been using a 1/64th of an ounce jig head. Not necessarily a trout magnet, even though I use those, just a 1/64th of an ounce ball head jig. I've been using the same soft plastic, a 2-in Bobby Garland pearl colored baby shad, but that jig head is half the size that I have been using. I like it! I have to fish even slower, and more patiently using that jig, but I'm having great success! I was able to put a pretty good beat down on the crappie this afternoon.
Sitting in the back of the spring, casting directly out as far as I could with that light jig, I would allow it to sink for about 30 seconds! Then I would start a painfully slow retrieve. Incorporating a couple twitches every now and then. It was those twitches that would trigger the bite today! In total, I probably caught 13 to 14 crappie. All of them wanted the jig to have a little bit of movement. Either a twitch or two, or a little jiggle jiggle jiggle jiggle. No matter what I had to do, it needed to be really deep! It's tough for me to say, because I was standing on the bank, and I was using a really light jig, but I was probably down there at about 14 or 15 feet.
The water at the spring is really clear! I could see my jig underwater to a depth of about four or five feet. At one point in time, I saw a crappie come up and hit my lure! The place is overwhelmingly loaded with fish. There are thousands of bluegill all around the edges, hanging close to the rocks, because, just off the edge of the cliffs in all directions there are countless largemouth bass of every size. There are some true giants in there! No doubt, they're going after some of the larger gizzard shad that you can see using their weird shaped mouth to pluck whatever it is they're eating off the side of the rocks.
An easy way to get those bass would be to take some live shiners from the bait shop, put one of those on a hook underneath a bobber at a depth of about one foot and then cast it near the bank and then leave it there until a big bass comes to take it. These bass don't really like to come up to eat right in front of you. So it'll be easier to get them if you cast at the bank to the left or the right. Basically, if they can't see you are there, they will feel comfortable and eat, and they are eating a lot! Seems like every time I go there, they are smashing bluegill, or some type of bait fish, into the rocks!

title: Trip Report #132
content_raw:
It's time to do some stair stepping...
Every year, I wait until winter begins before I start fishing the steps at Center Hill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/jyWKxSy2bXPu1JQh9
You're allowed to drive all the way to the base of the dam and park really close to the entrance, so that you can fish on the steps that are provided, just above where the generators discharge. There's a bathroom right there in the parking lot, but for the first time in my 33 years of fishing below Center Hill dam, it is closed for the winter. The bathroom at the top of the dam in the observation over look parking lot, remains the only open restroom in the area.
I always wait until this time of year because fishing at the steps is one heck of a workout. Going up and down those steps is very rigorous, and it will get you all hot and bothered, real quick! I like to go when it's brutally cold outside, that way I don't get too overheated coming back up those steps. I'm not exaggerating when I say it is one heck of a workout to fish at those steps. They are not normal stairs, they are 4 ft long, which makes getting up them even tougher.
Now that my time of year to fish at the steps has arrived, I'll be going there quite frequently. But I will only ever be fishing at the steps when the generators are scheduled to be on. Today, the generators were scheduled to turn on at 11:00a.m., and be on for the rest of the day. I decided to show up just after 11:00, and take advantage of that raging current, to try to catch trout. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
As always, if you're using Patreon on your phone, you will have to hold down on the link to make it work.
The generator turned on as scheduled, so when I got there, I immediately got to work. My favorite way to fish at the steps is with my 9-ft Shakespeare ugly stick. That's a medium action rod. The extra length allows me to throw my setup really far. It also allows me to fight big fish with ease. I have two different 9-ft Shakespeare ugly stick rods set up for fishing below Center Hill dam. One with 12 lb monofilament as the main line and one with relatively heavy braid, I believe it's around 30 lb. I like to use the one with monofilament to set up a Carolina rig to try to fish on the bottom.
On that pole, I will use a 1 oz barrel weight for the weight on my Carolina rig. Then I will add a bead, so that the weight doesn't crush my knot. Then I will tie my main line to a barrel swivel. Then I will attach 8 lb monofilament to the barrel swivel as my leader line. I like to use a really small diameter fishing line to attach my lures, because trout can be line shy. 8 lb monofilament is more than strong enough to pull in just about any fish out there. On the end of my leader, I put a number one eagle claw bait holder hook. On that hook, I can attach any number of small soft plastics. Today, I was using a sassy shad. I have two and a half inch and 3 inch soft plastics. That tends to be the perfect size.
On my other 9-ft rod, I attach a three-way swivel directly to my trunk line. On one side of the three-way swivel I attach 8 lb monofilament with a 1 oz pyramid weight. On the third side of the swivel, I put my 8 lb monofilament leader line. I typically run the same hook on that one as well, but today, I was running a 1/64th of an ounce trout magnet, with a 1 inch gulp minnow.
I always take a third setup. My 7 ft medium heavy bass rod with 15 lb braid as the trunk line and 12 lb monofilament as the leader line. I will attach the monofilament directly to the braid with a knot that is called an Acapulco knot. I did a video earlier this year about how to tie that, but I will redo that real soon. On the end of my monofilament, today I was using a 1/2 oz Cotton Cordell silver spoon. I started off with a gold spoon, and I could see trout coming up to the surface, but they wouldn't take the lure. That's when I switched to a silver lure, and ended up catching my first brown trout of the day.
The most important thing about fishing below Center Hill Dam is not what type of lure you are using, but how you are using it. For both of those 9 ft rods with sinkers, I want to fish that small soft plastic by bouncing it along the bottom. I stand on the steps and cast upstream towards the dam and then quickly real out any slack in the line. Once the weight sinks down to the bottom, you will start feeling it bouncing along the bottom, bump bump bump bump bump bump bump bump bump. If it settles down, quickly give that big fishing pole an upward twitch, that should dislodge your weight, and allow the lure to continue bumping on the bottom. This is my favorite method, because the fish will hook themselves! You don't have to feel for a bite, you just have to wait for it. It's the same way with a three-way rig, or a Carolina rig.
It's a lot more complicated to fish with a spoon. You need a relatively heavy spoon. Half of an ounce is the lightest weight you will be able to get away with. The most common, 1 oz spoon. A really heavy lure that allows you to yo-yo in front of these fish. Basically, you need to throw your spoon a little bit upstream towards the dam, and then get your rod tip up into the air, and allow that lure to sink for just a few seconds, before you twitch it back up near the surface. When you're doing it right, you can see your spoon coming up to the surface out in front of you, and you will see the trout come up and take the lure!
It's important to remember that you can put any number of lures on a three-way rig or a Carolina rig. You do not necessarily have to fish them on the bottom, that's just the way that I like to do it. You could put a spoon on one of those and then just retrieve the lure without letting it hit the bottom. Or you could put on any number of trout lures like a rooster tail or a rapala minnow. One of my favorite things to do, is to put on a couple of Berkeley powerbait Magnum power eggs for trout, with half of a night crawler. That gets them every time!

The bathroom at the top of the dam in the observation over look parking lot, remains the only open restroom in the area.

I always wait until this time of year because fishing at the steps is one heck of a workout. Going up and down those steps is very rigorous, and it will get you all hot and bothered, real quick! I like to go when it's brutally cold outside, that way I don't get too overheated coming back up those steps. I'm not exaggerating when I say it is one heck of a workout to fish at those steps. They are not normal stairs, they are 4 ft long, which makes getting up them even tougher.

Now that my time of year to fish at the steps has arrived, I'll be going there quite frequently. But I will only ever be fishing at the steps when the generators are scheduled to be on. Today, the generators were scheduled to turn on at 11:00a.m., and be on for the rest of the day. I decided to show up just after 11:00, and take advantage of that raging current, to try to catch trout. You can find the generating schedule for Center Hill dam, here...

<https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill>

As always, if you're using Patreon on your phone, you will have to hold down on the link to make it work.

The generator turned on as scheduled, so when I got there, I immediately got to work. My favorite way to fish at the steps is with my 9-ft Shakespeare ugly stick. That's a medium action rod. The extra length allows me to throw my setup really far. It also allows me to fight big fish with ease. I have two different 9-ft Shakespeare ugly stick rods set up for fishing below Center Hill dam. One with 12 lb monofilament as the main line and one with relatively heavy braid, I believe it's around 30 lb. I like to use the one with monofilament to set up a Carolina rig to try to fish on the bottom.

On that pole, I will use a 1 oz barrel weight for the weight on my Carolina rig. Then I will add a bead, so that the weight doesn't crush my knot. Then I will tie my main line to a barrel swivel. Then I will attach 8 lb monofilament to the barrel swivel as my leader line. I like to use a really small diameter fishing line to attach my lures, because trout can be line shy. 8 lb monofilament is more than strong enough to pull in just about any fish out there. On the end of my leader, I put a number one eagle claw bait holder hook. On that hook, I can attach any number of small soft plastics. Today, I was using a sassy shad. I have two and a half inch and 3 inch soft plastics. That tends to be the perfect size.

On my other 9-ft rod, I attach a three-way swivel directly to my trunk line. On one side of the three-way swivel I attach 8 lb monofilament with a 1 oz pyramid weight. On the third side of the swivel, I put my 8 lb monofilament leader line. I typically run the same hook on that one as well, but today, I was running a 1/64th of an ounce trout magnet, with a 1 inch gulp minnow.

I always take a third setup. My 7 ft medium heavy bass rod with 15 lb braid as the trunk line and 12 lb monofilament as the leader line. I will attach the monofilament directly to the braid with a knot that is called an Acapulco knot. I did a video earlier this year about how to tie that, but I will redo that real soon. On the end of my monofilament, today I was using a 1/2 oz Cotton Cordell silver spoon. I started off with a gold spoon, and I could see trout coming up to the surface, but they wouldn't take the lure. That's when I switched to a silver lure, and ended up catching my first brown trout of the day.

The most important thing about fishing below Center Hill Dam is not what type of lure you are using, but how you are using it. For both of those 9 ft rods with sinkers, I want to fish that small soft plastic by bouncing it along the bottom. I stand on the steps and cast upstream towards the dam and then quickly real out any slack in the line. Once the weight sinks down to the bottom, you will start feeling it bouncing along the bottom, bump bump bump bump bump bump bump bump bump. If it settles down, quickly give that big fishing pole an upward twitch, that should dislodge your weight, and allow the lure to continue bumping on the bottom. This is my favorite method, because the fish will hook themselves! You don't have to feel for a bite, you just have to wait for it. It's the same way with a three-way rig, or a Carolina rig.

It's a lot more complicated to fish with a spoon. You need a relatively heavy spoon. Half of an ounce is the lightest weight you will be able to get away with. The most common, 1 oz spoon. A really heavy lure that allows you to yo-yo in front of these fish. Basically, you need to throw your spoon a little bit upstream towards the dam, and then get your rod tip up into the air, and allow that lure to sink for just a few seconds, before you twitch it back up near the surface. When you're doing it right, you can see your spoon coming up to the surface out in front of you, and you will see the trout come up and take the lure!

It's important to remember that you can put any number of lures on a three-way rig or a Carolina rig. You do not necessarily have to fish them on the bottom, that's just the way that I like to do it. You could put a spoon on one of those and then just retrieve the lure without letting it hit the bottom. Or you could put on any number of trout lures like a rooster tail or a rapala minnow. One of my favorite things to do, is to put on a couple of Berkeley powerbait Magnum power eggs for trout, with half of a night crawler. That gets them every time!

title: Trip Report #133
content_raw:
Some crappie are really shallow...
Today, I had a client booked for the 4-Hour instructional, forward facing sonar trip, from my boat. He wanted to look at the lowrance eagle eye nine before he made his decision about purchasing one. The plan, find some fish, and then use the forward facing sonar to watch how the fish respond to our lures. Mission accomplished! We launched at 6:00 a.m. from Jefferson Springs boat ramp...
Jefferson Springs Boat Ramp. https://share.google/NFUVXh92FYWUGv71M
We didn't go far! From the boat ramp, you can see the bridge on Jefferson Pike that goes over the lake. We went right over there to the bridge pilings and then put out an anchor, and then caught crappie for 4 hours. We didn't catch great numbers of keepers, lots of the fish were kind of small. We only ended up with five that were over 10 inches. Those fish have been hanging out on those bridge pilings for the last few weeks, and I suspect they will stay there. At that spot, the water is 28 ft deep, and they have the opportunity to move up or down in the water column according to whatever temperature makes them happiest.
Speaking of temperature, the water at the surface of the lake at Jefferson Springs boat ramp was a balmy 58°! That's unbelievably warm for this time of year. We caught fish under the bridge until about 9:00. At that point in time, they kind of turned off. The bite had slowed down, so we started trolling around the bridge pilings, just to get a good feel for what everything looks like on forward facing sonar. We caught a few more little fish, but by and large, the bite was over.
I went home and got some lunch and then went right back out to Percy Priest lake. Yesterday, I caught fish on Couchville lake, which is right next to Percy Priest. The thing about those fish, they were in one foot of water! There are fish attractors at Couchville lake that are mostly exposed because the lake is so low. Despite that fact, crappie had made their way into the shallowest part of the lake, to hang out around those man-made structures. There are countless man-made fishing attractors on the banks of Percy Priest lake, so I wanted to go see if any crappie we're doing the same thing on Percy Priest as they were on Couchville.
I started at the handicap Fishing Pier in the parking lot at Stewart Creek boat ramp...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/r3PKtYDTPjU6iYBj4
This is the exact same setup that I had yesterday at couchville lake. Fish attractors everywhere in really shallow water. So I did what I always do, I used my ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament but this time I used a 1/64th of an ounce jig head instead of a 1/32nd ounce. Reason being, the water is so shallow, you don't want your jig head to sink down into the mud. You want to cast out, and then immediately get your retrieve started.
I got a couple of bites doing that, but I couldn't get any fish to commit. So I pulled out a bobber and put that jig underneath a fixed bobber at  18 inches of depth. I was making long casts, and then slowly retrieving that bobber on the surface and waiting for it to make the slightest movement that wasn't initiated by me. Eureka! I got a crappie to bite, and commit. I officially caught a crappie in the last few days of the year right at the bank on Percy Priest lake, in the fish attractors! But that would be the only one.
From there, I would move over to a spot that I found with my forward facing sonar at West Fork boat ramp...
West Fork Boat Ramp https://share.google/HUO7bO7OnuqWyD8L2
Park in the parking lot and walk towards the boat ramp. To the right of the boat ramp, you will see a trail that goes into the woods. This is a very short trail! Only about 100 ft, maybe less. It's well beaten, and it spits out just on the other side of a downed tree that is in the way. You will know you are in the right spot when you see a perfect concrete cylinder. It looks like concrete from an old fence post, but the metal fence post is gone. If you stand right in front of that, on those rocks in the water so you won't have to stand in the mud, there is a tree about 30 ft from the bank that stays loaded with crappie!
https://maps.app.goo.gl/Ei2WhqjKB7toMS418
That pin is in the general vicinity, but if you stand right in front of that concrete chunk, you will catch crappie! I was able to catch them a number of ways. Using that 1/64th of an ounce jig head and a pearl colored Bobby Garland and a slow retrieve. Adding a bobber to the equation and setting it to a depth of about 2 ft. Also, I was able to add a small split. When I first got there, I was catching them with just the jig head, casting it out about 30 ft and starting a slow retrieve as soon as the lure hit the surface. But then, I had to go a little lower and a little slower. So I added the bobber. When that wouldn't work, I took the bobber off, and added a really tiny split shot. After I did that, I would allow the lure to sink. I was counting it down to about 10 seconds before I would start my retrieve, and I was having great success!
Remember, crappie like a slow retrieve. If you're not having any luck, try slowing down. If you slow down so much that you get hung up, that was a little too slow. You're going to have to find the sweet spot in between getting hung up on that tree, and getting those fish to bite. That's the most fun part! Trying to figure out exactly what you have to do. Don't feel like putting in that much effort? Just bring a quarter pound of minnows. Put those underneath a bobber at a depth of 2 ft, and you will load a bucket with crappie!

title: Trip Report #134
content_raw:
I had the entire lake to myself...
Today, I went to Couchville Lake in Long Hunter State Park...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/bVgEs4Md5xYkwGYW6
I have wheels for my kayak, so I'm able to unload in the parking lot and then roll my kayak all the way to the water's edge. It's not close! In the past, you could drive to the water's edge. You are no longer able to do that. They have put up blockades and do not allow people to drive on the sidewalk. You will have to unload in the unloading zone in front of the sidewalk or in the parking lot. Either way, it doesn't look like anybody is fishing out there!
I expected the place to be packed. Just a few years ago, there would be half a dozen kayaks out there on a day like today. I found myself all alone for the entire day! I got there at 8:00 a.m., which is a little late, because the park opens at 7:00 a.m.
I paddled directly across from where you launch your kayak, to the main point on the lake. I'll drop you a pin right here. Keep in mind, if you are using Patreon on your phone, which most of us do, you will have to hold down on this pin so that it will take you to the link...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/LxQjYRPfDazFiRuT6
I go to this spot and drop an anchor in about 10 feet of water, and then just fish around me. It's good to fish on the main point of the lake if you can. You can catch all kinds of fish! I was targeting crappie, but when you sit here, you have no clue what you're going to catch! It's mostly going to be crappie, but you can catch just about anything. I've been fishing on this point for half a decade, and it's fantastic!
Today, the wind was brutal! Fishing for crappie is typically slow and methodical. The wind makes it hard to keep ultra light line in the water. It makes it hard to get the lure down, it just makes everything harder to do in general. Despite my best efforts to fish with the wind at my back, it seems like the crappie kept moving around, so that I had to cast into the wind. I did that for a couple of hours, and caught a couple handful of crappie. But it was a struggle! Almost out of the crappie we're really tiny. It seems like not enough people are going out there and keeping fish. Incidentally, there is no size limit for crappie on Couchville lake, because it's so overpopulated.
What I'm about to tell you next blew my mind. There is a fishing pier right where you load your kayak into the water. Unfortunately, the fishing pier has been rendered unsafe to use. It is therefore, out of service. Around the fishing pier, in the water, there are fish attractors, intended to attract crappie. This time of year, the tips of those attractors are out of the water. These things are no more than 3 ft tall. So that means they're sitting in about 2 ft of water, or less. Not somewhere you would expect to catch crappie on the last week of the year... Or would you?
To be honest with you, I did. I did expect to catch crappie there. The water temperature was 53°! That's crazy warm! I went over there with my ultra light rod and reel, with 4 lb monofilament, and a 1/32nd of an ounce jig head, with a 2-inch pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad, and beat the brakes off the crappie!
I caught about a dozen fish off of not only those fish attractors, but the actual fishing pier structure that was in the water. Every type of crappie, white crappie, black crappie, and black nose crappie. Casting across those corrugated pipes that they use for fish attractors, and slowly retrieving my jig between them, I was pulling them out left and right! Right at high noon! That got me thinking, there's a good chance, that on the south, shallow end of Percy Priest lake, crappie could be stacked up on those fish attractors, in great numbers! Who knows? There's only one way to find out!

title: Trip Report #135
content_raw:
Yesterday, I went muskie fishing on the Collins River in McMinnville Tennessee. The stretch of river that I did was 8 miles, and you need someone to help you shuttle if you're going to do this trip. I met a couple of buddies in McMinnville for breakfast, and then we went to where we were planning on ending our trip, at Shellsford road Collins river access...
https://share.google/lYCPYmvCAufAC7FN8
This is not a boat ramp. There is a trail through the woods to the edge of the water and you can carry or drag your kayak up to the parking lot. This is not a good spot to launch and try to go upstream and then come back down. The best way to utilize this location is to end your trip here, or begin your trip here. Since this would be the spot we were going to end, we got loaded up into one vehicle, left the other two vehicles at this location, and then headed up to where we were going to start our trip, at Myer's cove boat ramp...
Myers Cove Boat Ramp https://share.google/8THj0GzJ9pgkIvpsj
This is a boat ramp! Both of these locations are 24 hours, and completely free and public use. At the Myers cove boat ramp, the water is swift, but if you have a boat that can run really shallow, like a jet boat, you can launch there and go upstream or downstream. There was someone launching a really big jet boat when we were there, and he said he could go more than 10 miles upstream. That's not something I can do in my boat, because my propeller, but this place is great for people who own a jet boat!
The float from the boat ramp to Shellsford access is a little more than 8 miles of river. That type of trip is going to take at least 8 hours. It's almost impossible to get the perfect flow, yesterday was a little bit too fast. You take what you can get, when you have a chance to go, but you have to know what the flow is before you go out to McMinnville, because if you get there and it's too low, you will have to drag the entire 8 miles. If the water is too high, it could be too fast, and dangerous. There is a sweet spot, and it's measured in cubic feet per second.
Cubic feet per second is the way we measure the speed and volume of a river. One cubic foot is about the size of one basketball. Yesterday, the Collins River was flowing at 770 cubic feet per second when we started our trip. By the time we ended our trip, it had dropped to around 700 cubic feet per second. The sweet spot is between 400 and 800 cubic feet per second. When we started yesterday, we were near that 800 number, and the river was a little fast, so we didn't get to fish it as slowly and intently as we would have liked. If the cubic feet per second gets lower than 400, you will get stuck in some places on that 8 mile stretch and have to get out of your kayak and walk. To find the flow rate, or cubic feet per second, of the Collins river, you can look here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03421000/all-graphs/#period=P7D
When I went to grab the website to share with you just now, the river was at 612 cubic feet per second. That's a fantastic number! Not too fast and not too slow. If you get a chance, Christmas day would be a great day to kayak for muskie! But what are you going to do to catch one? I'm glad you asked...
Here's what I like to do. I grab my 7 ft, medium heavy rod. I put 80 lb braid on my reel, and then I attach a 100 lb steel leader, I like a 6-inch steel leader. From there, you can use whatever type of lure you like! A few weeks ago, my buddy was using a 1/8 of an ounce crappie jig with a 3-inch soft plastic on that same setup, and he caught a muskie! I always tell people, use your favorite lure. If you have a confidence lure, like a Ned rig or a buzzbait, throw that! The three of us were throwing white paddle tails. A very simple bass lure with a quarter ounce jig head and a 5 inch soft plastic. A confidence lure for Smallmouth, but when musky decide they want to eat, they eat whatever they see.
Yesterday, a few different Muskie came out and took a swipe at our lures, but only one of them got hooked up and in the net. It was probably 3 ft long, and a little less than 10 lb. It put up one heck of a fight, and it came really close to the end of the trip. I'd say about 7 miles into our 8 mile trip. That gives me a chance to explain the most important part of Muskie fishing, how to handle them.
You want a giant, rubber net. The biggest one you can find. You want the Muskie to be able to swim around in the net. Once we got the fish in the net, we got lucky, because the hook fell out. Quite often, especially when you're in kayaks, getting the muskie free from the hook can be a fiasco! Here's what you do in that situation... With the muskie in a position that water can flow freely over its gills, paddle your way to the bank. Once you get there, get out on the bank where you have firm footing, while keeping the Muskie in the water, and try to secure the hooks. You're definitely going to need footlong pliers, and you're also going to need something to cut the hooks in case you can't remove them. I like a small bolt cutter. Carry that with you when you go musky fishing.
There's a tool called a jaw spreader that is specifically made for Muskie and Pike. I do not have one of those, but I definitely should. It's on my Christmas wish list, and I'm hoping I get one tomorrow. Everyone should have a jaw spreader, just in case you're lure has pinned the mouth shut. Jaw spreaders will help you open the fish's mouth, so that you don't expose yourself to the toothy interior.
Once you have the hooks far away from the fish, and the fish in the net, swimming freely, now you're able to take a picture. Using your dominant hand, for me my right hand, grab the fish by the tail. That's the part that it uses to slash, that's where you want to hold it firm. Once you have the fish just above the tail, in the meaty part of the end of the fish, you can slide your left hand underneath the belly of the fish. content_markdown:
Yesterday, I went muskie fishing on the Collins River in McMinnville Tennessee. The stretch of river that I did was 8 miles, and you need someone to help you shuttle if you're going to do this trip. I met a couple of buddies in McMinnville for breakfast, and then we went to where we were planning on ending our trip, at Shellsford road Collins river access...

https://share.google/lYCPYmvCAufAC7FN8

This is not a boat ramp. There is a trail through the woods to the edge of the water and you can carry or drag your kayak up to the parking lot. This is not a good spot to launch and try to go upstream and then come back down. The best way to utilize this location is to end your trip here, or begin your trip here. Since this would be the spot we were going to end, we got loaded up into one vehicle, left the other two vehicles at this location, and then headed up to where we were going to start our trip, at Myer's cove boat ramp...

Myers Cove Boat Ramp https://share.google/8THj0GzJ9pgkIvpsj

This is a boat ramp! Both of these locations are 24 hours, and completely free and public use. At the Myers cove boat ramp, the water is swift, but if you have a boat that can run really shallow, like a jet boat, you can launch there and go upstream or downstream. There was someone launching a really big jet boat when we were there, and he said he could go more than 10 miles upstream. That's not something I can do in my boat, because my propeller, but this place is great for people who own a jet boat!

The float from the boat ramp to Shellsford access is a little more than 8 miles of river. That type of trip is going to take at least 8 hours. It's almost impossible to get the perfect flow, yesterday was a little bit too fast. You take what you can get, when you have a chance to go, but you have to know what the flow is before you go out to McMinnville, because if you get there and it's too low, you will have to drag the entire 8 miles. If the water is too high, it could be too fast, and dangerous. There is a sweet spot, and it's measured in cubic feet per second.

Cubic feet per second is the way we measure the speed and volume of a river. One cubic foot is about the size of one basketball. Yesterday, the Collins River was flowing at 770 cubic feet per second when we started our trip. By the time we ended our trip, it had dropped to around 700 cubic feet per second. The sweet spot is between 400 and 800 cubic feet per second. When we started yesterday, we were near that 800 number, and the river was a little fast, so we didn't get to fish it as slowly and intently as we would have liked. If the cubic feet per second gets lower than 400, you will get stuck in some places on that 8 mile stretch and have to get out of your kayak and walk. To find the flow rate, or cubic feet per second, of the Collins river, you can look here...

https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03421000/all-graphs/#period=P7D

When I went to grab the website to share with you just now, the river was at 612 cubic feet per second. That's a fantastic number! Not too fast and not too slow. If you get a chance, Christmas day would be a great day to kayak for muskie! But what are you going to do to catch one? I'm glad you asked...

Here's what I like to do. I grab my 7 ft, medium heavy rod. I put 80 lb braid on my reel, and then I attach a 100 lb steel leader, I like a 6-inch steel leader. From there, you can use whatever type of lure you like! A few weeks ago, my buddy was using a 1/8 of an ounce crappie jig with a 3-inch soft plastic on that same setup, and he caught a muskie! I always tell people, use your favorite lure. If you have a confidence lure, like a Ned rig or a buzzbait, throw that! The three of us were throwing white paddle tails. A very simple bass lure with a quarter ounce jig head and a 5 inch soft plastic. A confidence lure for Smallmouth, but when musky decide they want to eat, they eat whatever they see.

Yesterday, a few different Muskie came out and took a swipe at our lures, but only one of them got hooked up and in the net. It was probably 3 ft long, and a little less than 10 lb. It put up one heck of a fight, and it came really close to the end of the trip. I'd say about 7 miles into our 8 mile trip. That gives me a chance to explain the most important part of Muskie fishing, how to handle them.

You want a giant, rubber net. The biggest one you can find. You want the Muskie to be able to swim around in the net. Once we got the fish in the net, we got lucky, because the hook fell out. Quite often, especially when you're in kayaks, getting the muskie free from the hook can be a fiasco! Here's what you do in that situation... With the muskie in a position that water can flow freely over its gills, paddle your way to the bank. Once you get there, get out on the bank where you have firm footing, while keeping the Muskie in the water, and try to secure the hooks. You're definitely going to need footlong pliers, and you're also going to need something to cut the hooks in case you can't remove them. I like a small bolt cutter. Carry that with you when you go musky fishing.

There's a tool called a jaw spreader that is specifically made for Muskie and Pike. I do not have one of those, but I definitely should. It's on my Christmas wish list, and I'm hoping I get one tomorrow. Everyone should have a jaw spreader, just in case you're lure has pinned the mouth shut. Jaw spreaders will help you open the fish's mouth, so that you don't expose yourself to the toothy interior.

Once you have the hooks far away from the fish, and the fish in the net, swimming freely, now you're able to take a picture. Using your dominant hand, for me my right hand, grab the fish by the tail. That's the part that it uses to slash, that's where you want to hold it firm. Once you have the fish just above the tail, in the meaty part of the end of the fish, you can slide your left hand underneath the belly of the fish. Now you can lift the fish up, out of the net, but make sure to keep it over the water, and not hold it over the bank. If the fish thrashes, you want it to fall into the water, and not on to the ground.

Congratulations, you caught the fish of 10,000 casts! Make sure to share your picture on social media, and tell them Better Days sent you!

title: Trip Report #136
content_raw:
Crappie were shallow yesterday...
Yesterday, I had a client booked for the 4-hour instructional crappie fishing trip. He wanted to see my lowrance eagle eye 9 in action. We met at 6:30 a.m. at Jefferson Springs boat ramp...
Jefferson Springs Boat Ramp. https://share.google/5lSMx0xAbnT2ik9Gz
We got in and headed directly upstream, to a spot just below the confluence of the East Fork and West Fork Stones river, where I have been finding lots of crappie. It's just a little more than two miles from the boat ramp, and these fish have been sitting there, on this spot, for more than a month now. The water is shallow in this area, 13 ft of depth or less. They're hanging out on a bunch of stumps that are under the water. I'm going to drop a pin of exactly where I've been finding these fish...
https://goo.gl/maps/7N8fRBttPc2RhKLa6
We did a little bit of fishing for these fish, and we were getting good bites, but my client is already rather proficient at crappie fishing, so he wanted to cruise around and look at the fish finder more than just sitting somewhere and fishing. So that's what we did! After we found these fish, and took a good look at what they look like on the fish finder, we started working our way back to the boat ramp.
On our way back, we scanned The cliffs that we could see above the surface of the water and we scanned cliffs that were underneath the surface of the water, looking for crappie. Unfortunately, they're not really hanging on the cliffs right now. They seem to be in shallower areas, that have a mud bottom, and trees in the water. Most of the time, the tree has to be completely submerged, or they won't be hanging on it.
There's a spot on the side of the lake where I had found a bunch of crappie, and you could walk to if you park on Jefferson pike. I had gone there rather recently and caught lots of crappie standing on the bank. We went to scan that area, and none of those fish were there! The water may have gotten a little too shallow since they dropped the lake. I'm going to drop a pin on that location, just so you don't waste your time. It's a pretty long walk through the woods to get skunked...
https://goo.gl/maps/TWBw2nXpUpqfVARA9
One thing I did notice on the fish finder, as we were scanning this 2-mile stretch of lake, there are white bass and yellow bass everywhere! They swim in small schools, relative to the size of a school of crappie, and they move really fast. I had caught a bunch of white bass in this area a few weeks ago, during the afternoon bite. Those fish get fired up in the evening better than they do in the morning. They like to go to those shallow, mud flats, to target threadfin shad. But we weren't looking for white bass, so we didn't fish for those. We kept scanning the area, so he could get a good feel for forward facing sonar.
By the time we made it almost all the way back to the boat ramp, we were underneath the bridge on Jefferson Pike that goes over the lake. If you're coming from the boat ramp, the very first pillar in the water, on the south side of the bridge, was completely loaded with crappie! We put an anchor down, and sat there and caught a few of those fish so he could take some home to eat. These crappie were tightly schooled, hanging right next to the pillar, in 26 ft of water. But even though the water was really deep, they were suspended between 4 and 10 ft! We were able to cast ultralight setups directly over top of them, and start reeling as soon as the lure hit the surface.
Using ultralight rods and reels, with 4 lb monofilament, and a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a pearl colored body Garland baby shad, we would cast directly past the school of fish, and start a painfully slow retrieve, with the rod tip up at a 45° angle. As soon as that little soft plastic would get above the school of fish, one would come up and give it a thump! If you're unfamiliar with crappie fishing, that's the bite. You get a split second, where you feel a small thump, and you have to set the hook right then. They won't bite it multiple times, or chew on it like a bass. You need to have a quick hook set.
You could potentially catch those crappie from the bank, but only if you could cast a slip bobber setup about 75 yards. I happened to have mine with me in the boat, so I made a quick cast over to the bank to see if I could make it to that pillar from the bank. I could, but just barely. I would have to tweak my setup a little to make it all the way out there, it's a long way. But if you could, you could have a day at that spot, from the bank, catching crappie!
The water temperature on the south end of the lake, where the lake begins, was 51 and a half degrees! I was really surprised to see it that warm. But, it has been warm the last few days, and it will be warm going forward. So I expect these fish to stay put, on the trees that they have found. There won't be major fluctuations in temperature, so they should be particularly willing to bite. One major concern, it seems like the entire lake is chocolate milk brown! There wasn't any clear water that we could find yesterday, and most of it was filled with debris, logs, trash, and leaves from our recent heavy rainfall event. Don't let that discourage you, these fish still eat really well when the water is brown!

title: Trip Report #137
content_raw:
A cave you can kayak into...
Yesterday, I had high hopes that the crappie would pile up below Nice Mill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/mqZkdfZiKyyKaap3A
I got there at 5:00 a.m. just to make sure I got my favorite spot. I like to go down the trail and then to the right, where there is a cliff that overhangs the river. It's the most popular spot to stand, that isn't on the dam, and the only good spot to stand yesterday...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/i8WYTf929qPdnrPC9
We had a massive amount of rain on Friday, and that caused the Stones River to rise rapidly on Saturday. When that happens, and the water gets brown, and goes over the dam, crappie will school in great numbers, just below the dam. They do it all winter long, up until the time in which they spawn, usually late April. When that happens, I like to be there early in the morning with a minnow under a bobber. The river is really shallow in this area, so you only need about 2 ft of depth. I cast all the way across the heavy current, to a nice calm pocket that is created behind what is typically an island.
Lots of people show up to this spot to catch crappie, every time this situation presents itself. Unfortunately, yesterday, the crappy didn't show up. They will, you just never know when. So you have to give that spot a chance whenever the water is brown and flowing fast. But I couldn't get anything done there, so I went to another crappie spot, not far away on Percy Priest lake.
https://maps.app.goo.gl/pnqSaRyyHyixS6Ah6
That's where you can park on the side of Weekly lane. It's a parking spot on the side of the road that is public access to the lake. You are allowed to be there, but the road drops off really steep! You need to be real careful pulling in and out of this spot. You either need a high profile vehicle, or you need to take your time. Once you park there, there's a trail through the woods that takes you over to the cliffs. Once you get to the cliffs, you can start going downhill to this pin that I'm about to drop.
https://goo.gl/maps/qMkcpxRUn4DGvoa87
I found this spot with my forward facing sonar in my boat. Each time I've been there in my boat, I have caught lots of crappie! I've gone there three times now on the bank, and I have yet to have a good day. Yesterday, I only fished for about 20 minutes before I realized that the crappie either weren't there, or we're not going to bite. So I headed down the road to a third spot on Percy Priest lake. That's what you do when your crappie fishing. If you can't find crappie at the location you show up at, you need to go to another location. When you find crappie, you can almost always catch one. Where there is one, there are almost always more.
https://maps.app.goo.gl/A4CYcpEehvL8rURG7
That's a pin for a location on the side of Maddox road where, once again, it's really steep and you need to be super careful pulling in. You are allowed to be here, this is the side of Percy Priest lake. Take the trail through the woods to the pin that I'm about to drop.
https://maps.app.goo.gl/8YfNDWtTi4ojDaHk9
There's a cliff face right here with a tree that is in the water. It's just a tall tree trunk with no limbs. It's standing straight up and down on the cliff, so you will know exactly where to stand. Right beside it! You can climb down the cliff to be right on the water's edge. This spot, off of Maddox, is affectionately referred to as the brush pile. Fortunately, underneath the surface of the water, there are tons of trees! That means crappy love to hang out in this spot. Unfortunately, it means you're going to lose a lot of hooks. That's what happened to me yesterday. I got hung up, and broke off, lots! But I finally got a nice big slab crappie! Unfortunately, I didn't get to the spot until around 9:00 a.m. then it seemed like if the fish were biting, they quit.
To fish in this spot, you need to use an ultra light rod and reel with a very light jig head. Something like a 1/32nd ounce. This area is really shallow, only about 8 ft! Don't allow your jig head to sink. Cast out, and start a painfully slow retrieve, as soon as your lure hits the water. These fish will come up out of the branches to attack your lure. Another good way to catch crappie at this location, would be with a minnow under a bobber. I had Amino and some bobbers yesterday, but the wind was blowing in my face. When that happens, the bobber will blow back to the bank, rendering it useless.
When I caught my first and only crappie of the day, I realized where I was standing. Just a stone's throw away from a cave that I could kayak into. Not necessarily a fishing destination, more of an adventure spot! And adventure spot just for us, because no one else ever goes there LOL I didn't mention where it was in the video, and I'm about to tell you exactly how to get there, if you would like to kayak inside of a cave.
You're going to want to park on the side of Maddox road...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/notuSisjpyYAB8AS8
At this curve in the road, the lake is right there! There are a number of parking spaces, even though they're a little muddy. You're allowed to park here, and take your kayak down to the lake and drop in. Once you do, it's a short paddle around the corner and then into the cave! I'm going to drop you a pin of exactly where the mouth of the cave is...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/zT8JUikEJdnnjsyv5
You can only kayak into this cave when the water on Percy Priest Lake is below 494.5 ft in elevation. As of yesterday, the rainwater had brought the lake near that level, but the dam was starting to release water from the lake, which was dropping the level. That means, we will be able to kayak into this cave for the foreseeable future. To find the elevation of Percy Priest lake, look here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/j-percy-priest
There were some small largemouth bass in the cave, but they were really small. I still caught them, but they were really small. Nothing that serious fishermen would be concerned with, more of a place to go adventure! Take half a day and go explore a cave that is typically underwater!

title: Trip Report #138
content_raw:
The best stretch of Trout River in Middle Tennessee...
Yesterday, my buddy and I kayaked the first 6 miles of the Caney Fork River below Center Hill dam. We started at Buffalo Valley boat ramp...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/ci5yUrjeMTVBlRg1T
From there, it's 6 mi downstream to the second boat ramp below the dam, at Happy Hollow boat ramp...
Happy Hollow Boat Ramp https://share.google/kZc9NSInv1gZiz3fE
The number one factor you want to consider when kayaking down the Caney Fork river, is the generating schedule. Yesterday, the generators were scheduled to be off from 8:00 a.m. until 3:00 p.m. That would allow us enough time to facilitate a downstream trip, during which we could fish the entire six miles of river, relatively slowly. I don't recommend trying to kayak down this River while the generators are on. Yes, lots of people do it. No, I wouldn't recommend it. To find the generating schedule, you can look here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
We get there before the generators turned off. We wanted to do a little fishing below the dam, before we started working our way downstream. If you were to start heading downstream with the generating water, before it turned off, you would ride it all the way down to the end, relatively quickly, and you wouldn't be able to do much fishing. We wanted to wait until the generator is turned off completely, that way we could slowly float down and fish as we went. Typically, once you know the flow of the water, the hardest part is coordinating your shuttle. Here's how I handle that on the Caney Fork river.
Before I was scheduled to meet my friend at Happy Hollow boat ramp, downstream from the dam, I went up to Buffalo valley boat ramp, and dropped off my kayaks and all my fishing equipment. I like to set my stuff right on the side of the river, and then drive back to Happy Hollow to leave my vehicle. When I get there, I hop in with my buddy and we go up to the dam where my kayaks are waiting for us. Then we float back down where my vehicle is parked, and we are able to load up everything, then I drive him back up to the dam and drop him off at his vehicle. That's called logistics, and sometimes, it's really tough to figure out.
There's almost always people fishing at the dam. I don't worry about somebody taking my stuff. I've been doing it this way for several years, and I haven't had any problems. That doesn't mean it won't happen, but typically, there is safety in numbers. Just having other fishermen around, keeps people honest. So that's the way I've been facilitating these trips for the last few years.
Yesterday was a really tough day. We fished the entire 6 miles of river and we didn't even catch ten fish. I only caught one! We spent the majority of our time visiting and casting rooster tails. That would be the most effective lure on the day. Using ultralight rods and reels with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/8 of an ounce rooster tail, we were able to get a few little browns and a few little rainbows. Typically, I use a white rooster tail with a silver blade. Yesterday, trout weren't really interested in a silver blade. My friend was throwing a rooster tail with a gold blade, and he caught more than half a dozen fish.
It was an overcast sky, and that's the opposite of what I usually do. Typically, when the skies are overcast, I'm using silver blades for trout and doing pretty well. Yesterday, they wanted that gold blade. I usually save gold blades and gold spoons and even gold trout magnets for really sunny days. But sometimes, you have to let the fish tell you what they want. It was very clear yesterday. I didn't have any luck on my lures because they were the wrong size. Everything I had in my tackle box was a little too heavy from 1/6 of an ounce to 1/4 of an ounce! Those fish wanted a smaller presentation. 1/8 of an ounce was the magic number, but only if it had a gold blade.
Since I wasn't having any luck with my lures, I went to my tried and true method. A number 6 eagle claw bait holder hook with a split shot about one foot above the hook. One pink Berkeley Magnum floating power bait for trout, and half a Canadian nightcrawler. I dragged that setup along the bottom of the river for miles before I got my first bite! I wouldn't catch that fish, or the next fish that would bite, but eventually, a pretty little brown trout, a little more than a foot long, committed to my nightcrawler, and made his way into the video! That would be the only fish I would catch.
So what gives? Why didn't we catch a hundred fish like we usually do in the summertime. That one's easy! Because of the water level. Trout on the Caney Fork River hate when the water is falling. Most of the fish don't like it. So what does that mean? Basically, after the generators turn off, before the water gets all the way down, it's falling pretty fast. When it's going up, those fish feel real comfortable, exploring new areas. When it's going down, it starts squeezing them into smaller areas, and they hate the way that feels. I've been fishing out there for over 33 years, and the worst time to fish, is right after the generators turn off.
So why did we go yesterday right after the generators turned off? Easy answer, that was the only time we could go. Just because it's not going to be a stellar day of fishing, doesn't mean I won't go. Even if I know the conditions aren't favorable, I'll still opt for a day on the water, if it's possible! For us to catch that many fish, in those conditions, was actually pretty good! It's tough to catch anything while the water is dropping, and if you're floating downstream, just after generators turn off, you're going to be encountering water that is dropping the whole entire trip.
This time of year, they have to run the generators more because of the demand for electricity. Very rarely, will they turn the generators off for more than 4 or 5 hours at a time. When they do, that's your best opportunity to float the Caney.

title: Trip Report #139
content_raw:
The most bass I've ever seen in one spot...
This afternoon, I went to Spring Creek Spring...
https://share.google/hjPmhayVvXZ6AuF8t
It's a long walk from the side of Maddox road, but it's all public property, which means it belongs to us! Go over, under, or around the gate, trust me, you're allowed to be here! Take the path all the way until it ends at the spring. Did not go left or right off the path! Follow it all the way under the telephone lines until you get to the spring...
https://goo.gl/maps/na4v6UN4bDedFHJv8
When I got there, it was already 2:00. I started with my ultralight rod and reel and a 1/32nd ounce jig head. I had my favorite crappie soft plastic, a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad. Those crappie weren't having it! I tried fishing slow and low, then I tried fishing really slow and really low, but I couldn't get a crappie to bite. From the second I walked up, there were numerous amounts of largemouth bass everywhere! So I turned my attention to trying to get one of those.
I didn't have anything I needed! All I would have needed was a medium action bass rod with 8 lb monofilament and a bobber and a number one eagle claw bait holder hook with some shiners from Big Charlie's bait shop. What I'm about to say is not hyperbole... I would have put a shiner 4 inches underneath a bobber and cast it right next to the bank. These largemouth bass were feeding at the bank all the way around the spring, all afternoon! All I had was crappie gear. So I tried to catch a bluegill the best I could. My plan, put a small bluegill on a hook. That should get one as well!
I tried catching a bluegill for more than 30 minutes, but I couldn't get one on the hook. So I started jigging my crappie jig in front of the bass to see if I could get one of those. I managed to catch a couple little ones, but there were some true monsters roaming around in there! Among the fish you could see in the ultra clear water were largemouth and spotted bass, every kind of sunfish, the occasional crappie, and gizzard shad as big as dinner plates!
As I was trying to coax one of these small bass into a bite, a really big crappie came up and smashed my jig! At this point in time, it was right around 3:30, and the sun was starting to go down fast. There was a small bite window, maybe 25 minutes, where I could predictably get a crappie bite, and occasionally catch one. The late afternoon bite is one of the worst times of day to catch crappie, in my opinion. I would imagine that the spring would be on fire tomorrow morning! Perhaps, even overnight tonight.

title: Trip Report #140
content_raw:
The fish were still there...
Yesterday afternoon, I took my boat out at West Fork boat ramp...
West Fork Boat Ramp https://share.google/IIP4Sw9fS99RLs9iN
I was there 48 hours prior, on Saturday afternoon. When I got there, it was an impromptu trip, and I wasn't expecting what I saw, fish were everywhere! Lots of crappie on structure, in very shallow water! At the surface! In one or two foot of water. There were unbelievable amounts of bluegills as well as huge schools of white bass roaming around. They were even plenty of largemouth to catch! That stretch of the lake, which is basically the river, is shallow, and it was extremely warm. 51 and a half degrees.
Then the bottom dropped out. Saturday night, a massive cold front came through, and it was so cold, that I didn't go fishing Sunday. Monday afternoon, it got above freezing for the first time in 36 hours, so I headed down to the river to see if those fish had left the area. I suspected, that the drop in temperatures would cause the fish to leave shallow water and seek the refuge of deeper, warmer, more temperature stable water.
The only thing I was right about, was the temperature affecting the water temperature. The water had dropped seven degrees! Previously, the water temperature was 51 and a half, yesterday afternoon, it was 44 and a half degrees! That's a really big drop. The water in that area only gets to about 11 or 12 ft deep, at the deepest. So I expected fish to move far downstream, near the lake. And I was wrong!
The same fish were stacked up all over. Most of the fish were on the bank, except for the schools of white bass, which were constantly roaming. Don't get me wrong, yesterday was a really tough fishing day, but I was able to catch a few of each different kind of species. All of those fish are still there, in great numbers! So here's exactly where I found them.
At the boat ramp. Once again, I never left sight of the boat ramp. If you're standing on the boat ramp, looking out at the river, to the right, you can go over a downed tree that's in the way, and there is a stump that someone has chainsawed, that is laying over in front of a spot that is loaded! Out in front of that spot, the water gets about seven or eight feet deep pretty quick, and there is a tree stuck there. For some reason, fish are loaded on that tree, each time I've been there. It's a whole lot of bluegill, and occasionally, a school of crappie works its way in there. To fish that spot, I would use a minnow under a bobber at a depth of about 2 or 3 ft.
Across from the boat ramp, you can see trees in the water everywhere! They are typically in the lake when it is at summer pool, but now, most of the trees are out of the water, with only the treetops submerged. Every type of fish is hanging out underneath those trees! All the way up to the bank, as far out as five or six foot of depth. Pack your patience! These fish are really tough to get, once again, the best method is going to be a minnow under a bobber. Trying to cast and retrieve into those trees will get you hung up, a lot!
I'm not certain how cold it has to get before those fish leave the area, or if they ever will. I do know, we don't have any cold weather in the forecast. Temperatures are going to be relatively stable for the next 10 days, and I expect crappie fishing to be on fire! After all, crappie love consistency!
