title: Trip Report #141
content_raw:
I found them!
Saturday, I had a client booked for a 4-Hour forward facing sonar instructional trip. We were going to take his boat, and launch from Elm Hill boat ramp at 6:00 a.m...
Elm Hill Rush Boat Ramp https://share.google/m8y6dk42cu7j0Cm98
I chose this boat ramp because it's closer to where he lives, on the west side of middle Tennessee. If you've been reading my reports for a while, you know that, for the past few months, my buddy Chris and i, have been catching crappie off the cliffs at Elm Hill, fairly reliably! Saturday would be no different. We would take his boat directly across the cove to the cliffs in front of the boat ramp, look for a school of crappie with his forward facing sonar, find them, put out an anchor, and then catch a bunch of fish.
We never moved from that spot for the entire 4 hours. We didn't have to. These fish were biting pretty well, which gave us ample time to do lots of forward facing sonar instruction. The most important instruction when it comes to these fish, be patient. Typically, if you can find them, you can catch them. Especially if they're out in the open like this location, where they are suspended on a cliff face. Crappie can be much more difficult to catch when you find them in brush, or underneath tree limbs. That's another reason why this spot is a good location for beginners, these fish are hanging on the cliff itself, as opposed to underwater structure like trees, that can hang up your lures, and break you off.
We were using ultralight setups. 4 lb monofilament with 1/32nd ounce jig heads. That's my go-to when I'm trying to catch crappie. The only difference, when I'm in the boat, I will add a split shot to get that jig down faster. No point in fishing slow when you can see the lure and the fish on your screen. Just go ahead and get that lure down to them quickly, and start working in front of their face. That's typically a winning recipe!
These fish provided very little resistance. On the day, we caught dozens of fish. He was hoping to take a couple home to eat, he ended up with six nice fat slabs in the live well! A really good outing, in a really reliable spot, there's only one real drawback to this location, that's the cost. Unfortunately, even though Elm Hill boat ramp is public, it does have a gate that charges you $10 to get in. It's open 24 hours a day, so you don't have to worry about showing up and the boat ramp being closed. But you will always have to pay to get in. What we've been doing, and I'm not sure if it's legal or not, is that one of us has paid, and then the other follows them through the gate. Once you get to the parking lot, there is a porta john, which is nice.
After that trip, I headed back to Murfreesboro to get some quick lunch, to meet my second client of the day. We were scheduled to fish from 12:00 to 4: 00 p.m. Our plan was to fish the recently stocked trout in the West Fork Stones River below Nice Mill Dam...
Nice Mill Recreation Area https://share.google/6B4KMkJb0JOs4MqX9
THERE WERE A MILLION PEOPLE THERE SATURDAY AFTERNOON!
So we did the sensible thing and rescheduled. Then I found myself with some time on my hands, but not very much. As we all know, the Sun starts setting around 4:00, and it's dark before 5:00 p.m. So I raced home, hooked my boat up to my truck, and then went to West Fork boat ramp...
West Fork Boat Ramp https://share.google/qVZAkVeaHRhOrBHgz
This is the closest boat ramp to my house, therefore the easiest quick access. I hadn't taken my forward facing sonar to this boat ramp yet so I was excited to see if there were any fish on the shallow, tributary into the lake. When I got into the water, I was surprised to see that the temperature was 51 and a half degrees. That's a full five degrees warmer than the Elm Hill area where we were fishing in the morning. Also, the lake at West Fork boat ramp is really shallow. No more than 13 ft of depth in the center. I knew it was shallow, but I was surprised that it was so warm.
I WAS NEVER ABLE TO LEAVE THE BOAT RAMP AREA! As soon as I turned on my fish finder, there were crappie everywhere! The first school of crappie I started catching, we're off the bank at the boat ramp. I'm going to tell you exactly where these fish were, but I'm worried that our cold weather made them leave the area. The water temperature was 51 and a half degrees on Saturday, and that was our last warm day. The temperature bottomed out Saturday night, and I'm afraid that when the river temperature dropped, those fish may have left the area. Nevertheless, here's where they were...
If you're standing on the boat ramp and looking to your right, the exposed lake bed is all mud. There's a piece of tree trunk that someone cut with a chainsaw that is a perfect chair. It's literally sitting right in front of where you need to fish. I suspect someone planted the brush pile in this area. So if you're standing at the boat ramp look to your right and you will see a laid over stump that is perfect to use as a seat. Set that thing up, use it as a seat, and fish directly in front of you. Those fish are no more than 30 ft from the bank, and they're hanging out in a shallow brush pile. The best way to get them, would be with a bobber with 2 ft of depth and a minnow.
After I beat up those fish for a little while, I turned around to the other bank, away from the boat ramp, and it was absolutely overwhelmingly loaded with fish! First of all, there's a whole bunch of trees in the water directly across from the boat ramp. Every single one of those trees was loaded with bluegill and bass and crappie. While I was sitting there, catching fish after fish after fish, huge schools of white bass came through and attacked my lure! I have no idea why the river was so overwhelmingly loaded with fish, but I suspect it's been this way for most of the Fall. Unfortunately, I've been sleeping on the closest boat ramp to my house!
These fish are in the trees, but that doesn't make them harder to get, it kind of makes them easier to get. Instead of making long casts, and allowing my lure to sink to a certain depth, before I can start my retrieve, I'm free to make short casts, and even use a bobber! I didn't do it on Saturday, but it's a great idea! These trees are hanging off of the bank, and into the water. Those fish, are underneath the overhanging limbs. You can see the limbs out of the water. That gives you a tactical advantage. Now, all you need to do, is take a minnow, or one of those Bobby Garland's, underneath a bobber, at about 2 or 3 ft. Throw that in there next to those trees, and hold on tight!

We would take his boat directly across the cove to the cliffs in front of the boat ramp, look for a school of crappie with his forward facing sonar, find them, put out an anchor, and then catch a bunch of fish.

We never moved from that spot for the entire 4 hours. We didn't have to. These fish were biting pretty well, which gave us ample time to do lots of forward facing sonar instruction. The most important instruction when it comes to these fish, be patient. Typically, if you can find them, you can catch them. Especially if they're out in the open like this location, where they are suspended on a cliff face. Crappie can be much more difficult to catch when you find them in brush, or underneath tree limbs. That's another reason why this spot is a good location for beginners, these fish are hanging on the cliff itself, as opposed to underwater structure like trees, that can hang up your lures, and break you off.

We were using ultralight setups. 4 lb monofilament with 1/32nd ounce jig heads. That's my go-to when I'm trying to catch crappie. The only difference, when I'm in the boat, I will add a split shot to get that jig down faster. No point in fishing slow when you can see the lure and the fish on your screen. Just go ahead and get that lure down to them quickly, and start working in front of their face. That's typically a winning recipe!

These fish provided very little resistance. On the day, we caught dozens of fish. He was hoping to take a couple home to eat, he ended up with six nice fat slabs in the live well! A really good outing, in a really reliable spot, there's only one real drawback to this location, that's the cost. Unfortunately, even though Elm Hill boat ramp is public, it does have a gate that charges you $10 to get in. It's open 24 hours a day, so you don't have to worry about showing up and the boat ramp being closed. But you will always have to pay to get in. What we've been doing, and I'm not sure if it's legal or not, is that one of us has paid, and then the other follows them through the gate. Once you get to the parking lot, there is a porta john, which is nice.

After that trip, I headed back to Murfreesboro to get some quick lunch, to meet my second client of the day. We were scheduled to fish from 12:00 to 4: 00 p.m. Our plan was to fish the recently stocked trout in the West Fork Stones River below Nice Mill Dam...

Nice Mill Recreation Area https://share.google/6B4KMkJb0JOs4MqX9

THERE WERE A MILLION PEOPLE THERE SATURDAY AFTERNOON!

So we did the sensible thing and rescheduled. Then I found myself with some time on my hands, but not very much. As we all know, the Sun starts setting around 4:00, and it's dark before 5:00 p.m. So I raced home, hooked my boat up to my truck, and then went to West Fork boat ramp...

West Fork Boat Ramp https://share.google/qVZAkVeaHRhOrBHgz

This is the closest boat ramp to my house, therefore the easiest quick access. I hadn't taken my forward facing sonar to this boat ramp yet so I was excited to see if there were any fish on the shallow, tributary into the lake. When I got into the water, I was surprised to see that the temperature was 51 and a half degrees. That's a full five degrees warmer than the Elm Hill area where we were fishing in the morning. Also, the lake at West Fork boat ramp is really shallow. No more than 13 ft of depth in the center. I knew it was shallow, but I was surprised that it was so warm.

I WAS NEVER ABLE TO LEAVE THE BOAT RAMP AREA! As soon as I turned on my fish finder, there were crappie everywhere! The first school of crappie I started catching, we're off the bank at the boat ramp. I'm going to tell you exactly where these fish were, but I'm worried that our cold weather made them leave the area. The water temperature was 51 and a half degrees on Saturday, and that was our last warm day. The temperature bottomed out Saturday night, and I'm afraid that when the river temperature dropped, those fish may have left the area. Nevertheless, here's where they were...

If you're standing on the boat ramp and looking to your right, the exposed lake bed is all mud. There's a piece of tree trunk that someone cut with a chainsaw that is a perfect chair. It's literally sitting right in front of where you need to fish. I suspect someone planted the brush pile in this area. So if you're standing at the boat ramp look to your right and you will see a laid over stump that is perfect to use as a seat. Set that thing up, use it as a seat, and fish directly in front of you. Those fish are no more than 30 ft from the bank, and they're hanging out in a shallow brush pile. The best way to get them, would be with a bobber with 2 ft of depth and a minnow.

After I beat up those fish for a little while, I turned around to the other bank, away from the boat ramp, and it was absolutely overwhelmingly loaded with fish! First of all, there's a whole bunch of trees in the water directly across from the boat ramp. Every single one of those trees was loaded with bluegill and bass and crappie. While I was sitting there, catching fish after fish after fish, huge schools of white bass came through and attacked my lure! I have no idea why the river was so overwhelmingly loaded with fish, but I suspect it's been this way for most of the Fall. Unfortunately, I've been sleeping on the closest boat ramp to my house!

These fish are in the trees, but that doesn't make them harder to get, it kind of makes them easier to get. Instead of making long casts, and allowing my lure to sink to a certain depth, before I can start my retrieve, I'm free to make short casts, and even use a bobber! I didn't do it on Saturday, but it's a great idea! These trees are hanging off of the bank, and into the water. Those fish, are underneath the overhanging limbs. You can see the limbs out of the water. That gives you a tactical advantage. Now, all you need to do, is take a minnow, or one of those Bobby Garland's, underneath a bobber, at about 2 or 3 ft. Throw that in there next to those trees, and hold on tight!

title: Trip Report #142
content_raw:
The best winter time trout stocking location?
Today, TWRA stocked 1500 rainbow trout in the West Fork Stones river, at Nice Mill Dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/5Gn5QpEscJ27tEJq9
I got there at 9:00 a.m. the trout truck arrived at 9:46 a.m. When I took a quick count, there were 34 people fishing, and everybody was having a good time, and most people were catching fish!
Each one of these winter time stocking locations is unique unto itself. You never know exactly what these fish are going to bite after they are delivered, but if you know the lay of the land, it's easier to decide what type of trout lure will work best. Today, the West Fork Stones was running fast and shallow. The water below the dam is no more than knee deep in most places, and there's a lot of current. In a situation like that, I like to use a lure that moves through the water, so I can avoid hanging up on the bottom as much as possible.
Today, I took my 6 ft ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and started off with a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail. As it would turn out, that would be the only lure I would need. When you have 1500 rainbow trout directly in front of you, pretty much any lure will work. I'm going to tell you a few of the different setups that I saw people using that caught fish, in case maybe you'd like to do something a little different.
Lots of people were using a hook and a sinker on the bottom. Some people were using worms, some people had on a few kernels of corn, most people were using Berkeley powerbait for trout. Pretty much anything laying on the bottom is fair game for these fish, and those fishermen were limiting out quickly. The majority of fishermen were using exactly what I was using, a 1/8 of an ounce rooster tail, but there were a variety of different colors. Every color was working. There was a fly fisherman standing right next to me, and he was using a small strike indicator and a black zebra midge, size 20. He was having good luck as well.
At this location, all of the rainbow trout are between 8 and 12 inches long. They stock a whole lot of them in this particular location, but I have never seen them stock any big ones. These fish come from the Dale Hollow national fish hatchery in Celina Tennessee. They have a more than 2-hour journey to reach their destination at Nice Mill in Smyrna, so that explains why they usually show up right around 10:00 a.m.
This location will get stocked again in January and in February. That's typical for these winter stocking events, most locations get three separate stockings. This particular river, the West Fork Stones river, gets stocked in two different locations. Not only at Nice Mill, where we were today, but upstream 12 miles at Ransom Mill as well. At that location, they put 500 trout, but those trout are unable to go upstream any farther, so they make their way down. Today's trout, can easily make their way up over the dam. We were able to stand there and watch them do it! Bottom line, the 12 Mile stretch of river between Nice Mill and Ransom Mill in Murfreesboro will be full of trout up until the end of May.
Because Murfreesboro has such an extensive Greenway system, there's bank access to the first four miles of that stretch of river. The next 8 miles are out in the wilderness. The only way to get to those fish will be by kayak. That trip can be facilitated by launching at the Thompson Lane trailhead at the end of the Murfreesboro Greenway...
https://share.google/aR5sJxfIO3Vv4tReo
I wouldn't suggest anyone who isn't an extremely good kayaker, with white water paddling capabilities, attempt this trip. It's an all-day trip, it's 8 Miles long, there's lots of rapids and steep drops, and even the best kayakers get flipped on this stretch of river. You're going to want to take out at Nice Mill, where they put the fish in today. That stretch of river is going to be loaded with smallmouth bass. The side mission, try to find a pocket where some of these rainbow have schooled up, and catch a bunch of them!

title: Trip Report #143
content_raw:
The trout stocking location where the fish can't get away, and a place on Percy Priest to catch crappie from the bank...
Yesterday, I went to the trout stocking event in Fayetteville Tennessee...
https://share.google/Y60a8gpEzAnWt3yYM
That link is for Stone Bridge Memorial Park in Fayetteville. There is a horseshoe shaped pond that has three fountains and one bridge across the pond. They brought 250 trout, plus three sizable palomino, or albino trout. The best thing about this stocking location, is the fact that the fish can't get away. They can't swim away from this area. They will be in that pond until every single one of them is caught. But there's a lot of great things to like about this location!
It seems to be open all the time. There are not any gates that could be closed. That means there's lots of accessibility! You can walk all the way around the pond. Every bit of it. You can fish from both sides. So it's accessible, and it's easy to fish. There's also a public restroom for men and women. As well as picnic tables under a covered pavilion, and even some nice porch swings! The only thing it doesn't have, is a playground. But there are lots of ducks, and they have duck food available for a quarter, at a vending machine.
The fish weren't biting yesterday! I tried to catch the fish out of that pond for more than 3 hours! I was only able to generate one little bite. I got there at 7:30 a.m. but the truck didn't arrive until just after 9:00 a.m. I stayed until just after 12:00, and I only saw one person catch one fish the entire time. Unfortunately, it was one of those big albino trout. It ate a 1/8 oz white rooster tail. That's what most of us were throwing out there, rooster tails.
I tried every trout lure you can think of, I even took my fly rod and tried several different flies. This was one of those occasions where, when those trout got off the truck, they didn't bite. That doesn't happen very often. For what it's worth, there is a trout stocking event tomorrow in Smyrna Tennessee, on the West Fork Stones River, I will be there, and those fish will be biting. I like to get there around 8:30, just to make sure I am there when the truck shows up. They typically show up as early as 9:00, or as late as noon. Either way, I can guarantee you right now, that tomorrow night's report, will be a successful one, from Nice Mill Dam...
https://share.google/wXGdFhWrfm4Et3NhG
Today, there was very light wind. Just the right condition for trying to utilize forward facing sonar in the boat, for crappie, on Percy Priest lake. When there's too much wind, it's hard to stay in position on the school of fish that you're trying to catch. With a light wind, it's easier to sit on an anchor or to use the spot lock feature on your trolling motor, if you have that, which I do not. I have a rock. On a rope. I use that as an anchor. It's cheap, and effective. Today, it worked out really well! I launched from Stewart Creek boat ramp at just after 9:00 a.m...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/xeoC4jJiSrdsKnyYF
For the first few hours, my buddy and I found several different schools of crappie, but they were tucked up underneath trees so tightly, that we kept getting hung up and broke off. It would be after lunch time before I would find a school of fish that were suspended away from structure enough to fish for. Fortunately, those fish were in a very large school, and sitting right in front of a spot that we would be able to get to from the bank. I'm going to drop a pin on exactly where those fish were, right here...
https://goo.gl/maps/nArDvQXz3QkiUE599
To get to this spot on the cliffs, you have to park on the side of weekly lane. When you pull into this well-known parking space, the road drops off really steep! You need to pull in really slow, and you probably shouldn't go there if you have a low profile vehicle. I'm going to drop a pin on the parking space, then you'll have to take the trail through the woods. Use your phone like a compass to walk down the trail to the cliffs, and then walk along the cliffs until you get to the pin that I gave you on Google maps...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/XDSQ33cPF2S79TAe9?g_st=ac
Catching these fish was like taking candy from a baby. Using my ultralight rod and reel, with 4 lb monofilament, a 1/48th of an ounce jig head with a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad and a medium sized split shot, about 1 ft above my jig head, I was able to cast all the way to the cliff face and let my lure sink down to about 20 ft where these fish were. Once it got down to their depth, I would start a slow retrieve, with a couple little twitches, to entice the bite. That works really well! But that technique wouldn't work well from the bank. So here's what you're going to have to do if you're going to this spot to fish from the bank.
First of all, you'll know you're in the right spot, because there are a couple of very large tree trunks in the water to your left, and there is a fire pit... because someone else has been fishing for these crappie! Stand right in front of the fire pit and cast directly out into the lake. I would use an ultralight setup with 4 lb test and a 1/32nd ounce jig head. Don't put any other weight on there, you're going to want this thing to sink slow. Cast it as far as you can, that's probably about 60 to 70 ft, and then allow it to sink really slowly, for probably about 30 seconds. Then you should be near the bottom. Then you can start a really slow retrieve. If you're getting hung up, you'll need to go a little faster. Don't be afraid to break off! That's part of it!
Once you figure out how deep you can't go, start working your way up. These fish are sitting really low right now! Start as low as you can go, and then if you can't get any bites, start working your way up the water column. That's what I would do for the next few months of winter, pretty much everywhere from the bank. There aren't going to be very many days when these fish are going to be near the surface on Percy Priest Lake.

title: Trip Report #144
content_raw:
Tragedy at the trout stocking in Lebanon...
Yesterday, I went to the trout stocking event in Lebanon, Tennessee at Don Fox Park...
https://share.google/M2Vnie8RaVE2JoDyK
There's a little creek that runs right through the park, and the TWRA stocks 250 trout there, three different times, during the winter. Yesterday was their first trip to Lebanon from the Flintville hatchery. After the video I made yesterday, they may not return for the next 2 months. What happened yesterday, was completely avoidable.
I got to Don Fox park at 9:00 a.m. Typically, they don't show up at this location until well after 10:00 a.m. That wasn't the case yesterday! At 10 minutes after 9:00, the trout truck pulled in and drove down the greenway, to the water's edge. In the past, they had used nets to move the fish into the creek. Yesterday, they used a pipe and dump the fish in 6 in of water. By 9:20, everything was done, and they were on their way out of the park.
Not before they dropped 250 rainbow trout ranging in size from 6 in to 12 in, and three palomino trout. All three of the palomino trout were really good sized, a couple of pounds or more, and all three of them died as soon as they hit the creek. They never stood a chance to swim away and be caught. I picked one up that was laying on its side, and held it in the current, to try to encourage it to live, but it went belly up. So I told the agents from TWRA, as they were packing up, that these fish were dying. Their response, we lose a few of them from time to time.
I explained that I had recently had a trout dinner and didn't want to keep them, they said that someone else could. So three different people grabbed those trout up off the creek bed and put them in their buckets. A real shame, and it could have been avoided if they'd have been at a better location. That creek is simply too small to hold trout that size, and they never really stood a chance. They couldn't even sit up right without most of their torso being out of water.
That wasn't the worst of it. This creek, being so small, and so shallow, created a condition where these trout found themselves beached. Sideways on limestone rock, completely unable to get back to the creek. When I found these fish, lying on the bank, my new mission became returning them to the water, instead of trying to catch them. They were at least eight or nine trout in one area that we're going to die quickly, if someone didn't intervene. The TWRA was long gone, so I took it upon myself. Once I got the fish back into the creek, it was finally time to do a little fishing.
But there wasn't any feasible way to catch these fish. The water was way too shallow, and there was nowhere for them to sit and feed. You can step across the creek in about three big steps, so there was nowhere to hide from the fish, they could always see you. This created a condition where these trout swim downstream, as hard, and as fast, as they could. That's not something I ever see at the stocking events! Typically, the fish hang out right where they're put in the water, and are very easy to catch.
Yesterday, everything that could go wrong, did go wrong. The big fish they wanted to put in the water didn't make it, the little fish they wanted people to catch found themselves in a perilous situation, and the water they were stocked into did not provide any real fishing opportunities for the anglers of Tennessee.

So three different people grabbed those trout up off the creek bed and put them in their buckets. A real shame, and it could have been avoided if they'd have been at a better location. That creek is simply too small to hold trout that size, and they never really stood a chance. They couldn't even sit up right without most of their torso being out of water.

That wasn't the worst of it. This creek, being so small, and so shallow, created a condition where these trout found themselves beached. Sideways on limestone rock, completely unable to get back to the creek. When I found these fish, lying on the bank, my new mission became returning them to the water, instead of trying to catch them. They were at least eight or nine trout in one area that we're going to die quickly, if someone didn't intervene. The TWRA was long gone, so I took it upon myself. Once I got the fish back into the creek, it was finally time to do a little fishing.

But there wasn't any feasible way to catch these fish. The water was way too shallow, and there was nowhere for them to sit and feed. You can step across the creek in about three big steps, so there was nowhere to hide from the fish, they could always see you. This created a condition where these trout swim downstream, as hard, and as fast, as they could. That's not something I ever see at the stocking events! Typically, the fish hang out right where they're put in the water, and are very easy to catch.

Yesterday, everything that could go wrong, did go wrong. The big fish they wanted to put in the water didn't make it, the little fish they wanted people to catch found themselves in a perilous situation, and the water they were stocked into did not provide any real fishing opportunities for the anglers of Tennessee.

title: Trip Report #145
content_raw:
Three different fishing adventures...
On Saturday, I met my buddy at Jefferson Springs boat ramp, to take out my boat, to find some crappie...
https://share.google/9vJNqPFvpoJBSSUD4
We went upstream, a little more than a mile, to the exact same spot where I had been catching crappie, three Saturdays in a row...
https://goo.gl/maps/uq7jACyU3WuNf28D8?g_st=ac
Fortunately for us, they were still hanging out in this area. Unfortunately, there were not nearly as many fish in this school as there had been previously. Another downturn in luck, these fish were not sitting still. They were constantly moving from one underwater tree to another. In this area, there are a handful of trees underwater, that are laying in the mud. These fish were moving, from structure to structure, constantly. We were sitting in about 10 ft of water, and they were sitting in about 8 ft of water. When they would stack up, they would be as close to the surface as 2 ft. That's pretty shallow, and that makes them easier to spook, so we sat about 40 ft away, on an anchor.
Using ultralight rods and reels with 4 lb monofilament, a 1/32nd ounce jig head, with a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad, those crappie didn't stand a chance. I was using Pearl color, my buddy was using blue ice. That's his favorite. I really don't think it matters. We were catching doubles, out of the same school of fish, with two different color baits. After we caught a handful of crappie, as well as some small largemouth and a couple of white bass, those fish didn't want to cooperate. So we scanned around the area until we found an underwater cliff.
This was a completely different situation. These fish were on an underwater drop off at about 10 ft down. To get to these fish, I simply added a small split shot, about a foot above my jig head. That would allow my lure to get down to them quicker, so that I could catch them quicker! And to catch them we did. In a stunningly similar fashion to the first pile of fish that we found, we caught a handful of nice crappie, and some white bass, and some largemouth. All in all, a pretty good day.
Sunday, a different buddy and I, took his boat out of Bryant Grove boat ramp...
https://share.google/9xAgGOUYCvLfWqjbx
Our plan was to scan that area with his forward facing sonar and find some schools of crappie. We were able to do that. But it was very difficult! His forward facing sonar is attached to his trolling motor. That means, we could only point the forward facing sonar, in the direction that the trolling motor was pointed. So if we wanted to go straight, and look at a cliff, we wouldn't be able to do that. For what it's worth, if you have forward facing sonar, you need to have it on its own mount. So you can look around independently of the trolling motor movement.
We looked for more than 4 hours before it dawned on me, that it was just going to be too difficult to do with that setup. So we went over to the Hobson Pike bridge in hopes that the crappie would be stacked up on the bridge pilings. Fortunately for us, that's exactly what happened! On the south side of the bridge, at the second set of bridge pilings in the water, there were hundreds of crappie! They were mostly loaded up on the back side, if you're standing on the bank, looking at the bridge pilings. Occasionally, the majority of the school, would move in between the two bridge pilings. Each set of bridge pilings is two concrete pillars, and at the second set of pillars, they would hang out in between the two, and just passed the two, if you're looking at it from the bank.
Using the same crappie setup as the day before, and keeping that split shot on there, so that we could get down to those fish, we would cast past, or in between, the bridge pilings, and allow our lures to sink down to where those crappie were. The total depth of the water was about 25 ft, and the crappie were sitting between 15 and 20 ft. It was really hard to stay in position because it was really windy, but we were able to catch several crappie. Not unlike the schools of crappie I had found the day before, these crappie were constantly on the move around those bridge pilings. It made them tough to pin down, and after more than 6 hours of fishing, we called it a day.
Today, I went back down to the Duck River below Normandy Dam...
https://goo.gl/maps/xUmzAxF16exsqUog7?g_st=ac
I like to walk up and down the river. The entire bank is accessible for the first mile and a half below the dam. There are trails through the woods, and through the fields, and you can even walk right up next to the dam! The water has been coming out at a trickle, only 70 cubic feet per second. That's how we measure the flow of water, in cubic feet. One cubic foot, is about the size of one basketball. So that's 70 cubic feet or 70 basketballs per second, flowing out of the dam. That's not very much.
When the flow is slow and low, sometimes the fishing can be tough. Today, using my ultralight rod and reel, with 4 lb monofilament, I started with a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail. That was getting me some attention, but the the best way to get them today, was with a small red mosquito hook, one split shot, about a foot above that, and two pink Berkeley Magnum floating power bait power eggs for trout. Simply cast that setup into the Duck River below Normandy dam, get your rod tip up, allow the presentation to bounce along the bottom, and then wait for the bite. The trout practically hook themselves!
Recently, the TWRA stocked as many as 200 brood trout in that stretch of river. A brood trout is a trout that was used by the hatchery to create the next generation of trout, before it was released back into Tennessee's waterways, to be harvested by fishermen. These trout are relatively large, and highly sought after. By yours truly. But today, I wouldn't even sniff one. I was able to catch more than my limit of small, stocked rainbow trout, and they all came by way of patiently bouncing Berkeley power eggs on the bottom of the river.
I say patiently, because every single cast, if you didn't catch a fish, and even if you did, you would have to remove copious amounts of seaweed from your line. So much, that my fingers turned green! But that was the only way I could get these fish to bite. I had tried rapala minnows as well as roostertails, two lures that usually never let me down for trout. They just weren't having it today. I saw a few guys who were there using fly rods, they didn't catch anything. I had a couple of buddies there, one of them was using a fly rod, and he wasn't doing very well at all. That stretch of river is absolutely loaded with trout, but I keep going down there on bad days!

title: Trip Report #146
content_raw:
Crappie on the cliffs, trout on the rocks...
I got the Stewart Creek boat ramp this morning just after 7:30...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/FooZ2MCpHkr5VdPGs
There weren't any people there. There was only one boat trailer, and only two cars in the parking lot. One guy fishing for bass on the boat ramp, and another guy fishing way down the cliffs, presumably for crappie. I went directly through the woods next to the parking lot, to the cliffs, where I usually stand by the big tree that's down in the water. I didn't have high hopes, typically, when there's not anyone there, there aren't any crappie. I fished for the better part of an hour, very patiently, and intently, but I didn't even get a single bite. That's not uncommon, typically, crappie fishermen will change locations if they're not doing very well.
So I headed down to the end of Weekly Lane, just outside of Smyrna, to the boat ramp at Bryant's Grove...
https://share.google/0xCaio03w9gwN04BC
I saw two different vehicles that I recognized as crappie fishermen when I pulled in, so I figured they would be there. Just walk down to the boat ramp, and then carefully make your way along the bank, to the right, for a few hundred yards. Then, you will find yourself on a cliff. You will know you are in the right spot, when you see a big white cross. I'm not sure why it's there, it may have some writing on it or something, but it's a great landmark! Anywhere around that white cross is going to hold crappie right now!
When I got there, a few of the guys already had nice sized crappie in the bucket, and they added several more while I was there. These guys were dialed in! I was not. It took me a while to even get the first bite. I was using my seven and a half foot ultralight rod and reel, with 4 lb monofilament, and a 1/48th of an ounce jig head with a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad, when I finally got my first bite. The bite was hot, but your presentation had to be painfully slow!
Casting as far as I could, which was a probably about 60 ft, and then allowing the lure to sink for about 30 seconds, you could start your retrieve, but then you had to stop. And allow that lure to pendulum through the water. Then, start your retrieve again, and then stop. And allow the lure to pendulum through the water. The fish were far away from the cliff! Anytime someone would hook up, it would be at least 40 to 50 ft away. I couldn't say for sure, but it seems like the fish were suspended way out off the cliff, and relatively deep. When I finally had something figured out, and got my first crappie, it was a nice big slab! I threw it in the bucket for one of my buddies, and then headed out to my next location.
Today was trout stocking day at Percy Priest dam...
https://share.google/QMW6qi9OFYqnnahDo
Today, TWRA was scheduled to stock trout below Percy Priest dan. They always do it on this side, at Dodson chapel access. I got there at 10 minutes after 10:00, and I didn't know what to expect. I didn't know if they wanted the generators to be on, or off. I honestly, suspected, that they wanted the generators to be off. When they showed up, I quickly found out why they need the generators to be on. It's a long way from the parking lot down to the water's edge, and they have to run tubes. They only have enough to get so far, so they need the water to come up.
That meant, they needed the generators to be on. Today, the generating schedule for Percy Priest dam, was for the generators to turn on at 11:00 a.m. you can find that information, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/j-percy-priest
They got there just before 11:00, set everything up, and then we waited. And then 11:00 came, and we were still waiting. In my experience, it's uncommon for water release schedules to vary. When they didn't start the water at 11:00, I was pretty convinced that they weren't going to. The agents who were there, said they were going to wait just a little while longer. 10 minutes after 11:00, they blew the horn, signaling that water release was imminent. A few minutes later, they open the generator, and water began filling up the river basin. About 45 minutes after that, we were in business, and I learned something new! In the future, when they are scheduled to stop at Percy Priest, you can approximate their arrival time by looking at the generating schedule. They're going to want the water flowing before they show up with those fish. Or at least, scheduled to start very soon.
Today's truck was from the Dale Hollow national fish hatchery, and it had a little over 1,000 rainbow trout between 8 and 12 inches long. Before the fish were even out of the tube, the person (Patreon subscriber, Collin) standing next to me caught the first trout of the day! He was using a rooster tail, on an ultra light rod and reel, with 4 lb monofilament. That's exactly what I had! Unfortunately, TWRA had employed me to hold the tube down, so that it didn't go all wacky when they forced all the water and fish through, so I was the last one who got to pick up his rod and reel.
That wouldn't matter! These fish were going crazy, right out of the truck! Everybody on the bank, about 15 people, were all using rooster tails, and we were all smashing them! I had on a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail, and you could stand there and catch as many fish as you wanted to, one right after the other! So I started putting on different lures, and catching fish just for fun. I tried a few different little trout lures, and everything was working. Until it wasn't. After about 30 minutes of intense feeding, all of these fish stopped. Immediately, all at once. I stayed for about 45 minutes after the fish quit feeding, and I only saw one other fish get caught. It was magical while it lasted, a testament why you should try to show up on trout stocking day!

title: Trip Report #147
content_raw:
The Greenway in Springfield has been stocked with trout...
Yesterday, I went to Springfield Tennessee. They have a Greenway on the Sulfur Fork Creek where they stock about 500 trout.  They have Greenway trailheads to access the area, but those trailheads are far away from where they put the fish! Using Google maps, I figured out that, where they stock, is right next to the fairgrounds. Their county fairgrounds are always open to the public for parking, but yesterday, the gate that led to the greenway was locked. Not a big deal! You can park in the parking lot and then walk around the fence down to the greenway. It's really convenient, only a couple hundred yards...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/aAimrHiucMXWALn6A
That is the parking lot at the Robertson county fairgrounds. It is a very safe place to park! County Police have a station right there on the property! If the gate in the corner, next to the creek is closed, simply park at the end of the parking lot, where I dropped this pin, and walk around the fence. I know you are allowed to do this, because I got there early yesterday, and eventually, they unlocked the gate!
I got there just after 10:00 a.m. and there was only one other person there. He was one of the locals that's always there when they stock those trout. He gave me the lay of the land, and explained that, they dropped trout in two different places on that greenway. There are two bridges that go over the creek. At each one of those bridges, they stop and throw trout into the water. The one we were standing on, next to the fairgrounds, is where they dump the majority of the fish. If you go upstream on the greenway, about 3/4 of a mile away, they put a few more in there. But most people don't fish there.
On that bridge by the fairgrounds, where they dump the majority of the fish, there is a small dam. Above that dam, the water is a little bit deep, and it would probably be pretty difficult to wade. Below that dam, where they put the majority of the fish, is literally heaven for someone in waders! The creek is small, and has nice riffles and every once in awhile, a few nice pools to hold trout. It's not very big, so you may be able to wear something like muck boots, or even just hip waders. When they initially stock the trout, they typically stay right where they are put. Not long after that, they start to spread out. You can expect these fish to thin out, providing excellent opportunities up and down the creek.
As the creek moves away from where they stocked, downstream, it takes a bend to the right, and the greenway follows directly alongside. I didn't venture down that way, but the local guy I met told me, it's really pretty down that way, and the fish get stacked into small pools. They will stock this spot again in January as well as February. After that, near the end of February, or beginning of March, the creek will be loaded with fish. I plan on making a trip out there in the early spring, just to explore the greenway. It's a really nice area, the only drawback, no real bathrooms around. There is a gas station across the street, but it's a relatively busy highway, so be careful!
The fish they put in the creek we're about 10 to 12 inches, pretty typical in Middle Tennessee. Before they put the last trout in the river, I had already caught the first trout of the day. Using my ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament, a number six eagle claw bait holder hook, and a single medium sized split shot, about a foot up from the hook, I put on two pink Berkeley Magnum floating power bait for trout. Because we were elevated, on a bridge above the creek, I was able to drop my bait directly below me, and watch through the shallow clear water, as the pink bait would disappear.
Those trout are pretty well camouflaged from above! So you don't necessarily see them coming in to bite your lure, or bait. So what i do, is focus on the two pink balls on my hook. I just sit, and watch them intently, and if they disappear, I set the hook! I've only ever seen one other Middle Tennessee set up where you could fish directly above the trout, in that location, fishing from the bridge is illegal. In this location, it's encouraged! They have rod holders built into the bridge, on both sides. THIS MIGHT BE THE EASIEST PLACE TO CATCH A TROUT IN TENNESSEE!

The Greenway in Springfield has been stocked with trout...

Yesterday, I went to Springfield Tennessee. They have a Greenway on the Sulfur Fork Creek where they stock about 500 trout. They have Greenway trailheads to access the area, but those trailheads are far away from where they put the fish! Using Google maps, I figured out that, where they stock, is right next to the fairgrounds. Their county fairgrounds are always open to the public for parking, but yesterday, the gate that led to the greenway was locked. Not a big deal! You can park in the parking lot and then walk around the fence down to the greenway. It's really convenient, only a couple hundred yards...

https://maps.app.goo.gl/aAimrHiucMXWALn6A

That is the parking lot at the Robertson county fairgrounds. It is a very safe place to park! County Police have a station right there on the property! If the gate in the corner, next to the creek is closed, simply park at the end of the parking lot, where I dropped this pin, and walk around the fence. I know you are allowed to do this, because I got there early yesterday, and eventually, they unlocked the gate!

I got there just after 10:00 a.m. and there was only one other person there. He was one of the locals that's always there when they stock those trout. He gave me the lay of the land, and explained that, they dropped trout in two different places on that greenway. There are two bridges that go over the creek. At each one of those bridges, they stop and throw trout into the water. The one we were standing on, next to the fairgrounds, is where they dump the majority of the fish. title: Trip Report #148
content_raw:
Where to get giant rainbow trout, right now...
This morning, I arrived at 6:00 a.m. on the side of the river, below Normandy Dam...
https://goo.gl/maps/zdztRhKxwE6PNtSi8
My plan, find out if the rumors were true. Apparently, on Tuesday, TWRA put their annual stock of brood trout into the Duck river below Normandy dam. If you don't know, a brood trout is a giant trout that has been used for its eggs or milt. When TWRA has what they need, they return those fish back to Tennessee's waterways for us to catch. Each year, for the past few years, the spot where they have put up to a hundred of these fish, it's just below Normandy dam.
I got there this morning and there was no one else there. I had the entire place, from the dam, up to more than a mile downstream, all to myself. And the river was chocked full of trout! Hundreds and hundreds of little rainbow trout, and as many as a hundred of those big giant brood trout. I was using my ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail. I was able to catch plenty of those tiny rainbow trout, between 8 and 12 inches, but I never hooked into one of the really big trout. I did see them, attacking bait, and jumping out of the water. But I wasn't able to hook into one. A couple of my buddies went down there later in the day, and they caught a total of five of those big trout. Most of them weigh at least two and a half to 3 lb and some of them are in the four or five pound range.
At 8:00 a.m. I left Normandy and headed back to Murfreesboro. The West Fork Stones River was scheduled to receive its first trout stocking of the season, and I wanted to be there for the occasion. Typically, the trout truck shows up in Murfreesboro around 9:00 a.m. so I got there a little before that. Today, the truck didn't show up until around 10:00 a.m. Not a big deal, the trout truck is always right on time!
Today's location in Murfreesboro, was on the West Fork Stones River, at Ransom Mill Dam, on the Murfreesboro Greenway, at the Manson Pike trailhead...
Manson Pike Trailhead https://share.google/exLNMdvej8CNqkKIF
They usually bring around 500 to 600 trout, and today was no exception. One thing they did today, that they don't usually do for this location, was drop one, around 3 lb, female, palomino trout. If you don't know, that's also referred to as a lightning trout, or an albino trout. It's pretty much bright orange and incredible to look at! While I was there, I didn't see anyone catch that big girl. As far as I know, she's still in there.
I still had my ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament, but these fish didn't want anything to do with the rooster tail. There were 22 other fishermen down there, and the only thing that was working well was power bait on bottom. So I put on a number 6 eagle claw bait holder hook and about 1 ft above that hook I put one medium size split shot. I like to use Berkeley Magnum floating power bait for trout. I like pink color. I put two of those on my hook and cast that into the swift water, and allow it to settle off to the side of the current. You don't have to wait very long, with your rod tip up at a 45° angle, before you begin to feel a little tug. At that point, a quick little flip of the wrist is all it will take to set the hook.
I was able to hook, and land, three of these little 12-inch rainbow trout before I backed out and allowed the 22 other fishermen to have their fun. This isn't necessarily a location that I like to visit, unless it's the actual day of the stocking event. As soon as tomorrow, most of those fish will leave that little waterfall area below the dam, and go downstream. Not to worry, they will stock in this location again in January and February!

title: Trip Report #149
content_raw:
The most wonderful time of the year...
Yesterday, I took my kayak below Center Hill Dam...
Buffalo Valley Boat Ramp https://share.google/iowwNmj7wyn4Z7iGb
I launched just after 11:00, so that I could fish the last 2 hours of generating water, before they turned the generators off, at 1:00 p.m.
You can find the generating schedule, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
This is the second year I have gone to Center Hill Dam on December 1st, because that's the day they turn the orifice gate off. That makes it, the most wonderful time of the year! If you don't know, the orifice gate is a small gate, in the front, center of the dam, that allows 250 cubic feet of water per second to flow from the beginning of June until the end of November. For some reference, one cubic foot of water is about the size of one basketball. So the orifice gate releases 250 basketballs of water per second from the beginning of June until the end of November, every year. This is done in an effort to keep more flow in the river, so there is more dissolved oxygen for the fish.
My opinion on the matter, I never had any problems catching fish before they opened the orifice gate. I always caught great numbers, and plenty of very large fish. What we didn't have, before they started using the orifice gate every summer, was curly leafed pond weed. We had slippery, slimy, snotty moss, that was attached to pretty much every rock on the bottom of the river, but never tall grasses that grew all the way to the surface like curly leafed pond weed does. And now, it's here to stay. Mostly because of all the added nutrients. When they run the orifice gate, the water goes from clear, to cloudy. That cloudy water, is nutrients, that grass needs.
But all of that is behind us now! They did indeed turn off the orifice gate yesterday, and the fishing was stellar! There were several people standing on the steps, fishing the generating water. A few of them caught a few different fish. It looked like they were pretty dialed in. I tried my hand at fishing the generating water from my kayak, but I didn't have any luck. Things would turn around for me as soon as they turned the generator is off.
Once the generators are turned off, and there's no more water coming out of the dam, I feel comfortable to put my anchor out. It's a lot easier to catch fish when you're sitting still. That's one of the great advantages to standing on the steps, when you're fishing the generating water, you have the ability to plant yourself. That makes not only feeling the bite, and setting the hook, easier, but it makes getting dialed in easier. You know exactly where you're casting, every time, because you haven't moved. When you're drifting around in a kayak, it's tough to get dialed in. I love sitting on an anchor!
I like to set up directly in front of the center of the dam, about a hundred yards away. I typically face the dam, and cast that direction. I was doing that yesterday, with my ultralight rod and reel and a 1/32nd ounce jig head, with a 2-in pearl colored body Garland baby shad. My typical crappie setup, but yesterday, I added one medium size split shot, about a foot above the jig head. I had been using that recently, when using my forward facing sonar, to get my lure down faster. I hadn't noticed that it had a negative effect on catching crappie, so I was going to try it again, even though I wasn't using my forward facing sonar.
The first couple fish I caught were a sauger and a walleye. It's great that they are up there, but they were both too small to keep, and that's not really what I was targeting. I was allowing my crappie jig to get all the way to the bottom, and then starting a slow retrieve, with a couple little twitches. Fortunately, that same retrieve works great for walleye and saguer. But those weren't the fish I was looking for, so I started making casts in all directions around me. As it turned out, the crappie were behind me!
I turned my kayak to face away from the dam and started casting as far as I could, which was about 80 ft. After allowing that lure to sink all the way to the bottom, I would start my slow retrieve, and almost immediately hook up. These fish were sitting about 70 ft away, all the way at the bottom, in 10 ft of water. I was able to catch five crappie, pretty much back to back to back. I was finally dialed in, but it was much too late. I could feel the sun setting behind the giant hill to the southwest. At 3:09 p.m., the sun went behind the Earth, creating that afternoon, low light condition, that crappie hate. The same type of condition that sets them off pretty much every morning, shuts them down, pretty much every afternoon. That type of thing happens all over Middle Tennessee with crappie this time of year, so I packed in my things, and called it a day!
Today, December 2nd, the TWRA will be releasing trout at Shelby bottoms park in downtown Nashville...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/Vtmi11gjNhsXS8tF6
That's a pin of exactly where on the lake they will drop the fish. I typically get there between 8:00 and 9:00 a.m. just to make sure I'm there when they release the fish. Most of the time, they show up between 10:00 and 11:00, but they can be there as early as 9:00 a.m. if I was going to this location today, I would probably use a 1/8 of an ounce white rooster tail on an ultralight setup. Typically, those fish will eat right out of the truck! Usually, someone has one within the first 5 minutes of their release. I'm going to drop a  link to where you can find this information...
Trout Fishing & Stockings in Tennessee https://share.google/6oHCD9QCgHCe5xTCs
Tomorrow, December 3rd, they will be stocking Manson Pike trailhead in Murfreesboro. I plan on being there tomorrow. I typically get there just after 8:00 a.m. TWRA typically shows up around 9:00 a.m. Be there or be square!
https://share.google/WtsSGCBpxP1kKw34t

title: Trip Report #150
content_raw:
The crappie fishing method that can't be beat...
Yesterday, I had a client booked for the four hour, forward facing sonar, instructional crappie fishing trip. We met at 6:00 a.m. at Jefferson springs boat ramp...
Jefferson Springs Boat Ramp. https://share.google/L0HUK77PfjcPR956a
I have the lowrance eagle eye 9, forward facing sonar. He recently purchased the same unit, and wanted some in-depth instructions about how to use it properly. In my opinion, the best way to use forward facing sonar for crappie is to locate a school of fish, and then fish for them. I have tried looking at the screen to watch my lure, and I don't like that very much. The best method for using forward facing sonar, is to help you know exactly where the fish are, so you can line up your cast. Then, traditional crappie fishing methods work best!
My client wasn't very familiar with crappie fishing on purpose, so we went over some very specific details. We located a school of crappie, and anchored ourselves about 35 ft away from the center of the school. To start with, I had him figure out exactly how far he needed to cast to reach the school of fish. That can be achieved relatively easily by looking for your lure on the screen on your forward facing sonar device. After you know exactly where to cast, then we worked on exactly how retrieve.
Using an ultralight rod and reel, with 4 lb monofilament, and a 1/32nd ounce jig head, with a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad, I had him start a painfully slow retrieve as soon as the lure hit the surface. The school of fish that we found was on a slowly sloping mud bank with a couple of logs. Those logs were sitting on the bottom in 10 ft of water, the school of crappie, was suspended from the bottom, all the way up to about 2 ft from the surface! On this day, we would never have to allow our lure to sink any amount of time, in the entire 4 hours that we would fish.
Starting with a slow retrieve, as soon as the lure would hit the water, after a couple of turns of the reel, I would have him incorporate a twitch. Crappie love when a small soft plastic is moving through their area and then twitches, randomly. Most of the time, you don't have to twitch the lure very much. A quick twitch about four or five times on one cast is all you need. I like to space them out instead of clustering them up. Very rarely will you need to twitch, twitch, twitch, twitch, twitch. Most of the time, a slow steady retrieve with the occasional twitch, will do.
It didn't take long before he had the hang of it, and we were pulling crappie into the boat left and right. The first ever crappie that he had caught intentionally. Some were small, some were keepers, all of them were providing the thump that crappie fisherman live for! Since we had such a large, active school of fish, I showed him how easy it is to catch crappie with a minnow.
Using my medium light action 6 ft rod and reel, I was throwing minnows on a slip bobber set to a depth of about 4 ft. I probably didn't need a slip bobber for fish that were so shallow, but that's what I already had set up. I had purchased some minnows the day before for a trip below Center Hill Dam and I still had some left over. When that's the case, I always take them with me on whatever fishing adventure is next. You never know when fish will prefer a minnow over a lure. Yesterday, however, was not that day.
I was able to catch one nice crappie with a minnow, but they would let that minnow sit there in their midst, unaffected, for 20 minutes at a time. All the while, we would be catching crappie left and right using a Bobby Garland and a slow retrieval technique. I have an opinion about this, I believe, because the minnow is just sitting there, it doesn't get as much attention. We are able to make several casts in lots of different directions trying to find fish in this school that are willing to bite, while the minnow is just sitting there, not really doing much. I can't tell you how many times I have seen lures out fish live bait. I believe this to be the reason.
All the crappie with that we found yesterday were really shallow. 10 ft of water or less. We looked at structures like bridge pilings and cliff faces, but they were devoid of fish. These fish are currently hanging out in muddy areas where there are trees underneath the surface of the water. We didn't see any fish on trees that were poking out of the water or on any of the fish attractors, as they were far too shallow since the lowering the lake.

The best method for using forward facing sonar, is to help you know exactly where the fish are, so you can line up your cast. Then, traditional crappie fishing methods work best!

My client wasn't very familiar with crappie fishing on purpose, so we went over some very specific details. We located a school of crappie, and anchored ourselves about 35 ft away from the center of the school. To start with, I had him figure out exactly how far he needed to cast to reach the school of fish. That can be achieved relatively easily by looking for your lure on the screen on your forward facing sonar device. After you know exactly where to cast, then we worked on exactly how retrieve.

Using an ultralight rod and reel, with 4 lb monofilament, and a 1/32nd ounce jig head, with a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad, I had him start a painfully slow retrieve as soon as the lure hit the surface. The school of fish that we found was on a slowly sloping mud bank with a couple of logs. Those logs were sitting on the bottom in 10 ft of water, the school of crappie, was suspended from the bottom, all the way up to about 2 ft from the surface! On this day, we would never have to allow our lure to sink any amount of time, in the entire 4 hours that we would fish.

Starting with a slow retrieve, as soon as the lure would hit the water, after a couple of turns of the reel, I would have him incorporate a twitch. Crappie love when a small soft plastic is moving through their area and then twitches, randomly. Most of the time, you don't have to twitch the lure very much. A quick twitch about four or five times on one cast is all you need. I like to space them out instead of clustering them up. Very rarely will you need to twitch, twitch, twitch, twitch, twitch. Most of the time, a slow steady retrieve with the occasional twitch, will do.

It didn't take long before he had the hang of it, and we were pulling crappie into the boat left and right. The first ever crappie that he had caught intentionally. Some were small, some were keepers, all of them were providing the thump that crappie fisherman live for! Since we had such a large, active school of fish, I showed him how easy it is to catch crappie with a minnow.

Using my medium light action 6 ft rod and reel, I was throwing minnows on a slip bobber set to a depth of about 4 ft. I probably didn't need a slip bobber for fish that were so shallow, but that's what I already had set up. I had purchased some minnows the day before for a trip below Center Hill Dam and I still had some left over. When that's the case, I always take them with me on whatever fishing adventure is next. You never know when fish will prefer a minnow over a lure. Yesterday, however, was not that day.

I was able to catch one nice crappie with a minnow, but they would let that minnow sit there in their midst, unaffected, for 20 minutes at a time. All the while, we would be catching crappie left and right using a Bobby Garland and a slow retrieval technique. I have an opinion about this, I believe, because the minnow is just sitting there, it doesn't get as much attention. We are able to make several casts in lots of different directions trying to find fish in this school that are willing to bite, while the minnow is just sitting there, not really doing much. I can't tell you how many times I have seen lures out fish live bait. I believe this to be the reason.

All the crappie with that we found yesterday were really shallow. 10 ft of water or less. We looked at structures like bridge pilings and cliff faces, but they were devoid of fish. These fish are currently hanging out in muddy areas where there are trees underneath the surface of the water. We didn't see any fish on trees that were poking out of the water or on any of the fish attractors, as they were far too shallow since the lowering the lake.

title: Trip Report #151
content_raw:
What's biting at Center Hill Dam...
Yesterday, I had clients booked for the 6-hour fishing trip below Center Hill Dam, in my boat...
https://share.google/v3aU1iaCYWR0xwChd
The generators were scheduled to run from 3:00 a.m. until 11:00 a.m. so I scheduled our trip from 8:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. that way we could fish 3 hours with the generators on and 3 hours with the generators off. You can find the generating schedule, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
You must wear your life jacket at all times when on the water below Center Hill dam. Whether you're in a kayak or canoe or raft or a boat, life jacket usage is mandatory. If you launch from Buffalo valley boat ramp, you won't be hindered by the generating water. You will be on the side of the river where there is very little to no current and you can get out of the boat ramp with ease and make your way up to the base of the dam to do some fishing.
We wanted to catch every type of fish that swims below Center Hill dam. Fortunately for us, we were in my boat with forward facing sonar. Unfortunately for us, that forward facing sonar said there weren't any fish below Center Hill dam. When sitting right in the center of the deepest hole and looking around, there were very few, if any fish holding below the dam. I expected to see sturgeon on the bottom and striped bass swimming through in schools. Big balls of bait fish as well as tightly packed schools of crappie. We didn't see any of those things! There were a handful of gar and as usual, plenty of trout to catch.
We did our best focusing on catching trout, most of the time. We would take the boat beside the current and cast into the current with light setups. Using medium- light action rods, with six or eight pound monofilament, we were casting 1/2 oz spoons when we hooked up with our first brown trout of the day. That's a relatively heavy lure on such a light setup, but it makes it more fun to fight the fish. When I'm using a spoon from my boat, I like to cast into the heavy current, and get my rod tip up, and then drop my rod tip down, so that the lure flutters down in the water column, and then, lift my rod tip up and then drop it down, so that it flutters down in the water column. The whole time you're doing that, you have to be reeling so that your lure doesn't hit the bottom. A nice steady retrieve will do the trick, unless you're hitting bottom, then you need to speed it up a little.
If you're not aware, most of the area below the dam is extremely shallow. When the generators are turned off, the average depth out there is about 4 ft. With one generator on, the water level rises about 4 ft. So those areas that are typically 4 ft of water, we're 8 ft of water yesterday with a generators were on. It's really easy to get hung up with a half ounce lure when you only have 8 ft of water to work with. Once you get the feel, using a spoon during the generating water is my number one way to go after big trout. Unfortunately, yesterday morning, fish weren't feeding very heavily while they were generating, if they were, we couldn't get them to bite our lures.
After the generators turned off we spent some time sitting in the very center of the river below the dam. That's the deepest spot. When the water is all the way off, it's about 18 ft deep. That's where I like to sit and catch crappie and walleye and sometimes even sauger! We tried our best to get some walleye. We were using heavy jigs on the bottom with Charlie Brewer sliders, a known walleye lure. For all our patients, we would receive zero reward. The best other option is to fish in the corner where the water falls are.
We set up on an anchor in the corner between the two waterfalls and tried our best with every type of lure in the book. Roostertails, rapala minnows, you name it. Even my favorite little trout lure, a trout magnet with a 1-inch Gulp minnow. There was only one thing in my boat that would end up pulling in a few fish. I had an old box of worms laying in the corner.
Using ultralight rods and reels with 4 lb monofilament and a number 6 eagle claw bait holder hook with a single medium size split shot about a foot above the hook, and a pink Powerball power bait from Berkeley, we were able to put half a nightcrawler on that hook and start catching a few fish. Casting into the current that comes off the waterfall and allowing that worm to get down to the bottom, it wouldn't be long before a rainbow trout would pick that up and hook itself on its way into our net. Nothing to write home about, but it was the second fish of the day, and we were on to something.
The next fish that would come out in the exact same fashion would be a real bruiser! At almost 20 in long, it was a male rainbow trout that made our day! It was more than 2 lb of fierce fighting, beautiful fish, and it didn't want anything that we threw at it, until we put on that worm. Then, shortly thereafter my other client got into their first fish of the day, and then we had another one in the boat, and then, as quickly as our 6-hour started, it was over.
Those fish were really finicky when the day started. We had used nightcrawlers before they started to bite towards the end of our trip, but they didn't want anything to do with them. We even had a bucket of minnows, and we tried fishing with those, but we couldn't get a bite. If you've been reading my Pro reports for a while, you know that I typically don't pay much attention to things like wind direction or barometric pressure. But in a stunning situational circumstance, yesterday's weather started off with a bluebird sky and a North wind and at the end of our 6 hours the wind had turned around to the West and we were seeing clouds move in as well as airplanes forming condensation trails in the sky.
To me, it's worth noting, that I pointed this out to my clients. We had a tough morning catching any fish at all, we had only gotten one. Then, when I saw the first plane laying down tracks in the sky, I pointed it out to them. That was followed by more clouds and more condensation trails, and then, more bites! It's my contention, that when planes that are flying at 30,000 ft are laying down condensation trails, the fishing is typically good. I wouldn't say anything about yesterday's fishing was good, but it got better when we started seeing those trails.

title: Trip Report #152
content_raw:
Crappie are on the move...
Wednesday, I had a client booked for the 4-hour instructional bank fishing trip for crappie, on Percy Priest Lake. We started at spring creek spring...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/wfrCeesXv5cwJGpA8
I wanted to be fishing when the first little bit of light hit the sky, so we met at 5:30 a.m. on the side of Maddox road...
https://goo.gl/maps/b9UCb9s3n3fckCkQ8
From here, go over, under, or around the gate on the side of the road and take the trail that is now really wide. This area is for foot traffic only, so just ignore the gate. We used to be able to drive back there, but people abused that privilege. This is a wildlife management area, so I always wear my orange hat. I did see a hunter out here last week, and he was able to get a deer that day. Stay on the path, and wear something orange, and only go to the spring and you will be fine.
When we got there, we were the first people there. Lots of other people showed up shortly thereafter. My client wanted to learn the techniques that I use from the bank to catch crappie. He had the perfect setup! A seven and a half foot, ultra light rod and reel, with a 1/32nd ounce jig head and a Bobby Garland baby shad, on 4 lb fluorocarbon. Now he just needed a little bit of instruction.
We started the same way that I start when I go fishing there. Cast that lure out as far as you can and then start your retrieve. Rod tip up in the air, at about a 45° angle. A painfully slow retrieve, and every once in awhile, incorporate a small twitch. It's the painfully slow retrieve that's the most important part. Typically, when I'm trying to teach someone how to crappie fish, I'm constantly telling them to slow down their retrieve. As it turned out, that was all it would take for him. As I told him, slow it down, he would do so, and we got our first bite of the day.
Crappie don't bite like any other fish. Typically, it's just a quick thump. To imitate this for clients, I typically thump them lightly on their shoulder or arm. That way they can feel how slight the sensation is. Then I explain, that the feeling will be in the palm of their hand. The hand that is holding the rod and reel will be the only hand that will feel the bite. It will feel like a small thump inside of the center of your palm that resonates from the tip of the fishing pole. What I didn't tell him, was that you need to immediately snap the rod to life to set the hook.
When he got his first bite, he proudly explained, that he felt the thump! I realized my shortcoming, and informed him, that was his only opportunity to catch that fish. Then we talked about how bass fishermen have this tendency to delay the hook set. With bass fisherman, once you feel something, you say, " there she is " ,  and then you lower the rod tip and then slam the hook into the fish. You don't have that kind of time with crappie. They hit the lure by throwing their mouth out around it and then before they pull their mouth back, they can spit that lure out. It's a quick thump, and you have to snap the rod to life in that instant.
It wouldn't take long before we got our next bite. About 10 minutes to 6:00, when it was still a little dark out, the next small crappie would come up near the surface and provide a thump. My client set the hook with a quick swing, and pulled in his first ever crappie, that he caught on purpose. But it wouldn't be his last! By this point in time, there were a half a dozen people standing around fishing the bank at the spring. Everybody was fishing for crappie, most of these people were seasoned crappie fishermen. Unfortunately, we didn't see anybody else catch a single fish of any type. My client would go on to catch a couple more crappie that were too small to keep. We fished for a total of 2 hours and those three fish were the only ones that we saw caught.
Typically, when you find crappie, you're going to find lots of fish. There's a good chance that those fish just weren't biting very well at that point in time in the day. When you find three, you should find a lot more, but that wasn't the case. After 2 hours and only a few fish, and no one else catching anything, I decided we should move around the corner to try a more shallow spot. Where we were fishing in the spring, the water gets 20 ft deep. As we all know, these fish can move as shallow as just a few feet of water. Just around the corner from this location, you can park on the side of Lamar road and go to another spot on a cliff face where the water is between 8 and 12 ft deep. I've had good luck catching crappie there over the years, so we made our way over there to check it out.
https://maps.app.goo.gl/aQjD5tSXnkTAxf3WA
Be very careful pulling in and out of this spot. The road drops off dramatically and this spot is very muddy and has a lot of exposed rock. If you do not have a high profile vehicle, it may be difficult to get in or out of this location. But you are allowed to park here. The entire area is corps of engineer property. There are trails through the woods that lead you directly over to a relatively tall cliff face. By now, the lake has lowered enough that there are some exposed spots to stand down on the cliff face, closer to the water's edge. I have got crappie from end to end on this cliff, but I like to sit in the very center where there are some underwater brush piles...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/2ma2TAqax7FhHCww5
We spent the rest of our trip over here going over the finer details of a crappie retrieve. Counting the lure down until you find out the depth where the crappie live. Incorporating a twitch instead of just a slow retrieve, and even the importance of using a pendulum when you're standing on a cliff. This is actually the location where I developed that method. I was sitting on these cliffs that have relatively shallow water underneath them and only casting out in front of me about seven or eight feet and allowing the lure to pendulum back down to the rock face directly underneath me. I had figured out that crappie were biting as my lure got near the bank, just before I pulled it out, so I started trying to fish directly below me, and that was the method that I came up with to get them to bite. As that lure slowly swings back to the cliff, it provides the perfect action and slow presentation that crappie love!
Much like our first location, either these fish weren't there in great numbers or just weren't willing to bite. So we headed over to Stewart Creek boat ramp at the end of our trip just to see if maybe we guessed the wrong spot and they were a bunch of people over there catching crappie...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/fn6uYjxphvpNdXKT6
To my surprise, as we were pulling in, there were only two trucks that looks like they were fishing the cliffs. An older gentleman who I have fished with before was making his way back to his truck with an empty bucket. I didn't even have to get out of my car. I rolled my window down and I asked him for a fishing report. He said he had been there all morning and that nobody caught any fish. That settles it, these fish are on the move! So what does that mean?
They still go to their favorite areas and get caught every once in awhile, but they're not spending a lot of time sitting in one place. That is part of their fall pattern. When the water temperatures are cooling like this, they get on the move, chasing bait, trying to prepare for the winter, when they're metabolism slows down greatly. These fish will move side to side on a cliff or from tree to tree underwater, constantly! Especially when they have fluctuating temperatures. Last week we had temperatures that reached 70° in the afternoon, next week we won't have a day that reaches 50°. Be patient, the best time of year to catch crappie from the bank is coming soon!
When the weather stabilizes and cold temperatures are here to stay, these crappie will school up together, kind of like they are cuddling! They get together in great numbers, and they hang together all day long. When they find some good structure, with bait nearby, they rarely ever leave. When I find a school of crappie at a location in the winter time, I can usually go back to catch them several days in a row. I anticipate that will be the case for the months of December, January, and February. By the time we get to March, we will have those days that start to reach 70°, and the fish will start moving around, dramatically, again.
