So what does that mean?

They still go to their favorite areas and get caught every once in awhile, but they're not spending a lot of time sitting in one place. That is part of their fall pattern. When the water temperatures are cooling like this, they get on the move, chasing bait, trying to prepare for the winter, when they're metabolism slows down greatly. These fish will move side to side on a cliff or from tree to tree underwater, constantly! Especially when they have fluctuating temperatures. Last week we had temperatures that reached 70° in the afternoon, next week we won't have a day that reaches 50°. Be patient, the best time of year to catch crappie from the bank is coming soon!

When the weather stabilizes and cold temperatures are here to stay, these crappie will school up together, kind of like they are cuddling! They get together in great numbers, and they hang together all day long. When they find some good structure, with bait nearby, they rarely ever leave. When I find a school of crappie at a location in the winter time, I can usually go back to catch them several days in a row. I anticipate that will be the case for the months of December, January, and February. By the time we get to March, we will have those days that start to reach 70°, and the fish will start moving around, dramatically, again.

title: Trip Report #153
content_raw:
What's going on at cedar Creek spring...
Yesterday morning, I went bank fishing for Crappie at the spring on Percy Priest Lake...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/6Zh5siTVEEUhbAfV9
I got there about 30 minutes after sunrise, and parked on the side of Maddox road, and hiked in along the well-beaten path...
https://goo.gl/maps/zinusSgiQvypHY1n7
You can park at that pin, and then go under, over, or around the gate. I assure you, this is public property, and you are allowed to be here. It's a pretty long walk back to the spring. Most of the ground is relatively flat and you can't miss the trail. By now, so many people have gone back there, it's more like a road than a trail. When I got there yesterday, it was only myself and two other guys. We had plenty of room to fish and all of us were catching crappie.
Every year in winter, they lower the level of the lake, and the spring becomes a magical place. Because spring water flows constantly in that area, the water stays cooler in the summer, and warmer in the winter, and it becomes a haven for lots of fish. Right now, the spring is completely loaded with a few different types of fish. Lots of bluegills between two and three inches are hanging out in the shallows around the edges. Bigger bluegill, between five and seven inches are hanging out at the surface, scattered around the spring. Small bass, around 10 inches, are just off the edge of the bank, patrolling the area for tiny minnows. Several schools of very sizable largemouth bass are cruising from the deep spring up the cliff face, and occasionally attacking shad as they swim through. Yesterday, we saw largemouth knocking thread fin shad out of the water onto the bank! Seems like it might have been a good day for top water for those fish, but none of us were interested in targeting bass.
The main attraction at the spring is the crappie! Although I haven't found them in great numbers in the spring just yet, they will be soon. The colder it gets, the more they load up in there. One of the biggest reasons, that's where their bait goes. Lots of food is making its way into the spring right now. Not only the schools of thread fin shad that crappie like to eat, but lots of really big gizzard shad are hanging out. You can see them on the edges of the underwater cliff picking whatever it is they eat off the rocks. Now that all the ingredients for big crappie have arrived at the spring, it will only take water temperatures on the lake to drop four or five degrees for them to start making their way back there, in great numbers.
The three of us were using ultralight rod and reels and 1/32nd ounce jig heads. Each of us had a different color Bobby Garland baby shad but that didn't matter, we were each catching fish. One of the guys was retrieving his lure as soon as it hit the surface, without letting it sink. Another guy was allowing it to sink about six or seven seconds. I was allowing mine to drop all the way down like I do when I'm sitting in that spot. I like to cast out exactly 40 feet, lift my rod tip directly into the air, and then allow my lure to pendulum for about 27 seconds until it gets down into their area. Then I start to slowly retrieve it, with a couple of twitches. Lately, I've been having to twitch it a lot to get these fish to bite.
I stayed until about 10:30. There were a handful of keeper crappie that were caught between three of us, but not very many. Most of the fish were relatively small, and not very bitey. Crappie weren't providing their typical thump yesterday. We are having to be very patient, and, if you felt anything at all, you would just swing that hook. The bite was very subtle, so you didn't want to take a chance on missing it. My philosophy, if I feel anything, I make a hook set. If I swing and miss, that's okay, hook sets are free!
Those bass were attacking threadfin shad, and bluegills, in the shallows, even as I left. Some of the bass were in the three to four pound range. It looks like all of them were largemouth. They were coming up into 6 inches of water. If you would sit still enough, they wouldn't even know you were there, and they would come up right at your feet. It shouldn't be difficult to catch those bass. If it were me, I would probably get a small fly and put it on an ultra light rod and reel. Something that you should be using on a fly rod, but you don't have to make it that complicated. Just dip the fly in the water and catch one of those small 3-inch bluegills and put it on a hook underneath a bobber near the bank and eventually you will catch one of those big bass. You could probably even catch a whole lot of them!

title: Trip Report #154
content_raw:
Try before you buy, forward facing sonar...
Yesterday, I had a client who wanted to try forward facing sonar before he committed to purchasing it. I had been having luck finding schools of crappie over at Jefferson Springs boat ramp, so we met there yesterday morning at 6:15 a.m...
Jefferson Springs Boat Ramp. https://share.google/7bp1LP3PcpAsLiXAw
There were lots of boats and lots of people fishing from the bank, yesterday. We had to get about a mile or more away from the boat ramp before we could find some open water and not be too close to other fishermen. We were headed upstream away from the boat ramp in the direction of the confluence of the East Fork and West Fork Stones River. We were slowly scanning most of the way using the trolling motor and forward facing sonar to look at the cliffs, in search of crappie. We were cruising in 20 to 28 ft of water looking at steep cliffs, hoping to see schools of fish pressed up against the cliff face. That's the way I've been finding them recently.
We made it around a couple different bends in the river before my client pointed out that most of the other fishermen weren't fishing on the cliffs, they were fishing on the muddy side of the bank. The cliffs are deeper and typically that's where I find the crappie, the slowly sloping muddy sides tend to be shallow. But since we weren't finding any fish on the cliffs we made our way across to the shallower, slowly sloping side, and started scanning trees that were underwater. Part of the reason there are so many fishermen on this stretch of the lake is because there are so many underwater trees.
Forward facing sonar is great for eliminating water. Just because there are trees underwater doesn't mean there are fish on those trees. It didn't take us long before we found a small school of fish and caught a couple of bass and a couple of crappie. But that was a really small school and we decided to look for a different school of fish. Little did we know, not very far from where we were sitting, was the biggest school of crappie I've ever seen in my entire life. We put out an anchor and sat with the forward facing sonar pointed at the school of fish so we knew exactly where to cast.
Then, instead of looking at the screen to watch our crappie jigs, we just fished in that school of fish. We used the forward facing sonar to show us exactly where they were, and then crappie fished like regular. The only real difference today, from what I've been doing in the past, was the depth of the water. These fish were sitting in water that was only 8 ft deep! The school was so big that it expanded out to about 10 ft of depth. Most of the fish have been finding for the last few weeks have been 15 ft or deeper, so I've been using my ultralight setup with a 1/32nd ounce jig head and a medium split shot above the jig head. Unfortunately, that was getting us hung up and broke off. So we took the split shot off and started beating up these fish!
Using a 7 and 1/2 ft ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament a 1/32nd ounce jig head and a 2 inch Bobby Garland baby shad in Pearl color, we were able to put 17 big keeper slab crappie in the cooler! We did a 4-Hour trip. Catching some fish off of smaller schools and looking around until we found a monster school. Once you find a school of that many fish, you're going to be able to catch plenty!
These fish have been moving quite a bit. School of crappie are not sitting reliably anywhere in the last few days. They are still schooling together, so if you find them, they're easy to catch. But these schools are moving in real time. You can be sitting there catching fish and then watch the entire School swim away. It might be the rising and lowering of the water temperature due to the fact that it has gotten cold and then warm several different times this fall. It might just be because that's what they do in the fall. They may be chasing their bait. I'm not 100% certain.
I'm going to drop a pin where I found these fish, but it's only useful if you have a boat. There's no guarantee they're going to be on this particular tree, underwater, but they could still be nearby. Lots of people go there to fish, every day, so there's the potential that you could find crappie there, year round...
https://goo.gl/maps/TusgoBq7uYD6wzZp6

title: Trip Report #155
content_raw:
What a difference a day makes...
Yesterday, I hiked through the woods to a spot I had never fished, because I saw that it held crappie, on my fish finder, in my boat. When I got there, I caught crappie as fast as I could get my line in the water! So this morning, I went right back to the side of Jefferson Pike to hike into that spot again...
https://goo.gl/maps/hiCL1RZpjLgVUkCfA
That is where you are allowed to legally park to access the bank at Percy Priest Lake. When you're standing at this spot, take the trail to the right, and then shortly into the woods, you will see a gate. Go over, under, or around that gate. I assure you, this is public property, and you are allowed to be here. That gate is from a bygone era when people used to be allowed to drive around the lake. I have checked on my app, and this is all definitely public property.
When you take the trail on the right you go a little more than a tenth of a mile and then you will see a Sprite bottle hanging on a limb. From there, there is no trail down to where we are fishing. Because no one else is fishing there! Take a 45° angle off the path at that Sprite bottle and it will lead you through the woods, to the spot where you need to be...
https://goo.gl/maps/9G2EsU7hKb4VZVHY8
Yesterday when I went there, I just kept my maps open and tried to lead myself slowly to where I needed to be. That worked out just fine, and I ended up catching a whole bunch of crappie! Fast forward to this morning, and I got there a little bit earlier, about 30 minutes before sunrise at 6:00 a.m.
I fished for an entire hour without a bite. The non-stop action every cast from the day before had been replaced with a barren wasteland. No real rhyme or reason, but these crappie were not there! The only thing I can come up with, they have been on the move lately, and they took off. It's impossible for me to say exactly where they went, but I knew they weren't there. And that's a bummer! The way they bit yesterday, I was convinced I had us a new honey hole. No doubt, those fish will be there again, but they were not there this morning.
So I headed to the north side of the lake to meet my buddy to launch his boat at seven points boat ramp...
Seven Points Boat Ramp https://share.google/iYaeTeRmWbjwXwMl1
We had been catching crappie in this area on brush piles for several months now. Yesterday, he picked up livescope. The most advanced, most expensive, forward facing sonar you can get. Today, we went out to give it a shot. We never made it past the green channel marker at the point by the bank at seven points...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/hhMj9hx83RvE6ge19
Right out here by the green buoy that marks the channel, there were fish everywhere! Every kind of fish you could imagine. Lots of white bass and yellow bass and hybrid Bass. There was a boat on the other side of the buoy from us, they were fishing for largemouth, and each one of the guys in the boat were catching them. We were a couple hundred yards away on the other side of the buoy, in about 14 ft of water, targeting crappie sitting on a hump that was just off of the channel.
We were using ultralight setups with 4 lb monofilament and I was running a 1/16 of an ounce jig head with a 2-inch pearl colored body Garland baby shad. My favorite way to run that with forward facing sonar is with a medium size split shot about 10 inches above the jig. All I have to do is see the fish on the screen. If I can see them, I can catch them. That was the case this morning. When we finally found some fish, we just stayed where they were and caught them until it was time for him to go. We got several really nice crappie and as is typical, yellow bass make their way through the school of crappie occasionally. One of the yellow bass that came through I hooked up with, and it was an 11 inch Tennessee trophy fish!
That's something that I learned recently. Every true bass in that lake, yellow bass, white bass, hybrid bass and striped bass, all of them will eat a crappie jig. When you see them coming through, you can tell they're not crappie. Crappie tend to school up in a tight school and hang relatively close to structure and do very little moving. True bass come in in a roughly shaped school that gets longer than it does tall and they never stop moving. They swim through the area in a school together and attack any kind of bait they see. When you see them on the forward facing sonar, it's easy enough to just cast it them and give the lure a couple of quick twitches. That's usually all it takes to get one on the hook.
Once we were done catching all the fish we wanted to, we cruised around the area using his forward facing sonar to look at some of the brush piles that we had been frequenting. Because the lake has dropped several feet since summer pool, the brush piles that we were previously fishing in 20 ft of water we're now closer to 15 ft of water. Unfortunately, none of those reliable places where we had been catching crappie had any fish on them at all. Bottom line, if we didn't have forward facing sonar to tell us that there weren't any fish on those crappie structures, we may have spent a lot of time fishing at them.

title: Trip Report #156
content_raw:
I love it when a plan comes together...
This morning, I wanted to go find this spot on the bank...
https://goo.gl/maps/5sSeDbLTeCFE2quN6
I didn't know where to park, or how to get there, or if there would be a trail, so I didn't want to do it in the dark. So I started my morning at 5:45 a.m. at Stewart Creek boat ramp...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/JcgfHLLZRKCd650as
The past couple of months, the cliffs at Stewart Creek boat ramp have been packed with fishermen every morning. When I got there this morning, I was the only person there! I knew when I pulled in, there weren't going to be any fish there. If there were, there would be people fishing for them. But it was still too dark to try to go through the woods where I wanted to, so I hit the cliffs, to bide my time. It only took 15 or 20 minutes to figure out that not only could I not get a crappie bite, but there weren't any bait fish jumping and I didn't hear much activity on the surface of the water in general. That's pretty indicative of a spot where there's not a lot of fish.
So I headed across the street to the wildlife Management area, where I had seen a school of crappie with my forward facing sonar a couple of days before...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/zTTAEt95ufru75q79
That's where you can park on the side of the road, but it's really steep pulling in here! If you pull off too quickly, you're going to bottom out. It's not a bad place for a few cars to park, you just have to pull in and out slowly. If it's raining, it's going to be muddy. From here, there's a really good path through the woods to the water's edge. Once you get to the water's edge, the trail kind of goes away. I made my way off the trail to the right along the cliffs above the water's edge, until I got to the spot on the bank where I had not only seen crappie on the forward facing sonar, but caught several...
https://goo.gl/maps/UDSFCxy4eSWv46ut9
You'll know when you're in the right spot. It's pretty distinguishable. There's a fire pit, and as you look out at the lake, to your left, there are two big trees in the water. Unfortunately, this morning, just like across the road at Stewart creek, the fish in this area just weren't having it. I'm certain, at both spots, there were crappie. They always hang out in those locations. They just don't always eat. Those fish may have eaten overnight, or they may have been waiting a little later, either way, that's what crappie fishermen do. They change spots. After about 15 minutes, and only catching a largemouth bass and a white bass, I took off through the woods back to my car and headed to a third spot...
https://goo.gl/maps/mCUHwHHYE64UMXYGA
This is a spot on the side of the lake that I found yesterday with my forward facing sonar. There was a school of crappie that I knew were close enough to the bank for me to catch. I caught several of them yesterday, dropped a pin on this spot, and then waited until it got light enough outside for me to get lost in the woods trying to find it. After striking out at my first two locations, I made my way up Jefferson Pike to find a spot along the side of the road to park. It didn't take long! There are a handful of legal parking spots that have been carved out by the city, they are nicely kept and mowed and the gravel is compacted and smooth. This is the very first parking spot alongside this cliff. I parked at this spot so that I could make my way to the beginning of the cliff where it starts to drop off to deep water, from shallow muddy bank, to the cliff...
https://goo.gl/maps/iAWxeW6TdN8nREb4A
It's a quarter mile walk through the woods! The trail is not well beaten! As you park, facing the woods, there's a trail to the left and to the right. I made the mistake of taking the trail to the left. It's not a dead end, but there aren't any fish over there. So I headed back to my car, and took the trail to the right. You'll know you're going the right way, because there's an old gate there. As usual, on Percy Priest lake, you're allowed to be here! Go over, under, or around the gate. Then, you walk a little more than a tenth of a mile on a relatively distinguishable trail before you have to make a left and make your way down to the water's edge. I just kept the PIN on Google maps up on my phone and tried walking my way through there. Fortunately, there's not a lot of undergrowth, so you can pick your way through the trees and over all the downed leaves. But there is not a path!
Then when I got there, I didn't know exactly where to stand. I picked out a spot on the bank yesterday when I was in my boat, but it wasn't optimum. I was standing near a downed tree in the water and casting out in front of it, where I was catching those fish yesterday. As it turned out, I needed to be standing on the actual edge of the cliff. At this location, it goes from a flat muddy bank, to a cliff face. On that transition, there's a bunch of busted up rocks that you can stand on and cast straight out.
Using my seven and a half foot ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament, I figured out quickly that my typical 1/32nd ounce jig head would be a little too heavy because I got hung up and broke off. You're not standing on a cliff with deep water in front of you. You're standing on the transition. So the water out in front is very shallow for the first 20 or 30 ft and then it drops off underwater. That's where those fish are hanging out. Near the transition, between the muddy bank and the rocky bank, just off the underwater Cliff face in about 13 ft of water. It's not necessary to make a long cast, so I changed my lure to an even lighter lure, a 1/48th of an ounce jig head, with my usual 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad.
Making a cast of about 70 ft, and allowing my jig to sink exactly 10 seconds before I started a slow retrieve, I would incorporate a quick twitch after a few cranks of the real and that would be all it would take! For nine casts in a row I got a bite, and on most of those bites I landed a keeper crappie! This morning, this place, was on fire! I caught about a dozen crappie, and more than half of them were keepers! Catching these fish was made easier by the fact that there was no wind this morning. It may have been much more difficult if I had to make those long casts and combat any wind at all. Fortunately, when I got there, the rain hadn't moved in just yet, and the fish were fired up!

title: Trip Report #157
content_raw:
It's happening!
Before I acquired forward facing sonar for my boat, I knew I wanted to use it to find spots on the bank where I could catch crappie. Today, on only my second trip out with my boat and forward facing sonar, I found a fantastic spot to catch crappie from the bank!
After breakfast this morning, I launched my boat from Jefferson springs boat ramp...
https://share.google/678iBqiJdZyoMgSug
There's a cliff directly across from the boat ramp. On that cliff, directly in front of the boat ramp, there was a huge school of crappie, where I caught my first fish of the day. There was a guy who was walking through the woods with his dogs and I asked him how he got there. He said his neighborhood backs up to the lake, so they can walk through. So that's not an option, unless you know someone in the neighborhood. He said that crappie can be caught all up and down that cliff and that people are well aware of it. When I say directly in front of the boat ramp, I mean directly straight across in a straight line across the lake. It's not that far!
From there, I went under the bridge on Jefferson Pike and scanned the columns that hold the bridge up. Unfortunately, there weren't any crappie schooled up on those bridge pilings. The next spot as you're moving up Lake is the water intake plant. I've always heard lots of good things about people catching fish in that area, but there is a sign that says not to fish within a hundred feet! So I didn't. Then the river channel makes a bend to the left and runs up along another cliff face. That's where I found a school of crappie that we can walk to from the side of the road on Jefferson Pike.
I'm going to drop the pin here...
https://goo.gl/maps/uesYKtCiLK97VqBz8
I haven't walked through this area so I don't know exactly which trail to take or exactly where to park. I will figure all that out soon. You need to know that this is a wildlife management area, and if you're going to be walking through here this time of year, you should probably wear some bright orange in case there are any hunters. There's a very low likelihood, because this is a very heavily fished area. I caught a whole bunch of crappie at this spot, and there was a bunch of trash on the ground near there. It look like at least some people are already aware of the good crappie fishing there.
So let me break it down for you. These fish had moved to much shallower areas. Both school of crappie that I found today were near the bank, and they were in 13 ft of water or less. That means, the bottom of the lake was 13 ft deep. They were stacked up as high as 5 ft from the surface. That's really shallow! If you were standing at the bank, it would be easy to cast directly out from that spot with a 1/32nd ounce jig head on 4 lb monofilament and get past these fish, so that you could retrieve through them.
That's the way you would have to get them from the bank. I know that from experience. You can't put too much weight on when you're fishing from the bank because as you reel the lure back to yourself, the ground is coming up to you quickly. That causes you to get hung up way too much. Lighter lures are the way to go when you're standing on the bank. For me, from the boat, I've realized, the heavier the better. Today, I was throwing a 1/16th of an ounce jig head with a medium size split shot about 12 inches above it. That has been my go-to when trying to catch crappie using forward facing sonar from the boat.
It's not that these fish are so deep that a lighter lure won't get there, it's that I don't have to use a lighter lure. This heavier presentation allows me to cast it farther and more accurately against the wind. It allows my crappie jig to sink quickly to the desired depth before I start my retrieve. So far, the heavier setup hasn't hindered my ability to catch crappie, it's only made it easier.
Those were the only two school of crappie that I found, but as I went a little farther upstream, I was suddenly on a mud bank near the cliffs. 28 ft of water was only a cast away, but I was sitting in about 2 ft of water above a perfectly flat muddy area. That's when I saw a whole bunch of fish moving around really fast on the screen. They looked exactly like crappie, so I made a cast, and I caught one, and it was a white bass! Then the next one was a little striped bass, about the same size. Then the next one was a hybrid bass, a little bit bigger than the other two! I kept catching those fish for about 30 minutes until there were some guys who came from the woods to stand on the bank right there!
They said they were fishing for white bass, and I told them to start casting! They were using what looked like 1/4 oz white rooster tails. Immediately, they started catching fish! They just had to throw it as far as they could and get their rod tip up and start reeling really fast. This spot was on the other end of the same cliff where I found those crappie. It would be a different place where you had to park on Jefferson pike, but I'm going to drop the pin where I found those white bass, here...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/W4SM8cRvi9BpR5fX9
This spot was easy enough to find from the bank. I haven't been there yet, but those cliffs come to an abrupt end, and then the bank is all mud. That's where you stand! Right there on the last little rocks before it turns into mud. The ground out in front of you is very shallow, so you will have to run your lure very fast. One thing I know for sure, these white bass and hybrids go into these shallow coves and shallow areas to feed in the evening. I know that's why those guys showed up when they did! I'm not certain they will be there at any other point in time during the day, but at least that much, we've got figured out.

title: Trip Report #158
content_raw:
Return to Center Hill Dam...
It's been more than 9 weeks since I went fishing in my favorite spot in the world, below Center Hill Dam...
https://share.google/Fx6A0kSN75ZfUoLLN
This morning, I launched my kayak at 7:30 a.m. from Buffalo valley boat ramp, while the generators were on. There was one generator on, and it was scheduled to go off at 9:00 a.m.  You can find the generating schedule, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/center-hill
I prefer to fish for my kayak when the generators are off, but I went this morning because I was ready to get back up there! When the generators are on, I like to fish that generating water. I like to make long casts into the water and use lures that I can retrieve, that hopefully won't get hung up on the bottom. If you are in a boat or a kayak and you get hung up on the bottom and that generating water, when you try to pull your line to break it off, you pull your vessel into that heavy current. I don't like that! So I use lures that I can swim through the current and try to avoid the bottom altogether.
This morning, I was using my 6-ft 6-in medium action bass pole with 15 lb braid. I was throwing a quarter ounce white jig head with a 4 in white paddle tail into that heavy current, and retrieving it really slowly. That is a good way to catch walleye. Within a few casts, that's exactly what I did. I caught a small walleye. The bite was so quick that I figured I would catch a few more, so I tried patiently for about an hour. Unfortunately, that would be the only fish I would catch out of the generating water.
With about 20 minutes of generating to go, I was reeling that paddle tail slowly near the bottom, when I thought I felt a couple of bounces on the bottom. Then my rod doubled over and my line started to scream and a gigantic rainbow trout went flying out of the river and threw my paddle tail! It was the biggest rainbow I have seen this year, and it would have been the big fish of the day. But they gave me a high hopes that the big fish we're biting today.
Almost immediately after the generators turned off, one of the people who was fishing at the steps hooked into a gigantic fish. I couldn't tell at the time, but I later found out, it was a 22 inch Brown trout. I'm not certain what type of bait or lure they were using, but it looked like they were using a three-way rig with something like a paddle tail. Either way, it was the second big fish I had seen on the day, but it wouldn't be the last.
Once the generators went off, I made my way over to the waterfall in the corner. Using my ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament, I tied on my favorite trout lure, a 1/64th of an ounce trout magnet with a 1 inch gulp minnow from Berkeley. This is an extremely light setup, and you can't cast it very far. I like to sit right next to the water in the corner that is creating a little current against the wall. I cast into that current and allow my lure to suspend against my raised rod tip. You really don't even have to do anything, the fish will do all the work!
Holding that really light lure against the current and reeling it back and possibly slowly, sometimes incorporating a twitch, I caught a rainbow trout on the very first cast! That's when I realized that I had tied my gulp minnow and 1/64th of an ounce jig head on to the wrong rod and reel. I had it on the pole that had 6 lb monofilament and I wasn't able to cast it very far. So I switched it over to my ultra light that had 4 lb monofilament. After I made the change, I draped the lure over the front of my kayak. There was about 4 ft of line and it was dangling right off the front while I was tying a different lure on my other pole.
While it was dangling off the front of my kayak, my trout magnet got smashed by an over 20 inch female rainbow trout! Unfortunately, my camera wasn't recording, but I got a good video of her after the fight. I didn't have to fish to catch this fish. I just had to be in the right place at the right time. Having the right lure didn't hurt!
That trout magnet with a 1-in gulp minnow is a tiny presentation but it catches fish year round! The biggest factor for my success is knowing when to use which color jig head. Trout magnets come in three different colors, black, silver, and gold. I don't like the black ones at all. I've never had much success. I do have a tried and true method for using the silver or the gold ones. When I opened my tackle box today, I had the option of gold or silver. The sky was completely overcast. When that's the case, I use gold lures to fish for trout. Gold trout magnets. Gold spoons. Lures with gold spinners. When it is sunny out, I use silver. Silver trout magnets, silver spoons, rooster tails with a silver blade.
After I caught that fish, I immediately cut the gills and let it bleed out so I could take it home to have it for dinner. I didn't stay to fish any longer because I didn't have a stringer or a cooler so I immediately took that fish directly home. My plan was to stay up there until the generators kicked on again in the afternoon. But I wasn't planning on catching a trout that big, so my plans had to change!

Within a few casts, that's exactly what I did. I caught a small walleye. The bite was so quick that I figured I would catch a few more, so I tried patiently for about an hour. Unfortunately, that would be the only fish I would catch out of the generating water.

With about 20 minutes of generating to go, I was reeling that paddle tail slowly near the bottom, when I thought I felt a couple of bounces on the bottom. Then my rod doubled over and my line started to scream and a gigantic rainbow trout went flying out of the river and threw my paddle tail! It was the biggest rainbow I have seen this year, and it would have been the big fish of the day. But they gave me a high hopes that the big fish we're biting today.

Almost immediately after the generators turned off, one of the people who was fishing at the steps hooked into a gigantic fish. I couldn't tell at the time, but I later found out, it was a 22 inch Brown trout. I'm not certain what type of bait or lure they were using, but it looked like they were using a three-way rig with something like a paddle tail. Either way, it was the second big fish I had seen on the day, but it wouldn't be the last.

Once the generators went off, I made my way over to the waterfall in the corner. Using my ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament, I tied on my favorite trout lure, a 1/64th of an ounce trout magnet with a 1 inch gulp minnow from Berkeley. This is an extremely light setup, and you can't cast it very far. I like to sit right next to the water in the corner that is creating a little current against the wall. I cast into that current and allow my lure to suspend against my raised rod tip. You really don't even have to do anything, the fish will do all the work!

Holding that really light lure against the current and reeling it back and possibly slowly, sometimes incorporating a twitch, I caught a rainbow trout on the very first cast! That's when I realized that I had tied my gulp minnow and 1/64th of an ounce jig head on to the wrong rod and reel. I had it on the pole that had 6 lb monofilament and I wasn't able to cast it very far. So I switched it over to my ultra light that had 4 lb monofilament. After I made the change, I draped the lure over the front of my kayak. There was about 4 ft of line and it was dangling right off the front while I was tying a different lure on my other pole.

While it was dangling off the front of my kayak, my trout magnet got smashed by an over 20 inch female rainbow trout! Unfortunately, my camera wasn't recording, but I got a good video of her after the fight. I didn't have to fish to catch this fish. I just had to be in the right place at the right time. Having the right lure didn't hurt!

That trout magnet with a 1-in gulp minnow is a tiny presentation but it catches fish year round! The biggest factor for my success is knowing when to use which color jig head. Trout magnets come in three different colors, black, silver, and gold. I don't like the black ones at all. I've never had much success. I do have a tried and true method for using the silver or the gold ones. When I opened my tackle box today, I had the option of gold or silver. The sky was completely overcast. When that's the case, I use gold lures to fish for trout. Gold trout magnets. Gold spoons. Lures with gold spinners. When it is sunny out, I use silver. Silver trout magnets, silver spoons, rooster tails with a silver blade.

After I caught that fish, I immediately cut the gills and let it bleed out so I could take it home to have it for dinner. I didn't stay to fish any longer because I didn't have a stringer or a cooler so I immediately took that fish directly home. My plan was to stay up there until the generators kicked on again in the afternoon. But I wasn't planning on catching a trout that big, so my plans had to change!

title: Trip Report #159
content_raw:
I put forward facing sonar on my boat...
Today, I launched my boat from Stewart Creek boat ramp at around 9:30 a.m...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/FewoexVNdpxtbWT49
If you don't know, forward facing sonar is the technical name for tools like livescope. It's a fish finder that allows you to see what the fish are doing in real time. You can not only see the fish moving, but you can see your lure, and how they respond to it. The best way to use this tool, find the fish that you're looking for, and then fish for them. Today, I was looking for crappie, specifically, crappie that I can catch from the bank. Mission accomplished!
First of all, before I even got too far away from the boat ramp, I scanned the cliff adjacent to where I usually fish from the bank at Stewart Creek. I found some underwater trees and a really large school of crappie. They didn't want to bite, but that was just because I hadn't got dialed in yet. Turns out, that today, they didn't really care for my crappie jig moving through the water. They really wanted it to be sitting still, directly in front of their face. But we will get to that later. This school of fish was just a short cast away from a really nice spot to stand on the bank. I'm going to drop a pin here...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/hYSEmZmb1W5z3Bzq6
You have to walk all the way around the path from the boat ramp to the spot, and eventually the sidewalk path ends and you have to take a relatively well beaten path around to this point. You're going to be standing on the tallest of these five to six foot tall cliffs, just over the water. Cast directly out! I would use my ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad. I have never attempted to fish this spot from the bank, but I will soon.
From there, I went around the corner to the bridge on Weekly Lane that goes over the lake at the cliffs at Fate Sanders recreation area. Currently, the recreation area is closed for winter. Fortunately, there are a few parking spaces on the north side of the bridge as you're heading south. The perfect place to access the next spot where I found crappie...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/YJ3KyJVtRAMJN95n6
These fish were really conveniently placed! I plan on going to this spot in the future when it's a rainy day. You can stand underneath this bridge on a tremendously tall cliff and cast straight out in front of you. There was a really large school of crappie, but you're going to have to bring them up this crazy cliff! And it's really dangerous under there, you could easily slip off and fall into the lake. And it's probably like 40 ft straight up! My plan, go there with my medium action rof, about 7 ft, and use 8 lb monofilament so that I can drag those fish up the cliff face. This is a terribly treacherous spot to try to fish, but they are loaded up!
When I came back to the boat ramp, I went across the cove at Stewart Creek just passed the boat ramp, so that I could scan the cliffs that I stand on and catch crappie over there. I like to stand right here...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/gJPTCzpvzG2yUj5r8
There was somebody sitting there crappie fishing, so I didn't get very close, but my forward facing sonar shoots out 70 ft, and I was able to stay far enough away and I could easily tell, that spot is completely loaded. I figured it would be. There's always a lot of people catching fish there, Saturday morning there was a dozen people standing right there! But they weren't just in that one spot, they were also a little farther down the bank where there is a tree that sticks out of the water...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/kh3VtFa1AP17sgfX7
No one was standing at that tree so I went down there to scan it and pluck all of the crappie jigs off of it. That thing was loaded! I had been casting at crappie each time I had seen them, and wasn't having any luck. This time, because I was so close to the structure, when I was pulling those jigs off, I turned my forward facing sonar on down scan. What I saw was, lots of crappie hanging all around the tree. That's what I expected, I could see that from a distance. So I dropped my jig directly down into the down scan where I can watch it and it immediately got crushed!
As it turned out, the fish were willing to bite, just about anywhere that I could find them, they just weren't willing to chase anything. I was able to catch a few nice keeper crappie and a couple small crappie that I threw back simply by dropping my jig directly down to them and giving it a little twitch. That leads me to believe that, if I go to one of these locations on the bank and cast out with a minnow on a slip bobber, I could definitely catch some of these fish.
So here's what you're going to have to do. You're going to need a slip bobber. Basically, a bobber stop on your line at a depth of at least 15 ft to start. Cast directly out from one of these locations and allow that minnow to get all the way down and then work it slowly back to you. If you don't get a bite in a few casts, lower it down to 16 ft. These fish were hanging out as low as 20 feet. In each one of these locations, the water gets between 28 and 30 ft deep at the bottom.
That was what these fish had in common today. They were all holding between 15 and 20 ft in around 30 ft of water. I didn't find any fish that were in places where the bottom was only 20 ft deep or shallower. I even went into Fate Sanders Marina to look at the whole entire thing, and because most of the marina is in 11 ft of water or less, I didn't see anything that looked like a school of crappie! I didn't even see anything that looked like a school of bluegill. There's a good chance that the cooling water temperatures have forced these fish to start moving deeper, something that happens during the winter.
Today, the water temperature had dropped below 60° in each of the places that I fished. I didn't see any temperatures higher than 59°. When that happens, these fish like to school a lot heavier, together, because they get pushed out of the shallower areas into these cliff-like situations, where they find each other, and school in great numbers.

title: Trip Report #160
content_raw:
Busy Saturday morning...
This morning, I got to Stewart Creek boat ramp at around 5:30 a.m...
https://share.google/VgtNpFXkAaQeiOnSq
I usually just walk the short trail through the woods over to the cliffs, not very far from the parking lot at all...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/kzLXPZGYQ35XA25DA
There were a dozen people standing out there this morning! But that doesn't matter. As long as everybody is casting straight out, there's plenty of room! Some of the people who were fishing there recognized me, and invited me to come down and stand in between them. I was there at the golden hour, the time of day that had been most productive for me in the last couple of weeks, the first 40 minutes of daylight, just before the sun comes up. Unfortunately, the fish weren't feeling it. It took until sunrise before I saw the first fish caught.
A small crappie, at exactly 6:22 a.m. Then, an avalanche of catches! All the way up and down the bank, from sunrise, until a little after 8:00 a.m. crappie were biting hot and heavy! Everybody out there was casting jigs, most people were using the same thing I was, a 1/32nd ounce jig head and a Bobby Garland baby shad. I like to use Pearl color, the guys that were standing around me were using blue ice. I don't think the color was as important as the presentation.
Everybody was casting those light lures as far as they could, which isn't very far, and then allowing it to sink for just a few seconds before starting a painfully slow retrieve, with a few twitches Incorporated. That was all it would take today! You didn't necessarily need to let your lure sink for more than five or six seconds, but you needed to reel it back very slowly. Pretty much everybody out there is using an ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament. Some people are using 6 lb, but most people are not.
There were lots of short fish today. Seems like it was two to one short fish over keepers. What these fish lacked in length, they made up for in numbers. At one point in time, everybody around me was catching fish at the same time. As far as I could see down the bank, I could see other fishermen reeling in crappie. It was bizarre to see them get started later today than they usually do, but when they did, the bite lasted a little longer today.
Typically, the early morning bite window doesn't last more than 45 minutes to an hour. Don't get me wrong, you can still catch fish before and after, it just seems like there's a very hot bite right around sunrise everyday. That tends to happen after several days of consistent weather. Each day this week has gotten a little warmer. The longer we have consistent weather that doesn't dramatically change the water temperature, the easier it will be to pin down exactly what time these fish are feeding heaviest.
Here's what I'm seeing recently, and what I expect to continue through the next few days, until we get some significant rain on Thursday.
Fish are biting heavily at night! But not until about 10:00. The best night bite has been from 10:00 p.m. until about 4:00 a.m. at that point in time, they kind of slow down until sunrise. Then, right around sunrise, either just before 6:22, or just after, the fish feed heavily again for about an hour and a half. Then you hit the longest period of the day where the fish don't bite as much... From about 8:30 until about 1:00 p.m. when stuff picks up after lunch. Then you get the afternoon/evening bite, but it isn't nearly as prolific as the morning bite or even the overnight bite. Pretty much, from 1:00 p.m. until sunset, the crappie are biting pretty good, just not gangbusters, anywhere that I have been.

title: Trip Report #161
content_raw:
How we caught bigger crappie...
Yesterday, my buddy and I found a gigantic school of crappie at the cliffs at Elm Hill Rush boat ramp...
https://share.google/NUxQQe7ZQAg7H8Qe6
We caught several fish using ultralight rod and reels with 4 lb monofilament. Yesterday, for the first time, I tried adding a couple of split shots about a foot above the jig head that I typically use (1/32 oz) with a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad. That was to get down to the fish that were suspended at 20 ft of depth, quicker. Not only did it work, they were happy to eat my jig, several times in a row. But even though we caught a couple handful of crappie, only a few were keepers, and none of them were true giants.
Fast forward to this morning, we went to the same spot right at sunrise, except this time, we had minnows. Using a slip bobber setup set to about 18 ft of depth, the very first crappie we caught was 13 in long and over a pound! Then we caught at least four or five more really big super slab crappie as well as a handful of small crappie, before the school got wise to us and completely moved away. After we caught about a dozen fish, and they moved away, we could see them on the forward facing sonar, but we couldn't get them to bite. So we scooted directly across the lake to the seven points area where we had been catching crappie most of the fall.
We put some 5 gallon buckets with limbs to make brush piles in a spot over by seven points, but we have never seen any fish on that spot. Today wouldn't prove any different. They're still weren't any fish on our structures. So we looked at a couple of different places that had previously been in 20 ft of water, but since they dropped the lake level the last couple of days, these spots were only in about 16 and a half foot of water, and they didn't hold any fish. It's turning into that time of year really quick. The time of year where these fish like to sit on these deep cliffs, pretty much every day.
The level on Percy Priest Lake is getting lower for winter pool, and as that happens, the shallow water areas that these fish like to frequent, dry up. By the end of november, the lake will be down to 483 ft above sea level. Right now, is right around 487 ft, so it'll take the next couple of weeks for it to get all the way down. You can find the level of the lake, here...
https://tva.com/environment/lake-levels/j-percy-priest
Not only will that show you the surface level of the lake measured at the dam in feet above sea level, it will also show you what the generating schedule is for today, and also the next day. I haven't been able to confirm this yet, but I have heard that the crappie bite better when the dam is pulling water. I will pay particular attention going forward, and let you know if that's the case. If that turns out to be true, it would be really easy to look at that schedule and see when they are generating and plan your fishing trip at that time.
Since we couldn't find any crappie across the lake at the three or four usual spots that we try at seven points area, we came back to the Elm Hill area to scan the other side of the cliff. If you're standing on the boat ramp, we had been fishing on the cliffs directly out in front of the boat ramp, about a thousand yards away across cove. If you come out of the boat ramp and go to the left, there is another section of cliff face right there. It's the cliff that has the RVs parked there for camping. Using his forward facing sonar, we scanned all the way along that cliff. Unfortunately, that cliff didn't hold crappie like the other one did. We found a small school of fish, but it turned out to be bluegill.

title: Trip Report #162
content_raw:
We found the mother load...
This morning I meet my buddy at 7:30 a.m. to launch his boat at Elm Hill Rush boat ramp on Percy Priest Lake...
https://share.google/eIpk7Xf914Xo7zgYU
This is a very safe and secure boat ramp, because no one is ever there, because it cost $10 to launch! He likes to go there because it's close to his house. When we get there, he pays the $10 to go in, and I follow him through the gate without paying. I don't know if you're allowed to do that, but we've been doing that every time. It doesn't give you a ticket or any kind of verification that you paid, it just raises the gate when you pay $10. On your way out, the gate opens automatically.
If you're standing at the boat ramp looking directly out at the lake, The cove over to your right has a crappie condo fish attractor that was put in the lake by a fisherman and not by TWRA. We started over there looking for Crappie using his forward facing sonar and we could tell there were a few fish on the fish attractor but it was sitting in about 15 ft of water and that would prove to be a little too shallow.
That cove at the boat ramp is large. At least a quarter mile across. All the way across from the boat ramp in the same cove, there is a buoy that was put there by TWRA to mark fish  attractors that they had put in the water. Once again, these perfectly placed structures were a little bit too shallow, in 12 ft of water. We recently had a major cold front that dropped the temperature of the lake by nearly 10 degrees from just over 70° to just over 60°. We started looking for these fish in shallow water areas because everyone talks about how they move shallow when it gets colder. Unless it gets too cold.
That's exactly what happened. Directly across from that boat ramp if you're looking straight and not left or not right, but straight, you're staring a quarter mile across that cove at a giant cliff face. That cliff runs probably a thousand yards long and the water in front of that cliff is 20 to 30 ft deep. On that cliff, we found a school of crappie that was the biggest school of crappie we had ever seen on forward-facing sonar. It wasn't hundreds of fish. It was thousands of fish!
One thing we have figured out about fish that hang out on the cliffs, they move from side to side along the face of the cliff. Typically, the whole entire School of crappie will move in unison, back and forth along whatever cliff they are sitting in front of. Sometimes, they move really really slow. Sometimes they move rather quickly and you can see the entire school sliding away from one area to the left or to the right. You can follow them with forward facing sonar and continue casting at them, and continue catching them. But if you can't see them with that type of fish finder it's best to do what I usually do from the bank.
When I'm standing on a cliff on Percy Priest Lake, and fishing for crappie, I will cast left and right continuously searching to find those fish. When I get a bite in a particular direction, I keep casting that direction until I don't get a bite anymore. Typically, that indicates that they have moved on. It may be some time before they come back through, depending on how big a cliff you are sitting on. They tend to go all the way from one side of the cliff to the other. This cliff is huge, so they had a lot of room to roam.
Once we found them, all we had to do was cast into them, and we would get a bite. Using my 7 and 1/2 ft ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament, I dramatically altered my crappie lure today. Instead of my typical jig head, I was using a 1/64th of an ounce. That's half the size of the jig head I usually use. Above The jig head, at about 8 inches away, I put two fairly sizable split shots. Pretty heavy, so I could get down to the fish quickly. The top of the school of fish was at about 15 ft and the bottom was down near the bottom of the lake at about 25 ft. You had to get your jig head down to them in order to get them to bite.
In the past, we would cast out there with a 1/32nd ounce jig head and watch it on the screen sink painfully slow, until it got all the way down to the level where the fish were. I had recently seen other fishermen on YouTube using heavy weights to get their lure down there quicker. So that's what I tried to do today. On my first four casts, I not only got a bite, but I hooked up to, and landed crappie. Four fish in a row. Then, they started to move away from that area slowly.
They weren't necessarily moving because we caught a few of them, they just always do that! So we watched them slide about 30 ft away down the rock face, and then, turn around and come back. They literally came right back directly under the boat. We were sitting within inches of the cliff, sheltered from the wind. The boat wasn't moving, so they didn't necessarily know we were there. We just watched them. Anytime they would get close to us, we would cast into them and catch a few.
These were nice size fish! The majority of the ones we caught were keepers, but we weren't keeping any fish today, so we threw them all back. It's important to note, the reason we went over there to scan with his forward facing sonar is, each time we had launched at that location, we had seen a boat, sitting in front of those cliffs fishing. After we made our rounds in the cove looking for crappie in shallow water, we noticed that there was no one over on that cliff and decided to go see what they had been fishing for. It was crappie!

title: Trip Report #163
content_raw:
Muskie time in Tennessee...
We have a fairly small population of Muskie that live on the plateau in Middle Tennessee. Yesterday,  my buddy and I fished a 5-mile stretch of the Collins River in McMinnville Tennessee. We dropped in on private property on the side of the road and kayaked downstream to Myers cove boat ramp...
Myers Cove Boat Ramp https://share.google/a25BTEvlSilWkTVWW
The boat ramp is public access, the place where we launched our kayaks is not. There is no parking lot or public area to launch where we launched, you just have to know somebody. On this river, there are other public launching points that I will use throughout the year, depending on water levels. Yesterday, the river was running at just over 500 CFS when we started our trip, that's why I chose this particular stretch of river. It's a little further upstream and therefore subject to a little less flow than where the reading is being taken downstream. To see current stream data for the Collins river, check here...
https://waterdata.usgs.gov/monitoring-location/USGS-03421000/all-graphs/#period=P7D
I like to Target Muskie in Middle Tennessee during the late fall and winter and early spring. When it gets too warm, the water doesn't hold enough dissolved oxygen and it makes it hard for these fish to recover after being caught. Targeting them this time of year gives them the best chance at survival after a tough fight.
You need heavy equipment to Target muskie! A 7 ft heavy action rod with 65 lb braid is what I use. Yesterday, we were throwing lures that weighed several ounces and some people throw lures that way as much as a pound. To attach the lure to the line, we use a steel leader That's rated at least 100 lb. After you have the proper equipment, pretty much any giant lure will work. There are lots of different musky specific lures on the market, and we tried several of them yesterday.
You're going to need a really big net! Gigantic! Something that's big enough for a 40 inch fish to swim around in. It needs to be rubber, so that the hooks don't get tangled in it. You need jaw spreaders. If you don't know what job spreaders are, they're designed to open the toothy mouth of a muskie so you can retrieve a lure or a hook if it gets stuck down in their mouth and pins it closed. You going to need bolt cutters, so that you can cut any hooks if you cannot retrieve them. You're going to need long handled pliers so you can try to reach in to a thrashing fish's mouth and retrieve your hooks without getting stuck.
On our 5 Mile trip, we had two musky come out and swipe and then disappear back into the river. We had one muskie follow all the way to the boat and my buddy was able to figure eight until he caught it. I was able to catch one tiny muskie near the end of the trip.
Titan JR Lure |
SCHEELS.com
https://share.google/yYr6UL2HoRneoeaI7
The Titan Junior musky lure was what my buddy was throwing. He was having pretty good success because he got three fish to come out and one of them to commit. This is a very big, very expensive lure and I don't typically buy musky lures because of that reason. I catch my Muskie with regular bass lures, I just put them on my extra heavy rod and reel with my steel leader so that muskies teeth don't cut my line.
I was able to catch my Muskie on a 7-in weightless fluke with a four ot gamakatsu wormhook. I was using a white fluke and I rigged it weedless and I was casting it and twitching it with a slow retrieve. The thing about Muskie is, you never know what they're going to want to eat! So I just stick with what I know best. I like to fish for bass with flukes as well as paddle tails or Whopper ploppers on top water. All of these are good options for Muskie as I have caught multiple Muskie with each one of these lures. I've also caught them on Ned rigs and drop shots with a plastic worm, you name it, I've seen a musky eat it!
So here's what you need to know if you want to go out to the Collins river. Never under any circumstance, do you want to try to go out there and fish with the current over 1,000 CFS on that graph that I just shared with you. At that point, the river is too fast and it can be dangerous. There are a handful of boat ramps, but they're not really boat ramps. They're access points. Only one spot, at meyer's cove, is there an actual boat ramp. Here are a couple other public locations on the river.
Shellsford Rd Collins River Access https://share.google/4JCYq8rUfiK8m6dGm
https://share.google/iA3Rzebgs9n9vu9xg
Wanamaker Landing Collins River Access https://share.google/d1SiYZE15cfUu5Orh
As we get deeper into the cold weather months, I'll explain in more detail the stretches of river between these points, how long the trips are, and what type of obstacles, if any may be in the way. Over the course of the next few months, I will hit every stretch of this River targeting not only musky, but trophy smallmouth bass.

title: Trip Report #164
content_raw:
Did you see the frost flowers?
Today I went to the spring on Percy Priest Lake to catch crappie, but primarily to walk that long trail and check out all the really pretty frost flowers...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/HaiwfjqKrM7drq957
To get to the spring, park on the side of Maddox road and go under, over, or around the gate that says, "foot traffic only"...
https://goo.gl/maps/6K3hdqxRxJuKWiqf9
This is all public property, and the trail is a quarter mile long. By now, I've walked it so many times, it's really wide and well beaten! This is a wildlife management area, so be sure to wear something bright orange! Hunters are allowed to use this area, right now it's muzzleloader season. Stay on the path.
Once you get back to the spring, it looks like you're in the back of a cul-de-sac! The way the spring has carved out the lake makes it the perfect shape and size! I like to stand right in the very back, in the deepest part of the spring, on one of the many rocks overlooking the lake. I've been hitting this spot consistently for the last 7 to 10 days. The crappie bite was fantastic until the front came through and then it got really tough. Now, more than 2 days removed from the front that came through Saturday night into Sunday, the fish have become acclimated and the bite was on fire!
For the past few trips there, I was having to fish really deep. Allowing my lure to sink for more than 30 seconds most of the time. What I was doing, was casting my 1/32nd ounce jig head with a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland exactly 40 ft and allowing it to pendulum off the tip of my rod. I would hold my rod straight up at a 45° angle and allow that jig to slowly sink for most of a minute before I started to slowly work it back to me. Today, they were feeding much higher in the water column.
Using my 7 1/2 ft ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament I was casting the same distance, about 40 ft straight out in front of me, but I was starting my retrieve after the lure sank 17 seconds. When I first got there, I started fishing really deep, but I wasn't having very good results. That's why I started fishing a little shallower. I was already fishing as deep as I could go, the only other way was up. Fortunately, when that's happening, you can get the fish quicker, because you don't have to wait so long!
The bite was fire hot. The temperature outside was 23⁰ and the wind chill was 18⁰, but the crappie couldn't be happier! I've been complaining about the way crappie bite during the fall. During the winter, they give you a distinct thump. Then you know to set the hook. This fall, it has been more of a finicky nibble or even a very faint bite and sometimes they just sit with the lure in their mouth and don't move and you don't feel anything at all. That makes it really hard to get the lure in their mouth and the hook to stick consistently. This morning, I did not have that problem.
After allowing the lure to sink for 17 seconds, I would start a painfully slow retrieve and every once in awhile incorporate a small twitch or even a twitch twitch and then continue my retrieve. That was it. That was all I had to do! They did the rest of the work for me. Reeling as painfully slow as I could, and incorporating the occasional twitch, they were hitting the lure with a massive thump! That's when you give them a quick flip of the wrist to set that hook!
This morning I was giving them the beans. Basically, it was every cast or every other cast. I walked in just after 5:30 and I started fishing at 5:45 a.m. by 6:22 I had caught about 12 fish and seven of them were nice slab keeper crappie. Then, sunrise happened, and the bite slowed down to a trickle. A little more than 30 minutes between daylight and sunrise, and then it was like pulling teeth. One fish would bite every 15 or 20 minutes.
During that window, when fish were easy to catch, all of the fish were biting at once. They were likely chasing bait and getting full. By the time the bite slows down, typically what has happened, is all the fish are satiated. When that happened, I packed up my things and called it a day!

title: Trip Report #165
content_raw:
Did the cold front change anything?
You better believe it! I have no idea what was going on with those fish today, but I could not catch a crappie. In my experience, crappie love consistency, and a dramatic change in the weather that results in a dramatic change in water temperature typically puts them off for a couple of days. This morning I got started at 5:45 a.m. on the side of North Lamar road...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/ddjJpmhYECRn5UJH7
You're allowed to park on the side of the road here because all of the property from the roadside to the lake is public. But this spot is very tough to pull into because there's a lot of mud and big rocks and the road falls off pretty sharply. If you don't have a high profile vehicle or you're not used to going off-road, you may not even want to try this spot! That being said, there's enough room there for probably four or five cars. There is a trail through the woods that leads directly to the lakes edge.
This spot is a channel swing. Basically, before the reservoir was built, a creek carved out a crescent moon shape in the rock face creating a small cliff. At this spot, right now, the water is about 15 ft deep. It's not a spot that I go to very often, but it holds really good crappie because they're are sunken logs out in front of these cliffs. I haven't been there recently so I wouldn't know if the crappie bite had been very good there, but I couldn't get any bites today. So I went right around the corner to another spot that typically holds crappie when the weather gets cooler.
https://maps.app.goo.gl/CP18GFVw1KoGY7Yu6
There's tons of parking along Maddox road here because all of this area is public except for one driveway. It's very obvious where you are allowed to park, there's lots of well-beaten spaces off the side of the road. Unfortunately, because they're so well beaten, they get very muddy this time of year. Once again, you're going to have to proceed with caution. Once you get parked, there are any number of trails through the woods over to the lakes edge.
There's a couple of coves here that both hold water even when the lake goes all the way down to Winter pool. I wasn't able to generate a crappie bite there this morning, but there are signs all around this area that the fishing must be pretty good. I spent the better part of an hour and a half cleaning up just the aluminum cans from this spot. There are half a dozen fire pits and it looks like lots of people fish for catfish at this spot because there were buckets of chicken livers. Alternatively, people could be using chicken livers on bottom to catch hybrid bass. That's a very popular method for getting those fish in Percy Priest Lake.
Since I was unable to get a bite, I got some cleaning done and then went home to get something to eat. After breakfast,and lunch, I went back out to Maddox road to walk over to the spring. When you park at this spot, the parking isn't as treacherous...
https://goo.gl/maps/tu8SXxZoiY4iXvdT8
There's a gate that says the area is for foot traffic only. It's a TWRA wildlife Management area and you are allowed to be there, but I suggest you wear bright orange as it is hunting season and people are allowed to hunt there with muzzleloaders, currently. Stay on the very wide, well beaten path and you should be able to make your way all the way back to the spring after a little more than a quarter mile hike...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/sfN4VSSHWFke5SYy8

I don't like to walk around the edges, I like to stand in the very back of the spring. I was using my 6 ft ultralight rod and reel as opposed to my seven and a half foot because there was so much wind today. That rod has 4 lb monofilament. I tried every size jig head in the bag from 1/64th of an ounce up to 1/8 of an ounce and every size in between. The reason I used so many different jig heads is because I couldn't generate a bite. So I was trying to work the water column at different depths and at different speeds. But none of that would matter.
These fish weren't having it today. They hate the dramatic change in water conditions. Don't get me wrong, they can still be caught, but I would have had to drastically change up my location. The method for catching crappie doesn't change dramatically. Either dangle a minnow in front of their face or run a small soft plastic on a light jig head with ultralight gear. The problem for me today, they weren't where they had been recently, and if they were, they weren't willing to eat.
After I'd been there a little while, another gentleman showed up who had a bucket of minnows. I asked him if I could have one and he agreed. I took off my jig head and put on a number 6 eagle claw bait holder hook and one small split shot about 6 inches away. I put on a small minnow and casted into the corner where I had seen multiple gigantic largemouth bass sitting the entire time I was crappie fishing.
I had been there the better part of an hour and a half and these fish, five or six, had made their way in and out of the shallows several different times. Each one of them were largemouth bass that looked to be at least two or three pounds and some of them were much larger than that. I dropped my minnow right where they had been moving in and out from in an attempt to get one of them to eat. Unfortunately, a small bluegill ate my minnow and got himself hooked.
At first I was bummed out because he ate my minnow and I didn't want to ask for another one, but then I realized I should probably use that bluegill for bait. So I took that number six eagle claw bait holder hook and I ran it through its upper lip and I casted it right back into the shallows beside me. Within about 3 minutes my line started to slowly move away. The bluegill was sitting on the bottom and I suspected maybe he was swimming so I opened my bail and let him have some slack. Then he started to swim really fast and I realized that one of those bass had him in his mouth!
I leaned back into the fish ever so slightly and I was able to get that tiny little hook to set into the corner of that big bass's mouth! After a few minutes of fighting that fish, I got him to the bank. But he was down at the surface of the water and I was up on an elevated rock face and I couldn't reach him. I suspected the line would break, and it did, just about the time that I figured it would. Not a big deal, after all, the biggest fish of the day tends to get away. But I learned something extremely valuable.
For the last few weeks, that area of the lake has been filled with small largemouth bass, most of them not even a quarter of a pound. Last week, slightly larger bass made their way into the spring. I was able to catch a few that were right at 3/4 of a pound. As of this morning, with that water temperature screaming downward, some true Giants had made their way back into the spring! And it wasn't really that hard to get one of them on the hook!
In the near future, I'll go back there with the intention of catching some of those bass. I already know they have a pension for bluegills, so that's what I will feed them! I'll probably take my fly rod so that I can use a tiny fly to catch really small bluegills. Something that we learned today, after I hooked that one fish, we could still see the other bass hanging out, but we couldn't get them to bite. The only other bluegill that we could catch were fairly sizable, and they were probably a little too big. Seems like the best size would be about three and a half to 4 inches at most. Just a quick snack that goes down easy!
I'll definitely be bringing heavier equipment. Something like a 7 ft bass rod with medium action and eight to 12 lb monofilament, so I can pull the fi
sh up on the bank and not break it off.

title: Trip Report #166
content_raw:
Finicky fish in the fog...
Friday night we had heavy rain, Saturday morning, the fog was as thick as it could be, just before sunrise, at Stewart Creek boat ramp...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/c84StrtcPxBjSF3gN
If you're looking straight down the boat ramp, go left through the woods. It's about 150 ft of well-beaten trail directly to the edge of a cliff overlooking the lake. The water directly out in front of you gets to be about 20 ft deep really quick off that cliff. I have developed a method that works fantastic to catch crappie standing on the cliffs on Percy Priest Lake.
Using my 6 ft ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad, I was casting exactly 60 ft directly out in front of me and then closing the bail on my spinning rod. I immediately get my rod tip up and then allow The lure to sink for 27 seconds. Yesterday, no more or no less than 27 seconds or I wouldn't get a bite. After it got down to the desired depth, I would start a painfully slow retrieve. One slow turn of the handle and then a twitch. Another slow turn and a couple of twitches. Then boom! That's where you would get the bite. If I didn't get one all the way down there, I would reel my lure back up and start the process again. Sometimes, if you're not quick enough reeling it in, you're going to get hung on the cliff. That's part of it, just break off, and quickly retie.
The bite was hot! Every single time I got my lure to the right spot, these crappie would bite. But the bite was very finicky! I've been complaining all fall that crappie don't do their typical thump every single time. Much of this season, they do what amounts to a little peck or a small nibble. That can make it really hard to set the hook! That's what I was battling yesterday morning. Don't get me wrong, I caught my fair share of fish, probably around 12 to 15 in all, with some of them being nice size keepers. But I had twice as many bites!
At first, I started allowing a split second pause after I would feel the bite, before I tried to set the hook. That did not work. Time and time again, I would swing and miss. So I went back to swinging as fast as I could, as soon as I felt something. That hooked a few fish, but I also missed my fair share. So I tried playing it by ear. Unfortunately, that's the way it has to be right now... Or at least, yesterday morning.
If I felt a thump, I went ahead with a fast hookset. If I started to feel a little nibble, I would hesitate ever so slightly and continue to slowly retrieve the lure without any twitches or pauses. That nibble would slowly turn into a little more pressure, and I would set the hook. I still missed a few doing it that way, but I also got several!
Unfortunately, yesterday was the end of a long stretch of warm weather where we had days that started off in the 40s and 50s and afternoons that ended in the upper 60s and lower 70s. The rain that came through the night before didn't necessarily change the temperature of the water, so that didn't really affect the fish much, in my opinion. The cold front that followed that rain, Saturday night into Sunday, will have affected these fish greatly! The last time we saw a cold front this impactful, fish moved from feeding in 20 ft of water up to about 15 ft of water!
That bodes well for catching these fish from the bank, but I will have to figure out a few more locations that are in shallower water. Hopefully, they will move up onto the fish attractors that are near the bank at lots of different boat ramps. There are fish attractors at this particular boat ramp all the way around the cove. If the crappie move up into those areas, you guys will be the first to know!
