title: Trip Report #167
content_raw:
Fantastic fishing before the storm?
Why does it seem like the fishing is always so good right before a storm? I'll tell you why...
This morning, I got to the side of Maddox road at about 5:35 a.m...
https://goo.gl/maps/fRT65m7mipHPGbax9
You're legally allowed to park here on the side of the road and then go past the gate that says foot traffic only... There is a quarter mile, well beaten trail, all the way to my favorite fishing spot on Percy Priest lake, the spring!
https://maps.app.goo.gl/mtbavbykphJxdmSg7
I like to get there early, in an effort to get on that sunrise bite. My target this morning, trophy crappie. I've been catching plenty of keeper crappie, but I wanted to try and specifically Target really big ones. My weapon of choice, my 7 and 1/2 ft ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a 2 inch pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad. I went to the same Rock in the very back of the spring, where you come to first it when you come off the trail. I picked up exactly where I left off.
I would cast exactly 40 ft directly out in front of me and then keep my rod tip up and allow my jig to sink on a pendulum from the tip of my rod, that way I could feel if a crappie bites while it's on its way down. Lately, they haven't been hitting it on the fall, but this is the most effective way to get the presentation across to these fish. They are sitting about 15 ft out in front of the bank at about 15 to 20 ft of depth. I've been allowing my lure to slowly pendulum right directly in front of them. Then, after a count of about 40 seconds, I start slowly working it back up the rock face. But a slow retrieval is not enough to make them bite.
What it takes, is a fair amount of jiggling. In the past, I've always Incorporated a slight twitch, or even a pause, to actuate the bite. These fall crappie need that lure to be jiggling! So after I count my lure down, and it gets into position, I give it a jiggle jiggle jiggle and then start slowly reeling it back. After a couple slow turns of the handle on the reel, I give it another jiggle jiggle jiggle. When I jiggle, I stop retrieving. When I stop jiggling, I continue my retrieve. Typically, if they're going to bite, it's when the lure sits still, just after the jiggle.
Don't give up on these fish too quick! Just because you think the lure is close to the bank, or all the way back to you, that doesn't mean you should reel it in. Take a chance on getting hung up on the cliff in front of you. If you're not getting hung up, you're not fishing. These fish will come within a foot or two of the surface while following your lure. Give them a chance to hit it before it gets out of the water. You'd be surprised how shallow they will come before they realize that bait is going to get away from them and they finally strike at it.
I caught a few fish, and then I caught a really nice fishing pole. It was a lews, one piece American hero baitcasting rod and a cast King Spartacus 2 baitcaster reel. The reel had a nasty backlash, and it looked like someone had intentionally thrown it from the spot where I was fishing into the lake. It was practically brand new, and everything was in perfect working order! After I'd caught plenty of crappie, I was convinced I wasn't going to get a trophy. I had one that went right around 13 in, but a trophy is 14 in. So I threw back oh probably 20 fish and I kept that rod and reel and then I went to get some breakfast.
After breakfast, I met my buddy over at cason Lane trailhead on the Murfreesboro Greenway...
https://share.google/L0HGpoOzS3hWZH45d
As soon as you get on the greenway and start walking upstream along the river, there is a bridge that goes over a creek that feeds into the river. There's a fairly steep path down to the edge of the creek and there's some slippery mud where you can make your way into the water. We had on our chest waders so we were able to get into the water. Our intention, use a cast net to catch some bait fish and then catch some bass. But the bait fish didn't want to have anything to do with us!
It took about a half an hour of some really good cast net throws into some really good spots that would only net us one or sometimes two fish. After wading up and down the River we finally made our way into the creek where we were able to get a couple handful. With only 10 bait fish, we decided to hop out of the river and make our way downstream. As you walk downstream on the greenway, it's significantly elevated above the river, and you are able to see into the clear water. We found a trail down to the water and headed down there with our freshly acquired Creek minnows.
Standing on what amounts to a small Cliff above the river we were able to see some largemouth and some spotted bass. Using six and a half foot medium action rods with 10 lb monofilament and a hook with no sinker and no bobber, my buddy was able to land the first little bass of the day, which was a largemouth. He was able to see the fish eat his bait, and then set the hook!
The next couple of fish took a little more work. After we pulled one out of there, they were kind of wise to us. After all, the river in that area is only about 40 ft wide and about 2 to 3 ft deep. If we can see those fish, they can see us. But they can't help themselves when they see live bait. They have to eat. It would take a little more patience, but if you stand still, and allow those fish to forget you were there, they will make their way back through the river in front of you, looking for food.
The second fish that took the bait was a beautiful Smallmouth bass. Probably about 14 in long and 3/4 of a pound. Not a big fish by any means, but significantly bigger than the first little large mouth. The third and final fish we would catch we had seen cruising around for a while. Because of the magnification of the water, we thought it was probably two to three pounds and a large mouth. When we finally got it to take the bait, it was probably more like one and a half pound.
It was a really nice spotted bass! At right around 15 in, it was only a few inches shy of being a trophy fish, which is no small task in a stretch of river this tiny, and overfished. But there it was, the black bass trifecta! A largemouth, a spotted, and a smallmouth bass. We do have one more type of bass in that stretch of river, it's called a mean mouth. If we could have got one of those, it would have been a grand slam home run! Maybe next time, but that will have to wait...
So why were the fish so eager to oblige today before the storm? Consistency! Fish love consistency! When you have several days of consistent weather, all in a row, it's much easier to figure out what to do to catch these fish. Extreme fluctuations in weather change where they feed and what they feed on. We had several days in a row this week with cool mornings and warm sunny afternoons. After several of those in a row, it's much easier to be dialed in on where you can catch what types of species and what you should use to catch them. I can assure you, the fish didn't know the storm was coming, they don't even know what a meteorologist is!

There's a fairly steep path down to the edge of the creek and there's some slippery mud where you can make your way into the water. We had on our chest waders so we were able to get into the water. Our intention, use a cast net to catch some bait fish and then catch some bass. But the bait fish didn't want to have anything to do with us!

It took about a half an hour of some really good cast net throws into some really good spots that would only net us one or sometimes two fish. After wading up and down the River we finally made our way into the creek where we were able to get a couple handful. With only 10 bait fish, we decided to hop out of the river and make our way downstream. As you walk downstream on the greenway, it's significantly elevated above the river, and you are able to see into the clear water. We found a trail down to the water and headed down there with our freshly acquired Creek minnows.

Standing on what amounts to a small Cliff above the river we were able to see some largemouth and some spotted bass. Using six and a half foot medium action rods with 10 lb monofilament and a hook with no sinker and no bobber, my buddy was able to land the first little bass of the day, which was a largemouth. He was able to see the fish eat his bait, and then set the hook!

The next couple of fish took a little more work. After we pulled one out of there, they were kind of wise to us. After all, the river in that area is only about 40 ft wide and about 2 to 3 ft deep. If we can see those fish, they can see us. But they can't help themselves when they see live bait. They have to eat. It would take a little more patience, but if you stand still, and allow those fish to forget you were there, they will make their way back through the river in front of you, looking for food.

The second fish that took the bait was a beautiful Smallmouth bass. Probably about 14 in long and 3/4 of a pound. Not a big fish by any means, but significantly bigger than the first little large mouth. The third and final fish we would catch we had seen cruising around for a while. Because of the magnification of the water, we thought it was probably two to three pounds and a large mouth. When we finally got it to take the bait, it was probably more like one and a half pound.

It was a really nice spotted bass! At right around 15 in, it was only a few inches shy of being a trophy fish, which is no small task in a stretch of river this tiny, and overfished. But there it was, the black bass trifecta! A largemouth, a spotted, and a smallmouth bass. We do have one more type of bass in that stretch of river, it's called a mean mouth. If we could have got one of those, it would have been a grand slam home run! Maybe next time, but that will have to wait...

So why were the fish so eager to oblige today before the storm? Consistency! Fish love consistency! When you have several days of consistent weather, all in a row, it's much easier to figure out what to do to catch these fish. Extreme fluctuations in weather change where they feed and what they feed on. We had several days in a row this week with cool mornings and warm sunny afternoons. After several of those in a row, it's much easier to be dialed in on where you can catch what types of species and what you should use to catch them. I can assure you, the fish didn't know the storm was coming, they don't even know what a meteorologist is!

title: Trip Report #168
content_raw:
Hybrid bass hunting on Percy Priest Lake
This morning, I'm at my buddy at 5:30 a.m. at Elm Hill Rush boat ramp...
https://share.google/8veC2UhXIB6xA6ypx
We went across the lake all the way up by the dam to the Nashville shores area. A friend of ours had been on a very good early morning hybrid bass bite in that area for the last couple of days. This morning, there was nothing going on out there. Just the typical handful of early morning largemouth bass hitting top water near the bank and what looked like hundreds of gar, everywhere. Not a big deal, while we were there, we decided to try and scope out some of the fish attractors near the dam.
The first one we went to, was directly out in front of Nashville shores. It's a crazy shallow area right out in between the dam and the Nashville shores area, and it's only accessible by boat. The wind was blowing us all over the place, even early this morning, so it was really hard to fish where we needed to. The fish attractor was clearly marked with a buoy, but even getting a cast in that direction against the wind, or with the wind, or beside the wind, was hard to do. And then, during your retrieval, the wind would make it even harder to work the lure effectively. Despite that fact, the first and only fish that we would catch all day came from that fish attractor, on a crappie jig.
I was using my favorite crappie setup for windy days. My 6 ft ultralight rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad. Casting to the fish attractor buoy and allowing my lure to sink for at least 10 to 12 seconds, before starting a slow retrieve, was how I garnered the only bite I would get. But what a bite it was!
Quick backstory, a buddy of mine catches lots of really big bluegill on this particular section of the lake. He's been doing it consistently for the last few years, and I've never really tried my hand at it. Full disclosure, today, I was trying to catch crappie. But the biggest bluegill I've ever seen in person had other plans!
Using a painfully slow retrieve, and incorporating lots of little twitches, more like a jiggle, I was able to make a Tennessee trophy bluegill commit to my crappie jig. It was right at 10 and a half inches and almost exactly 1 lb at .96. Unfortunately, it was the only fish we would catch on the day, but we would keep trying for a little while longer.
From the fish a tractor in front of Nashville shores, we crossed the lake to another buoy that was marking fish attractors in the water just out in front of the recreation area by the dam...
https://maps.app.goo.gl/tojebjwM9hcKMmFw6
When you park in this parking lot by the lake, you can see the buoy that marks the fish attractor. It has a picture of a fish and the four letter word that says "fish". That thing was loaded! First of all, you can easily cast to it from the bank. There was nobody else there fishing, and it looked like a fantastic spot! We had forward facing sonar on his boat and we were able to see these fish. We were able to clearly see that they weren't going to bite. Unfortunately for us, we didn't have any minnows.
it's pretty much a sure thing, right now, if you find deep enough fish attractors on Percy Priest lake, there's going to be crappie there. And if you have minnows and a slip bobber setup, you should be able to easily get them. This is hands down the most accessible fish attractor that's in the deepest water that I have found. I haven't got a chance to go out there and fish from the bank just yet, but I will be doing it soon! When I go, I'm going to take my favorite setup, but I'm also going to take minnows.

title: Trip Report #169
content_raw:
Catching crappie on command!
This morning, I went back to the spring on Percy Priest Lake...
https://share.google/gm5gefoHMyJXL6f8W
To get back there, you have to park on the side of Maddox road...
https://goo.gl/maps/5svbraCaWcn6LDQRA
There's a well beaten path from the side of the road all the way to the spring!
I got there at around 5:35 and by 5:45 this morning I had already caught two crappie! I've got that location completely dialed in right now. This morning, I was using my 7 and 1/2 ft ultralight rod with 4 lb monofilament line and a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a 2-in pearl colored body Garland baby shad. I picked up exactly where I left off yesterday...
Sitting in the very back of the spring, facing directly out, I cast exactly 40 feet of line out and then lift my rod tip up into the air and allow that jig head to slowly fall to a depth of about 20 ft. I like to keep the rod tip up, because sometimes as that jig is falling, these fish will bite. Most of the time they do not, but it's good to be able to feel if they do. Once that lure gets all the way down I start a painfully slow retrieve back up to the surface. Sometimes I give it a twitch, sometimes I give it a pause, sometimes I give it a little jiggle. Very rarely, do they want it only moving, they almost always want some sort of little action.
That's not always the case for crappie! Most of the time, I can just use a straight slow retrieve. I think it has something to do with the fall bite. I haven't done a whole lot of crappie fishing in the fall, but I'm starting to realize that, crappie all over the lake, like the jig to have a little bit of action as it's coming in.
I sat there and patiently, retrieved the lure like that for a couple of hours until they completely quit biting right around 7:30. So I went to get some breakfast, and then grabbed a bass rod so that I could throw some Ned rigs, and went right back to the spring. I got there around 10:00 a.m., and on my first two casts, I caught back to back largemouth and spotted bass. The spring always has largemouth bass, 24/7, 365, but right now it's completely loaded with tiny large mouth and spotted bass.
To catch these bass, I like a 7 ft medium, ultra fast action rod. I'm using 8 lb monofilament and casting a 1/10 of an ounce Ned rig head from z-man paired with a  z-man peanut butter jelly Ned rig soft plastic. All around the bank in this area there are boulders where you can drop that Ned rig in and work it on the bottom. You're guaranteed to catch bass, but you're also guaranteed to get hung up and lose your Ned rig. It's part of it!
After I had my fun catching a few largemouth, I picked up my crappie rod, which I had to alter slightly, because of the stiff west wind. The wind was blowing pretty hard before I left the house, so I opted for my 6-ft ultra light rod and reel with 4 lb monofilament instead of my seven and a half foot rod. By using a shorter rod, I was able to keep the line a little lower to the surface of the water, and out of the wind as much. Too much wind on the line makes the jig move in ways that you don't want it to. You need to know exactly what your lure is doing, and you don't want the wind to affect that.
I picked right back up where I left off in the morning, casting directly out in front of me to 40 ft, and getting my rod tip up, and allowing that lure to sink for a long time! Until it pendulums, almost all the way back to me. Then I start that slow painful retrieve with a couple little twitches every now and then. Sure enough, there were still some nice slab crappie hanging out! There was another gentleman in the spring, fishing from the bank so I gave him a couple of nice big crappie, cleaned up all the aluminum cans I could find on the bank, and then called it a day! Today, I finished fishing by around 1:00 p.m. Yesterday afternoon, I was beating up the same exact fish, at the same exact spot, but I didn't get started until 12:33 p.m.
What I'm trying to say is, I think this spot is overwhelmingly loaded. These fish are feeding heavily anytime I show up, and this spot is notorious for being fantastic at night. No doubt, they're feeding heavily at night right now. They're feeding heavily all the time!

title: Trip Report #170
content_raw:
Getting dialed in...
Crappie all over the country respond well to jigs and soft plastics. That much we know, but every day is a different day, and each day, you have to get dialed in. Getting dialed in looks different, every day. Being dialed in means you have the exact lure at the exact depth at the exact speed and the exact cadence that your target fish desires. Today, I fished at two different places. One spot where I am still learning exactly what to do and another spot where I know exactly what to do. The difference between my success rate is staggering!
I started the morning 45 minutes before sunrise at Stewart Creek boat ramp...
Stewart Creek Boat Ramp https://share.google/qI1kQKR8bfzVou58G
I walked over to these cliffs and I was the first one there this morning. It didn't make any difference, the fish didn't start biting until sunrise. At that point, I caught my very first crappie of the day. Using my favorite crappie fishing method, a tight line, with 4 lb stren monofilament and a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a 2-in pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad. Tight line just means there's no bobber in between my lure and my rod tip. You simply cast your lure out, either begin your retrieval, or allow it to sink a little bit. That's my favorite way to get them!
Right then, another fisherman showed up and stood right next to where I was fishing and absolutely started wearing them out! Quite frankly, it was a welcome sight! I was struggling to catch fish with my method, and he was catching them quickly and easily. There were a few differences in our setups, which allowed him to be what I considered, dialed in. First of all, he was using 6 lb monofilament instead of four. And most importantly, he was using a 1/16 of an ounce jig head, twice as heavy as the one I was throwing! The next biggest difference, I was using pearl white while he had a tube that had a brown body and chartreuse yellow tail.
That was it. Those were the only differences. We were casting to the same spot, and we were using the same retrieve. But he caught fish five to one over me! Fast forward to this afternoon, in a spot where I have been dialed in for more than a year, and it was my turn to beat the brakes off the crappie! After lunch, I headed over to Maddox road to walk through the woods to cedar Creek spring...
https://goo.gl/maps/seGVPDL2KcJytEmv5
When I got there, I was careful to creep up slowly from the woods so that the fish weren't alerted to my presence. Yesterday, when I got there, they were bluegill all over the surface, either sunning, or looking for something to eat. Today, there were all of those bluegill, and dozens and dozens of largemouth bass! They were everywhere! I caught a few of them, with my crappie jig, and a crappie retrieve, but as fun as that was, I wanted to try to get those crappie.
This is where being dialed in at this location came in handy. I've been catching fish from this Bank really well. Not just this season, but last winter as well. It takes some getting used to, but this spot is loaded! Today, I found the fish in the very back of the spring, just like I did yesterday. As you approach, the spring looks like a cul-de-sac. No need to walk up or down the left side. Just walk straight to the back of it, and start casting out directly in front of you.
Here's how I got them in good numbers today... After patiently casting and retrieving and allowing my lure to sink to several different depths at several different positions away from the bank, I settled on a spot that was about 40 ft out. I would cast to that location, and get my rod tip up, and then allow my 132nd ounce jig head to slowly pendulum all the way back to me until that jig had reached down to just over a depth of about 20 ft. At that point, it's hanging over and underwater cliff, and I would start to bring it up slowly, incorporating a few small twitches. They were hammering it every time!
I caught a few nice slabs, and several fish were back to back to back. I had to be slow, and deliberate, and I had to do it exactly the same way, each cast, or I wouldn't get a bite! In total, I caught five Big slab crappie that were all over 11 to 12 in. I caught a handful of crappie that would have been keepers, over the 10 inch mark, but I threw them back. I probably caught 10 to 15 short crappie, and another five or six largemouth bass. When I say the spring is loaded, I mean it's absolutely loaded!

title: Trip Report #171
content_raw:
Fantastic news about crappie fishing!
This morning I went to clean up Stewart Creek boat ramp at around 9:00 a.m...
https://share.google/bcKtBFT3DzCvHCOSP
A short walk through the woods, there are some cliffs that have access to deep water right off the bank...
A buddy of mine was there, he usually crappie fishes there in the winter time. He said that every morning, the crappie have been biting good! Lots of people are using minnows, but he always uses a 1/32nd ounce jig head with a bobby garland. My favorite color is Pearl white, but he always uses something with chartreuse. Today he had red and chartreuse. Typically, he uses black and chartreuse. Either way, apparently, the bite has been hot on these cold mornings! By the time I got there, nothing was really biting.
I did some cleaning and made the place look real nice, and then when I was in the parking lot, I noticed a different buddy who was over on the fishing pier. If you look at the picture above, it's a handicap accessible fishing pier, just to the right of the boat ramp. The water out in front of it is no more than eight or nine feet deep, but he reported that he had some nice crappie catches this morning using a bobber and a minnow...
He was fishing about 4 to 5 ft deep and he had some nice slab crappie on his stringer, one of them was 14 and 1/2 in, a Tennessee trophy crappie! That's really good news! I wasn't 100% certain that crappie would come up into the shallows and hang around the fish attractors that are in Percy Priest lake, but that's what surrounds that handicap accessible fishing pier, and that's where he was catching them.
He had the same report as my other buddy over on the cliffs, once it got to be about 9:00 a.m., the bite turned off.
I went home to get some lunch, and then I went back out to spring Creek spring...
https://share.google/CGA8mUeJZSqco1AiF
There's only one place to legally park to get to this spot, on the side of Maddox road...
https://goo.gl/maps/sPnvf7m9Etw9Sct57
Park here on the side of the road, and you will see a gate that says foot traffic only. Go under or over or around the gate and take the well-beaten path all the way to the spring, I'll draw you a map.
I stood in the very back of the spring, right where you first walk into. On my first cast, using my 7 1/2 ft ultralight rod and reel, with 4 lb monofilament and a 1/32nd ounce jig head, with a 2 inch pearl colored Bobby Garland baby shad, I caught a tiny largemouth bass, and then another one on my second cast, and then another one on my fourth cast! Totaled up, I caught about 10 small largemouth and spotted bass in the hour and a half that I was at the spring. To catch these fish, I wasn't casting directly out into the center of the spring, I was casting along the edges. They were tucked up in the rocks that make up the floor of the spring. I would simply cast parallel to the bank, and get my rod tip up quickly, so that the lure couldn't sink too fast, and then roll it back to me real slow with a couple little twitches.
Once I had my fun catching a couple handful of little bass, I turned my attention to trying to catch a crappie. Sitting on the same rock, in the very back of the spring, casting out as far as I could with the same jig head, I would allow it to sink all the way to the bottom before I started my retrieve. Those rocks sit up on somewhat of a cliff that goes straight down 20 or more feet. As I was bringing my jig head up that sheer Rock wall, I got my first thump of the day, a nice big slab crappie! I got it on the bank, and in my bucket, and it was only a few minutes later before I got another one!
Using an incredibly patient, slow retrieve, and incorporating not only some twitches, but a little bit of jiggling, was what it would take to entice the only two crappie that I could catch today. But both crappie were really nice size, and that bodes well for the future. It was much later in the season before I started going to the spring last year, I'm looking forward to a really long winter season of catching lots o
f slab crappie out at the spring!

title: Trip Report #172
content_raw:
A long tough day...
Yesterday, I meet my buddy at Elm Hill boat ramp to launch his boat at 6:30 a.m...
https://share.google/6Olrq8njWKc5saBB4
We were hoping to see hybrid Bass attacking on top water first thing in the morning, but that didn't happen. So we started targeting crappie on brush piles.
We fished the same handful of brush piles that we had been fishing in recent weeks, in 20 ft of water, for several hours. They were holding some fish, that we could see on the fish finder, but they were mostly bluegill and yellow bass. We've seen this before, recently. On Percy Priest lake, crappie like to sit in a depth of 20 ft, pretty much year-round. If they are not on structure, in 20 ft of water, they went shallow. Rarely, if ever, would you find them any deeper than 20 ft. So if you can't find them at 20 ft, it's time to start looking shallower.
To Target crappie we always look for underwater structure like brush piles. When someone says they're looking for a brush pile, on this lake, that refers to structure that has been placed, underwater, by other fishermen. One such spot, that we fished yesterday, was a place in 20 ft of water where we dropped three different five gallon buckets filled with concrete and limbs from a Osage orange tree. We use a traditional downscan fish finder to look for anything on the bottom of the lake that isn't flat, that rises up, that could hold fish. Then we throw a buoy marker so that we know where to cast, and then we fish around that area until we either catch a bunch of fish or 20 - 30 minutes have passed, and we haven't gotten any bites, then we move on.
Yesterday, we couldn't catch any crappie on those types of structures in 20 ft of water. So we started looking a little closer to the bank for the same types of structures. The first spot we came across was in 9 ft of water. It was holding tons of fish! My buddy caught several short crappie, and we each caught one keeper crappie. We were using minnows. We had our ultralight setups with slip bobbers. When we were fishing in 20 ft of water, we were running the depth of the slip bobber down to about 15 ft. When we found this brush pile in 9 ft of water, we had to raise the level up to about 4 ft. We caught a handful of fish, but after more than an hour, a handful isn't enough, so we moved on again.
Eventually, we came upon an actual fish attractor. Structure, put in the lake by TWRA, specifically to attract crappie. We had made our way around the lake for around 10 hours and had only caught two keeper crappie when we got back to the boat ramp where we had launched. In that cove, there is a buoy directly across from the boat ramp that marks fish attractors. This is probably one of my new favorite fish attractors on the lake! It's massive in scope and it's not as shallow as most of the other ones. When the lake is at winter pool, it's as deep as 20 ft!
That's great news for the future. During the cold weather months, all the way up until the middle of June, crappie will go shallow all over the lake. They're starting to do that now!  So, despite the fact that we had found a tremendous fish attractor, it didn't have any fish on it. It is still a little too deep. But, unlike most fish attractors, it will be viable during winter pool. Most fish attractors on that Lake get exposed when the lake gets dropped to Winter pool. This one should hold crappie all winter long!
In the same cove, on the same side as the boat ramp, someone, who was not TWRA, dropped three tremendous fish attractors in the cove. If you launch from the boat ramp and you're looking out at the lake, all the way up in the cove to your right. There are what looks like high-rise condos for Crappie. They're sitting in about 15 ft of water, and they were loaded with fish! I caught a couple crappie, even a nice big slab keeper crappie with my minnow. And my buddy Chris caught five keeper crappie real quick with his 1/32nd ounce jig head and a pearl colored body Garland.
I just threw in there with my minnow set to a depth of about 10 ft and watched my bobber until it went under. He was casting across to the other side and allowing his jig to get to a depth of about 10 ft, before he started a slow retrieve. Some fish would react to the slow retrieve, but he had the most luck when he gave the lure a little action. While retrieving, he would give it a pause, and that would sometimes trigger a bite. Or, he would give it a little twitch, and that also triggered a bite. We were there at around 5:00 p.m., just as it was starting to get low light. That may have had something to do with our success. Either way, that's a fantastic spot that you could get to with any boat or kayak, or potentially, if you feel like you could cast a hundred yards, you may be able to get there from the bank!
Unfortunately, it cost $10 to utilize this boat ramp. There is a gate with an automatic payment machine that will accept cash or a card and then raise the arm so that you can go into the parking lot. If it weren't for that, this would be an
ideal fishing spot.

title: Trip Report #173
content_raw:
I go fishing everyday. I take people on guided trips and I make YouTube videos when I'm not guiding. I'm licensed to take people fishing in the state of Tennessee. My target species range from trout and crappie in the winter time to muskie in the spring and fall. We target walleye during the heat of the summer, mostly at night, and I offer multiple different kayak trips targeting smallmouth bass all summer long. For more than a year before I started my patreon account, I was sending detailed, daily emails containing all the pertinent information about each days fishing trip.
Comprehensive reporting about exactly where I was fishing and what I was targeting. What types of methods that I was using as well as any equipment or lures. Also, what type of success did I have, if any. No detail is too small when you're trying to be successful at catching fish. So I include information about environmental factors like weather and animal activity as well as any fish that I see being caught.
Patreons would visit my page with the hopes of becoming better fishermen and garnering new fishing locations. I tell people exactly where I go fishing, because there are thousands of good public fishing locations that most people don't know about. That type of information is highly sought after, as location is the most important factor when it comes to catching fish.
